<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Must Know</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 01</div>

    <h3>What is AWS Auto Scaling?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED</span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS Auto Scaling is the ability to automatically
        adjust application capacity according to demand.

        In EC2-based architectures, an
        <strong>Auto Scaling Group (ASG)</strong> can
        automatically launch or terminate EC2 instances based
        on configured scaling policies.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Low Traffic
        â†’ Fewer Instances

        <br>

        High Traffic
        â†’ More Instances

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose an application normally needs 2 EC2
            instances.

            During a sale, traffic suddenly increases.

            The ASG can launch additional instances so the
            application can handle the increased load.

            When traffic decreases, unnecessary instances can
            be terminated.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "AWS Auto Scaling automatically adjusts application
            capacity based on demand. With EC2 Auto Scaling
            Groups, instances can be launched or terminated
            according to scaling policies while maintaining
            the desired capacity."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 02</div>

    <h3>What is an Auto Scaling Group?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ TOP INTERVIEW QUESTION</span>

    <p class="answer">

        An <strong>Auto Scaling Group</strong> is a logical
        group of EC2 instances that AWS manages as a unit.

        It maintains the desired number of instances and can
        automatically scale the group based on policies.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Launch Template

        â†“

        Auto Scaling Group

        â†“

        EC2 Instances

        â†“

        Load Balancer

    </div>

    <div class="important">

        The three important ASG capacity values are:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Minimum Capacity</strong>
        â†’ Lowest number of instances ASG should maintain.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Desired Capacity</strong>
        â†’ Target number of instances ASG tries to maintain.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Maximum Capacity</strong>
        â†’ Highest number of instances ASG can launch.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An Auto Scaling Group manages a collection of EC2
            instances and maintains the configured desired
            capacity. It can scale between the minimum and
            maximum capacity based on scaling policies."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 03</div>

    <h3>What are minimum, desired and maximum capacities?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Setting</th>
            <th>Meaning</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Minimum</td>
            <td>Lowest number of instances the ASG should maintain.</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Desired</td>
            <td>Number of instances the ASG attempts to maintain normally.</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Maximum</td>
            <td>Upper limit of instances the ASG can launch.</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            If:

            <br><br>

            Min = 2

            <br>

            Desired = 3

            <br>

            Max = 6

            <br><br>

            The ASG normally maintains 3 instances and can
            scale down to 2 or up to 6.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Minimum defines the lowest capacity, desired is the
            normal target capacity, and maximum defines the
            highest number of instances the Auto Scaling Group
            can launch."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 04</div>

    <h3>What is a Launch Template?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A Launch Template contains the configuration required
        to launch EC2 instances.

        It can define:

        <br><br>

        â†’ AMI

        <br>

        â†’ Instance type

        <br>

        â†’ Key pair

        <br>

        â†’ Security groups

        <br>

        â†’ IAM instance profile

        <br>

        â†’ Storage configuration

        <br>

        â†’ User data

        <br>

        â†’ Network configuration

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Why is it important?</strong>

        <p>

            When an ASG needs to launch a new instance, it needs
            to know what configuration the new EC2 instance
            should have.

            The Launch Template provides that configuration.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A Launch Template defines the configuration used
            to launch EC2 instances. Auto Scaling Groups can
            use the template to consistently create instances
            with the required AMI, instance type, security
            groups, IAM role and user data."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 05</div>

    <h3>How does Auto Scaling work with a Load Balancer?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ EXTREMELY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The Load Balancer distributes incoming traffic across
        healthy EC2 instances.

        The Auto Scaling Group manages the number of EC2
        instances.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Users

        â†“

        Load Balancer

        â†“

        â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”

        â”‚ EC2 Instance â”‚

        â”œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”¤

        â”‚ EC2 Instance â”‚

        â”œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”¤

        â”‚ EC2 Instance â”‚

        â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜

        â†‘

        Auto Scaling Group

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time Scenario</strong>

        <p>

            Traffic increases â†’ ASG launches instances.

            <br>

            New instances pass health checks â†’ LB begins
            sending traffic to them.

            <br>

            Traffic decreases â†’ ASG terminates unnecessary
            instances.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The Load Balancer distributes traffic across
            healthy instances, while the Auto Scaling Group
            dynamically adjusts the number of instances based
            on demand. Together they provide scalability and
            high availability."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 06</div>

    <h3>What are the different Auto Scaling policies?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Important scaling approaches include:

        <br><br>

        <strong>1. Target Tracking Scaling</strong>

        <br>
        Maintains a target metric value.

        <br><br>

        <strong>2. Step Scaling</strong>

        <br>
        Changes capacity by different amounts depending on how
        far a metric moves beyond thresholds.

        <br><br>

        <strong>3. Simple Scaling</strong>

        <br>
        Older policy approach using a single adjustment and
        cooldown behavior.

        <br><br>

        <strong>4. Scheduled Scaling</strong>

        <br>
        Scales based on a known schedule.

        <br><br>

        <strong>5. Predictive Scaling</strong>

        <br>
        Uses historical patterns to forecast future demand for
        supported workloads.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Common Auto Scaling strategies include target
            tracking, step scaling, scheduled scaling and
            predictive scaling. Target tracking is commonly
            used when I want the ASG to maintain a target metric
            such as average CPU utilization."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 07</div>

    <h3>What is Target Tracking Scaling?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Target tracking automatically adjusts capacity to
        maintain a selected metric close to a target value.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose target CPU utilization is configured as
            <strong>50%</strong>.

            <br><br>

            CPU stays significantly above the target â†’
            ASG can add capacity.

            <br><br>

            CPU stays below the target â†’
            ASG can reduce capacity.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Target tracking scaling adjusts the number of
            instances to maintain a target value for a selected
            metric, such as average CPU utilization."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 08</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ COMMON</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Horizontal Scaling</th>
            <th>Vertical Scaling</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Add more instances</td>
            <td>Increase resources of one instance</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Scale out / scale in</td>
            <td>Scale up / scale down</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Common with Auto Scaling Groups</td>
            <td>Changes instance size/resources</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ§  Easy Example</strong>

        <p>

            2 EC2 â†’ 5 EC2

            = Horizontal Scaling

            <br><br>

            t3.medium â†’ larger instance type

            = Vertical Scaling

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Horizontal scaling means adding or removing
            instances, also called scale out and scale in.
            Vertical scaling means increasing or decreasing
            resources of an individual instance."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q9 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 09</div>

    <h3>What is scale out and scale in?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>Scale Out</strong> means adding more instances.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Scale In</strong> means removing instances.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Scale Out:

        <br>

        2 EC2 â†’ 3 EC2 â†’ 4 EC2 â†’ 5 EC2

        <br><br>

        Scale In:

        <br>

        5 EC2 â†’ 4 EC2 â†’ 3 EC2

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Scale out increases the number of instances to
            handle higher demand, while scale in decreases the
            number of instances when demand falls."

        </p>

    </div>

<!-- Q10 -->

        â†’ EC2

        â†’ EC2

        <br>

        â†’ EC2

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<!-- Q12 -->

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 12</div>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</span>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

            serving application traffic. For load-balanced
            applications, I can configure the ASG to use ELB

        </p>

<!-- Q13 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 13</div>

    <h3>What is cooldown in Auto Scaling?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A cooldown period was designed to prevent an ASG from
        immediately performing additional scaling actions while
        the previous scaling action was still taking effect.

        Modern Auto Scaling generally relies heavily on
        policy-specific behavior and warm-up settings, so in
        interviews it is important to distinguish classic
        cooldown from instance warm-up.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸŽ¯ Remember:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Cooldown</strong> â†’ helps avoid rapid repeated
        scaling actions.

        <br>

        <strong>Instance Warmup</strong> â†’ gives a newly launched
        instance time to initialize before metrics are used for
        scaling decisions.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Cooldown historically helped prevent repeated
            scaling actions immediately after a scale event.
            In modern ASG configurations, instance warm-up and
            policy-specific behavior are also important for
            controlling scaling decisions."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q14 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 14</div>

    <h3>What is instance warm-up?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Instance warm-up gives a newly launched EC2 instance
        time to initialize before its metrics are fully used in
        scaling calculations.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose a new instance needs 3 minutes to install
            dependencies, start Docker containers and become
            ready.

            The scaling configuration should account for this
            startup period rather than immediately treating the
            instance as fully contributing capacity.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Instance warm-up allows newly launched instances
            time to initialize before their metrics are fully
            considered for scaling decisions. This helps avoid
            unnecessary repeated scaling."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q15 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 15</div>

    <h3>What is Scheduled Scaling?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Scheduled scaling changes ASG capacity according to a
        predefined schedule.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            An e-commerce application receives heavy traffic
            every evening.

            You can schedule additional capacity before the

            the traffic window.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Scheduled scaling is useful when demand follows a
            predictable pattern. I can configure the ASG to
            change its capacity at predefined times."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q16 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 16</div>

    <h3>What is a Lifecycle Hook?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A lifecycle hook pauses an instance during an Auto
        Scaling lifecycle transition so that custom actions
        can be performed.

        Important transitions include:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Launching

        <br>

        â†’ Terminating

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Before terminating an instance, a lifecycle hook
            can provide time to perform a custom action such as
            collecting logs or completing cleanup.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An Auto Scaling lifecycle hook temporarily pauses
            an instance during launch or termination so that
            custom initialization, cleanup or other automation
            can run before the lifecycle transition continues."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q17 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 17</div>

    <h3>What is a termination policy?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        selects when scaling in.

        The goal is to make the termination decision consistent
        with the configured policy and group state.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Interview Thinking</strong>

        <p>

            Termination policies influence that decision.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A termination policy determines how Auto Scaling
            selects instances to terminate when the group scales
            in. It can help control which instance is removed."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q18 -->

<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 01</div>

    <h3>
        Traffic suddenly increases from 1,000 users to 50,000 users. What happens?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        In a properly configured architecture:

        <br><br>

        1. Load increases on the application.

        <br>

        2. CloudWatch metrics reflect the increased workload.

        <br>

        3. Auto Scaling policy detects the scaling condition.

        <br>

        4. ASG launches additional EC2 instances.

        <br>

        5. New instances initialize.

        <br>

        6. Load Balancer health checks verify them.

        <br>

        7. Healthy instances start receiving traffic.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would use an ALB in front of an Auto Scaling Group.
            CloudWatch metrics and the configured scaling policy
            would trigger scale-out when demand increases.
            Newly launched instances would pass health checks
            before receiving production traffic."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 02</div>

    <h3>
        CPU is 90%, but Auto Scaling is not launching instances. What do you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ TROUBLESHOOTING</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would check step by step:

        <br><br>

        <strong>1.</strong> Is the ASG scaling policy attached?

        <br>

        <strong>2.</strong> Is the policy using the expected
        metric?

        <br>

        <strong>3.</strong> Is the desired capacity already equal
        to maximum capacity?

        <br>

        <strong>4.</strong> Is there an active alarm or scaling
        condition?

        <br>

        <strong>5.</strong> Is the Launch Template valid?

        <br>

        <strong>6.</strong> Are there EC2 capacity/quota issues?

        <br>

        <strong>7.</strong> Is instance warm-up or another
        scaling constraint affecting the decision?

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would first verify the ASG min, desired and max
            capacity, then check the scaling policy and its
            CloudWatch metric or alarm. I would also inspect
            scaling activity history, launch template
            configuration, EC2 capacity errors and quotas."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

        â†’ Security groups

        <br>

        â†’ Load Balancer health checks

        <br>

        â†’ Target group configuration

        <br>

        â†’ Application port

        <br>

        â†’ AMI configuration

        <br>

        â†’ Instance warm-up

        <br>

        â†’ ASG activity history

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would check the ASG activity history and determine
            why instances are being marked unhealthy. Then I

            target group health checks, ports, security groups

        </p>

    </div>

<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 04</div>

    <h3>
        How would you design a highly available EC2 application?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ ARCHITECTURE QUESTION</span>

<div class="important">

    <strong>ðŸ§  Auto Scaling One-Minute Revision</strong>

    <br><br>

    <strong>ASG</strong>
    = Manages EC2 capacity.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Launch Template</strong>
    = Defines how new EC2 instances are launched.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Minimum</strong>
    = Lowest capacity.

    <br>

    <strong>Desired</strong>
    = Normal target capacity.

    <br>

    <strong>Maximum</strong>
    = Highest allowed capacity.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Scale Out</strong>
    = Add instances.

    <br>

    <strong>Scale In</strong>
    = Remove instances.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Target Tracking</strong>
    = Maintain target metric.

    <br>

    <strong>Step Scaling</strong>
    = Different capacity adjustments based on metric deviation.

    <br>

    <strong>Scheduled Scaling</strong>
    = Scale at predefined times.

    <br>

    <strong>Predictive Scaling</strong>
    = Forecast demand from historical patterns.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Health Check</strong>
    = Detect unhealthy instances.

    <br>

    <strong>Lifecycle Hook</strong>
    = Pause launch/termination for custom actions.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Golden Architecture:</strong>

    <br><br>

    Users â†’ ALB â†’ ASG â†’ EC2 â†’ Multi-AZ

    <br><br>

    CloudWatch â†’ Scaling Policy â†’ ASG

<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 01</div>

    <h3>What is AWS CLI?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS CLI stands for <strong>AWS Command Line Interface</strong>.

        It is a command-line tool that allows us to interact
        with AWS services using commands instead of manually
        using the AWS Management Console.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Instead of opening the S3 console and checking
            buckets manually, we can run:

        </p>

        <pre>aws s3 ls</pre>

        <p>

            This lists the S3 buckets accessible using the
            configured AWS credentials.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "AWS CLI is a command-line interface provided by AWS
            that allows us to manage and automate AWS resources
            using commands. It is useful for administration,
            scripting and DevOps automation."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 02</div>

    <h3>Why do we use AWS CLI in DevOps?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS CLI is useful because DevOps work involves
        automation.

        Instead of performing repetitive tasks manually through
        the console, commands can be executed through scripts,
        CI/CD pipelines and automation tools.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Developer

        â†’

        GitHub / Jenkins

        â†’

        AWS CLI Commands

        â†’

        AWS Resources

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            A CI/CD pipeline can use AWS CLI to upload build
            artifacts to S3 or interact with ECR, ECS, EC2 and
            other AWS services.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "In DevOps, AWS CLI helps automate AWS operations.
            We can use it inside shell scripts and CI/CD
            pipelines instead of performing repetitive tasks
            manually through the AWS Console."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 03</div>

    <h3>How do you configure AWS CLI?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The commonly used command is:

    </p>

    <pre>aws configure</pre>

    <p class="answer">

        It asks for:

        <br><br>

        â†’ AWS Access Key ID

        <br>

        â†’ AWS Secret Access Key

        <br>

        â†’ Default AWS Region

        <br>

        â†’ Default output format

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <pre>aws configure</pre>

        <p>

            Then configure the required values.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="important">

        âš ï¸ Never hard-code or expose AWS access keys in GitHub
        repositories, source code or public files.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I can configure AWS CLI using the aws configure
            command, which stores the CLI configuration for the
            selected profile. In production automation, I prefer
            temporary credentials or IAM roles rather than
            hard-coded long-lived access keys."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 05</div>

    <h3>How do you check which AWS identity is being used?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Use:

    </p>

    <pre>aws sts get-caller-identity</pre>

    <p class="answer">

        This is one of the most useful troubleshooting commands.

        It tells us the AWS account and identity associated with
        the credentials currently being used.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose Terraform or AWS CLI gives an
            <strong>AccessDenied</strong> error.

            Before changing permissions, I can verify which
            identity is actually being used.

        </p>

        <pre>aws sts get-caller-identity</pre>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I use aws sts get-caller-identity to verify which
            AWS identity and account my CLI session is using.
            It is very useful when troubleshooting credentials
            or permissions."

        </p>

    </div>

<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 06</div>

    <h3>What is an AWS CLI profile?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A profile is a named set of AWS CLI configuration and
        credential settings.

        Profiles are useful when working with multiple AWS
        accounts or environments.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <pre>aws configure --profile dev</pre>

        <pre>aws configure --profile prod</pre>

        <p>

            Then select a profile while running a command:

        </p>

        <pre>aws s3 ls --profile dev</pre>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "AWS CLI profiles allow me to maintain separate
            configurations for different AWS accounts or
            environments. I can select a specific profile using
            the --profile option."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 07</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between AWS CLI and AWS Management Console?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ COMMON</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Both can manage AWS resources, but the method is
        different.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        AWS Console

        â†’

        GUI / Browser

        <br><br>

        AWS CLI

        â†’

        Commands / Scripts / Automation

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The AWS Management Console is a graphical interface,
            while AWS CLI provides command-line access. CLI is
            particularly useful for automation, scripting and
            CI/CD pipelines."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 08</div>

    <h3>How do you specify an AWS region using CLI?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A region can be specified directly using:

    </p>

    <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances --region ap-south-1</pre>

    <p class="answer">

        Or a default region can be configured using:

    </p>

    <pre>aws configure</pre>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            If your resources are in Mumbai:

        </p>

        <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances --region ap-south-1</pre>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 12</div>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>aws s3</strong> provides high-level,
        easier-to-use commands for common S3 operations.

        <br><br>

        <strong>aws s3api</strong> provides direct access to
        individual S3 API operations.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Examples</strong>

        <pre>aws s3 ls</pre>

        <pre>aws s3 cp file.txt s3://my-bucket/</pre>

        <pre>aws s3api list-buckets</pre>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            tasks, while aws s3api exposes individual S3 API
            operations and gives more direct control."

<!-- Q17 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 17</div>

    <h3>How can AWS CLI output be filtered?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS CLI supports options such as
        <strong>--query</strong> for JMESPath expressions.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances \
```

--query "Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId"</pre>

```
        <p>

            This extracts instance IDs instead of displaying the
            entire response.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I use the --query option with JMESPath expressions
            to extract only the required fields from AWS CLI
            output."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q18 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 18</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between --query and --filter?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        They work at different levels.

        <br><br>

        <strong>--filters</strong>
        are service-specific request filters that can limit
        resources returned by the AWS API.

        <br><br>

        <strong>--query</strong>
        processes the returned response using JMESPath and
        extracts the information you need.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        Easy memory:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Filter â†’ Ask AWS for fewer resources.</strong>

        <br>

        <strong>Query â†’ Select fields from the response.</strong>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Q19 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 19</div>

    <h3>Where does AWS CLI store configuration?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS CLI commonly uses configuration files under the
        user's AWS directory.

        On Linux/macOS:

    </p>

    <pre>~/.aws/</pre>

    <p class="answer">

        Common files include:

    </p>

    <pre>~/.aws/config
```

~/.aws/credentials</pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        On Windows, the AWS directory is typically under the
        user's profile directory.

    </p>

</article>


<!-- Q20 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 20</div>

    <h3>What is the AWS_DEFAULT_REGION environment variable?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        It can be used to provide a default AWS region to AWS
        SDKs and CLI behavior where applicable.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Linux/macOS</strong>

        <pre>export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=ap-south-1</pre>

        <strong>PowerShell</strong>

        <pre>$env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-south-1"</pre>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q21 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 21</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between AWS CLI and SDK?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS CLI is a command-line tool used by users and
        scripts.

        AWS SDKs are software libraries that developers use
        inside applications written in supported programming
        languages.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "AWS CLI is mainly used from the command line and
            automation scripts, while AWS SDKs allow application
            code to interact programmatically with AWS services."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q22 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 22</div>

    <h3>How do you delete an S3 object using CLI?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <pre>aws s3 rm s3://my-bucket/file.txt</pre>

    <p class="answer">

        To remove objects recursively from a prefix:

    </p>

    <pre>aws s3 rm s3://my-bucket/folder/ --recursive</pre>

    <div class="important">

        âš ï¸ Always verify the bucket and path before using
        recursive delete commands.

    </div>

</article>


<!-- ======================================================
     â­â­
======================================================= -->

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­â­ Less Frequently Asked</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q23 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 23</div>

    <h3>What is the AWS CLI --dry-run option?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Some AWS CLI operations support <strong>--dry-run</strong>
        to test whether the command would succeed without
        actually performing the requested operation.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <pre>aws ec2 run-instances --dry-run ...</pre>

        <p>

            The exact behavior depends on the API operation.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q24 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 24</div>

    <h3>What is pagination in AWS CLI?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Some AWS APIs return large result sets in multiple
        pages.

        AWS CLI generally handles pagination automatically, but
        pagination behavior can be controlled with CLI options
        such as:

    </p>

    <pre>--no-paginate</pre>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Why useful?</strong>

        <p>

            When troubleshooting or scripting, controlling
            pagination can make output easier to process.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- ======================================================
     ðŸŽ¯ SCENARIOS

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>ðŸŽ¯ Real-Time Interview Scenarios</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 01</div>

    <h3>
        AWS CLI says AccessDenied. How will you troubleshoot?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would troubleshoot systematically.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 1:</strong>
        Check the current identity.

    </p>

    <pre>aws sts get-caller-identity</pre>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>Step 2:</strong>
        Check which profile/credentials are being used.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 3:</strong>
        Verify the IAM policy permissions.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 4:</strong>
        Check resource policies such as S3 bucket policies
        where applicable.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 5:</strong>
        Check region and resource ARN.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "First I would run aws sts get-caller-identity to
            confirm which identity is being used. Then I would
            check the IAM permissions, resource policy, resource
            ARN and region. I would also verify that the CLI is
            using the expected profile or role."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 02</div>

    <h3>
        You have Dev and Production AWS accounts. How would you manage them using CLI?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would use separate AWS CLI profiles or, preferably in
        production environments, role-based access with
        appropriate identity management.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <pre>aws configure --profile dev</pre>

        <pre>aws configure --profile prod</pre>

        <p>

            Then:

        </p>

        <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances --profile dev</pre>

        <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances --profile prod</pre>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "For separate environments I can use named CLI
            profiles, but for production I prefer role-based
            access and temporary credentials rather than
            storing long-lived access keys."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 03</div>

    <h3>
        Your command is working in one region but not another. What will you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would check:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Current/default region

        <br>

        â†’ Explicit <code>--region</code>

        <br>

        â†’ Whether the resource exists in that region

        <br>

        â†’ IAM permissions

        <br>

        â†’ Resource-specific regional behavior

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances --region ap-south-1</pre>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 04</div>

    <h3>
        Your Jenkins pipeline needs to upload a build artifact to S3. How would you do it securely?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS SCENARIO</span>

    <div class="flow">

        Git Push

        â†’

        Jenkins

        â†’

        Build

        â†’

        AWS Authentication

        â†’

        AWS CLI

        â†’

        S3

    </div>

    <p class="answer">

        I would avoid storing AWS access keys directly inside
        the Jenkinsfile.

        Instead, I would use an appropriate IAM role or secure
        credential mechanism with least-privilege permissions.

    </p>

    <pre>aws s3 cp build.zip s3://my-bucket/releases/</pre>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would integrate Jenkins with AWS using a secure
            IAM-based authentication mechanism and least
            privilege. The pipeline can then use AWS CLI to
            upload the artifact to the required S3 bucket without
            hard-coding credentials in the Jenkinsfile."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <h3 class="command-title">Configure a profile</h3>

    <pre>aws s3 ls</pre>

    <h3 class="command-title">Download from S3</h3>

    <h3 class="command-title">List EC2 instances</h3>

    <h3 class="command-title">Specify region</h3>

    <pre>aws ec2 describe-instances --region ap-south-1</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Use a profile</h3>

    <pre>aws s3 ls --profile dev</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Get command help</h3>

    <pre>aws ec2 help</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Filter response with query</h3>

<div class="important">

    <strong>ðŸ§  AWS CLI One-Minute Revision</strong>

    <br><br>

    <strong>AWS CLI</strong>
    = Command-line tool to interact with AWS.

    <br><br>

    <strong>aws configure</strong>
    = Configure CLI credentials/settings.

    <br>

    <strong>aws sts get-caller-identity</strong>
    = Check current AWS identity.

    <br>

    <strong>--profile</strong>
    = Select a named CLI profile.

    <br>

    <strong>--region</strong>
    = Specify AWS region.

    <br>

    <strong>--query</strong>
    = Extract required fields using JMESPath.

    <br>

    <strong>aws s3</strong>
    = High-level S3 commands.

    <br>

    <strong>aws s3api</strong>
    = Direct S3 API operations.

    <br><br>

    <strong>DevOps Flow:</strong>

    <br><br>

    Git â†’ CI/CD â†’ AWS CLI â†’ AWS Service

    <br><br>

    <strong>Security Rule:</strong>

    <br>

    Never hard-code AWS access keys in source code or
    repositories. Prefer IAM roles and temporary credentials
    wherever possible.

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Very Frequently Asked</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 01</div>

    <h3>What is Amazon CloudWatch?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Amazon CloudWatch is an AWS monitoring and observability
        service.

        It helps us monitor AWS resources, applications and
        infrastructure by collecting and analyzing metrics,
        logs and other operational data.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Simple Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we have an EC2 server running our application.

            We can use CloudWatch to monitor things such as:

            <br><br>

            â†’ CPU utilization

            <br>
            â†’ Network activity

            <br>
            â†’ Status-related metrics

            <br>
            â†’ Application logs

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon CloudWatch is an AWS monitoring and
            observability service used to collect metrics and
            logs, create alarms and dashboards, and monitor the
            health and performance of AWS resources and
            applications."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 02</div>

    <h3>What are the main components of CloudWatch?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Important CloudWatch concepts include:

        <br><br>

        ðŸ“Š <strong>Metrics</strong>

        <br>

        ðŸ“ <strong>Logs</strong>

        <br>

        ðŸš¨ <strong>Alarms</strong>

        <br>

        ðŸ“ˆ <strong>Dashboards</strong>

        <br>

        âš¡ <strong>Events / EventBridge integration</strong>

        <br>

        ðŸ“‹ <strong>Logs Insights</strong>

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        AWS Resources / Applications

        â†’

        CloudWatch

        â†’

        Metrics + Logs

        â†’

        Alarms / Dashboards / Actions

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The major CloudWatch capabilities I use are metrics,
            logs, alarms, dashboards and log analysis. These help
            monitor infrastructure and applications and trigger
            actions when defined conditions occur."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 03</div>

    <h3>What is a CloudWatch Metric?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A metric is a time-ordered set of data points used to
        measure the performance or behavior of a resource or
        application.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ EC2 Example</strong>

        <p>

            EC2 can publish metrics such as:

            <br><br>

            â†’ CPUUtilization

            <br>
            â†’ NetworkIn

            <br>
            â†’ NetworkOut

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="important">

        Easy memory:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Metric = numerical measurement.</strong>

        <br><br>

        Example: CPU utilization = 82%

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A CloudWatch metric is a time-series measurement
            used to monitor the performance or health of a
            resource. For example, EC2 CPUUtilization is a
            CloudWatch metric."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 04</div>

    <h3>What is a CloudWatch Alarm?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A CloudWatch Alarm watches a metric and performs an
        action when the metric crosses a defined threshold for a
        specified evaluation period.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Metric

        â†’

        Threshold

        â†’

        Alarm

        â†’

        Action

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose an EC2 instance has CPU utilization above
            80%.

            We can create an alarm that changes state when the
            configured condition remains true.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A CloudWatch alarm monitors a metric against a
            configured threshold and changes state when the
            condition is met. It can then be used to trigger an
            action such as an SNS notification or an
            Auto Scaling-related action."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 05</div>

    <h3>What are the states of a CloudWatch Alarm?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ COMMON</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A CloudWatch alarm has three main states:

        <br><br>

        ðŸŸ¢ <strong>OK</strong>

        <br>

        The metric is within the configured condition.

        <br><br>

        ðŸ”´ <strong>ALARM</strong>

        <br>

        The configured alarm condition has been met.

        <br><br>

        âšª <strong>INSUFFICIENT_DATA</strong>

        <br>

        There is not enough data to determine the state.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The three CloudWatch alarm states are OK, ALARM and
            INSUFFICIENT_DATA."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 06</div>

    <h3>What is CloudWatch Logs?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        CloudWatch Logs provides centralized collection and
        monitoring of log data from applications, services and
        AWS resources.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Application logs from an EC2-hosted application can
            be sent to CloudWatch Logs and then searched and
            analyzed.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "CloudWatch Logs allows us to collect, store and
            analyze log data from applications and AWS
            resources. It is useful for troubleshooting application
            and infrastructure issues."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 07</div>

    <h3>What is a Log Group and Log Stream?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A <strong>Log Group</strong> is a collection of log
        streams that share the same retention, monitoring and
        access-control settings.

        <br><br>

        A <strong>Log Stream</strong> is a sequence of log events
        from the same source or related source.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Log Group

        â†’

        Log Stream 1

        <br>

        â†’

        Log Stream 2

        <br>

        â†’

        Log Stream 3

    </div>

    <div class="important">

        Easy memory:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Log Group = container/category</strong>

        <br>

        <strong>Log Stream = individual sequence of logs</strong>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 08</div>

    <h3>What is a CloudWatch Dashboard?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A CloudWatch Dashboard provides a visual representation
        of metrics and monitoring information in one place.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            A dashboard can display:

            <br><br>

            EC2 CPU

            <br>

            Application metrics

            <br>

            ALB metrics

            <br>

            Database metrics

            <br>

            Error-related metrics

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q9 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 09</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between CloudWatch Metrics and Logs?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <div class="important">

        <strong>Metrics â†’ numbers used for monitoring.</strong>

        <br><br>

        <strong>Logs â†’ detailed event records.</strong>

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Example</strong>

        <p>

            Metric:

            <br>

            CPU = 90%

            <br><br>

            Log:

            <br>

            "Application failed to connect to database."

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Metrics provide numerical time-series data for
            monitoring performance, while logs contain detailed
            records of application or system events. Metrics are
            useful for thresholds and alarms, while logs are
            useful for troubleshooting."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

     â­â­â­â­

<!-- Q10 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 10</div>

    <h3>How do you monitor an EC2 instance using CloudWatch?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS QUESTION</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EC2 publishes standard monitoring metrics to CloudWatch.

        We can view these metrics, create alarms and build
        dashboards.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2

        â†’

        CloudWatch Metrics

        â†’

        Alarm

        â†’

        SNS / Auto Scaling / Action

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Create an alarm when average CPU utilization remains
            above a defined threshold.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I monitor EC2 through CloudWatch metrics such as
            CPU utilization and network metrics. I can create
            alarms on those metrics and use dashboards for
            visualization."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q11 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 11</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between Basic and Detailed Monitoring for EC2?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EC2 basic monitoring provides metrics at a lower
        frequency, while detailed monitoring provides more
        frequent monitoring data.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        Interview memory:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Basic â†’ 5-minute monitoring</strong>

        <br>

        <strong>Detailed â†’ 1-minute monitoring</strong>

        <br><br>

        Availability and pricing should be considered when
        choosing monitoring options.

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q12 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 12</div>

    <h3>What is CloudWatch Agent?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The CloudWatch Agent is software that can collect
        additional system-level metrics and logs from servers.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Why do we need it?</strong>

        <p>

            Standard EC2 monitoring does not provide every
            operating-system-level metric.

            For example, you may want to monitor memory
            utilization or collect application/system logs.

            The CloudWatch Agent can be configured for this.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The CloudWatch Agent is installed on supported
            servers when we need additional system metrics or
            log collection beyond the default metrics provided
            by the service."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q13 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 13</div>

    <h3>What is CloudWatch Logs Insights?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        CloudWatch Logs Insights is used to interactively query
        and analyze log data stored in CloudWatch Logs.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            If an application is returning many errors, Logs
            Insights can help search the logs and identify
            patterns.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "CloudWatch Logs Insights provides a query-based way
            to search and analyze CloudWatch log data, which is
            useful during troubleshooting and incident analysis."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q14 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 14</div>

    <h3>Can CloudWatch send notifications?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Yes.

        CloudWatch alarms can integrate with services such as
        Amazon SNS to send notifications.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        CloudWatch Metric

        â†’

        Alarm

        â†’

        SNS

        â†’

        Notification

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Example</strong>

        <p>

            If an EC2 CPU alarm enters ALARM state, an SNS topic
            can be used to notify subscribed endpoints.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q15 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 15</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between CloudWatch and CloudTrail?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <div class="important">

        <strong>CloudWatch â†’ Monitoring and observability.</strong>

        <br><br>

        <strong>CloudTrail â†’ API activity and account activity
        auditing.</strong>

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Easy Example</strong>

        <p>

            CloudWatch:

            <br>

            "Why is my EC2 CPU high?"

            <br><br>

            CloudTrail:

            <br>

            "Who performed this AWS API action?"

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "CloudWatch is primarily used for monitoring metrics,
            logs and application or infrastructure health.
            CloudTrail records AWS API activity and is mainly
            used for auditing and tracking actions performed in
            an AWS account."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q16 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 16</div>

    <h3>What is a custom CloudWatch metric?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A custom metric is application or system monitoring data
        that you publish to CloudWatch yourself.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose your application has a metric called:

            <br><br>

            <strong>OrdersProcessed</strong>

            <br><br>

            Your application can publish that metric to
            CloudWatch for monitoring.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Q17 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 17</div>

    <h3>What are CloudWatch dimensions?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Dimensions are name/value pairs that identify and
        distinguish metrics.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Example</strong>

        <p>

            An EC2 CPU metric can be associated with dimensions
            such as the instance identifier.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q18 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 18</div>

    <h3>What is metric namespace?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A namespace is a container used to organize metrics.

        AWS services publish metrics into service-specific
        namespaces, and custom applications can use custom
        namespaces.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Memory Trick</strong>

        <p>

            <strong>Namespace â†’ Category</strong>

            <br>

            <strong>Metric â†’ Measurement</strong>

            <br>

            <strong>Dimension â†’ Identifier</strong>

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q19 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 19</div>

    <h3>What is metric retention in CloudWatch?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        CloudWatch retains metric data for different periods
        depending on the resolution and age of the data.

        Older high-resolution data is aggregated into lower
        resolution periods over time.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        For interviews, understand the main idea:

        <br><br>

        <strong>CloudWatch does not keep every metric data point
        forever at its original resolution.</strong>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q20 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 20</div>

    <h3>What is an alarm threshold?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A threshold is the value or condition against which a
        monitored metric is evaluated.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Example</strong>

        <pre>CPUUtilization > 80%</pre>

        <p>

            If the configured evaluation criteria are met,
            the alarm can enter the ALARM state.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =====================================================
     â­â­

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­â­ Less Frequently Asked</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q21 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 21</div>

    <h3>What is high-resolution monitoring in CloudWatch?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        CloudWatch supports high-resolution custom metrics with
        shorter periods than standard one-minute metrics.

        These are useful when applications need more granular
        monitoring.

    </p>

</article>


<!-- Q22 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 22</div>

    <h3>What is CloudWatch anomaly detection?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        CloudWatch anomaly detection uses statistical modeling
        to identify expected metric behavior and can help
        identify values outside the expected pattern.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Example</strong>

        <p>

            Instead of using only a fixed CPU threshold, anomaly
            detection can help identify unusual behavior based
            on historical patterns.

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q23 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 23</div>

    <h3>What is CloudWatch Contributor Insights?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­ BONUS</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Contributor Insights helps identify top contributors to
        patterns in time-series data, such as the sources
        generating the most traffic or other activity.

    </p>

</article>

    <h2>ðŸŽ¯ Real-Time Interview Scenarios</h2>

<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 01</div>

    <h3>
        Your EC2 server CPU suddenly reaches 95%. What will you do?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        First, I would verify the CloudWatch CPU metric and
        understand when the increase started.

        Then I would correlate the metric with application logs
        and other infrastructure metrics.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        CPU Spike

        â†’

        CloudWatch Metric

        â†’

        Check Logs

        â†’

        Identify Cause

        â†’

        Take Action

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>Possible causes</strong>

        <p>

            â†’ Traffic increase

            <br>

            â†’ Application process consuming CPU

            <br>

            â†’ Background job

            <br>

            â†’ Resource sizing issue

            <br>

            â†’ Unexpected workload

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would first verify the CPU metric in CloudWatch
            and identify the time of the spike. Then I would
            check application and system logs, traffic metrics
            and running processes to determine the root cause.
            Based on the cause, I may optimize the application,
            scale the workload or increase capacity."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 02</div>

    <h3>
        You want an alert whenever EC2 CPU goes above 80%. How will you implement it?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2

        â†’

        CPUUtilization

        â†’

        CloudWatch Alarm

        â†’

        SNS

        â†’

        Notification

    </div>

    <p class="answer">

        I would create a CloudWatch alarm on the
        CPUUtilization metric with the required threshold and
        evaluation period, and configure an appropriate action
        such as SNS notification.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would create a CloudWatch alarm on the EC2
            CPUUtilization metric. I would configure the
            threshold and evaluation period and connect the
            alarm to SNS so the required team or endpoint is
            notified when the alarm enters ALARM state."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 03</div>

    <h3>
        Your application is failing, but CPU and memory look normal. What will you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would not assume the infrastructure is healthy just
        because CPU is normal.

        I would check:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Application logs

        <br>

        â†’ CloudWatch Logs

        <br>

        â†’ Logs Insights

        <br>

        â†’ Load Balancer metrics

        <br>

        â†’ Error rates

        <br>

        â†’ Database connectivity

        <br>

        â†’ Recent deployments/configuration changes

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would correlate infrastructure metrics with
            application logs. Normal CPU does not necessarily
            mean the application is healthy. I would use
            CloudWatch Logs and Logs Insights to identify errors
            and correlate them with recent deployments,
            dependencies and traffic."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 04</div>

    <h3>
        How would you monitor an application running on multiple EC2 instances?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would centralize application logs in CloudWatch Logs,
        monitor infrastructure metrics, create CloudWatch
        dashboards and configure alarms for important
        conditions.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2-1 â”€â”
        <br>
        EC2-2 â”€â”¼â†’ CloudWatch â†’ Dashboard / Alarms
        <br>
        EC2-3 â”€â”˜

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 5 -->

<article class="question scenario">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 05</div>

    <h3>
        CloudWatch Alarm is showing INSUFFICIENT_DATA. What does it mean?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        It means CloudWatch does not currently have enough
        information to determine whether the alarm condition is
        true or false.

        I would investigate whether the metric is being
        published correctly and whether there is enough recent
        data.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "INSUFFICIENT_DATA means the alarm does not have
            enough metric data to determine its state. I would
            check whether the metric is being published and
            whether the configured evaluation period and data
            points are appropriate."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <h2>ðŸ› ï¸ Useful CloudWatch CLI Commands</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>

<article class="question">

    <h3 class="command-title">List CloudWatch alarms</h3>

    <pre>aws cloudwatch describe-alarms</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">List metric information</h3>

    <pre>aws cloudwatch list-metrics</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Get metric statistics</h3>

    <pre>aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Describe alarm history</h3>

    <pre>aws cloudwatch describe-alarm-history</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">List dashboards</h3>

    <pre>aws cloudwatch list-dashboards</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Describe dashboard</h3>

    <pre>aws cloudwatch get-dashboard --dashboard-name MyDashboard</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">List log groups</h3>

    <pre>aws logs describe-log-groups</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">List log streams</h3>

    <pre>aws logs describe-log-streams --log-group-name MyLogGroup</pre>


    <h3 class="command-title">Start a Logs Insights query</h3>

    <pre>aws logs start-query</pre>

<div class="important">

    <strong>ðŸ§  CloudWatch One-Minute Revision</strong>

    <br><br>

    <strong>CloudWatch</strong>
    = AWS monitoring and observability service.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Metric</strong>
    = Numerical/time-series measurement.

    <br>

    <strong>Logs</strong>
    = Detailed event records.

    <br>

    <strong>Alarm</strong>
    = Watches a metric and reacts to configured conditions.

    <br>

    <strong>Dashboard</strong>
    = Visual monitoring view.

    <br>

    <strong>Log Group</strong>
    = Collection/container of log streams.

    <br>

    <strong>Log Stream</strong>
    = Sequence of log events.

    <br>

    <strong>CloudWatch Agent</strong>
    = Collect additional system metrics and logs.

    <br>

    <strong>Logs Insights</strong>
    = Query and analyze CloudWatch logs.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Remember:</strong>

    <br>

    CloudWatch â†’ Monitor

    <br>

    CloudTrail â†’ Audit AWS API activity

    <br>

    SNS â†’ Notify

    <br>

    Auto Scaling â†’ Scale
