<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 01</div>

    <h3>What is Amazon EBS?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Amazon EBS stands for <strong>Elastic Block Store</strong>.

        It provides persistent block-level storage volumes
        that can be attached to EC2 instances.

        Think of EBS like a virtual hard disk for an EC2
        instance.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2 Instance

        â†’

        EBS Volume

        â†’

        Persistent Data

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Easy Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose an EC2 instance contains an application
            and its data.

            If the instance is stopped and started again,
            the EBS volume can retain the data.

            Therefore EBS provides persistent storage
            separately from the compute instance.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon EBS is a persistent block storage service
            designed for EC2. An EBS volume can be attached to
            an EC2 instance and is commonly used for operating
            system disks, application data and databases."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 02</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between EBS and instance store?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Feature</th>
            <th>EBS</th>
            <th>Instance Store</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Storage Type</td>
            <td>Persistent block storage</td>
            <td>Temporary local storage</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Data Persistence</td>
            <td>Designed to persist independently of instance lifecycle</td>
            <td>Data can be lost when the instance is stopped/terminated depending on lifecycle</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Network Attached</td>
            <td>Yes</td>
            <td>Physically attached to host</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Typical Use</td>
            <td>OS, application data, databases</td>
            <td>Temporary/cache/scratch workloads</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ§  Easy Memory Trick</strong>

        <p>

            <strong>EBS = Persistent Disk</strong>

            <br>

            <strong>Instance Store = Temporary Local Disk</strong>

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EBS provides persistent block storage that is
            independent from the lifecycle of the EC2 compute
            resource. Instance store is temporary local storage
            physically attached to the host and is suitable for
            temporary data."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 03</div>

    <h3>What are the main EBS volume types?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The major EBS volume families you should know are:

        <br><br>

        <strong>gp3</strong>

        <br>
        General-purpose SSD. A common choice for general
        workloads.

        <br><br>

        <strong>gp2</strong>

        <br>
        Previous-generation general-purpose SSD.

        <br><br>

        <strong>io2</strong>

        <br>
        Provisioned IOPS SSD for I/O-intensive workloads.

        <br><br>

        <strong>st1</strong>

        <br>
        Throughput-oriented HDD, suitable for large sequential
        workloads.

        <br><br>

        <strong>sc1</strong>

        <br>
        Lower-cost HDD designed for infrequently accessed
        throughput-oriented workloads.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸ’¡ In most modern general-purpose application
        architectures, <strong>gp3</strong> is an important
        volume type to understand.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EBS provides different volume types based on
            workload requirements. gp3 is commonly used for
            general-purpose SSD workloads, io2 is used for
            high-performance IOPS-intensive workloads, while
            st1 and sc1 are throughput-oriented HDD options."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 04</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between gp3 and io2?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Feature</th>
            <th>gp3</th>
            <th>io2</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Type</td>
            <td>General-purpose SSD</td>
            <td>Provisioned IOPS SSD</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Use Case</td>
            <td>General applications</td>
            <td>High I/O intensive workloads</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Performance</td>
            <td>Good general-purpose performance</td>
            <td>High and predictable IOPS</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Typical Workload</td>
            <td>Web servers, applications, DevOps workloads</td>
            <td>High-performance databases and critical I/O workloads</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "gp3 is a general-purpose SSD suitable for most
            application workloads, while io2 is designed for
            workloads that require high and predictable IOPS,
            such as demanding database workloads."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 05</div>

    <h3>What is an EBS snapshot?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS
        volume.

        Snapshots are stored in Amazon S3-managed infrastructure
        and can be used to create new EBS volumes or restore
        data.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EBS Volume

        â†’

        ðŸ“¸ Snapshot

        â†’

        Backup

        â†’

        New EBS Volume

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Before performing a risky production change,
            you can create a snapshot of the relevant EBS
            volume.

            If recovery is required, the snapshot can be used
            to create a new volume.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an
            EBS volume. It can be used for backup, recovery,
            migration and creating new EBS volumes."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 06</div>

    <h3>What is Amazon EFS?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Amazon EFS stands for <strong>Elastic File System</strong>.

        It provides managed, elastic file storage that can be
        accessed concurrently by multiple compute resources.

        EFS uses the NFS protocol.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2-A

        â†˜

        <br>

        EC2-B

        â†’

        ðŸ“ EFS

        â†

        EC2-C

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose three EC2 instances are running a web
            application and all need access to the same uploaded
            files.

            Instead of storing those files separately on each
            EC2 instance, an EFS file system can provide shared
            file storage.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon EFS is a managed elastic file storage
            service that provides shared file storage using
            NFS. Multiple supported compute resources can mount
            and access the same file system."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 07</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between EBS and EFS?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ TOP INTERVIEW QUESTION</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Feature</th>
            <th>EBS</th>
            <th>EFS</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Storage Model</td>
            <td>Block storage</td>
            <td>File storage</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Access</td>
            <td>Attached to EC2 according to supported configuration</td>
            <td>Shared file system</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Protocol</td>
            <td>Block device</td>
            <td>NFS</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Multi-Instance Access</td>
            <td>Limited by volume and attachment capabilities</td>
            <td>Designed for concurrent access</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Typical Use</td>
            <td>OS disks, databases, application disks</td>
            <td>Shared files, content, common application storage</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ§  Easy Memory Trick</strong>

        <p>

            <strong>EBS = One virtual hard disk</strong>

            <br><br>

            <strong>EFS = Shared network file system</strong>

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EBS is block storage primarily attached to EC2,
            while EFS is a managed shared file system accessed
            using NFS. EBS is commonly used for operating
            system and application disks, while EFS is useful
            when multiple instances need shared files."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 08</div>

    <h3>Can multiple EC2 instances access the same EFS?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ COMMON</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Yes.

        EFS is designed to provide shared file storage that
        multiple supported compute resources can access
        concurrently.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2-1 â”€â”

        <br>

        EC2-2 â”€â”¼â”€â”€â†’ EFS

        <br>

        EC2-3 â”€â”˜

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Yes. Amazon EFS is a shared file system, so
            multiple EC2 instances can mount and access the same
            EFS file system concurrently."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q9 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 09</div>

    <h3>Can EBS be attached to multiple EC2 instances?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ TRICK QUESTION</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The normal EBS usage model is one volume attached to one
        EC2 instance at a time.

        However, certain EBS volume types and supported EC2
        configurations provide multi-attach capabilities.

        Therefore, don't simply say "EBS can never be attached
        to multiple instances."

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸŽ¯ <strong>Interview Tip:</strong>

        Say:

        <br><br>

        "Normally an EBS volume is attached to a single EC2
        instance, but specific supported configurations such
        as EBS Multi-Attach allow certain io2 volumes to be
        attached to multiple supported instances in the same
        Availability Zone."

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q10 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 10</div>

    <h3>What is EBS encryption?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EBS encryption protects data at rest on EBS volumes.

        AWS Key Management Service (KMS) can be used to manage
        the encryption keys.

        Encryption can cover:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Data at rest

        <br>

        â†’ Snapshots

        <br>

        â†’ Volumes created from encrypted snapshots

        <br>

        â†’ Data moving between the instance and the EBS volume
        depending on supported implementation

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EBS encryption protects EBS data at rest and uses
            AWS KMS for key management. Encrypted snapshots and
            volumes can also be created from encrypted EBS
            resources."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q11 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 11</div>

    <h3>What is EFS mount target?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

    <p class="answer">

        An EFS mount target provides network access to an EFS
        file system from a specific Availability Zone.

        It is associated with a subnet and security group.

        EC2 instances use the mount target to connect to the
        EFS file system.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2 in AZ-A

        â†’

        Mount Target AZ-A

        â†’

        EFS

        <br><br>

        EC2 in AZ-B

        â†’

        Mount Target AZ-B

        â†’

        EFS

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An EFS mount target provides a network endpoint
            through which resources in an Availability Zone can
            access the EFS file system. It is created in a
            subnet and associated with security groups."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q12 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 12</div>

    <h3>How do you mount EFS on an EC2 instance?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS PRACTICAL</span>

    <p class="answer">

        A common approach is to install the EFS mount helper,
        create a mount directory and mount the file system.

    </p>

    <pre>
```

sudo mkdir -p /mnt/efs

sudo mount -t efs fs-XXXXXXXX:/ /mnt/efs </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        The exact commands depend on the operating system and
        whether encryption-in-transit is enabled.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Verify Mount</strong>

        <pre>
```

df -h </pre>

```
    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would install the required EFS mount helper,
            create a mount point and mount the EFS file system.
            Then I would verify the mount using commands such
            as df -h and confirm that security groups allow
            NFS traffic."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Q13 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 13</div>

    <h3>What is EBS volume resizing?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EBS volumes can generally be modified to increase
        storage capacity and, for supported volume types,
        adjust performance characteristics.

        After increasing the volume size, the operating system
        filesystem may also need to be expanded.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        AWS EBS Volume

        â†’

        Increase Size

        â†’

        OS Detects Larger Disk

        â†’

        Expand Partition / Filesystem

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Linux Example</strong>

        <pre>
```

lsblk

df -h </pre>

```
        <p>

            After resizing the EBS volume in AWS, verify the
            device and expand the partition/filesystem as
            required by the operating system and filesystem type.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "After increasing an EBS volume size, I verify that
            the operating system sees the larger block device.
            Then I expand the partition and filesystem if
            required so the application can use the additional
            capacity."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q14 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 14</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between EBS snapshot and AMI?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Snapshot</th>
            <th>AMI</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Backup of EBS volume</td>
            <td>Machine image used to launch EC2 instances</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Primarily storage-level backup</td>
            <td>Instance template / image</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Can create EBS volumes</td>
            <td>Can launch EC2 instances</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time backup of an EBS
            volume. An AMI is a machine image that can be used
            to launch EC2 instances and can reference one or
            more snapshots."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q15 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 15</div>

    <h3>What is EFS performance mode?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS provides performance modes that determine how the
        file system behaves for different workloads.

        The key concept to remember is that performance mode
        selection is related to workload characteristics and
        throughput/latency requirements.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸ’¡ Interview focus:

        Don't memorize random values.

        Understand that EFS performance configuration should
        match the application's file access pattern and
        performance requirements.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EFS performance configuration is selected based on
            application access patterns and performance
            requirements. I would evaluate the workload's
            latency and throughput characteristics before
            selecting the appropriate configuration."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q16 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 16</div>

    <h3>What is EFS throughput mode?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS throughput mode controls how throughput is provided
        to the file system.

        Modern EFS supports modes such as:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Elastic

        <br>
        â†’ Provisioned

        <br>
        â†’ Bursting

        <br><br>

        The correct mode depends on workload characteristics
        and traffic patterns.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EFS throughput mode determines how file-system
            throughput is provided. Elastic can adapt to
            workload demand, while Provisioned allows a
            configured throughput level. Bursting uses a model
            based on file system size and workload behavior."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q17 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 17</div>

    <h3>What is EFS storage class?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS supports storage classes designed for different
        access patterns and cost requirements.

        Common concepts include:

        <br><br>

        â†’ EFS Standard

        <br>

        â†’ EFS Infrequent Access

        <br>

        â†’ EFS Archive

        <br><br>

        Lifecycle management can move files between appropriate
        storage classes based on access patterns.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EFS provides storage classes for frequently and
            infrequently accessed data, including Archive for
            long-term infrequently accessed data. Lifecycle
            policies can help optimize storage cost."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q18 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 18</div>

    <h3>What security group rules are required for EFS?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ PRACTICAL</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS uses NFS.

        Therefore, the EC2 instances that mount EFS need network
        connectivity to the EFS mount target on the NFS port.

    </p>

    <pre>
```

NFS
TCP
Port 2049 </pre>

```
    <div class="flow">

        EC2 Security Group

        â†’

        TCP 2049

        â†’

        EFS Mount Target Security Group

    </div>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸ” Best Practice:

        Allow TCP 2049 from the application's EC2 security
        group rather than allowing it broadly from the entire
        internet.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EFS uses NFS, so the EC2 instances need network
            access to the EFS mount target on TCP port 2049.
            I would allow that traffic using security groups
            with least privilege."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =====================================================
     â­â­â­
====================================================== -->

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­â­â­ Medium Priority</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 19</div>

    <h3>What is EFS Access Point?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        An EFS Access Point provides an application-specific
        entry point into an EFS file system.

        It can enforce a configured root directory and POSIX
        identity for access.

        This is especially useful when multiple applications
        share one EFS file system but should have isolated
        access paths.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Application A:

            <br>
            `/app-a`

            <br><br>

            Application B:

            <br>
            `/app-b`

            <br><br>

            Each application can use a different access point.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An EFS Access Point provides an application-specific
            access path into an EFS file system and can enforce
            a POSIX identity and root directory."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q20 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 20</div>

    <h3>What is EFS encryption in transit?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS supports encryption at rest and encryption in
        transit.

        Encryption in transit protects data while it is moving
        between the client and EFS.

        TLS can be used through the EFS mount helper.

    </p>

    <pre>
```

sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-XXXXXXXX:/ /mnt/efs </pre>

```
    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EFS supports encryption at rest and encryption in
            transit. For encryption in transit, the EFS mount
            helper can establish a TLS-protected connection."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q21 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 21</div>

    <h3>What happens if an EC2 instance is terminated?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The behavior depends on the EBS volume's
        <strong>DeleteOnTermination</strong> setting.

        For a root volume, it is commonly configured to delete
        when the instance terminates.

        Additional EBS volumes can be configured to persist
        after instance termination.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸŽ¯ Interview Tip:

        Always say:

        <br><br>

        "It depends on the DeleteOnTermination setting."

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Whether an EBS volume is deleted when an EC2
            instance terminates depends on its DeleteOnTermination
            configuration. I verify this setting before
            terminating production instances."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =====================================================
     â­â­
====================================================== -->

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­â­ Less Frequently Asked</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q22 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 22</div>

    <h3>What is EBS Multi-Attach?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EBS Multi-Attach allows a supported EBS volume to be
        attached to multiple supported EC2 instances in the
        same Availability Zone.

        It is designed for specific clustered application
        architectures and requires application-level
        coordination to safely manage shared block storage.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EBS Multi-Attach allows certain supported io2
            volumes to be attached to multiple supported EC2
            instances in the same Availability Zone. The
            application must be designed to safely coordinate
            concurrent access."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q23 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 23</div>

    <h3>Can EBS volumes be moved across Availability Zones?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        An EBS volume is associated with a specific Availability
        Zone.

        To use its data in another Availability Zone, a common
        approach is to create a snapshot and then create a new
        volume from that snapshot in the target Availability
        Zone.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EBS Volume

        â†’

        Snapshot

        â†’

        Target AZ

        â†’

        New EBS Volume

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An EBS volume is AZ-specific. To move its data to
            another Availability Zone, I can create a snapshot
            and create a new EBS volume from that snapshot in
            the target AZ."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q24 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 24</div>

    <h3>What is EFS One Zone?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS provides Regional file systems designed for
        multi-AZ availability and One Zone file systems that
        store data within a single Availability Zone.

        One Zone can be useful for workloads where lower storage
        cost is more important and the availability trade-off
        is acceptable.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EFS One Zone stores data in a single Availability
            Zone and can provide a lower-cost option for
            appropriate workloads. Regional EFS provides
            multi-AZ storage for higher availability."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =====================================================
     â­
====================================================== -->

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>â­ Bonus Questions</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Q25 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 25</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between block, file and object storage?</h3>

    <span class="label">â­ IMPORTANT CONCEPT</span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Storage</th>
            <th>Example</th>
            <th>Used For</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Block</td>
            <td>EBS</td>
            <td>OS disks, databases, applications</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>File</td>
            <td>EFS</td>
            <td>Shared directories and files</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Object</td>
            <td>S3</td>
            <td>Images, backups, logs, documents</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ§  Easy Memory Trick</strong>

        <p>

            EBS â†’ Disk

            <br>

            EFS â†’ Folder

            <br>

            S3 â†’ Bucket / Objects

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =====================================================
     ðŸŽ¯ REAL TIME SCENARIOS
====================================================== -->

<div class="priority-title">
    <h2>ðŸŽ¯ Real-Time EBS & EFS Scenarios</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>
</div>


<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 01</div>

    <h3>
        EC2 says the EBS volume is full. What will you do?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

    <p class="answer">

        First I check disk usage:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

df -h </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        Then identify which directories are consuming space:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

sudo du -sh /* 2>/dev/null </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        Then:

        <br><br>

        1. Clean unnecessary data/logs if safe.

        <br>

        2. Increase EBS volume size if required.

        <br>

        3. Expand the partition/filesystem.

        <br>

        4. Verify using `df -h`.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would first identify what is consuming the disk
            using df and du. If cleanup is not enough, I would
            increase the EBS volume size and then expand the
            filesystem. Finally, I would verify the available
            space."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 02</div>

    <h3>
        EC2 cannot mount EFS. What will you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

    <p class="answer">

        Follow the network path.

        <br><br>

        <strong>1. DNS</strong>

        <br>
        Confirm the instance can resolve the EFS endpoint.

        <br><br>

        <strong>2. Mount Target</strong>

        <br>
        Confirm the EFS mount target exists for the relevant
        Availability Zone/network.

        <br><br>

        <strong>3. Security Group</strong>

        <br>
        Check TCP 2049.

        <br><br>

        <strong>4. Network ACL / Routing</strong>

        <br>
        Verify network connectivity.

        <br><br>

        <strong>5. EFS Mount Helper</strong>

        <br>
        Confirm required packages are installed.

        <br><br>

        <strong>6. File System Policy / IAM</strong>

        <br>
        If using IAM authorization, verify permissions.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would first check the EFS mount target and network
            connectivity, especially TCP 2049. Then I would
            verify DNS, security groups, NACLs, routing and the
            EFS mount helper. If IAM authorization is enabled,
            I would also verify the relevant permissions."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 03</div>

    <h3>
        Three EC2 instances need access to the same uploaded files. EBS or EFS?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ SCENARIO</span>

    <p class="answer">

        EFS is generally the better fit because the requirement
        is shared file access across multiple instances.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        EC2-1

        â†˜

        <br>

        EC2-2

        â†’

        EFS

        â†

        EC2-3

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would choose EFS because multiple EC2 instances
            need concurrent access to the same shared file
            system. EFS is designed for this shared file
            storage requirement."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 04</div>

    <h3>
        Your database requires consistently high IOPS. Which EBS type would you consider?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would consider an appropriate provisioned-IOPS SSD
        such as io2, after evaluating the database workload,
        required IOPS, throughput, latency and cost.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "For a database requiring consistently high and
            predictable IOPS, I would evaluate io2 because it
            is designed for provisioned IOPS workloads. I would
            still size it based on measured application
            requirements."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 05</div>

    <h3>
        You terminated an EC2 instance and lost its root disk data. Why?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

    <p class="answer">

        The root EBS volume may have had
        <strong>DeleteOnTermination</strong> enabled.

        Before terminating an instance, production data should
        be stored and protected according to the application's
        backup and persistence requirements.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The root EBS volume may have been configured with
            DeleteOnTermination enabled. I would check the
            volume's lifecycle configuration and ensure
            production data has appropriate backups before
            terminating instances."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- =====================================================
     ðŸ§  REVISION
====================================================== -->

<div class="important">

    <strong>ðŸ§  EBS & EFS One-Minute Revision</strong>

    <br><br>

    <strong>EBS</strong>
    = Persistent block storage.

    <br><br>

    <strong>EFS</strong>
    = Managed shared file storage using NFS.

    <br><br>

    <strong>gp3</strong>
    = General-purpose SSD.

    <br><br>

    <strong>io2</strong>
    = Provisioned IOPS SSD for demanding workloads.

    <br><br>

    <strong>Snapshot</strong>
    = Point-in-time backup of EBS volume.

    <br><br>

    <strong>EBS Encryption</strong>
    = Encryption at rest using AWS KMS.

    <br><br>

    <strong>EFS Mount Target</strong>
    = Network access point for EFS in an Availability Zone.

    <br><br>

    <strong>EFS Port</strong>
    = NFS TCP 2049.

    <br><br>

    <strong>EBS</strong>
    = Think "virtual hard disk".

    <br><br>

    <strong>EFS</strong>
    = Think "shared network folder".

    <br><br>

    <strong>Most Important Comparison</strong>

    <br><br>

    EC2 OS / Database Disk â†’ EBS

    <br>

    Shared Files Across Instances â†’ EFS

    <br>

    Images / Backups / Objects â†’ S3

</div>

<!-- =================================================
     5 STAR QUESTIONS
================================================= -->

<div class="priority-title">

    <h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Must Know</h2>

    <div class="line"></div>

</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 01
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is Amazon EC2?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is an AWS service
        that provides resizable virtual servers called
        <strong>instances</strong> in the cloud.

        Instead of purchasing and maintaining a physical
        server, we can launch an EC2 instance with the
        required CPU, memory, storage and networking
        configuration.

        We can then install an operating system,
        applications and other software on that instance.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we have a web application that needs
            a Linux server.

            Instead of buying a physical server, we can
            launch an EC2 instance, install Docker,
            deploy our application and expose it through
            a Load Balancer.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon EC2 is a compute service provided by AWS
            that allows us to launch and manage virtual
            servers in the cloud. We can choose the instance
            type, operating system, storage and networking
            configuration based on our application
            requirements."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>What is an EC2 instance?</li>

            <li>What is an AMI?</li>

            <li>What are instance types?</li>

            <li>What happens when an instance is stopped?</li>

            <li>What is the difference between stop and terminate?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 02
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an EC2 instance?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An EC2 instance is a virtual server running inside
        AWS.

        When we launch an EC2 instance, AWS allocates
        computing resources such as CPU, memory, networking
        and storage according to the configuration we select.

        The instance runs an operating system such as
        Amazon Linux, Ubuntu or Windows Server.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            If our application requires 4 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM,
            we can select an EC2 instance type that provides
            those resources and deploy our application on it.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An EC2 instance is a virtual machine provided by
            AWS. It gives us configurable compute resources
            such as CPU, memory, networking and storage,
            allowing us to run applications without managing
            physical servers."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>How do you launch an EC2 instance?</li>

            <li>What is an instance type?</li>

            <li>How do you connect to Linux EC2?</li>

            <li>How do you secure an EC2 instance?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 03
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an AMI in AWS?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        AMI stands for <strong>Amazon Machine Image</strong>.

        It is a template used to create EC2 instances.

        An AMI can contain the operating system,
        application configuration, installed software
        and other required settings.

        When we launch an EC2 instance, we select an AMI
        as the starting template.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we configured an Ubuntu EC2 server with
            Docker, Java and our application dependencies.

            We can create a custom AMI from that configured
            server and use it to launch additional instances
            with the same base configuration.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An AMI is a template used to launch EC2
            instances. It contains the operating system and
            can also contain software and configuration
            required by the application."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>What is a custom AMI?</li>

            <li>Can we create an AMI from an existing EC2?</li>

            <li>Can an AMI be copied to another region?</li>

            <li>What is the relationship between AMI and EBS?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 04
    </div>

    <h3>
        What are EC2 instance types?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        EC2 instance types define the compute resources
        available to an EC2 instance.

        Different instance families are optimized for
        different workloads.

        For example:

        <br><br>

        <strong>General Purpose</strong> â€”
        balanced CPU, memory and networking.

        <br>

        <strong>Compute Optimized</strong> â€”
        workloads requiring high CPU performance.

        <br>

        <strong>Memory Optimized</strong> â€”
        workloads requiring large amounts of RAM.

        <br>

        <strong>Storage Optimized</strong> â€”
        workloads requiring high local storage performance.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            A normal web application may use a
            general-purpose instance.

            A CPU-intensive application may require a
            compute-optimized instance.

            A large in-memory database may require a
            memory-optimized instance.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EC2 instance types determine the compute
            resources provided to an instance. AWS offers
            different instance families optimized for
            general-purpose, compute-intensive,
            memory-intensive and storage-intensive
            workloads."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>What is an instance family?</li>

            <li>How do you choose an instance type?</li>

            <li>What are vCPUs?</li>

            <li>What is the difference between CPU and memory optimized instances?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 05
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is the difference between stopping and terminating an EC2 instance?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>Stop:</strong>

        The instance is shut down, but its EBS-backed
        storage can remain available.

        The instance can usually be started again.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Terminate:</strong>

        The instance is permanently deleted.

        The instance cannot be started again after
        termination.

        Therefore, termination should be used carefully.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose a development server is not required
            overnight.

            We can stop the instance and start it again
            the next morning.

            If the server is permanently no longer required,
            we can terminate it.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Stopping an EC2 instance shuts it down while
            allowing it to be started again later.
            Terminating an instance permanently removes it,
            so it cannot be restarted."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>What happens to the public IP after stopping?</li>

            <li>What happens to EBS volumes?</li>

            <li>Does stopping an instance stop all charges?</li>

            <li>What happens to instance-store data?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 06
    </div>

    <h3>
        How do you connect to a Linux EC2 instance?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        For a Linux EC2 instance, we commonly connect using
        <strong>SSH</strong>.

        We need the appropriate private key, the instance's
        reachable IP or hostname, and network access through
        the Security Group.

        SSH normally uses port 22.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            After launching an Ubuntu EC2 instance, we can
            connect from a terminal using the instance's
            public IP and the corresponding private key.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I connect to a Linux EC2 instance using SSH.
            I make sure the instance is reachable, port 22
            is allowed from the required source in the
            Security Group, and I use the correct private
            key with the appropriate SSH username."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’» Example Command</strong>

        <pre>ssh -i my-key.pem ubuntu@&lt;public-ip&gt;</pre>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>Why is port 22 required?</li>

            <li>What if SSH connection times out?</li>

            <li>What if the key permission is incorrect?</li>

            <li>What is the difference between public and private IP?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =================================================
     IMPORTANT CONCEPTS
================================================= -->

<div class="priority-title">

    <h2>â­â­â­â­ High Priority</h2>

    <div class="line"></div>

</div>


<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 07
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is a Security Group in EC2?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A Security Group is a virtual firewall associated
        with AWS resources such as EC2 instances.

        It controls network traffic using inbound and
        outbound rules.

        Security Groups are stateful, meaning response
        traffic for an allowed connection is automatically
        allowed.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            For a web server, we may allow HTTP on port 80
            and HTTPS on port 443 from the internet.

            For SSH, instead of allowing port 22 from
            everyone, we should restrict access to a
            trusted IP range.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A Security Group acts as a stateful virtual
            firewall for an EC2 instance. It controls
            inbound and outbound traffic through rules."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>Are Security Groups stateful or stateless?</li>

            <li>Can a Security Group deny traffic?</li>

            <li>Security Group vs NACL?</li>

            <li>Can one EC2 have multiple Security Groups?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 08
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is EBS and how is it related to EC2?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Amazon EBS stands for Elastic Block Store.

        It provides persistent block-level storage that can
        be attached to EC2 instances.

        The operating system and application data can be
        stored on EBS volumes.

        Unlike temporary instance-store storage, EBS data
        is designed to persist independently of the running
        instance lifecycle in many common scenarios.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            If an EC2 instance is used as an application
            server, an EBS volume can be used to store
            application files, logs or database data.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "EBS is persistent block storage for EC2.
            We can attach EBS volumes to EC2 instances and
            use them for operating-system, application or
            data storage."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =================================================
     SCENARIO QUESTIONS
================================================= -->

<div class="priority-title">

    <h2>ðŸŽ¯ Real-Time EC2 Scenarios</h2>

    <div class="line"></div>

</div>


<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 01
    </div>

    <h3>
        Your EC2 instance is running, but you cannot connect using SSH. What will you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        TROUBLESHOOTING APPROACH
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would troubleshoot layer by layer instead of
        immediately assuming that the EC2 instance itself
        is down.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ› ï¸ Troubleshooting Checklist</strong>

        <p>

            1. Check whether the instance is actually
            running.

            <br>

            2. Verify the correct public IP or reachable
            private address.

            <br>

            3. Check the Security Group and confirm that
            TCP port 22 is allowed from the required source.

            <br>

            4. Check the subnet route table and internet
            connectivity if using a public IP.

            <br>

            5. Check Network ACL rules.

            <br>

            6. Verify the SSH username.

            <br>

            7. Verify the correct private key.

            <br>

            8. Check whether the operating system's SSH
            service is running.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "If SSH is failing, I first check the EC2
            instance state and connectivity. Then I verify
            the IP address, Security Group port 22 rule,
            subnet routing, Network ACLs, SSH credentials
            and finally the SSH service on the operating
            system."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 02
    </div>

    <h3>
        Your EC2 application is running but users cannot access the website. How would you troubleshoot it?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        PRODUCTION SCENARIO
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would check the complete request path from the
        client to the application.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ› ï¸ Troubleshooting Flow</strong>

        <p>

            Client

            â†’
            DNS

            â†’
            Load Balancer / Public IP

            â†’
            Security Group

            â†’
            Network ACL

            â†’
            EC2

            â†’
            Application

            â†’
            Application Port

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would first identify whether the problem is
            DNS, network connectivity, security rules,
            EC2 availability or the application itself.
            I would verify the Security Group, routes,
            listening ports, application process and logs
            before making changes."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<div class="priority-title">

    <h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Must Know</h2>

    <div class="line"></div>

</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 01
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is AWS IAM?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        IAM stands for
        <strong>Identity and Access Management</strong>.

        AWS IAM is a service used to control
        <strong>who can access AWS resources</strong>
        and <strong>what actions they are allowed to perform</strong>.

        In simple words:

        <br><br>

        <strong>
            IAM = Authentication + Authorization + Access Control
        </strong>

        <br><br>

        Authentication answers:

        <br>

        <strong>
            "Who are you?"
        </strong>

        <br><br>

        Authorization answers:

        <br>

        <strong>
            "What are you allowed to do?"
        </strong>

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ‘¤ Identity

        â†’

        ðŸ” IAM

        â†’

        ðŸ“œ Policy

        â†’

        â˜ï¸ AWS Resource

        <br>

        User / Role

        â†’

        Permission

        â†’

        Action

    </div>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose a DevOps engineer needs to restart an EC2
            instance.

            We should not give unrestricted administrator
            permissions just because the engineer needs EC2
            access.

            Instead, we can provide only the required
            permissions according to the job requirement.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "AWS IAM is a service used to securely control
            authentication and authorization for AWS
            resources. It allows us to create identities,
            define permissions using policies and provide
            users or workloads only the access they require."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 02
    </div>

    <h3>
        What are the main components of IAM?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        The important IAM concepts are:

        <br><br>

        ðŸ‘¤ <strong>Users</strong> â€”
        identities generally representing people or
        applications that need long-term credentials.

        <br><br>

        ðŸ‘¥ <strong>Groups</strong> â€”
        collections of IAM users used to manage permissions
        for multiple users.

        <br><br>

        ðŸŽ­ <strong>Roles</strong> â€”
        identities with permissions that can be assumed by
        trusted principals such as AWS services, users or
        federated identities.

        <br><br>

        ðŸ“œ <strong>Policies</strong> â€”
        documents that define permissions.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ‘¤ USER

        +

        ðŸ‘¥ GROUP

        +

        ðŸŽ­ ROLE

        +

        ðŸ“œ POLICY

        â†“

        ðŸ” PERMISSIONS

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The main IAM concepts are users, groups, roles
            and policies. Users represent identities, groups
            help organize users and permissions, roles provide
            assumable permissions, and policies define what
            actions are allowed or denied."

        </p>

    </div>

<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 03
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an IAM User?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An IAM User is an identity created in an AWS account.

        A user can have credentials and permissions assigned
        through IAM policies.

        Historically, IAM users are commonly used for
        individual people or specific long-term credentials,
        although AWS generally recommends temporary
        credentials and federation where appropriate.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Imagine a company has a developer who needs to
            work with AWS.

            The organization can use centralized identity
            federation or other appropriate access mechanisms.
            If an IAM user is used, its permissions should
            follow least privilege and MFA should be enabled
            where applicable.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An IAM user is an identity in an AWS account that
            can be granted permissions to access AWS
            resources. For human access, organizations often
            prefer federation and temporary credentials,
            while IAM users can still be used for specific
            requirements."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 04
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an IAM Group?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An IAM Group is a collection of IAM users.

        Groups help simplify permission management.

        Instead of attaching the same policy individually to
        ten developers, we can put the users into a group and
        attach the required permissions to that group.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ‘¤ Developer 1

        â†˜

        ðŸ‘¥ DevOps Group

        â†—

        ðŸ‘¤ Developer 2

        <br>

        DevOps Group

        â†’

        ðŸ“œ Required Policies

    </div>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose 20 developers need read-only access to
            CloudWatch.

            Instead of managing 20 users separately, we can
            create a Developers group and attach the required
            policy to that group.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An IAM group is a collection of IAM users.
            Groups allow us to manage common permissions for
            multiple users centrally."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 05
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an IAM Role?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An IAM Role is an identity that defines a set of
        permissions that can be assumed by a trusted
        principal.

        Unlike a typical IAM user access-key setup, a role
        does not require permanent credentials to be embedded
        in the workload.

        Roles are heavily used in DevOps and cloud
        architectures.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ EC2

        â†’

        ðŸŽ­ IAM Role

        â†’

        ðŸ” Temporary Credentials

        â†’

        ðŸª£ S3

    </div>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Most Important DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose an EC2 server needs to download files from
            S3.

            A bad approach is to put an IAM user's access key
            and secret key inside the EC2 server.

            A better approach is:

            <br><br>

            EC2 â†’ IAM Role â†’ S3 permissions.

            <br><br>

            AWS provides temporary credentials to the
            workload through the role.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An IAM role is an identity with permissions that
            can be assumed by trusted principals. Roles are
            commonly used by AWS services and workloads such
            as EC2 because they provide temporary credentials
            instead of requiring long-term access keys to be
            stored on the server."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Interviewer May Ask</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>Why use a role instead of access keys?</li>

            <li>How does EC2 get credentials from a role?</li>

            <li>What is a trust policy?</li>

            <li>What is sts:AssumeRole?</li>

        </ul>

<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 06
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an IAM Policy?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An IAM Policy is a JSON document that defines
        permissions.

        It answers questions such as:

        <br><br>

        <strong>
            What action?
        </strong>

        <br>

        <strong>
            On which resource?
        </strong>

        <br>

        <strong>
            Is it allowed or denied?
        </strong>

        <br><br>

        A policy commonly contains:

        <br>

        <strong>Effect</strong> â†’ Allow or Deny

        <br>

        <strong>Action</strong> â†’ API operation

        <br>

        <strong>Resource</strong> â†’ AWS resource

        <br>

        <strong>Condition</strong> â†’ Optional conditions

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Simple Policy Structure</strong>

        <pre>
```

{
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "s3:GetObject",
"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*"
} </pre>

```
        <p>

            This example grants permission to retrieve
            objects from the specified S3 bucket path.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An IAM policy is a JSON-based permission document
            that defines which actions are allowed or denied
            on which AWS resources, optionally under specific
            conditions."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 07
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is the difference between Authentication and Authorization?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        BASIC BUT VERY IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>Authentication</strong> means verifying
        identity.

        <br><br>

        It answers:

        <br>

        <strong>
            "Who are you?"
        </strong>

        <br><br>

        <strong>Authorization</strong> means determining
        permissions.

        <br><br>

        It answers:

        <br>

        <strong>
            "What are you allowed to do?"
        </strong>

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Easy Example</strong>

        <p>

            Logging into AWS with valid credentials:

            <br>

            â†’ Authentication

            <br><br>

            Being allowed to launch an EC2 instance:

            <br>

            â†’ Authorization

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Authentication verifies who the identity is,
            while authorization determines what that
            authenticated identity is permitted to do."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 08
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is the difference between IAM User and IAM Role?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        VERY FREQUENT INTERVIEW QUESTION
    </span>

    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ‘¤ IAM User

        â†’

        Long-term identity

        <br><br>

        ðŸŽ­ IAM Role

        â†’

        Assumable identity

        â†’

        Temporary credentials

    </div>


    <p class="answer">

        An IAM User is a persistent identity within an AWS
        account.

        An IAM Role is an identity that can be assumed by a
        trusted principal and is commonly used to provide
        temporary credentials.

        In modern cloud architectures, roles are especially
        important for workloads and federated human access.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            <strong>Developer workstation:</strong>

            <br>

            Use appropriate federated/temporary access.

            <br><br>

            <strong>EC2 â†’ S3:</strong>

            <br>

            Attach an IAM role to EC2 rather than storing
            long-term access keys on the server.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An IAM user is a persistent identity, while an
            IAM role is an assumable identity that provides
            temporary credentials. Roles are preferred for
            AWS workloads because they avoid embedding
            long-term access keys in servers or applications."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q9 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 09
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is the Principle of Least Privilege?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ SECURITY
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Least privilege means giving an identity only the
        permissions it actually needs to perform its task.

        We should avoid giving unnecessary permissions.

        For example:

        <br><br>

        If an application only needs to read S3 objects,
        giving it:

        <br>

        <strong>
            s3:GetObject
        </strong>

        is better than giving:

        <br>

        <strong>
            AdministratorAccess
        </strong>

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            A CI/CD pipeline only needs permission to push
            images to a specific ECR repository.

            Instead of giving the pipeline full AWS
            AdministratorAccess, create permissions only for
            the required ECR actions and resources.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The principle of least privilege means providing
            only the minimum permissions required to perform
            a specific task. It reduces the potential impact
            of compromised credentials or applications."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q10 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 10
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is a Trust Policy?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A role has two important permission concepts:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Trust Policy</strong> â†’
        defines <strong>who can assume the role</strong>.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Permissions Policy</strong> â†’
        defines <strong>what the role can do after it is
        assumed</strong>.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        WHO CAN ASSUME?

        â†’

        ðŸ¤ Trust Policy

        <br><br>

        WHAT CAN THEY DO?

        â†’

        ðŸ“œ Permissions Policy

    </div>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ EC2 Example</strong>

        <p>

            EC2 needs to use an IAM role.

            The role's trust relationship allows the EC2
            service principal to assume the role.

            The permissions policy then determines what the
            role can do, for example access S3.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The trust policy of an IAM role defines which
            principals are allowed to assume the role.
            The permissions policy defines what actions the
            role can perform after it is assumed."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Q14 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 14
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an inline policy?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        MEDIUM
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An inline policy is a policy embedded directly into
        a single IAM identity such as a user or role.

        It has a one-to-one relationship with that identity.

        Inline policies can be useful when the permission
        should be tightly coupled to one identity, although
        customer managed policies are often easier to
        reuse and manage centrally.

    </p>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An inline policy is embedded directly into a
            specific IAM identity and has a one-to-one
            relationship with that identity."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

        What happens if an IAM policy has both Allow and Deny?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        INTERVIEW TRICK
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An explicit Deny overrides an Allow.

        This is one of the most important IAM evaluation
        concepts.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        Allow

        +

        Explicit Deny

        â†“

        âŒ DENIED

    </div>


    <div class="example">

            Suppose a user receives:

            <br><br>

            Policy A â†’ Allow S3 access

            <br>

            Policy B â†’ Explicitly Deny access to a specific
            bucket

            <br><br>

            The explicit Deny wins for the request covered by
            that Deny.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit Deny
            overrides an Allow."

        </p>

<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 01
    </div>

    <h3>
        An EC2 instance needs access to S3. How would you provide access securely?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would create an IAM role with the minimum required
        S3 permissions and attach that role to the EC2
        instance.

        I would avoid storing long-term access keys directly
        on the EC2 server.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        EC2

        â†’

        IAM Role

        â†’

        Temporary Credentials

        â†’

        S3

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance
            and grant the role only the required S3
            permissions. This avoids storing long-term access
            keys on the server and follows least privilege."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 02
    </div>

    <h3>
        Your application is getting AccessDenied when calling an AWS API. How do you troubleshoot?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ PRODUCTION QUESTION
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would troubleshoot from identity to permission.

        First identify the principal making the API call.

        Then check:

        <br><br>

        1. Which IAM user or role is being used?

        <br>

        2. Does the identity have the required action?

        <br>

        3. Is the resource ARN correct?

        <br>

        4. Are there conditions restricting access?

        <br>

        5. Is there an explicit Deny?

        <br>

        6. Are SCPs or permissions boundaries involved?

        <br>

        7. Is the request coming from the expected account,
        Region or network context?

    </p>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "For AccessDenied, I first identify the principal
            and API operation. Then I review identity and
            resource policies, resource ARNs, conditions and
            explicit Denies. In an organization, I would also
            check controls such as SCPs and permissions
            boundaries."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 03
    </div>

    <h3>
        A developer stored AWS access keys inside GitHub. What would you do immediately?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        ðŸš¨ SECURITY INCIDENT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would treat the credentials as compromised.

        The immediate priority is to stop unauthorized use
        and then investigate.

        Depending on the credential type and setup, I would
        revoke or deactivate the exposed credentials,
        investigate CloudTrail activity, rotate credentials
        where applicable, remove the secret from the
        repository/history as appropriate, and move the
        workload toward short-lived credentials such as IAM
        roles or OIDC-based federation.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        ðŸš¨ Exposed Secret

        â†’

        ðŸ”’ Revoke / Rotate

        â†’

        ðŸ”Ž Investigate CloudTrail

        â†’

        ðŸ§¹ Remove Secret

        â†’

        ðŸ›¡ï¸ Use Short-Lived Credentials

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would treat the exposed credentials as
            compromised. I would immediately revoke or
            rotate them, investigate usage through logging,
            remove the secret from the source-control
            workflow, and replace long-lived credentials with
            short-lived role or OIDC-based authentication
            wherever possible."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 04
    </div>

    <h3>
        Why should we avoid giving AdministratorAccess to a CI/CD pipeline?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        DEVSECOPS
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Because a CI/CD pipeline is an automated workload.

        If its credentials are compromised, AdministratorAccess
        could allow an attacker to modify or delete a large
        portion of the AWS environment.

        The safer design is to give the pipeline only the
        permissions required for its deployment task.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            If the pipeline only deploys to ECS and pushes
            images to ECR, it should not automatically receive
            permissions to modify unrelated IAM, billing,
            networking or production resources.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "CI/CD pipelines should follow least privilege.
            Giving AdministratorAccess increases the blast
            radius if the pipeline credentials or runner are
            compromised. I would create a deployment role
            containing only the required permissions."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>
