    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 01</div>

    <h3>What is a Load Balancer?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A load balancer distributes incoming application traffic
        across multiple backend targets such as EC2 instances,
        containers or IP addresses.

        Its main purpose is to improve:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Availability

        <br>
        â†’ Scalability

        <br>
        â†’ Fault tolerance

        <br>
        â†’ Traffic distribution

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ‘¤ Users

        â†’

        âš–ï¸ Load Balancer

        â†’

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ EC2-A

        <br>
        â†“

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ EC2-B

        <br>
        â†“

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ EC2-C

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose an application has three EC2 instances.

            Instead of users connecting directly to one EC2
            instance, they connect to the Load Balancer.

            The Load Balancer distributes requests among
            healthy backend instances.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A Load Balancer distributes incoming traffic across
            multiple healthy backend targets. It improves
            application availability, scalability and fault
            tolerance by preventing traffic from depending on
            a single server."

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Common Follow-ups</strong>

<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 02</div>

    <h3>What are the types of AWS Load Balancers?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS Elastic Load Balancing provides several load
        balancing options.

        The major ones to know are:

        <br><br>

        <strong>1. Application Load Balancer (ALB)</strong>

        <br>
        Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS load balancing.

        <br><br>

        <strong>2. Network Load Balancer (NLB)</strong>

        <br>
        Layer 4 TCP/UDP/TLS load balancing.

        <br><br>

        <strong>3. Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)</strong>

        <br>
        Used to deploy and scale network virtual appliances.

        <br><br>

        <strong>4. Classic Load Balancer (CLB)</strong>

        <br>
        Older generation load balancer. For new architectures,
        ALB or NLB is generally preferred depending on the
        requirement.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The main AWS Elastic Load Balancing options are
            Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer,
            Gateway Load Balancer and the older Classic Load
            Balancer. ALB is mainly used for HTTP/HTTPS
            applications, NLB for high-performance Layer 4
            traffic, and GWLB for network appliances."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 03</div>

    <h3>What is an Application Load Balancer (ALB)?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW FOR DEVOPS
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An Application Load Balancer operates at
        <strong>Layer 7</strong> of the OSI model.

        It is designed for HTTP and HTTPS applications.

        ALB can make routing decisions based on application-level
        information such as:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Hostname

        <br>
        â†’ URL path

        <br>
        â†’ HTTP headers

        <br>
        â†’ Query parameters

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        User

        â†’

        ALB : 443

        â†’

        Target Group

        â†’

        EC2 : 8080

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Path-Based Routing Example</strong>

        <p>

            `/api/*`

            â†’

            API target group

            <br><br>

            `/web/*`

            â†’

            Web target group

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Application Load Balancer is a Layer 7 load
            balancer designed for HTTP and HTTPS traffic. It
            supports advanced application-level routing such
            as host-based and path-based routing."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 04</div>

    <h3>What is a Network Load Balancer (NLB)?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A Network Load Balancer operates primarily at
        <strong>Layer 4</strong>.

        It is designed for high-performance network traffic
        such as TCP, UDP and TLS use cases.

        NLB is useful when very high throughput, low latency,
        static IP requirements or non-HTTP protocols are needed.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Client

        â†’

        NLB

        â†’

        TCP / UDP

        â†’

        Target

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            If an application uses a custom TCP protocol rather
            than HTTP, NLB can be a better fit than ALB.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Network Load Balancer is a Layer 4 load balancer
            designed for high-performance TCP, UDP and TLS
            traffic. It is useful when low latency, high
            throughput or network-level load balancing is
            required."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 05</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between ALB and NLB?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE
    </span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Feature</th>
            <th>ALB</th>
            <th>NLB</th>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>OSI Layer</td>
            <td>Layer 7</td>
            <td>Layer 4</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Main Traffic</td>
            <td>HTTP / HTTPS</td>
            <td>TCP / UDP / TLS</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Path Routing</td>
            <td>Yes</td>
            <td>No HTTP path routing</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Host Routing</td>
            <td>Yes</td>
            <td>No HTTP host routing</td>
        </tr>

        <tr>
            <td>Typical Use</td>
            <td>Web applications / APIs</td>
            <td>High-performance network traffic</td>
        </tr>

    </table>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Easy Memory Trick</strong>

        <p>

            <strong>ALB = Application-level decisions</strong>

            <br>

            "Which URL or hostname?"

            <br><br>

            <strong>NLB = Network-level decisions</strong>

            <br>

            "Which TCP/UDP target?"

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "ALB works at Layer 7 and is mainly used for HTTP/HTTPS
            applications with features such as host and path
            based routing. NLB works at Layer 4 and is designed
            for high-performance TCP, UDP and TLS traffic."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 06</div>

    <h3>What is a Target Group?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A Target Group is a logical group of backend targets
        that a load balancer sends traffic to.

        Depending on the load balancer and configuration,
        targets can include:

        <br><br>

        â†’ EC2 instances

        <br>
        â†’ IP addresses

        <br>
        â†’ Containers through supported integrations

        <br>
        â†’ Lambda functions for ALB use cases

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        ALB

        â†’

        Target Group

        â†’

        EC2-1

        <br>
        â†“

        EC2-2

        <br>
        â†“

        EC2-3

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            An ALB receives HTTPS traffic on port 443.

            The target group may forward that traffic to
            application servers listening on port 8080.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A target group is a logical collection of backend
            targets that receive traffic from a load balancer.
            It also contains settings such as the target port
            and health check configuration."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 07</div>

    <h3>What is a Listener?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A Listener checks for incoming connection requests on
        a configured protocol and port.

        For example:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

HTTPS : 443
HTTP  : 80 </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        The listener then uses listener rules to determine
        where the request should go.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Client

        â†’

        Listener : 443

        â†’

        Listener Rule

        â†’

        Target Group

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A listener checks for incoming connection requests
            on a configured protocol and port. For an ALB,
            listener rules can then route requests to the
            appropriate target group."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 08</div>

    <h3>What is a health check in a Load Balancer?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A health check allows the load balancer to determine
        whether a registered target is healthy enough to receive
        traffic.

        For an HTTP application, an example health check might be:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

Protocol: HTTP
Port: 8080
Path: /health </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        If the target fails health checks, the load balancer
        stops routing new traffic to that unhealthy target.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we have:

            <br><br>

            EC2-A â†’ healthy

            <br>

            EC2-B â†’ unhealthy

            <br>

            EC2-C â†’ healthy

            <br><br>

            The Load Balancer sends traffic only to the healthy
            targets.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A load balancer health check periodically verifies
            whether a registered target is healthy. If a target
            fails the configured health checks, the load
            balancer stops sending new traffic to it until it
            becomes healthy again."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 09</div>

    <h3>What is path-based routing?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ ALB FAVORITE
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Path-based routing allows an ALB to route requests to
        different target groups depending on the URL path.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        /api/*

        â†’

        API Target Group

        <br><br>

        /payment/*

        â†’

        Payment Target Group

        <br><br>

        /web/*

        â†’

        Web Target Group

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Microservices Example</strong>

        <p>

            A single ALB can expose:

            <br><br>

            example.com/api

            â†’ API service

            <br>

            example.com/payment

            â†’ Payment service

            <br>

            example.com/orders

            â†’ Order service

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Path-based routing allows an ALB to route HTTP or
            HTTPS requests to different target groups based on
            the URL path. It is commonly used in microservices
            architectures."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 10</div>

        â†’

        Web Target Group

        â†’

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

            Balancer to route HTTP or HTTPS requests to

            hostname."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q11 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 11</div>

    <h3>How does an ALB distribute traffic?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        The ALB receives client requests through its listener,
        evaluates listener rules and forwards matching requests
        to a target group.

        The target group contains registered targets and
        health-check information.

        Only healthy targets are eligible to receive new
        traffic.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Client

        â†“

        ALB

        â†“

        Listener

        â†“

        Listener Rule

        â†“

        Target Group

        â†“

        Healthy Targets

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "The ALB accepts client requests through a listener,
            evaluates its listener rules, selects the relevant
            target group and forwards the request to eligible
            healthy targets."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q12 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 12</div>

    <h3>Why do we use a Load Balancer with Auto Scaling?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Auto Scaling changes the number of backend instances
        according to demand.

        The Load Balancer provides a stable entry point and
        distributes traffic across the currently healthy
        instances.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Users

        â†“

        Load Balancer

        â†“

        Auto Scaling Group

        â†“

        EC2-1

        EC2-2

        EC2-3

        â†•

        Scale Out / Scale In

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            During normal traffic:

            <br>
            2 EC2 instances

            <br><br>

            During high traffic:

            <br>
            Auto Scaling launches additional instances.

            <br><br>

            The Load Balancer automatically routes traffic
            to the healthy registered instances.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Auto Scaling manages the number of backend instances,
            while the Load Balancer distributes traffic among
            healthy instances. Together they provide scalability
            and high availability."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 13</div>

    <h3>What is cross-zone load balancing?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Cross-zone load balancing allows load balancing across
        targets in different Availability Zones rather than
        restricting distribution to targets associated with
        only the receiving zone.

        Exact behavior and configuration details depend on the
        load balancer type.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            AZ-A has 2 healthy targets.

            <br>

            AZ-B has 5 healthy targets.

            <br><br>

            Cross-zone behavior can help distribute traffic
            more evenly across available targets according to
            the load balancer's configuration.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Cross-zone load balancing allows a load balancer
            to distribute traffic across targets in multiple
            Availability Zones. The exact default and
            configuration behavior depends on the load balancer
            type."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q14 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 14</div>

    <h3>What is connection draining / deregistration delay?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­ COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        When a target is being removed from service, the load
        balancer can allow existing connections or requests to
        complete instead of immediately terminating traffic.

        This helps prevent users from experiencing interrupted
        requests during deployments or scale-in events.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ DevOps Deployment Example</strong>

        <p>

            During deployment, an old application server is
            removed.

            Instead of killing active requests immediately,
            deregistration delay allows existing traffic to
            finish while new traffic is sent to healthy targets.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Deregistration delay allows existing connections or
            requests to finish when a target is being removed
            from service. It helps provide graceful deployments
            and reduces interrupted requests."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q15 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 15</div>

    <h3>Can an ALB route traffic to different ports?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Yes.

        The Load Balancer listener can accept traffic on one
        port and the target group can forward it to a configured
        target port.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Client

        â†’

        HTTPS : 443

        â†’

        ALB

        â†’

        Target Group

        â†’

        EC2 : 8080

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Users access:

            <br>

            HTTPS : 443

            <br><br>

            Application servers listen on:

            <br>

            HTTP : 8080

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Yes. A load balancer can listen on one port and
            forward traffic to a target group configured for
            another target port, depending on the protocol and
            load balancer configuration."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q16 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 16</div>

    <h3>Where should an internet-facing ALB be deployed?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An internet-facing ALB is associated with subnets that
        have network connectivity suitable for internet-facing
        access, typically public subnets in multiple
        Availability Zones.

        The ALB itself provides the public-facing entry point;
        backend application instances can remain in private
        subnets.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        ðŸŒ Internet

        â†“

        Public Subnets

        â†“

        ALB

        â†“

        Private App Subnets

        â†“

        Application Servers

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An internet-facing ALB is placed across appropriate
            public subnets in multiple Availability Zones.
            Backend application servers can remain in private
            subnets and receive traffic from the ALB."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        </p>

    </div>

<!-- Q18 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 18</div>

    <h3>What is SSL/TLS termination at the Load Balancer?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        SSL/TLS termination means the Load Balancer handles the
        HTTPS encryption/decryption from the client.

        For example:

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Client

        â†’

        HTTPS : 443

        â†’

        ALB

        â†’

        HTTP : 8080

        â†’

        Application

    </div>

    <p class="answer">

        This can reduce the TLS processing burden on backend
        servers.

        The exact architecture should be selected based on
        security requirements.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "TLS termination means the load balancer terminates
            the client's HTTPS connection. It decrypts the
            request and can forward it to backend targets using
            the configured protocol and port."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 19</div>

    <h3>What is weighted routing in ALB?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        ALB listener rules can use weighted forwarding to send
        different proportions of traffic to multiple target
        groups.

        This is useful for controlled releases and testing.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Canary Deployment</strong>

        <p>

            Version 1:

            <br>
            90% traffic

            <br><br>

            Version 2:

            <br>
            10% traffic

            <br><br>

            If version 2 is stable, the percentage can be
            increased gradually.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Weighted forwarding allows an ALB listener rule to
            distribute traffic across multiple target groups
            using configured weights. It can be useful for
            canary or controlled deployments."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q20 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 20</div>

    <h3>What happens when all targets become unhealthy?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­ TROUBLESHOOTING
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        If the target group has no healthy targets, requests
        cannot be successfully served by normal healthy-target
        routing.

        The exact response and behavior depend on the
        load-balancer configuration and failure scenario.

        The first troubleshooting step is to determine why
        the health checks are failing.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ What to check</strong>

        <p>

            â†’ Health check path

            <br>
            â†’ Health check port

            <br>
            â†’ Application process

            <br>
            â†’ Security Group

            <br>
            â†’ NACL

            <br>
            â†’ Route table

            <br>
            â†’ Application response code

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "If all targets are unhealthy, the load balancer has
            no healthy backend target to serve normal traffic.
            I would immediately troubleshoot the health check
            path, port, application response and network
            security configuration."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q21 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 21</div>

    <h3>Can a Load Balancer distribute traffic across multiple Availability Zones?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Yes.

        For high availability, load balancers are commonly
        configured across multiple Availability Zones.

        Backend targets can also be distributed across
        multiple Availability Zones.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Internet

        â†“

        ALB

        â†™          â†˜

        AZ-A        AZ-B

        â†“            â†“

        EC2         EC2

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Yes. AWS load balancers can be configured across
            multiple Availability Zones. This improves
            availability and helps applications continue
            operating if one Availability Zone has a problem."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q22 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 22</div>

    <h3>What is sticky session / session persistence?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Sticky sessions allow a client's requests to be routed
        to the same target for a period of time, when the
        relevant load balancer feature is enabled and supported.

        This can be useful for applications that maintain
        session state locally on a backend server.

    </p>

    <div class="important">

        ðŸ’¡ Better architecture:

        Whenever possible, design applications to be
        stateless and store session state in shared services
        such as databases or caches rather than relying on
        one specific backend instance.

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Sticky sessions keep a client's requests associated
            with the same backend target for a configured period.
            They can help legacy stateful applications, but
            stateless application design is generally preferred."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <h3>What is the difference between internet-facing and internal ALB?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­
    </span>

    <table class="compare">

        <tr>
            <th>Feature</th>
            <th>Internet-Facing</th>
            <th>Internal</th>

<!-- Q24 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 24</div>

    <h3>What is Gateway Load Balancer?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Gateway Load Balancer is designed for deploying,
        scaling and managing virtual network appliances such
        as firewalls, intrusion detection systems and other
        security appliances.

        It operates using network-level technologies suited
        for transparent appliance insertion.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            Traffic can be inspected by a security appliance
            fleet before reaching application workloads.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Gateway Load Balancer is used to deploy and scale
            third-party and custom virtual network appliances,
            such as firewalls and inspection systems."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <h2>â­ Bonus</h2>
    <div class="line"></div>

<!-- Q25 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 25</div>

    <h3>Can we use an ALB for non-HTTP traffic?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        ALB is designed for HTTP and HTTPS application traffic.

        If the application requires general TCP or UDP
        load balancing, an NLB is normally considered instead.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "ALB is designed for HTTP and HTTPS application
            traffic. For TCP or UDP network-level load balancing,
            NLB is generally the appropriate choice."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 01</div>

    <h3>
        ALB is reachable, but it returns 503. How do you troubleshoot?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A common cause is that the target group does not have
        healthy targets.

        I would check:

        <br><br>

        1. Target group health status

        <br>

        2. Health check path

        <br>

        3. Health check port

        <br>

        4. Application is running

        <br>

        5. Security group allows ALB â†’ target traffic

        <br>

        6. NACLs

        <br>

        7. Application response

        <br>

        8. Target registration

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        Client

        â†’

        ALB âœ…

        â†’

        Target Group âŒ

        â†’

        No Healthy Target

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would first check the target group's health
            status. Then I would verify the health check path,
            port, application process, target registration and
            security group and NACL rules between the ALB and
            the backend."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 02</div>

    <h3>
        Target is registered but showing unhealthy. What do you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I follow the traffic path.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 1:</strong>

        Check health check protocol.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 2:</strong>

        Check health check port.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 3:</strong>

        Check health check path.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 4:</strong>

        Test the application locally on the EC2 instance.

        <pre>
```

curl http://localhost:8080/health </pre>

```
        <strong>Step 5:</strong>

        Check the EC2 security group.

        It should allow traffic from the Load Balancer's
        security group on the application port.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Step 6:</strong>

        Check NACL and routing.

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would verify the health check configuration first,
            then test the endpoint directly from the instance.
            After that I would check the target security group,
            NACLs, routing and application logs."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

        â­â­â­â­
    </span>

        I would check the complete request path:

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        DNS

        â†’

        ALB

        â†’

        Listener

        â†’

        Target Group

        â†’

        Health Check

        â†’

        Application

    </div>

    <p class="answer">

        Specifically:

        <br><br>

        â†’ DNS record

        <br>

        â†’ ALB listener

        <br>

        â†’ Security Group

        <br>

        â†’ Target group

        <br>

        â†’ Target health

        <br>

        â†’ Application port

        <br>

        â†’ Application logs

    </p>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 04</div>

    <h3>
        You deploy a new version and suddenly all targets become unhealthy. What could be wrong?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS SCENARIO
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Possible reasons:

        <br><br>

        â†’ New application is listening on a different port

        <br>

        â†’ Health check path changed

        <br>

        â†’ Application startup takes longer

        <br>

        â†’ Security group changed

        <br>

        â†’ Environment variable/configuration issue

        <br>

        â†’ Application returns an unexpected status code

        <br>

        â†’ Deployment broke the health endpoint

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Production Approach</strong>

        <p>

            First check target health details.

            Then check application logs.

            Test the health endpoint directly.

            If necessary, rollback the deployment.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "After a deployment I would first compare the new
            version's port and health endpoint with the target
            group configuration. Then I would check application
            logs and target health details. If the new release
            is confirmed as the cause, I would rollback or shift
            traffic back to the previous healthy version."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Scenario 5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">SCENARIO 05</div>

    <h3>
        How would you design a highly available ALB architecture?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ ARCHITECTURE
    </span>

    <div class="flow">

        ðŸŒ Users

        â†“

        âš–ï¸ ALB

        â†™             â†˜

        AZ-A           AZ-B

        â†“               â†“

        App-1           App-2

        â†“               â†“

        Private Database Tier

    </div>

    <p class="answer">

        I would:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Use multiple Availability Zones

        <br>

        â†’ Place the ALB across multiple subnets/AZs

        <br>

        â†’ Run backend instances across multiple AZs

        <br>

        â†’ Configure health checks

        <br>

        â†’ Use Auto Scaling where appropriate

        <br>

        â†’ Keep application servers private where possible

        <br>

        â†’ Use security groups with least privilege

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would deploy the ALB across multiple Availability
            Zones and place backend application instances across
            multiple AZs. I would configure health checks and
            Auto Scaling, keep backend instances private where
            possible and use security groups to allow only the
            required traffic."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Load Balancer
    </strong>

    = Distributes traffic across backend targets.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        ALB
    </strong>

    = Layer 7 = HTTP/HTTPS = Host/Path routing.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        NLB
    </strong>

    = Layer 4 = TCP/UDP/TLS = High performance.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Target Group
    </strong>

    = Backend targets + health checks.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Listener
    </strong>

    = Protocol + Port + Rules.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Health Check
    </strong>

    = Determines whether target is healthy.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Path Routing
    </strong>

    = `/api` â†’ API target group.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Host Routing
    </strong>

    = `api.example.com` â†’ API target group.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        ALB + Auto Scaling
    </strong>

    = Scalable + highly available application.

    <br><br>

    <strong>
        Production Flow
    </strong>

    <h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Must Know</h2>

    <div class="line"></div>

<!-- Q1 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 01
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is Amazon S3?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Amazon S3 stands for
        <strong>Simple Storage Service</strong>.

        It is an AWS object storage service used to store
        and retrieve data from anywhere over the internet
        or through AWS services.

        S3 is designed to provide highly durable and
        scalable storage.

        Instead of storing files on a server's local disk,
        we can store them as objects inside S3.

    </p>


    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ‘¤ Application

        â†’
        
        ðŸª£ S3 Bucket

        â†’

        ðŸ“¦ Object

        â†’

        ðŸ’¾ Stored Data

    </div>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose our application allows users to upload
            profile pictures.

            Instead of storing thousands of images directly
            on an EC2 server, we can upload those images to
            S3 and store the S3 object reference in our
            application/database.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon S3 is an object storage service provided
            by AWS. It is used to store and retrieve objects
            such as files, images, videos, backups and logs.
            S3 provides scalable storage with high durability
            and supports features such as versioning,
            lifecycle management, encryption and access
            control."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>What is a bucket?</li>

            <li>What is an object?</li>

            <li>What is object storage?</li>

            <li>How is S3 different from EBS?</li>

<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 02
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is a bucket in S3?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A bucket is a container used to store objects in S3.

        Think of a bucket as the top-level storage location
        where we keep files and other objects.

        Each object belongs to a bucket.

        Bucket-level configuration can include things such
        as access controls, versioning, lifecycle rules,
        encryption settings and other policies.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            If we build an e-commerce application, we might
            have a bucket for product images and another
            bucket for application backups.

            Inside the bucket we can organize objects using
            key prefixes such as:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

product-images/
phones/
laptops/

backups/
database/
application/ </pre>

```
    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An S3 bucket is a logical container in which
            objects are stored. We can configure bucket-level
            settings such as access policies, versioning,
            lifecycle rules and encryption."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>Can we have folders inside an S3 bucket?</li>

            <li>What makes an S3 bucket name unique?</li>

            <li>Can a bucket be public?</li>

            <li>Can we change a bucket's region?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 03
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an object in S3?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CLEAR CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An object is the actual piece of data stored in S3.

        An object consists mainly of:

        <br><br>

        <strong>Data</strong> â€”
        the actual file content.

        <br>

        <strong>Key</strong> â€”
        the unique name/path used to identify the object
        within a bucket.

        <br>

        <strong>Metadata</strong> â€”
        information associated with the object.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we upload:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

profile.jpg </pre>

```
        <p>

            to:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

nandu-app-bucket/users/1001/profile.jpg </pre>

```
        <p>

            Here the file is the object and the complete
            object key identifies where it is logically
            located in the bucket.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An S3 object is the actual data stored in a
            bucket. An object has data, a key that identifies
            it, and metadata associated with it."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 04
    </div>

    <h3>
        Is S3 file storage, block storage or object storage?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        VERY COMMON CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 is an <strong>object storage</strong> service.

        This is an important distinction.

        <br><br>

        <strong>S3 â†’ Object Storage</strong>

        <br>

        <strong>EBS â†’ Block Storage</strong>

        <br>

        <strong>EFS â†’ File Storage</strong>

        <br><br>

        Object storage manages data as objects rather than
        presenting a traditional block device or shared
        filesystem.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Easy Way to Remember</strong>

        <p>

            S3 â†’ Files as objects

            <br>

            EBS â†’ Disk-like block storage for EC2

            <br>

            EFS â†’ Shared filesystem

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon S3 is object storage. EBS provides block
            storage and EFS provides managed file storage.
            The correct choice depends on the application's
            storage requirement."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 05
    </div>

    <h3>
        What are S3 storage classes?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 storage classes are different storage options
        designed for different access patterns.

        Common classes include:

        <br><br>

        <strong>S3 Standard</strong> â€”
        frequently accessed data.

        <br>

        <strong>S3 Intelligent-Tiering</strong> â€”
        useful when access patterns are unpredictable.

        <br>

        <strong>S3 Standard-IA</strong> â€”
        infrequently accessed data that still needs quick
        access.

        <br>

        <strong>S3 One Zone-IA</strong> â€”
        infrequently accessed data stored in a single
        Availability Zone.

        <br>

        <strong>S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval</strong> â€”
        archive data that still needs very fast retrieval.

        <br>

        <strong>S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval</strong> â€”
        archive data where retrieval can take longer.

        <br>

        <strong>S3 Glacier Deep Archive</strong> â€”
        very long-term archival data with infrequent access.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            A company may keep active application assets in
            S3 Standard, move older data to an appropriate
            infrequent-access or archive class through
            lifecycle rules, and use Deep Archive for
            long-term retention.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 provides multiple storage classes based on
            access frequency and retrieval requirements.
            For example, Standard is suitable for frequently
            accessed data, while Glacier classes are designed
            for archival workloads."

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>When would you use Intelligent-Tiering?</li>

            <li>Standard vs Standard-IA?</li>

            <li>What is Glacier?</li>

            <li>How can lifecycle rules help reduce storage cost?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 06
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is S3 Versioning?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 Versioning allows S3 to maintain multiple versions
        of an object in the same bucket.

        If an object is overwritten or deleted, previous
        versions can remain available depending on the
        bucket's versioning state and lifecycle configuration.

        This helps protect against accidental deletion or
        accidental overwrites.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we have:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

config.json â†’ Version 1
config.json â†’ Version 2
config.json â†’ Version 3 </pre>

```
        <p>

            If Version 3 contains a mistake, we may be able
            to recover an earlier version instead of losing
            the previous data.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 Versioning keeps multiple versions of objects
            in a bucket. It helps protect data from accidental
            deletion and overwrites and can support recovery
            of previous object versions."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 07
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an S3 Lifecycle Rule?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An S3 Lifecycle Rule automatically performs actions
        on objects based on conditions such as object age.

        We can use lifecycle rules to transition objects
        between storage classes or expire objects when they
        are no longer required.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Imagine application logs are stored in S3.

            We may configure a lifecycle policy such as:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

Day 0      â†’ S3 Standard
Day 30     â†’ Infrequent Access
Day 90     â†’ Archive
Day 365    â†’ Delete </pre>

```
        <p>

            The exact policy should be chosen based on the
            application's retention and compliance needs.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 Lifecycle Rules automate object management.
            They can transition objects to different storage
            classes or expire objects based on defined
            conditions such as age."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    </div>

    <h3>
        How do you secure an S3 bucket?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        SECURITY
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 security should be designed using multiple
        controls rather than depending on only one setting.

        Important controls include:

        <br><br>

        â€¢ IAM policies

        <br>
        â€¢ Bucket policies

        <br>
        â€¢ Block Public Access

        <br>
        â€¢ Encryption

        <br>
        â€¢ Versioning where appropriate

        <br>
        â€¢ Least-privilege permissions

        <br>
        â€¢ Logging and monitoring

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            If an application needs to upload files to S3,
            instead of making the bucket public, we can give
            the application's IAM role only the required S3
            permissions.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I secure S3 using least-privilege IAM or resource
            policies, Block Public Access, encryption,
            appropriate bucket configuration, and monitoring.
            I avoid making buckets public unless there is a
            specific justified requirement."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q9 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 09
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is the difference between IAM Policy and S3 Bucket Policy?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        HIGH PRIORITY
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        Both are authorization mechanisms, but they are
        attached differently.

        <br><br>

        <strong>IAM Policy</strong> is attached to IAM
        identities such as users, groups or roles.

        <br><br>

        <strong>Bucket Policy</strong> is a resource-based
        policy attached directly to an S3 bucket.

        Bucket policies are especially useful for defining
        access to the bucket as a resource, including
        cross-account scenarios.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Simple Example</strong>

        <p>

            An EC2 instance can use an IAM role with
            permissions to access an S3 bucket.

            Alternatively, an S3 bucket policy can explicitly
            allow a particular principal to perform
            specific actions on the bucket.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An IAM policy is an identity-based policy
            attached to an IAM principal, while an S3 bucket
            policy is a resource-based policy attached to
            the bucket. Both can participate in determining
            whether an S3 request is authorized."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q10 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 10
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is S3 encryption?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        SECURITY
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 encryption protects object data at rest.

        Common server-side encryption approaches include:

        <br><br>

        <strong>SSE-S3</strong> â€”
        encryption using S3-managed keys.

        <br>

        <strong>SSE-KMS</strong> â€”
        encryption using AWS Key Management Service keys,
        providing additional key-management and auditing
        capabilities.

        <br>

        <strong>SSE-C</strong> â€”
        the customer provides the encryption key with the
        request.

        S3 also supports client-side encryption where the
        data is encrypted before being uploaded.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            For sensitive application backups, a company may
            choose SSE-KMS so encryption is integrated with
            KMS key management and access controls.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 supports server-side encryption such as
            SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS. SSE-KMS is useful when we need
            AWS KMS-based key management and additional
            control over key usage."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q11 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 11
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is S3 Replication?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        HIGH PRIORITY
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 Replication automatically copies objects from one
        S3 bucket to another bucket according to configured
        replication rules.

        Common use cases include:

        <br><br>

        â€¢ Disaster recovery

        <br>
        â€¢ Compliance

        <br>
        â€¢ Cross-region data copies

        <br>
        â€¢ Centralized data management

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            A company has production data in one AWS Region
            and wants a copy in another Region for disaster
            recovery.

            S3 replication can be configured to copy
            eligible objects to the destination bucket.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 Replication automatically copies objects from
            a source bucket to a destination bucket according
            to replication rules. It can be used for disaster
            recovery, compliance and cross-region data
            requirements."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

    <h3>
        What is S3 Transfer Acceleration?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 Transfer Acceleration helps speed up uploads and
        downloads to S3 by using AWS edge locations and the
        AWS global network.

        It can be useful when users are geographically far
        from the S3 bucket's Region and large amounts of data
        need to be transferred.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            files to an S3 bucket located in one Region,
            Transfer Acceleration may improve transfer
            performance depending on network conditions.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 Transfer Acceleration uses AWS edge locations
            and the AWS global network to accelerate data
            transfers to and from S3, especially for
            geographically distributed users."

        </p>

    </div>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 14
    </div>

    <h3>
        What is an S3 presigned URL?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        PRACTICAL CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A presigned URL provides temporary access to a
        specific S3 object without requiring the recipient
        to have direct AWS credentials.

        The URL is generated with a defined expiration time
        and permissions based on the credentials and request
        used to generate it.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            A private S3 bucket contains a user's resume.

            Instead of making the bucket public, the
            application can generate a temporary presigned
            URL so the user can download the file.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A presigned URL provides temporary access to a
            specific S3 object. It allows us to share private
            objects without making the entire bucket public."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        QUESTION 15
    </div>

    <h3>
        Does S3 have folders like a traditional filesystem?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        CONCEPT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        S3 is an object storage service rather than a
        traditional hierarchical filesystem.

        What appears as folders in the S3 console is based
        on object key prefixes.

        For example:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

app/logs/2026/08/application.log </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        Here:

        <br>

        <strong>app/logs/2026/08/</strong>
        is a key prefix.

        <br>

        <strong>application.log</strong>
        is the object name portion.

    </p>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "S3 does not use traditional filesystem folders.
            The folder-like structure shown in the console is
            based on object key prefixes."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<div class="priority-title">

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 01
    </div>

    <h3>
        Your application gets AccessDenied when trying to upload an object to S3. What will you check?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        TROUBLESHOOTING
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would check authorization systematically.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ› ï¸ Troubleshooting Flow</strong>

        <p>

            Application

            â†’

            IAM Principal / Role

            â†’

            IAM Policy

            â†’

            Bucket Policy

            â†’

            Block Public Access / Resource Restrictions

            â†’

            S3 Object

        </p>

        <br>

        I would also verify that the request is using the
        correct bucket, Region and credentials, and check
        whether encryption with KMS introduces additional
        permissions requirements.

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "For an S3 AccessDenied error, I first identify
            which IAM principal is making the request.
            Then I check its IAM permissions, the bucket
            policy, public-access settings and any applicable
            resource restrictions. If KMS encryption is
            involved, I also verify the required KMS
            permissions."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 02
    </div>

    <h3>
        A developer accidentally deleted an important S3 object. How can you recover it?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        PRODUCTION SCENARIO
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        If S3 Versioning was enabled before the deletion,
        previous versions of the object may still be
        available.

        In a versioned bucket, a normal deletion can create
        a delete marker rather than immediately removing all
        previous versions.

        The exact recovery approach depends on the bucket's
        versioning state and lifecycle configuration.

    </p>


    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Production bucket has versioning enabled.

            Developer deletes:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

production-config.json </pre>

```
        <p>

            We inspect the object's versions, identify the
            required previous version and restore/recover it
            according to the application's recovery procedure.

        </p>

    </div>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "If S3 Versioning was enabled, I would check the
            object's previous versions and delete markers.
            We can use the previous version to recover the
            required data."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">
        SCENARIO 03
    </div>

    <h3>
        Your S3 bucket contains sensitive company data. The team asks you to make the bucket public for easier access. What would you do?
    </h3>

    <span class="label">
        SECURITY SCENARIO
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        I would not make a sensitive bucket public simply for
        convenience.

        First I would understand the actual access
        requirement.

        If users need temporary access, a presigned URL may
        be appropriate.

        If an application needs access, an IAM role with
        least-privilege permissions is usually preferable.

        If a public website is genuinely required, I would
        separate public assets from sensitive data and design
        the access model accordingly.

    </p>


    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "I would avoid making sensitive S3 data publicly
            accessible. I would first identify who needs
            access and provide the minimum required
            permissions using IAM roles, bucket policies or
            temporary presigned URLs. I would follow the
            principle of least privilege."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 01</div>

    <h3>What is Amazon VPC?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        VPC stands for <strong>Virtual Private Cloud</strong>.

        Amazon VPC allows us to create a logically isolated
        virtual network inside AWS.

        Within a VPC, we can control:

        <br><br>

        â†’ IP address ranges

        <br>
        â†’ Subnets

        <br>
        â†’ Route tables

        <br>
        â†’ Internet connectivity

        <br>
        â†’ Network security

        <br>
        â†’ Private connectivity

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        ðŸŒ VPC

        â†’

        ðŸ§© Subnets

        â†’

        ðŸ›£ï¸ Route Tables

        â†’

        ðŸ” Security

        â†’

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ Resources

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Real-Time Example</strong>

        <p>

            Suppose we are deploying an application on EC2.

            Instead of placing servers randomly on the AWS
            network, we create a VPC and decide which servers
            should be public and which should remain private.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Amazon VPC is a logically isolated virtual network
            in AWS where we can define IP ranges, subnets,
            routing and network security for our resources."

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Possible Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>

            <li>What is a route table?</li>
            <li>What is an Internet Gateway?</li>

        </ul>

    </div>

<!-- Q2 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 02</div>

    <h3>What is a CIDR block?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        CIDR stands for <strong>Classless Inter-Domain Routing</strong>.

        CIDR notation represents an IP address range using
        an address followed by a prefix length.

        Example:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

10.0.0.0/16 </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        The <strong>/16</strong> indicates the network prefix
        length.

        A larger prefix number means a smaller address range.

        For example:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

10.0.0.0/16
10.0.1.0/24
10.0.2.0/24 </pre>

```
    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            A common VPC design might use:

            <br><br>

            VPC â†’ 10.0.0.0/16

            <br>

            Public subnet â†’ 10.0.1.0/24

            <br>

            Private subnet â†’ 10.0.2.0/24

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "CIDR is a notation used to define an IP address
            range. In a VPC, we use CIDR blocks to define the
            VPC and subnet address ranges."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q3 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 03</div>

    <h3>What is a subnet?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A subnet is a smaller IP address range inside a VPC.

        Subnets allow us to divide a VPC into separate network
        segments.

        Each subnet belongs to one Availability Zone.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        VPC: 10.0.0.0/16

        <br><br>

        â”œâ”€â”€ Public Subnet â†’ 10.0.1.0/24

        <br>

        â”œâ”€â”€ Public Subnet â†’ 10.0.2.0/24

        <br>

        â”œâ”€â”€ Private Subnet â†’ 10.0.11.0/24

        <br>

        â””â”€â”€ Private Subnet â†’ 10.0.12.0/24

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Why use subnets?</strong>

        <p>

            We can put internet-facing load balancers in public
            subnets and application servers in private subnets.

            This creates network separation.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A subnet is a logical subdivision of a VPC's IP
            address range. Each subnet is associated with one
            Availability Zone and can be used to separate
            workloads based on network requirements."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q4 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 04</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between a public subnet and a private subnet?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        The key difference is the subnet's routing configuration.

        A subnet is considered <strong>public</strong> when its
        route table has a route to an Internet Gateway.

        A subnet is considered <strong>private</strong> when it
        does not have a direct route to an Internet Gateway.

        A private subnet can still have outbound internet access
        through a NAT Gateway when appropriately configured.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        PUBLIC

        <br>

        EC2

        â†’

        Route Table

        â†’

        Internet Gateway

        â†’

        ðŸŒ Internet

        <br><br>

        PRIVATE

        <br>

        EC2

        â†’

        Route Table

        â†’

        NAT Gateway

        â†’

        Internet Gateway

        â†’

        ðŸŒ Internet

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Production Example</strong>

        <p>

            Public subnet:

            <br>
            â†’ Application Load Balancer

            <br><br>

            Private subnet:

            <br>
            â†’ Application servers

            <br>
            â†’ Databases

            <br>
            â†’ Internal services

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway,
            allowing supported resources to communicate with the
            internet when their other network configuration also
            permits it. A private subnet does not have a direct
            route to an Internet Gateway. It can use a NAT Gateway
            for outbound internet access."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q5 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 05</div>

    <h3>What is an Internet Gateway?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        An Internet Gateway, or <strong>IGW</strong>, is a
        VPC component that provides a path between a VPC and
        the internet.

        For an IPv4 public subnet, the route table normally
        contains a default route:

    </p>

    <pre>
```

0.0.0.0/0 â†’ Internet Gateway </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        The subnet alone is not enough. The instance also needs
        appropriate addressing and security configuration.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Simple Example</strong>

        <p>

            EC2 in public subnet

            <br>

            â†’ route table has 0.0.0.0/0 to IGW

            <br>

            â†’ EC2 has a public IPv4 address

            <br>

            â†’ security rules allow required traffic

            <br>

            â†’ internet communication can work.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "An Internet Gateway is a VPC component that enables
            communication between a VPC and the internet. A
            public subnet typically has a default route pointing
            to the Internet Gateway."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q6 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 06</div>

    <h3>What is a NAT Gateway?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        NAT stands for <strong>Network Address Translation</strong>.

        A NAT Gateway allows resources in private subnets to
        initiate outbound connections to the internet without
        requiring those resources to have public IP addresses.

        It does not provide unsolicited inbound internet access
        to the private resources.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ Private EC2

        â†’

        ðŸ›£ï¸ Private Route Table

        â†’

        NAT Gateway

        â†’

        Internet Gateway

        â†’

        ðŸŒ Internet

    </div>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ DevOps Example</strong>

        <p>

            A private EC2 instance needs to download security
            updates or install packages.

            Instead of giving the EC2 instance a public IP,
            we can route outbound traffic through a NAT Gateway.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A NAT Gateway allows resources in private subnets
            to initiate outbound internet connections while
            keeping those resources without public IP addresses.
            It is deployed in a public subnet and uses an
            Elastic IP for IPv4 internet connectivity."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q7 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 07</div>

    <h3>What is a Route Table?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        A route table contains rules that determine where network
        traffic should be sent.

        Each route has:

        <br><br>

        â†’ Destination

        <br>
        â†’ Target

    </p>

    <pre>
```

Destination       Target

10.0.0.0/16       local
0.0.0.0/0         igw-xxxxxxxx </pre>

```
    <p class="answer">

        The <strong>local</strong> route allows communication
        within the VPC's CIDR.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

        <p>

            If a public subnet needs internet connectivity,
            its route table can contain:

        </p>

        <pre>
```

0.0.0.0/0 â†’ Internet Gateway </pre>

```
    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A route table contains routing rules that determine
            where traffic from a subnet should be sent. For
            example, a public subnet can have a default route
            to an Internet Gateway."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q8 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 08</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between Security Group and NACL?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ EXTREMELY IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <div class="flow">

        SECURITY GROUP

        â†’

        ðŸ–¥ï¸ ENI / Resource

        <br><br>

        NACL

        â†’

        ðŸ§© Subnet

    </div>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>Security Group:</strong>

        <br>
        â†’ Works at the resource/network-interface level

        <br>
        â†’ Stateful

        <br>
        â†’ Supports allow rules

        <br>
        â†’ Commonly used for instance-level access control

        <br><br>

        <strong>Network ACL:</strong>

        <br>
        â†’ Works at subnet boundary

        <br>
        â†’ Stateless

        <br>
        â†’ Supports allow and deny rules

        <br>
        â†’ Rules are evaluated in order

    </p>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "Security Groups are stateful virtual firewalls
            associated with network interfaces and support
            allow rules. Network ACLs operate at the subnet
            level, are stateless, support both allow and deny
            rules, and are evaluated in rule order."

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="followup">

        <strong>ðŸ”Ž Very Common Follow-ups</strong>

        <ul>
            <li>Which one is stateful?</li>
            <li>Which one supports deny rules?</li>
            <li>Where does NACL work?</li>
            <li>Where does Security Group work?</li>
            <li>Which is evaluated first?</li>
        </ul>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q9 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 09</div>

    <h3>What is the difference between a default VPC and a custom VPC?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        AWS accounts can have a default VPC in supported Regions.

        AWS creates common networking components for the default
        VPC, making it convenient for initial workloads.

        A custom VPC is designed by us according to application
        requirements.

    </p>

    <div class="example">

        <strong>ðŸ’¡ Production Example</strong>

        <p>

            For a production environment, we normally design
            our own CIDR ranges, public and private subnets,
            routing, NAT, security and connectivity rather than
            depending on the default VPC design.

        </p>

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "A default VPC is an AWS-provided VPC with common
            networking configuration for convenience. A custom
            VPC is designed and configured according to the
            application's networking and security requirements."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- Q10 -->

<article class="question">

    <div class="question-number">QUESTION 10</div>

    <h3>Can a subnet span multiple Availability Zones?</h3>

    <span class="label">
        â­â­â­â­â­ TRICK QUESTION
    </span>

    <p class="answer">

        <strong>No.</strong>

        An AWS subnet is associated with exactly one
        Availability Zone.

        A VPC can span multiple Availability Zones, but each
        individual subnet belongs to one AZ.

    </p>

    <div class="flow">

        VPC

        <br>

        â”œâ”€â”€ AZ-A â†’ Subnet-A

        <br>

        â””â”€â”€ AZ-B â†’ Subnet-B

    </div>

    <div class="interview-answer">

        <strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

        <p>

            "No. A subnet is associated with one Availability
            Zone. To build a multi-AZ architecture, we create
            separate subnets in multiple Availability Zones."

        </p>

    </div>

</article>


<!-- =====================================================
     â­â­â­â­
