<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 11</div>

<h3>What is storage replication?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Replication means maintaining copies of data in multiple
locations or storage systems.

It can improve resilience and availability and may support
disaster recovery depending on the architecture.

</p>

<div class="flow">

Original Data

â†“

Replication

â†™     â†“     â†˜

Copy A   Copy B   Copy C

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>

"Storage replication maintains copies of data across multiple
storage locations or systems. It can improve resilience and
support availability or disaster recovery requirements."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 12</div>

<h3>What is data redundancy?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Redundancy means maintaining additional copies or components so
that the system can continue operating or recover when one
component fails.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>

Instead of relying on a single copy of important data, an
architecture may maintain additional copies according to its
recovery requirements.

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 13</div>

<h3>What are storage classes?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Storage classes are different storage tiers designed for
different access patterns, performance requirements and cost
requirements.

Frequently accessed data can use a storage tier optimized for
frequent access, while infrequently accessed or archival data
can use lower-cost tiers with different retrieval characteristics.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ AWS S3 Example</strong>

<p>

Frequently accessed data

â†’ Standard storage

<br><br>

Infrequently accessed data

â†’ Infrequent Access class

<br><br>

Long-term archive

â†’ Glacier storage classes

</p>

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>

"Storage classes provide different storage tiers optimized for
different access patterns and cost requirements. Frequently
accessed data can use standard storage, while infrequently
accessed or archival data can use lower-cost tiers."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 14</div>

<h3>How do you choose the right storage type?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ SCENARIO</span>

<p class="answer">

The choice depends on:

<br><br>

â†’ Type of data

<br>
â†’ Access pattern

<br>
â†’ Performance requirements

<br>
â†’ Sharing requirements

<br>
â†’ Durability and availability requirements

<br>
â†’ Cost

<br>
â†’ Recovery requirements

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>

Images and videos

â†’ Object Storage

<br><br>

Database disk

â†’ Block Storage

<br><br>

Shared application files

â†’ File Storage

<br><br>

Long-term archive

â†’ Archive-oriented storage tier

</p>

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>

"I choose storage based on the workload rather than choosing
one storage type for everything. I consider data type, access
pattern, performance, sharing requirements, durability,
availability, recovery and cost."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 15</div>

<h3>What is ephemeral storage?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Ephemeral storage is temporary storage whose lifetime is tied to
the underlying compute resource or its lifecycle, depending on
the service.

It should not be treated as the primary location for data that
must survive resource replacement.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>

Temporary cache

â†’ Ephemeral storage can be suitable.

<br><br>

Important customer database

â†’ Use persistent storage and backups.

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 16</div>

<h3>What is persistent storage?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Persistent storage is designed to preserve data beyond the
lifecycle of a particular compute process or instance, depending
on the service and configuration.

It is used when data must survive compute replacement or restart.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ Example</strong>

<p>

Application server is replaced.

<br>

Persistent storage keeps important application data available
according to the storage configuration.

</p>

</div>

</article>

<div class="line"></div>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 17</div>

<h3>What is data lifecycle management?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Lifecycle management automatically moves data between storage
classes or deletes data according to predefined policies.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ Example</strong>

<p>

New data

â†“

Frequently accessed storage

â†“

After 30 days

â†“

Infrequent Access

â†“

After 180 days

â†“

Archive

â†“

After retention period

â†“

Delete

</p>

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>

"Lifecycle management automates storage transitions and
retention actions based on rules such as object age or access
patterns. It helps optimize storage cost and manage data
retention."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 18</div>

<h3>What is data archiving?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Archiving means moving data that is rarely accessed into
long-term storage designed to reduce storage cost.

Archived data may have higher retrieval latency or retrieval
cost depending on the storage tier.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>

Company logs from five years ago may rarely be accessed.

Instead of keeping them in expensive frequently accessed
storage, the organization can move them to an archive tier.

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 19</div>

<h3>What is encryption at rest?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ SECURITY FAVORITE</span>

<p class="answer">

Encryption at rest protects stored data by encrypting it while it
is stored on disks or storage systems.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>

Database data

â†“

Encrypted Storage

â†“

Even if someone gains access to the underlying storage medium,
the stored data is protected by encryption.

</p>

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>

"Encryption at rest protects stored data by encrypting it on the
storage system. It is an important security control for
protecting sensitive information."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 20</div>

<h3>What is encryption in transit?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Encryption in transit protects data while it is moving between
systems or across a network.

TLS is commonly used to secure network communication.

</p>

<div class="important">

<strong>ðŸ§  Easy Memory</strong>

<br><br>

At Rest â†’ Data is stored.

<br>

In Transit â†’ Data is moving.

</div>

</article>

<div class="line"></div>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 21</div>

<h3>What is storage IOPS?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

IOPS stands for Input/Output Operations Per Second.

It represents the number of input/output operations a storage
system can perform per second.

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>

Database workloads with many small read/write operations may
require high IOPS.

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question">

<div class="question-number">QUESTION 22</div>

<h3>What is storage throughput?</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Storage throughput is the amount of data that can be transferred
between storage and a system over a period of time.

</p>

<div class="important">

<strong>ðŸ§  IOPS vs Throughput</strong>

<br><br>

IOPS â†’ Number of operations.

<br>

Throughput â†’ Amount of data transferred.

</div>

</article>

<article class="question scenario">

<div class="question-number">SCENARIO 01</div>

<h3>
Where would you store images uploaded by users?
</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

I would generally use object storage because images are

</p>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>

"I would store user-uploaded images in object storage such as
Amazon S3 because it is designed for scalable storage of
unstructured objects. I can also use lifecycle policies,
versioning and appropriate access controls based on the
requirements."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question scenario">

<div class="question-number">SCENARIO 02</div>

<h3>
Where would you store an EC2 operating system disk?
</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

Block storage is the appropriate model because an operating
system requires disk-like block-level storage.

</p>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Answer</strong>

<p>

"I would use block storage such as Amazon EBS for an EC2
operating system disk because the instance requires persistent
disk-like storage."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question scenario">

<div class="question-number">SCENARIO 03</div>

<h3>
Three application servers need access to the same files. What storage would you choose?
</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

I would use shared file storage.

</p>

<div class="flow">

Application Server 1 â”€â”

Application Server 2 â”€â”¼â†’ Shared File Storage

Application Server 3 â”€â”˜

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Answer</strong>

<p>

"I would use a shared file-storage service such as Amazon EFS
when multiple application servers need concurrent access to the
same file system."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question scenario">

<div class="question-number">SCENARIO 04</div>

<h3>
Your storage cost is increasing rapidly. How would you optimize it?
</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ COST OPTIMIZATION</span>

<p class="answer">

I would first understand the data access pattern and identify
unused, old and infrequently accessed data.

Then I would:

<br><br>

â†’ Use appropriate storage classes

<br>
â†’ Configure lifecycle policies

<br>
â†’ Archive old data

<br>
â†’ Delete unnecessary data according to retention requirements

<br>
â†’ Review snapshots and backups

<br>
â†’ Monitor storage growth

</p>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>

"I would analyze storage usage and access patterns, move
infrequently accessed data to lower-cost storage tiers, automate
transitions with lifecycle policies, remove unnecessary data
according to retention requirements, and review backup and
snapshot retention."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question scenario">

<div class="question-number">SCENARIO 05</div>

<h3>
A production database server is terminated. How will you recover the data?
</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­â­ DISASTER RECOVERY</span>

<p class="answer">

The recovery method depends on the architecture, but I would
use persistent storage, backups or snapshots that were configured
before the failure.

</p>

<div class="flow">

Production Database

â†“

Automated Backup / Snapshot

â†“

Failure

â†“

Restore

â†“

New Database Environment

</div>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>

"I would restore the database using the available persistent
storage, snapshots or backups according to the recovery
procedure. This is why backup schedules, retention policies and
tested recovery procedures are important for production
systems."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="question scenario">

<div class="question-number">SCENARIO 06</div>

<h3>
You need to store five years of rarely accessed logs. What would you consider?
</h3>

<span class="label">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p class="answer">

I would consider an archive-oriented storage tier with lifecycle
management.

The important factors are:

<br><br>

â†’ Retention requirement

<br>
â†’ Access frequency

<br>
â†’ Retrieval time

<br>
â†’ Retrieval cost

<br>
â†’ Compliance requirements

<br>
â†’ Storage cost

</p>

<div class="interview-answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Answer</strong>

<p>

"For long-term, rarely accessed logs, I would consider an
archive storage tier and use lifecycle policies to automatically
transition logs after the required retention period while
considering retrieval requirements."

</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- QUICK FIRE -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<div class="priority-title">
<h2>ðŸ§  Quick-Fire Interview Questions</h2>
<div class="line"></div>
</div>

<article class="question">

<h3>Rapid Revision</h3>

<p class="answer">

<strong>Q:</strong> What is cloud storage?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Provider-managed storage delivered through cloud
services.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Three major storage types?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Object, Block and File.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Object storage?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Stores data as objects; ideal for unstructured data.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Block storage?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Disk-like storage for compute workloads.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> File storage?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Shared hierarchical file system.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> AWS object storage example?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Amazon S3.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> AWS block storage example?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Amazon EBS.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> AWS file storage example?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Amazon EFS.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Durability?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Protection of data from loss over time.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Availability?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> How consistently the service can be accessed.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Backup?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Separate copy used for recovery.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Snapshot?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Point-in-time representation of storage.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Replication?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Maintaining copies of data.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Storage class?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Storage tier optimized for an access pattern and cost.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Lifecycle management?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Automatically moves or deletes data based on policies.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Encryption at rest?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Protecting stored data through encryption.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Encryption in transit?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Protecting data while it moves across networks.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> IOPS?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Input/output operations per second.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Throughput?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Amount of data transferred over a period.

</p>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- WHAT IS LINUX -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>What is Linux?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux is an open-source operating system kernel that is used as
the foundation of many operating systems and server environments.
</p>

<p>
In practical usage, the term "Linux" commonly refers to Linux
distributions that include the Linux kernel together with system
utilities, libraries and applications.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Simple Example</strong>

<p>
When you launch an AWS EC2 instance using Amazon Linux or Ubuntu,
you are running a Linux-based operating system.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux is an open-source operating system kernel. Linux-based
distributions combine the kernel with system utilities,
libraries and applications to provide a complete operating
system environment. Linux is widely used for servers, cloud
infrastructure and DevOps."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- WHY LINUX -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>Why is Linux important in DevOps?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
Linux is widely used in cloud and server environments, making
Linux administration an important DevOps skill.
</p>

<p>

â†’ AWS EC2 servers frequently run Linux

<br>
â†’ Docker containers commonly use Linux-based environments

<br>
â†’ Kubernetes nodes commonly run Linux

<br>
â†’ CI/CD tools are commonly deployed on Linux

<br>
â†’ Web servers and application servers commonly use Linux

<br>
â†’ Shell scripting is widely used for automation

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time DevOps Example</strong>

<p>
A DevOps engineer may connect to an EC2 Linux server through SSH,
check CPU usage, inspect logs, restart a service and troubleshoot
network connectivity.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux is important in DevOps because many cloud servers,
containers, CI/CD systems and production workloads run on Linux.
It also provides powerful command-line tools and scripting
capabilities for automation and troubleshooting."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- KERNEL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>

<h2>What is the Linux Kernel?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The kernel is the core component of the operating system.
It manages communication between hardware and software and
controls important system resources.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Applications

â†“

Shell / System Libraries

â†“

<strong>Linux Kernel</strong>

â†“

CPU â€¢ Memory â€¢ Disk â€¢ Network â€¢ Hardware

</div>

<h3>Major responsibilities of the Kernel</h3>

<p>

â†’ Process management

<br>
â†’ Memory management

<br>
â†’ Device management

<br>
â†’ File system management

<br>
â†’ Networking

<br>
â†’ Security and access control

</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"The Linux kernel is the core of the operating system. It
manages system resources such as CPU, memory, devices, storage
and networking and provides the interface between applications
and hardware."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SHELL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>

<h2>What is a Shell?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A shell is a command-line interface that allows users to interact
with the operating system by executing commands.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User

â†“

Shell

â†“

Kernel

â†“

Hardware / System Resources

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<p>
When you type:

</p>

<pre>ls
pwd
cd /var/log
systemctl status nginx</pre>

<p>
the shell interprets the commands and requests the operating
system to perform the required operations.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A shell is a command-line interface between the user and the
operating system. It interprets user commands and communicates
with the operating system to execute them."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- BASH -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>

<h2>What is Bash?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Bash stands for Bourne Again Shell. It is one of the most widely
used shells in Linux environments.
</p>

<p>
Bash can execute commands interactively and can also run shell
scripts for automation.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<pre>#!/bin/bash

echo "Hello DevOps"</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Bash is a widely used Linux shell and scripting language. It
allows users to execute commands interactively and automate tasks
using shell scripts."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- DISTRIBUTIONS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>

<h2>What is a Linux Distribution?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A Linux distribution is a complete operating system built around
the Linux kernel along with system utilities, libraries,
package-management tools and applications.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Distribution</th>
<th>Common Usage</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Ubuntu</td>
<td>Cloud, servers, development</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Amazon Linux</td>
<td>AWS environments</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>RHEL</td>
<td>Enterprise environments</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CentOS / Rocky / AlmaLinux</td>
<td>Server environments</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Debian</td>
<td>Servers and general Linux usage</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A Linux distribution is a complete operating system built using
the Linux kernel together with system utilities, libraries,
package managers and other software. Examples include Ubuntu,
Amazon Linux and Red Hat Enterprise Linux."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ROOT -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>

<h2>What is the Root User?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
The root user is the Linux superuser with extensive privileges
over the system.
</p>

<p>
The root user can perform administrative operations such as
installing software, modifying system configuration and changing
permissions.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
Because root has extensive privileges, administrative access
should be used carefully.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Root is the Linux superuser with extensive administrative
privileges. Because unrestricted root access can be dangerous,
administrative operations should be performed carefully and
preferably through controlled privilege escalation."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SUDO -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>

<h2>What is sudo?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
<code>sudo</code> allows an authorized user to execute a command
with elevated privileges.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<pre>sudo apt update

sudo systemctl restart nginx</pre>

</div>

<p>
Instead of logging in directly as root, an administrator can
grant controlled administrative privileges to users.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"sudo allows an authorized user to execute specific commands with
elevated privileges without directly logging in as the root
user."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- FILESYSTEM -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>

<h2>What is the Linux File System?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux organizes files and directories in a hierarchical structure
starting from the root directory represented by <code>/</code>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

/

â”œâ”€â”€ bin

â”œâ”€â”€ etc

â”œâ”€â”€ home

â”œâ”€â”€ var

â”œâ”€â”€ tmp

â”œâ”€â”€ usr

â”œâ”€â”€ opt

â””â”€â”€ root

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Directory</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/</td>
<td>Root of the filesystem</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/home</td>
<td>User home directories</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/etc</td>
<td>System configuration files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/var</td>
<td>Variable data such as logs</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/tmp</td>
<td>Temporary files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/usr</td>
<td>User-space programs and resources</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/opt</td>
<td>Optional/additional application software</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/root</td>
<td>Home directory of the root user</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux uses a hierarchical filesystem that starts at the root
directory /. Important directories include /etc for configuration,
/var for variable data and logs, /home for user directories and
/tmp for temporary files."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ABSOLUTE RELATIVE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 10</div>

<h2>Absolute Path vs Relative Path</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Absolute Path</th>
<th>Relative Path</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Starts from the root directory</td>
<td>Starts from the current directory</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: /var/log/app.log</td>
<td>Example: logs/app.log</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Complete location</td>
<td>Location relative to current directory</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<pre>pwd
/home/nandu

cd /var/log</pre>

<p>
<code>/var/log</code> is an absolute path.

If the current directory is <code>/home/nandu</code>:

</p>

<pre>cd projects</pre>

<p>
<code>projects</code> is a relative path.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>

<h2>CLI vs GUI</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>CLI</th>
<th>GUI</th>
</tr>

</p>

<div class="number">REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<div class="number">QUICK INTERVIEW</div>

<h2>â­â­â­ Quick Questions</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is Linux?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> An open-source kernel used as the foundation
of many operating systems.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is the kernel?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Core component that manages system resources
and communicates with hardware.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a shell?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Command-line interface used to interact with
the operating system.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is Bash?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A widely used Linux shell and scripting
language.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a Linux distribution?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A complete OS built around the Linux kernel
with utilities and software.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is root?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Linux superuser with extensive privileges.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is sudo?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Runs authorized commands with elevated
privileges.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is /etc?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Common location for system configuration
files.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is /var?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Stores variable data such as logs.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is /home?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Contains users' home directories.

</p>

<h2>ls â€” List Files and Directories</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

The <code>ls</code> command lists files and directories in the

<th>Purpose</th>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<h2>cp â€” Copy Files and Directories</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>cp</code> command copies files or directories from one

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<pre>cp app.txt backup.txt

<p>
The <code>-r</code> option is used to copy directories

</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"The cp command copies files and directories. For directories,
the recursive option -r is commonly used."
</p>

<h2>mv â€” Move or Rename</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>mv</code> command is used to move files or directories
and can also be used to rename them.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<pre>mv app.txt /tmp/

mv project /opt/project</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"The mv command is used to move files or directories. It can also
rename a file or directory when the source and destination are in
the same location."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- RM -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 08</div>

<h2>rm â€” Remove Files and Directories</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>rm</code> command removes files and directories.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<pre>rm app.txt

rm -r project

rm -f app.txt

rm -rf project</pre>

<p>
Be extremely careful with <code>rm -rf</code> because it can
recursively and forcefully delete data.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"The rm command removes files and directories. The -r option
allows recursive deletion of directories, while -f forces
deletion without interactive confirmation. It should be used
carefully."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- FIND -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 09</div>

<h2>find â€” Search Files and Directories</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
The <code>find</code> command searches for files and directories
based on conditions such as name, type, size and modification
time.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<pre>find /var/log -name "*.log"

find /home -name "app.txt"

find . -type f

find . -type d

find /tmp -type f -size +100M</pre>

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Option</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>-name</code></td>
<td>Search by name</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>-type f</code></td>
<td>Search files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>-type d</code></td>
<td>Search directories</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>-size</code></td>
<td>Search based on file size</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time DevOps Example</strong>

<p>
If a production server has many log files and you need to find
all <code>.log</code> files under <code>/var/log</code>:
</p>

<pre>find /var/log -type f -name "*.log"</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"find is a powerful Linux command used to search files and
directories based on conditions such as name, type and size. It
is frequently useful during server troubleshooting."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
In Linux, files and directories whose names begin with a dot

</p>

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<div class="answer">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ Create a Project Directory Structure</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS PRACTICAL</span>

<p>
Suppose you need to create a basic application structure on a
Linux server.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Step 4 â€” Verify</strong>

<strong>Step 5 â€” Create backup</strong>

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ File or Directory Not Found</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>

</p>

<p>

<br>
â†’ Incorrect filename

<br>
â†’ Case-sensitive filename

<br>
â†’ File was moved

<br>
â†’ File was deleted

</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>
"First I would check the current working directory using pwd and
list its contents using ls -la. If the file is not there, I would
use find to locate it and verify the exact filename and path."
</p>

<h1>Linux <span>Logs, Cron & Environment</span></h1>

<!-- LOGS -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>
<h2>What are Linux Logs?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux logs record events generated by the operating system,
services, applications and other components. They are essential
for troubleshooting.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Problem
<br>â†“
<br>Check Status
<br>â†“
<br>Check Logs
<br>â†“
<br>Identify Error
<br>â†“
<br>Fix Root Cause
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"Linux logs provide information about system and application
events. I use them to investigate failures, authentication
problems, service issues and unexpected behavior."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>
<h2>Where are Linux Logs stored?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Traditional Linux systems commonly store many logs under:
</p>

<pre>/var/log/</pre>

<p>
Examples you may encounter include:
</p>

<pre>
/var/log/syslog
/var/log/messages
/var/log/auth.log
/var/log/secure
/var/log/kern.log
</pre>

<div class="note">
<strong>Important:</strong>
<p>
Exact log files depend on the Linux distribution and its logging
configuration. Modern systems may rely heavily on systemd's
journal.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>
<h2>How do you read a log file?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h3>Read entire file</h3>
<pre>cat /var/log/syslog</pre>

<h3>Read page by page</h3>
<pre>less /var/log/syslog</pre>

<h3>Show last lines</h3>
<pre>tail /var/log/syslog</pre>

<h3>Follow new log entries</h3>
<pre>tail -f /var/log/syslog</pre>

<h3>Search inside a log</h3>
<pre>grep "error" /var/log/syslog</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸ”¥ DevOps Favorite</strong>
<p>
<code>tail -f</code> is extremely useful when watching an application
log while reproducing a problem.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>
<h2>What is journalctl?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>journalctl</code> is used to query and inspect logs collected by
systemd's journal.
</p>

<pre>journalctl</pre>

<h3>View logs for a service</h3>
<pre>journalctl -u nginx</pre>

<h3>Follow service logs</h3>
<pre>journalctl -u nginx -f</pre>

<h3>Show recent logs</h3>
<pre>journalctl --since "1 hour ago"</pre>

<h3>Show current boot logs</h3>
<pre>journalctl -b</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"I use journalctl to inspect systemd journal logs, especially when
troubleshooting services managed by systemd."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>
<h2>What is dmesg?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>dmesg</code> displays messages from the kernel ring buffer and
can help investigate kernel and hardware-related events.
</p>

<pre>dmesg</pre>

<p>
For readable timestamps on systems supporting the option:
</p>

<pre>dmesg -T</pre>

<div class="note">
<strong>Use cases:</strong>
<p>
Hardware detection, driver messages, kernel events and some
boot/device troubleshooting.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>
<h2>How do you troubleshoot a failed service?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME</span>

<p>
Suppose nginx is not working.
</p>

<div class="flow">
systemctl status
<br>â†“
<br>journalctl
<br>â†“
<br>Configuration Check
<br>â†“
<br>Port Check
<br>â†“
<br>Fix
<br>â†“
<br>Restart
</div>

<pre>
systemctl status nginx
journalctl -u nginx --no-pager
ss -lntp
</pre>

<p>
Then validate the configuration if the service supports a config
test command before restarting.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"I first check the service status, then inspect its logs, verify
configuration and dependencies, check whether the expected port is
available, fix the root cause and restart the service."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- CRON -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>
<h2>What is Cron?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Cron is a time-based job scheduling mechanism commonly used to run
commands or scripts automatically at specified times.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Schedule
<br>â†“
<br>Cron
<br>â†“
<br>Command / Script
<br>â†“
<br>Automatic Execution
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"Cron is used to schedule recurring tasks such as backups, cleanup
scripts, reports and maintenance jobs."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>
<h2>What is Crontab?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A crontab contains scheduled commands for a user.
</p>

<h3>Open current user's crontab</h3>
<pre>crontab -e</pre>

<h3>List current user's cron jobs</h3>
<pre>crontab -l</pre>

<h3>Remove current user's crontab</h3>
<pre>crontab -r</pre>

<div class="warning">
<strong>âš ï¸ Careful:</strong>
<p>
<code>crontab -r</code> removes the user's crontab. Do not run it
unless you intentionally want to remove the scheduled jobs.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>
<h2>Crontab Syntax</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<pre>
* * * * * command
â”‚ â”‚ â”‚ â”‚ â”‚
â”‚ â”‚ â”‚ â”‚ â””â”€â”€ Day of week
â”‚ â”‚ â”‚ â””â”€â”€â”€â”€ Month
â”‚ â”‚ â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Day of month
â”‚ â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Hour
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Minute
</pre>

<table>
<tr><th>Position</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>Minute</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>Hour</td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>Day of month</td></tr>
<tr><td>4</td><td>Month</td></tr>
<tr><td>5</td><td>Day of week</td></tr>
</table>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 10</div>
<h2>Common Cron Examples</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h3>Every minute</h3>
<pre>* * * * * /path/to/script.sh</pre>

<h3>Every day at midnight</h3>
<pre>0 0 * * * /path/to/script.sh</pre>

<h3>Every day at 2:30 AM</h3>
<pre>30 2 * * * /path/to/script.sh</pre>

<h3>Every Sunday at 3:00 AM</h3>
<pre>0 3 * * 0 /path/to/script.sh</pre>

<h3>Every 5 minutes</h3>
<pre>*/5 * * * * /path/to/script.sh</pre>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 11</div>
<h2>Important Cron Pitfall</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS</span>

<p>
Cron runs with a limited environment compared with an interactive
shell. A script that works manually may fail under cron because
commands, paths or environment variables are different.
</p>

<div class="example">
<strong>Better:</strong>
<pre>/usr/bin/python3 /opt/scripts/backup.py</pre>

<p>
Using an explicit executable path can make scheduled jobs more
predictable.
</p>
</div>

<p>
Always use absolute paths where appropriate and capture output/error
logs for important jobs.
</p>
</article>

<!-- ENVIRONMENT -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>
<h2>What is an Environment Variable?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
An environment variable is a named value made available to a
process through its environment.
</p>

<pre>echo $HOME</pre>

<p>
Common examples:
</p>

<pre>
HOME
PATH
USER
SHELL
PWD
LANG
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"Environment variables provide configuration values to processes
without requiring those values to be hard-coded into the program."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>
<h2>How do you view Environment Variables?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h3>Print one variable</h3>
<pre>echo $PATH</pre>

<h3>Show exported environment</h3>
<pre>env</pre>

<h3>Another commonly used command</h3>
<pre>printenv</pre>

<h3>Inspect shell variables and functions too</h3>
<pre>set</pre>

<div class="note">
<strong>Remember:</strong>
<p>
<code>env</code> and <code>printenv</code> primarily show environment
variables, while <code>set</code> can include shell variables and
functions.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 14</div>
<h2>How do you create an Environment Variable?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h3>Shell variable</h3>
<pre>APP_ENV=production</pre>

<h3>Export it to child processes</h3>
<pre>export APP_ENV=production</pre>

<h3>Verify</h3>
<pre>echo $APP_ENV</pre>

<div class="warning">
<strong>Important:</strong>
<p>
A shell variable does not automatically become part of the
environment inherited by child processes. <code>export</code> makes
it an exported environment variable.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>
<h2>What is PATH?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>PATH</code> is a colon-separated list of directories that the
shell searches when you execute a command without specifying its
full path.
</p>

<pre>echo $PATH</pre>

<p>
Example structure:
</p>

<pre>
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
</pre>

<div class="example">
<strong>Example:</strong>
<p>
When you run <code>python3</code>, the shell searches directories
listed in PATH for an executable named python3.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 16</div>
<h2>How do you find the location of a command?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>
which python3
</pre>

<p>
You can also use:
</p>

<pre>
command -v python3
</pre>

<p>
For shell command resolution, <code>command -v</code> is often a
portable and useful choice.
</p>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 17</div>
<h2>What is .bashrc?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>~/.bashrc</code> is a shell startup configuration file commonly
used by interactive Bash shells.
</p>

<p>
It can contain:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Aliases</li>
<li>Functions</li>
<li>Environment setup</li>
<li>PATH modifications</li>
<li>Shell configuration</li>
</ul>

<p>
After modifying it, you can reload it in the current shell:
</p>

<pre>source ~/.bashrc</pre>

<div class="warning">
<strong>Important:</strong>
<p>
Startup files differ depending on the shell and whether the shell
is interactive or login. Do not assume every shell uses .bashrc.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>
<h2>What is Shell?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A shell is a command interpreter that provides an interface for
interacting with the operating system.
</p>

<table>
<tr><th>Shell</th><th>Example</th></tr>
<tr><td>Bash</td><td>Common Linux shell</td></tr>
<tr><td>sh</td><td>Traditional shell interface</td></tr>
<tr><td>Zsh</td><td>Interactive shell used on many systems</td></tr>
</table>

<p>
Check the current user's configured shell:
</p>

<pre>echo $SHELL</pre>

</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 19</div>
<h2>Useful Shell Basics for DevOps</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h3>Command substitution</h3>
<pre>echo "Today is $(date)"</pre>

<h3>Variable</h3>
<pre>NAME="Nandu"
echo $NAME</pre>

<h3>Exit status</h3>
<pre>echo $?</pre>

<p>
An exit status of <code>0</code> generally indicates success, while
a non-zero status generally indicates some form of failure.
</p>

<h3>Pipe</h3>
<pre>ps aux | grep nginx</pre>

<h3>Redirect output</h3>
<pre>command &gt; output.txt</pre>

<h3>Append output</h3>
<pre>command &gt;&gt; output.txt</pre>

<h3>Redirect errors</h3>
<pre>command 2&gt; error.log</pre>

<h3>Redirect output and errors</h3>
<pre>command &gt; output.log 2&gt;&amp;1</pre>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 20</div>
<h2>What is chmod vs chown?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ QUICK REVISION</span>

<p>
These were covered in the permissions module, but remember the
difference:
</p>

<table>
<tr><th>Command</th><th>Purpose</th></tr>
<tr><td>chmod</td><td>Change permissions</td></tr>
<tr><td>chown</td><td>Change owner/group ownership</td></tr>
</table>

<pre>
chmod 755 script.sh
chown user:group file.txt
</pre>

</article>

<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Application Started but Immediately Stopped</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<pre>
systemctl status app.service
journalctl -u app.service --no-pager
</pre>

<p>
Then check:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Configuration</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>File permissions</li>
<li>Dependencies</li>
<li>Port conflicts</li>
<li>Application logs</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">
Service Failed
<br>â†“
<br>Status
<br>â†“
<br>Logs
<br>â†“
<br>Environment / Config
<br>â†“
<br>Dependencies
<br>â†“
<br>Fix Root Cause
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Script Works Manually but Fails in Cron</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
Possible reasons:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Different PATH</li>
<li>Missing environment variables</li>
<li>Relative paths</li>
<li>Different working directory</li>
<li>Permissions</li>
<li>Different user</li>
</ul>

<p>
Use absolute paths and log output.
</p>

<pre>
/usr/bin/python3 /opt/scripts/job.py &gt;&gt; /var/log/job.log 2&gt;&amp;1
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"Cron has a different execution environment, so I verify PATH,
environment variables, permissions, user context and absolute paths,
then capture stdout and stderr for troubleshooting."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Command: "command not found"</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Check whether the command exists:
</p>

<pre>
command -v kubectl
which kubectl
</pre>

<p>
Then inspect:
</p>

<pre>echo $PATH</pre>

<p>
If the executable exists outside PATH, either use its full path or
configure PATH appropriately.
</p>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Application Cannot Read an Environment Variable</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS</span>

<pre>
echo $APP_ENV
env | grep APP_ENV
</pre>

<p>
If the variable exists in your interactive shell but not in the
application, check how the application is started.
</p>

<p>
For systemd services, inspect the service configuration and its
environment rather than assuming your interactive shell's variables
are inherited.
</p>
</article>

<h2>Linux Final Cheat Sheet</h2>

<div class="note">

<strong>Logs</strong>
â†’ Troubleshoot system and application events.

<br><br>

<strong>/var/log</strong>
â†’ Common location for traditional log files.

<br><br>

<strong>journalctl</strong>
â†’ Query systemd journal logs.

<br><br>

<strong>dmesg</strong>
â†’ Kernel ring-buffer messages.

<br><br>

<strong>tail -f</strong>
â†’ Follow new lines in a log.

<br><br>

<strong>cron</strong>
â†’ Schedule recurring tasks.

<br><br>

<strong>crontab -e</strong>
â†’ Edit user's scheduled jobs.

<br><br>

<strong>Environment Variable</strong>
â†’ Configuration/value available to a process.

<br><br>

<strong>export</strong>
â†’ Export a shell variable to child processes.

<br><br>

<strong>PATH</strong>
â†’ Directories searched for executable commands.

<br><br>

<strong>.bashrc</strong>
â†’ Common Bash interactive-shell configuration file.

<br><br>

<strong>$?</strong>
â†’ Exit status of the previous command.

<br><br>

<strong>|</strong>
â†’ Pipe output from one command into another.

<br><br>

<strong>></strong>
â†’ Redirect/overwrite output.

<br><br>

<strong>>></strong>
â†’ Append output.

<br><br>

<strong>2></strong>
â†’ Redirect standard error.

</div>

<article class="card">
<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL LINUX INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> Where do Linux logs commonly exist?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Many traditional logs are under <code>/var/log</code>, while systemd systems commonly use the journal.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is journalctl?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A command used to query systemd journal logs.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot a failed systemd service?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Check <code>systemctl status</code>, inspect <code>journalctl -u</code>, verify configuration, dependencies,
permissions and ports.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is cron?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A mechanism for scheduling recurring commands or
scripts.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is crontab?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A user's scheduled-job configuration.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Why can a cron job fail even though the script
works manually?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Cron may have a different environment, PATH,
user, working directory or permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is an environment variable?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A named value made available to a process through
its environment.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is PATH?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A list of directories searched for executable
commands.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does export do?<br> <strong>A:</strong> It places a shell variable into the environment
inherited by child processes.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does $? mean?<br> <strong>A:</strong> The exit status of the previous command.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot "command not found"?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Verify the executable exists, inspect PATH and
use <code>command -v</code> or the executable's full path.

</p>
</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>Why is Network Troubleshooting Important in DevOps?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Applications in DevOps environments depend heavily on network
communication between users, load balancers, containers,
Kubernetes services, databases, APIs and cloud resources.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User

â†“

DNS

â†“

Load Balancer

â†“

Application

â†“

Database

</div>

<p>
A failure at any layer can make an application appear unavailable.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Network troubleshooting is important in DevOps because modern
applications depend on communication between multiple services.
I troubleshoot systematically from DNS and connectivity through
ports, routing, firewalls and application-level responses."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 02 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>What is traceroute?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>traceroute</code> is used to identify the network hops
between the source system and a destination.
</p>

<pre>traceroute google.com</pre>

<p>
On some Linux distributions, the command may need to be installed
first.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Why use it?</strong>

<p>
If a remote server is unreachable, traceroute can help identify
where along the network path packets stop receiving expected
responses.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Traceroute helps identify the network path and intermediate hops
between a source and destination, which can help locate routing
or connectivity problems."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 03 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>

<h2>What is the difference between ping and traceroute?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ping</th>
<th>traceroute</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Tests basic reachability</td>
<td>Shows network path/hops</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Measures response time</td>
<td>Helps identify path issues</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually targets one destination</td>
<td>Shows intermediate routing hops</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Ping checks basic reachability and latency, while traceroute
helps identify the path and intermediate hops taken toward the
destination."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 04 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>

<h2>What is curl -v?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
The <code>-v</code> option makes curl display detailed information
about the connection.
</p>

<pre>curl -v http://localhost:8080</pre>

<p>
It can reveal useful details such as connection attempts,
request/response headers and TLS-related information for HTTPS.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Useful for:</strong>

<ul>
<li>HTTP connection debugging</li>
<li>Checking response headers</li>
<li>Understanding redirects</li>
<li>Troubleshooting TLS/HTTPS</li>
<li>Verifying application endpoints</li>
</ul>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 05 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>

<h2>How do you check only HTTP response headers?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>curl -I https://example.com</pre>

<p>
This sends a HEAD request when supported and displays response
headers without retrieving the normal response body.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Useful headers</strong>

<pre>
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: ...
Server: ...
</pre>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 06 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>

<h2>How do you test a specific TCP port?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY USEFUL</span>

<p>
A simple approach is using tools such as <code>nc</code> when
available.
</p>

<pre>nc -zv server-ip 8080</pre>

<p>
This can help determine whether a TCP connection to the specified
port can be established.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Remember</strong>

<p>
A successful TCP connection only proves that the network path and
port are reachable. It does not prove that the application itself
is functioning correctly.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 07 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>

<h2>What is localhost?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>localhost</code> refers to the local machine itself.
It commonly resolves to loopback addresses such as:
</p>

<pre>
127.0.0.1
::1
</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example</strong>

<pre>curl http://localhost:8080</pre>

<p>
This tests the application from the same machine rather than from
another network host.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 08 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>

<h2>Why test localhost first?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
Testing localhost helps separate application problems from
external network problems.
</p>

<div class="flow">

curl localhost:8080

â†“

Works?

â†“

YES â†’ Investigate external network

NO â†’ Investigate application/service

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I test the application locally first. If localhost works but
remote access fails, I focus on network, firewall, routing or
security controls. If localhost itself fails, I investigate the
application or service."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 09 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>

<h2>What is a socket?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A socket is an endpoint used for network communication.
A network connection is commonly associated with an IP address,
port and transport protocol.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example</strong>

<pre>
192.168.1.10:8080
</pre>

<p>
This identifies an endpoint using an IP address and port.
</p>

</div>

<p>
The <code>ss</code> command is commonly used to inspect sockets.
</p>

<pre>ss -tulpn</pre>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 10 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 10</div>

<h2>What is a listening port?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A listening port indicates that a service is waiting for incoming
network connections.
</p>

<pre>ss -lntp</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example</strong>

<p>
If an application is expected on port 8080 but no process is
listening on 8080, remote clients cannot establish a normal TCP
connection to that service.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 11 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 11</div>

<h2>What does 0.0.0.0 mean when a service binds to it?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
When a service listens on <code>0.0.0.0</code> for IPv4, it
generally means it is listening on all IPv4 interfaces on that
host, subject to firewall and network controls.
</p>

<pre>ss -lntp</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Compare</strong>

<pre>
127.0.0.1:8080
</pre>

<p>
Usually accessible only locally.

<pre>
0.0.0.0:8080
</pre>

<p>
Generally listening on all IPv4 interfaces.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Security Note</strong>

<p>
Listening on all interfaces does not mean the service should be
publicly exposed. Firewall, security groups and network design
still matter.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>

<h2>How do you check DNS resolution step by step?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<pre>
hostname
nslookup example.com
dig example.com
cat /etc/resolv.conf
</pre>

<div class="flow">

Hostname

â†“

Resolver Configuration

â†“

DNS Query

â†“

DNS Response

â†“

IP Address

â†“

Application Connection

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I first verify the hostname and use nslookup or dig to check
whether DNS returns an expected address. If resolution fails, I
inspect resolver configuration and DNS infrastructure."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>

<h2>DNS works but application still fails â€” why?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</span>

<p>
Successful DNS resolution only proves that the hostname can be
resolved. The application can still fail because of:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Wrong port</li>
<li>Firewall/security-group rules</li>
<li>Routing issues</li>
<li>Service not running</li>
<li>Application errors</li>
<li>TLS problems</li>
<li>Load balancer health issues</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

DNS âœ“

â†“

IP âœ“

â†“

TCP Connection ?

â†“

Port ?

â†“

Application ?

â†“

HTTP Response ?

</div>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 15</div>

<h2>502 Bad Gateway</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
A 502 response commonly means a gateway or proxy received an
invalid or unsuccessful response from an upstream server.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User

â†“

Nginx / Load Balancer

â†“

Upstream Application

â†“

âŒ Failure

â†“

502

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Is backend application running?</li>
<li>Is backend port correct?</li>
<li>Can proxy reach backend?</li>
<li>Is backend returning a valid response?</li>
<li>Check application and proxy logs.</li>
</ul>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 16 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 16</div>

<h2>503 Service Unavailable</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
503 generally means the service is currently unavailable.
Possible causes include overloaded services, unavailable
upstreams, maintenance or unhealthy backend instances.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>DevOps approach</strong>

<pre>
systemctl status app
journalctl -u app
ss -lntp
curl localhost:8080
</pre>

<p>
For load-balanced environments, also check backend health and
target registration.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 17 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 17</div>

<h2>504 Gateway Timeout</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A 504 commonly means a gateway or proxy did not receive a timely
response from an upstream service.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Client

â†“

Proxy / Load Balancer

â†“

Backend

â†“

No timely response

â†“

504

</div>

<p>
Investigate backend latency, network connectivity, application
performance and timeout configuration.
</p>

</article>

<!-- 18 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>

<h2>What is TLS/HTTPS troubleshooting?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
HTTPS adds TLS encryption to HTTP. Problems can occur because of
certificate validation, hostname mismatch, expired certificates,
unsupported protocols or trust-chain issues.
</p>

<pre>curl -v https://example.com</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Certificate validity</li>
<li>Hostname</li>
<li>Certificate chain</li>
<li>Server configuration</li>
<li>Client trust store</li>
<li>System time</li>
</ul>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<!-- 19 -->

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 19</div>

<h2>How does system time affect HTTPS?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
TLS certificate validation depends on time validity. If a system
clock is significantly incorrect, certificates may appear not
yet valid or expired.
</p>

<pre>date</pre>

<p>
On systemd-based systems:
</p>

<pre>timedatectl</pre>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO 20</div>

<h2>Website is not opening</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST PRACTICE</span>

<div class="flow">

1. DNS

â†“

2. IP Reachability

â†“

3. TCP Port

â†“

4. HTTP Response

â†“

5. Application

â†“

6. Logs

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre>
nslookup app.example.com

ping server-ip

nc -zv server-ip 443

curl -v https://app.example.com

ss -lntp

journalctl -u nginx
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I troubleshoot from the outside inward. First I verify DNS,
then network reachability, then TCP port connectivity, then the
HTTP response. If the request reaches the server but fails, I
inspect the proxy, application and system logs."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO 21</div>

<h2>Application works on localhost but not from another machine</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

localhost works âœ“

â†“

Check listening address

â†“

Check firewall

â†“

Check security group

â†“

Check routing

â†“

Check client connectivity

</div>

<h3>First checks</h3>

<pre>
ss -lntp
ip addr
ip route
curl localhost:8080
</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common cause</strong>

<p>
The application may be bound only to <code>127.0.0.1</code>.
In that case, remote systems cannot directly connect to it.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ================================================= -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO 22</div>

<h2>Port is listening but connection still fails</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
If <code>ss</code> shows the port listening but clients cannot
connect, investigate:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Listening address</li>
<li>Firewall rules</li>
<li>Cloud security groups</li>
<li>Network ACLs</li>
<li>Routing</li>
<li>Load balancer configuration</li>
<li>Client-side restrictions</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A listening socket proves the application has opened the port,
but external connectivity can still fail because of binding,
firewall, security-group, routing or load-balancer issues."
</p>

</div>

</article>

â†’ Detailed HTTP/HTTPS debugging.

â†’ Inspect HTTP response headers.

â†’ Test TCP connectivity to a port.

<br><br>

<strong>localhost</strong>
â†’ Local machine / loopback.

<br><br>

<strong>Listening Port</strong>
â†’ Service waiting for incoming connections.

<br><br>

<strong>127.0.0.1</strong>
â†’ Loopback address.

<br><br>

<strong>0.0.0.0</strong>
â†’ All IPv4 interfaces when used as a bind/listen address.

â†’ Successful HTTP response.

<br><br>

â†’ Resource not found.

<br><br>

â†’ Gateway/upstream response problem.

<br><br>

â†’ Service unavailable.

<br><br>

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is traceroute?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A tool used to identify network hops between
source and destination.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Difference between ping and traceroute?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Ping tests basic reachability; traceroute
helps identify the network path.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does curl -v do?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Shows detailed HTTP/HTTPS connection and
response information.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does localhost mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> The local machine, commonly represented by
127.0.0.1 for IPv4.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a listening port?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A port where a service is waiting for incoming
network connections.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Application works locally but not remotely.
What do you check?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Binding address, firewall, security groups,
routing and network connectivity.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> DNS resolves but application doesn't work.
Why?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> DNS only confirms name resolution. The port,
service, firewall, routing or application can still fail.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is 502?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A gateway/proxy received an invalid or
unsuccessful response from an upstream server.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is 504?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A gateway/proxy timed out waiting for an
upstream response.

</p>

</article>

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>What is Linux Networking?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux networking allows a server to communicate with other
systems, applications and network services using interfaces,
IP addresses, routes, ports and network protocols.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Application

â†“

TCP / UDP

â†“

IP

â†“

Network Interface

â†“

Network

â†“

Remote Server

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux networking provides the mechanisms required for a system
to communicate with other systems using network interfaces,
IP addressing, routing, ports and network protocols."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- IP -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>What is an IP Address?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
An IP address identifies a device or network interface on an IP
network and allows systems to communicate with each other.
</p>

<h3>IPv4 Example</h3>

<pre>192.168.1.10</pre>

<h3>Private IP</h3>

<p>
Private IP addresses are commonly used inside internal networks.
For example:
</p>

<pre>10.0.0.10
172.16.1.10
192.168.1.10</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"An IP address identifies a network interface and allows systems
to communicate across an IP network."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- IP COMMAND -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 03</div>

<h2>How do you check the IP address in Linux?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<pre>ip addr</pre>

<p>
A shorter commonly used form:
</p>

<pre>ip a</pre>

<p>
To view a particular interface:
</p>

<pre>ip addr show eth0</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Useful related command</strong>

<pre>ip link</pre>

<p>
Shows network interfaces and their state.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ROUTING -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>

<h2>What is Routing?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Routing determines where network packets should be sent to reach
their destination.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>View routing table</strong>

<pre>ip route</pre>

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application

â†“

Destination IP

â†“

Routing Table

â†“

Next Hop / Interface

â†“

Destination

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Routing determines the path or next hop used to deliver packets
toward their destination. Linux maintains a routing table that
can be inspected using ip route."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- DEFAULT ROUTE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>

<h2>What is a Default Route?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A default route is used when no more specific route exists for
the destination.
</p>

<pre>ip route</pre>

<p>
You may see something similar to:
</p>

<pre>default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Meaning</strong>

<p>
Traffic for destinations not covered by more specific routes is
sent through the configured default gateway.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PING -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 06</div>

<h2>What is ping?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>ping</code> is commonly used to test IP-level reachability
and observe round-trip response time using ICMP.
</p>

<pre>ping 8.8.8.8</pre>

<pre>ping google.com</pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
A failed ping does not always mean the application or server is
down. ICMP may be blocked by a firewall or security policy.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I use ping as a basic connectivity test. However, I don't rely
on ping alone because ICMP may be blocked even when application
traffic is working."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PORTS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>

<h2>What is a Port?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A port identifies a network service or endpoint on a host.
TCP and UDP use port numbers to distinguish services.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Service</th>
<th>Common Port</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SSH</td>
<td>22</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTP</td>
<td>80</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTPS</td>
<td>443</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>DNS</td>
<td>53</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MySQL</td>
<td>3306</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>PostgreSQL</td>
<td>5432</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A port identifies a network service on a host. For example,
SSH commonly uses port 22 and HTTPS commonly uses port 443."
</p>

</div>

</article>

</p>

<pre>ss -tulpn</pre>

<th>Meaning</th>

</p>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
<code>curl</code> is a command-line tool used to communicate with

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

DNS, or Domain Name System, translates domain names into IP

â†“

<h2>/etc/hosts</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>/etc/hosts</code> file provides local hostname-to-IP
mappings.
</p>

<pre>cat /etc/hosts</pre>

<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>

<h2>/etc/resolv.conf</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
This file commonly contains DNS resolver configuration such as
nameserver information, although on modern Linux systems it may
be managed dynamically by another service.
</p>

<pre>cat /etc/resolv.conf</pre>

<p>
The actual resolver configuration depends on the Linux
distribution and network management system.
</p>

<div class="number">QUESTION 16</div>

<h2>netstat vs ss</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>netstat</code> is a traditional networking command, while
<code>ss</code> is the modern tool commonly preferred on Linux
systems.
</p>

<pre>netstat -tuln</pre>

<pre>ss -tuln</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"ss is generally preferred on modern Linux systems for inspecting
sockets and listening ports, while netstat is an older commonly
known tool."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- TCP UDP -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 17</div>

<h2>TCP vs UDP</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>TCP</th>
<th>UDP</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Connection-oriented</td>
<td>Connectionless</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Reliable delivery</td>
<td>No built-in delivery guarantee</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Ordered byte stream</td>
<td>Datagrams</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More protocol overhead</td>
<td>Lower overhead</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common examples</strong>

<p>
HTTP/HTTPS commonly use TCP-based connections, while DNS can
use both UDP and TCP depending on the situation.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"TCP provides reliable, connection-oriented communication, while
UDP is connectionless and has lower protocol overhead but does not
provide TCP's delivery guarantees."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- FIREWALL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>

<h2>Firewall & Network Access</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A firewall controls which network traffic is allowed or denied
based on configured rules.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Client

â†“

Network Firewall / Security Group

â†“

Server

â†“

Application Port

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>Real-Time Example</strong>

<p>
An application listens on port 8080, but the firewall blocks
incoming traffic to that port. The service can be running
correctly while clients still cannot connect.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"If a service is running but unreachable, I check the service
binding and port first, then firewall or security-group rules,
routing and network connectivity."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- CONNECTION REFUSED -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 19</div>

<h2>Connection Refused</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
A connection refused error often means the destination host is
reachable but no service is accepting the connection on that
port, or a device is actively rejecting it.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Connection Refused

â†“

Check Application

â†“

Check Listening Port

â†“

ss -tulpn

â†“

Check Bind Address

â†“

Check Firewall

â†“

Test Again

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>ss -tulpn | grep 8080
curl http://localhost:8080</pre>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- TIMEOUT -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 20</div>

<h2>Connection Timeout</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
A timeout often indicates that traffic is not receiving a response
within the expected period.
</p>

<p>Possible causes include:</p>

<ul>
<li>Firewall blocking traffic</li>
<li>Security group/network ACL rules</li>
<li>Routing problems</li>
<li>Network path failure</li>
<li>Service not reachable</li>
<li>Incorrect IP or port</li>
</ul>

<div class="example">

<pre>ping server-ip
ip route
ss -tulpn
curl -v http://server-ip:8080</pre>

</div>

</article>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
If a hostname cannot be resolved, investigate DNS configuration

â†“

â†“

â†“

Check DNS

â†“

cat /etc/resolv.conf</pre>

<!-- REAL TIME APP -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application is running but users cannot access it</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<div class="flow">

Application Running?

â†“

Check Process

â†“

Check Listening Port

â†“

Check IP / Bind Address

â†“

Check Local curl

â†“

Check Firewall / Security Group

â†“

Check Route

â†“

Check DNS

â†“

Test From Client

</div>

<h3>Useful Commands</h3>

<pre>ps aux | grep application
ss -tulpn

ip route
curl http://localhost:8080
curl http://server-ip:8080
nslookup app.example.com</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would troubleshoot layer by layer. First I verify that the
application process is running and listening on the expected
port. Then I test locally with curl, verify the server IP and
route, inspect firewall or security-group rules, and finally

</p>
