<div class="note">

<strong>IP Address</strong>
â†’ Identifies a network interface.

<br><br>

â†’ Check IP addresses.

<br><br>

â†’ Check routing table.

<br><br>

â†’ Used when no more specific route exists.

<br><br>

<strong>ping</strong>
â†’ Basic ICMP reachability test.

<br><br>

<strong>Port</strong>
â†’ Identifies a network service endpoint.

<br><br>

<strong>ss</strong>
â†’ Inspect listening sockets.

<br><br>

<strong>curl</strong>
â†’ Test HTTP/HTTPS endpoints.

<br><br>

<strong>DNS</strong>
â†’ Resolves names to IP addresses.

<br><br>

<strong>nslookup / dig</strong>
â†’ Troubleshoot DNS.

<br><br>

<strong>/etc/hosts</strong>
â†’ Local hostname mapping.

<br><br>

<strong>/etc/resolv.conf</strong>
â†’ DNS resolver configuration.

<br><br>

<strong>TCP</strong>
â†’ Reliable, connection-oriented communication.

<br><br>

<strong>UDP</strong>
â†’ Connectionless, lower-overhead communication.

<br><br>

<strong>Connection Refused</strong>
â†’ Check service and listening port.

<br><br>

<strong>Connection Timeout</strong>
â†’ Check firewall, routing and network path.

<br><br>

<strong>DNS Failure</strong>
â†’ Check resolver and DNS records.

</div>

</article>

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check the IP address?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>ip addr</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check the routing table?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>ip route</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check listening ports?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>ss -tulpn</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is DNS?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> DNS translates domain names into IP addresses
and provides other DNS records.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot DNS?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Use <code>nslookup</code> or <code>dig</code> and
inspect resolver configuration.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is curl used for?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Testing HTTP/HTTPS endpoints and connectivity.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Connection refused â€” what do you check?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Check whether the service is running and
whether the expected port is listening.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Connection timeout â€” what do you check?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Check firewall/security rules, routing,
network path, IP and port.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Ping is failing. Is the server definitely down?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> No. ICMP may be blocked even when application
traffic is working.

</p>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>
<h2>What is Linux Networking?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux networking allows a server to communicate with other systems
through network interfaces, IP addresses, routing, DNS and ports.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Application
<br>â†“
<br>Port
<br>â†“
<br>IP Address
<br>â†“
<br>Network Interface
<br>â†“
<br>Network
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"Linux networking involves configuring and troubleshooting network
interfaces, IP addressing, routing, DNS, ports and connectivity
between systems."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>
<h2>What is an IP Address?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
An IP address identifies a network interface or endpoint on an IP
network.
</p>

<h3>IPv4 Example</h3>
<pre>192.168.1.10</pre>

<h3>IPv6 Example</h3>
<pre>2001:db8::10</pre>

<table>
<tr><th>Type</th><th>Example</th></tr>
<tr><td>IPv4</td><td>192.168.1.10</td></tr>
<tr><td>IPv6</td><td>2001:db8::10</td></tr>
</table>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>
<h2>How do you check the IP address?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<pre>ip addr</pre>

<p>
A commonly used shorter form is:
</p>

<pre>ip a</pre>

<p>
This displays network interfaces and their assigned addresses.
</p>

<div class="note">
<strong>Modern command:</strong>
<p>
Prefer the <code>ip</code> command for current Linux administration.
Older systems may also contain commands such as <code>ifconfig</code>.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>
<h2>What is a Network Interface?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A network interface is the software-visible connection through which
a Linux system communicates over a network.
</p>

<p>
Examples commonly include:
</p>

<pre>
eth0
ens5
enp0s3
lo
</pre>

<p>
The exact interface name depends on the system.
</p>

<h3>Loopback</h3>
<pre>lo</pre>

<p>
The loopback interface is used for communication within the local
system. Its commonly used IPv4 address is <code>127.0.0.1</code>.
</p>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>
<h2>How do you check network interfaces?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ip link</pre>

<p>
For addresses and interfaces together:
</p>

<pre>ip addr</pre>

<p>
To inspect a specific interface:
</p>

<pre>ip addr show eth0</pre>

</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>
<h2>What is a MAC Address?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A MAC address is a hardware/link-layer address associated with a
network interface.
</p>

<pre>ip link</pre>

<p>
The output contains a value such as:
</p>

<pre>link/ether 02:42:ac:11:00:02</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"A MAC address identifies a network interface at the data-link
layer, while an IP address is used for communication at the network
layer."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>
<h2>What is the Default Gateway?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A default gateway is the router used when traffic does not have a
more specific route in the routing table.
</p>

<pre>ip route</pre>

<div class="flow">
Linux Server
<br>â†“
<br>Default Gateway
<br>â†“
<br>Other Network
<br>â†“
<br>Internet
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>
<h2>What is a Routing Table?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
A routing table tells Linux where network traffic should be sent.
</p>

<pre>ip route</pre>

<p>
Typical information includes:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Destination network</li>
<li>Gateway</li>
<li>Network interface</li>
<li>Route metric</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"The routing table determines where packets should be forwarded
based on their destination."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>
<h2>What is DNS?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
DNS stands for <strong>Domain Name System</strong>. It translates
domain names into IP addresses and can provide other DNS records.
</p>

<div class="flow">
google.com
<br>â†“
<br>DNS Lookup
<br>â†“
<br>IP Address
<br>â†“
<br>Server
</div>

<p>
Without DNS, users and applications would often need to use IP
addresses directly instead of domain names.
</p>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 10</div>
<h2>How do you test DNS resolution?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>
nslookup example.com
</pre>

<p>
Another commonly used command:
</p>

<pre>
dig example.com
</pre>

<p>
On systems using systemd-resolved, you may also encounter:
</p>

<pre>
resolvectl status
</pre>

</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 11</div>
<h2>What is /etc/hosts?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>/etc/hosts</code> provides local hostname-to-IP mappings.
</p>

<pre>
127.0.0.1 localhost
192.168.1.20 app-server
</pre>

<p>
The local hosts file can be useful for testing or simple local
name resolution.
</p>

<div class="warning">
<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>
<p>
Changes to <code>/etc/hosts</code> affect the local system and do not
create a global DNS record.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>
<h2>What is a Port?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A port identifies a network service endpoint on a host.
</p>

<table>
<tr><th>Service</th><th>Common Port</th></tr>
<tr><td>SSH</td><td>22</td></tr>
<tr><td>HTTP</td><td>80</td></tr>
<tr><td>HTTPS</td><td>443</td></tr>
<tr><td>DNS</td><td>53</td></tr>
<tr><td>FTP</td><td>21</td></tr>
<tr><td>MySQL</td><td>3306</td></tr>
<tr><td>PostgreSQL</td><td>5432</td></tr>
</table>

<div class="note">
<strong>Remember:</strong>
<p>
The port numbers above are common defaults, not guarantees that a
service must always use those ports.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>
<h2>How do you check listening ports?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<pre>ss -tulnp</pre>

<p>
Common flags:
</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>-t</strong> â†’ TCP</li>
<li><strong>-u</strong> â†’ UDP</li>
<li><strong>-l</strong> â†’ Listening</li>
<li><strong>-n</strong> â†’ Numeric output</li>
<li><strong>-p</strong> â†’ Process information where permitted</li>
</ul>

<div class="example">
<strong>Example:</strong>
<pre>ss -lntp</pre>
<p>
Useful when checking whether an application is actually listening
on the expected TCP port.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 14</div>
<h2>What is ping?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
<code>ping</code> tests basic IP connectivity by sending ICMP
Echo Requests and waiting for replies.
</p>

<pre>ping 8.8.8.8</pre>

<p>
To stop continuous output:
</p>

<pre>Ctrl + C</pre>

<div class="warning">
<strong>Important:</strong>
<p>
A failed ping does not automatically mean the host is down.
ICMP may be blocked by a firewall or security policy.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>
<h2>What is curl?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
<code>curl</code> is commonly used to transfer data and test HTTP/HTTPS
endpoints.
</p>

<pre>curl https://example.com</pre>

<p>
To inspect response headers:
</p>

<pre>curl -I https://example.com</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>DevOps Use:</strong>
<p>
Use curl to verify whether an application endpoint is responding
and to inspect HTTP responses during troubleshooting.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 16</div>
<h2>What is traceroute?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Traceroute helps identify the network path taken toward a
destination by showing intermediate hops.
</p>

<pre>traceroute example.com</pre>

<p>
On some Linux distributions you may need to install the command
first.
</p>

<div class="note">
<strong>Use case:</strong>
<p>
Useful when investigating where packets may be experiencing
routing or connectivity problems.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 17</div>
<h2>TCP vs UDP</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<table>
<tr>
<th>TCP</th>
<th>UDP</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Connection-oriented</td>
<td>Connectionless</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reliable ordered delivery</td>
<td>No built-in delivery guarantee</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>More protocol overhead</td>
<td>Lower overhead</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Common for HTTP/HTTPS and SSH</td>
<td>Common for DNS and streaming/real-time use cases</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"TCP provides connection-oriented and reliable ordered delivery,
while UDP is connectionless and has lower protocol overhead but
does not provide TCP's delivery guarantees."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>
<h2>What is localhost?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>localhost</code> refers to the local machine.
</p>

<pre>127.0.0.1</pre>

<p>
IPv6 loopback:
</p>

<pre>::1</pre>

<div class="example">
<strong>Example:</strong>

<p>
This tests a service listening on port 8080 on the same machine.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Application is not reachable on its port</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
Suppose an application should be running on port 8080.

</p>

<pre>

</pre>

<p>

</p>

<li>Check application logs</li>
<li>Verify configuration</li>

<p>

</p>

<ul>
<li>Firewall</li>
<li>Cloud security group</li>
<li>Network ACL</li>
<li>Routing</li>
<li>Listening address</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">
Application
<br>â†“
<br>Listening Port?
<br>â†“
<br>Local curl?
<br>â†“
<br>Firewall / Security Rules
<br>â†“
<br>Remote Client
</div>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>DNS works differently than IP connectivity</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
If this works:
</p>

<pre>ping 8.8.8.8</pre>

<p>
but this fails:
</p>

<pre>ping example.com</pre>

the problem may involve DNS resolution rather than basic IP

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Approach</strong>
<p>
"I separate the problem into layers. First I test IP connectivity,

</p>
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Server has no Internet connectivity</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

</p>

</pre>

<div class="flow">
Interface
<br>â†“
<br>IP Address
<br>â†“
<br>Default Route
<br>â†“
<br>Gateway
<br>â†“
<br>Internet IP
<br>â†“
<br>DNS
</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Container Networking â€” Basic Concept</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Containers have their own networking model and may communicate
through container networks, host networking or published ports,
depending on configuration.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Client
<br>â†“
<br>Host Port
<br>â†“
<br>Container Port
<br>â†“
<br>Application
</div>

<p>
For example, a web application listening on container port 8080
might be published to a host port such as 80.
</p>

<pre>docker run -p 80:8080 image-name</pre>

<p>
This means host port 80 is published to container port 8080.
</p>
</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 22</div>
<h2>What is a Firewall?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>

</p>

<p>
Linux environments may use tools such as:
</p>

<pre>

firewalld
nftables
</pre>

<p>

</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"A firewall filters network traffic according to rules and helps

</p>
</div>
</article>

<div class="number">ðŸ§  FINAL REVISION</div>
<h2>Linux Networking Cheat Sheet</h2>

<div class="note">

<strong>IP Address</strong>
â†’ Identifies an endpoint/interface on an IP network.

<br><br>

<strong>Network Interface</strong>
â†’ Connection used for network communication.

<br><br>

<strong>MAC Address</strong>
â†’ Link-layer address of a network interface.

<br><br>

<strong>Default Gateway</strong>
â†’ Next-hop router for traffic without a more specific route.

<br><br>

<strong>Routing Table</strong>
â†’ Determines where packets should be sent.

<br><br>

<strong>DNS</strong>
â†’ Resolves domain names to IP addresses and other records.

<br><br>

<strong>Port</strong>
â†’ Identifies a service endpoint.

<br><br>

<strong>ping</strong>
â†’ Basic ICMP connectivity test.

<br><br>

<strong>curl</strong>
â†’ HTTP/API testing and data transfer.

<br><br>

<strong>ss</strong>
â†’ Inspect sockets and listening ports.

<br><br>

<strong>TCP</strong>
â†’ Reliable, connection-oriented transport.

<br><br>

<strong>UDP</strong>
â†’ Connectionless, lower-overhead transport.

<br><br>

<strong>localhost</strong>
â†’ Local machine.

<br><br>

<strong>Least-layer troubleshooting</strong>
â†’ Interface â†’ Route â†’ Connectivity â†’ DNS â†’ Port â†’ Application.

</div>
</article>

<article class="card">
<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check an IP address?<br> <strong>A:</strong> <code>ip addr</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check the routing table?<br> <strong>A:</strong> <code>ip route</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check listening ports?<br> <strong>A:</strong> <code>ss -lntp</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is DNS?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A system that resolves domain names and provides
other DNS records.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is the difference between TCP and UDP?<br> <strong>A:</strong> TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable
ordered delivery; UDP is connectionless with lower overhead.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does ping test?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Basic IP connectivity using ICMP, where permitted.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot an application that is
not reachable?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Check the application, listening port, local
connectivity, firewall/security rules, routing and DNS.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> If IP works but domain name does not, what do
you check?<br> <strong>A:</strong> DNS configuration and name resolution.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> If an application works on localhost but not
from another machine?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Check the listening address, firewall, cloud
security rules, routing and published/exposed port.

</p>
</article>

</main>

<h2>ping</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>ping</code> command is commonly used to test network
reachability using ICMP echo requests.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>ping google.com</pre>

<pre>ping 8.8.8.8</pre>

<p>

ICMP requests.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>

ICMP may be blocked by firewalls or security rules even when
TCP-based application traffic works.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"ping uses ICMP echo requests to test basic network reachability.
However, a failed ping does not necessarily mean the application
is unavailable because ICMP may be blocked."
</p>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A firewall controls network traffic according to defined rules.

</p>

<div class="example">

</p>

<!-- CONNECTIVITY TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application is not reachable â€” How do you troubleshoot?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

Application Not Reachable

â†“

Is the process running?

â†“

Is the port listening?

â†“

Is local connectivity working?

â†“

Does DNS resolve?

â†“

Is routing correct?

â†“

Firewall / Security Group?

â†“

Application Logs

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>1. Check process</strong>

<pre>ps aux | grep nginx</pre>

<strong>2. Check listening port</strong>

<pre>sudo ss -tulpn</pre>

<strong>3. Test locally</strong>

<pre>curl http://localhost:8080</pre>

<strong>4. Test DNS</strong>

<pre>nslookup example.com</pre>

<strong>5. Check route</strong>

<pre>ip route</pre>

<strong>6. Test remote connectivity</strong>

<pre>ping SERVER_IP</pre>

<strong>7. Test HTTP endpoint</strong>

<pre>curl -v http://SERVER_IP:8080</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would troubleshoot layer by layer. First I would confirm the
application process is running, then verify that the expected port
is listening. I would test the service locally with curl, check
DNS resolution and routing, then verify firewall or cloud security
rules and finally inspect application and system logs."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PORT CLOSED -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Port 8080 is not reachable</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<div class="example">

<strong>Step 1 â€” Is application running?</strong>

<pre>ps aux | grep java</pre>

<strong>Step 2 â€” Is port listening?</strong>

<pre>sudo ss -tulpn | grep 8080</pre>

<strong>Step 3 â€” Test locally</strong>

<pre>curl http://localhost:8080</pre>

<strong>Step 4 â€” Check firewall</strong>

<p>
Verify host firewall rules and cloud security controls.
</p>

<strong>Step 5 â€” Check application logs</strong>

<p>
Look for startup failures, binding errors or configuration
problems.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would first verify that the application is running and that
port 8080 is actually listening. Then I would test the endpoint
locally. If it works locally but not remotely, I would investigate
the host firewall, cloud security rules, routing and network path."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<div class="flow">

curl localhost:8080

â†“

âŒ Fails

â†’ Application / Service issue

<br><br>

curl localhost:8080

â†“

âœ… Works

â†“

Remote access fails

â†’ Network / Firewall / Routing issue

</div>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 23</div>

<h2>ping vs curl</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ping</th>
<th>curl</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Tests ICMP reachability</td>
<td>Tests application/network protocols such as HTTP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not test HTTP application behavior</td>
<td>Can test HTTP response/status/headers</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"ping tests basic ICMP reachability, while curl can test the
actual application endpoint such as an HTTP service. Therefore
curl is often more useful when troubleshooting web applications."
</p>

</div>

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is an IP address?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A logical address used to identify a host or
network interface.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a port?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A logical endpoint used to identify a network
service.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does ping do?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Tests basic ICMP reachability.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is DNS?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Resolves domain names to IP addresses and
supports other DNS records.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check listening ports?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>ss -tulpn</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you test an HTTP application?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Use <code>curl</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot DNS?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Use <code>nslookup</code> or <code>dig</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check Linux routes?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>ip route</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> ping vs curl?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> ping tests ICMP reachability; curl tests an
application/network protocol endpoint such as HTTP.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot an unreachable
application?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Check process â†’ port â†’ localhost â†’ DNS â†’
routing â†’ firewall/security rules â†’ logs.

</p>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>What are Linux File Permissions?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux file permissions control who can read, modify or execute
a file or directory.
</p>

<p>
The three basic permissions are:
</p>

<p>
â†’ <strong>r</strong> = Read

<br>
â†’ <strong>w</strong> = Write

<br>
â†’ <strong>x</strong> = Execute
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example</strong>

<pre>-rwxr-xr--</pre>

<p>
This permission string tells us which operations are allowed for
the owner, group and others.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux permissions control access to files and directories.
The basic permissions are read, write and execute, and they are
assigned separately to the owner, group and other users."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- OWNERSHIP -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>Linux File Ownership</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Every Linux file and directory has an owner and an associated
group.
</p>

<div class="flow">

File

â†“

<strong>Owner</strong> + <strong>Group</strong>

â†“

Permissions

â†“

User Access

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Check ownership</strong>

<pre>ls -l</pre>

<p>Example output:</p>

<pre>-rw-r--r-- 1 nandu devops 1200 app.log</pre>

<p>
Here:
</p>

<p>
Owner â†’ <strong>nandu</strong>

<br>
Group â†’ <strong>devops</strong>
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux associates each file with an owner and a group. Permissions
are then defined for the owner, group members and other users."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- LS -L -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>

<h2>How do you check permissions?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
Use the <code>ls -l</code> command.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>ls -l app.sh</pre>

<th>Meaning</th>

<td><code>nandu</code></td>
<td>Owner</td>

<td><code>devops</code></td>
<td>Group</td>
</tr>

</table>

<!-- R W X -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>

<h2>What do r, w and x mean?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>File</th>
<th>Directory</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>r</strong></td>
<td>Read file contents</td>
<td>List directory contents</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>w</strong></td>
<td>Modify file</td>
<td>Create/delete/rename entries</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>x</strong></td>
<td>Execute file</td>
<td>Enter/access directory</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="note">

<strong>ðŸ§  Important:</strong>

<p>
Execute permission on a directory means you can access/traverse
that directory. Directory permissions behave differently from
file permissions.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"For files, read allows viewing contents, write allows modifying
contents and execute allows running the file. For directories,
read allows listing entries, write allows modifying directory
entries and execute allows traversing or accessing the directory."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- THREE GROUPS -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>

<h2>Owner, Group and Others</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux permissions are divided into three categories.
</p>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Owner</strong>

â†“

<strong>Group</strong>

â†“

<strong>Others</strong>

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Category</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Owner</td>
<td>User who owns the file</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Group</td>
<td>Users belonging to the associated group</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Others</td>
<td>All other users</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example</strong>

<pre>-rwxr-x---</pre>

<p>

Owner â†’ <strong>rwx</strong>

<br>

Group â†’ <strong>r-x</strong>

<br>

Others â†’ <strong>---</strong>

</p>

</div>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>chmod</code> command changes permissions on files and

</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Symbolic Mode</strong>

<pre>chmod u+x script.sh

<th>Meaning</th>

<td>User / Owner</td>

<td>Group</td>
</tr>

<td><code>o</code></td>
<td>Others</td>

<td>All</td>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<!-- NUMERIC -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>

<h2>Numeric Permissions in Linux</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
Linux permissions can also be represented using numeric values.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>Value</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Read (r)</td>
<td>4</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Write (w)</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Execute (x)</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>

</table>

<p>
The values are added together for each permission group.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example: 755</strong>

<pre>7 = 4 + 2 + 1 = rwx

5 = 4 + 1 = r-x

5 = 4 + 1 = r-x</pre>

<p>
Therefore:
</p>

<pre>755 = rwxr-xr-x</pre>

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Example: 644</strong>

<pre>6 = 4 + 2 = rw-

4 = r--

4 = r--</pre>

<p>
Therefore:
</p>

<pre>644 = rw-r--r--</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"In numeric Linux permissions, read is 4, write is 2 and execute
is 1. The values are added for owner, group and others. For
example, 755 represents rwxr-xr-x and 644 represents rw-r--r--."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<h2>Common Permission Values</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Value</th>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>Typical Usage</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>777</td>
<td>rwxrwxrwx</td>
<td>Full access to everyone â€” usually avoid</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>755</td>
<td>rwxr-xr-x</td>
<td>Executable scripts/directories</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>700</td>
<td>rwx------</td>
<td>Owner only</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>644</td>
<td>rw-r--r--</td>
<td>Regular files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>600</td>
<td>rw-------</td>
<td>Private/sensitive files</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
Avoid blindly using <code>chmod 777</code>. It grants read, write
and execute permissions to everyone and can create security
risks.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- CHOWN -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 09</div>

<h2>chown â€” Change Ownership</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>chown</code> command changes the owner and optionally
the group of a file or directory.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<pre>sudo chown nandu app.log

sudo chown nandu:devops app.log

sudo chown -R nandu:devops /opt/app</pre>

<p>
The <code>-R</code> option applies the ownership change
recursively.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"chown is used to change the owner of a file or directory. It can
also change the associated group, and the -R option applies the
change recursively."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- CHGRP -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 10</div>

<h2>chgrp â€” Change Group Ownership</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­</span>

<p>
The <code>chgrp</code> command changes the group associated with
a file or directory.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>sudo chgrp devops app.log

sudo chgrp -R devops /opt/app</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"chgrp is used to change the group ownership of a file or
directory."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- WHOAMI ID -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 11</div>

<h2>whoami and id</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
These commands help identify the current user and group
information.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>whoami

id</pre>

<p>
<code>whoami</code> displays the current username.
</p>

<p>
<code>id</code> displays the user ID, group ID and group
membership information.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- UMASK -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>

<h2>What is umask?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW</span>

<p>
<code>umask</code> defines the default permission restrictions
applied when new files and directories are created.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Check current umask</strong>

<pre>umask</pre>

<p>
A common value is:
</p>

<pre>0022</pre>

</div>

<p>
The exact resulting permissions depend on the system's default
base permissions and the umask value.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"umask defines default permission restrictions for newly created
files and directories. It prevents certain permission bits from
being granted by default."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- EXECUTABLE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>

<h2>How do you make a script executable?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
Use <code>chmod +x</code>.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>chmod +x deploy.sh

./deploy.sh</pre>

<p>
You can verify it using:
</p>

<pre>ls -l deploy.sh</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would add execute permission using chmod +x and then execute
the script using ./script-name.sh."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SSH KEY -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 14</div>

<h2>Why are SSH private key permissions important?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ AWS / DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
SSH private keys contain sensitive authentication material and
should not be accessible to other users.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Common permission</strong>

<pre>chmod 400 my-key.pem</pre>

<p>
Then connect:

</p>

<pre>ssh -i my-key.pem ec2-user@SERVER-IP</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
If an SSH private key is too permissive, SSH may reject it for
security reasons. Always protect private keys appropriately.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"SSH private keys should have restrictive permissions so that
other users cannot read them. A common practice is chmod 400 or
another appropriately restrictive permission depending on the
environment."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- REAL-TIME DEVOPS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application cannot read its configuration file</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
Suppose an application is running on a Linux server but cannot
read its configuration file.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Check User

â†“

Check File

â†“

Check Ownership

â†“

Check Permissions

â†“

Fix Ownership / Permissions

â†“

Test Application

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>Step 1 â€” Identify current user</strong>

<pre>whoami
id</pre>

<strong>Step 2 â€” Check file permissions</strong>

<pre>ls -l /opt/app/config.yaml</pre>

<strong>Step 3 â€” Change ownership if required</strong>

<pre>sudo chown appuser:appgroup /opt/app/config.yaml</pre>

<strong>Step 4 â€” Set appropriate permissions</strong>

<pre>sudo chmod 640 /opt/app/config.yaml</pre>

<strong>Step 5 â€” Verify</strong>

<pre>ls -l /opt/app/config.yaml</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"First I would identify which user the application is running as.
Then I would inspect the file's ownership and permissions using
ls -l. If required, I would correct the owner or group using
chown and set the minimum required permissions using chmod. I
would then test the application again."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SECURITY PRINCIPLE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>

<h2>What is the Principle of Least Privilege?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ SECURITY MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The principle of least privilege means giving users, processes
and applications only the permissions they actually need.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>âŒ Bad Practice</strong>

<pre>chmod 777 application.conf</pre>

<strong>âœ… Better Approach</strong>

<pre>chmod 640 application.conf</pre>

<p>
Then assign the appropriate owner and group.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Least privilege means granting only the minimum permissions
required for a user or application to perform its task. This
reduces the security impact of accidental or unauthorized access."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">TROUBLESHOOTING</div>

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Permission Denied â€” What would you check?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
When a Linux command returns "Permission denied", I would inspect
the current user, file ownership, permissions and directory
access.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>whoami

id

ls -l file.txt

ls -ld /path/to/directory</pre>

<p>
Then, depending on the requirement:

</p>

<pre>sudo chown user:group file.txt

sudo chmod 640 file.txt</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"For a permission denied issue, I would first identify the
current user and groups, then inspect the file and parent
directory permissions. I would verify ownership and only make
the minimum required permission or ownership change. I would
avoid blindly granting broad permissions such as 777."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- QUICK QUESTIONS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUICK INTERVIEW</div>

<h2>â­â­â­ Quick Questions</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What are the three basic Linux permissions?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Read, write and execute.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What are the three permission categories?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Owner, group and others.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is chmod?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Changes file or directory permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is chown?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Changes file or directory ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is chgrp?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Changes group ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 755 mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> rwxr-xr-x.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 644 mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> rw-r--r--.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 400 mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> r--------.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is umask?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Controls default permission restrictions for
new files and directories.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Why avoid chmod 777?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> It grants broad permissions to everyone and
can create security risks.

</p>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  FINAL REVISION â€” LINUX PERMISSIONS</h2>

<br><br>

<strong>Others</strong>
â†’ Everyone else.

<br><br>

<strong>chmod</strong>
â†’ Change permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>chown</strong>
â†’ Change owner/group ownership.

<br><br>

â†’ Change group.

<br><br>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>What is a Process?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A process is a running instance of a program.
When Linux executes a program, the operating system creates a
process to manage its execution and resources.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Simple Example</strong>

<pre>./application</pre>

<p>
When the application starts running, Linux creates a process
for it.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A process is a running instance of a program. Linux assigns
resources and a process ID to each running process."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PID -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>What is PID?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
PID stands for <strong>Process ID</strong>.
Linux assigns a unique process identifier to each running
process.
</p>

<pre>ps</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example</strong>

<pre>
PID     COMMAND
1245    nginx
2480    java
</pre>

<p>
Here <code>1245</code> and <code>2480</code> are process IDs.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"PID is the unique identifier assigned by Linux to a running
process. It is commonly used to inspect or manage that process."
</p>

</div>

</article>

</p>

<pre>ps aux</pre>

<p>
To find a specific process:
</p>

<pre>ps aux | grep nginx</pre>

<h2>top & htop</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>top</code> provides a live view of running processes and

</p>

<pre>top</pre>

<p>
If installed, <code>htop</code> provides a more interactive

<!-- ZOMBIE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>

<h2>What is a Zombie Process?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
A zombie process is a process that has finished execution but
still has an entry in the process table because its parent has
not yet collected its exit status.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Child Process

â†“

Finishes Execution

â†“

Exit Status Remains

â†“

Parent Has Not Collected It

â†“

Zombie

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A zombie is a terminated child process whose exit status has
not yet been collected by its parent process."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- KILL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 07</div>

<h2>How do you terminate a process?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
The <code>kill</code> command sends a signal to a process.
</p>

<pre>kill PID</pre>

<p>
For example:
</p>

<pre>kill 2480</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Force termination</strong>

<pre>kill -9 2480</pre>

<p>
SIGKILL immediately terminates the process and cannot be caught
or handled by the process.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
Do not use <code>kill -9</code> as the first option. Prefer a
normal termination signal when possible so the application has
an opportunity to clean up resources.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SIGNALS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>

<h2>Important Linux Signals</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Signal</th>
<th>Number</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SIGTERM</td>
<td>15</td>
<td>Request graceful termination</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SIGKILL</td>
<td>9</td>
<td>Force termination</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SIGHUP</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>Hangup; meaning depends on application</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SIGSTOP</td>
<td>19</td>
<td>Stop process</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SIGCONT</td>
<td>18</td>
<td>Continue stopped process</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Tip</strong>

<p>
"SIGTERM is generally preferred for graceful shutdown. SIGKILL
is used when a process does not terminate normally."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- BACKGROUND -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>

<h2>Foreground vs Background Process</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A foreground process occupies the current terminal session.
A background process can continue while the shell is available
for other commands.
</p>

<h3>Run in background</h3>

<pre>./application &</pre>

<h3>Show jobs</h3>

<pre>jobs</pre>

<h3>Move process to background</h3>

<pre>bg</pre>

<h3>Bring process to foreground</h3>

<pre>fg</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A foreground process uses the current terminal, while a
background process runs without blocking the shell from accepting
other commands."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- NOHUP -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 10</div>

<h2>nohup</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>nohup</code> allows a command to continue running after the
terminal session is closed, subject to the application's behavior
and environment.
</p>

<pre>nohup ./application &amp;</pre>

<p>
Output is commonly redirected to <code>nohup.out</code> if not
otherwise redirected.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Production Note</strong>

<p>
For production services, systemd, containers or orchestration
platforms are generally preferable to manually keeping processes
alive with nohup.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SERVICE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 11</div>

<h2>What is a Service?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A service is a long-running program that provides functionality
to other applications, users or system components.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Examples</strong>

<ul>
<li>SSH service</li>
<li>Nginx</li>
<li>Docker daemon</li>
<li>Database service</li>
<li>Application service</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A service is a long-running process that provides a specific
system or application function and can commonly be managed by
a service manager such as systemd."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SYSTEMCTL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 12</div>

<h2>systemctl</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>systemctl</code> is used to interact with systemd-managed
services and units on systems using systemd.
</p>

<h3>Check status</h3>

<pre>systemctl status nginx</pre>

<h3>Start service</h3>

<pre>sudo systemctl start nginx</pre>

<h3>Stop service</h3>

<pre>sudo systemctl stop nginx</pre>

<h3>Restart service</h3>

<pre>sudo systemctl restart nginx</pre>

<h3>Reload configuration</h3>

<pre>sudo systemctl reload nginx</pre>

<h3>Enable at boot</h3>

<pre>sudo systemctl enable nginx</pre>

<h3>Disable at boot</h3>

<pre>sudo systemctl disable nginx</pre>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ENABLE VS START -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>

<h2>start vs enable</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>start</td>
<td>Start service now</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>enable</td>
<td>Configure service to start automatically at boot</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>restart</td>
<td>Stop and start service</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>reload</td>
<td>Reload configuration without a full restart when supported</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>stop</td>
<td>Stop service</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"systemctl start starts a service immediately, while systemctl
enable configures it to start automatically during boot."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SYSTEMD -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 14</div>

<h2>What is systemd?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
systemd is a system and service manager used by many modern
Linux distributions.
</p>

<p>
It manages services, startup, dependencies, units and system
state.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Boot

â†“

systemd

â†“

Units / Services

â†“

Applications

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"systemd is a system and service manager used by many Linux
distributions to initialize the system and manage services,
units and dependencies."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- LOGS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>

<h2>What are Linux Logs?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Logs record events generated by the operating system, services
and applications. They are essential for troubleshooting,
auditing and monitoring.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common log locations</strong>

<pre>/var/log/</pre>

<p>
Examples may include:
</p>

<pre>/var/log/syslog
/var/log/messages
/var/log/auth.log</pre>

<p>
Exact files vary by Linux distribution and configuration.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- JOURNALCTL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 16</div>

<h2>journalctl</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>journalctl</code> is used to query logs collected by the
systemd journal.
</p>

<h3>View logs</h3>

<pre>journalctl</pre>

<h3>View logs for a service</h3>

<pre>journalctl -u nginx</pre>

<h3>Follow logs live</h3>

<pre>journalctl -u nginx -f</pre>

<h3>Recent logs</h3>

<pre>journalctl -u nginx -n 100</pre>

<h3>Logs since boot</h3>

<pre>journalctl -b</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I use journalctl to inspect systemd journal logs. For example,
journalctl -u service-name helps investigate why a service failed
or restarted."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- TAIL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 17</div>

<h2>tail &amp; grep for Log Troubleshooting</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<h3>Last lines</h3>

<pre>tail -n 50 /var/log/syslog</pre>

<h3>Follow log file</h3>

<pre>tail -f /var/log/syslog</pre>

<h3>Search errors</h3>

<pre>grep "ERROR" application.log</pre>

<h3>Combine commands</h3>

<pre>tail -f application.log | grep ERROR</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>DevOps Usage</strong>

<p>
During deployment, you can follow application logs in real time
and search for errors to identify startup failures.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SERVICE FAILED -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 18</div>

<h2>Service Failed to Start</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

Service Failed

â†“

systemctl status

â†“

journalctl -u service

â†“

Check Configuration

â†“

Check Port

â†“

Check Permissions

â†“

Fix

â†“

Restart

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre>systemctl status nginx

journalctl -u nginx -n 100

ss -tulpn</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"If a service fails to start, I first check systemctl status,
then inspect journalctl logs for the exact error. I also verify
configuration, permissions, dependencies and whether the required
port is already in use."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PORT ALREADY IN USE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 19</div>

<h2>Port Already in Use</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS SCENARIO</span>

<p>
If an application cannot start because its port is already
occupied, identify the process using that port.
</p>

<pre>ss -tulpn | grep 8080</pre>

<p>
Then inspect the process:
</p>

<pre>ps aux | grep 8080</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Typical situation</strong>

<p>
Application A is already listening on port 8080.
Application B tries to bind to the same port and fails.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- HIGH CPU -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 20</div>

<h2>High CPU Usage</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<div class="flow">

High CPU

â†“

top / htop

â†“

Identify PID

â†“

ps

â†“

Check Application

â†“

Inspect Logs

â†“

Take Corrective Action

</div>

<pre>top

ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"For high CPU usage, I first identify the process consuming CPU
using top or ps. Then I investigate its logs and workload before
deciding whether the issue requires configuration changes,
scaling, restart or application-level investigation."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- HIGH MEMORY -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 21</div>

<h2>High Memory Usage</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>free -h</pre>

<pre>ps aux --sort=-%mem | head</pre>

<p>
Use <code>free -h</code> to inspect memory availability and
<code>ps</code> to identify processes consuming significant
memory.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>DevOps Scenario</strong>

<p>
If a Java application repeatedly consumes memory and gets killed,
investigate JVM configuration, application behavior, container
limits and system memory pressure.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 22</div>

<h2>Disk Usage: df vs du</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<h3>df</h3>

<pre>df -h</pre>

<p>
Shows filesystem-level disk space usage.
</p>

<h3>du</h3>

<pre>du -sh /var/log/*</pre>

<p>
Shows disk usage of files/directories.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>df -h</td>
<td>Filesystem free/used space</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>du -sh</td>
<td>Directory/file space usage</td>
</tr>

</table>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- LOG DISK FULL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ TROUBLESHOOTING 23</div>

<h2>Disk Full Because of Logs</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

Application Logs

â†“

Disk Usage Increases

â†“

df -h

â†“

Find Large Directories

â†“

du -sh

â†“

Check Log Rotation

â†“

Clean / Rotate Safely

</div>

<pre>df -h

du -sh /var/log/*</pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
Do not blindly delete active application or system logs in
production. Investigate log rotation, retention and the service
that is generating excessive logs.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PROCESS VS SERVICE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 24</div>

<h2>Process vs Service</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Process</th>
<th>Service</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Running instance of a program</td>
<td>Long-running system/application function</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Has a PID</td>
<td>Can be managed by service manager</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be temporary</td>
<td>Usually designed to provide ongoing functionality</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A process is an executing instance of a program, while a service
is typically a long-running component managed by a service manager
such as systemd."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- REAL WORLD -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application Deployment Troubleshooting</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST PRACTICE</span>

<p>
Suppose you deployed a Java application as a Linux service and
users report that the application is unavailable.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Deployment

â†“

systemctl status app

â†“

Is Service Running?

â†“

journalctl -u app

â†“

Application Logs

â†“

Check Port

â†“

ss -tulpn

â†“

curl localhost:8080

â†“

Network / Firewall

â†“

Application Available

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre>systemctl status app

journalctl -u app -n 100

ss -tulpn | grep 8080

curl http://localhost:8080

df -h

free -h

top</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would start with the service status, inspect systemd logs,
verify that the application is listening on the expected port,
test the endpoint locally with curl, and then check system
resources, firewall and network connectivity."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  FINAL REVISION â€” PROCESSES, SERVICES &amp; LOGS</h2>

<div class="note">

<strong>Process</strong>
â†’ Running instance of a program.

<br><br>

<strong>PID</strong>
â†’ Unique process identifier.

<br><br>

<strong>ps</strong>
â†’ Process snapshot.

<br><br>

<strong>top / htop</strong>
â†’ Live resource monitoring.

<br><br>

<strong>kill</strong>
â†’ Send signal to a process.

<br><br>

<strong>SIGTERM</strong>
â†’ Graceful termination request.

<br><br>

<strong>SIGKILL</strong>
â†’ Force termination.

<br><br>

<strong>Zombie</strong>
â†’ Finished child process awaiting parent collection.

<br><br>

<strong>systemd</strong>
â†’ System and service manager.

<br><br>

<strong>systemctl</strong>
â†’ Manage systemd services.

<br><br>

<strong>start</strong>
â†’ Start now.

<br><br>

<strong>enable</strong>
â†’ Start automatically at boot.

<br><br>

<strong>journalctl</strong>
â†’ Query systemd journal logs.

<br><br>

<strong>tail -f</strong>
â†’ Follow a log file live.

<br><br>

<strong>df -h</strong>
â†’ Filesystem disk usage.

<br><br>

<strong>du -sh</strong>
â†’ Directory/file disk usage.

<br><br>

<strong>free -h</strong>
â†’ Memory usage.

<!-- INTERVIEW -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a process?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A running instance of a program.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is PID?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Process ID assigned to a running process.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check running processes?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>ps aux</code> or <code>top</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you terminate a process?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Use <code>kill PID</code>; use SIGKILL only
when necessary.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a zombie process?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A terminated child process whose exit status
has not yet been collected by its parent.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is systemd?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A system and service manager used by many
modern Linux distributions.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is systemctl?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A command used to manage systemd services and
units.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Difference between start and enable?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Start runs the service now; enable configures
it to start automatically at boot.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check service logs?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>journalctl -u service-name</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot high CPU?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Use <code>top</code> or <code>ps</code> to
identify the process, then investigate its workload and logs.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot a service that won't
start?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Check <code>systemctl status</code>, inspect
<code>journalctl</code>, verify configuration, dependencies,
permissions, ports and resources.

</p>

</article>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>What is Linux Security?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux security controls who can access files, directories,
processes and system resources and what actions they are allowed
to perform.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User

â†“

Authentication

â†“

Authorization

â†“

Permissions

â†“

Resource Access

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ DevOps Example</strong>

<p>
An application should be able to read its configuration files,
but it should not have permission to modify sensitive system
files.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux security uses users, groups, permissions, ownership and
privilege controls to restrict access to system resources and
protect applications and data."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- USERS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>What is a Linux User?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A user is an identity under which processes and commands run.
Linux associates each user with a UID, or User ID.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>View current user</strong>

<pre>whoami</pre>

<strong>View user identity</strong>

<pre>id</pre>

<strong>List users</strong>

<pre>cat /etc/passwd</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"A Linux user is an identity used to authenticate and control
access to system resources. Each user has a unique UID."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ROOT -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>

<h2>What is the root user?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
The root user is the Linux superuser with extensive privileges
over the operating system.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>whoami</pre>

<p>
If the output is:
</p>

<pre>root</pre>

<p>
the current shell is running as the root user.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Security Principle</strong>

<p>
Avoid using root unnecessarily. Use the least privilege required
to perform an operation.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Root is the Linux superuser with administrative privileges.
For security, administrative access should be limited and used
only when necessary."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- GROUPS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>

<h2>What is a Linux Group?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
A group is a collection of users that can share permissions to
files, directories and other resources.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Check groups of current user</strong>

<pre>groups</pre>

<strong>Detailed identity</strong>

<pre>id</pre>

</div>

<div class="flow">

Users

â†“

Group

â†“

Shared Permissions

â†“

Resources

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux groups allow administrators to manage permissions for
multiple users collectively instead of configuring permissions
individually."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- PERMISSIONS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>

<h2>Linux File Permissions</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux permissions control what the owner, group and other users
can do with a file or directory.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>ls -l</pre>

<p>Example:</p>

<pre>-rwxr-xr--</pre>

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
<th>Numeric Value</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>r</td>
<td>Read</td>
<td>4</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>w</td>
<td>Write</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>x</td>
<td>Execute</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>

</table>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- PERMISSION STRUCTURE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>

<h2>How do you read rwxr-xr-x?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

rwx

Owner

â†“

r-x

Group

â†“

r-x

Others

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Section</th>
<th>Permission</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Owner</td>
<td>rwx</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Group</td>
<td>r-x</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Others</td>
<td>r-x</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"The first permission set belongs to the owner, the second to
the group and the third to others. In rwxr-xr-x, the owner has
read, write and execute permissions, while group and others have
read and execute permissions."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- CHMOD -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 07</div>

<h2>chmod</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>chmod</code> changes the permissions of files and
directories.
</p>

<h3>Symbolic Mode</h3>

<pre>chmod u+x script.sh
chmod g+w file.txt
chmod o-r file.txt</pre>

<h3>Numeric Mode</h3>

<pre>chmod 755 script.sh
chmod 644 file.txt</pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Number</th>
<th>Permissions</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>7</td>
<td>rwx</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>6</td>
<td>rw-</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>5</td>
<td>r-x</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>4</td>
<td>r--</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>0</td>
<td>---</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"chmod is used to modify file and directory permissions. Numeric
permissions represent read, write and execute values using
4, 2 and 1."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- 755 -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>

<h2>What does chmod 755 mean?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<div class="flow">

7 â†’ rwx

â†“

5 â†’ r-x

â†“

5 â†’ r-x

</div>

<p>
Therefore:
</p>

<pre>Owner  â†’ rwx
Group  â†’ r-x
Others â†’ r-x</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common use</strong>

<p>
Executable scripts may commonly use 755 when they need to be
executed by users other than the owner.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- 644 -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>

<h2>What does chmod 644 mean?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>6 â†’ rw-
4 â†’ r--
4 â†’ r--</pre>

<p>
So:
</p>

<pre>Owner  â†’ read + write
Group  â†’ read
Others â†’ read</pre>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common use</strong>

<p>
Regular text or configuration files may commonly use a 644-style
permission when they do not need to be executable.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- CHOWN -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 10</div>

<h2>chown</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>chown</code> changes file or directory ownership.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Change owner</strong>

<pre>sudo chown nandu file.txt</pre>

<strong>Change owner and group</strong>

<pre>sudo chown nandu:devops file.txt</pre>

<strong>Recursive ownership change</strong>

<pre>sudo chown -R nandu:devops /app</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Be careful with -R</strong>

<p>
Recursive ownership changes affect everything below the specified
directory. Always verify the path before using it.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"chown changes the owner and group ownership of files and
directories. It is commonly used to ensure applications have the
correct ownership for accessing their files."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<div class="number">COMMAND 11</div>

<h2>chgrp</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>chgrp</code> changes the group ownership of a file or
directory.
</p>

<pre>sudo chgrp devops file.txt</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Memory Trick</strong>

<p>
<strong>chown</strong> â†’ Change owner<br>
<strong>chgrp</strong> â†’ Change group
</p>

</div>

</article>

<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>

<h2>What is sudo?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>sudo</code> allows an authorized user to execute a command

</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>sudo apt update</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"sudo allows authorized users to execute specific commands with
elevated privileges without logging in directly as the root
user."
</p>

</div>

<h2>/etc/sudoers</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
The sudoers configuration defines which users or groups are

<!-- UMASK -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 14</div>

<h2>What is umask?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
<code>umask</code> controls the default permission bits that are
removed when new files and directories are created.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>umask</pre>

<strong>Example</strong>

<pre>umask 022</pre>

</div>

<p>
A commonly encountered 022 umask results in:
</p>

<pre>New file       â†’ 644
New directory  â†’ 755</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"umask defines which permission bits are masked when new files
and directories are created. It helps control their default
permissions."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- SPECIAL PERMISSIONS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>

<h2>Special Permissions</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Linux supports special permission bits that provide additional
access-control behavior.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SUID</td>
<td>Executable runs with owner's privileges</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SGID</td>
<td>Executable/group inheritance behavior</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Sticky Bit</td>
<td>Controls deletion in shared directories</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common example</strong>

<pre>ls -ld /tmp</pre>

<p>
The <code>/tmp</code> directory commonly has the sticky bit.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- STICKY -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 16</div>

<h2>What is Sticky Bit?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
The sticky bit on a shared directory restricts users from deleting
or renaming files owned by other users, subject to the system's
permission model.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>ls -ld /tmp</pre>

<p>
You may see a permission pattern containing:
</p>

<pre>drwxrwxrwt</pre>

<p>
The <code>t</code> represents the sticky bit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"The sticky bit is commonly used on shared directories so users
cannot freely delete or rename files belonging to other users."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- ACL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 17</div>

<h2>What is ACL?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
ACL stands for Access Control List. It provides more granular
permissions than the traditional owner-group-other model.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>View ACL</strong>

<pre>getfacl file.txt</pre>

<strong>Set an ACL entry</strong>

<pre>setfacl -m u:nandu:r file.txt</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"ACL provides fine-grained access control by allowing additional
users or groups to receive specific permissions beyond the
traditional owner, group and others model."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>

<h2>What is SSH?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
SSH, or Secure Shell, is a protocol used to securely connect to
remote systems and execute commands.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>ssh user@server-ip</pre>

<strong>Using a private key</strong>

<pre>ssh -i key.pem user@server-ip</pre>

</div>

<div class="flow">

Local Machine

â†“

SSH

â†“

Remote Server

â†“

Authentication

â†“

Shell Access

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"SSH is a secure protocol used for remote login and command
execution. In cloud environments it is commonly used by
administrators and DevOps engineers to access Linux servers."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- SSH KEY -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 19</div>

<h2>SSH Key-Based Authentication</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
SSH key authentication uses a public-private key pair instead of
a password.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Private Key

â†“

Client

â†“

Public Key

â†“

Server

â†“

Authentication

</div>

<p>
The private key should remain secret, while the public key can be
placed on the server.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common key location</strong>

<pre>~/.ssh/id_rsa
~/.ssh/id_ed25519</pre>

<strong>Authorized public keys</strong>

<pre>~/.ssh/authorized_keys</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>ðŸ” Security Rule</strong>

<p>
Never share your private SSH key. Store it securely and protect
its permissions.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- SSH PERMISSIONS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 20</div>

<h2>Common SSH Permission Problem</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME</span>

<p>
SSH may reject a private key if its permissions are too open.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>chmod 400 key.pem</pre>

<p>
or, depending on the environment and security requirements:
</p>

<pre>chmod 600 key.pem</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"If SSH reports that a private key is too open, I would verify
the key's ownership and permissions and restrict access so that
unauthorized users cannot read the private key."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- FILE ACCESS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 21</div>

<h2>File vs Directory Permissions</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>File</th>
<th>Directory</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Read</td>
<td>Read file contents</td>
<td>List directory entries</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Write</td>
<td>Modify file</td>
<td>Create/delete/rename entries subject to other permissions</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Execute</td>
<td>Execute program/script</td>
<td>Access/traverse directory</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Read, write and execute have different practical meanings on
files and directories. On a directory, execute permission is
especially important because it allows traversal and access to
entries."
</p>

</div>

</article>
