<!-- REAL TIME -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application cannot read its configuration file</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

Application Error

â†“

ls -l config-file

â†“

Check Owner

â†“

Check Group

â†“

Check Permissions

â†“

Check Parent Directory

â†“

Fix Ownership/Permissions

â†“

Test Application

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>ls -l /app/config/application.yml

id appuser

namei -l /app/config/application.yml</pre>

<p>
Then, if appropriate:
</p>

<pre>sudo chown appuser:appgroup /app/config/application.yml
sudo chmod 640 /app/config/application.yml</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Don't simply use chmod 777</strong>

<p>
Fix the actual ownership or permission requirement instead of
giving everyone unrestricted access.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would first inspect the file ownership and permissions, then
verify the application's user and group. I would also check
permissions on the parent directories. I would make the smallest
permission or ownership change necessary and then test again."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- 777 -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 22</div>

<h2>Why should you avoid chmod 777?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
<code>777</code> gives read, write and execute permissions to the
owner, group and others.
</p>

<pre>777 â†’ rwxrwxrwx</pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>ðŸš¨ Security Risk</strong>

<p>
Giving everyone write and execute access can allow unauthorized
modification or execution and increase the attack surface.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I avoid chmod 777 because it grants excessive permissions to
everyone. I follow the principle of least privilege and grant
only the permissions required by the application or user."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- USER CREATION -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">COMMAND 23</div>

<h2>User & Group Management</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<div class="example">

<strong>Create user</strong>

<pre>sudo useradd nandu</pre>

<strong>Create group</strong>

<pre>sudo groupadd devops</pre>

<strong>Add user to group</strong>

<pre>sudo usermod -aG devops nandu</pre>

<strong>Verify</strong>

<pre>id nandu</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
Use <code>-aG</code> when adding supplementary groups so existing
supplementary group memberships are not unintentionally replaced.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- SECURITY BEST PRACTICES -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 25</div>

<h2>Linux Security Best Practices</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<ul>
<li>Follow the principle of least privilege.</li>
<li>Avoid unnecessary root access.</li>
<li>Use SSH keys where appropriate.</li>
<li>Protect private SSH keys.</li>
<li>Avoid chmod 777.</li>
<li>Keep systems and packages updated.</li>
<li>Use strong authentication practices.</li>
<li>Restrict unnecessary network access.</li>
<li>Monitor logs and authentication activity.</li>
<li>Use service-specific users where appropriate.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I follow least privilege, minimize root access, secure SSH
authentication, protect private keys, avoid excessive
permissions, keep systems updated and monitor logs for suspicious
activity."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<h2>Permission Denied â€” What Will You Check?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

â†“

â†“

Check Group

Check Parent Directories

â†“

Check ACL

â†“

Fix Minimum Required Permission

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>whoami
id
ls -l file.txt
namei -l /path/to/file
getfacl file.txt</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>
"First I identify the user running the command. Then I check the
file's owner, group and permissions. I also verify permissions on
parent directories and check ACLs if necessary. Finally, I apply
the minimum required permission or ownership change."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<h2>ðŸ§  FINAL REVISION â€” LINUX SECURITY</h2>

<div class="note">

<strong>User</strong>
â†’ Identity on Linux.

<br><br>

<strong>Group</strong>
â†’ Collection of users.

<br><br>

<strong>root</strong>
â†’ Superuser.

<br><br>

<strong>r</strong>
â†’ Read = 4.

<br><br>

<strong>w</strong>
â†’ Write = 2.

<br><br>

<strong>x</strong>
â†’ Execute = 1.

<br><br>

<strong>chmod</strong>
â†’ Change permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>chown</strong>
â†’ Change ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>chgrp</strong>
â†’ Change group.

<br><br>

<strong>sudo</strong>
â†’ Execute command with elevated privileges.

<br><br>

<strong>umask</strong>
â†’ Controls default permission mask.

<br><br>

<strong>SUID / SGID / Sticky Bit</strong>
â†’ Special permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>ACL</strong>
â†’ Fine-grained permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>SSH</strong>
â†’ Secure remote access.

<br><br>

<strong>chmod 755</strong>
â†’ rwxr-xr-x

<br><br>

<strong>chmod 644</strong>
â†’ rw-r--r--

<br><br>

<strong>chmod 777</strong>
â†’ rwxrwxrwx â†’ generally avoid.

<br><br>

<strong>ðŸ”¥ Permission Denied</strong>

<br><br>

â†“

id

â†“

â†“

â†“

<!-- FINAL INTERVIEW -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is chmod?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Changes file and directory permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is chown?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Changes file or directory ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 755 mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 644 mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Owner rw-, group r--, others r--.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Why avoid 777?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> It gives excessive permissions to everyone.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is sudo?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Allows authorized users to execute commands with
elevated privileges.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is umask?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Controls permission bits masked from newly
created files and directories.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is ACL?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Provides fine-grained access control beyond the
basic owner/group/other permission model.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is SSH?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Secure protocol for remote login and command
execution.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot Permission Denied?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Check current user, ownership, group,
permissions, parent directory permissions and ACLs, then apply
the minimum required fix.

</p>

</article>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>
<h2>What is SSH?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
SSH stands for <strong>Secure Shell</strong>. It is a network protocol
used to securely connect to and manage remote systems.
</p>

<pre>ssh username@server-ip</pre>

<div class="example">
<strong>Example:</strong>
<pre>ssh ec2-user@13.233.10.20</pre>
<p>
This establishes a secure remote shell session with the server.
</p>
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"SSH is a secure remote-access protocol used to connect to and
manage Linux servers over an encrypted connection."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 02 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>
<h2>Why is SSH important in DevOps?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<ul>
<li>Access Linux servers remotely</li>
<li>Perform troubleshooting</li>
<li>Manage cloud instances</li>
<li>Transfer files</li>
<li>Run administrative commands</li>
<li>Debug application and infrastructure issues</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">
Developer / DevOps Engineer
<br>â†“
<br>SSH
<br>â†“
<br>Cloud / Linux Server
<br>â†“
<br>Application / Infrastructure
</div>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>
<h2>Basic SSH Command</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ssh username@hostname</pre>

<p>
You can also specify a custom SSH port using <code>-p</code>.
</p>

<pre>ssh -p 2222 username@server-ip</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Remember:</strong>
<p>
Default SSH port is <strong>22</strong>.
</p>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>
<h2>Password Authentication vs SSH Key Authentication</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Password</th>
<th>SSH Key</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>User enters password</td>
<td>Uses cryptographic key pair</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Can be harder to manage at scale</td>
<td>Common for server automation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>More dependent on password security</td>
<td>Can provide stronger authentication</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"SSH key authentication uses a public and private key pair instead
of relying on a password. It is widely used for secure and automated
server access."
</p>
</div>

<!-- 05 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>
<h2>What is an SSH Key Pair?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
An SSH key pair consists of:
</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>Private key</strong> â€” kept secret on the client.</li>
<li><strong>Public key</strong> â€” placed on the remote server.</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">
Private Key
<br>ðŸ”
<br>Client
<br>â†“
<br>Authentication
<br>â†“
<br>Server
<br>ðŸ”“
<br>Public Key
</div>

<div class="warning">
<strong>âš ï¸ IMPORTANT</strong>
<p>
Never share your private key. Protect it like a password.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 06 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>
<h2>How do you generate an SSH key?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ssh-keygen -t ed25519</pre>

<p>
This generates an Ed25519 key pair on systems that support it.
RSA is also commonly encountered:
</p>

<pre>ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096</pre>

<p>
The generated files commonly include a private key and a public key
ending in <code>.pub</code>.
</p>
</article>

<!-- 07 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>
<h2>What is authorized_keys?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
On Linux servers, the user's SSH public keys are commonly stored in:
</p>

<pre>~/.ssh/authorized_keys</pre>

<p>
When a matching private key is used by the client, SSH can
authenticate the user without requiring the normal password flow.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"The authorized_keys file contains public keys that are allowed to
authenticate for a particular Linux user."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 08 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>
<h2>What are SSH file permissions?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</span>

<p>
SSH is sensitive to permissions on key files.
A private key should not be broadly readable by other users.
</p>

<pre>chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519</pre>

<p>
The SSH directory itself is commonly restricted as well:
</p>

<pre>chmod 700 ~/.ssh</pre>

<div class="warning">
<strong>Common problem:</strong>
<p>
If a private key is too permissive, SSH may refuse to use it.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 09 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>
<h2>How do you specify an SSH private key?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ssh -i my-key.pem ec2-user@server-ip</pre>

<p>
The <code>-i</code> option specifies the identity/private-key file.
</p>

<div class="example">
<strong>AWS example:</strong>
<pre>ssh -i nandu-key.pem ec2-user@&lt;EC2-PUBLIC-IP&gt;</pre>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 10 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 10</div>
<h2>What is SCP?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
SCP stands for <strong>Secure Copy Protocol</strong>. It is used to
securely copy files between systems over SSH.
</p>

<h3>Local â†’ Remote</h3>
<pre>scp file.txt user@server:/home/user/</pre>

<h3>Remote â†’ Local</h3>
<pre>scp user@server:/home/user/file.txt .</pre>

<h3>Directory</h3>
<pre>scp -r project/ user@server:/home/user/</pre>
</article>

<article class="card">

<h2>SCP vs SSH</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>SSH</th>
<th>SCP</th>
</tr>

<td>Remote shell/access</td>
<td>File transfer</td>

<td>Run commands remotely</td>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>
<h2>What is rsync?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<p>
<code>rsync</code> is commonly used to synchronize files and
directories efficiently between locations.
</p>

<pre>rsync -av project/ user@server:/home/user/project/</pre>

<p>
It can transfer only changed portions/files depending on the
synchronization scenario, making it useful for repeated transfers.
</p>
</article>

<!-- 13 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>
<h2>SCP vs rsync</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<table>
<tr>
<th>SCP</th>
<th>rsync</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Simple file copying</td>
<td>Synchronization</td>
</tr>

<td>Easy for one-time transfers</td>
<td>Useful for repeated transfers</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Less synchronization-focused</td>
<td>Efficient for changed data</td>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>SSH Connection Refused</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST PRACTICE</span>

<pre>ssh user@server-ip</pre>

<p>
If you receive:</p>

<pre>Connection refused</pre>

<p>
the target host may be reachable, but the connection is being
actively refused. Investigate whether the SSH service is running
and whether the expected port is listening.
</p>

<pre>
systemctl status ssh
systemctl status sshd
ss -lntp
</pre>

<div class="note">
<strong>Also check:</strong>
<ul>
<li>Correct IP address</li>
<li>Correct SSH port</li>
<li>Firewall rules</li>
<li>Cloud security-group rules</li>
<li>SSH service configuration</li>
</ul>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 15 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>SSH Connection Timed Out</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ssh: connect to host server port 22: Connection timed out</pre>

<p>
A timeout commonly points toward a network path or filtering
problem rather than simply an SSH authentication failure.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Client
<br>â†“
<br>Network
<br>â†“
<br>Firewall / Security Group
<br>â†“
<br>Server
<br>â†“
<br>Port 22
</div>

<p>
Check routing, security groups, firewalls, network ACLs and whether
the server is reachable.
</p>
</article>

<!-- 16 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>
<h2>Permission Denied (publickey)</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<pre>Permission denied (publickey)</pre>

<p>
This usually means SSH key authentication did not succeed.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>
<ul>
<li>Correct username</li>
<li>Correct private key</li>
<li>Correct server public key</li>
<li>Private-key permissions</li>
<li><code>authorized_keys</code></li>
<li>SSH configuration</li>
</ul>

<pre>chmod 600 my-key.pem</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>
<p>
"For public-key authentication failures, I verify the username,
private key, corresponding public key, authorized_keys and SSH
permissions before checking the SSH daemon configuration."
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 17 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 17</div>
<h2>How do you debug SSH in detail?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ssh -v user@server-ip</pre>

<p>
For more detailed debugging:
</p>

<pre>ssh -vvv user@server-ip</pre>

<p>
Verbose output can help identify where authentication or connection

</p>

<!-- 18 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>
<h2>What is SSH Agent?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>ssh-agent</code> can hold private keys in memory so that SSH
operations can use them without repeatedly supplying the key
passphrase.
</p>

<pre>
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
</pre>

<p>
This is especially useful when working with multiple SSH operations
during a session.
</p>
</article>

<!-- 19 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 19</div>
<h2>What is known_hosts?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
SSH commonly stores information about previously contacted servers
in:
</p>

<pre>~/.ssh/known_hosts</pre>

<p>
This helps SSH detect unexpected changes to a server's host key.
</p>

<div class="warning">
<strong>âš ï¸ Security Concept</strong>
<p>
Do not blindly ignore host-key warnings. They can indicate a
legitimate server change, but they can also indicate a
man-in-the-middle attack.
</p>
</div>
</article>

<!-- 20 -->

<article class="card">
<div class="number">QUESTION 20</div>
<h2>What is the SSH configuration file?</h2>
<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
The client-side configuration is commonly:
</p>

<pre>~/.ssh/config</pre>

<p>
It allows convenient host-specific settings.
</p>

<pre>
Host myserver
    HostName 192.168.1.20
    User ubuntu
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
</pre>

<p>
Then connect simply with:</p>

<pre>ssh myserver</pre>

</article>

<article class="card">

<br>â†“

<p>
In modern CI/CD pipelines, dedicated deployment mechanisms and

</p>

<article class="card">
<div class="number">ðŸ§  FINAL REVISION</div>
<h2>SSH & Remote Access Cheat Sheet</h2>

<div class="note">

<strong>SSH</strong>
â†’ Secure remote access.

<br><br>

<strong>Port 22</strong>
â†’ Default SSH port.

<br><br>

<strong>ssh user@server</strong>
â†’ Connect to remote server.

<br><br>

<strong>ssh -i key.pem user@server</strong>
â†’ Use specific private key.

<br><br>

<strong>ssh -v</strong>
â†’ Verbose debugging.

<br><br>

<strong>authorized_keys</strong>
â†’ Stores allowed public keys.

<br><br>

<strong>known_hosts</strong>
â†’ Stores known server host-key information.

<br><br>

<strong>SCP</strong>
â†’ Secure file copy.

<br><br>

<strong>rsync</strong>
â†’ Efficient file synchronization.

<br><br>

<strong>chmod 600 private-key</strong>
â†’ Restrict private-key permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>Connection refused</strong>
â†’ Check service/port/listener/firewall.

<br><br>

<strong>Connection timed out</strong>
â†’ Check network path/firewall/security controls.

<br><br>

<strong>Permission denied (publickey)</strong>
â†’ Check user/key/authorized_keys/permissions.

</div>
</article>

<!-- 23 -->

<article class="card">
<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>
<strong>Q:</strong> What is SSH?<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A secure protocol for remote access to systems.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is the default SSH port?<br> <strong>A:</strong> 22.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is the difference between public and private keys?<br> <strong>A:</strong> The public key is placed on the server; the private
key remains secret with the client.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is SCP?<br> <strong>A:</strong> A command used to securely copy files over SSH.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> SCP vs rsync?<br> <strong>A:</strong> SCP is simple file copying; rsync is designed for
efficient synchronization.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does Permission denied (publickey) mean?<br> <strong>A:</strong> SSH public-key authentication failed.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you debug SSH?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Use <code>ssh -v</code> or <code>ssh -vvv</code>
and check keys, usernames, permissions and server configuration.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Connection timed out vs refused?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Timeout commonly indicates a network/filtering
issue; refused means the destination actively rejected the connection,
often because the service is not listening or access is being rejected.

</p>
</article>

</main>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux storage is used to store operating system files,

Physical Disk

â†“

Partition

â†“

Filesystem

â†“

Mount Point

â†“

Files & Directories

<h2>What is a Block Device?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A block device provides storage that can be accessed in fixed-size

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Mounting makes a filesystem available at a directory in the

â†“

<div class="answer">

<p>
UUID stands for Universally Unique Identifier. Filesystems can

<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>

<h2>What is an Inode?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
An inode stores metadata about a filesystem object such as file
type, permissions, ownership and timestamps, along with pointers
to the file's data blocks.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Check inode usage</strong>

<pre>df -i</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ Real-Time Problem</strong>

<p>
A server can report "No space left on device" even when
<code>df -h</code> shows free disk space if the filesystem has
run out of inodes.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"An inode stores filesystem metadata about a file. If a filesystem
runs out of inodes, new files may not be created even when there
is still free disk capacity."
</p>

</div>

<!-- DISK FULL -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Disk is 100% full. What will you do?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<div class="flow">

Disk Alert

â†“

df -h

â†“

Identify Full Filesystem

â†“

du -sh *

â†“

Find Large Directories

â†“

Check Logs / Temporary Files

â†“

Clean Safely

â†“

Verify df -h Again

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>Step 1 â€” Check filesystem usage</strong>

<pre>df -h</pre>

<strong>Step 2 â€” Find large directories</strong>

<pre>sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var</pre>

<strong>Step 3 â€” Check logs</strong>

<pre>sudo du -sh /var/log/*</pre>

<strong>Step 4 â€” Check inode usage</strong>

<pre>df -i</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Never blindly delete files</strong>

<p>
Do not randomly remove system files or active application files.
First identify what is consuming space and understand whether it
is safe to remove, rotate or archive it.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"First I would use df -h to identify the full filesystem. Then I
would use du to locate large directories or files. I would also
check inode usage with df -i. After identifying the cause, I would
safely clean, rotate or archive unnecessary data and verify the
available space again."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- DELETED FILE -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>df shows high usage but du doesn't show the same usage</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
One possible cause is a deleted file that is still held open by a
running process.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Find deleted-but-open files</strong>

<pre>sudo lsof +L1</pre>

</div>

<div class="flow">

File Deleted

â†“

Process Still Has File Open

â†“

Disk Blocks Still Occupied

â†“

df Shows Usage

â†“

du Does Not Show Deleted File

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"If df shows significantly more usage than du, I would investigate
deleted files that are still held open by running processes using
lsof. The disk space is released when the process closes the file."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- STORAGE TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ DEVOPS TROUBLESHOOTING</div>

<h2>New Disk Attached but Not Visible in Application</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<div class="flow">

Disk Attached

â†“

lsblk

â†“

Partition?

â†“

Filesystem?

â†“

â†“

â†“

</div>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Answer</strong>

<p>
"I would first confirm that Linux detects the block device using
lsblk. Then I would check whether it has a filesystem, verify the
mount point and confirm that the filesystem is mounted. Finally,
I would verify /etc/fstab if persistent mounting is required and
check whether the application is using the correct path."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- FINAL QUESTIONS -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you check disk usage?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>df -h</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you find which directory is consuming space?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Use <code>du</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> df vs du?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> df shows filesystem usage; du shows file and
directory usage.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you list disks?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> <code>lsblk</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is mounting?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Attaching a filesystem to a directory.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is /etc/fstab?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Persistent filesystem mount configuration.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is an inode?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> A filesystem data structure containing metadata
about a file.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What happens if inodes are exhausted?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> New files may not be created even if disk
capacity is still available.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is LVM?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Logical Volume Manager, used for flexible
storage management.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What do PV, VG and LV mean?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Physical Volume, Volume Group and Logical Volume.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot a full disk?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> df -h â†’ du â†’ inspect logs/files â†’ df -i â†’
check deleted open files â†’ clean safely â†’ verify again.

</p>

</article>

<!-- REDIRECTION -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">CONCEPT 13</div>

<h2>Input and Output Redirection</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux provides operators to redirect command input and output.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Operator</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>&gt;</code></td>
<td>Write output to a file and overwrite it</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>&gt;&gt;</code></td>
<td>Append output to a file</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>&lt;</code></td>
<td>Use a file as command input</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>2&gt;</code></td>
<td>Redirect standard error</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Examples</strong>

<pre>ls > files.txt

echo "hello" >> app.log

command 2> error.log

command > output.log 2>&1</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
<code>&gt;</code> overwrites the destination file.
Use <code>&gt;&gt;</code> when you want to append instead.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux redirection allows command input and output to be
redirected. The greater-than operator writes or overwrites a
file, double greater-than appends output, and 2> redirects
standard error."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<!-- DEVOPS LOG FLOW -->

<!-- ===================================================== -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application is throwing errors. How would you check the logs?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<div class="flow">

Application

â†“

Log File

â†“

tail

â†“

grep

â†“

wc / sort / awk

â†“

Identify Problem

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>Step 1 â€” Watch recent logs</strong>

<pre>tail -f app.log</pre>

<strong>Step 2 â€” Find errors</strong>

<pre>grep "ERROR" app.log</pre>

<strong>Step 3 â€” Count errors</strong>

<pre>grep "ERROR" app.log | wc -l</pre>

<strong>Step 4 â€” Search recursively</strong>

<pre>grep -r "ERROR" /var/log/</pre>

<strong>Step 5 â€” Extract useful information</strong>

<pre>grep "ERROR" app.log | awk '{print $1,$2,$NF}'</pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"First I would inspect the latest logs using tail or tail -f.
Then I would use grep to filter ERROR or WARN messages. If
necessary, I would combine grep with wc, sort or awk to count,
sort or extract useful information. Based on the error pattern,
I would investigate the application, system or dependency
causing the issue."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<h2>â­ Important DevOps Command Combinations</h2>

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUICK INTERVIEW</div>

<h2>â­â­â­ Quick Questions</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is cat?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Displays file contents and can concatenate
files.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> cat vs less?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> cat prints content directly; less provides
interactive viewing of large files.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> head?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Displays the beginning of a file.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> tail?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Displays the end of a file.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Why is tail -f important?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> It continuously follows new log entries.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is grep?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Searches text or patterns in files/output.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is a pipe?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Passes output from one command to another.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is awk?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Powerful text-processing and field-extraction
tool.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is sed?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Stream editor used for text transformation and
replacement.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does >> do?

<br>
<strong>A:</strong> Appends output to a file.

</p>

</article>

<h1>Linux <span>Users, Groups & Permissions</span></h1>

<!-- 01 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 01</div>

<h2>Why does Linux use Users and Groups?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux uses users and groups to control who can access resources
and what actions they are allowed to perform.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User

â†“

Group Membership

â†“

File Ownership

â†“

Permissions

â†“

Access

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"Linux uses users and groups to implement access control.
Files and directories have ownership and permissions that determine
which users can read, modify or execute them."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 02 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 02</div>

<h2>How do you check the current user?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>whoami</pre>

<p>
The <code>whoami</code> command prints the username associated with
the current session.
</p>

<pre>id</pre>

<p>
The <code>id</code> command provides the user ID, primary group and
supplementary group information.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Useful commands:</strong>

<pre>
whoami
id
groups
</pre>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 03 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 03</div>

<h2>What is UID and GID?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux internally identifies users and groups using numeric IDs.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Term</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>UID</td>
<td>User ID</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>GID</td>
<td>Group ID</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre>id username</pre>

<p>
This displays the UID, primary GID and supplementary groups.
</p>

</article>

<!-- 04 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 04</div>

<h2>How do you create a user?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>sudo useradd username</pre>

<p>
On many systems, administrators then configure a password:</p>

<pre>sudo passwd username</pre>

<p>
A more user-friendly command on many Linux distributions is:</p>

<pre>sudo adduser username</pre>

<div class="note">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
The exact availability and behavior of <code>adduser</code> versus
<code>useradd</code> depends on the Linux distribution.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 05 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 05</div>

<h2>How do you delete a user?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>sudo userdel username</pre>

<p>
To remove the user's home directory as part of deletion:</p>

<pre>sudo userdel -r username</pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Be careful</strong>

<p>
The <code>-r</code> option can remove the user's home directory
and associated local files. Use it only when appropriate.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 06 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 06</div>

<h2>How do you modify a user?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>sudo usermod [options] username</pre>

<h3>Example: Add user to a group</h3>

<pre>sudo usermod -aG developers username</pre>

<p>
The <code>-aG</code> combination appends the user to supplementary
groups without removing existing supplementary group memberships.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important</strong>

<p>
Using <code>-G</code> without <code>-a</code> can replace the user's
supplementary group list.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 07 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 07</div>

<h2>What is a Linux group?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A group is a collection of users used to simplify access control.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example:</strong>

<p>
Instead of giving permissions separately to 10 developers, you can
create a <code>developers</code> group and assign permissions to
the group.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 08 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 08</div>

<h2>How do you create a group?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>sudo groupadd developers</pre>

<p>
Check group membership:</p>

<pre>groups username</pre>

<p>
Or:</p>

<pre>id username</pre>

</article>

<!-- 09 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 09</div>

<h2>What are /etc/passwd, /etc/group and /etc/shadow?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>File</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/etc/passwd</td>
<td>User account information</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/etc/group</td>
<td>Group information</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>/etc/shadow</td>
<td>Password hashes and password aging information</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Security</strong>

<p>
The shadow file contains sensitive authentication information and
should be protected from unauthorized access.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 10 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 10</div>

<h2>What is sudo?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>sudo</code> allows an authorized user to execute commands with
elevated privileges, according to the system's sudo configuration.
</p>

<pre>sudo systemctl restart nginx</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"sudo allows authorized users to execute specific commands with
elevated privileges without needing to log in directly as the
root user."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 11 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 11</div>

<h2>What is root?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
The root account is the traditional Linux superuser account with
extremely broad administrative privileges.
</p>

<p>
Because root can modify critical system resources, normal
administration should use controlled privilege escalation where
possible.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ DevOps Best Practice</strong>

<p>
Avoid running everything as root. Use least privilege and
<code>sudo</code> where appropriate.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 12 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 12</div>

<h2>What are File Permissions?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
Linux permissions define what the owner, group and others can do
with a file or directory.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
<th>Numeric</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>r</td>
<td>Read</td>
<td>4</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>w</td>
<td>Write</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>x</td>
<td>Execute</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>

</table>

</article>

<!-- 13 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 13</div>

<h2>Explain rwx permissions</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY COMMON</span>

<pre>-rwxr-xr--</pre>

<p>
The permissions are divided into three groups:
</p>

<div class="flow">

Owner
â†’ rwx

Group
â†’ r-x

Others
â†’ r--

</div>

<p>
Therefore:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Owner â†’ read, write, execute</li>
<li>Group â†’ read, execute</li>
<li>Others â†’ read only</li>
</ul>

</article>

<!-- 14 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 14</div>

<h2>What does the first character mean?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>-rwxr-xr--</pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Character</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>-</td>
<td>Regular file</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>d</td>
<td>Directory</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>l</td>
<td>Symbolic link</td>
</tr>

</table>

<p>
The remaining nine characters represent owner, group and other
permissions.
</p>

</article>

<!-- 15 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 15</div>

<h2>What is chmod?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>chmod</code> changes file or directory permissions.
</p>

<h3>Symbolic</h3>

<pre>
chmod u+x script.sh
chmod g+w file.txt
chmod o-r file.txt
</pre>

<h3>Numeric</h3>

<pre>chmod 755 script.sh</pre>

</article>

<!-- 16 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 16</div>

<h2>Understand chmod 755</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</span>

<p>
Calculate each permission group:
</p>

<pre>
7 = 4 + 2 + 1 = rwx

5 = 4 + 1 = r-x

5 = 4 + 1 = r-x
</pre>

<p>
Therefore:</p>

<pre>chmod 755 script.sh</pre>

<div class="flow">

Owner â†’ rwx

Group â†’ r-x

Others â†’ r-x

</div>

</article>

<!-- 17 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 17</div>

<h2>Common Permission Values</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>644</td>
<td>Owner read/write, others read</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>755</td>
<td>Owner full access, others read/execute</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>700</td>
<td>Owner full access only</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>600</td>
<td>Owner read/write only</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<strong>Common use:</strong>

<p>
Private SSH keys commonly need restrictive permissions such as
<code>600</code>.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 18 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 18</div>

<h2>What is chown?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<p>
<code>chown</code> changes file ownership.
</p>

<pre>sudo chown user file.txt</pre>

<p>
Change owner and group:</p>

<pre>sudo chown user:developers file.txt</pre>

<p>
Recursive ownership change:</p>

<pre>sudo chown -R user:developers project/</pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Caution</strong>

<p>
Recursive ownership changes can affect many files. Always verify
the target path before using <code>-R</code>.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 19 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 19</div>

<h2>What is chgrp?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>chgrp</code> changes the group ownership of a file or directory.
</p>

<pre>sudo chgrp developers project/</pre>

<p>
In many cases, <code>chown user:group</code> is used when changing
both owner and group together.
</p>

</article>

<!-- 20 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 20</div>

<h2>How do you check ownership and permissions?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<pre>ls -l</pre>

<p>
Example:</p>

<pre>
-rwxr-xr-- 1 nandu developers 1200 Aug 12 deploy.sh
</pre>

<div class="flow">

Permissions
â†’ Owner
â†’ Group
â†’ Size
â†’ Date
â†’ File

</div>

</article>

<!-- 21 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Permission denied while running a script</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</span>

<pre>./deploy.sh</pre>

<p>
If you get:</p>

<pre>Permission denied</pre>

<p>
First inspect permissions:</p>

<pre>ls -l deploy.sh</pre>

<p>
If execute permission is missing:</p>

<pre>chmod +x deploy.sh</pre>

<p>
Then:</p>

<pre>./deploy.sh</pre>

</article>

<!-- 22 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Application cannot write to a directory</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
Check:
</p>

<pre>
ls -ld /path/to/directory
id application-user
</pre>

<p>
Verify:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Directory owner</li>
<li>Group ownership</li>
<li>Write permission</li>
<li>Application's running user</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Strong Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I first identify which Linux user the application runs as.
Then I check the directory's ownership and permissions and make
the smallest required permission or ownership change."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 23 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Why should we avoid chmod 777?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<pre>chmod 777 file</pre>

<p>
This gives read, write and execute permissions to owner, group
and others.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Security Risk</strong>

<p>
It grants broad access and violates least-privilege principles
in many situations. Do not use 777 as a default fix for permission
problems.
</p>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"I avoid chmod 777 because it grants excessive permissions.
Instead, I identify the required user or group and provide only
the minimum permissions necessary."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 24 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 24</div>

<h2>What is the principle of least privilege?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS + SECURITY</span>

<p>
Least privilege means giving users, processes and services only
the permissions they actually need.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Required Access

â†“

Minimum Permission

â†“

Reduced Attack Surface

â†“

Better Security

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>DevOps Example:</strong>

<p>
If an application only needs write access to one directory, do
not give it root access to the entire server.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 25 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 25</div>

<h2>File vs Directory Permissions</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</span>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Permission</th>
<th>File</th>
<th>Directory</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>r</td>
<td>Read file contents</td>
<td>List directory entries</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>w</td>
<td>Modify file</td>
<td>Create/delete/rename entries, subject to other controls</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>x</td>
<td>Execute program</td>
<td>Traverse/access directory</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="note">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Directory permissions behave differently from file permissions.
A directory's execute permission is especially important for
traversing/accessing paths.
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 26 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">QUESTION 26</div>

<h2>What is umask?</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
<code>umask</code> influences the default permissions assigned to
newly created files and directories by removing permission bits
from their base creation modes.
</p>

<pre>umask</pre>

<p>
Example:</p>

<pre>umask 022</pre>

<p>
The exact resulting permissions depend on whether a file or
directory is being created and the system's base mode.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"umask defines which permission bits are masked when new files
and directories are created."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 27 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>Docker / DevOps Permission Problem</h2>

<span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<p>
A containerized application writes files to a host-mounted
directory, but the application receives permission denied.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Container Process User

â†“

Mounted Volume

â†“

Host Directory

â†“

Host Ownership / Permissions

</div>

<p>
Check the UID/GID used by the process and the ownership and
permissions of the mounted directory.
</p>

<pre>
ls -ln /host/path
id
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>ðŸŽ¤ Interview Answer</strong>

<p>
"In containerized environments, I check the UID/GID of the
application process and compare it with the ownership and
permissions of the mounted host directory."
</p>

</div>

</article>

<!-- 28 -->

<article class="card">

<div class="number">ðŸ§  FINAL REVISION</div>

<h2>Users, Groups & Permissions Cheat Sheet</h2>

<div class="note">

<strong>whoami</strong>
â†’ Current username.

<br><br>

<strong>id</strong>
â†’ UID, GID and group information.

<br><br>

<strong>useradd</strong>
â†’ Create user.

<br><br>

<strong>usermod</strong>
â†’ Modify user.

<br><br>

<strong>userdel</strong>
â†’ Delete user.

<br><br>

<strong>groupadd</strong>
â†’ Create group.

<br><br>

<strong>groups</strong>
â†’ Show group membership.

<br><br>

<strong>sudo</strong>
â†’ Controlled privilege escalation.

<br><br>

<strong>/etc/passwd</strong>
â†’ User account information.

<br><br>

<strong>/etc/group</strong>
â†’ Group information.

<br><br>

<strong>/etc/shadow</strong>
â†’ Sensitive password-related information.

<br><br>

<strong>chmod</strong>
â†’ Change permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>chown</strong>
â†’ Change owner/group ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>chgrp</strong>
â†’ Change group ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>r = 4</strong>
â†’ Read.

<br><br>

<strong>w = 2</strong>
â†’ Write.

<br><br>

<strong>x = 1</strong>
â†’ Execute.

<br><br>

<strong>755</strong>
â†’ rwx r-x r-x.

<br><br>

<strong>644</strong>
â†’ rw- r-- r--.

<br><br>

<strong>600</strong>
â†’ rw- --- ---.

<br><br>

<strong>Least Privilege</strong>
â†’ Give only required access.

<br><br>

<strong>Avoid chmod 777</strong>
â†’ Do not grant unnecessary broad permissions.

</div>

</article>

<!-- 29 -->

<article class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ FINAL INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</h2>

<p>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is UID?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Numeric identifier assigned to a Linux user.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is GID?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Numeric identifier assigned to a Linux group.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Difference between chmod and chown?<br> <strong>A:</strong> chmod changes permissions; chown changes ownership.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 755 mean?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Owner has rwx; group and others have r-x.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What does 644 mean?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Owner has rw-; group and others have r--.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Why chmod 777 is bad?<br> <strong>A:</strong> It grants broad read/write/execute access and can
create unnecessary security risk.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> What is sudo?<br> <strong>A:</strong> It allows authorized users to execute commands
with elevated privileges.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Where are Linux users stored?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Account information is commonly represented in <code>/etc/passwd</code>; sensitive password information is in <code>/etc/shadow</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> Why are groups useful?<br> <strong>A:</strong> They simplify permission management for multiple
users.

<br><br>

<strong>Q:</strong> How do you troubleshoot permission denied?<br> <strong>A:</strong> Check the current user, file ownership,
permissions, directory traversal permissions and application
runtime user before changing anything.

</p>

</article>

<h1>Git <span>Architecture</span></h1>

<p>
Working Directory, Staging Area, Local Repository,
Remote Repository, HEAD and the complete Git workflow.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>1. Explain Git Architecture.</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git architecture describes how Git manages our code from the
time we modify a file until the changes are stored in a remote
repository.
</p>

<p>
The main areas are:
</p>

<ol>
<li>Working Directory</li>
<li>Staging Area</li>
<li>Local Repository</li>
<li>Remote Repository</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">
<strong>Working Directory</strong>
<br>
Modify files
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†’</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>Staging Area</strong>
<br>
git add
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†’</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>Local Repository</strong>
<br>
git commit
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†’</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>Remote Repository</strong>
<br>
git push
</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>2. What is the Working Directory?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
The Working Directory is the actual folder where we work on
our project files.
</p>

<p>
When we create, modify or delete files, those changes initially
exist in the Working Directory.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example:</strong>

<pre>
project/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ app.py
â”œâ”€â”€ Dockerfile
â””â”€â”€ README.md
</pre>

<p>
Suppose we modify <code>app.py</code>. The modified file exists
in the Working Directory, but it is not yet staged or committed.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>3. What is the Staging Area?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
The Staging Area is an intermediate area where we select the
changes that should be included in the next commit.
</p>

<p>
We move changes from the Working Directory to the Staging Area
using <code>git add</code>.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git add app.py
</pre>

<p>
Now <code>app.py</code> is staged and ready to be committed.
</p>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Interview Point:</strong>

<p>
The staging area gives developers control over exactly which
changes should be included in the next commit.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>4. What is the Local Repository?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
The Local Repository is the Git repository stored on the
developer's local machine.
</p>

<p>
When we execute <code>git commit</code>, staged changes are
recorded in the local repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git add .
git commit -m "Add application changes"
</pre>

<p>
The commit is created locally. It has not necessarily been
sent to GitHub yet.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>5. What is the Remote Repository?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A Remote Repository is a Git repository hosted on another
system or service, such as GitHub.
</p>

<p>
It allows developers to share code and collaborate with
other team members.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git push origin main
</pre>

<p>
This sends local commits to the remote repository.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>6. Explain the complete Git workflow.</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A typical Git workflow starts with modifying files in the
Working Directory.
</p>

<p>
Then we stage the required changes using <code>git add</code>,
create a commit using <code>git commit</code>, and finally
send the commit to the Remote Repository using <code>git push</code>.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">
Working Directory
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“ git add</div>

<div class="box">
Staging Area
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“ git commit</div>

<div class="box">
Local Repository
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“ git push</div>

<div class="box">
Remote Repository
</div>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
# 1. Check changes
git status

# 2. Stage changes
git add .

# 3. Create commit
git commit -m "Update application"

# 4. Send to GitHub
git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>7. What happens internally when you run git add?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
When we run <code>git add</code>, Git takes the current version
of the selected changes from the Working Directory and places
them into the Staging Area.
</p>

<p>
It tells Git which changes should be included in the next commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git add app.py
</pre>

<pre>
Working Directory
       â†“
    git add
       â†“
Staging Area
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>8. What happens when you run git commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git commit</code> takes the staged changes and records them
as a new commit in the Local Repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git commit -m "Add login functionality"
</pre>

<p>
A commit is created with a unique commit ID/hash.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>9. What is the difference between git add and git commit?</h2>

<table class="compare">

<tr>
<th>git add</th>
<th>git commit</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Moves changes to staging area</td>
<td>Records staged changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not create a commit</td>
<td>Creates a new commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Working Directory â†’ Staging</td>
<td>Staging â†’ Local Repository</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git add .
git commit -m "Add feature"
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>10. What is the difference between git commit and git push?</h2>

<table class="compare">

<tr>
<th>git commit</th>
<th>git push</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates a commit locally</td>
<td>Sends commits to remote repository</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not require internet</td>
<td>Normally requires access to remote</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Local operation</td>
<td>Remote synchronization operation</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
<strong>Commit = save the version locally.</strong><br>
<strong>Push = send the commits to the remote repository.</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>11. What is HEAD in Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
HEAD is a reference that points to the current location in
the Git history, normally the latest commit of the currently
checked-out branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
main
  â†“
HEAD
  â†“
Latest Commit
</pre>

<p>
If we switch to another branch, HEAD normally moves to that branch.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>12. What is the .git directory?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
The <code>.git</code> directory contains Git's internal repository
metadata.
</p>

<p>
It stores information required for commits, branches, references,
configuration and Git's object database.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
my-project/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ app.py
â”œâ”€â”€ README.md
â”‚
â””â”€â”€ .git/
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important:</strong>

<p>
Deleting the <code>.git</code> directory removes the Git repository
metadata from that project directory.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>13. Why does Git use a staging area?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
The staging area allows us to choose exactly which changes should
go into the next commit.
</p>

<p>
This helps developers create clean and meaningful commits.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
app.py
README.md
config.yml

git add app.py README.md
git commit -m "Update application documentation"
</pre>

<p>
Here, only the selected files are included in the commit.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>14. What is the difference between local and remote repositories?</h2>

<table class="compare">

<tr>
<th>Local Repository</th>
<th>Remote Repository</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Exists on developer's machine</td>
<td>Hosted on a remote server/platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for local development</td>
<td>Used for sharing and collaboration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>git commit stores changes here</td>
<td>git push sends commits here</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</div>

<h2>15. How does Git fit into a DevOps CI/CD pipeline?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git usually acts as the source-control system for the DevOps pipeline.
A developer pushes code to GitHub, which can trigger a CI/CD pipeline.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">Developer</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Git / GitHub</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Build & Test</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Docker Image</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Deployment</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Real-time Example:</strong>

<p>
A developer pushes a change to GitHub. GitHub Actions or Jenkins
detects the change, runs tests, builds the application or Docker
image and continues the deployment pipeline.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>16. You committed a change but haven't pushed it. Where is it?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
The commit exists in the <strong>Local Repository</strong>.
It has not yet reached the Remote Repository.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
Working Directory
       â†“
Staging Area
       â†“
Local Repository  â† Commit exists here
       
Remote Repository â† Not updated yet
</pre>

</div>

<p>
To send it to the remote repository:
</p>

<pre>
git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>17. A developer says "I committed my code, so why can't my teammate see it?"</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Because <code>git commit</code> only stores the changes in the
developer's local repository.
</p>

<p>
The developer must push the commit to the remote repository.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

<p>
The teammate can then fetch or pull the updated changes.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- FOLLOW UP -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸŽ¯ FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS</div>

<h2>Interview Follow-ups</h2>

<ul>

<li>What is the difference between Working Directory and Staging Area?</li>

<li>What is the difference between Staging Area and Local Repository?</li>

<li>What happens internally during git add?</li>

<li>What happens internally during git commit?</li>

<li>What happens internally during git push?</li>

<li>What is HEAD?</li>

<li>What is a commit hash?</li>

<li>What is the .git directory?</li>

<li>Why does Git use a staging area?</li>

<li>What is the difference between git push and git pull?</li>

<li>What happens if you delete the .git directory?</li>

<li>How does Git integrate with Jenkins?</li>

<li>How does GitHub trigger a CI/CD pipeline?</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- QUICK REVISION -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ§  QUICK REVISION</div>

<h2>Git Architecture â€” One-Minute Revision</h2>

<div class="diagram">

<br>
Modify files
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“ git add</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>2. Staging Area</strong>
<br>
Select changes
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“ git commit</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>3. Local Repository</strong>
<br>
Store commits
</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“ git push</div>

<div class="box">

<br>
Share with team
</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>ðŸŽ¯ Interview Shortcut:</strong>

<p>
<strong>Working Directory â†’ git add â†’ Staging â†’ git commit â†’
Local Repository â†’ git push â†’ Remote Repository</strong>
</p>

<div class="icon">ðŸ”€</div>

<h1>Git <span>Basics</span></h1>

<p>
Core Git concepts, version control, Git vs GitHub,
Git workflow and essential interview fundamentals.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>1. What is Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git is a distributed version control system used to track changes
in source code and collaborate with multiple developers.
</p>

<p>
It allows developers to maintain different versions of their code,
create branches, merge changes and restore previous versions when required.
</p>

<div class="example">

<strong>Example:</strong>

<pre>
Developer
   â†“
Modify Code
   â†“
git add
   â†“
git commit
   â†“
Local Repository
   â†“
git push
   â†“
GitHub
</pre>

</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ DevOps Point:</strong>

Git is the foundation of many CI/CD pipelines because tools like
Jenkins and GitHub Actions can trigger builds whenever code is pushed.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>2. Why is Git used in DevOps?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git provides version control and collaboration for application
and infrastructure code.
</p>

<p>
In DevOps, Git can store application source code,
Dockerfiles, Kubernetes manifests and Terraform configurations.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<strong>Real-time DevOps Example:</strong>

<pre>
Developer pushes code
        â†“
GitHub
        â†“
CI Pipeline
        â†“
Build
        â†“
Test
        â†“
Docker Image
        â†“
Deployment
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>3. What is Version Control?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Version control is a system that records changes made to files
over time so that developers can track, compare and restore
different versions.
</p>

<p>
Git is a distributed version control system.
</p>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Simple Example:</strong>

<p>
Suppose today's application works correctly but tomorrow a developer
introduces a bug. Git allows us to identify the change and restore
the previous working version.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>4. What is the difference between Git and GitHub?</h2>

<table class="compare">

<tr>
<th>Git</th>
<th>GitHub</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Version control system</td>
<td>Cloud platform for hosting Git repositories</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs locally</td>
<td>Runs as a web service</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Tracks code changes</td>
<td>Provides collaboration features</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CLI based</td>
<td>Web UI + Git integration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Created by Linus Torvalds</td>
<td>GitHub is a hosting/collaboration platform</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview line:</strong>

<p>
"Git is the version control tool, whereas GitHub is a platform
that hosts Git repositories and provides collaboration features
such as pull requests, issues and code reviews."
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>5. Is Git centralized or distributed?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git is a <strong>distributed version control system (DVCS)</strong>.
</p>

<p>
Every developer's local repository contains the project's history,
so developers can perform many Git operations without depending
on the remote repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
GitHub Remote Repository
          â†‘
       git push
          â†‘
Developer Local Repository
          â†‘
       git commit
          â†‘
      Working Code
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>6. What are the main areas in a Git workflow?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
The commonly discussed Git workflow contains three local areas:
</p>

<ol>
<li><strong>Working Directory</strong></li>
<li><strong>Staging Area</strong></li>
<li><strong>Local Repository</strong></li>
</ol>

<p>
There is also a <strong>Remote Repository</strong>, such as a repository
hosted on GitHub.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
Working Directory
       â†“
    git add
       â†“
Staging Area
       â†“
  git commit
       â†“
Local Repository
       â†“
   git push
       â†“
Remote Repository
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>7. What is a Git repository?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A Git repository is a directory that contains the project's files
and Git metadata used to track changes and maintain version history.
</p>

<p>
The hidden <code>.git</code> directory stores important Git metadata.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
my-project/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ app.py
â”œâ”€â”€ README.md
â””â”€â”€ .git/
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>8. What does git init do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git init</code> initializes a new Git repository
inside the current directory.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
mkdir my-project
cd my-project

git init
</pre>

<p>
After running this command, Git creates a hidden
<code>.git</code> directory.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>9. What does git clone do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git clone</code> creates a local copy of an existing
remote Git repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git clone https://github.com/user/project.git
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Unlike <code>git init</code>, clone is normally used when
the repository already exists remotely.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>10. What is a Git commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A commit is a snapshot of the staged changes stored in the
local Git repository.
</p>

<p>
Each commit has a unique identifier called a commit hash.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git add app.py

git commit -m "Add application configuration"
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>11. What is the purpose of git status?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git status</code> shows the current state of the working
directory and staging area.
</p>

<p>
It helps us identify modified, untracked and staged files.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>12. What is the purpose of git log?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git log</code> displays the commit history of a repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git log

git log --oneline
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- REAL TIME -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>13. A developer accidentally deleted a file. How can Git help?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
First, check the repository status and history.
If the deleted file was previously committed, Git can restore
the version from a previous commit.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status

git log -- filename

git restore filename
</pre>

</div>

<p>
The exact recovery command depends on whether the deletion is
committed or still only present in the working directory.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- FOLLOW UP -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸŽ¯ FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS</div>

<h2>Interview Follow-ups You Should Prepare</h2>

<ul>

<li>What is the difference between git pull and git fetch?</li>

<li>What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?</li>

<li>What is the difference between git reset and git revert?</li>

<li>What is a branch in Git?</li>

<li>What is HEAD in Git?</li>

<li>What is a detached HEAD state?</li>

<li>What is .gitignore?</li>

<li>How do you undo the last commit?</li>

<li>How do you recover a deleted branch?</li>

<li>How do you handle a merge conflict?</li>

</ul>
