<div class="icon">ðŸŒ¿</div>

<h1>Git <span>Branches & Merging</span></h1>

<p>
Git branches, switching, merging, fast-forward merge,
three-way merge, conflicts and real-time DevOps workflows.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>1. What is a Git branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A Git branch is a movable pointer to a sequence of commits.
It allows developers to work on different features or fixes
independently without directly affecting the main branch.
</p>

<p>
In simple terms, a branch provides an isolated line of
development.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
main
  |
  A
  |
  B
  |
  C
</pre>

<p>
We can create a feature branch from the current commit:
</p>

<pre>
git branch feature-login
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong>

<p>
Branches are mainly used to isolate development work such as
features, bug fixes and release work.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>2. Why do we use Git branches?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
We use branches so multiple developers can work on different
features or fixes independently.
</p>

<p>
This reduces the risk of directly changing production or
main development code.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
main
 |
 +---- feature-login
 |
 +---- feature-payment
 |
 +---- bugfix
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>DevOps Example:</strong>

<p>
One developer works on a login feature while another fixes a
production bug. Both can work on separate branches and later
merge their completed changes into the appropriate branch.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>3. How do you create a new branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
We can create a branch using <code>git branch</code>.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git branch feature-login
</pre>

<p>
This creates the branch but does not switch to it.
</p>

<p>
To create and switch to a branch:</p>

<pre>
git switch -c feature-login
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>4. How do you switch between branches?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Modern Git recommends <code>git switch</code> for changing
branches.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git switch feature-login
</pre>

<p>
Older Git workflows commonly use:</p>

<pre>
git checkout feature-login
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
<code>git switch</code> is specifically designed for branch
switching, while <code>git checkout</code> has multiple uses.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>5. How do you create and switch to a branch in one command?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git switch -c feature-login
</pre>

<p>
Older syntax:</p>

<pre>
git checkout -b feature-login
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>6. How do you list Git branches?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>List local branches:</p>

<pre>
git branch
</pre>

<p>List local and remote branches:</p>

<pre>
git branch -a
</pre>

<p>List remote branches:</p>

<pre>
git branch -r
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>7. How do you rename a branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Rename the current branch:
</p>

<pre>
git branch -m new-name
</pre>

<p>
Rename another local branch:
</p>

<pre>
git branch -m old-name new-name
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>8. How do you delete a Git branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Delete a merged local branch:
</p>

<pre>
git branch -d feature-login
</pre>

<p>
Force delete a branch:
</p>

<pre>
git branch -D feature-login
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong>

<p>
<code>-d</code> performs a safer deletion and normally refuses
to delete a branch whose changes have not been merged.
</p>

<p>
<code>-D</code> forces the deletion.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>9. What is Git merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git merge combines changes from one branch into another branch.
</p>

<p>
For example, after completing a feature, we can merge the
feature branch into the main branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git switch main

git merge feature-login
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>10. Explain a typical feature branch workflow.</h2>

<div class="answer">

<ol>
<li>Start from the main branch.</li>
<li>Create a feature branch.</li>
<li>Develop the feature.</li>
<li>Commit the changes.</li>
<li>Push the branch to the remote repository.</li>
<li>Create a Pull Request.</li>
<li>Review and test the changes.</li>
<li>Merge into the target branch.</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git switch main

git pull origin main

git switch -c feature-login

# Make changes

git add .

git commit -m "Add login feature"

git push -u origin feature-login
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>11. What is a fast-forward merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A fast-forward merge occurs when the target branch has not
received any new commits after the feature branch was created.
</p>

<p>
Git can simply move the target branch pointer forward without
creating an additional merge commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">A</div>
<div class="arrow">â†’</div>
<div class="box">B</div>
<div class="arrow">â†’</div>
<div class="box">C</div>

<p>Feature branch contains the latest commits.</p>

<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">main pointer moves forward</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>12. What is a three-way merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A three-way merge occurs when both the target branch and the
feature branch have diverged after a common ancestor.
</p>

<p>
Git uses three commits to perform the merge:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Common ancestor</li>
<li>Tip of the current branch</li>
<li>Tip of the branch being merged</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
        feature
           C
          /
A ---- B
          \
           D
          main
</pre>

<p>
Because both branches contain different commits after the
common ancestor, Git may create a merge commit.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>13. What is a merge conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically determine
which changes should be kept while combining branches.
</p>

<p>
This commonly happens when two branches modify the same part
of the same file differently.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
<<<<<<< HEAD
production configuration
=======
development configuration
>>>>>>> feature
</pre>

<p>
The developer must manually decide which version should remain.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</div>

<h2>14. How do you resolve a merge conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<ol>
<li>Identify the conflicted files.</li>
<li>Open the files and inspect conflict markers.</li>
<li>Choose or combine the correct changes.</li>
<li>Remove the conflict markers.</li>
<li>Stage the resolved file.</li>
<li>Complete the merge commit if required.</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status

# Fix the conflicted file

git add app.py

git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Never blindly accept changes during a production conflict.
Understand which code should actually be preserved.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>15. What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>git merge</th>
<th>git rebase</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Combines branch histories</td>
<td>Replays commits on top of another base</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can create a merge commit</td>
<td>Usually creates a linear history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Preserves existing commit topology</td>
<td>Rewrites commit history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Generally safer for shared branches</td>
<td>Should be used carefully on shared branches</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Shortcut:</strong>

<p>
<strong>Merge = combine histories.</strong><br>
<strong>Rebase = move/replay commits onto a new base.</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>16. How do you push a new branch to GitHub?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
After creating and committing the branch locally, use:
</p>

<pre>
git push -u origin feature-login
</pre>

<p>
The <code>-u</code> option establishes the upstream relationship,
making future pushes and pulls easier.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>17. What is the difference between a local branch and a remote branch?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Local Branch</th>
<th>Remote-Tracking Branch</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Exists in the local repository</td>
<td>Represents the state of a branch on a remote</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: main</td>
<td>Example: origin/main</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for local development</td>
<td>Used to track remote branch state</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>18. Why should developers avoid directly working on the main branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Direct development on main can introduce incomplete,
untested or unstable changes into the shared branch.
</p>

<p>
Feature branches allow changes to be developed, tested,
reviewed and validated before merging.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">Feature Branch</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Code Review</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">CI Tests</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Main</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>19. How would you handle a production bug while working on a feature?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
I would not mix the production fix with my unfinished feature.
I would create a separate bug-fix or hotfix branch from the
appropriate production branch.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git switch main

git pull origin main

git switch -c hotfix-login

# Fix the issue

git add .

git commit -m "Fix login production issue"

git push -u origin hotfix-login
</pre>

<p>
Then the change can go through review, testing and deployment.
</p>

</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q20 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ CI/CD SCENARIO</div>

<h2>20. How are Git branches used in CI/CD?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Different branches can trigger different CI/CD workflows
depending on the organization's branching strategy.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">feature/*</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>
<div class="box">Build + Test</div>

<div class="box">develop</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>
<div class="box">Integration Environment</div>

<div class="box">main</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>
<div class="box">Production Pipeline</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Example:</strong>

<p>
A feature branch may run unit tests and security scans.
A merge into main may trigger the production deployment pipeline,
depending on the organization's CI/CD design.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>21. You are on the wrong branch and have uncommitted changes. What should you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
First, I would check the status and decide whether the changes
should be committed or temporarily stashed.
</p>

<pre>
git status
git stash
</pre>

<p>
Then switch to the correct branch:</p>

<pre>
git switch correct-branch
</pre>

<p>
If needed, restore the changes:</p>

<pre>
git stash pop
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>22. What happens if two developers modify the same lines?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Git may detect a merge conflict when their branches are merged.
The conflicting file must be reviewed manually and the correct
changes selected before the merge can be completed.
</p>

</div>

</div>

Create + switch

Delete merged branch

    â†“
Force delete

Merge feature into current branch

Check current branch / changes

</strong>
</p>

<div class="icon">ðŸ”€</div>

<h1>Git <span>Commands</span></h1>

<p>
Essential Git commands for DevOps interviews, daily development,
branch management, collaboration and CI/CD workflows.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>1. What is git init?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git init</code> initializes a new Git repository in the
current directory.
</p>

<p>
It creates a hidden <code>.git</code> directory that contains
Git's repository metadata.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
mkdir my-project
cd my-project

git init
</pre>

<p>Check the repository:</p>

<pre>
git status
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong>

<p>
<code>git init</code> is normally used when starting a new local
project that is not already a Git repository.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>2. What is git clone?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git clone</code> creates a local copy of an existing
remote Git repository.
</p>

<p>
It downloads the repository, its history and branches needed
for normal development.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git clone https://github.com/example/project.git
</pre>

<p>
After cloning, Git automatically creates a directory containing
the project.
</p>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
<strong>git init = create a new repository</strong><br>
<strong>git clone = copy an existing repository</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>3. What is git status?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git status</code> shows the current state of the working
directory and staging area.
</p>

<p>
It tells us which files are modified, staged, untracked or
ready to be committed.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status
</pre>

<p>Typical output can show:</p>

<pre>
modified: app.py
untracked: Dockerfile
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>DevOps Usage:</strong>

<p>
Before committing changes, I usually run <code>git status</code>
to verify exactly what has changed.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>4. What is git add?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git add</code> moves changes from the Working Directory
into the Staging Area.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git add app.py
</pre>

<p>Stage all modified files:</p>

<pre>
git add .
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
<code>git add</code> does not create a commit. It only prepares
the selected changes for the next commit.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>5. What is git commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git commit</code> records the staged changes in the
Local Repository as a new commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git commit -m "Add login feature"
</pre>

<p>
Every commit receives a unique commit identifier/hash.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>6. What is git push?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git push</code> uploads local commits to a remote repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git push origin main
</pre>

<p>
Here <code>origin</code> is the remote repository name and
<code>main</code> is the branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
<strong>commit â†’ local repository</strong><br>
<strong>push â†’ remote repository</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>7. What is git pull?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git pull</code> gets changes from the remote repository
and integrates them into the current local branch.
</p>

<p>
Conceptually, it performs a fetch followed by an integration
operation, commonly a merge.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git pull origin main
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Real-time Example:</strong>

<p>
If another developer pushed changes to GitHub, I can use
<code>git pull</code> to bring those changes into my local branch.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>8. What is git fetch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git fetch</code> downloads new commits and references
from the remote repository without automatically merging them
into the current working branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git fetch origin
</pre>

<p>
After fetching, we can inspect the remote changes before deciding
whether to merge or rebase them.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>9. git pull vs git fetch?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>git fetch</th>
<th>git pull</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Downloads remote changes</td>
<td>Downloads and integrates changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not directly update current branch</td>
<td>Usually updates current branch</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Safer for inspecting changes first</td>
<td>Convenient for regular synchronization</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Shortcut:</strong>

<p>
<strong>fetch = download and inspect</strong><br>
<strong>pull = download and integrate</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>10. What is git diff?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git diff</code> shows the differences between different
states of files.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git diff
</pre>

<p>
Shows unstaged changes.
</p>

<pre>
git diff --staged
</pre>

<p>
Shows changes that are currently staged.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>11. What is git log?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git log</code> displays the commit history of the repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git log
</pre>

<p>Compact history:</p>

<pre>
git log --oneline
</pre>

<p>Graph view:</p>

<pre>
git log --oneline --graph --all
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>12. What is git remote?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git remote</code> is used to manage connections between
the local repository and remote repositories.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git remote -v
</pre>

<p>
This displays the URLs configured for the remote repository.
</p>

<pre>
git remote add origin https://github.com/example/project.git
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>13. What is git show?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git show</code> displays information about a specific
Git object, commonly a commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git show
</pre>

<p>Show a specific commit:</p>

<pre>
git show abc123
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ VERY USEFUL</div>

<h2>14. What is git stash?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git stash</code> temporarily stores uncommitted changes
so that we can work on another branch without committing
unfinished work.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git stash
</pre>

<p>View stashes:</p>

<pre>
git stash list
</pre>

<p>Restore the latest stash:</p>

<pre>
git stash pop
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Real-time Scenario:</strong>

<p>
I am working on Feature A, but suddenly I need to switch to
a production bug-fix branch. If my current changes are not
ready for a commit, I can stash them, switch branches, fix
the issue and later restore my changes.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>15. What is git tag?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A Git tag is a reference used to mark a specific point in
Git history, commonly used for releases.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git tag v1.0.0

git push origin v1.0.0
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>DevOps Example:</strong>

<p>
A team can tag a production release as
<code>v1.0.0</code>, making it easy to identify exactly which
code version was deployed.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>16. Explain a basic Git workflow using commands.</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
For a normal development task, I first check the repository,
modify the required files, review the changes, stage them,
commit them and push the commit to the remote repository.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status

# Review changes
git diff

# Stage changes
git add .

# Create commit
git commit -m "Add application changes"

# Push to GitHub
git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</div>

<h2>17. How are Git commands used in a CI/CD workflow?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git acts as the source-control layer of the CI/CD pipeline.
A developer pushes code to GitHub, which can trigger Jenkins
or GitHub Actions.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">Developer</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“ git push</div>

<div class="box">GitHub</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“ webhook / trigger</div>

<div class="box">Jenkins / GitHub Actions</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan</div>
<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Deploy</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIOS -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>18. You changed a file but don't want to commit it yet. What will you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
If I need to temporarily save the changes while switching
branches, I can use <code>git stash</code>.
</p>

<pre>
git stash
</pre>

<p>
Later:

<pre>
git stash pop
</pre>

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>19. Your teammate pushed new changes. How do you get them?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
For normal synchronization, I can use:</p>

<pre>

</pre>

<p>
If I want to inspect the changes before integrating them:</p>

<pre>

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>20. You committed locally, but GitHub does not show the commit. Why?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Because <code>git commit</code> only creates the commit in the
local repository.
</p>

<p>
I need to push it:</p>

<pre>
git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>21. You want to know which files changed before committing. What do you use?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git status
git diff
</pre>

<p>
<code>git status</code> gives the state of files, while
<code>git diff</code> shows the actual content differences.
</p>

</div>

<header>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Git & GitHub</a>

<h1>Git <span>Merge Conflicts</span></h1>

<p>
Understand why merge conflicts occur, how Git identifies them,
and how to resolve them safely in real DevOps environments.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Merge conflicts are one of the most common practical Git interview
topics. In real projects, multiple developers may modify the same
file at the same time. Git may not be able to automatically decide
which change should be kept.
</p>

<p>
A DevOps engineer should know how to identify, resolve, verify and
safely complete a conflicted merge.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>1. What is a Git Merge Conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>merge conflict</strong> occurs when Git cannot automatically
combine changes from two branches because the same part of a file
has been changed differently.

</div>

<h3>Simple Example</h3>

<pre><code>main branch
    |
    A
    |
    B  â† Version 1

feature branch
    |
    A
    |
    C  â† Version 2

Both changed the same lines.

Git cannot decide which version should be kept.</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically combine
changes from different branches, usually because the same lines
or nearby parts of a file were modified differently. We manually
resolve the conflict, stage the resolved file and complete the merge."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>2. Why do Merge Conflicts occur?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Conflicts commonly occur when two branches modify the same lines
of the same file differently.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<p>Developer A changes:</p>

<pre><code>PORT=8080</code></pre>

<p>Developer B changes the same line to:</p>

<pre><code>PORT=9090</code></pre>

<p>
When Git tries to merge both branches, it cannot automatically
choose between <code>8080</code> and <code>9090</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>3. Does every merge create a conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>No.</strong>

Most merges can be completed automatically by Git.

A conflict occurs only when Git cannot determine which change
should be preserved.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>Developer A â†’ file1.txt
Developer B â†’ file2.txt

Different files
      â†“
Git can usually merge automatically</code></pre>

<p>
If both developers modify the same section of the same file,
a conflict may occur.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>4. How do you reproduce a merge conflict?</h2>

<p>Start from the main branch:</p>

<pre><code>git switch main

git switch -c feature-a</code></pre>

<p>Modify the same line in a file and commit:</p>

<pre><code>git add .
git commit -m "Change configuration"</code></pre>

<p>Create another branch from the original main:</p>

<pre><code>git switch main
git switch -c feature-b</code></pre>

<p>
Modify the same line differently and commit again.
</p>

<p>Now try to merge one branch into the other:</p>

<pre><code>git switch feature-a

git merge feature-b</code></pre>

<p>
Git may report a merge conflict.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>5. What does Git show when a conflict occurs?</h2>

<p>
Git marks the conflicting section inside the file.
</p>

<h3>Conflict Markers</h3>

<pre><code>&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt; HEAD

PORT=8080

=======

PORT=9090

&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt; feature-b</code></pre>

<h3>Meaning</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Marker</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt; HEAD</code></td>
<td>Current branch changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>=======</code></td>
<td>Separator between changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt; feature-b</code></td>
<td>Incoming branch changes</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>6. How do you check which files have conflicts?</h2>

<pre><code>git status</code></pre>

<p>
Git identifies files that are currently in a conflicted state.
</p>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>On branch feature-a

You have unmerged paths.

Unmerged paths:
    both modified:   app.py</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview tip:</strong>

<br><br>

The first command you should normally run after seeing a merge
conflict is:

<br><br>

<code>git status</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>7. How do you resolve a merge conflict?</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>1. Check status</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>2. Open conflicted file</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>3. Decide which changes to keep</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>4. Remove conflict markers</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>5. Test the code</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>6. git add</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>7. Complete merge</strong>

</div>

<h3>Step 1 â€” Check status</h3>

<pre><code>git status</code></pre>

<h3>Step 2 â€” Open the conflicted file</h3>

<p>
Look for the conflict markers.
</p>

<h3>Step 3 â€” Choose the correct content</h3>

<p>
Keep the correct version or combine both changes if required.
</p>

<h3>Step 4 â€” Remove conflict markers</h3>

<p>
The final file must not contain:
</p>

<pre><code>&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;&lt;
=======
&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Step 5 â€” Test</h3>

<p>
Run the appropriate application tests before completing the merge.
</p>

<h3>Step 6 â€” Stage the resolved file</h3>

<pre><code>git add app.py</code></pre>

<h3>Step 7 â€” Complete the merge</h3>

<pre><code>git commit</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>8. What is the purpose of git add after resolving a conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

After manually resolving a conflict, Git needs to know that the
file has been resolved.

Running <code>git add</code> stages the resolved version and marks
the conflict as resolved.

</div>

<pre><code>git add app.py

git status</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>9. Can you abort a merge conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Yes.</strong>

If you do not want to continue with the merge, you can abort it.

</div>

<pre><code>git merge --abort</code></pre>

<p>
This attempts to return the working tree to the state it had
before the merge started.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<br><br>

Do not blindly delete or overwrite files to solve a conflict.
First understand what changes are present and use Git's merge
state safely.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>10. What is the difference between resolving and aborting a merge?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Action</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Resolve conflict</td>
<td>Keep or combine the required changes and complete the merge</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git merge --abort</code></td>
<td>Cancel the current merge attempt</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>11. How do you check whether conflicts are resolved?</h2>

<pre><code>git status</code></pre>

<p>
After resolving all conflicts and staging the files, Git should
no longer show them as unmerged.
</p>

<h3>Then verify the changes</h3>

<pre><code>git diff --cached</code></pre>

<p>
This lets you inspect what is staged before completing the merge.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>12. What happens if you run git commit before resolving conflicts?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Git normally prevents the merge from being completed while
unmerged files remain.

You must resolve the conflicts and stage the resolved files first.

</div>

<pre><code>git status

# resolve conflicts

git add .

git commit</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>13. Can a merge conflict happen during git pull?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Yes.</strong>

A <code>git pull</code> typically fetches remote changes and then
integrates them into the current branch. If the local and remote
changes conflict, Git can report a merge conflict.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git pull origin main

# conflict occurs

git status

# resolve files

git add .

git commit</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>14. How can you reduce merge conflicts in a team?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Keep branches short-lived.</li>

<li>Pull the latest changes regularly.</li>

<li>Communicate before modifying heavily shared files.</li>

<li>Keep commits small and focused.</li>

<li>Use pull requests and code reviews.</li>

<li>Run CI tests before merging.</li>

<li>Avoid unnecessary large changes in shared files.</li>

</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>DevOps perspective:</strong>

<br><br>

Good Git practices reduce conflicts, but they cannot completely
eliminate them in a collaborative development environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>15. Real-Time DevOps Scenario: Production deployment conflict</h2>

<div class="answer">

Suppose two developers are working on an application.

Developer A changes the Kubernetes deployment configuration.

Developer B changes the same deployment file for a different
environment.

Both create pull requests.

When the second branch is merged, Git reports a conflict.

</div>

<h3>DevOps Resolution</h3>

<pre><code>git switch feature-a

git pull origin main

# Resolve conflict

git status

# Edit the file

git add deployment.yaml

# Run tests

git commit

git push</code></pre>

<p>
The pull request can then be reviewed again before merging.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>16. What is the safest approach when resolving a conflict?</h2>

<div class="success">

<strong>Understand â†’ Resolve â†’ Test â†’ Stage â†’ Review â†’ Commit</strong>

</div>

<p>
Never resolve conflicts simply by choosing "ours" or "theirs"
without understanding the business or application requirement.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>17. What are "ours" and "theirs" in a merge conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

During a normal merge:

<br><br>

<strong>ours</strong> generally refers to the current branch.

<br><br>

<strong>theirs</strong> generally refers to the branch being merged in.

</div>

<p>
Git can provide options such as:
</p>

<pre><code>git checkout --ours file.txt
git checkout --theirs file.txt</code></pre>

<p>
Modern Git also supports restore-style workflows, but these
commands should be used carefully because they can discard changes.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Interview point:</strong>

Do not say "always choose ours" or "always choose theirs."
The correct choice depends on which change is required.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>18. Merge Conflict Troubleshooting Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Merge Conflict
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git status</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Identify conflicted files
<br>
â†“
<br>
Open files
<br>
â†“
<br>
Understand both changes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Resolve manually
<br>
â†“
<br>
Remove conflict markers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Run tests
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git add</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git commit</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git push</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- FOLLOW UPS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ Common Interview Follow-up Questions</h2>

<ul>

<li>What is a merge conflict?</li>

<li>Why does Git create merge conflicts?</li>

<li>How do you resolve a merge conflict?</li>

<li>What does <code>git status</code> show during a conflict?</li>

<li>What are Git conflict markers?</li>

<li>What does <code>git merge --abort</code> do?</li>

<li>Can <code>git pull</code> cause a merge conflict?</li>

<li>What is the difference between ours and theirs?</li>

<li>How do you verify a conflict is resolved?</li>

<li>How can teams reduce merge conflicts?</li>

</ul>

</div>

<!-- 1 FUNDAMENTALS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Git Fundamentals</h2>

<h3>Q1. What is Git?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Git is a distributed version control system used to track changes
in source code and enable developers to collaborate safely.
</div>

<h3>Q2. Why is Git distributed?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Each developer normally has a complete local repository containing
the project history, so many Git operations can be performed locally.
</div>

<h3>Q3. Git vs GitHub?</h3>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Git</th>
<th>GitHub</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Version control system</td>
<td>Hosting and collaboration platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs locally</td>
<td>Provides remote repositories</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Tracks project history</td>
<td>Provides PRs, reviews, issues and CI integrations</td>
</tr>
</table>

<h3>Q4. What is a Git repository?</h3>

<div class="answer">
A Git repository contains project files together with Git metadata
and version history.
</div>

<h3>Q5. What are Working Tree, Staging Area and Repository?</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Area</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Working Tree</td>
<td>Current files and modifications</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Staging Area</td>
<td>Changes selected for the next commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Repository</td>
<td>Committed project history</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 2 COMMANDS -->

<div class="card">

<tr>

<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<td>Initialize repository</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git clone &lt;url&gt;</code></td>
<td>Clone repository</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git status</code></td>
<td>Check repository status</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git add .</code></td>
<td>Stage changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git commit -m "message"</code></td>
<td>Create commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git log</code></td>
<td>View history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git diff</code></td>
<td>View changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git branch</code></td>
<td>List branches</td>
</tr>

<td>Create and switch branch</td>
</tr>

<td>Merge branch</td>
</tr>

<td>Rebase branch</td>
</tr>

<td>Download remote changes</td>
</tr>

</tr>

</tr>

<td>Move HEAD / branch reference</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git revert</code></td>
<td>Create reversing commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git reflog</code></td>
<td>View local reference history</td>
</tr>

</table>

<!-- 3 BRANCH -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Branches & Branching</h2>

<h3>What is a branch?</h3>

<div class="answer">
A branch is a movable reference to a commit that allows independent
development without directly changing another branch.
</div>

<h3>Why use branches?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Feature isolation</li>
<li>Parallel development</li>
<li>Bug fixes</li>
<li>Code review</li>
<li>Production protection</li>
</ul>

<pre><code>main
 â”œâ”€â”€ feature/login
 â”œâ”€â”€ feature/payment
 â””â”€â”€ bugfix/api-error</code></pre>

<pre><code>git branch
git switch main
git switch -c feature/login
git branch -d feature/login</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 4 MERGE REBASE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Merge vs Rebase</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Merge</th>
<th>Rebase</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Combines histories</td>
<td>Replays commits onto another base</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can create merge commit</td>
<td>Usually creates linear history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not rewrite existing commits</td>
<td>Rewrites commit history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Safer for shared branches</td>
<td>Use carefully on shared branches</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>git switch main
git merge feature/login

git switch feature/login
git rebase main</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Avoid rebasing shared commits when other developers depend on them.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 CONFLICT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Merge Conflict</h2>

<h3>What is a merge conflict?</h3>

<div class="answer">
A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically determine
which changes should be kept.
</div>

<pre><code>git merge feature/login

# Resolve conflicting files

git add .
git commit</code></pre>

<h3>During rebase</h3>

<pre><code>git rebase main

# Resolve conflict

git add .
git rebase --continue</code></pre>

<h3>Abort</h3>

<pre><code>git merge --abort
git rebase --abort</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

I inspect the conflicting files, understand both changes,
resolve the conflict carefully, stage the resolved files and
complete the merge or rebase.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 RESET REVERT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Reset vs Revert</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Reset</th>
<th>Revert</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Moves HEAD / branch reference</td>
<td>Creates a new reversing commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can rewrite local history</td>
<td>Preserves existing history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for local work</td>
<td>Preferred for shared history</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Reset modes</h3>

<pre><code>git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1</code></pre>

<h3>Revert</h3>

<pre><code>git revert &lt;commit-id&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Be careful with <code>git reset --hard</code> because uncommitted
changes can be lost.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 STASH -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Git Stash</h2>

<h3>Why use stash?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Git stash temporarily stores uncommitted changes so you can switch
to another task without creating an unfinished commit.
</div>

<pre><code>git stash
git stash list
git stash pop
git stash apply
git stash drop</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

You are working on a feature when an urgent production bug arrives.
Stash the unfinished work, switch to the bugfix branch, fix the issue,
then restore your previous work.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 REMOTE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Remote, Fetch, Pull & Push</h2>

<h3>What is origin?</h3>

<div class="answer">
<code>origin</code> is the conventional default name for a remote
repository.
</div>

<pre><code>git remote -v
git remote add origin &lt;URL&gt;

git fetch origin
git pull origin main
git push origin main</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Fetch</th>
<th>Pull</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Downloads remote updates</td>
<td>Downloads and integrates changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not merge into current branch</td>
<td>Can update current branch</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 9 PR -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. GitHub Pull Request</h2>

<div class="answer">
A Pull Request is a request to merge changes from one branch into
another, usually with code review and automated checks.
</div>

<div class="flow">

Feature Branch
<br>
â†“
<br>
Push
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pull Request
<br>
â†“
<br>
Code Review
<br>
â†“
<br>
CI Checks
<br>
â†“
<br>
Approval
<br>
â†“
<br>
Merge

</div>

<h3>Why are PRs important?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Code review</li>
<li>CI validation</li>
<li>Quality control</li>
<li>Audit trail</li>
<li>Team collaboration</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 10 PROTECTION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Branch Protection</h2>

<ul>
<li>Require Pull Requests</li>
<li>Require approvals</li>
<li>Require CI checks</li>
<li>Restrict direct pushes</li>
<li>Protect production branches</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

A developer accidentally pushes untested code to <code>main</code>.
Branch protection with PR reviews and required CI checks can prevent
unsafe direct changes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 TAGS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Git Tags & Releases</h2>

<div class="answer">
Tags identify specific versions or release points in Git history.
</div>

<pre><code>git tag

git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0"

git push origin v1.0.0

git push origin --tags

git show v1.0.0</code></pre>

<h3>Semantic Versioning</h3>

<pre><code>MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

1.4.2

1 = breaking change
4 = new feature
2 = bug fix</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

CI/CD pipelines can use release tags such as <code>v2.0.0</code>
to trigger controlled production deployments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 CHERRY PICK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Cherry-Pick</h2>

<div class="answer">
Cherry-pick applies the changes from a specific commit onto the
current branch.
</div>

<pre><code>git cherry-pick &lt;commit-id&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A bug fix exists in development, but production needs only that
specific fix. Cherry-pick the required commit instead of merging
all development changes.

</div>

<pre><code>git cherry-pick &lt;commit-id>

# Resolve conflict
git add .
git cherry-pick --continue

# Abort
git cherry-pick --abort</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 REFLOG -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Reflog & Recovery</h2>

<div class="answer">
Reflog records local movements of references such as HEAD and branch
pointers.
</div>

<pre><code>git reflog</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If a developer accidentally resets a branch and appears to lose a
commit, reflog can often help locate the previous commit reference.

</div>

<pre><code>git reflog

git reset --hard &lt;recovered-commit&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Reflog is primarily local and is not a permanent remote backup.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 LOG -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. Git Log & Investigation</h2>

<pre><code>git log
git log --oneline
git log --graph --oneline --all
git show &lt;commit-id&gt;

git diff
git diff HEAD
git diff main..feature</code></pre>

<h3>Best interview command</h3>

<pre><code>git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 15 GITIGNORE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. .gitignore</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>.gitignore</code> specifies files and directories that Git should
normally ignore when detecting untracked files.
</div>

<pre><code>.env
*.log
node_modules/
.terraform/
*.tfstate
*.pem</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Adding a file to <code>.gitignore</code> does not automatically remove
a file that is already tracked.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 CLEAN -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 16. Git Clean</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>git clean</code> removes untracked files from the working tree.
</div>

<pre><code>git clean -n
git clean -f</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Always use <code>git clean -n</code> first to inspect what would be removed.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 HOOKS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Git Hooks</h2>

<div class="answer">
Git hooks are scripts that execute automatically at specific Git
lifecycle events.
</div>

<ul>
<li>pre-commit</li>
<li>commit-msg</li>
<li>pre-push</li>
<li>post-merge</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">
A pre-commit hook can run formatting, linting or validation before
allowing a commit.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 BISECT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. Git Bisect</h2>

<div class="answer">
Git bisect uses binary search through commit history to identify
the commit that introduced a bug.
</div>

<pre><code>git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good &lt;known-good-commit&gt;

# Continue marking commits good/bad

git bisect reset</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 19 SUBMODULE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 19. Git Submodules</h2>

<div class="answer">
A Git submodule allows one repository to include another repository
at a specific commit.
</div>

<pre><code>git submodule add &lt;repository-url&gt;
git submodule update --init --recursive</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 20 LFS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 20. Git LFS</h2>

<div class="answer">
Git LFS is designed for large files by keeping pointers in Git while
large objects are managed separately.
</div>

<p>
It is useful for large binaries, media and other files that are not
ideal for normal Git object storage.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 21 SECURITY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Git Security</h2>

<h3>Should secrets be committed?</h3>

<div class="answer">
<strong>No.</strong> Passwords, API keys, AWS credentials, tokens and
private keys should never be committed to Git.
</div>

<h3>Best practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Secret managers</li>
<li>GitHub encrypted secrets</li>
<li>Secret scanning</li>
<li>Credential rotation</li>
<li>Never commit private keys</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

If a secret is accidentally pushed, deleting the file is not enough.
Treat the credential as compromised and rotate it immediately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 CI CD -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Git + CI/CD</h2>

<div class="flow">

Git Push
<br>
â†“
<br>
GitHub
<br>
â†“
<br>
CI Trigger
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Test
<br>
â†“
<br>
Security Scan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Registry
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deployment

</div>

<h3>Common CI/CD triggers</h3>

<ul>
<li>Push</li>
<li>Pull Request</li>
<li>Tag</li>
<li>Schedule</li>
<li>Manual trigger</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

Git acts as the source of truth for application code and CI/CD
configuration. Pushes and Pull Requests can trigger CI, while tags
can trigger controlled release pipelines.

</div>

<pre><code>main

         â†“

         â†“

<!-- 24 SCENARIOS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Most Important Real-Time Scenarios</h2>

<h3>Scenario 1 â€” Bad code pushed to main</h3>

<div class="scenario">
Use <code>git revert</code> for a shared branch because it preserves
history through a new reversing commit.
</div>

<pre><code>git revert &lt;bad-commit&gt;
git push origin main</code></pre>


<h3>Scenario 2 â€” Accidentally deleted commit</h3>

<div class="scenario">
Use <code>git reflog</code> to locate the previous commit and recover it.
</div>

<pre><code>git reflog
git reset --hard &lt;commit-id&gt;</code></pre>


<h3>Scenario 3 â€” Only one production fix is required</h3>

<div class="scenario">
Use <code>git cherry-pick</code> instead of merging an entire development
branch.
</div>

<pre><code>git switch production
git cherry-pick &lt;fix-commit&gt;</code></pre>


<h3>Scenario 4 â€” Branch is behind main</h3>

<pre><code>git fetch origin

# Merge approach
git merge origin/main

# Rebase approach
git rebase origin/main</code></pre>


<h3>Scenario 5 â€” Push rejected</h3>

<div class="scenario">
The remote contains commits that your local branch does not have.
Fetch and integrate the remote changes before pushing again.
</div>

<pre><code>git fetch origin
git pull --rebase origin main
git push origin main</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Do not blindly use <code>git push --force</code> on a shared branch.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 PRODUCTION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Production Rollback Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A production deployment failed.

First identify the currently deployed version and the last known-good
release. If releases are tagged, redeploy the known-good version or
immutable artifact instead of rewriting production Git history.

</div>

<pre><code>git tag
git show v1.4.0</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Known-Good Tag
<br>
â†“
<br>
Known-Good Artifact
<br>
â†“
<br>
Redeploy
<br>
â†“
<br>
Verify

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 TRAPS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 26. Common Git Interview Traps</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Question</th>
<th>Correct Answer</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Is GitHub Git?</td>
<td>No. Git is the version control system; GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does git fetch merge?</td>
<td>No. It downloads remote updates without merging them.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does git pull only download?</td>
<td>No. It fetches and integrates changes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Is reset the same as revert?</td>
<td>No. Reset moves references; revert creates a reversing commit.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Is rebase always better than merge?</td>
<td>No. It depends on the workflow and shared-history requirements.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does .gitignore remove tracked files?</td>
<td>No.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can deleting a secret remove it completely?</td>
<td>No. Rotate the secret and clean history when appropriate.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can reflog recover everything?</td>
<td>No. It is local and entries can expire.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

git init

git show &lt;commit&gt;
git diff

# Stage / Commit

# Branch
git branch
git switch main

# Merge
git merge feature/name

# Rebase
git rebase main
git rebase --abort
git rebase --continue

# Remote
git remote -v
git fetch origin
git pull origin main
git push origin main

# Stash
git stash
git stash list
git stash pop
git stash apply
git stash drop

# Reset / Revert
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git revert &lt;commit&gt;

# Tags
git tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release"
git push origin v1.0.0

# Cherry-pick
git cherry-pick &lt;commit&gt;
git cherry-pick --continue
git cherry-pick --abort

# Recovery
git reflog

# Clean
git clean -n
git clean -f

# Bug Investigation
git bisect start
git bisect good
git bisect bad
git bisect reset</code></pre>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Git in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

Git is a distributed version control system used to track source
code changes and enable collaboration.

Developers normally work on feature branches, commit their changes
and push them to a remote repository such as GitHub.

A Pull Request is then used for code review and automated CI checks
before merging changes into the main branch.

Git provides commands such as merge, rebase, reset, revert, stash,
cherry-pick and reflog for handling different development scenarios.

In DevOps, Git acts as the source of truth for application code and
CI/CD configuration. Tags can identify releases and commits or tags
can trigger automated build, test, security scanning and deployment
pipelines.

For production safety, I would use protected branches, code review,
CI validation, secure secret management and controlled releases.

</div>

<div class="icon">ðŸ”€</div>

<h1>Git <span>Merge & Rebase</span></h1>

<p>
Understand merge, fast-forward merge, three-way merge,
rebase, conflicts, interactive rebase and real-time DevOps scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>1. What is Git Merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git merge is used to combine the changes from one branch into
another branch.
</p>

<p>
For example, after completing a feature, we can merge the
feature branch into the main branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git switch main

git merge feature-login
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
The branch you are currently on is the branch that receives
the changes.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>2. How does Git Merge work?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Git examines the commit history of both branches and determines
how the histories can be combined.
</p>

<p>
Depending on the commit structure, Git may perform a
<strong>fast-forward merge</strong> or a
<strong>three-way merge</strong>.
</p>

</div>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">main</div>

<div class="arrow">â†“</div>

<div class="box">Common Ancestor</div>

<div class="arrow">â†™ â†˜</div>

<div class="box">Feature</div>

<div class="box">Main</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>3. What is a Fast-Forward Merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A fast-forward merge happens when the target branch has not
diverged from the branch being merged.
</p>

<p>
Git simply moves the target branch pointer forward.
No additional merge commit is required.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
Before:

A --- B --- C
      \
       feature


After:

A --- B --- C
           â†‘
          main
          feature
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Example:</strong>

<p>
If main has no new commits after the feature branch was created,
Git can simply move main forward to the latest feature commit.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>4. What is a Three-Way Merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A three-way merge is used when both branches have new commits
after their common ancestor.
</p>

<p>
Git uses three points:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Common ancestor</li>
<li>Current branch tip</li>
<li>Incoming branch tip</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
        C --- D
       /
A --- B
       \
        E --- F

B = Common Ancestor

C,D = Feature branch

E,F = Main branch
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<p>
Because both branches changed independently, Git may create a
new merge commit.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</div>

<h2>5. What is a Merge Commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A merge commit is a special commit created when Git combines
two diverged branch histories.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
        C
       / \
A --- B   M
       \ /
        D

M = Merge Commit
</pre>

</div>

<p>
A merge commit normally has two parent commits.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>6. What is Git Rebase?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git rebase moves or replays commits from one branch on top of
another base commit.
</p>

<p>
It is commonly used to create a cleaner, more linear commit
history.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
Before:

A --- B --- C
       \
        D --- E
             feature


After rebase:

A --- B --- C --- D' --- E'
                       feature
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
The rebased commits are recreated, so their commit IDs change.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>7. How do you rebase a feature branch onto main?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git switch feature-login

git rebase main
</pre>

<p>
Git takes the feature commits and replays them on top of the
latest main branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
Before:

A --- B --- C       main
       \
        D --- E     feature


After:

A --- B --- C --- D' --- E'
                          feature
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>8. What is the difference between Merge and Rebase?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Merge</th>
<th>Rebase</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Combines histories</td>
<td>Replays commits</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can create a merge commit</td>
<td>Usually creates a linear history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Preserves existing commit history</td>
<td>Rewrites commit history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not normally change existing commit IDs</td>
<td>Rebased commits receive new IDs</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Safer for shared branches</td>
<td>Needs caution on shared branches</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Shortcut:</strong>

<p>
<strong>Merge = preserve and combine histories.</strong>
</p>

<p>
<strong>Rebase = replay commits onto a new base.</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</div>

<h2>9. Why does rebase create a cleaner history?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Rebase removes unnecessary merge commits from the feature
development history and creates a more linear sequence of commits.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
Merge:

A --- B -------- M
       \        /
        C --- D


Rebase:

A --- B --- C' --- D'
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<p>
A linear history can make it easier to understand when changes
were introduced and troubleshoot commit history.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>10. Why should you be careful when rebasing a shared branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Rebase rewrites commit history.
Because commit IDs can change, rebasing a branch that other
developers are already using can cause synchronization problems.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Important Interview Point:</strong>

<p>
Avoid rebasing shared/public branches unless the team has
specifically agreed on that workflow.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>11. What is a Merge Conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically determine
which changes should be kept.
</p>

<p>
This commonly happens when two branches modify the same lines
of the same file differently.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
<<<<<<< HEAD
version from main
=======
version from feature
>>>>>>> feature-login
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>12. How do you resolve a merge conflict?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<ol>
<li>Run <code>git status</code>.</li>
<li>Identify the conflicted files.</li>
<li>Open the files.</li>
<li>Understand both versions.</li>
<li>Choose or combine the correct changes.</li>
<li>Remove conflict markers.</li>
<li>Stage the resolved files.</li>
<li>Complete the merge.</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status

# Fix the file manually

git add app.py

git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict"
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REBASE CONFLICT</div>

<h2>13. How do you resolve a conflict during rebase?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
When a conflict occurs during rebase, Git pauses the rebase.
We resolve the file manually and then continue the rebase.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status

# Fix the conflicted file

git add app.py

git rebase --continue
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>14. How do you abort a rebase?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git rebase --abort
</pre>

<p>
This cancels the current rebase operation and returns the branch
to the state it was in before the rebase started.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>15. How do you skip a problematic commit during rebase?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git rebase --skip
</pre>

<p>
This tells Git to skip the current commit being replayed.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Use carefully:</strong>

<p>
Only skip a commit when you understand why that commit is no
longer required.
</p>

</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>16. What is Interactive Rebase?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Interactive rebase allows us to modify, reorder, combine or
remove commits before sharing the history.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git rebase -i HEAD~3
</pre>

<p>
This opens the last three commits for interactive editing.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FOLLOW-UP</div>

<h2>17. What can you do with interactive rebase?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<ul>
<li>Reorder commits</li>
<li>Squash commits</li>
<li>Change commit messages</li>
<li>Edit commits</li>
<li>Drop commits</li>
<li>Combine multiple commits</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
pick   abc123 Add login page
squash def456 Fix login page
pick   ghi789 Add validation
</pre>

<p>
The <code>squash</code> operation combines commits.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>18. What is git merge --no-ff?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
The <code>--no-ff</code> option forces Git to create a merge commit
even when a fast-forward merge is possible.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git merge --no-ff feature-login
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<p>
Teams may use this when they want the history to clearly show
that a feature branch was merged.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>19. Your feature branch is behind main. What would you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
I would first update my local main branch and then bring the
latest main changes into my feature branch.
</p>

<p>
Depending on the team's workflow, I can use merge or rebase.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git switch main

git pull origin main

git switch feature-login

git rebase main
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<p>
If the team does not allow rebasing shared branches, I would
use merge instead.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q20 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>20. You have local commits and main has new commits. How do you update your feature branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
One approach is to rebase the feature branch onto the latest main:
</p>

<pre>
git switch main
git pull origin main

git switch feature-login
git rebase main
</pre>

<p>
This keeps the feature commits on top of the latest main history.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q21 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ PRODUCTION SCENARIO</div>

<h2>21. Would you rebase main in production?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Normally, I would avoid rewriting history on a shared production
or main branch.
</p>

<p>
For shared branches, merge is generally safer because it preserves
the existing history.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Key Point:</strong>

<p>
Do not treat rebase as simply a "better merge". They solve
different workflow needs.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q22 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ CI/CD SCENARIO</div>

<h2>22. How does merge/rebase affect CI/CD?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
CI pipelines commonly run when branches are pushed or when Pull
Requests are created or updated.
</p>

<p>
If a branch is rebased, the commit IDs change, so the CI system
may see the rebased commits as new commits.
</p>

<p>
After resolving conflicts or rebasing, the branch should be
tested again before merging.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q23 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW TRAP</div>

<h2>23. Is rebase safer than merge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>No. It depends on the situation.</strong>

<p>
Rebase provides a cleaner history but rewrites commits.
Merge preserves the existing history and is generally safer
for shared branches.
</p>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Good interview answer:</strong>

<p>
"I would use rebase for keeping my private feature branch
up to date and maintaining a linear history, but I would avoid
rewriting history on shared branches."
</p>

</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q24 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ SCENARIO</div>

<h2>24. You started a rebase and got many conflicts. What would you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<ol>
<li>Check the current rebase state.</li>
<li>Review the conflicted files.</li>
<li>Resolve each conflict carefully.</li>
<li>Stage the resolved files.</li>
<li>Run <code>git rebase --continue</code>.</li>
<li>Repeat until the rebase completes.</li>
<li>If the rebase is no longer appropriate, use <code>git rebase --abort</code>.</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git status

# Resolve conflict

git add .

git rebase --continue

# If necessary:
git rebase --abort
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q25 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME DEVOPS</div>

<h2>25. A developer force-pushed after rebasing. What should the team be careful about?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Because rebase rewrites history, a force push can replace the
remote branch history.
</p>

<p>
Other developers who already based work on the old history may
need to reconcile their local branches.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Force-pushing shared branches can disrupt other developers.
It should be done only when the team workflow permits it.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- COMMANDS -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ§  QUICK COMMAND REVISION</div>

<h2>Git Merge & Rebase Commands</h2>

<div class="example">

<pre>
# Merge
git switch main
git merge feature

# Force merge commit
git merge --no-ff feature

# Rebase
git switch feature
git rebase main

# Continue rebase
git rebase --continue

# Abort rebase
git rebase --abort

# Skip current commit
git rebase --skip

# Interactive rebase
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# Check status
git status

# View history
git log --oneline --graph --all
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- FINAL REVISION -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸŽ¯ FINAL INTERVIEW REVISION</div>

<h2>Merge vs Rebase â€” Remember This</h2>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">
<strong>MERGE</strong>
<br>
Combine histories
<br>
Preserves history
<br>
May create merge commit
<br>
Safer for shared branches
</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>REBASE</strong>
<br>
Replay commits
<br>
Linear history
<br>
Rewrites commit IDs
<br>
Use carefully on shared branches
</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>ðŸ”¥ One-Line Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
"Git merge combines two branch histories while preserving their
existing commits, whereas Git rebase replays commits onto a new
base to create a cleaner linear history, but it rewrites commit
history."
</p>

</div>

</div>
