<header>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Git & GitHub</a>

<h1>Git <span>Remote & GitHub</span></h1>

<p>
Remote repositories, GitHub, origin, upstream, push, pull, fetch,
tracking branches and practical DevOps workflows.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ GIT & GITHUB â€” DEVOPS MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Git is primarily the version control system, while GitHub is a
platform that hosts Git repositories and provides collaboration
features such as pull requests, code reviews, issues and CI/CD
integration.
</p>

<p>
Understanding how local Git repositories communicate with remote
repositories is essential for DevOps interviews.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>1. What is a Remote Repository?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>remote repository</strong> is a Git repository hosted at
another location, usually on a server or cloud platform such as
GitHub.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>Local Repository
      |
      | git push
      â†“
Remote Repository
      |
   GitHub</code></pre>

<p>
The local repository contains your working copy and Git history,
while the remote repository allows teams to share and collaborate
on the project.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"A remote repository is a Git repository hosted on a remote server
or platform such as GitHub. Developers use commands like push, pull
and fetch to exchange changes between the local and remote
repositories."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>2. What is GitHub?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>GitHub</strong> is a cloud-based platform for hosting and
collaborating on Git repositories.

</div>

<p>
GitHub provides features such as:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Repository hosting</li>
<li>Pull requests</li>
<li>Code reviews</li>
<li>Issues</li>
<li>GitHub Actions</li>
<li>Access control</li>
<li>Branch protection</li>
<li>Collaboration</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Important:</strong>

Git and GitHub are not the same thing.

<br><br>

Git = distributed version control system

<br>

GitHub = platform for hosting and collaborating around Git repositories

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>3. What is the difference between Git and GitHub?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Git</th>
<th>GitHub</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Version control system</td>
<td>Git repository hosting and collaboration platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs locally</td>
<td>Cloud/web platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Tracks changes</td>
<td>Hosts repositories and enables collaboration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Works from command line</td>
<td>Provides web UI, APIs and collaboration features</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>4. How do you check configured remote repositories?</h2>

<pre><code>git remote -v</code></pre>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>origin  https://github.com/user/project.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/user/project.git (push)</code></pre>

<p>
This shows the remote name and its fetch/push URLs.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>5. What is origin in Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>origin</strong> is the conventional default name given to a
remote repository when it is cloned or when a remote is added
using that name.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git remote -v

origin  https://github.com/user/project.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/user/project.git (push)</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Origin is simply a commonly used name for a Git remote. It is not
a special server or protocol; it is a remote name that points to
a repository URL."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>6. How do you add a remote repository?</h2>

<pre><code>git remote add origin https://github.com/user/project.git</code></pre>

<p>
This connects the local repository to the specified remote
repository using the name <code>origin</code>.
</p>

<h3>Verify</h3>

<pre><code>git remote -v</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>7. How do you remove a remote?</h2>

<pre><code>git remote remove origin</code></pre>

<p>
This removes the remote configuration from the local repository.
It does not delete the remote repository itself.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>8. What is git push?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>git push</code> sends commits from the local repository to a
remote repository.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git push origin main</code></pre>

<p>
This pushes the local <code>main</code> branch to the
<code>main</code> branch on the remote named <code>origin</code>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Local Commit
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git push</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Remote Repository

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>9. What is git fetch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>git fetch</code> downloads changes and references from a remote
repository without automatically merging those changes into the
current working branch.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git fetch origin</code></pre>

<p>
After fetching, you can inspect the remote changes before deciding
what to merge or rebase.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>10. What is git pull?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>git pull</code> retrieves changes from a remote repository and
integrates them into the current branch.

</div>

<h3>Typical concept</h3>

<pre><code>git pull

â‰ˆ

git fetch
+
integration step</code></pre>

<p>
The exact integration behavior depends on the configured Git
settings and options; it can involve a merge or rebase.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>11. Difference between git fetch and git pull</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>git fetch</th>
<th>git pull</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Downloads remote updates</td>
<td>Downloads and integrates updates</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not automatically update current branch</td>
<td>Updates the current branch through integration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Safer for inspecting changes first</td>
<td>Convenient for regular synchronization</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Fetch downloads remote changes without integrating them into my
current branch. Pull downloads the changes and then integrates them
into the current branch."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>12. How do you push a new local branch to GitHub?</h2>

<pre><code>git switch -c feature/login

git add .

git commit -m "Add login feature"

git push -u origin feature/login</code></pre>

<p>
The <code>-u</code> option establishes an upstream tracking
relationship between the local and remote branch.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>13. What is an upstream branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An upstream branch is the remote branch that a local branch tracks
by default for operations such as push and pull.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git push -u origin feature/login</code></pre>

<p>
After this, the local <code>feature/login</code> branch tracks
<code>origin/feature/login</code>.
</p>

<p>
Later, you can often simply use:
</p>

<pre><code>git push
git pull</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>14. What does git clone do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>git clone</code> creates a local copy of a remote Git repository,
including its Git history and remote-tracking information.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git clone https://github.com/user/project.git</code></pre>

<p>
After cloning, Git normally configures the remote repository under
the name <code>origin</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>15. What is a remote-tracking branch?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A remote-tracking branch is a local reference that represents the
state of a branch on a remote repository.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>origin/main
origin/development
origin/feature/login</code></pre>

<p>
These references are updated when Git communicates with the remote,
for example through <code>git fetch</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>16. How do you see remote branches?</h2>

<pre><code>git branch -r</code></pre>

<p>
To see both local and remote branches:
</p>

<pre><code>git branch -a</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>17. What is upstream in Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

In Git workflows, <strong>upstream</strong> can refer to the original
repository from which a fork was created.

It is also commonly used as a remote name.

</div>

<h3>Fork workflow example</h3>

<pre><code>origin   â†’ your GitHub fork
upstream â†’ original project repository</code></pre>

<p>
This is especially common in open-source development.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>18. Origin vs Upstream</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Remote</th>
<th>Common Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>origin</td>
<td>Your primary remote repository or fork</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>upstream</td>
<td>Original repository in a fork-based workflow</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

These names are conventions, not fixed Git keywords.
You can technically name remotes differently.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>19. What happens when you push code to GitHub?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Local Changes
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git add</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git commit</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git push</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
GitHub Remote Repository
<br>
â†“
<br>
CI/CD Pipeline
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build â†’ Test â†’ Deploy

</div>

<p>
In a DevOps environment, pushing code to GitHub can trigger
automated CI/CD workflows such as GitHub Actions or other
pipeline systems.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>20. Real-Time DevOps Scenario: Developer pushes code</h2>

<div class="answer">

A developer completes a feature locally and needs to share it with
the team.

</div>

<pre><code>git status

git add .

git commit -m "Add payment validation"

git push -u origin feature/payment</code></pre>

<p>
The branch becomes available on GitHub, where the developer can
open a pull request for review.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>21. Real-Time DevOps Scenario: Get latest changes before starting work</h2>

<p>
A developer wants to synchronize their local main branch with
the latest remote changes.
</p>

<pre><code>git switch main

git fetch origin

git pull origin main</code></pre>

<p>
In a team workflow, the exact synchronization strategy may use
merge or rebase according to the team's Git policy.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>22. What should you do if git push is rejected?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A push can be rejected when the remote branch contains commits
that are not present in the local branch.

</div>

<h3>Typical message</h3>

<pre><code>! [rejected] main -> main
! [rejected] non-fast-forward</code></pre>

<h3>Basic approach</h3>

<pre><code>git fetch origin

git pull origin main

# Resolve conflicts if required

git push origin main</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not blindly use <code>git push --force</code> on a shared branch.
Understand the reason for rejection first.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>23. What is a non-fast-forward push?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A non-fast-forward rejection usually means the remote branch has
advanced and the local branch does not contain those remote commits.

Git rejects the push to prevent accidentally overwriting remote
history.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>24. How do you rename a remote?</h2>

<pre><code>git remote rename origin upstream</code></pre>

<p>
This changes the remote name locally.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>git remote -v</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>25. How do you change a remote URL?</h2>

<pre><code>git remote set-url origin https://github.com/user/new-project.git</code></pre>

<p>
This is useful when a repository moves or the remote URL needs
to be changed.
</p>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>27. Why is GitHub important in DevOps?</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub acts as an important collaboration and source-control

It can integrate source code with CI/CD, security scanning,
code review, issue tracking and deployment automation.

<div class="icon">â†©ï¸</div>

<h1>Git <span>Reset, Revert & Reflog</span></h1>

<p>
Recover mistakes, undo commits safely, restore files and understand
Git history using reset, revert, restore and reflog.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>1. What is git reset?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git reset</code> moves the current branch pointer to another
commit and can also modify the staging area and working directory
depending on the reset mode.
</p>

<p>
It is mainly used to undo local commits or unstage changes.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reset HEAD~1
</pre>

<p>
This moves the current branch back by one commit using the default
mixed reset.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Be very careful with reset on shared branches because it can rewrite
branch history.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>2. What are the three types of git reset?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>The three commonly discussed reset modes are:</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>--soft</strong></li>
<li><strong>--mixed</strong></li>
<li><strong>--hard</strong></li>
</ul>

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Reset</th>
<th>HEAD</th>
<th>Staging Area</th>
<th>Working Directory</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>--soft</td>
<td>Moves</td>
<td>Preserved</td>
<td>Preserved</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>--mixed</td>
<td>Moves</td>
<td>Reset</td>
<td>Preserved</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>--hard</td>
<td>Moves</td>
<td>Reset</td>
<td>Reset</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>3. What is git reset --soft?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A soft reset moves HEAD to the specified commit but keeps the
changes staged.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reset --soft HEAD~1
</pre>

<p>
The last commit is removed from the branch history, but its changes
remain staged so they can be recommitted.
</p>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Use case:</strong>

<p>
Useful when you want to modify or combine recent commits without
losing the changes.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>4. What is git reset --mixed?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A mixed reset moves HEAD and resets the staging area, but it keeps
the changes in the working directory.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
</pre>

<p>
This is also the default behavior when no reset mode is specified.
</p>

<pre>
git reset HEAD~1
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
The files are not deleted. The changes simply become unstaged.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DANGEROUS / MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>5. What is git reset --hard?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
A hard reset moves HEAD, resets the staging area and resets the
working directory to match the target commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reset --hard HEAD~1
</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Be Careful:</strong>

<p>
Uncommitted changes can be permanently lost when using
<code>--hard</code>.
</p>

<p>
Do not use it blindly, especially on important work.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</div>

<h2>6. Explain reset --soft, --mixed and --hard in simple terms.</h2>

<div class="answer">

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">
<strong>SOFT</strong>
<br>
Commit removed
<br>
Changes staged
</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>MIXED</strong>
<br>
Commit removed
<br>
Changes unstaged
</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>HARD</strong>
<br>
Commit removed
<br>
Changes discarded
</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Easy memory trick:</strong>

<p>
<strong>Soft â†’ Keep staged</strong><br>
<strong>Mixed â†’ Keep files</strong><br>
<strong>Hard â†’ Throw away local changes</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>7. What is git revert?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git revert</code> creates a new commit that reverses the
changes introduced by an earlier commit.
</p>

<p>
Unlike reset, revert does not remove the original commit from
the shared history.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git revert abc123
</pre>

</div>

<div class="success">

<strong>Production-Friendly:</strong>

<p>
Revert is generally safer for shared branches because it preserves
the existing history and adds a new commit that undoes the change.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>8. What is the difference between git reset and git revert?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>git reset</th>
<th>git revert</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Moves branch pointer</td>
<td>Creates a new commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can rewrite history</td>
<td>Preserves existing history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for local changes</td>
<td>Safer for shared branches</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can remove commits from branch history</td>
<td>Original commit remains visible</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can discard working-tree changes with --hard</td>
<td>Does not simply erase the original commit</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Shortcut:</strong>

<p>
<strong>Reset = move history.</strong>
</p>

<p>
<strong>Revert = create a new commit that undoes history.</strong>
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS FAVORITE</div>

<h2>9. If a bad commit is already pushed to production, would you use reset or revert?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
I would generally prefer <code>git revert</code> because the commit
has already been shared and possibly deployed.
</p>

<p>
Revert preserves the existing history and creates a new commit
that reverses the bad change.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git revert &lt;bad-commit-id&gt;

git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

<div class="success">

<strong>Production principle:</strong>

<p>
For a shared branch, prefer a history-preserving rollback such
as revert rather than rewriting the branch with reset.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>10. You committed the wrong changes locally. What would you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
If the commit has not been pushed and I want to keep the changes,
I can use a soft or mixed reset depending on whether I want the
changes staged or unstaged.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reset --soft HEAD~1
</pre>

<p>
Or:</p>

<pre>
git reset HEAD~1
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>11. You accidentally committed a password or secret. What should you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
First, I would treat the secret as compromised and rotate or
revoke it immediately.
</p>

<p>
Then I would remove it from the repository and follow the team's
secret-remediation process.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Simply deleting the secret in a later commit does not necessarily
remove it from Git history.
</p>

<p>
For sensitive credentials, history cleanup may also be required,
depending on where the secret was exposed.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>12. What is git restore?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
<code>git restore</code> is used to restore files in the working
tree or staging area.
</p>

<p>
It separates file restoration tasks from the older
<code>git checkout</code> command.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git restore app.py
</pre>

<p>
Restore a staged file back to the working tree:</p>

<pre>
git restore --staged app.py
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<p>
<code>git restore</code> is mainly about restoring file contents
and staging state, while <code>git reset</code> can move the branch
pointer.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>13. What is git reflog?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
Git reflog records updates to local references such as HEAD and
branch pointers.
</p>

<p>
It can help recover commits or branch positions that are no longer
reachable through the normal branch history.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reflog
</pre>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Reflog is extremely useful when you accidentally reset, rebase,
or move a branch pointer and need to find the previous position.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</div>

<h2>14. Can you recover a commit after git reset --hard?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Yes, often you can if the commit is still available in the local reflog.</strong>

<p>
First check:
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reflog
</pre>

</div>

<p>
Find the previous commit ID and reset back to it if appropriate:
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reset --hard &lt;commit-id&gt;
</pre>

</div>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

<p>
Recovery is not guaranteed forever. Git eventually prunes unreachable
objects according to repository maintenance and retention behavior.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>15. You accidentally ran git reset --hard HEAD~3. What would you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<ol>
<li>Do not panic.</li>
<li>Check the reflog.</li>
<li>Identify the previous HEAD position.</li>
<li>Verify the commit.</li>
<li>Move the branch back to the correct commit.</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git reflog

# Find the previous HEAD

git reset --hard &lt;previous-commit-id&gt;
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</div>

<h2>16. What does HEAD mean in Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
HEAD is a reference that normally points to the currently checked
out branch or commit.
</p>

<p>
When you make a new commit, the branch and HEAD move forward.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
A --- B --- C
            â†‘
           HEAD
            |
           main
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>17. What does HEAD~1 mean?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
<code>HEAD~1</code> means the first parent of the current commit,
which is commonly the previous commit in a normal linear history.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
A --- B --- C
            â†‘
           HEAD

HEAD~1 = B

HEAD~2 = A
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>18. What is the difference between git restore and git reset?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>git restore</th>
<th>git reset</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Restores file contents</td>
<td>Can move branch pointer</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can unstage files</td>
<td>Can change staging state</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not normally move branch history</td>
<td>Can rewrite branch history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for file-level recovery</td>
<td>Useful for commit-level/local history changes</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED</div>

<h2>19. Can you reset a pushed commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Technically, yes, but resetting a pushed commit changes the local
branch history and usually requires a force push to update the
remote branch.
</p>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Production Warning:</strong>

<p>
Avoid rewriting shared branch history just to remove a pushed
commit. For a bad shared commit, <code>git revert</code> is usually
the safer approach.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q20 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW FAVORITE</div>

<h2>20. What is git revert HEAD?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
It creates a new commit that reverses the changes introduced by
the current HEAD commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git revert HEAD
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q21 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>21. How do you undo the latest commit but keep the changes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Use a soft reset:
</p>

<pre>
git reset --soft HEAD~1
</pre>

<p>
The commit is removed from the branch history while the changes
remain staged.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q22 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>22. How do you undo the latest commit and keep the files but unstage them?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git reset HEAD~1
</pre>

<p>
This is the default mixed reset.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q23 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DANGEROUS COMMAND</div>

<h2>23. How do you completely remove the latest local commit and its changes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<pre>
git reset --hard HEAD~1
</pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>âš ï¸ Warning:</strong>

<p>
This can discard uncommitted changes. Verify the working tree
before using it.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q24 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>24. A deployment commit broke production. What is the safest Git rollback approach?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
If the bad commit is already part of a shared production branch,
I would normally create a revert commit rather than rewrite the
shared history.
</p>

<div class="example">

<pre>
git revert &lt;bad-commit&gt;

git push origin main
</pre>

</div>

<p>
Then the CI/CD pipeline can validate and deploy the rollback,
according to the team's process.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q25 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME DEVOPS SCENARIO</div>

<h2>25. A developer says "I deleted my commit with reset --hard." How would you investigate?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
I would first inspect the local reflog:
</p>

<pre>
git reflog
</pre>

<p>
Then I would identify the commit that existed before the reset and
verify it before recovering it.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q26 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW TRAP</div>

<h2>26. Does git revert delete the original commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>No.</strong>

<p>
The original commit remains in the history. Revert creates another
commit whose changes reverse the original commit.
</p>

</div>

<div class="example">

<pre>
A --- B --- C --- R

C = Bad commit
R = Revert commit
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q27 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­ IMPORTANT</div>

<h2>27. Does git reset delete a commit permanently?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
Reset can make a commit unreachable from the current branch,
but that does not always mean the commit immediately disappears
from the local repository.
</p>

<p>
The reflog may still contain the previous reference, allowing
recovery for some time.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q28 -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ REAL-TIME SCENARIO</div>

<h2>28. A developer accidentally reset the wrong branch. What should they do first?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>First: stop making more destructive changes.</strong>

<p>
Then check:
</p>

<pre>
git reflog
</pre>

<p>
Identify the previous branch position and recover it carefully.
</p>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>Good interview wording:</strong>

<p>
"I would first inspect reflog instead of immediately running more
reset commands, because reflog can show the previous HEAD positions."
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- COMMAND CHEAT SHEET -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ§  QUICK COMMAND REVISION</div>

<h2>Git Recovery Command Cheat Sheet</h2>

<div class="example">

<pre>
# Undo latest commit, keep changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo latest commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset HEAD~1

# Undo latest commit and discard local changes
git reset --hard HEAD~1

# Undo a shared commit safely
git revert &lt;commit-id&gt;

# Restore a working-tree file
git restore app.py

# Unstage a file
git restore --staged app.py

# View local reference history
git reflog

# View commit history
git log --oneline --graph --all
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- COMPARISON -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸŽ¯ FINAL COMPARISON</div>

<h2>Reset vs Revert vs Restore vs Reflog</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Main Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>reset</strong></td>
<td>Move branch pointer / change staging and working tree depending on mode</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>revert</strong></td>
<td>Create a new commit that reverses an earlier commit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>restore</strong></td>
<td>Restore file contents or unstage files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>reflog</strong></td>
<td>Find previous local HEAD/reference positions for recovery</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- MEMORY -->

<div class="question">

<div class="badge">ðŸ”¥ INTERVIEW MEMORY TRICK</div>

<h2>Remember These Four Words</h2>

<div class="diagram">

<div class="box">
<strong>RESET</strong>
<br>
Move
</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>REVERT</strong>
<br>
Reverse
</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>RESTORE</strong>
<br>
Recover File
</div>

<div class="box">
<strong>REFLOG</strong>
<br>
Recover History
</div>

</div>

<div class="tip">

<strong>One-line answer:</strong>

<p>
"Reset changes the branch position, revert creates a commit that
undoes a previous commit, restore handles file/staging restoration,
and reflog helps recover previous local reference positions."
</p>

</div>

</div>

<header>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Git & GitHub</a>

<h1>Git <span>Stashing</span></h1>

<p>
Temporarily save uncommitted changes, switch branches safely,
restore work and handle practical DevOps scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ GIT STASH â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Git stash is used when you have uncommitted changes in your working
directory but need to temporarily switch to another branch or
perform another Git operation.
</p>

<p>
Instead of committing unfinished work, you can temporarily store
those changes using <code>git stash</code> and restore them later.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>1. What is Git Stash?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Git stash</strong> temporarily saves your uncommitted changes
and cleans the working directory so you can work on something else.

</div>

<h3>Basic command</h3>

<pre><code>git stash</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Uncommitted Changes
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>git stash</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Changes Temporarily Stored
<br>
â†“
<br>
Clean Working Directory

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Git stash temporarily stores my uncommitted changes and gives me
a clean working directory. I can later restore those changes using
commands such as git stash pop or git stash apply."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>2. Why do we use Git Stash?</h2>

<p>
A common situation is that you are working on one feature and
suddenly need to switch to another branch.
</p>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>feature/login
     |
     | Uncommitted changes
     â†“
Urgent production bug
     |
     â†“
Need to switch to main / hotfix branch</code></pre>

<p>
Instead of creating an unnecessary commit, you can stash the
unfinished changes.
</p>

<pre><code>git stash

git switch main</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>3. What does git stash do?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash</code></pre>

<p>
By default, Git saves changes to tracked files that are modified or
staged and restores the working tree to a clean state.
</p>

<div class="warning">

Important: ordinary <code>git stash</code> does not include
untracked files by default.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>4. How do you see your stashes?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash list</code></pre>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>stash@{0}: WIP on feature/login
stash@{1}: WIP on main
stash@{2}: WIP on feature/payment</code></pre>

<p>
The most recent stash is normally referenced as
<code>stash@{0}</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>5. How do you restore stashed changes?</h2>

<p>There are two commonly used commands:</p>

<pre><code>git stash apply</code>

<code>git stash pop</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Behavior</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash apply</code></td>
<td>Restores the stash but keeps it in the stash list</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash pop</code></td>
<td>Restores the stash and removes it from the stash list if applied successfully</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>6. Difference between git stash apply and git stash pop?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The key difference is whether the stash remains in the stash list.

</div>

<pre><code>git stash apply

â†’ Restore changes
â†’ Keep stash</code></pre>

<pre><code>git stash pop

â†’ Restore changes
â†’ Remove stash if successfully applied</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I use git stash apply when I want to restore the changes but keep
the stash as a backup. I use git stash pop when I want to restore
the changes and remove that stash entry after successful
application."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>7. How do you stash with a message?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash push -m "Login feature work"</code></pre>

<p>
A descriptive message makes it easier to identify a stash later.
</p>

<h3>Check it</h3>

<pre><code>git stash list</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>8. How do you stash untracked files?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Use the <code>-u</code> option.

</div>

<pre><code>git stash -u</code></pre>

<p>
This includes untracked files in the stash.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

<br><br>

<code>git stash</code> â†’ tracked changes

<br>

<code>git stash -u</code> â†’ tracked + untracked changes

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>9. How do you stash ignored files too?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash -a</code></pre>

<p>
The <code>-a</code> option includes ignored files as well as tracked
and untracked files.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Includes</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash</code></td>
<td>Tracked changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash -u</code></td>
<td>Tracked + untracked</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash -a</code></td>
<td>Tracked + untracked + ignored</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>10. How do you apply a specific stash?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash list

git stash apply stash@{1}</code></pre>

<p>
This applies the specific stash instead of the latest one.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>11. How do you remove a specific stash?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash drop stash@{1}</code></pre>

<p>
This removes that stash entry.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>12. How do you delete all stashes?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash clear</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

This permanently removes all stash entries from the repository's
stash list. Use it carefully.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>13. Can you create a branch from a stash?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Yes. Git provides <code>git stash branch</code> for this purpose.

</div>

<pre><code>git stash branch feature/login stash@{0}</code></pre>

<p>
Git creates a new branch starting from the commit where the stash
was originally created and then attempts to apply the stash.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>14. What is git stash show?</h2>

<pre><code>git stash show</code></pre>

<p>
It shows a summary of the changes contained in a stash.
</p>

<h3>More detailed view</h3>

<pre><code>git stash show -p</code></pre>

<p>
The <code>-p</code> option displays the actual patch/diff.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>15. Does git stash create a commit?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Git stash internally stores the stashed state using Git objects,
but from the developer's workflow perspective it is not a normal
branch commit that you push to GitHub.

</div>

<p>
A stash is primarily a temporary local storage mechanism for
uncommitted work.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>16. Is Git stash shared with the team?</h2>

<div class="answer">

No. Git stash is normally local to your repository.

</div>

<p>
A stash is not pushed to GitHub using <code>git push</code>.
If another developer needs your work, create a proper commit and
push it through the normal Git workflow.
</p>

<div class="warning">

Do not use Git stash as a replacement for Git commits when work
needs to be shared with the team.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>17. What happens if stash apply causes conflicts?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A stash can conflict with changes already present in the target
branch.

</div>

<h3>Typical workflow</h3>

<pre><code>git stash apply

# Conflict occurs

git status

# Resolve conflicted files

git add .

# Continue your normal workflow</code></pre>

<p>
The conflict must be resolved manually just like other Git
conflicts.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>18. Real-Time Scenario: Urgent production bug</h2>

<p>
You are working on a new feature but your manager asks you to fix
a production issue immediately.
</p>

<pre><code># Current feature work

git status

# Temporarily save unfinished changes

git stash push -m "WIP login feature"

# Move to the required branch

git switch main

# Fix production issue

git add .
git commit -m "Fix production issue"

git push origin main</code></pre>

<p>
After the urgent work is complete, return to the feature branch.
</p>

<pre><code>git switch feature/login

git stash pop</code></pre>

<div class="success">

Your unfinished feature work can now be restored and continued.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>19. Real-Time Scenario: Multiple stashes</h2>

<pre><code>git stash push -m "Login UI"
git stash push -m "Payment API"
git stash push -m "Monitoring changes"</code></pre>

<h3>View them</h3>

<pre><code>git stash list</code></pre>

<p>
You can then choose the required stash using its reference.
</p>

<pre><code>git stash apply stash@{1}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>20. When should you NOT use Git stash?</h2>

<ul>
<li>When work needs to be shared with teammates</li>
<li>When the changes represent a meaningful completed unit</li>
<li>When you need a permanent history of the work</li>
<li>When the work should be reviewed through a pull request</li>
</ul>

<div class="success">

Use a proper Git commit when the work should become part of the
project history.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>21. Git Stash vs Git Commit</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Git Stash</th>
<th>Git Commit</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Temporary storage</td>
<td>Permanent project history</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Normally local</td>
<td>Can be pushed to remote</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for unfinished work</td>
<td>Useful for meaningful changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Not normally shared with team</td>
<td>Can be shared through GitHub</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>22. DevOps Interview Scenario: You have uncommitted changes but need to pull latest code. What do you do?</h2>

<div class="answer">

First determine whether the local changes are ready to commit. If
they are unfinished, temporarily stash them.

</div>

<pre><code>git status

git stash push -m "WIP"

git pull origin main

git stash pop</code></pre>

<p>
If conflicts occur while applying the stash, resolve them before
continuing.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Better real-world answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I first check whether my changes can be committed safely. If they
are incomplete, I can stash them, synchronize with the remote
branch, and then restore the work. In a team environment I also
follow the repository's merge/rebase policy."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>23. Common Git Stash Commands</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash</code></td>
<td>Stash tracked changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash push -m "message"</code></td>
<td>Create named stash</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash -u</code></td>
<td>Include untracked files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash -a</code></td>
<td>Include ignored files too</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash list</code></td>
<td>List stashes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash show</code></td>
<td>Show stash summary</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash show -p</code></td>
<td>Show stash diff</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash apply</code></td>
<td>Apply latest stash and keep it</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash pop</code></td>
<td>Apply latest stash and remove it if successful</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash drop</code></td>
<td>Remove a stash</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash clear</code></td>
<td>Remove all stashes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git stash branch branch-name</code></td>
<td>Create branch from stash</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

<header>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Git & GitHub</a>

<h1>Git <span>Tags & Releases</span></h1>

<p>
Git tags, annotated tags, versioning, releases, rollback strategies
and practical DevOps deployment workflows.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­ GIT TAGS â€” IMPORTANT FOR DEVOPS</strong>

<p>
Git tags are used to mark specific points in Git history, commonly
for software releases such as <code>v1.0.0</code>,
<code>v2.0.0</code> or <code>v2.1.3</code>.
</p>

<p>
In DevOps, tags are especially useful for identifying exactly which
version of source code was built and deployed.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>1. What is a Git Tag?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>Git tag</strong> is a reference that points to a specific
Git object, commonly a commit.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>v1.0.0
v1.1.0
v2.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
Instead of remembering a commit hash, teams can use a meaningful
version name to identify a release.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Git tags are used to mark specific points in the repository history.
They are commonly used to identify software releases and stable
versions."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>2. Why are Git Tags important in DevOps?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Tags provide a stable reference to the exact source-code version
used for a release or deployment.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Code Changes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Commit
<br>
â†“
<br>
Git Tag <code>v1.0.0</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
CI Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Production Deployment

</div>

<p>
This makes releases traceable and helps teams identify exactly
which version is running in an environment.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>3. How do you list Git tags?</h2>

<pre><code>git tag</code></pre>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>v1.0.0
v1.1.0
v1.2.0
v2.0.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>4. How do you create a lightweight tag?</h2>

<pre><code>git tag v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
This creates a lightweight tag pointing to the current commit.
</p>

<h3>Tag a specific commit</h3>

<pre><code>git tag v1.0.0 abc1234</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>5. What is an annotated tag?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An annotated tag is a full Git object containing metadata such as
the tagger, date and message.

</div>

<h3>Create one</h3>

<pre><code>git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release version 1.0.0"</code></pre>

<p>
Annotated tags are generally preferred for official releases
because they contain release metadata.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>6. Lightweight Tag vs Annotated Tag</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Lightweight Tag</th>
<th>Annotated Tag</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple reference</td>
<td>Full Git object</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Minimal metadata</td>
<td>Contains tagger, date and message</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for simple references</td>
<td>Preferred for official releases</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>git tag v1.0.0</code></td>
<td><code>git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release"</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"A lightweight tag is a simple pointer to a commit. An annotated
tag is a Git object containing metadata such as the tagger, date
and message. Annotated tags are commonly preferred for releases."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>7. How do you view information about a tag?</h2>

<pre><code>git show v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
This displays information about the tag and the referenced commit.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>8. How do you push a tag to GitHub?</h2>

<h3>Push one tag</h3>

<pre><code>git push origin v1.0.0</code></pre>

<h3>Push all tags</h3>

<pre><code>git push origin --tags</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Creating a tag locally does not automatically make it available on
the remote repository. You need to push it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>9. How do you delete a local tag?</h2>

<pre><code>git tag -d v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
This removes the tag from your local repository.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>10. How do you delete a remote tag?</h2>

<pre><code>git push origin --delete v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
This removes the tag from the remote repository.
</p>

<h3>Alternative syntax</h3>

<pre><code>git push origin :refs/tags/v1.0.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>11. How do you checkout a tag?</h2>

<pre><code>git checkout v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
This places you at the commit referenced by the tag.
</p>

<div class="warning">

If you make new commits from a tag without creating a branch, you
can end up in a detached HEAD state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>12. What is detached HEAD when checking out a tag?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit instead of
pointing to a local branch.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git checkout v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
You can inspect or test that version safely. If you need to develop
from that point, create a branch.
</p>

<pre><code>git switch -c hotfix-from-v1.0.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>13. How do you create a tag on a specific commit?</h2>

<pre><code>git tag -a v1.0.0 abc1234 -m "Release v1.0.0"</code></pre>

<p>
The tag will point to the specified commit instead of the current
HEAD.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>14. How do you list tags matching a pattern?</h2>

<pre><code>git tag -l "v1.*"</code></pre>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>v1.0.0
v1.1.0
v1.2.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>15. What is semantic versioning?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Semantic Versioning commonly follows the format:

<br><br>

<strong>MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH</strong>

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MAJOR</td>
<td>Breaking or incompatible changes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MINOR</td>
<td>Backward-compatible new functionality</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>PATCH</td>
<td>Backward-compatible bug fixes</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>1.4.2

1 â†’ Major
4 â†’ Minor
2 â†’ Patch</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>16. What is a GitHub Release?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A GitHub Release is a published release associated with a Git tag,
providing a convenient way to distribute and document a specific
version of a project.

</div>

<p>
A release can include:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Version number</li>
<li>Release notes</li>
<li>Changelog</li>
<li>Links to source code</li>
<li>Build artifacts</li>
<li>Binary files</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- Q17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>17. Git Tag vs GitHub Release</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Git Tag</th>
<th>GitHub Release</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Git reference</td>
<td>GitHub publishing feature</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Points to a Git object</td>
<td>Usually associated with a tag</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can exist without GitHub</td>
<td>Requires GitHub platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for version identification</td>
<td>Used for publishing/documenting a release</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- Q18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>18. Real-Time DevOps Scenario: Release a production version</h2>

<p>
Suppose version <code>1.4.0</code> has passed testing and is ready
for production.
</p>

<pre><code>git switch main

git pull origin main

git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release v1.4.0"

git push origin v1.4.0</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Git Commit
<br>
â†“
<br>
<code>v1.4.0</code>
<br>
â†“
<br>
CI/CD Pipeline
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build & Test
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Production

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>19. How can CI/CD use Git tags?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A CI/CD pipeline can be configured to trigger when a version tag
is pushed.

</div>

<h3>Example concept</h3>

<pre><code>git push origin v2.0.0

        â†“

CI/CD detects tag

        â†“

Build application

        â†“

Run tests

        â†“

Build Docker image

        â†“

Push image

        â†“

Deploy version 2.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
This creates a clear relationship between source-code versions and
deployments.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>20. Why are immutable version tags useful in DevOps?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A release tag provides a stable identifier for the source version
that was intended for a particular release.

</div>

<p>
This improves:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Traceability</li>
<li>Rollback planning</li>
<li>Release auditing</li>
<li>Deployment tracking</li>
<li>Incident investigation</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

In production workflows, teams should establish a policy for
protecting release tags and avoiding accidental tag movement.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>21. How would you rollback to an earlier tagged version?</h2>

<p>
First identify the desired stable tag.
</p>

<pre><code>git tag

git show v1.3.0</code></pre>

<p>
For inspection or creating a branch from that version:
</p>

<pre><code>git switch -c rollback-v1.3.0 v1.3.0</code></pre>

<p>
In a real production environment, rollback is usually handled
through the deployment system rather than rewriting the main
branch history.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>DevOps interview point:</strong>

<br><br>

"I would prefer redeploying a known-good version such as a release
tag or corresponding immutable artifact rather than rewriting
production Git history."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>22. Can you move an existing tag?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Yes, technically a tag can be deleted and recreated at another
commit, but moving an already-published release tag is generally
discouraged.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>git tag -d v1.0.0

git tag v1.0.0 &lt;new-commit&gt;

git push origin v1.0.0 --force</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Avoid moving published production tags unless your team's release
policy explicitly allows it. Prefer creating a new version such as
<code>v1.0.1</code>.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Q23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>23. Real-Time Scenario: Production is running v2.1.0</h2>

<p>
An incident occurs and you discover that <code>v2.0.5</code> was
the last known-good release.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Production
<br>
â†“
<br>
v2.1.0 âŒ
<br>
â†“
<br>
Known-good release
<br>
â†“
<br>
v2.0.5 âœ…
<br>
â†“
<br>
Redeploy

</div>

<p>
The tag provides a reliable reference for locating the source
version associated with the earlier release.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Q24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>24. How do you find which commit a tag points to?</h2>

<pre><code>git rev-list -n 1 v1.0.0</code></pre>

<p>
You can also inspect the tag with:
</p>

<pre><code>git show v1.0.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- Q25 -->

<div class="card">

</tr>

<td>List matching tags</td>
</tr>

</tr>

<tr>
<td>Delete local</td>
<td><code>git tag -d v1.0.0</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Delete remote</td>
<td><code>git push origin --delete v1.0.0</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Inspect</td>
<td><code>git show v1.0.0</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

</main>

<div class="icon">ðŸ³</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Docker</a>

<h1>Docker <span>Basics</span></h1>

<p>
Docker fundamentals, architecture, containers, images, registries,
Docker Engine, Docker vs Virtual Machines and real DevOps interview scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Docker is one of the most important technologies for DevOps.
Before learning Docker commands, Dockerfiles, networking or Compose,
you should understand what Docker actually solves and how its
architecture works.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker Image</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker Container</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Engine
<br>
â†“
<br>
Host Operating System

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Docker?</h2>

<h3>Q. What is Docker?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Docker is a containerization platform used to package an application
and its dependencies into a portable image that can run consistently
across different environments.
</div>

<h3>Why do we use Docker?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Consistent application environments</li>
<li>Fast application startup</li>
<li>Application isolation</li>
<li>Portable deployments</li>
<li>Efficient resource usage</li>
<li>Easy CI/CD integration</li>
<li>Microservices deployment</li>
<li>Scalable application packaging</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Docker is a containerization platform that packages applications
and their dependencies into portable images. These images can be
used to create isolated containers, providing consistency across
development, testing and production environments."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Containers vs Virtual Machines</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Containers</th>
<th>Virtual Machines</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Share the host OS kernel</td>
<td>Each VM normally includes a guest OS</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Lightweight</td>
<td>Heavier</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Start quickly</td>
<td>Usually slower startup</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Lower resource overhead</td>
<td>Higher resource overhead</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for application isolation</td>
<td>Provides stronger full OS-level isolation</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container image contains application and dependencies</td>
<td>VM image includes an entire operating system</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Virtual Machine
<br>
Application
â†“
Libraries
â†“
Guest OS
â†“
Hypervisor
â†“
Host OS
<br><br>

Container
<br>
Application
â†“
Libraries
â†“
Container
â†“
Docker Engine
â†“
Host OS

</div>

<h3>Important interview point</h3>

<div class="answer">
Containers are not simply "small virtual machines". They use
OS-level isolation and share the host kernel, while VMs virtualize
hardware and run guest operating systems.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Docker Architecture</h2>

<p>
Docker uses a client-server architecture. The Docker CLI communicates
with the Docker daemon, which manages Docker objects such as images,
containers and networks.
</p>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Docker CLI</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker API
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker Daemon</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Images â€¢ Containers â€¢ Networks â€¢ Volumes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container Runtime
<br>
â†“
<br>
Containers

</div>

<h3>Docker Client</h3>

<div class="answer">
The Docker client is the command-line interface used to send commands
to the Docker daemon.
</div>

<h3>Docker Daemon</h3>

<div class="answer">
The Docker daemon manages Docker objects such as containers, images,
networks and volumes and performs requested operations.
</div>

<h3>Docker Engine</h3>

<div class="answer">
Docker Engine is the technology used to build and run containers.
It includes the Docker daemon, API and supporting container runtime
components.
</div>

<h3>Docker Registry</h3>

<div class="answer">
A registry stores and distributes container images. Docker Hub is a
popular public registry, while organizations can also use private
registries.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Docker Image</h2>

<h3>Q. What is a Docker image?</h3>

<div class="answer">
A Docker image is an immutable, versioned package used as the
template for creating containers. It contains the application,
dependencies and filesystem layers required by the container.
</div>

<h3>Image characteristics</h3>

<ul>
<li>Read-only template</li>
<li>Versionable</li>
<li>Portable</li>
<li>Made of filesystem layers</li>
<li>Can create multiple containers</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Dockerfile
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker build</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker run</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Docker Container</h2>

<h3>Q. What is a container?</h3>

<div class="answer">
A container is a running or stopped instance created from a Docker
image. It provides an isolated environment in which an application
and its dependencies can execute.
</div>

<h3>Image vs Container</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Image</th>
<th>Container</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Template</td>
<td>Instance created from the template</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Immutable filesystem layers</td>
<td>Has a writable container layer</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used to create containers</td>
<td>Runs the application</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be stored in a registry</td>
<td>Normally runs on a host</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Docker Image Layers</h2>

<p>
Docker images are built using layers. Each Dockerfile instruction
that creates filesystem changes can contribute to an image layer.
</p>

<pre><code>FROM ubuntu

RUN apt-get update

RUN apt-get install -y nginx

COPY app /app</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Layer 4 â†’ Application files
<br>
Layer 3 â†’ Nginx installation
<br>
Layer 2 â†’ Package metadata / changes
<br>
Layer 1 â†’ Base image
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker Image</strong>

</div>

<h3>Why are layers useful?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Image reuse</li>
<li>Build caching</li>
<li>Faster builds when cache is valid</li>
<li>Reduced storage through shared layers</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">
A change to an earlier Dockerfile instruction can invalidate the
cache for subsequent instructions, potentially making later build
steps execute again.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Docker Registry</h2>

<h3>Q. What is a container registry?</h3>

<div class="answer">
A container registry is a service used to store, version and
distribute container images.
</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<ul>
<li>Docker Hub</li>
<li>Amazon ECR</li>
<li>GitHub Container Registry</li>
<li>Azure Container Registry</li>
<li>Google Artifact Registry</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Push
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Container Registry</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pull
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deployment Environment

</div>

<h3>Common commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker login

docker tag myapp:1.0 username/myapp:1.0

docker push username/myapp:1.0

docker pull username/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Docker Container Lifecycle</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Image</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
docker create
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Created</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
docker start
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Running</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
docker stop
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Stopped</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
docker rm
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Removed</strong>

</div>

<h3>Important distinction</h3>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker stop</code> stops a container but keeps it.
<code>docker rm</code> removes the container.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What happens when you run docker run?</h2>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker run nginx</code></pre>

<h3>High-level flow</h3>

<ol>
<li>Docker checks whether the image exists locally.</li>
<li>If required, Docker pulls the image from a registry.</li>
<li>A container is created from the image.</li>
<li>Filesystem and networking are configured.</li>
<li>The container's configured process is started.</li>
</ol>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"When I execute docker run, Docker checks for the requested image.
If it is unavailable locally, Docker pulls it from the configured
registry. It then creates the container, configures its runtime
environment and starts the container's main process."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Docker Port Mapping</h2>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Browser
<br>
â†“
<br>
Host Port <strong>8080</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container Port <strong>80</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Nginx

</div>

<div class="answer">
The format is <code>HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT</code>.
Port publishing makes a container port reachable through the
specified host port.
</div>

<div class="warning">
<code>EXPOSE</code> in a Dockerfile documents an intended container
port; it does not by itself publish the port to the host.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Docker Environment Variables</h2>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -e APP_ENV=production myapp</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Environment variables allow configuration to be supplied to the
container without hard-coding environment-specific values into
the application image.
</div>

<h3>Important DevOps principle</h3>

<div class="warning">
Do not put passwords, API keys or cloud credentials directly inside
Dockerfiles or images. Use appropriate secret-management mechanisms.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Container Isolation</h2>

<p>
Containers provide process, filesystem and network isolation using
Linux kernel features.
</p>

<h3>Important technologies</h3>

<ul>
<li>Namespaces â€” isolate processes and system resources</li>
<li>cgroups â€” control and account for resource usage</li>
<li>Union / layered filesystems â€” support image layers</li>
</ul>

<h3>Namespaces</h3>

<div class="answer">
Namespaces provide isolated views of resources such as processes,
network interfaces, mounts and hostnames.
</div>

<h3>cgroups</h3>

<div class="answer">
Control groups allow resource usage such as CPU and memory to be
controlled and monitored for processes.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Docker vs Docker Compose</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Docker</th>
<th>Docker Compose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can manage individual containers</td>
<td>Defines and manages multi-container applications</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commands can be executed individually</td>
<td>Configuration is commonly defined in YAML</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for individual workloads</td>
<td>Useful for application stacks</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

Example application:

<br><br>

Frontend + Backend + Database

<br><br>

Compose can define these services together, including their
networks, volumes and configuration.

</div>

<p>
Detailed Compose concepts will be covered in the dedicated
<code>docker-compose.html</code> section.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Docker in DevOps</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>

<br>

<br>

</div>

<h3>Why Docker is important in CI/CD</h3>

<ul>
<li>Consistent build environment</li>
<li>Portable artifacts</li>
<li>Repeatable deployments</li>
<li>Easy integration with CI systems</li>
<li>Works well with Kubernetes and container platforms</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Real-Time Scenario: "It works on my machine"</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

An application works correctly on a developer's laptop but fails
in the test or production environment.

<br><br>

<strong>Docker approach:</strong>

Package the application together with its runtime dependencies into
an image and use the same image across environments.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Containerization helps reduce environment differences by packaging
the application and its dependencies into a consistent image. The
same tested image can then move through CI/CD environments."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Scenario: Container exits immediately</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A container starts and immediately stops.

<br><br>

<strong>First checks:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Check container status</li>
<li>Check container logs</li>
<li>Inspect the configured command</li>
<li>Check environment variables</li>
<li>Verify application startup errors</li>
</ul>

</div>

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
A container normally remains running only while its main process
is running. If that process exits, the container stops.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: Container cannot be reached</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

The application is running inside a container but cannot be reached
from the browser.

<br><br>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Is the container running?</li>
<li>Is the application listening on the expected container port?</li>
<li>Was the host port published?</li>
<li>Are host firewall/security rules allowing the port?</li>
<li>Is the application bound to the correct interface?</li>
</ul>

</div>

<pre><code>docker ps

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

</div>

<!-- FINAL -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If the Interviewer Says: "Explain Docker in 1 Minute"</h2>

<div class="interview">

" Docker is a containerization platform used to package an
application and its dependencies into a portable image.

That image can be used to create containers that run consistently
across different environments.

Docker uses a client-server architecture where the Docker CLI
communicates with the Docker daemon. Images can be stored in
container registries such as Docker Hub or Amazon ECR.

Compared with virtual machines, containers are generally more
lightweight because they share the host operating system kernel.

In DevOps, Docker is commonly used in CI/CD to build a consistent
application image, scan it, push it to a registry and deploy the
same tested artifact across environments.

Important Docker concepts include images, containers, Dockerfiles,
networking, volumes, Compose, security and container
troubleshooting."

</div>

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER COMMANDS â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
You do not need to memorize every Docker command for an interview.
Focus on the commands used daily for building, running, inspecting,
troubleshooting and cleaning Docker workloads.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker run</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container

<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Docker Version & Information</h2>

<h3>Check Docker version</h3>

<pre><code>docker --version

docker version</code></pre>

<p>
<code>docker --version</code> gives the CLI version, while
<code>docker version</code> provides client and server/daemon details.
</p>

<h3>System information</h3>

<pre><code>docker info</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker info</code> is useful when troubleshooting the Docker
environment because it provides information about the daemon,
containers, images, storage driver and runtime configuration.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Working with Docker Images</h2>

<h3>List images</h3>

<pre><code>docker images

docker image ls</code></pre>

<h3>Pull an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker pull nginx

docker pull nginx:latest</code></pre>

<h3>Remove an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker rmi nginx

docker image rm nginx</code></pre>

<h3>Inspect an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker image inspect nginx</code></pre>

<h3>View image history</h3>

<pre><code>docker history nginx</code></pre>

<h3>Tag an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker tag myapp:latest username/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview point:</strong>

<br><br>

Image commands are commonly used to inspect, version, tag, pull,
push and remove application images.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. docker run</h2>

<h3>Basic command</h3>

<pre><code>docker run nginx</code></pre>

<h3>Run in background</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d nginx</code></pre>

<p>
<code>-d</code> runs the container in detached mode.
</p>

<h3>Assign a name</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d --name web nginx</code></pre>

<h3>Publish a port</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

<h3>Set environment variable</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d \
--name app \
-e APP_ENV=production \
myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Run interactively</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -it ubuntu bash</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker run</code> creates and starts a new container from an
image. It can also configure the container's name, ports,
environment variables, volumes, network and command.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. List Containers</h2>

<h3>Running containers</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps</code></pre>

<h3>All containers</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -a</code></pre>

<h3>Only container IDs</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -q</code></pre>

<h3>All container IDs</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -aq</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker ps</code></td>
<td>Shows running containers</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker ps -a</code></td>
<td>Shows running and stopped containers</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker ps -q</code></td>
<td>Shows IDs of running containers</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Container Lifecycle</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker create</code></td>
<td>Create a container without starting it</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker start</code></td>
<td>Start a stopped container</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker stop</code></td>
<td>Gracefully stop a running container</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker restart</code></td>
<td>Restart a container</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker pause</code></td>
<td>Pause container processes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker unpause</code></td>
<td>Resume paused processes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker kill</code></td>
<td>Forcefully stop a container using a signal</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker rm</code></td>
<td>Remove a container</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker stop web

docker start web

docker restart web

docker rm web</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
A stopped container is not automatically deleted. You must remove
it separately with <code>docker rm</code> unless another cleanup
mechanism handles it.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Docker Logs</h2>

<h3>View logs</h3>

<pre><code>docker logs web</code></pre>

<h3>Follow logs</h3>

<pre><code>docker logs -f web</code></pre>

<h3>Show recent logs</h3>

<pre><code>docker logs --tail 100 web</code></pre>

<h3>Show timestamps</h3>

<pre><code>docker logs -t web</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Production scenario:</strong>

A container is repeatedly stopping.

First check:

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container-name&gt;</code></pre>

The logs may reveal application startup errors, configuration
problems or missing dependencies.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. docker exec</h2>

<h3>Execute a command inside a running container</h3>

<pre><code>docker exec web ls</code></pre>

<h3>Open a shell</h3>

<pre><code>docker exec -it web bash</code></pre>

<p>
If Bash is unavailable, a minimal image may provide <code>sh</code>.
</p>

<pre><code>docker exec -it web sh</code></pre>

<h3>Check environment</h3>

<pre><code>docker exec web env</code></pre>

<h3>Check processes</h3>

<pre><code>docker exec web ps</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker exec</code> runs a new process inside an already running
container. It is commonly used for troubleshooting and inspection.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. docker inspect</h2>

<h3>Inspect a container</h3>

<pre><code>docker inspect web</code></pre>

<p>
This returns detailed JSON information about the container.
</p>

<h3>Common things to investigate</h3>

<ul>
<li>Container IP address</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Port mappings</li>
<li>Mounts</li>
<li>Network configuration</li>
<li>Container state</li>
<li>Restart information</li>
<li>Image used</li>
</ul>

<h3>Inspect an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker image inspect nginx</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

When an application cannot connect to another container, inspect
the network configuration before changing random settings.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Container Resource Usage</h2>

<h3>Live resource usage</h3>

<pre><code>docker stats</code></pre>

<h3>Specific container</h3>

<pre><code>docker stats web</code></pre>

<p>
This displays live CPU, memory, network and block I/O information.
</p>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>High CPU scenario:</strong>

If an application suddenly consumes excessive CPU:

<pre><code>docker stats

docker logs web

docker inspect web</code></pre>

Then investigate the application process and host resources.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Copy Files To / From Containers</h2>

<h3>Host â†’ Container</h3>

<pre><code>docker cp ./config.yml web:/app/config.yml</code></pre>

<h3>Container â†’ Host</h3>

<pre><code>docker cp web:/app/logs.txt ./logs.txt</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker cp</code> copies files or directories between the local
filesystem and a container.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Container Port Inspection</h2>

<h3>Show published ports</h3>

<pre><code>docker port web</code></pre>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx

docker port web</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Use <code>docker port</code> when you want a quick view of the
container's published port mappings.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Docker Attach vs Exec</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>docker exec</th>
<th>docker attach</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Starts a new process inside the container</td>
<td>Attaches to the container's existing main process</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly safer for troubleshooting</td>
<td>Can interact directly with the main process</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: open a shell</td>
<td>Example: attach to process output</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>docker exec -it web sh

docker attach web</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Be careful when using <code>docker attach</code> because interacting
with the main process can affect the container depending on how the
application handles input and signals.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Docker Rename</h2>

<pre><code>docker rename old-name new-name</code></pre>

<p>
Renames an existing container without changing the image.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Docker Rename / Tag / Versioning</h2>

<h3>Tag an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker tag myapp:latest myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Registry tag</h3>

<pre><code>docker tag myapp:1.0 username/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Push</h3>

<pre><code>docker push username/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Pull</h3>

<pre><code>docker pull username/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>DevOps best practice:</strong>

<br><br>

Use meaningful immutable version tags for releases rather than
depending only on a mutable tag such as <code>latest</code>.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Docker System Cleanup</h2>

<h3>Check Docker disk usage</h3>

<pre><code>docker system df</code></pre>

<h3>Remove unused resources</h3>

<pre><code>docker system prune</code></pre>

<h3>More aggressive cleanup</h3>

<pre><code>docker system prune -a</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Be careful with cleanup commands.

<code>docker system prune -a</code> can remove unused images and
other unused Docker resources. Always understand what is unused
before running cleanup on an important host.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Removing Containers & Images</h2>

<h3>Remove stopped container</h3>

<pre><code>docker rm web</code></pre>

<h3>Force remove running container</h3>

<pre><code>docker rm -f web</code></pre>

<h3>Remove unused containers</h3>

<pre><code>docker container prune</code></pre>

<h3>Remove unused images</h3>

<pre><code>docker image prune</code></pre>

<h3>Remove unused networks</h3>

<pre><code>docker network prune</code></pre>

<h3>Remove unused volumes</h3>

<pre><code>docker volume prune</code></pre>

</div>
