<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Troubleshooting Scenarios</h2>

<h3>Scenario 1 â€” Container is not running</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Scenario 2 â€” Container exits immediately</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<p>
Check the exit status, logs and main process configured for the
container.
</p>

<h3>Scenario 3 â€” Application is unreachable</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps

docker port &lt;container&gt;

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Scenario 4 â€” High memory usage</h3>

<pre><code>docker stats</code></pre>

<h3>Scenario 5 â€” Docker host disk is full</h3>

<pre><code>docker system df

docker system prune</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Do not immediately delete everything. Identify unused images,
containers, volumes and build cache first.
</div>

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If the Interviewer Says: "Which Docker Commands Do You Use Daily?"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"I commonly use <code>docker ps</code> and
<code>docker ps -a</code> to check containers,
<code>docker logs</code> for troubleshooting,
<code>docker exec</code> to inspect a running container,
and <code>docker inspect</code> for detailed configuration.

For images I use commands such as <code>docker pull</code>,
<code>docker images</code>, <code>docker tag</code> and
<code>docker push</code>.

For container lifecycle management I use
<code>docker start</code>, <code>docker stop</code>,
<code>docker restart</code> and <code>docker rm</code>.

For resource and disk troubleshooting I use
<code>docker stats</code> and <code>docker system df</code>.
I use cleanup commands carefully, especially on production hosts."

</div>

<h1>Docker <span>Compose</span></h1>

<p>
Multi-container application management using Docker Compose,
YAML configuration, services, dependencies, environment variables,
networks, volumes and real-time DevOps scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="card intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER COMPOSE â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Docker Compose is used to define and manage multi-container
applications using a YAML configuration file.
</p>

<div class="flow">

docker-compose.yml
<br>
â†“
<br>
Services
<br>
â†“
<br>
Networks + Volumes + Configuration
<br>
â†“
<br>
Multiple Containers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Stack

</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview definition:</strong>
Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container
applications using a YAML file that describes services, networks,
volumes and configuration.
</div>

</div>


<!-- WHY COMPOSE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Why Do We Need Docker Compose?</h2>

<div class="answer">
Running multiple containers manually can become difficult.
Compose allows the entire application stack to be described as
configuration and started with a small number of commands.
</div>

<h3>Example application</h3>

<ul>
<li>Frontend</li>
<li>Backend API</li>
<li>MySQL</li>
<li>Redis</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Frontend
â†“
<br>
Backend
â†“
<br>
MySQL
<br>
+
<br>
Redis

</div>

<p>
Instead of maintaining many separate <code>docker run</code>
commands, these services can be defined in one Compose file.
</p>

</div>


<!-- FILE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is docker-compose.yml?</h2>

<div class="answer">
The Compose YAML file defines how the application's services should
be built, configured, connected and run.
</div>

<h3>Basic structure</h3>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend:1.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  database:
    image: mysql:8
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: example</code></pre>

<p>
Modern Docker Compose uses the <code>docker compose</code> command.
The older <code>docker-compose</code> command is also seen in older
projects.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SERVICES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is a Service in Docker Compose?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A service represents a containerized application component defined
inside the Compose configuration.
</div>

<pre><code>services:

  frontend:
    image: nginx

  backend:
    image: my-backend

  database:
    image: mysql:8</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Here:

<strong>frontend</strong> â†’ service

<strong>backend</strong> â†’ service

<strong>database</strong> â†’ service

Compose uses these definitions to create and manage the
corresponding containers.

</div>

</div>


<!-- IMAGE VS BUILD -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. image vs build</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>image</th>
<th>build</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses an existing Docker image.</td>
<td>Builds an image from a Dockerfile/context.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for official or prebuilt images.</td>
<td>Useful for your application source code.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Using an image</h3>

<pre><code>services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:latest</code></pre>

<h3>Using build</h3>

<pre><code>services:
  backend:
    build: ./backend</code></pre>

<h3>Build with Dockerfile</h3>

<pre><code>services:
  backend:
    build:
      context: ./backend
      dockerfile: Dockerfile</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- PORTS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 5. Ports in Compose</h2>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
The left side is the host port and the right side is the
container port.
</div>

<div class="flow">

Host :8080
<br>
â†“
<br>
Backend Container :8080

</div>

<p>
Port publishing is mainly needed when the service must be reached
from outside the Compose network.
</p>

</div>


<!-- ENVIRONMENT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Environment Variables</h2>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend
    environment:
      DB_HOST: database
      DB_PORT: 3306
      APP_ENV: production</code></pre>

<h3>Using .env</h3>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend
    environment:
      DB_HOST: ${DB_HOST}
      DB_PORT: ${DB_PORT}</code></pre>

<p><strong>.env</strong></p>

<pre><code>DB_HOST=database
DB_PORT=3306</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not put real passwords, API keys or cloud credentials directly
into source-controlled Compose files.

</div>

</div>


<!-- VOLUMES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Volumes in Compose</h2>

<p>
Compose can define named volumes for persistent application data.
</p>

<pre><code>services:

  database:
    image: mysql:8
    volumes:
      - mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql

volumes:
  mysql-data:</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

MySQL Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
/var/lib/mysql
<br>
â†“
<br>
mysql-data
<br>
â†“
<br>
Persistent Storage

</div>

</div>


<!-- NETWORK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Networks in Compose</h2>

<p>
Compose can create networks that allow services to communicate.
</p>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend
    networks:
      - app-network

  database:
    image: mysql:8
    networks:
      - app-network

networks:
  app-network:</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Services on the same Compose network can normally communicate
using their service names.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SERVICE DNS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Service Name as Hostname</h2>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend

  database:
    image: mysql:8</code></pre>

<p>
The backend can normally reach the database using:
</p>

<pre><code>DB_HOST=database</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not use the container IP as the application's permanent database
hostname. Service names provide a more stable Compose-level
communication mechanism.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DEPENDS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. depends_on</h2>

<h3>Why use depends_on?</h3>

<div class="answer">
It expresses a startup/shutdown dependency between Compose services.
</div>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend
    depends_on:
      - database

  database:
    image: mysql:8</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important interview point:</strong>

<code>depends_on</code> controls service dependency/startup ordering,
but it does not automatically guarantee that the database is ready
to accept connections.

</div>

</div>


<!-- HEALTHCHECK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Healthchecks</h2>

<p>
A healthcheck can be used to determine whether a service is actually
ready or healthy.
</p>

<pre><code>services:

  database:
    image: mysql:8
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: example

    healthcheck:
      test:
        - CMD-SHELL
        - mysqladmin ping -h localhost -pexample
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5</code></pre>

<p>
Healthchecks are useful when an application depends on another
service becoming operational rather than merely starting.
</p>

</div>


<!-- RESTART -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Restart Policies</h2>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    image: my-backend
    restart: unless-stopped</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Policy</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>no</code></td>
<td>Do not automatically restart.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>always</code></td>
<td>Restart the container according to Docker's restart behavior.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>on-failure</code></td>
<td>Restart when the container exits with a failure.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>unless-stopped</code></td>
<td>Restart unless it has been explicitly stopped.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- COMMANDS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Most Important Docker Compose Commands</h2>

<pre><code># Start services
docker compose up

# Start in background
docker compose up -d

# Build images
docker compose build

# Build and start
docker compose up --build

# List services/containers
docker compose ps

# View logs
docker compose logs

# Follow logs
docker compose logs -f

# Logs for one service
docker compose logs backend

# Stop and remove Compose resources
docker compose down

# Execute command inside service container
docker compose exec backend sh

# Restart services
docker compose restart

# Pull configured images
docker compose pull</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- UP DOWN -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. docker compose up vs down</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker compose up</code></td>
<td>Creates/starts the application services.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker compose up -d</code></td>
<td>Runs services in detached mode.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker compose up --build</code></td>
<td>Builds images and starts services.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>docker compose down</code></td>
<td>Stops and removes Compose-created containers and networks.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

Be aware of persistent volumes before using destructive cleanup
options. Do not remove database storage accidentally.

</div>

</div>


<!-- REAL WORLD -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Real-Time Backend + MySQL Example</h2>

<h3>docker-compose.yml</h3>

<pre><code>services:

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      DB_HOST: database
      DB_PORT: 3306
      DB_NAME: appdb
      DB_USER: appuser
      DB_PASSWORD: example
    depends_on:
      database:
        condition: service_healthy

  database:
    image: mysql:8
    environment:
      MYSQL_DATABASE: appdb
      MYSQL_USER: appuser
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: example
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: rootexample
    volumes:
      - mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql
    healthcheck:
      test:
        - CMD-SHELL
        - mysqladmin ping -h localhost -prootexample
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  mysql-data:</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>
â†“
<br>
docker compose up
<br>
â†“
<br>
Backend Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
Compose Network
<br>
â†“
<br>
Database Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
mysql-data Volume

</div>

</div>


<!-- THREE TIER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Three-Tier Application Using Compose</h2>

<pre><code>services:

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    depends_on:
      - database

  database:
    image: mysql:8
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/mysql

volumes:
  db-data:</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Architecture:</strong>

Frontend handles user requests.

Backend handles business logic.

Database stores persistent data.

Compose manages the complete local multi-container stack.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PROJECT STRUCTURE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Typical Compose Project Structure</h2>

<pre><code>my-project/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ docker-compose.yml
â”œâ”€â”€ .env
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ frontend/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ Dockerfile
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ source-code
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ backend/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ Dockerfile
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ source-code
â”‚
â””â”€â”€ README.md</code></pre>

<p>
This structure keeps service-specific Dockerfiles close to their
application source while Compose coordinates the overall stack.
</p>

</div>


<!-- COMPOSE OVERRIDES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. Development vs Production Configuration</h2>

<p>
Teams may use different Compose configurations for different
environments.
</p>

<pre><code>docker-compose.yml
docker-compose.dev.yml
docker-compose.prod.yml</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

For example, development might mount source code into the container
for rapid iteration, while production should generally use a
versioned image rather than a developer's local source directory.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECRETS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Secrets in Docker Compose</h2>

<div class="warning">

Never commit production passwords, AWS credentials, private keys or
API tokens into a Git repository.

</div>

<h3>Better approaches</h3>

<ul>
<li>Environment-specific secret injection</li>
<li>CI/CD secret stores</li>
<li>Cloud secret managers</li>
<li>Docker/Swarm secrets where applicable</li>
<li>Kubernetes Secrets for Kubernetes deployments</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would avoid hardcoding secrets in Compose files. For production,
I would inject secrets through the CI/CD or deployment platform and
prefer a dedicated secret-management solution."

</div>

</div>


<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Docker Compose Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Step 1 â€” Check services</h3>

<pre><code>docker compose ps</code></pre>

<h3>Step 2 â€” Check logs</h3>

<pre><code>docker compose logs backend

docker compose logs database</code></pre>

<h3>Step 3 â€” Inspect container</h3>

<pre><code>docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Step 4 â€” Enter container</h3>

<pre><code>docker compose exec backend sh</code></pre>

<h3>Step 5 â€” Verify configuration</h3>

<pre><code>docker compose config</code></pre>

<p>Check:</p>

<ul>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Port mappings</li>
<li>Service names</li>
<li>Network configuration</li>
<li>Volume mounts</li>
<li>Healthchecks</li>
<li>Application logs</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- COMMON ISSUES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Common Interview Scenarios</h2>

<h3>Scenario 1 â€” Backend cannot connect to database</h3>

<div class="scenario">

Check whether both services are running, whether they share the
appropriate network, whether the backend uses the database service
name as hostname, and whether the database is actually ready.

</div>

<h3>Scenario 2 â€” Port already in use</h3>

<pre><code>docker compose ps

docker ps</code></pre>

<p>
Choose another host port or stop the process/container occupying
the required port.
</p>

<h3>Scenario 3 â€” Database data disappeared</h3>

<div class="scenario">

Check whether the database was using a persistent named volume.
Containers should not be treated as the durable storage layer for
database data.

</div>

<h3>Scenario 4 â€” Configuration changed but container still uses old value</h3>

<pre><code>docker compose up -d --build</code></pre>

<p>
Also verify the effective Compose configuration and environment
variables.
</p>

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Docker Compose in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Docker Compose is used to define and run multi-container
applications from a YAML configuration file.

For example, a typical application may contain frontend, backend
and database services. Instead of running each container manually,
I can define these services in a Compose file.

Each service can specify an image or build context, ports,
environment variables, volumes, networks and dependencies.

Services can communicate using their Compose service names, and
named volumes can be used to persist database data.

I can start the complete stack using docker compose up -d,
check logs with docker compose logs, inspect the services with
docker compose ps, and stop the stack using docker compose down.

In a DevOps workflow, Compose is useful for local development,
integration testing and consistent multi-container environments."

</div>

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ FINAL DOCKER INTERVIEW REVISION</strong>

<p>
Use this page immediately before a DevOps interview. The detailed
Docker topics are covered in the other Docker files. This page
connects those concepts into interview-ready answers and real-time
scenarios.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Dockerfile
â†“
<br>
Image
â†“
<br>
Container
â†“
<br>
Network + Volume
â†“

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Docker?</h2>

<div class="answer">
Docker is a containerization platform used to package an application
together with its dependencies into a portable container image.
</div>

<h3>Why Docker?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Consistent application environments</li>
<li>Lightweight compared with traditional VMs</li>
<li>Fast application startup</li>
<li>Isolation between applications</li>
<li>Portable deployment</li>
<li>Useful for CI/CD and microservices</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Interview answer:</strong><br><br>
"Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a
container image so that the application can run consistently across
different environments."
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Docker vs Virtual Machine</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Docker Container</th>
<th>Virtual Machine</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Shares host OS kernel</td>
<td>Includes a guest OS</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Lightweight</td>
<td>Heavier</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Starts quickly</td>
<td>Usually slower to start</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Uses fewer resources</td>
<td>Uses more resources</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Application-level isolation</td>
<td>Full OS-level virtualization</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="flow">
Hardware
â†’ Host OS
â†’ Docker Engine
â†’ Containers
</div>

<div class="flow">
Hardware
â†’ Hypervisor
â†’ Virtual Machines
â†’ Guest OS
â†’ Application
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Docker Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">
Docker CLI
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Daemon
<br>
â†“
<br>
Images / Containers / Networks / Volumes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Registry
</div>

<h3>Main components</h3>

<ul>
<li><strong>Docker Client:</strong> Sends commands to Docker.</li>
<li><strong>Docker Daemon:</strong> Manages Docker objects and container lifecycle.</li>
<li><strong>Docker Engine:</strong> Provides the Docker runtime environment.</li>
<li><strong>Docker Image:</strong> Read-only template used to create containers.</li>
<li><strong>Container:</strong> Running instance of an image.</li>
<li><strong>Registry:</strong> Stores and distributes images.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Image vs Container</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Image</th>
<th>Container</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Immutable template</td>
<td>Running instance of an image</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Used to create containers</td>
<td>Runs the application</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Stored locally or in registry</td>
<td>Runs on Docker host</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Simple memory trick:</strong><br><br>
Image = blueprint<br>
Container = running object created from the blueprint
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Dockerfile â†’ Image â†’ Container</h2>

<pre><code>Dockerfile
    â†“
docker build
    â†“
Docker Image
    â†“
docker run
    â†“
Container</code></pre>

<h3>Most important commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0 .

docker run -d -p 8080:80 myapp:1.0

docker ps

docker stop &lt;container&gt;

docker rm &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Dockerfile â€” Must Know Instructions</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Instruction</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>FROM</code></td>
<td>Defines base image</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>WORKDIR</code></td>
<td>Sets working directory</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>COPY</code></td>
<td>Copies files into image</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>RUN</code></td>
<td>Executes commands while building image</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ENV</code></td>
<td>Defines environment variables</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>EXPOSE</code></td>
<td>Documents intended container port</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>CMD</code></td>
<td>Provides default runtime command</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ENTRYPOINT</code></td>
<td>Defines the main executable</td>
</tr>
</table>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>FROM nginx:alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

EXPOSE 80

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. CMD vs ENTRYPOINT</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>CMD</th>
<th>ENTRYPOINT</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Default command/arguments</td>
<td>Main executable</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Can be easily overridden</td>
<td>More strongly defines container purpose</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Often used for defaults</td>
<td>Often used for executable behavior</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="interview">
A common pattern is using <code>ENTRYPOINT</code> for the main
application and <code>CMD</code> for default arguments.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Docker Image Layers & Caching</h2>

<div class="answer">
Docker images are built from layers. Docker can reuse unchanged
layers from previous builds, which can make builds faster.
</div>

<h3>Best practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Use a suitable small base image</li>
<li>Order Dockerfile instructions carefully</li>
<li>Copy dependency files before application source when appropriate</li>
<li>Use <code>.dockerignore</code></li>
<li>Avoid unnecessary packages</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">
If application source changes frequently but dependencies rarely
change, placing dependency installation before copying the frequently
changing source can improve build-cache reuse.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Multi-Stage Docker Build</h2>

<div class="answer">
A multi-stage build uses multiple stages in one Dockerfile so that
build dependencies can be separated from the final runtime image.
</div>

<pre><code>FROM node:20 AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install

COPY . .
RUN npm run build


FROM nginx:alpine

COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Why?</strong> Smaller final images, fewer unnecessary build
dependencies and a cleaner production runtime.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Container Lifecycle</h2>

<div class="flow">
Created
â†“
Running
â†“
Paused
â†“
Stopped
â†“
Removed
</div>

<pre><code>docker create
docker start
docker stop
docker restart
docker pause
docker unpause
docker rm</code></pre>

<h3>Important distinction</h3>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker stop</code> stops a container while preserving it.
<code>docker rm</code> removes the container.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Important Docker Commands</h2>

<pre><code># Images
docker images
docker pull nginx
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker rmi &lt;image&gt;

# Containers
docker ps
docker ps -a
docker run -d nginx
docker stop &lt;container&gt;
docker start &lt;container&gt;
docker restart &lt;container&gt;
docker rm &lt;container&gt;

# Logs
docker logs &lt;container&gt;
docker logs -f &lt;container&gt;

# Inspect
docker inspect &lt;container&gt;

# Execute
docker exec -it &lt;container&gt; sh

# Resources
docker stats

# Networks
docker network ls

# Volumes
docker volume ls</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Port Mapping</h2>

<div class="answer">
Containers have their own network namespace. Port publishing maps a
host port to a container port.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

<div class="flow">
Host Port 8080
â†“
Docker Port Mapping
â†“
Container Port 80
</div>

<div class="warning">
<code>EXPOSE</code> in a Dockerfile does not itself publish the port.
Use <code>-p</code> or an appropriate Compose configuration to
publish a port.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Docker Networking</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Network</th>
<th>Typical Use</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>bridge</td>
<td>Common default network for containers</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>host</td>
<td>Container shares host networking</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>none</td>
<td>No normal network connectivity</td>
</tr>
</table>

<h3>Container-to-container communication</h3>

<div class="answer">
On a user-defined Docker network, containers can communicate using
container/service names rather than relying on hard-coded IP addresses.
</div>

<pre><code>docker network create app-net

docker run -d --name db --network app-net postgres

docker run -d --name app --network app-net myapp</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Volumes vs Bind Mounts</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Docker Volume</th>
<th>Bind Mount</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Managed by Docker</td>
<td>Uses a host filesystem path</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Good for persistent application data</td>
<td>Useful when host path control is needed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Portable Docker-managed storage</td>
<td>Tightly connected to host filesystem</td>
</tr>
</table>

<pre><code>docker volume create app-data

docker run -d \
  -v app-data:/var/lib/data \
  myapp</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
Containers are generally ephemeral, so persistent application data
should not depend only on the container's writable layer.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Docker Compose</h2>

<div class="answer">
Docker Compose is used to define and run multi-container
applications using a declarative YAML configuration.
</div>

<pre><code>services:

  app:
    image: myapp:1.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example</code></pre>

<pre><code>docker compose up -d

docker compose ps

docker compose logs

docker compose down</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">
Typical example: application container + database + cache + reverse
proxy running together as one development/test environment.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Docker Registry</h2>

<div class="answer">
A Docker registry stores and distributes container images.
Docker Hub is one example; organizations can also use private
registries such as Amazon ECR or other enterprise registries.
</div>

<div class="flow">
Developer
â†“
docker build
â†“
Image
â†“
docker tag
â†“
docker push
â†“
Registry
â†“
docker pull
â†“
Deployment Environment
</div>

<pre><code>docker login

docker tag myapp:1.0 username/myapp:1.0

docker push username/myapp:1.0

docker pull username/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Docker Security</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use trusted/minimal base images</li>
<li>Scan images for vulnerabilities</li>
<li>Do not store secrets in Dockerfiles</li>
<li>Do not bake credentials into images</li>
<li>Run containers as non-root where practical</li>
<li>Keep images and dependencies updated</li>
<li>Use read-only filesystems where appropriate</li>
<li>Limit Linux capabilities</li>
<li>Use private registries for sensitive workloads</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">
Never put passwords, API keys, AWS credentials or private keys directly
inside a Dockerfile or image.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Dockerfile Secrets â€” Common Trap</h2>

<div class="warning">
Do NOT do this:
<br><br>
<code>ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=secret</code>
<br><br>
The secret can become part of the image configuration/history.
</div>

<h3>Better approach</h3>

<ul>
<li>Inject secrets at runtime</li>
<li>Use CI/CD secret management</li>
<li>Use cloud secret managers</li>
<li>Use Docker/BuildKit secret mechanisms when build-time secrets are required</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. HEALTHCHECK</h2>

<div class="answer">
A Docker health check allows Docker to determine whether a container's
application is responding as expected.
</div>

<pre><code>HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
A container can be running while the application inside it is unhealthy.
That is why process status and application health are not always the
same thing.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 20. Resource Limits</h2>

<div class="answer">
Containers can be constrained so one workload does not consume
unbounded host resources.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run -d \
  --memory="512m" \
  --cpus="1.0" \
  myapp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">
In production, resource requests/limits should be designed according
to workload behavior and the orchestration platform being used.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Docker Troubleshooting â€” Container Exits Immediately</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Problem:</strong> Container starts and immediately stops.
</div>

<h3>Investigation</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;

docker image inspect &lt;image&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Common causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Main process exited</li>
<li>Incorrect CMD/ENTRYPOINT</li>
<li>Application crashed</li>
<li>Missing environment variable</li>
<li>Incorrect configuration</li>
<li>Port/configuration issue</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Troubleshooting: Container Cannot Reach Another Container</h2>

<div class="scenario">
Check whether both containers are attached to the same user-defined
network and whether the application is listening on the expected port.
</div>

<pre><code>docker network ls

docker network inspect app-net

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
Use service/container names on a user-defined network rather than
hard-coding dynamic container IP addresses.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Troubleshooting: Image Build Is Too Large</h2>

<ul>
<li>Check the Dockerfile layers</li>
<li>Use a smaller runtime base image</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds</li>
<li>Add a proper <code>.dockerignore</code></li>
<li>Remove unnecessary build artifacts</li>
<li>Avoid installing unnecessary packages</li>
</ul>

<pre><code>docker images

docker history myapp:1.0</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Real-Time Scenario: Application Works Locally but Not in Docker</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Approach:</strong>
<br><br>
I would compare the local and container environments, inspect logs,
verify environment variables, check exposed/listening ports, inspect
the container filesystem and verify dependencies.
</div>

<pre><code>docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker exec -it &lt;container&gt; sh

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Real-Time Scenario: Container Is Using Too Much CPU</h2>

<pre><code>docker stats</code></pre>

<p>
Then investigate the application process, workload pattern, memory
usage and logs. Resource limits can be configured where appropriate.
</p>

<pre><code>docker update --cpus="1.0" &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Real-Time Scenario: Image Has a Vulnerability</h2>

<div class="scenario">
Do not simply ignore the finding. Identify the vulnerable package or
base image, update the dependency/base image, rebuild the image and
scan again before deployment.
</div>

<div class="flow">
Image
â†“
Security Scan
â†“
Vulnerability
â†“
Update Dependency/Base Image
â†“
Rebuild
â†“
Rescan
â†“
Deploy
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Docker + CI/CD</h2>

<div class="flow">
Git Push
â†“
CI Pipeline
â†“
Build
â†“
Unit Tests
â†“
Docker Build
â†“
Security Scan
â†“
Tag Image
â†“
Push Registry
â†“
Deploy
â†“
Health Check
</div>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Interview answer:</strong><br><br>
"In a DevOps pipeline, Docker provides a consistent packaging format.
After code is pushed, CI can build the image, run tests and security
scans, tag the image, push it to a registry and deploy the immutable
image to the target environment."
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Image Tagging Strategy</h2>

<div class="answer">
Avoid relying only on mutable tags such as <code>latest</code> for
production deployments. Prefer immutable or traceable version tags.
</div>

<pre><code>myapp:1.4.2
myapp:2026-08-12
myapp:&lt;commit-sha&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">
A CI pipeline can build an image tagged with the Git commit SHA.
That makes it easier to identify exactly which source revision was
deployed.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Docker vs Kubernetes</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Docker</th>
<th>Kubernetes</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Containerization platform</td>
<td>Container orchestration platform</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Builds and runs containers</td>
<td>Manages containers/workloads across clusters</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Useful for local development and container runtime workflows</td>
<td>Provides scheduling, scaling, service discovery and orchestration</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="interview">
Docker and Kubernetes are not simply replacements for each other.
Docker focuses on container workflows, while Kubernetes orchestrates
containerized workloads across a cluster.
</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Docker in a Real DevOps Project</h2>

<div class="flow">
Developer
â†“

â†“

â†“

â†“
Trivy / Security Scan
â†“
Docker Image
â†“
Amazon ECR / Registry
â†“
Kubernetes / ECS
â†“
Load Balancer
â†“

â†“
Monitoring
</div>

<p>
This is the type of end-to-end flow a DevOps interviewer may expect
you to explain when discussing hands-on Docker experience.
</p>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If the Interviewer Says: "Explain Docker in 1 Minute"</h2>

<div class="interview">

" Docker is a containerization platform used to package applications
and their dependencies into portable images.

A Dockerfile defines how the image is built, and a container is a
running instance of that image.

Docker provides networking for container communication and volumes
for persistent data. Docker Compose can be used to define
multi-container applications.

In a DevOps pipeline, I can build a Docker image from source code,
run tests and security scans, tag the image with a traceable version
such as a Git commit SHA, push it to a container registry and deploy
that image to a platform such as Kubernetes or ECS.

For production, I would focus on small and secure images, multi-stage
builds, vulnerability scanning, secret management, resource limits,
health checks and immutable image versions."

</div>

</div>

Security â†’ Registry â†’ CI/CD â†’ Deployment â†’ Monitoring
</strong>

<br><br>

That is what turns a basic Docker answer into a DevOps-level answer.

<h1>Docker <span>Images & Containers</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Docker images, containers,
layers, lifecycle, storage, logs, inspection, resource usage,

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER IMAGES & CONTAINERS â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Docker images and containers are among the most frequently discussed
Docker concepts in DevOps interviews. You should understand not only
the commands but also what happens internally when a container starts.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Dockerfile
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker Image</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Container</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Process + Filesystem + Network
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application

</div>

</div>


<!-- IMAGE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Docker Image?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A Docker image is an immutable, read-only template containing the
application code, dependencies, libraries, configuration and
filesystem layers required to create a container.
</div>

<h3>Interview answer</h3>

<div class="interview">
A Docker image is a packaged application environment. It contains
everything required to run the application except the running
container process itself.
</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker pull nginx

docker images</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- CONTAINER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is a Docker Container?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A container is a running or stopped instance of a Docker image.
It provides an isolated environment for running application
processes.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run nginx

docker ps

docker ps -a</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker run</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Process

</div>

<h3>Important point</h3>

<p>
An image is a template. A container is an instance created from
that template.
</p>

</div>


<!-- IMAGE VS CONTAINER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Docker Image vs Container</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Image</th>
<th>Container</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Read-only template</td>
<td>Running/stopped instance of an image</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used to create containers</td>
<td>Used to run applications</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Immutable</td>
<td>Has a writable container layer</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be stored in registry</td>
<td>Runs on Docker Engine</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: nginx:latest</td>
<td>Example: running nginx container</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- LAYERS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Docker Image Layers</h2>

<div class="answer">
Docker images are built from layers. Each Dockerfile instruction
that creates filesystem changes can contribute a layer to the image.
Layers are cached and reused when possible.
</div>

<pre><code>FROM ubuntu

RUN apt-get update

RUN apt-get install -y nginx

COPY index.html /var/www/html/</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Base Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Package Layer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Layer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image

</div>

<h3>Why are layers important?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Image reuse</li>
<li>Build caching</li>
<li>Faster builds</li>
<li>Reduced storage through shared layers</li>
<li>Efficient image distribution</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- WRITABLE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is the Container Writable Layer?</h2>

<div class="answer">
When a container starts, Docker adds a writable layer above the
read-only image layers. Changes made inside the container are stored
in this writable layer unless persistent storage is used.
</div>

<div class="warning">
The writable container layer is not the correct place for important
persistent application data.
</div>

<h3>Production solution</h3>

<p>
Use volumes or external storage for data that must survive container
replacement.
</p>

</div>


<!-- LIFECYCLE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Docker Container Lifecycle</h2>

<div class="flow">

Created
<br>
â†“
<br>
Running
<br>
â†“
<br>
Stopped
<br>
â†“
<br>
Removed

</div>

<pre><code>docker create nginx

docker start &lt;container&gt;

docker stop &lt;container&gt;

docker restart &lt;container&gt;

docker rm &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Useful command</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -a</code></pre>

<p>
This displays both running and stopped containers.
</p>

</div>


<!-- RUN -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What happens when you run docker run?</h2>

<pre><code>docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

<p>Conceptually Docker:</p>

<ol>
<li>Checks whether the image exists locally.</li>
<li>Pulls the image from a registry if required.</li>
<li>Creates a container from the image.</li>
<li>Adds the writable container layer.</li>
<li>Configures networking.</li>
<li>Applies the port mapping.</li>
<li>Starts the container's main process.</li>
</ol>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"docker run is a high-level command that creates and starts a
container from an image, including configuration such as ports,
environment variables, volumes and networking."

</div>

</div>


<!-- DETACHED -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 8. Foreground vs Detached Mode</h2>

<h3>Foreground</h3>

<pre><code>docker run nginx</code></pre>

<p>
The terminal remains attached to the container process.
</p>

<h3>Detached</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d nginx</code></pre>

<p>
The container runs in the background.
</p>

<h3>Attach</h3>

<pre><code>docker attach &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Be careful with <code>docker attach</code>. Depending on the process
and terminal handling, exiting the attached session can affect the
foreground process.
</div>

</div>


<!-- EXEC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. docker exec vs docker attach</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>docker exec</th>
<th>docker attach</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs a new command inside a running container</td>
<td>Attaches to the container's existing main process</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly used for troubleshooting</td>
<td>Used to interact with the main process</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>docker exec -it web /bin/bash

docker exec -it web sh</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
For production troubleshooting, <code>docker exec</code> is commonly
more useful because it allows you to run a separate diagnostic
command without replacing or directly controlling the main process.
</div>

</div>


<!-- INSPECT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Docker Inspect</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker inspect</code> provides detailed low-level information
about Docker objects such as containers, images, networks and
volumes.
</div>

<pre><code>docker inspect web

docker inspect nginx

docker inspect web --format '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}'</code></pre>

<h3>What can you investigate?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Container configuration</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Mounts</li>
<li>Network settings</li>
<li>Container IP</li>
<li>Port bindings</li>
<li>Image information</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- LOGS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Container Logs</h2>

<pre><code>docker logs web

docker logs -f web

docker logs --tail 100 web

docker logs --since 10m web</code></pre>

<h3>Production scenario</h3>

<div class="scenario">

The application is returning errors after deployment.

First check:

<pre><code>docker ps

docker logs web

docker inspect web</code></pre>

Then investigate the application, network, configuration and
dependencies.

</div>

</div>


<!-- STATS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Docker Stats</h2>

<pre><code>docker stats

docker stats web</code></pre>

<p>
This displays live resource usage for running containers.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CPU</td>
<td>Container CPU usage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Memory</td>
<td>Memory usage and limits</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Network I/O</td>
<td>Network traffic</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Block I/O</td>
<td>Storage I/O</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- RESOURCE LIMITS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Container Resource Limits</h2>

<p>
Containers can be configured with resource constraints to prevent
one workload from consuming excessive host resources.
</p>

<pre><code>docker run -d \
  --name web \
  --memory=512m \
  --cpus=1 \
  nginx</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>DevOps scenario:</strong>

One container consumes excessive CPU and memory, affecting other
applications on the host.

Resource limits can reduce the blast radius, while the root cause
should still be investigated.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PORT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Container Port Mapping</h2>

<div class="answer">
The <code>-p</code> option publishes a container port on the Docker
host.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Port</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>8080</td>
<td>Host port</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>80</td>
<td>Container port</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Client
<br>
â†“
<br>
Host :8080
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container :80
<br>
â†“
<br>
Nginx

</div>

</div>


<!-- ENV -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Environment Variables</h2>

<pre><code>docker run -d \
  --name app \
  -e APP_ENV=production \
  nginx</code></pre>

<h3>Check environment</h3>

<pre><code>docker inspect app</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Do not use ordinary environment variables as the preferred long-term
solution for highly sensitive production secrets. Use an appropriate
secret-management mechanism.
</div>

</div>


<!-- NAMING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 16. Container Naming</h2>

<pre><code>docker run -d --name my-nginx nginx

docker ps

docker stop my-nginx

docker start my-nginx

docker rm my-nginx</code></pre>

<p>
Explicit names make operational commands easier and clearer.
</p>

</div>


<!-- COPY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Copy Files To/From Containers</h2>

<pre><code>docker cp file.txt web:/tmp/file.txt

docker cp web:/var/log/app.log ./app.log</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Useful during troubleshooting when you need to temporarily extract
a file from a container for investigation.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DIFF -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. docker diff</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker diff</code> shows filesystem changes made inside a
container compared with its original image state.
</div>

<pre><code>docker diff web</code></pre>

<p>
It can show added, changed and deleted files.
</p>

</div>


<!-- COMMIT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 19. docker commit</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>docker commit</code> creates a new image from a container's
current filesystem state.
</div>

<pre><code>docker commit web my-custom-image:v1</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

In normal DevOps workflows, prefer rebuilding an image from a
Dockerfile rather than manually committing container changes.
Dockerfiles provide reproducibility and version-controlled builds.

</div>

</div>


<!-- REMOVE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 20. Removing Containers and Images</h2>

<pre><code>docker stop web

docker rm web

docker rmi nginx:latest</code></pre>

<h3>Force removal</h3>

<pre><code>docker rm -f web</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Be careful with removal commands in production. Verify the target
container and understand whether persistent data is stored outside
the container.
</div>

</div>


<!-- PRUNE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 21. Docker Prune</h2>

<pre><code>docker container prune

docker image prune

docker network prune

docker volume prune

docker system prune</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Prune commands remove unused Docker objects. Always understand what
will be deleted before using them on an important host.

</div>

</div>


<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Container Troubleshooting Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

<!-- EXIT CODES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Container Exited â€” What Do You Check?</h2>

<div class="answer">

First check the container status and exit code, then inspect the
logs and configuration.

</div>

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;

docker logs &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A common reason is that the container's main process completed or
crashed. Containers remain alive only while their main process is
running.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PID 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Why does a container stop when the application exits?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A container is fundamentally tied to its main process. When the
container's primary process exits, the container stops.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run ubuntu echo "Hello"

docker ps -a</code></pre>

<p>
The command completes, so there is no long-running foreground process
keeping the container alive.
</p>

</div>


<!-- PERSISTENCE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Why shouldn't important data be stored only inside a container?</h2>

<div class="answer">
Containers are replaceable. Recreating or removing a container can
remove data stored only in its writable layer.
</div>

<div class="flow">

Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Volume / External Storage</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Persistent Data

</div>

<p>
Persistent data should be stored using Docker volumes or appropriate
external storage depending on the application architecture.
</p>

</div>


<!-- REGISTRY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Image Naming and Tags</h2>

<pre><code>nginx:latest

nginx:1.27

myuser/myapp:v1.0.0

registry.example.com/team/app:1.2.0</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>registry.example.com</td>
<td>Registry hostname</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>team/app</td>
<td>Repository</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>1.2.0</td>
<td>Tag</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

Avoid relying on <code>latest</code> for controlled production
deployments. Explicit version tags or immutable image references
make deployments easier to reproduce.

</div>

</div>

<!-- IMMUTABILITY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Why are immutable images important?</h2>

<div class="answer">
An immutable deployment uses a specific image version rather than
changing the contents of a running container manually.
</div>

<p>
This improves reproducibility, rollback and debugging.
</p>

<div class="scenario">

Instead of manually modifying a production container:

<pre><code>myapp:v1
   â†“
myapp:v2
   â†“
myapp:v3</code></pre>

Deploy a new tested image version and replace the old container.

</div>

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Docker Images & Containers in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

"A Docker image is an immutable template containing the application,
dependencies and filesystem layers required to run an application.

A container is an instance of that image with a writable layer and
a running process.

When I run a container, Docker creates the container, configures its
networking and storage, and starts its main process.

For troubleshooting, I commonly use docker ps -a, docker logs,
docker inspect, docker stats and docker exec.

For production workloads, I avoid storing important data only in
the container writable layer and use persistent storage.

I also prefer versioned images instead of relying on latest so that
deployments are reproducible and rollbacks are easier."

</div>

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="card intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER NETWORKING & STORAGE â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Containers are isolated by default, but real applications usually
need containers to communicate with each other and persist data.
Docker networking provides communication, while volumes and mounts
provide persistent storage.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Container
â†“
<br>
Network
â†“
<br>
Container-to-Container Communication
<br><br>
Container
â†“
<br>
Volume / Bind Mount
â†“
<br>
Persistent Data

</div>

</div>


<!-- NETWORK BASICS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Docker Networking?</h2>

<div class="answer">
Docker networking allows containers to communicate with each other,
the host machine and external networks.
</div>

<h3>Why is networking required?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Application container needs database access</li>
<li>Frontend needs backend API</li>
<li>Backend needs Redis</li>
<li>Containers need DNS-based service discovery</li>
<li>Applications need controlled external connectivity</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Frontend Container
â†“
<br>
Backend Container
â†“
<br>
Database Container

</div>

</div>


<!-- NETWORK TYPES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Docker Network Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Network</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>bridge</code></td>
<td>Default network for containers on a Docker host.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>host</code></td>
<td>Container shares the host's network namespace.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>none</code></td>
<td>Disables normal container networking.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Custom bridge</td>
<td>Allows controlled communication and Docker DNS between containers.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Overlay</td>
<td>Used for communication across multiple Docker hosts, commonly with orchestrated environments.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Useful commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker network ls

docker network inspect bridge

docker network create my-network

docker network inspect my-network

docker network rm my-network</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- CUSTOM NETWORK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Why use a Custom Bridge Network?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A custom bridge network provides better isolation and allows
containers on that network to communicate using container names.
</div>

<pre><code>docker network create app-network

docker run -d \
  --name backend \
  --network app-network \
  nginx

docker run -d \
  --name frontend \
  --network app-network \
  nginx</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Interview scenario:</strong>

Suppose a backend application connects to MySQL.

Instead of hardcoding a container IP address, place both containers
on the same custom network and connect using the database container
name.

Example:

<pre><code>DB_HOST=mysql</code></pre>

Docker's embedded DNS can resolve the container/service name.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DNS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Docker DNS</h2>

<h3>Q. How do containers find each other?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Containers connected to the same user-defined network can generally
communicate using container or service names instead of relying on
manually assigned IP addresses.
</div>

<pre><code>docker network create app-network

docker run -d \
  --name mysql \
  --network app-network \
  mysql

docker run -d \
  --name backend \
  --network app-network \
  my-backend</code></pre>

<p>
The backend can use <code>mysql</code> as the database hostname when
the containers are attached to the same user-defined network.
</p>

<div class="warning">

Do not design applications around hardcoded container IP addresses.
Container IPs can change when containers are recreated.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PORTS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Docker Port Mapping</h2>

<h3>Q. What is port mapping?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Port mapping connects a port on the Docker host to a port exposed
by a container.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Port</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>8080</code></td>
<td>Host port</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>80</code></td>
<td>Container port</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Browser
<br>
â†“
<br>
Host :8080
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container :80

</div>

<h3>Common commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps

docker port &lt;container&gt;

docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- EXPOSE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 6. EXPOSE vs -p</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>EXPOSE</th>
<th>-p</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Documents the intended container port.</td>
<td>Publishes/maps a port from host to container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not by itself publish the port.</td>
<td>Makes the service reachable through the published host port.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>EXPOSE 8080</code></pre>

<pre><code>docker run -p 8080:8080 my-app</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<code>EXPOSE</code> documents which port the application listens on
inside the container. <code>-p</code> actually publishes a host port
to the container port.

</div>

</div>


<!-- HOST NETWORK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 7. Host Network</h2>

<div class="answer">
With host networking, the container uses the host's network stack
instead of getting a separate network namespace in the usual way.
</div>

<pre><code>docker run --network host nginx</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Host networking reduces network isolation and is not the default
choice for normal application containers. Use it only when there is
a clear requirement.

</div>

</div>


<!-- VOLUMES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Why do Docker Containers Need Persistent Storage?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A container's writable layer is tied to the container lifecycle.
If the container is removed, data stored only there should not be
treated as durable application storage.
</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

A MySQL container stores database files inside its container
filesystem. If the container is deleted and recreated without
persistent storage, the database data can be lost.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application
â†“
<br>
Container
â†“
<br>
Persistent Volume
â†“
<br>
Data survives container replacement

</div>

</div>


<!-- VOLUME TYPES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Docker Volume vs Bind Mount</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Named Volume</th>
<th>Bind Mount</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed by Docker.</td>
<td>Uses a specific host filesystem path.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for persistent application data.</td>
<td>Useful when host files need to be directly shared.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Docker manages the storage location.</td>
<td>User controls the host path.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Named volume</h3>

<pre><code>docker volume create app-data

docker volume ls

docker volume inspect app-data

docker run -d \
  --name mysql \
  -v app-data:/var/lib/mysql \
  mysql</code></pre>

<h3>Bind mount</h3>

<pre><code>docker run -d \
  -v C:\myapp:/app \
  my-image</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- VOLUME COMMANDS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Important Volume Commands</h2>

<pre><code>docker volume ls

docker volume create my-volume

docker volume inspect my-volume

docker volume rm my-volume

docker volume prune</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Be careful with <code>docker volume prune</code>. It can remove
unused volumes and permanently delete data stored in them.

</div>

</div>


<!-- READ ONLY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. Read-Only Mounts</h2>

<p>
A mount can be made read-only when the container should be able to
read data but should not modify it.
</p>

<pre><code>docker run -v app-data:/data:ro my-image</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This can be useful when a container only needs to consume
configuration or shared data and should not have write access.

</div>

</div>


<!-- NETWORK + VOLUME REAL TIME -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Real-Time Scenario: Backend + Database</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Requirement:</strong>

Run a backend application and MySQL database as separate containers.

<br><br>

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Create a custom network for communication and a named volume for
database persistence.

</div>

<pre><code>docker network create app-network

docker volume create mysql-data

docker run -d \
  --name mysql \
  --network app-network \
  -v mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql \
  mysql

docker run -d \
  --name backend \
  --network app-network \
  my-backend</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Backend
<br>
â†“
<br>
app-network
<br>
â†“
<br>
mysql
<br>
â†“
<br>
mysql-data

</div>

</div>


<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Networking Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Problem: Container cannot reach another container</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;

docker network ls

docker network inspect &lt;network&gt;</code></pre>

<p>Check:</p>

<ul>
<li>Are both containers running?</li>
<li>Are they attached to the same network?</li>
<li>Is the hostname correct?</li>
<li>Is the application actually listening on the expected port?</li>
<li>Is the service binding to the correct interface?</li>
<li>Are host firewall or security rules involved?</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- PORT TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Port Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Application works inside the container but cannot be accessed from
the host.

</div>

<pre><code>docker ps

docker port &lt;container&gt;

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker exec -it &lt;container&gt; sh</code></pre>

<p>
Then verify the application is listening on the expected container
port and that the required host-to-container port mapping exists.
</p>

</div>


<!-- VOLUME TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. Volume Troubleshooting</h2>

<pre><code>docker volume ls

docker volume inspect my-volume

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Check:</h3>

<ul>
<li>Is the correct volume attached?</li>
<li>Is the mount path correct?</li>
<li>Does the container user have permission?</li>
<li>Is the mount read-only?</li>
<li>Is the application writing to the expected directory?</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="card">

<!-- CHEAT SHEET -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Docker Networking & Volumes Cheat Sheet</h2>

<pre><code># Networks
docker network ls

docker network rm app-network

# Run on network

# Ports

docker port &lt;container&gt;

# Volumes
docker volume ls
docker volume create app-data
docker volume inspect app-data
docker volume rm app-data
docker volume prune

# Named volume
docker run -d \
  -v app-data:/data \
  my-image

# Read-only volume
docker run -d \
  -v app-data:/data:ro \
  my-image

# Bind mount
docker run -d \
  -v C:\myapp:/app \
  my-image

# Troubleshooting

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker exec -it &lt;container&gt; sh</code></pre>

<h2>ðŸš€ 60-Second Revision</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Networking</strong>
<br>
Containers communicate through Docker networks.

<br><br>

<strong>Custom Bridge</strong>
<br>
Provides isolated container communication and DNS-based discovery.

<br><br>

<strong>Port Mapping</strong>
<br>
<code>-p HOST:CONTAINER</code>

<br><br>

<strong>Volumes</strong>
<br>
Persist application data beyond the container lifecycle.

<br><br>

<strong>Bind Mount</strong>
<br>
Maps a host path directly into a container.

<br><br>

<strong>Production Thinking</strong>
<br>
Network isolation + persistent storage + least privilege +
proper troubleshooting.

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Docker Networking & Volumes in an Interview</h2>

<div class="interview">

" Docker networking allows containers to communicate with each other,
the host and external networks.

For application architectures, I would normally create a custom
network so containers can communicate using service or container
names instead of hardcoded IP addresses.

Port publishing such as 8080:80 maps a host port to a container port.

For persistent data, I would use Docker volumes instead of relying
only on the container's writable layer. Named volumes are managed
by Docker, while bind mounts map a specific host directory.

For example, in a backend and MySQL setup, both containers can share
a custom network while MySQL uses a persistent volume for its data.

During troubleshooting I would check the container status, logs,
network configuration, port mappings, DNS/name resolution and volume
mounts."

</div>

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER REGISTRY â€” INTERVIEW FOCUS</strong>

<p>
A Docker registry is a storage and distribution system for
container images. Developers build images locally or through CI,
push them to a registry, and deployment systems pull those images
from the registry.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Registry
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pull
<br>
â†“
<br>
Server / Kubernetes / ECS

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Docker Registry?</h2>

<h3>Q. What is a Docker registry?</h3>

<div class="answer">

A Docker registry is a service that stores and distributes
container images. Developers and CI/CD pipelines can push images
to a registry, while servers or orchestration platforms can pull
those images for deployment.

</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<ul>
<li>Docker Hub</li>
<li>Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)</li>
<li>Google Artifact Registry</li>
<li>Azure Container Registry</li>
<li>GitHub Container Registry</li>
<li>Self-hosted Docker Registry</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Registry vs Repository vs Image vs Container</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Term</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Registry</td>
<td>Service that stores and distributes container images.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Repository</td>
<td>A collection of related image versions/tags inside a registry.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Image</td>
<td>Immutable package/template used to create containers.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container</td>
<td>Running instance created from an image.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Registry
<br>
â†“
<br>
Repository
<br>
â†“
<br>
Image Tag
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker.io/nandinireddem/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>Value</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Registry</td>
<td>docker.io</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Repository / namespace</td>
<td>nandinireddem/myapp</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Tag</td>
<td>v1.0</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Docker Hub</h2>

<h3>Q. What is Docker Hub?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Docker Hub is a hosted container registry service commonly used
to store, share and distribute Docker images.

</div>

<h3>Login</h3>

<pre><code>docker login</code></pre>

<h3>Pull an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker pull nginx:latest</code></pre>

<h3>List local images</h3>

<pre><code>docker images</code></pre>

<h3>Push an image</h3>

<pre><code>docker push username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Docker Image Tagging</h2>

<h3>Q. Why do we tag Docker images?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Tags identify different versions or variants of an image.
They allow CI/CD pipelines and deployment systems to reference
a specific image version.

</div>

<h3>Tag syntax</h3>

<pre><code>registry/namespace/repository:tag</code></pre>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker tag myapp:latest nandinireddem/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<p>
The <code>docker tag</code> command creates another reference to
the same image. It does not rebuild the image.
</p>

<h3>Verify</h3>

<pre><code>docker images</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Complete Push Workflow</h2>

<h3>Step 1 â€” Build image</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:v1.0 .</code></pre>

<h3>Step 2 â€” Login</h3>

<pre><code>docker login</code></pre>

<h3>Step 3 â€” Tag image</h3>

<pre><code>docker tag myapp:v1.0 username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Step 4 â€” Push</h3>

<pre><code>docker push username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Step 5 â€” Pull from another machine</h3>

<pre><code>docker pull username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Dockerfile
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker build</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“

<br>
â†“

<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Push vs Pull</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Push</th>
<th>Pull</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uploads an image</td>
<td>Downloads an image</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually performed after build</td>
<td>Usually performed before deployment</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Developer / CI pipeline commonly performs it</td>
<td>Server / Kubernetes / ECS commonly performs it</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>docker push username/myapp:v1.0

docker pull username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Public vs Private Registry</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Public</th>
<th>Private</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Images can be publicly accessible</td>
<td>Access is restricted</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for public/open-source images</td>
<td>Preferred for proprietary application images</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Lower access-control requirements</td>
<td>Requires authentication and authorization</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>DevOps scenario:</strong>

A company has a proprietary application image. The image should
not be publicly downloadable.

The team should use a private registry such as a private ECR
repository and configure the deployment environment with appropriate
permissions to pull the image.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Docker Registry Authentication</h2>

<h3>Q. Why is authentication required?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Private registries require authentication so that only authorized
users, systems or workloads can push and/or pull images.

</div>

<h3>Docker Hub</h3>

<pre><code>docker login</code></pre>

<h3>Logout</h3>

<pre><code>docker logout</code></pre>

<h3>Security best practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Do not hard-code registry passwords in Dockerfiles.</li>
<li>Do not commit registry credentials to Git.</li>
<li>Use CI/CD secret management.</li>
<li>Use short-lived credentials where supported.</li>
<li>Apply least-privilege permissions.</li>
<li>Use private repositories for proprietary images.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. AWS ECR</h2>

<h3>Q. What is Amazon ECR?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) is a managed AWS container
registry used to store, manage and deploy container images.

</div>

<h3>Why use ECR?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Private container image storage</li>
<li>AWS IAM integration</li>
<li>Works with ECS</li>
<li>Works with EKS</li>
<li>Works with CI/CD pipelines</li>
<li>Supports image scanning features</li>
<li>Integrates with AWS infrastructure</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. AWS ECR Push Workflow</h2>

<h3>Step 1 â€” Create ECR repository</h3>

<pre><code>aws ecr create-repository \
    --repository-name myapp \
    --region ap-south-1</code></pre>

<h3>Step 2 â€” Authenticate Docker to ECR</h3>

<pre><code>aws ecr get-login-password \
    --region ap-south-1 |
docker login \
    --username AWS \
    --password-stdin \
    &lt;ACCOUNT_ID&gt;.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com</code></pre>

<h3>Step 3 â€” Build image</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:v1.0 .</code></pre>

<h3>Step 4 â€” Tag image</h3>

<pre><code>docker tag myapp:v1.0 \
&lt;ACCOUNT_ID&gt;.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Step 5 â€” Push</h3>

<pre><code>docker push \
&lt;ACCOUNT_ID&gt;.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Docker Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Tag
<br>
â†“
<br>
ECR Login
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Push
<br>
â†“
<br>
ECR Repository
<br>
â†“
<br>
ECS / EKS
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container Deployment

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. ECR Pull Workflow</h2>

<h3>Authenticate</h3>

<pre><code>aws ecr get-login-password \
    --region ap-south-1 |
docker login \
    --username AWS \
    --password-stdin \
    &lt;ACCOUNT_ID&gt;.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com</code></pre>

<h3>Pull</h3>

<pre><code>docker pull \
&lt;ACCOUNT_ID&gt;.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

In a production environment, you normally configure the compute
platform's IAM permissions so the workload can pull private images.
You should not manually store long-lived AWS access keys on servers
just to pull images.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Docker Registry in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Git Push
<br>
â†“
<br>
CI Pipeline
<br>
â†“
<br>
Run Tests
<br>
â†“
<br>
Security Scan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Tag
<br>

<br>
Registry Login
<br>
â†“

Docker Push
<br>

<br>
ECR / Docker Hub
<br>

<br>
