</div>

<h3>Typical pipeline commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:$VERSION .

docker tag myapp:$VERSION \
$REGISTRY/myapp:$VERSION

docker push \
$REGISTRY/myapp:$VERSION</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"In CI/CD, after the application passes tests and security checks,
the pipeline builds a Docker image, tags it with a unique version,
authenticates to the container registry, and pushes the image.
The deployment stage then references that image from the registry."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Image Tagging Strategy</h2>

<h3>Bad approach</h3>

<pre><code>myapp:latest</code></pre>

<p>
Using only <code>latest</code> makes it harder to identify exactly
which version was deployed.
</p>

<h3>Better approaches</h3>

<pre><code>myapp:v1.0.0

myapp:2026-08-12

myapp:build-152

myapp:git-a83f21c</code></pre>

<h3>Recommended production concept</h3>

<div class="answer">

Use immutable, traceable image references whenever possible.
A deployment should be able to identify exactly which application
build is running.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Why Avoid Using latest in Production?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>latest</code> tag is mutable. A new image can be pushed
with the same tag, meaning the same deployment configuration can
resolve to a different image later.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Today:

<pre><code>myapp:latest â†’ version 1.0</code></pre>

Later:

<pre><code>myapp:latest â†’ version 1.1</code></pre>

The tag stayed the same, but the image changed.

A production deployment is easier to audit when it references
a specific immutable version or image digest.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Image Digest</h2>

<h3>Q. What is an image digest?</h3>

<div class="answer">

An image digest is a content-based identifier for a specific image
manifest. It can be used to reference an exact image version rather
than relying only on a mutable tag.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>myapp@sha256:abcdef123456...</code></pre>

<h3>Tag vs Digest</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Tag</th>
<th>Digest</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Human-friendly name</td>
<td>Content-based identifier</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be moved to another image</td>
<td>Identifies a specific image manifest</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Easy for releases</td>
<td>Useful for exact, reproducible references</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 16. Image Pull Policy</h2>

<h3>Why does image pulling matter?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Deployment platforms need to determine when an image should be
downloaded from the registry rather than using a locally cached
image.

</div>

<h3>Kubernetes example</h3>

<pre><code>image: myrepo/myapp:v1.0
imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent</code></pre>

<p>
The exact image-pull behavior depends on the configured image
reference and pull policy.
</p>

<div class="interview">

For production deployments, prefer versioned image references
instead of relying on mutable tags such as <code>latest</code>.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Registry vs Docker Hub</h2>

<div class="answer">

"Registry" is the general concept. Docker Hub is one specific
hosted registry service.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Registry</th>
<th>Docker Hub</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>General concept/service</td>
<td>Specific hosted platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be self-hosted or cloud-managed</td>
<td>Hosted by Docker</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be private or public depending on implementation</td>
<td>Provides public and private repository options</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. What Happens During docker push?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker authenticates to the registry, checks which image layers
are already present remotely, and uploads the layers and image
metadata that the registry does not already have.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Local Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Registry Authentication
<br>
â†“
<br>
Compare Layers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Upload Missing Layers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Upload Manifest / Metadata
<br>
â†“
<br>
Registry Stores Image

</div>

<h3>Important point</h3>

<p>
Docker images consist of layers. If the registry already contains
a layer, it generally does not need to upload the same layer again.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 19. What Happens During docker pull?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker contacts the registry, retrieves the image manifest and
downloads the required layers that are not already available
locally.

</div>

<div class="flow">

docker pull
<br>
â†“
<br>
Registry
<br>
â†“
<br>
Image Manifest
<br>
â†“
<br>
Required Layers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Local Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Registry Security</h2>

<h3>Important practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Use private repositories for proprietary images.</li>
<li>Use least-privilege IAM permissions.</li>
<li>Protect registry credentials.</li>
<li>Enable image vulnerability scanning where available.</li>
<li>Scan images before deployment.</li>
<li>Use trusted base images.</li>
<li>Keep base images updated.</li>
<li>Do not embed secrets in images.</li>
<li>Use immutable versioning where possible.</li>
<li>Restrict who can push production images.</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

A Docker image should not contain passwords, API keys, AWS access
keys, private keys or other secrets. Anything baked into an image
can potentially be extracted by someone who can access the image.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Real-Time Scenario: Docker Push Denied</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

You run:

<pre><code>docker push username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

and receive an authorization or access-denied error.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ol>
<li>Are you logged in?</li>
<li>Is the repository name correct?</li>
<li>Do you have permission to push?</li>
<li>Is the registry URL correct?</li>
<li>Are you using the correct AWS account/region for ECR?</li>
<li>Does the repository exist?</li>
</ol>

<h3>Docker Hub</h3>

<pre><code>docker login

docker push username/myapp:v1.0</code></pre>

<h3>ECR</h3>

<p>
Verify ECR authentication and IAM permissions.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Real-Time Scenario: ECS Cannot Pull Image</h2>

<div class="scenario">

An ECS task starts but fails because it cannot pull the private
image from ECR.

</div>

<h3>Possible causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect image URI</li>
<li>Incorrect image tag</li>
<li>Image does not exist in ECR</li>
<li>Task execution role lacks required ECR permissions</li>
<li>Network connectivity problem</li>
<li>Wrong AWS region</li>
<li>Repository access issue</li>
</ul>

<h3>Investigation</h3>

<pre><code>aws ecr describe-images \
    --repository-name myapp \
    --region ap-south-1</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would first verify the image URI, repository, tag and region.
Then I would check whether the image exists in ECR and verify the
ECS task execution role and its permissions to pull the image.
Finally, I would check the task and service events for the exact
pull failure."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Real-Time Scenario: Image Exists Locally but Deployment Fails</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A Docker image runs successfully on your laptop, but ECS or
Kubernetes cannot deploy it.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Was the image actually pushed to the registry?</li>
<li>Is the deployment using the correct registry URI?</li>
<li>Is the tag correct?</li>
<li>Can the workload authenticate to the registry?</li>
<li>Is the image architecture compatible with the target?</li>
<li>Are network and IAM permissions correct?</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

"Works on my machine" does not mean the production environment can
pull the same image. The registry, authentication, architecture,
network and deployment configuration must also be correct.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. CI/CD Scenario â€” Build and Push to ECR</h2>

<pre><code>Developer
   â†“
GitHub
   â†“
GitHub Actions
   â†“
Checkout Code
   â†“
Run Tests
   â†“
Trivy / Security Scan
   â†“
Docker Build
   â†“
ECR Login
   â†“
Docker Tag
   â†“
Docker Push
   â†“
ECS / EKS Deployment</code></pre>

<h3>Conceptual pipeline</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:$GIT_SHA .

docker tag myapp:$GIT_SHA \
$ECR_URI/myapp:$GIT_SHA

docker push \
$ECR_URI/myapp:$GIT_SHA</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The Git commit SHA is useful as an image tag because it creates
a direct relationship between the deployed container image and
the source-code revision.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 25. Why Use Commit SHA as Image Tag?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Git commit SHA provides a unique reference to a source-code
revision. Using it as an image tag improves traceability between
source code, CI builds and deployed containers.

</div>

<pre><code>Git Commit
a83f21c
   â†“
Docker Image
myapp:a83f21c
   â†“
Registry
   â†“
Deployment</code></pre>

<h3>Benefits</h3>

<ul>
<li>Traceability</li>
<li>Easy rollback</li>
<li>Better debugging</li>
<li>Clear CI/CD history</li>
<li>Reduced ambiguity compared with latest</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 26. Registry Cleanup</h2>

<h3>Why clean old images?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Container registries can accumulate old image versions, increasing
storage usage and making repository management harder.

</div>

<h3>Good practice</h3>

<ul>
<li>Define an image retention policy.</li>
<li>Keep required production versions.</li>
<li>Remove obsolete development images.</li>
<li>Use lifecycle policies where supported.</li>
<li>Never delete images that active deployments still depend on.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

For ECR, lifecycle policies can automatically expire images based
on rules such as image age or the number of images retained.

</div>

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If the Interviewer Says: "Explain Docker Registry"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"A Docker registry is a service used to store and distribute
container images.

In a typical DevOps workflow, the developer pushes code to Git,
and the CI pipeline builds and tests the Docker image. After
security scanning, the pipeline tags the image with a unique
version such as the Git commit SHA and pushes it to a private
registry such as Amazon ECR.

During deployment, platforms such as ECS or Kubernetes pull the
required image from the registry using the appropriate permissions.

For production, I prefer traceable versioned image tags or image
digests instead of relying only on the latest tag. I would also
use private repositories, least-privilege access, image scanning
and lifecycle policies to improve security and registry management."

</div>

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="card intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKER SECURITY â€” MUST KNOW</strong>

<p>
Docker security is about reducing the attack surface of container
images, containers, the Docker daemon and the host system.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Source Code

Runtime Security
<br>
â†“
<br>
Monitoring
<br>
â†“
<br>
Secure Deployment

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview definition:</strong>

Docker security involves securing the image supply chain, Dockerfile,
container runtime, secrets, daemon, host interaction and deployment
environment to reduce vulnerabilities and unauthorized access.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SHARED RESPONSIBILITY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What Does Docker Security Include?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Layer</th>
<th>Security Focus</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Source Code</td>
<td>Secure dependencies and avoid committed secrets.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Dockerfile</td>
<td>Trusted base images, non-root user, minimal packages.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Image</td>
<td>Vulnerability scanning and provenance.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container</td>
<td>Least privilege, capabilities and filesystem controls.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Docker Daemon</td>
<td>Restrict access to Docker control interfaces.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Host</td>
<td>Patch OS and protect Docker runtime.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Network</td>
<td>Restrict unnecessary connectivity.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Secrets</td>
<td>Use dedicated secret-management mechanisms.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- ROOT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why Should Containers Not Run as Root?</h2>

<div class="answer">

By default, some containers may run processes as root inside the
container. Running applications as a dedicated non-root user follows
the principle of least privilege and can reduce the impact of a
container compromise.

</div>

<h3>Dockerfile example</h3>

<pre><code>FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN addgroup -S appgroup \
    && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

USER appuser

CMD ["node","server.js"]</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Non-root containers are an important defense, but they do not replace
other security controls.

</div>

</div>


<!-- USER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. USER Instruction</h2>

<pre><code>USER appuser</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The Dockerfile <code>USER</code> instruction specifies the user that
will run subsequent commands and, unless overridden, the main
container process.

</div>

<h3>Check the running user</h3>

<pre><code>docker exec &lt;container&gt; id</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Interview scenario:</strong>

An application does not require root privileges.

I would create a dedicated application user and switch to it with
<code>USER</code> before starting the application.

</div>

</div>


<!-- VULNERABILITIES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Container Image Vulnerabilities</h2>

<div class="answer">

Container images can contain vulnerable operating-system packages,
application dependencies or libraries.

</div>

<h3>Common causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Old base images</li>
<li>Unpatched OS packages</li>
<li>Outdated application dependencies</li>
<li>Unused packages</li>
<li>Unmaintained libraries</li>
<li>Untrusted third-party images</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Base Image
<br>
+
<br>
OS Packages
<br>
+
<br>
Application Dependencies
<br>
â†“
<br>
Potential Vulnerabilities

</div>

</div>


<!-- TRIVY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Image Scanning with Trivy</h2>

<div class="answer">

Trivy is a security scanner commonly used to detect vulnerabilities
and other security issues in container images and related artifacts.

</div>

<pre><code>trivy image myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<h3>Typical CI/CD flow</h3>

<div class="flow">

Build Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Trivy Scan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Vulnerabilities?
<br>
â†“
<br>
Fail / Continue
<br>
â†“
<br>
Registry
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deployment

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would integrate image scanning into CI/CD so that known
high-severity vulnerabilities can be detected before an image is
promoted to a production environment."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SEVERITY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Vulnerability Severity</h2>

<p>
Security scanners commonly classify vulnerabilities by severity,
for example:
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Severity</th>
<th>Typical Interpretation</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CRITICAL</td>
<td>Very high potential impact; usually requires immediate attention.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HIGH</td>
<td>Significant risk requiring prompt remediation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MEDIUM</td>
<td>Moderate risk evaluated according to environment and exposure.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>LOW</td>
<td>Lower-risk finding that should still be tracked.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

A scanner finding does not automatically mean the application is
exploitable in your exact environment. Teams should assess severity,
exposure, exploitability and business impact.

</div>

</div>


<!-- MINIMAL IMAGE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Why Use Minimal Base Images?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A smaller runtime image generally contains fewer packages and
components, which can reduce the attack surface and image size.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>FROM python:3.13-slim</code></pre>

<p>
Minimal does not automatically mean secure. The image must still be
maintained and scanned.
</p>

</div>


<!-- TRUSTED -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Use Trusted Base Images</h2>

<div class="answer">

Base images should come from trusted sources and should be regularly
updated and scanned.

</div>

<h3>Bad practice</h3>

<pre><code>FROM random-image:latest</code></pre>

<h3>Better practice</h3>

<pre><code>FROM python:3.13-slim</code></pre>

<p>
In enterprise environments, organizations may also maintain approved
internal base images.
</p>

</div>


<!-- LATEST -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 9. Why Avoid latest in Production?</h2>

<pre><code>FROM nginx:latest</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The <code>latest</code> tag is mutable. A future build can therefore
use a different image than an earlier build.

</div>

<p>Prefer controlled versions:</p>

<pre><code>FROM nginx:1.29-alpine</code></pre>

<p>
For stronger reproducibility, an image digest can be pinned.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECRETS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 10. How Should Secrets Be Handled?</h2>

<div class="warning">

Never hardcode passwords, API keys, cloud credentials or private
keys into Dockerfiles or source code.

</div>

<h3>Do not do this</h3>

<pre><code>ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=supersecret</code></pre>

<h3>Better options</h3>

<ul>
<li>Cloud secret managers</li>
<li>CI/CD secret stores</li>
<li>Runtime secret injection</li>
<li>Docker/Swarm secrets where applicable</li>
<li>Kubernetes Secrets with appropriate protection</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

"I would keep secrets outside the image and inject them at deployment
or runtime using the platform's secret-management mechanism."

</div>

</div>


<!-- IMAGE HISTORY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Why Deleting a Secret From Dockerfile Is Not Enough</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose a secret was accidentally included in an image layer.

Later you remove the line from the Dockerfile.

That does not necessarily make the previously built image or its
layers safe.

</div>

<h3>Correct response</h3>

<ol>
<li>Immediately rotate/revoke the exposed credential.</li>
<li>Stop using the compromised credential.</li>
<li>Remove the secret from source/history where appropriate.</li>
<li>Rebuild the image.</li>
<li>Scan the new image.</li>
<li>Review registry and CI/CD exposure.</li>
</ol>

<div class="warning">

Treat an exposed credential as compromised. Do not assume deleting
the visible file makes the credential safe.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DOCKER SOCKET -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Why Is /var/run/docker.sock Sensitive?</h2>

<pre><code>-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The Docker socket provides access to the Docker daemon API. Giving a
container access to the host Docker socket can effectively grant very
powerful control over Docker-managed resources.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not mount the Docker socket into containers unless there is a
specific, well-understood requirement and the security implications
have been accepted.

</div>

<h3>Interview question</h3>

<p>
<strong>Why is Docker socket access dangerous?</strong>
</p>

<p>
Because access to the Docker daemon can allow powerful operations
against containers, images, volumes and potentially the host.
</p>

</div>


<!-- PRIVILEGED -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What Does --privileged Do?</h2>

<pre><code>docker run --privileged myimage</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Privileged mode significantly expands the capabilities available to
a container and reduces many of Docker's normal isolation
restrictions.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Avoid <code>--privileged</code> unless there is a legitimate,
documented requirement. It should not be used as a default solution
for permission problems.

</div>

</div>


<!-- CAPABILITIES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Linux Capabilities</h2>

<div class="answer">

Linux capabilities divide traditional root privileges into smaller
privilege sets. Docker can add or drop capabilities for containers.

</div>

<h3>Drop unnecessary capabilities</h3>

<pre><code>docker run \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  myimage</code></pre>

<h3>Add only what is required</h3>

<pre><code>docker run \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  myimage</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Principle:</strong>

Give the container only the privileges it actually needs.

</div>

</div>


<!-- READ ONLY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Read-Only Root Filesystem</h2>

<pre><code>docker run \
  --read-only \
  myimage</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

A read-only root filesystem prevents normal writes to the container's
root filesystem.

</div>

<p>
If the application needs writable storage, explicitly provide the
required writable volume or temporary filesystem.
</p>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>docker run \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp \
  myimage</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- NETWORK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Container Network Security</h2>

<div class="answer">

Containers should only communicate with the services they actually
need to reach.

</div>

<h3>Good practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Use dedicated Docker networks.</li>
<li>Do not expose unnecessary ports.</li>
<li>Publish only required host ports.</li>
<li>Separate application tiers where appropriate.</li>
<li>Restrict external access with firewalls/security groups.</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Internet
<br>
â†“
<br>
Reverse Proxy
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Network
<br>
â†“
<br>
Backend
<br>
â†“
<br>
Database Network

</div>

</div>


<!-- PORTS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. EXPOSE vs Published Ports</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>EXPOSE</th>
<th>-p / --publish</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Documents the container port in image metadata.</td>
<td>Publishes a container port through the host.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not make the port externally reachable by itself.</td>
<td>Creates host-to-container port mapping.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>EXPOSE 8080</code></pre>

<pre><code>docker run -p 8080:8080 myimage</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- RESOURCE LIMITS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Resource Limits</h2>

<div class="answer">

Resource limits can reduce the impact of runaway or compromised
containers consuming excessive host resources.

</div>

<h3>Memory</h3>

<pre><code>docker run --memory=512m myimage</code></pre>

<h3>CPU</h3>

<pre><code>docker run --cpus="1.0" myimage</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Production scenario:</strong>

A container has a memory leak and continuously consumes host memory.

A suitable memory limit can prevent that single container from
consuming unlimited memory and affecting other workloads.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PIDS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 19. PID Limits</h2>

<pre><code>docker run --pids-limit=100 myimage</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

A PID limit restricts the number of processes that a container can
create.

This can help reduce the impact of process-exhaustion attacks or
runaway applications.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECCOMP -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 20. Seccomp</h2>

<div class="answer">

Seccomp is a Linux kernel security mechanism that can restrict the
system calls a process is allowed to make.

Docker uses a default seccomp profile unless configured otherwise.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

The goal is to reduce the available kernel attack surface by limiting
unnecessary system calls.

</div>

</div>


<!-- APPARMOR SELINUX -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 21. AppArmor and SELinux</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Technology</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>AppArmor</td>
<td>Mandatory access-control mechanism based on application profiles.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SELinux</td>
<td>Mandatory access-control framework using security labels and policies.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<p>
Both can provide additional host-level controls around what processes
and containers are allowed to access.
</p>

</div>


<!-- DOCKER DAEMON -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Why Protect the Docker Daemon?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Docker daemon has powerful control over containers, images,
networks, volumes and host resources.

Therefore, unauthorized access to the daemon is highly sensitive.

</div>

<h3>Best practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Restrict access to the Docker socket.</li>
<li>Do not expose the daemon unnecessarily.</li>
<li>Use appropriate access controls.</li>
<li>Protect the host operating system.</li>
<li>Keep Docker components updated.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SOCKET VS CLI -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. Docker CLI vs Docker Daemon</h2>

<div class="flow">

Docker CLI

<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Daemon
<br>
â†“
<br>
Containers / Images / Networks / Volumes

</div>

<div class="answer">

The Docker CLI is a client. The Docker daemon performs the actual
management operations.

</div>

</div>

<!-- REGISTRY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 25. Secure Container Registry Practices</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use private repositories for sensitive images.</li>
<li>Restrict push/pull permissions.</li>
<li>Enable vulnerability scanning.</li>
<li>Use immutable/versioned image tags where possible.</li>
<li>Remove obsolete vulnerable images according to policy.</li>
<li>Protect registry credentials.</li>
<li>Use image signing/provenance where supported.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

A CI pipeline should authenticate to the registry using a short-lived
or securely stored credential rather than exposing a developer's
personal password.

</div>

</div>

<!-- ROOT SCENARIO -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Scenario â€” Container Is Running as Root</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A production container runs its application as UID 0.

<br><br>

<strong>Approach:</strong>

Create a dedicated user, ensure the application files have the
correct ownership, switch to that user with <code>USER</code>, then
test the application.

</div>

</div>


<!-- TRIVY SCENARIO -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Scenario â€” Trivy Finds Critical Vulnerabilities</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Do not simply ignore the scan.</strong>

<br><br>

First identify which package is vulnerable and whether a fixed
version is available.

Then update the base image or dependency, rebuild the image and scan
again.

</div>

<div class="flow">

â†“

<br>
â†“
<br>
Find Fixed Version
<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

</div>

<!-- SOCKET SCENARIO -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Scenario â€” Container Requests Docker Socket</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Question:</strong>

A monitoring or automation container asks for:

<pre><code>/var/run/docker.sock</code></pre>

Would you approve it immediately?

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong>

No. I would first understand why the access is required, assess the
security implications, look for alternatives and restrict access as
much as possible.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PRIVILEGED SCENARIO -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Scenario â€” Developer Uses --privileged</h2>

<div class="warning">

Do not treat <code>--privileged</code> as a general fix for permission
errors.

</div>

<div class="interview">

"I would identify the exact operation requiring additional
privileges and grant only the necessary capability or device access,
instead of enabling full privileged mode."

</div>

</div>


<!-- INCIDENT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Scenario â€” Secret Found in Docker Image</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Immediate actions:</strong>

<ol>
<li>Revoke or rotate the secret.</li>
<li>Determine where it was exposed.</li>
<li>Remove it from source and image build process.</li>
<li>Clean repository history if necessary.</li>
<li>Rebuild the image.</li>
<li>Scan the rebuilt image.</li>
<li>Check logs, registries and CI systems for exposure.</li>
</ol>

</div>

<div class="warning">

The first priority is credential rotation, not merely deleting the
secret from a file.

</div>

</div>


<!-- BEST PRACTICES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Docker Security Best Practices</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Practice</th>
<th>Reason</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Non-root user</td>
<td>Reduce process privileges.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Minimal image</td>
<td>Reduce attack surface.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Trusted base image</td>
<td>Reduce supply-chain risk.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Image scanning</td>
<td>Identify known vulnerabilities.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>No hardcoded secrets</td>
<td>Prevent credential exposure.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Drop capabilities</td>
<td>Reduce Linux privileges.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Read-only filesystem</td>
<td>Reduce unauthorized filesystem changes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Resource limits</td>
<td>Reduce resource exhaustion impact.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Restricted Docker socket</td>
<td>Protect Docker daemon control.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controlled networking</td>
<td>Reduce unnecessary connectivity.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Versioned images</td>
<td>Improve reproducibility.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h2>ðŸ”¥ Interview Follow-Up Questions</h2>

<ul>

<li>Is running as non-root enough to secure a container?</li>

<li>Does a smaller image automatically mean a secure image?</li>

<li>Can a Docker image contain secrets even after deleting the file?</li>

<li>Why is Docker socket equivalent to powerful host access?</li>

<li>What is the difference between --cap-drop and --privileged?</li>

<li>Why would you use a read-only filesystem?</li>

<li>How do resource limits improve security?</li>

<li>How would you prioritize vulnerabilities found by Trivy?</li>

<li>What would you do if the base image has a critical CVE?</li>

<li>How would you prevent vulnerable images from reaching production?</li>

<li>How would you secure a private container registry?</li>

<li>What is defense in depth for containers?</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- CHEAT SHEET -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Final Docker Security Cheat Sheet</h2>

<pre><code># Run as limited user
docker run --user 10001 myimage

# Memory limit
docker run --memory=512m myimage

# CPU limit
docker run --cpus="1.0" myimage

# Read-only filesystem
docker run --read-only myimage

# Temporary writable area
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myimage

# Drop capabilities
docker run --cap-drop=ALL myimage

# Check image
trivy image myimage:1.0

# Check running containers
docker ps

# Inspect container
docker inspect &lt;container&gt;

# Check running user
docker exec &lt;container&gt; id

# Check image history
docker history myimage:1.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- RAPID REVISION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸš€ 60-Second Docker Security Revision</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Trusted Image</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Minimal Base</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Secure Dockerfile</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Non-Root User</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Image Scan</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>No Hardcoded Secrets</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Drop Capabilities</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Read-Only FS</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Resource Limits</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Restricted Network</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Protected Docker Daemon</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Secure CI/CD</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- ONE MINUTE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Docker Security in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Docker security starts from the image build process and continues
through container runtime and deployment.

I would use trusted and appropriately minimal base images, scan
images for vulnerabilities using tools such as Trivy, and keep
dependencies updated.

Containers should run as non-root users whenever possible, and I
would avoid unnecessary privileges such as privileged mode or
excessive Linux capabilities.

Secrets should never be hardcoded into Dockerfiles or images. They
should be injected securely through the deployment platform or a
secret-management solution.

I would also restrict Docker socket access, control network exposure,
use resource limits, and consider read-only filesystems and security
profiles.

In CI/CD, I would scan images before pushing or promoting them and
apply security policies before production deployment.

The overall principle is least privilege, minimal attack surface,
secure supply chain and defense in depth."

</div>

</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Docker</a>

<h1>Dockerfile <span>Advanced</span></h1>

<p>
Production-focused Dockerfile concepts, instructions, image layers,
build cache, multi-stage builds, security, optimization and
high-frequency DevOps interview scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="card intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ DOCKERFILE â€” FINAL INTERVIEW REVISION</strong>

<p>
A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions used by Docker
to build an image.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Dockerfile
<br>
â†“
<br>
docker build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application

</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview definition:</strong>
A Dockerfile is a declarative set of instructions used to build a
Docker image containing an application, its dependencies and the
runtime configuration required to execute it.
</div>

</div>


<!-- BASIC STRUCTURE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Basic Dockerfile Structure</h2>

<pre><code>FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm install

COPY . .

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["npm", "start"]</code></pre>

<h3>Flow</h3>

<div class="flow">

FROM
â†’ Base Image

<br>â†“<br>

WORKDIR
â†’ Working Directory

<br>â†“<br>

COPY
â†’ Application Files

<br>â†“<br>

RUN
â†’ Build/Install Dependencies

<br>â†“<br>

EXPOSE
â†’ Document Application Port

<br>â†“<br>

CMD
â†’ Default Runtime Command

</div>

</div>


<!-- FROM -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. FROM</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>FROM</code> defines the base image from which the Docker image
is built.
</div>

<pre><code>FROM ubuntu:24.04

FROM python:3.13-slim

FROM node:22-alpine</code></pre>

<h3>Why is FROM important?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Provides the operating-system/runtime foundation.</li>
<li>Determines available tools and libraries.</li>
<li>Influences final image size.</li>
<li>Can affect security and compatibility.</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">
Prefer trusted, maintained and appropriately sized base images.
Avoid using <code>latest</code> when deterministic builds are
important.
</div>

</div>


<!-- TAGS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 3. Why Pin Image Versions?</h2>

<p>Instead of:</p>

<pre><code>FROM node:latest</code></pre>

<p>Prefer a controlled version:</p>

<pre><code>FROM node:22-alpine</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Pinning a meaningful image version improves build reproducibility
because the base image does not unexpectedly change just because
the tag <code>latest</code> was updated.
</div>

<p>
For stronger supply-chain reproducibility, organizations can also
pin images by immutable digest when appropriate.
</p>

</div>


<!-- WORKDIR -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. WORKDIR</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>WORKDIR</code> sets the working directory for subsequent
Dockerfile instructions and the default working directory of the
container.
</div>

<pre><code>WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN npm install</code></pre>

<p>
Using <code>WORKDIR</code> is preferable to repeatedly using
<code>RUN cd /app</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- COPY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. COPY</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>COPY</code> copies files from the Docker build context into the
image.
</div>

<pre><code>COPY package.json /app/

COPY . .

COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist</code></pre>

<h3>Most important use</h3>

<p>
The <code>--from</code> option is heavily used in multi-stage builds
to copy artifacts from one build stage into another.
</p>

</div>


<!-- ADD -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 6. COPY vs ADD</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>COPY</th>
<th>ADD</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple file/directory copying.</td>
<td>Provides additional behavior such as archive extraction for
supported local archives and URL handling.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually preferred for clarity.</td>
<td>Use only when its additional behavior is intentionally needed.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Interview answer:</strong>
"I generally prefer COPY because it has simpler and more explicit
behavior. I use ADD only when I specifically need its additional
features."
</div>

</div>


<!-- RUN -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. RUN</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>RUN</code> executes commands while the image is being built.
Its result becomes part of an image layer.
</div>

<pre><code>RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

RUN npm ci

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt</code></pre>

<h3>Important distinction</h3>

<table>
<tr>
<th>RUN</th>
<th>CMD</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build-time instruction.</td>
<td>Default runtime command.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates image-layer changes.</td>
<td>Runs when a container starts.</td>
</tr>
</table>

</div>


<!-- CMD -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. CMD</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>CMD</code> specifies the default command or arguments for a
container.
</div>

<pre><code>CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]</code></pre>

<p>
A Dockerfile normally has one effective CMD instruction; if multiple
CMD instructions exist, the last one takes effect.
</p>

<h3>Override CMD</h3>

<pre><code>docker run myimage
docker run myimage sh</code></pre>

<p>
The command supplied at container runtime can replace the default
CMD command.
</p>

</div>


<!-- ENTRYPOINT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. ENTRYPOINT</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>ENTRYPOINT</code> defines the primary executable of a container.
</div>

<pre><code>ENTRYPOINT ["python"]

CMD ["app.py"]</code></pre>

<p>
Conceptually this runs:</p>

<pre><code>python app.py</code></pre>

<h3>Override ENTRYPOINT</h3>

<pre><code>docker run --entrypoint sh myimage</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- CMD VS ENTRYPOINT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 10. CMD vs ENTRYPOINT</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>CMD</th>
<th>ENTRYPOINT</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides a default command/arguments.</td>
<td>Defines the main executable.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be replaced by a runtime command.</td>
<td>Usually remains the main executable unless explicitly overridden.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Often used for default arguments.</td>
<td>Useful when the container should behave like a specific executable.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Common pattern</h3>

<pre><code>ENTRYPOINT ["python"]

CMD ["app.py"]</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Interview answer:</strong>
"ENTRYPOINT defines the main executable, while CMD commonly
provides default arguments or a default command. They can also be
used together."
</div>

</div>


<!-- SHELL VS EXEC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. Shell Form vs Exec Form</h2>

<h3>Exec form</h3>

<pre><code>CMD ["node", "server.js"]

ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]</code></pre>

<h3>Shell form</h3>

<pre><code>CMD node server.js

RUN echo hello</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
For application ENTRYPOINT/CMD definitions, exec form is generally
preferred because it gives clearer process behavior and signal
handling.
</div>

</div>


<!-- ENV -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. ENV</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>ENV</code> sets environment variables in the image and makes
them available to processes running in containers created from it.
</div>

<pre><code>ENV APP_ENV=production
ENV PORT=8080</code></pre>

<p>
Values can be overridden at runtime:
</p>

<pre><code>docker run -e APP_ENV=staging myimage</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Do not use ENV to bake passwords, API keys or other sensitive
credentials into an image.
</div>

</div>


<!-- ARG -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. ARG</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>ARG</code> defines a build-time variable that can be supplied
to <code>docker build</code>.
</div>

<pre><code>ARG NODE_VERSION=22

FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine</code></pre>

<p>Build with:</p>

<pre><code>docker build --build-arg NODE_VERSION=22 -t myapp .</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- ARG VS ENV -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 14. ARG vs ENV</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ARG</th>
<th>ENV</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Mainly build-time.</td>
<td>Available to processes in the resulting image/container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can influence image construction.</td>
<td>Defines runtime environment variables.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Not automatically available as a runtime environment variable.</td>
<td>Persists as image configuration.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>ARG APP_VERSION=1.0

ENV APP_ENV=production</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Do not treat ARG or ENV as a secure secret-storage mechanism.
Build arguments can be exposed through build metadata/history in
some workflows.
</div>

</div>


<!-- EXPOSE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. EXPOSE</h2>

<pre><code>EXPOSE 8080</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
<code>EXPOSE</code> documents the port on which the application listens
inside the container. It does not publish the port to the host by
itself.
</div>

<p>Host publishing happens at runtime, for example:</p>

<pre><code>docker run -p 8080:8080 myimage</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- USER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. USER â€” Run as Non-Root</h2>

<div class="warning">
Running an application as root inside a container can increase the
impact of a container compromise.
</div>

<pre><code>FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .

USER node

CMD ["npm", "start"]</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Using a non-root user is an important container security practice
when the application supports it.
</div>

</div>


<!-- LABEL -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. LABEL</h2>

<pre><code>LABEL maintainer="devops-team"
LABEL version="1.0"
LABEL description="Production API"</code></pre>

<p>
Labels add metadata to images and can help with organization,
automation and image management.
</p>

</div>


<!-- DOCKERIGNORE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. .dockerignore</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>.dockerignore</code> prevents unnecessary files from being sent
as part of the Docker build context.
</div>

<pre><code>.git
.gitignore
node_modules
.env
*.log
coverage
Dockerfile*</code></pre>

<h3>Why is it important?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Reduces build context size.</li>
<li>Improves build performance.</li>
<li>Prevents unnecessary files from entering build context.</li>
<li>Helps avoid accidentally copying local files.</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">
Do not rely on .dockerignore as your only security control. Never
put secrets into a Docker build context in the first place.
</div>

</div>


<!-- LAYERS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Docker Image Layers</h2>

<p>
Many Dockerfile instructions contribute filesystem changes that can
be represented as image layers.
</p>

<pre><code>FROM node:22-alpine
        â†“
COPY package.json
        â†“
RUN npm ci
        â†“
COPY source
        â†“
CMD</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Docker can reuse unchanged build layers through its build cache.
This is one reason Dockerfile instruction order matters.
</div>

</div>


<!-- CACHE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Docker Build Cache</h2>

<h3>Bad ordering</h3>

<pre><code>COPY . .

RUN npm ci</code></pre>

<p>
Any source-code change may invalidate the COPY layer and cause
dependency installation to run again.
</p>

<h3>Better ordering</h3>

<pre><code>COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm ci

COPY . .</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Dependency files change less frequently than application source in
many projects, so separating them can allow Docker to reuse the
dependency-installation layer.
</div>

</div>


<!-- APT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 21. Package Installation Best Practice</h2>

<h3>Less efficient</h3>

<pre><code>RUN apt-get update

RUN apt-get install -y curl</code></pre>

<h3>Better</h3>

<pre><code>RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Combining related package-management commands helps avoid stale
package indexes and unnecessary intermediate filesystem data.
</div>

</div>


<!-- MULTI STAGE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Multi-Stage Builds</h2>

<div class="answer">
Multi-stage builds use multiple <code>FROM</code> stages so build
tools and intermediate artifacts can be separated from the final
runtime image.
</div>

<h3>Example â€” Node.js</h3>

<pre><code>FROM node:22-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm ci

COPY . .

RUN npm run build


FROM nginx:alpine

COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Builder Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Install Dependencies
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
dist/
<br>
â†“
<br>
Final Runtime Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Nginx

</div>

</div>


<!-- WHY MULTI STAGE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Why Use Multi-Stage Builds?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Smaller final images.</li>
<li>Build tools stay out of runtime image.</li>
<li>Reduced attack surface.</li>
<li>Cleaner production images.</li>
<li>Better separation between build and runtime.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

A Java application may need Maven and JDK to compile, but the
production container may only need a smaller JRE/runtime environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- JAVA -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Production Java Multi-Stage Example</h2>

<pre><code>FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY pom.xml .

RUN mvn dependency:go-offline

COPY src ./src

RUN mvn clean package -DskipTests


FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre

WORKDIR /app

COPY --from=builder /app/target/app.jar app.jar

USER 10001

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","app.jar"]</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
The first stage contains Maven and build dependencies. The final
stage contains only the runtime required to execute the JAR.
</div>

</div>


<!-- PYTHON -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 25. Python Production Pattern</h2>

<pre><code>FROM python:3.13-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

RUN useradd --create-home appuser

USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["python", "app.py"]</code></pre>

<p>
The exact production setup depends on the Python framework and
application architecture, but the important concepts are dependency
installation, minimal runtime image and non-root execution.
</p>

</div>


<!-- HEALTH -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 26. HEALTHCHECK</h2>

<pre><code>HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s \
            --timeout=5s \
            --retries=3 \
            CMD wget --spider -q http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
A healthcheck defines a command Docker can use to determine whether
a container is healthy.
</div>

<div class="warning">
A healthcheck does not magically fix an unhealthy application.
It only reports health status to the container runtime/orchestrator.
</div>

</div>


<!-- STOPSIGNAL -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 27. STOPSIGNAL</h2>

<pre><code>STOPSIGNAL SIGTERM</code></pre>

<p>
Specifies the system call signal sent to the container's main
process when Docker requests the container to stop.
</p>

<p>
Correct signal handling becomes particularly important for graceful
shutdown of web servers and applications.
</p>

</div>


<!-- VOLUME -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 28. VOLUME</h2>

<pre><code>VOLUME ["/data"]</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
The VOLUME instruction declares a mount point intended for
persistent or externally managed data.
</div>

<p>
In modern deployments, the actual storage mechanism is usually
chosen by the runtime or orchestrator rather than relying only on
the Dockerfile.
</p>

</div>


<!-- BUILD CONTEXT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. Docker Build Context</h2>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp .</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
The final <code>.</code> specifies the build context sent to the
Docker builder.
</div>

<p>
The Dockerfile can only access files available in the build context
unless another supported build mechanism is used.
</p>

<div class="scenario">

A huge project directory can make builds slower because the build
context itself becomes large. A good <code>.dockerignore</code> helps
reduce unnecessary context.

</div>

</div>


<!-- TAG -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Build and Tag an Image</h2>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0 .

docker images

docker run myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<p>
Use meaningful version tags for controlled deployments.
</p>

<div class="warning">
For production release workflows, avoid treating mutable tags such
as <code>latest</code> as your only deployment identifier.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SECURITY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Dockerfile Security Best Practices</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use trusted and maintained base images.</li>
<li>Prefer minimal runtime images where practical.</li>
<li>Pin meaningful versions or immutable digests.</li>
<li>Run as a non-root user.</li>
<li>Do not bake secrets into images.</li>
<li>Use .dockerignore.</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds.</li>
<li>Scan images for vulnerabilities.</li>
<li>Keep dependencies updated.</li>
<li>Use read-only filesystems where appropriate.</li>
<li>Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities at runtime.</li>
<li>Keep the final image focused on runtime requirements.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECRETS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Why Should Secrets Not Be in Dockerfiles?</h2>

<p>Never do this:</p>

<pre><code>ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=xxxxx
ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=xxxxx</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Even if the container is later removed, secrets embedded in an
image may remain accessible through image metadata, layers or
registries.

</div>

<h3>Better approach</h3>

<pre><code>docker run \
  -e API_KEY="$API_KEY" \
  myapp:1.0</code></pre>

<p>
For production, prefer the secret-management facilities provided by
the deployment platform or cloud provider.
</p>

</div>


<!-- ROOT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Why Run Containers as Non-Root?</h2>

<div class="answer">
If an attacker compromises an application process, running it as a
non-root user can reduce the privileges available inside the
container.
</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>RUN addgroup -S appgroup \
    && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

USER appuser</code></pre>

<p>
The exact commands depend on the Linux distribution used by the base
image.
</p>

</div>


<!-- CMD ENTRYPOINT SCENARIO -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Interview Scenario â€” CMD vs ENTRYPOINT</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Question:</strong>

You have:

<pre><code>ENTRYPOINT ["python"]
CMD ["app.py"]</code></pre>

What happens with:

<pre><code>docker run myimage</code></pre>

<strong>Answer:</strong>

It effectively starts:

<pre><code>python app.py</code></pre>

If the user supplies another argument:

<pre><code>docker run myimage test.py</code></pre>

The CMD arguments are replaced, resulting conceptually in:

<pre><code>python test.py</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- CACHE SCENARIO -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 35. Interview Scenario â€” Build Became Slow</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Every source-code change causes dependency installation to run
again.

<br><br>

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Separate dependency files from frequently changing source files.

</div>

<pre><code>COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
This allows Docker to reuse the dependency layer when only source
files change.
</div>

</div>


<!-- SIZE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 36. How to Reduce Docker Image Size?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use an appropriately small base image.</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds.</li>
<li>Remove build tools from runtime.</li>
<li>Use .dockerignore.</li>
<li>Install only required packages.</li>
<li>Clean package-manager caches when appropriate.</li>
<li>Copy only required runtime artifacts.</li>
<li>Avoid unnecessary files.</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would first identify what is contributing to the image size,
then use a suitable base image, multi-stage builds, .dockerignore,
dependency optimization and a runtime-only final stage."

</div>

</div>


<!-- DEBUG -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 37. Debugging a Dockerfile Build</h2>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:debug .

docker history myapp:debug

docker inspect myapp:debug</code></pre>

<h3>Useful questions</h3>

<ul>
<li>Which Dockerfile instruction failed?</li>
<li>Is the build context correct?</li>
<li>Does the file being copied exist?</li>
<li>Are dependency versions compatible?</li>
<li>Did a cache layer cause unexpected behavior?</li>
<li>Is the final image actually containing the application?</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- PRODUCTION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 38. Production Dockerfile Checklist</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Area</th>
<th>Check</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Base Image</td>
<td>Trusted, maintained and appropriately sized</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Versioning</td>
<td>Use controlled versions or immutable digests</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Security</td>
<td>Non-root user where possible</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Secrets</td>
<td>No credentials baked into image</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build</td>
<td>Multi-stage where useful</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Cache</td>
<td>Order instructions for effective caching</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Context</td>
<td>Use .dockerignore</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runtime</td>
<td>Only required files and dependencies</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Health</td>
<td>Healthcheck where appropriate</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Scanning</td>
<td>Scan images before deployment</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Dockerfile in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

"A Dockerfile contains instructions used to build a Docker image.

I normally start with a trusted base image using FROM, set the
working directory using WORKDIR, copy dependency files and install
them with RUN, then copy the application source.

For runtime configuration I can use ENV, while ARG is mainly used
for build-time variables. EXPOSE documents the application's
container port.

For production images I prefer multi-stage builds so build tools do
not remain in the final runtime image. I also use .dockerignore,
appropriate image versions, non-root users and image scanning.

For the application process, I use ENTRYPOINT and CMD depending on
whether I want to define a fixed executable, default arguments or
both.

The goal is to create a reproducible, secure, small and
production-ready image."

</div>

<h1>Dockerfile <span>Interview Guide</span></h1>

<p>
Important Dockerfile concepts, instructions, optimization,
multi-stage builds, security, troubleshooting and DevOps interview
questions.
</p>

</header>

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<strong>â­â­â­â­â­ Dockerfile â€” Must Know</strong>

<p>
A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions used by Docker
to build a container image.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Dockerfile
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker build</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>docker run</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Container

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Dockerfile?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Dockerfile is a text-based file containing instructions that Docker
uses to automatically build a container image.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>FROM nginx:alpine

COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/

EXPOSE 80

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Basic Dockerfile Structure</h2>

<pre><code>FROM base-image

WORKDIR /app

COPY application-files /app/

RUN installation-command

EXPOSE port

ENV VARIABLE=value

CMD ["command"]</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview point:</strong>

<br><br>

The Dockerfile describes how the image should be built and what
should happen when a container starts.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Important Dockerfile Instructions</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Instruction</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>FROM</code></td>
<td>Defines the base image.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>WORKDIR</code></td>
<td>Sets the working directory inside the image/container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>COPY</code></td>
<td>Copies files from the build context into the image.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ADD</code></td>
<td>Copies files and provides additional features such as archive extraction.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>RUN</code></td>
<td>Executes commands while building the image.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>CMD</code></td>
<td>Provides the default command for starting a container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ENTRYPOINT</code></td>
<td>Defines the main executable for the container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ENV</code></td>
<td>Defines environment variables.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ARG</code></td>
<td>Defines build-time variables.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>EXPOSE</code></td>
<td>Documents the port the application listens on.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>USER</code></td>
<td>Specifies the user used to run subsequent commands/container process.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>LABEL</code></td>
<td>Adds metadata to an image.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>HEALTHCHECK</code></td>
<td>Defines a container health check.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. FROM</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>FROM</code> specifies the base image from which the Docker image
is built.

</div>

<pre><code>FROM ubuntu:24.04

FROM python:3.12-slim

FROM nginx:alpine</code></pre>

<h3>Why use small base images?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Smaller image size</li>
<li>Faster downloads</li>
<li>Smaller attack surface</li>
<li>Faster deployments</li>
</ul>

</div>

<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. RUN</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>RUN</code> executes commands during image build time.

</div>

<pre><code>FROM ubuntu:24.04

RUN apt-get update

RUN apt-get install -y curl</code></pre>

<h3>Better approach</h3>

<pre><code>RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*</code></pre>

<p>
Combining related commands can reduce unnecessary image layers and
clean package metadata in the same layer.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. CMD vs RUN</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>RUN</th>
<th>CMD</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs during image build.</td>
<td>Provides the default command when the container starts.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates image layers.</td>
<td>Does not execute during build.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>RUN npm install

CMD ["npm", "start"]</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy way to remember:</strong>

<br><br>

RUN = <strong>Build time</strong>
<br>
CMD = <strong>Container start time</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. CMD vs ENTRYPOINT</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>CMD</th>
<th>ENTRYPOINT</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Default command or arguments.</td>
<td>Defines the main executable.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be replaced by a docker run command.</td>
<td>Normally remains the executable unless overridden with appropriate options.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>ENTRYPOINT ["python"]

CMD ["app.py"]</code></pre>

<p>
Docker effectively starts the container with the executable and its
default arguments.
</p>

<h3>Override CMD</h3>

<pre><code>docker run image other.py</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. COPY vs ADD</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>COPY</th>
<th>ADD</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple file/directory copying.</td>
<td>Provides extra functionality.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually preferred for clarity.</td>
<td>Can automatically extract local tar archives.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>COPY package.json /app/

ADD package.tar.gz /app/</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Best practice:</strong>

<br><br>

Prefer <code>COPY</code> unless you specifically need functionality
provided by <code>ADD</code>.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. WORKDIR</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>WORKDIR</code> sets the working directory for subsequent
Dockerfile instructions and the default working directory of the
container.

</div>

<pre><code>WORKDIR /app

COPY . .

RUN npm install

CMD ["npm", "start"]</code></pre>

<p>
It is generally preferable to <code>WORKDIR</code> over repeatedly
using <code>cd</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. COPY and Docker Build Context</h2>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0 .</code></pre>

<p>
The final <code>.</code> represents the build context.
Docker can copy files only from within the build context, subject to
Dockerfile and ignore rules.
</p>

<h3>.dockerignore</h3>

<pre><code>node_modules/
.git/
*.log
.env
terraform.tfstate</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>DevOps scenario:</strong>

If the build context is huge because it contains Git history,
dependencies or logs, builds can become slower.

Use <code>.dockerignore</code> to exclude unnecessary files.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. ENV vs ARG</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ARG</th>
<th>ENV</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Primarily available during image build.</td>
<td>Available to processes running in the container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be supplied using <code>--build-arg</code>.</td>
<td>Can be set using <code>-e</code> at runtime.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Not automatically a runtime environment variable.</td>
<td>Persists as image configuration.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>ARG APP_VERSION=1.0

ENV APP_ENV=production</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not use Dockerfile <code>ARG</code> or <code>ENV</code> as a safe
place for secrets. Build arguments and image configuration can become
visible through image metadata/history depending on how they are used.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. EXPOSE</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>EXPOSE</code> documents the port on which the application inside
the container listens.

</div>

<pre><code>EXPOSE 8080</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

EXPOSE does not publish the port to the host.

</div>

<p>
To publish a port, use <code>docker run -p</code>.
</p>

<pre><code>docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. USER</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>USER</code> instruction specifies which user should run
subsequent Dockerfile commands and, by default, the container process.

</div>

<pre><code>FROM nginx:alpine

RUN adduser -D appuser

USER appuser</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Running applications as a non-root user is generally preferred for
better container security when the application supports it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. HEALTHCHECK</h2>

<pre><code>HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s \
    CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

A health check allows Docker to determine whether the application
inside a container is responding as expected.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

In production, an application process may still exist while the
application itself is unhealthy. A health check helps distinguish
these situations.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Docker Image Layers</h2>

<div class="answer">

Many Dockerfile instructions create filesystem layers in the image.
Docker can reuse unchanged layers through its build cache.

</div>

<pre><code>FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]</code></pre>

<h3>Why COPY requirements first?</h3>

<p>
If application source code changes but the dependency file does not,
Docker can often reuse the dependency installation layer.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Docker Build Cache</h2>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0 .</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Docker attempts to reuse previously built layers when the relevant
instruction and inputs have not changed.

</div>

<h3>Bad ordering</h3>

<pre><code>COPY . .

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt</code></pre>

<h3>Better ordering</h3>

<pre><code>COPY requirements.txt .

RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY . .</code></pre>

<p>
This improves cache reuse when only application source code changes.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Multi-Stage Builds</h2>

<div class="answer">

Multi-stage builds use multiple <code>FROM</code> instructions so that
build dependencies can remain in an intermediate stage while only
the required runtime artifacts are copied into the final image.

</div>

<pre><code>FROM node:22 AS builder

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm ci

COPY . .

RUN npm run build


FROM nginx:alpine

COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80

CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Benefit:</strong>

The final image contains the runtime application instead of all the
Node.js build dependencies.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Why use Multi-Stage Builds?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Smaller production images</li>
<li>Lower attack surface</li>
<li>Separate build and runtime environments</li>
<li>Cleaner production containers</li>
<li>Reduced unnecessary dependencies</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I use multi-stage Docker builds to separate the build environment
from the runtime environment. The builder stage contains compilers
and development dependencies, while the final stage contains only
the artifacts and runtime dependencies required by the application."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Dockerfile Best Practices</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use trusted and appropriately small base images.</li>
<li>Pin important dependency versions where appropriate.</li>
<li>Use <code>.dockerignore</code>.</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds.</li>
<li>Run as a non-root user.</li>
<li>Keep images minimal.</li>
<li>Combine related package installation and cleanup.</li>
<li>Order instructions for cache efficiency.</li>
<li>Do not store secrets in images.</li>
<li>Scan images for vulnerabilities.</li>
<li>Use clear and maintainable Dockerfiles.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Dockerfile Security</h2>

<h3>Never do this</h3>

<pre><code>ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=xxxxx
ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=xxxxx</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Secrets can become part of image configuration or history.
Never bake cloud credentials, passwords or API keys into an image.

</div>

<h3>Better approach</h3>

<pre><code>docker run \
  -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID \
  -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY \
  myapp</code></pre>

<p>
For production, use the secret-management mechanism provided by the
platform, such as AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets with
appropriate controls, or CI/CD secret stores.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Dockerfile vs Docker Image vs Container</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Dockerfile</th>
<th>Image</th>
<th>Container</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Instructions</td>
<td>Built artifact/template</td>
<td>Running instance of an image</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used to build image</td>
<td>Used to create containers</td>
<td>Runs application</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Dockerfile
<br>
â†“ build
<br>
Docker Image
<br>
â†“ run
<br>
Container

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. ENTRYPOINT + CMD Real Example</h2>

<pre><code>FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY app.py .

ENTRYPOINT ["python"]

CMD ["app.py"]</code></pre>

<p>
The entrypoint defines the executable and CMD supplies the default
argument.
</p>

<pre><code>docker run myapp

docker run myapp another.py</code></pre>

<p>
The second command replaces the default CMD argument while keeping
the entrypoint.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. Shell Form vs Exec Form</h2>

<h3>Shell form</h3>

<pre><code>CMD python app.py</code></pre>

<h3>Exec form</h3>

<pre><code>CMD ["python", "app.py"]</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Exec form is generally preferred because it executes the process
directly and provides more predictable signal handling.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Dockerfile Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Problem: Build is very slow</h3>

<ul>
<li>Check build context size.</li>
<li>Use <code>.dockerignore</code>.</li>
<li>Optimize layer ordering.</li>
<li>Reuse build cache.</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds where appropriate.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Problem: Image is very large</h3>

<ul>
<li>Use a smaller suitable base image.</li>
<li>Remove unnecessary packages.</li>
<li>Use multi-stage builds.</li>
<li>Clean package caches.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Problem: Application works locally but not in container</h3>

<ul>
<li>Check application listening address.</li>
<li>Check exposed/published ports.</li>
<li>Check environment variables.</li>
<li>Check filesystem paths.</li>
<li>Check logs.</li>
<li>Check dependencies.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Real-Time Scenario: Image Size is Huge</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A Java/Node/Python application produces a 1.5 GB Docker image.

<br><br>

<strong>Approach:</strong>

1. Inspect image layers.
<br>
2. Remove unnecessary dependencies.
<br>
3. Use a suitable slim runtime image.
<br>
4. Use multi-stage builds.
<br>
5. Add a proper <code>.dockerignore</code>.
<br>
6. Scan and verify the final image.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Real-Time Scenario: Secret Accidentally Added</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A developer accidentally adds an AWS access key to a Dockerfile.

<br><br>

<strong>Immediate response:</strong>

Treat the credential as compromised and rotate/revoke it immediately.

Then remove the secret from the Dockerfile and review image and
repository history as appropriate.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Simply deleting the line from the latest Dockerfile does not guarantee
that the credential is absent from previous image layers or Git
history.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Real-Time Scenario: Container Starts and Immediately Exits</h2>

<div class="answer">

A container normally remains alive while its main process is running.
If that process exits, the container stops.

</div>

<h3>Debug</h3>

<pre><code>docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

<p>
Check the Dockerfile's <code>CMD</code>/<code>ENTRYPOINT</code>, logs,
environment variables and application startup command.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Real-Time Scenario: Build Works but Application Cannot Be Reached</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<br><br>

1. Application listening port
<br>
2. <code>EXPOSE</code>
<br>
3. Host-to-container port mapping
<br>
4. Application binding address
<br>
5. Container status
<br>
6. Container logs

</div>

<pre><code>docker ps

docker logs &lt;container&gt;

docker port &lt;container&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Important Docker Build Commands</h2>

<pre><code># Build image
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .

# Build without cache
docker build --no-cache -t myapp:1.0 .

# Build with argument
docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=2.0 -t myapp:2.0 .

# List images
docker images

# Inspect image
docker inspect myapp:1.0

# View image history
docker history myapp:1.0

# Run container
docker run -d --name myapp -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0</code></pre>

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Dockerfile in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

"A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions used to build
a Docker image.

I normally start with a suitable base image using FROM, set the
working directory using WORKDIR, copy the required application files,
install dependencies using RUN, and define the startup behavior using
ENTRYPOINT and CMD.

I use .dockerignore to reduce the build context and optimize
instruction ordering to improve Docker layer caching.

For production images, I prefer multi-stage builds so that build-time
dependencies are not included in the final runtime image.

From a security perspective, I avoid storing secrets in Dockerfiles,
use trusted minimal base images, scan images for vulnerabilities and
prefer running applications as a non-root user.

The final image can then be pushed to a registry and deployed through
the CI/CD pipeline."

</div>
