<header>
<div class="icon">âš™ï¸</div>
<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Kubernetes</a>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>Config & Storage</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused revision covering ConfigMaps, Secrets, Volumes,
Persistent Volumes, PVCs, StorageClasses and real-time production scenarios.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Why Config & Storage Matter</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes applications usually need two things outside the container image:
<strong>configuration</strong> and <strong>persistent data</strong>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Application Container
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>ConfigMap / Secret</strong>
â†’ Application Configuration
<br><br>
<strong>Volume / PVC</strong>
â†’ Persistent Application Data

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A Java application runs in Kubernetes.

The application image contains the code, but database URLs,
environment-specific configuration and passwords should not be
hardcoded inside the image.

ConfigMaps can store normal configuration, Secrets can store
sensitive values, and PVCs can provide persistent storage for
application data.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a ConfigMap?</h2>

<h3>Interview Question</h3>

<div class="answer">
A <strong>ConfigMap</strong> is a Kubernetes object used to store
non-sensitive configuration data separately from application code
and container images.
</div>

<h3>Why do we use ConfigMaps?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Keep configuration outside the container image</li>
<li>Use different configuration for different environments</li>
<li>Avoid rebuilding images for configuration changes</li>
<li>Provide configuration as environment variables or files</li>
</ul>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  APP_ENV: production
  LOG_LEVEL: INFO
  APP_PORT: "8080"</code></pre>

<h3>Using ConfigMap as environment variables</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:v1
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I use ConfigMaps to externalize non-sensitive application
configuration from the container image. This allows the same image
to be promoted across environments while configuration can vary
between development, staging and production."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is a Secret?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A <strong>Secret</strong> is a Kubernetes object designed to hold
sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, API keys and credentials.
</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  DB_USERNAME: admin
  DB_PASSWORD: mypassword</code></pre>

<h3>Using Secret in a Pod</h3>

<pre><code>env:
- name: DB_USERNAME
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: db-secret
      key: DB_USERNAME

- name: DB_PASSWORD
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: db-secret
      key: DB_PASSWORD</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Kubernetes Secrets are not automatically equivalent to a fully secure
external secrets manager. In production, protect access using RBAC
and encryption at rest, and consider external secret-management
solutions when appropriate.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. ConfigMap vs Secret</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ConfigMap</th>
<th>Secret</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Non-sensitive configuration</td>
<td>Sensitive configuration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Environment variables</td>
<td>Passwords / tokens / keys</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Application settings</td>
<td>Credentials</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Not intended for secrets</td>
<td>Designed for sensitive values</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy interview line:</strong>

<br><br>

"ConfigMap is for non-sensitive configuration, while Secret is for
sensitive configuration such as credentials and tokens."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. How can ConfigMap and Secret be consumed?</h2>

<p>They can commonly be consumed in two ways:</p>

<h3>1. Environment Variables</h3>

<pre><code>envFrom:
- configMapRef:
    name: app-config

- secretRef:
    name: db-secret</code></pre>

<h3>2. Mounted as Files</h3>

<pre><code>volumes:
- name: config-volume
  configMap:
    name: app-config

containers:
- name: app
  image: myapp:v1
  volumeMounts:
  - name: config-volume
    mountPath: /etc/config</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

An NGINX application may need a configuration file.
Instead of rebuilding the Docker image whenever the configuration
changes, the configuration can be stored in a ConfigMap and mounted
inside the Pod.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is a Volume in Kubernetes?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A Kubernetes Volume provides storage that can be mounted into
containers running inside a Pod.
</div>

<p>
A container's writable filesystem is tied to the container lifecycle.
When a container is replaced, data stored only inside that writable
layer may be lost.
</p>

<h3>Basic volume example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: volume-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-storage
      mountPath: /data

  volumes:
  - name: app-storage
    emptyDir: {}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is emptyDir?</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>emptyDir</code> creates temporary storage when a Pod is assigned
to a node. The storage exists for the lifetime of the Pod.
</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time use case:</strong>

A Pod has two containers. One container generates temporary files and
another container processes them.

Both containers can mount the same <code>emptyDir</code> volume and
share those temporary files.

</div>

<div class="warning">

When the Pod is deleted from the node, the <code>emptyDir</code>
data is deleted.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is PersistentVolume?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A <strong>PersistentVolume (PV)</strong> is a cluster-level storage
resource provisioned for persistent application data.
</div>

<p>
A PV represents storage that exists independently of a particular
Pod's lifecycle.
</p>

<h3>Concept</h3>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
PVC
<br>
â†“
<br>
PV
<br>
â†“
<br>
Storage Backend

</div>

<p>
The storage backend could be cloud block storage, network storage,
or another Kubernetes-supported storage implementation.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is PersistentVolumeClaim?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A <strong>PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)</strong> is a request for
persistent storage made by a user or workload.
</div>

<p>
Instead of directly selecting a physical storage device, the
application requests storage through a PVC.
</p>

<h3>Example PVC</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi</code></pre>

<h3>Using PVC in a Pod</h3>

<pre><code>volumes:
- name: app-storage
  persistentVolumeClaim:
    claimName: app-pvc

containers:
- name: app
  image: nginx
  volumeMounts:
  - name: app-storage
    mountPath: /data</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. PV vs PVC</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>PV</th>
<th>PVC</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Actual Kubernetes storage resource</td>
<td>Request for storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Cluster-level resource</td>
<td>Requested by workload/user</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides storage</td>
<td>Consumes/claims storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually associated with a storage backend</td>
<td>Specifies required capacity/access characteristics</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Simple interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"PV is the storage resource, while PVC is the request for that
storage. Pods normally consume the PVC rather than directly
managing the underlying storage."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What is StorageClass?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A <strong>StorageClass</strong> defines classes of storage and enables
dynamic provisioning of PersistentVolumes.
</div>

<p>
Without dynamic provisioning, administrators may need to create PVs
manually. With a StorageClass, Kubernetes can provision storage
through the configured storage provisioner when a PVC requests it.
</p>

<div class="flow">

PVC
<br>
â†“
<br>
StorageClass
<br>
â†“
<br>
Provisioner
<br>
â†“
<br>
Persistent Volume
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Dynamic vs Static Provisioning</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Static Provisioning</th>
<th>Dynamic Provisioning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Admin creates PV manually</td>
<td>PV is provisioned automatically</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More manual work</td>
<td>Automation-friendly</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for predefined storage</td>
<td>Common in cloud Kubernetes environments</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time AWS example:</strong>

An application requests a 20Gi PVC. The configured StorageClass
can dynamically provision the required cloud storage instead of
the administrator manually creating every PV.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Access Modes</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Mode</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ReadWriteOnce</code></td>
<td>Volume can be mounted read-write by a node according to the storage backend's capabilities.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ReadOnlyMany</code></td>
<td>Volume can be mounted read-only by multiple nodes where supported.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>ReadWriteMany</code></td>
<td>Volume can be mounted read-write by multiple nodes where supported.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

Do not assume every storage backend supports every access mode.
The actual capability depends on the storage implementation.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. What happens when a Pod using a PVC is deleted?</h2>

<div class="answer">
Deleting a Pod does not automatically mean the persistent data is
deleted. The PVC and the underlying storage can remain available
for another Pod, depending on the storage lifecycle and reclaim
configuration.
</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A database Pod crashes.

Kubernetes creates a replacement Pod.

The replacement Pod can mount the same PVC and continue using the
persistent database data, assuming the storage can be attached to
the new Pod.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. What is a Reclaim Policy?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A PV reclaim policy determines what happens to the underlying
storage after the PVC is deleted.
</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Policy</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Retain</td>
<td>Keep the PV/storage for manual recovery or cleanup.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Delete</td>
<td>Delete the associated dynamically provisioned storage where supported.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Recycle</td>
<td>Legacy behavior and generally not used in modern Kubernetes.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

For production databases, storage lifecycle must be chosen carefully.
Accidental deletion of a claim should not automatically destroy
critical data without an intentional recovery strategy.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Kubernetes Storage Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Scenario: PVC is stuck in Pending</h3>

<p>First inspect the PVC:</p>

<pre><code>kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc &lt;pvc-name&gt;</code></pre>

<p>Then inspect StorageClasses:</p>

<pre><code>kubectl get storageclass
kubectl describe storageclass &lt;storage-class-name&gt;</code></pre>

<p>Also inspect Pods and cluster events:</p>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

<h3>Common causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>No suitable StorageClass</li>
<li>StorageClass/provisioner problem</li>
<li>Insufficient storage capacity</li>
<li>Unsupported access mode</li>
<li>Storage backend problem</li>
<li>Topology or node constraints</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. ConfigMap/Secret Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Check objects</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get configmap
kubectl get secret</code></pre>

<h3>Inspect configuration</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl describe configmap app-config
kubectl describe secret db-secret</code></pre>

<h3>Check Pod</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

The application starts but cannot connect to the database.

I would verify:

<br><br>

1. Secret exists<br>
2. Correct Secret key is referenced<br>
3. Environment variable is injected correctly<br>
4. Database hostname and port are correct<br>
5. Pod logs show the actual application error

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Secret Security in Production</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use least-privilege RBAC</li>
<li>Restrict who can read Secrets</li>
<li>Enable encryption at rest where appropriate</li>
<li>Avoid committing secrets to Git</li>
<li>Rotate credentials</li>
<li>Use external secret-management systems when appropriate</li>
<li>Never print secrets in application logs</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

Base64 encoding is not the same thing as encryption.
Do not describe Kubernetes Secret data as secure simply because it
is base64-encoded.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Scenario: Database in Kubernetes</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

A PostgreSQL database is running inside Kubernetes.

The Pod gets deleted because of a node failure.

<br><br>

<strong>Problem:</strong>

If database files were stored only inside the container's writable
layer, the replacement Pod could lose the data.

<br><br>

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Use a PVC backed by persistent storage.

</div>

<div class="flow">

PostgreSQL Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
PVC
<br>
â†“
<br>
PV / Dynamic Provisioning
<br>
â†“
<br>
Persistent Storage

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would not depend on the container writable layer for database
persistence. I would use a PVC backed by an appropriate persistent
storage system, define the storage lifecycle carefully, and also
maintain backups because persistent storage alone is not a complete
backup strategy."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 19. ConfigMap vs Baking Configuration into Docker Image</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Docker Image Configuration</th>
<th>Kubernetes ConfigMap</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Configuration becomes part of image</td>
<td>Configuration is externalized</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Often requires rebuilding image</td>
<td>Same image can be used across environments</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less flexible for environment changes</td>
<td>Better separation of application and configuration</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>DevOps principle:</strong>

Build the application image once and inject environment-specific
configuration during deployment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Most Asked Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

</ol>

</div>


<!-- FOLLOW UPS -->

<div class="card">

â†’ Non-sensitive configuration

<strong>Secret</strong>
â†’ Sensitive configuration

<br><br>

â†’ Storage mounted into Pod

<br><br>

â†’ Temporary Pod storage

<br><br>

â†’ Persistent storage resource

<br><br>

â†’ Request for persistent storage

<br><br>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Kubernetes Storage"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes provides different mechanisms for configuration and
storage.

For non-sensitive application configuration, I use ConfigMaps,
while sensitive values such as credentials are stored in Secrets.

For storage, a Pod can use volumes. For temporary data,
emptyDir can be used, but for persistent application data I use
PersistentVolumeClaims.

A PVC represents the application's request for storage and can be
bound to a PersistentVolume. In dynamic provisioning, a
StorageClass and its provisioner can automatically create the
required storage.

For production workloads such as databases, I would use persistent
storage with an appropriate access mode and reclaim policy, secure
Secrets using RBAC and encryption controls, and maintain backups
because storage persistence is not a substitute for backups."

</div>

<header>

<div class="icon">ðŸ”‘</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Kubernetes</a>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>ConfigMaps & Secrets</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering configuration management, Secrets,
environment variables, volume mounts, security practices,
troubleshooting and real-time DevOps scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
Applications should not normally have environment-specific
configuration hard-coded inside the container image.
Kubernetes provides <strong>ConfigMap</strong> and
<strong>Secret</strong> for separating configuration from application
images.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application
<br>
+
<br>
<strong>ConfigMap</strong> â†’ Non-sensitive configuration
<br>
<strong>Secret</strong> â†’ Sensitive configuration
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

The same application image is deployed to Dev, QA and Production.

The application code remains unchanged, while values such as
database host, application mode and API credentials are supplied
through Kubernetes configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a ConfigMap?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>ConfigMap</strong> stores non-confidential configuration
data as key-value pairs or configuration files.

It helps keep environment-specific configuration separate from
the container image.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  APP_ENV: production
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  API_URL: https://api.example.com</code></pre>

<h3>View it</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get configmap
kubectl describe configmap app-config</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is a Secret?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>Secret</strong> stores sensitive information such as
passwords, tokens, API keys or credentials.

Kubernetes Secrets are intended for sensitive data, but simply
storing a value in a Secret does not automatically make it strongly
protected in every environment.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: admin
  password: MyStrongPassword</code></pre>

<h3>View Secret metadata</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get secret
kubectl describe secret db-secret</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not commit real passwords, API keys or cloud credentials into
Git repositories.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. ConfigMap vs Secret</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ConfigMap</th>
<th>Secret</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Non-sensitive configuration</td>
<td>Sensitive configuration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>URLs, feature flags, log levels</td>
<td>Passwords, tokens, credentials</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be consumed as env variables</td>
<td>Can be consumed as env variables</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be mounted as files</td>
<td>Can be mounted as files</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration such as application
settings and URLs. I use Secrets for sensitive values such as
passwords, tokens and credentials. Both can be consumed by Pods
through environment variables or mounted files."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Using ConfigMap as Environment Variables</h2>

<h3>ConfigMap</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  APP_ENV: production
  LOG_LEVEL: info</code></pre>

<h3>Pod</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-config</code></pre>

<p>
The keys from the ConfigMap become environment variables inside the
container.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Using Secret as Environment Variables</h2>

<h3>Secret</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  DB_USERNAME: admin
  DB_PASSWORD: MyStrongPassword</code></pre>

<h3>Pod</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: database-client
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    envFrom:
    - secretRef:
        name: db-secret</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Environment variables can potentially be exposed through application
debugging, process inspection, logs or other operational mechanisms.
Use the consumption method appropriate for your security requirements.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. ConfigMap using individual environment variable</h2>

<pre><code>env:
- name: APP_ENV
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: app-config
      key: APP_ENV</code></pre>

<p>
This is useful when the container should receive only a specific
configuration value instead of the entire ConfigMap.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Secret using individual key</h2>

<pre><code>env:
- name: DB_PASSWORD
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: db-secret
      key: DB_PASSWORD</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time use:</strong>

An application needs only the database password.

Instead of importing every Secret key into the container, expose
only the required key.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Mount ConfigMap as a Volume</h2>

<h3>ConfigMap</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  application.properties: |
    app.name=myapp
    log.level=INFO</code></pre>

<h3>Pod</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-volume-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config-volume
      mountPath: /etc/app

  volumes:
  - name: config-volume
    configMap:
      name: app-config</code></pre>

<p>
The ConfigMap data is exposed as files inside
<code>/etc/app</code>.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 9. Mount Secret as a Volume</h2>

<h3>Pod example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-volume-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - name: secret-volume
      mountPath: /etc/secrets
      readOnly: true

  volumes:
  - name: secret-volume
    secret:
      secretName: db-secret</code></pre>

<p>
Each Secret key is exposed as a file inside the mounted directory.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. stringData vs data</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>data</th>
<th>stringData</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Values are represented as base64-encoded data in the manifest.</td>
<td>Allows plain string values in the manifest.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly seen when inspecting Secret manifests.</td>
<td>Kubernetes converts the values into the Secret's data representation.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: example
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: admin
  password: password123</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

Do not assume a base64-encoded Secret is safe to expose.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Why not hard-code configuration in Docker image?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Hard-coding environment-specific values inside an image creates
deployment and maintenance problems.

For example, the same image should ideally be reusable across
development, staging and production while configuration changes
independently.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Same Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Dev Config
<br>
QA Config
<br>
Production Config

</div>

<div class="interview">

This follows the DevOps principle of separating application code
from environment-specific configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. ConfigMap update behavior</h2>

<div class="answer">

How a Pod observes a ConfigMap update depends on how the ConfigMap
is consumed.

Mounted ConfigMap volumes can eventually reflect updates, while
environment variables populated from ConfigMaps are not dynamically
updated inside an already-running container.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If an application reads configuration from environment variables,
you normally need to restart or recreate the Pod to load the updated
environment values.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. Secret update behavior</h2>

<div class="answer">

The same important distinction applies to Secrets.

A Secret consumed as an environment variable does not automatically
change inside a running process when the Secret object changes.

Mounted Secret volumes can reflect updates according to Kubernetes'
volume update behavior.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Even when Kubernetes updates a mounted Secret, the application must
be designed to re-read or reload the file if it needs the new value
without restarting.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Immutable ConfigMap / Secret</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes supports immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets.

This can prevent accidental modification of configuration after
creation and is useful when configuration should remain fixed for
the lifetime of a deployment.

</div>

<h3>ConfigMap example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
immutable: true
data:
  APP_ENV: production</code></pre>

<h3>Secret example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-secret
immutable: true
type: Opaque
stringData:
  API_KEY: example</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

If configuration needs to change, create a new ConfigMap or Secret
and update the workload reference as part of a controlled deployment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. How to create ConfigMap using kubectl?</h2>

<h3>From literals</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl create configmap app-config \
  --from-literal=APP_ENV=production \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info</code></pre>

<h3>From file</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl create configmap app-config \
  --from-file=application.properties</code></pre>

<h3>From env file</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl create configmap app-config \
  --from-env-file=.env</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. How to create Secret using kubectl?</h2>

<h3>From literal</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl create secret generic db-secret \
  --from-literal=username=admin \
  --from-literal=password='MyStrongPassword'</code></pre>

<h3>From file</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl create secret generic app-secret \
  --from-file=credentials.txt</code></pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get secrets
kubectl describe secret db-secret</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Avoid putting real secrets directly into shell history or shared
terminal sessions. Prefer a secure secret-management workflow.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Troubleshooting: ConfigMap not found</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Pod fails because it references a ConfigMap that does not exist in
the Pod's namespace.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get configmap -n dev

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n dev

kubectl get configmap app-config -n dev</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

ConfigMaps and Pods are namespace-scoped. The ConfigMap must normally
exist in the same namespace as the workload referencing it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Troubleshooting: Secret not found</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A Deployment references <code>db-secret</code>, but the Pod cannot
start correctly because the Secret is missing.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get secret -n production

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n production

kubectl get deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt; -n production -o yaml</code></pre>

<p>
Verify the Secret name, namespace and referenced key.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Real-Time Scenario: Dev, QA and Production</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose the application image is:

<pre><code>mycompany/payment-app:v1.5</code></pre>

The application is deployed into three environments.

<br><br>

<strong>Dev:</strong> LOG_LEVEL=debug

<br>

<strong>QA:</strong> LOG_LEVEL=info

<br>

<strong>Production:</strong> LOG_LEVEL=warn

<br><br>

The same application image can be reused while each environment
provides its own ConfigMap.

</div>

<div class="interview">

This avoids rebuilding the Docker image just because environment
configuration changed.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Real-Time Scenario: Database Password Rotation</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A production database password must be rotated.

A good approach is to update the credential through the approved
secret-management process, update the Kubernetes Secret, and ensure
the application reloads or restarts as required.

</div>

<div class="flow">

New Credential
<br>
â†“
<br>
Secret Management
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Secret
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Reload / Restart
<br>
â†“
<br>
Verify Connection

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not update credentials by manually editing application source code
or committing the new password to Git.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Real-Time Scenario: Secret accidentally committed to Git</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

An AWS access key or database password was accidentally committed.

<br><br>

<strong>Immediate response:</strong>

1. Treat the credential as compromised.<br>
2. Revoke or rotate it immediately.<br>
3. Remove it from active configuration.<br>
4. Investigate repository history and exposure.<br>
5. Clean repository history when appropriate.<br>
6. Use secret scanning to prevent recurrence.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Deleting the file in a later commit does not automatically remove
the secret from Git history.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. ConfigMap & Secret with Deployment</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payment-app
spec:
  replicas: 2

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payment

    spec:
      containers:
      - name: payment
        image: mycompany/payment:v1.0

        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: payment-config

        - secretRef:
            name: payment-secret</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This is a common production pattern:

<strong>Image</strong> contains application code.

<strong>ConfigMap</strong> provides normal configuration.

<strong>Secret</strong> provides sensitive configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. ConfigMap vs Docker ENV</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Docker ENV</th>
<th>Kubernetes ConfigMap</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be baked into the image definition</td>
<td>Managed separately from the image</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less flexible for multiple environments</td>
<td>Designed for Kubernetes configuration management</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Image may contain environment-specific defaults</td>
<td>Same image can be reused across environments</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

In Kubernetes deployments, I prefer externalizing environment-specific
configuration through ConfigMaps and Secrets rather than rebuilding
images for every environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Security Best Practices</h2>

<ul>
<li>Never store production secrets in Git.</li>
<li>Use RBAC to limit Secret access.</li>
<li>Use encryption at rest where appropriate.</li>
<li>Rotate credentials.</li>
<li>Use external secret managers when required.</li>
<li>Do not print Secrets in application logs.</li>
<li>Use dedicated Secrets for different environments.</li>
<li>Use immutable Secrets when appropriate.</li>
<li>Give workloads only the permissions they need.</li>
<li>Scan repositories for leaked credentials.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

For a production AWS workload, an organization may integrate
Kubernetes with a dedicated cloud secret-management solution instead
of manually managing long-lived credentials in Git.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 25 -->

<div class="card">

<!-- FINAL REVISION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸš€ 60-Second ConfigMap & Secret Revision</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>ConfigMap</strong>
â†’ Non-sensitive configuration

<br><br>

<strong>Secret</strong>
â†’ Sensitive configuration

<br><br>

<strong>envFrom</strong>
â†’ Load all keys

<br><br>

<strong>configMapKeyRef</strong>
â†’ Load one ConfigMap key

<br><br>

<strong>secretKeyRef</strong>
â†’ Load one Secret key

<br><br>

<strong>Volume Mount</strong>
â†’ Configuration as files

<br><br>

<strong>Immutable</strong>
â†’ Prevent modification

<br><br>

â†’ Control who can access Secrets

<br><br>

â†’ Stronger centralized secret management

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain ConfigMaps and Secrets"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"ConfigMaps and Secrets allow us to separate configuration from the
application container image.

I use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive values such as environment
settings, application URLs and log levels.

For sensitive information such as passwords, tokens and API keys,
I use Kubernetes Secrets and restrict access through RBAC.

Both ConfigMaps and Secrets can be consumed through environment
variables or mounted as files.

For production, I avoid committing Secrets to Git, use appropriate
encryption and access controls, rotate credentials and consider an
external secret-management solution when required.

This allows us to reuse the same application image across Dev, QA
and Production while managing environment-specific configuration
separately."

</div>

</div>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>Ingress, Helm & Monitoring</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Ingress, Ingress Controllers,
TLS routing, Helm, Charts, Releases, Values, Prometheus, Grafana,

</p>

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Big Picture</h2>

<p>
Ingress, Helm and Monitoring solve three different production
problems in Kubernetes.
</p>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Ingress</strong>
<br>
External HTTP/HTTPS traffic â†’ Kubernetes Services

<br><br>â†“

<strong>Helm</strong>
<br>
Package + install + upgrade Kubernetes applications

<br><br>â†“

<strong>Monitoring</strong>
<br>
Observe metrics â†’ dashboards â†’ alerts â†’ troubleshoot

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A company runs a web application on Kubernetes.

Users access:

<pre><code>https://shop.example.com</code></pre>

Ingress routes the request to the correct Service.

Helm is used to install and upgrade the application.

Prometheus collects metrics and Grafana displays dashboards for
CPU, memory, request rate, latency and application health.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ================= INGRESS ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Kubernetes Ingress?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Ingress is a Kubernetes API object used to define HTTP and HTTPS
routing rules for traffic entering the cluster.

It can route requests based on hostnames and URL paths to backend
Services.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Internet
<br>
â†“
<br>
Load Balancer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Ingress Controller
<br>
â†“
<br>
Ingress Rules
<br>
â†“
<br>
Service
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Ingress provides HTTP and HTTPS routing into Kubernetes Services.
It allows us to expose multiple applications using host-based or
path-based routing through a common entry point."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is an Ingress Controller?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An Ingress resource only defines routing rules.

An <strong>Ingress Controller</strong> is the component that actually
implements those rules and processes incoming traffic.

Examples include:

<ul>
<li>NGINX Ingress Controller</li>
<li>Traefik</li>
<li>HAProxy</li>
<li>Cloud-provider ingress/load-balancer controllers</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Creating an Ingress object without an appropriate Ingress Controller
does not automatically make the application reachable.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Basic Ingress YAML</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress

metadata:
  name: shop-ingress

spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx

  rules:
  - host: shop.example.com

    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix

        backend:
          service:
            name: shop-service
            port:
              number: 80</code></pre>

<p>
Requests for <code>shop.example.com</code> are routed to
<code>shop-service</code>.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Path-Based Routing</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress

metadata:
  name: app-ingress

spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx

  rules:
  - host: example.com

    http:
      paths:

      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix

        backend:
          service:
            name: api-service
            port:
              number: 80

      - path: /web
        pathType: Prefix

        backend:
          service:
            name: web-service
            port:
              number: 80</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

example.com/api
â†’ API Service

<br><br>

example.com/web
â†’ Web Service

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Host-Based Routing</h2>

<pre><code>rules:

- host: api.example.com

  http:
    paths:
    - path: /
      pathType: Prefix

      backend:
        service:
          name: api-service
          port:
            number: 80

- host: shop.example.com

  http:
    paths:
    - path: /
      pathType: Prefix

      backend:
        service:
          name: shop-service
          port:
            number: 80</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Production example:</strong>

<pre><code>api.example.com
        â†“
API Service

shop.example.com
        â†“
Shop Service</code></pre>

One cluster can serve multiple applications through the ingress
layer.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Ingress TLS</h2>

<div class="answer">

Ingress can terminate HTTPS/TLS traffic using a Kubernetes TLS
Secret.

</div>

<pre><code>spec:

  tls:
  - hosts:
    - shop.example.com

    secretName: shop-tls

  rules:
  - host: shop.example.com

    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix

        backend:
          service:
            name: shop-service
            port:
              number: 80</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Client:

<code>HTTPS</code>

â†“

Ingress Controller terminates TLS

â†“

Service

â†“

Pod

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Ingress vs Service</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Service</th>
<th>Ingress</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides stable networking for Pods.</td>
<td>Provides HTTP/HTTPS routing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can expose applications using ClusterIP, NodePort or LoadBalancer.</td>
<td>Routes based on host/path rules.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Works at the Service/networking layer.</td>
<td>Primarily handles HTTP/HTTPS application routing.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Simple answer:</strong>

"Service provides stable access to Pods, while Ingress provides
HTTP/HTTPS routing from outside the cluster to those Services."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 8. Ingress troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="scenario">

If an application is not reachable through Ingress, check:

<pre><code>kubectl get ingress
kubectl describe ingress &lt;ingress-name&gt;

kubectl get ingressclass

kubectl get svc
kubectl get pods

kubectl get endpoints
kubectl get events</code></pre>

</div>

<p>
Verify the Ingress class, hostname, Service name, Service port,
backend endpoints and Ingress Controller logs.
</p>

</div>


<!-- ================= HELM ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is Helm?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes.

It helps package, install, upgrade, configure and manage Kubernetes
applications using reusable <strong>Charts</strong>.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Helm Chart
<br>
â†“
Templates + Values
<br>
â†“
Helm
<br>
â†“
Kubernetes Manifests
<br>
â†“
Kubernetes API
<br>
â†“
Resources

</div>

<div class="interview">

"Helm is commonly used to package Kubernetes applications and
simplify repeatable deployments by using charts, templates and
values."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What is a Helm Chart?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Helm Chart is a collection of files that describes a Kubernetes
application.

A typical chart contains templates, default values and chart
metadata.

</div>

<h3>Typical structure</h3>

<pre><code>myapp/
â”œâ”€â”€ Chart.yaml
â”œâ”€â”€ values.yaml
â””â”€â”€ templates/
    â”œâ”€â”€ deployment.yaml
    â”œâ”€â”€ service.yaml
    â”œâ”€â”€ ingress.yaml
    â””â”€â”€ _helpers.tpl</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Important Helm files</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>File</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Chart.yaml</td>
<td>Chart metadata such as name and version.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>values.yaml</td>
<td>Default configurable values.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>templates/</td>
<td>Kubernetes manifest templates.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>_helpers.tpl</td>
<td>Reusable Helm template helpers.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Helm values.yaml</h2>

<pre><code>replicaCount: 2

image:
  repository: nginx
  tag: "1.27"

service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 80</code></pre>

<p>
Templates can consume these values using Helm template expressions.
</p>

<pre><code>replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}

image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Helm install</h2>

<pre><code>helm install myapp ./myapp</code></pre>

<p>
This creates a Helm release from the chart.
</p>

<h3>Specify values</h3>

<pre><code>helm install myapp ./myapp \
  --set replicaCount=3</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Helm upgrade</h2>

<pre><code>helm upgrade myapp ./myapp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose production currently runs:

<pre><code>replicas: 2</code></pre>

You change the values to:

<pre><code>replicas: 4</code></pre>

Then:

<pre><code>helm upgrade myapp ./myapp</code></pre>

Helm applies the updated release configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Helm rollback</h2>

<div class="answer">

Helm tracks release revisions, allowing you to roll back to a
previous revision.

</div>

<pre><code>helm history myapp

helm rollback myapp 2</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Production deployment v3 causes an outage.

If revision 2 was stable:

<pre><code>helm rollback myapp 2</code></pre>

This provides a fast recovery mechanism.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Helm release</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Helm release is a deployed instance of a Helm Chart.

The same chart can have different releases.

</div>

<pre><code>helm install dev-app ./myapp
helm install prod-app ./myapp</code></pre>

<p>
Here the same chart is used to create two different releases.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Helm important commands</h2>

<pre><code># Add repository
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts

# Update repositories
helm repo update

# Search charts
helm search repo prometheus

# Install
helm install myapp ./mychart

# List releases
helm list

# List all namespaces
helm list -A

# Show values
helm get values myapp

# Show release
helm get all myapp

# History
helm history myapp

# Upgrade
helm upgrade myapp ./mychart

# Rollback
helm rollback myapp 1

# Uninstall
helm uninstall myapp</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. helm template</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>helm template</code> renders Kubernetes manifests locally without
actually installing the release.

</div>

<pre><code>helm template myapp ./mychart</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Very useful in CI/CD to inspect generated manifests before applying
them to a cluster.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Helm vs kubectl</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>kubectl</th>
<th>Helm</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Directly interacts with Kubernetes resources.</td>
<td>Manages applications through reusable charts.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Works with individual manifests/resources.</td>
<td>Provides templating, values and release management.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Excellent for troubleshooting and direct operations.</td>
<td>Excellent for repeatable application packaging/deployment.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Helm real-time CI/CD usage</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A DevOps pipeline receives a new application image.

Pipeline:

<pre><code>Git Push
   â†“
CI Build
   â†“
Docker Image
   â†“
Container Registry
   â†“
Helm values updated
   â†“
helm upgrade
   â†“
Kubernetes Deployment
   â†“
Health Checks
   â†“
Monitoring</code></pre>

Helm makes it easier to maintain environment-specific values without
creating completely separate manifests for every environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ================= MONITORING ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. What is Kubernetes Monitoring?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes monitoring means collecting and analyzing information
about cluster nodes, Pods, containers, applications and workloads.

It helps teams detect failures, resource problems, performance
issues and capacity requirements.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Applications
<br>
â†“
<br>
Metrics
<br>
â†“
<br>
Prometheus
<br>
â†“
<br>
Grafana
<br>
â†“
<br>
Dashboard
<br>
â†“
<br>
Alert
<br>
â†“
<br>
DevOps Engineer

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Prometheus</h2>

<div class="answer">

Prometheus is a monitoring and alerting system commonly used with
Kubernetes.

It collects time-series metrics and stores them for querying and
alerting.

</div>

<h3>Examples of metrics</h3>

<ul>
<li>CPU usage</li>
<li>Memory usage</li>
<li>Request rate</li>
<li>HTTP errors</li>
<li>Latency</li>
<li>Pod/container metrics</li>
<li>Node metrics</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Grafana</h2>

<div class="answer">

Grafana is commonly used to visualize metrics through dashboards.

It can connect to Prometheus and display Kubernetes and application
metrics in graphs, tables and panels.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example dashboard:

<pre><code>Cluster CPU
Cluster Memory
Node Health
Pod Count
Pod Restarts
HTTP Request Rate
HTTP Error Rate
Application Latency</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Prometheus vs Grafana</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Prometheus</th>
<th>Grafana</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Collects and stores metrics.</td>
<td>Visualizes metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides PromQL querying.</td>
<td>Provides dashboards and panels.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can perform alerting.</td>
<td>Can visualize and route alerts depending on configuration.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy answer:</strong>

"Prometheus is primarily the metrics collection and monitoring
system, while Grafana is primarily used to visualize those metrics
through dashboards."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. What is PromQL?</h2>

<div class="answer">

PromQL is Prometheus Query Language.

It is used to query and analyze time-series metrics stored in
Prometheus.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>up</code></pre>

<p>
Shows whether monitored targets are currently up.
</p>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>rate(http_requests_total[5m])</code></pre>

<p>
Calculates the per-second rate of increase over the selected
five-minute range.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Kubernetes Monitoring Stack</h2>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes Cluster
<br>
â†“
<br>

A common production setup may use the

Prometheus, Grafana and related Kubernetes monitoring components.

</div>

<div class="card">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Why use monitoring in production?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Without monitoring, engineers may know that an application is down
only after users report the problem.

Monitoring provides visibility into:

<ul>
<li>Resource usage</li>
<li>Application performance</li>
<li>Errors</li>
<li>Latency</li>
<li>Pod restarts</li>
<li>Node failures</li>
<li>Capacity trends</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. What should you monitor?</h2>

</tr>

</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pods</td>
<td>Restarts, CPU, memory, status</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Application</td>
<td>Request rate, errors, latency</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Network</td>
<td>Traffic, failures, latency</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Storage</td>
<td>Capacity, I/O, volume health</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Pod CrashLoopBackOff monitoring</h2>

<div class="scenario">

If a Pod repeatedly crashes:

<pre><code>kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous</code></pre>

Monitoring can help identify:

<ul>
<li>Frequent restarts</li>
<li>Application errors</li>
<li>Memory pressure</li>
<li>Probe failures</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Alerting</h2>

<div class="answer">

Monitoring tells us what is happening.

Alerting notifies engineers when defined conditions require
attention.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Examples:

<pre><code>High CPU
High memory
Pod repeatedly restarting
Node unavailable
High HTTP 5xx rate
High application latency
Low disk space</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 32. Metrics Server vs Prometheus</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Metrics Server</th>
<th>Prometheus</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides basic resource metrics.</td>
<td>Full-featured monitoring and time-series database.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used by commands such as kubectl top.</td>
<td>Used for extensive metrics collection, querying and alerting.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly supports resource-based HPA.</td>
<td>Can provide richer/custom metrics depending on setup.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

Do not treat Metrics Server and Prometheus as interchangeable
products. They solve overlapping but different monitoring needs.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Real-Time Scenario â€” Deployment fails after Helm upgrade</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose:

<pre><code>helm upgrade myapp ./mychart</code></pre>

completes but the application is unhealthy.

Check:

<pre><code>helm history myapp

helm status myapp

kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

If the previous release was stable:

<pre><code>helm rollback myapp &lt;revision&gt;</code></pre>

Then investigate the failed chart/configuration before trying the
upgrade again.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 35. Real-Time Scenario â€” Ingress returns 404</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl get ingress
kubectl describe ingress &lt;ingress-name&gt;

kubectl get ingressclass

kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpoints</code></pre>

Verify:

<ul>
<li>Hostname is correct.</li>
<li>Path is correct.</li>
<li>IngressClass is correct.</li>
<li>Service exists.</li>
<li>Service port matches.</li>
<li>Service has healthy endpoints.</li>
<li>Ingress Controller is running.</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 36. Real-Time Scenario â€” High CPU Alert</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Prometheus detects high CPU usage.

Grafana displays the affected Pods.

Engineer checks:

<pre><code>kubectl top pods
kubectl top nodes
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Then determine whether the cause is:

<ul>
<li>Traffic increase</li>
<li>Bad application behavior</li>
<li>Insufficient resource requests/limits</li>
<li>Missing autoscaling</li>
</ul>

If appropriate, HPA can increase replicas.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Ingress, Helm and Monitoring"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In Kubernetes, I use Ingress to expose HTTP and HTTPS applications
through routing rules based on hostnames and paths. An Ingress
Controller implements those rules and forwards traffic to Services.

For application deployment and packaging, I use Helm. A Helm Chart
contains templates and configurable values. Helm allows me to install,
upgrade, inspect and rollback application releases consistently
across environments.

For monitoring, Prometheus collects time-series metrics from the
cluster and applications, while Grafana provides dashboards and
visualization. I monitor CPU, memory, Pod restarts, node health,
request rate, errors and latency.

In a production setup, these components work together: Ingress
handles external traffic, Helm manages application deployments, and
Prometheus with Grafana provides observability."

</div>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>Probes, Scheduling & Autoscaling</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Liveness, Readiness and Startup
Probes, resource requests and limits, QoS, scheduling, taints,
tolerations, affinity, HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler and
real-time production scenarios.
</p>

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Big Picture</h2>

<p>
Three important areas control how Kubernetes keeps applications
healthy and places workloads efficiently:
</p>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Probes</strong>
<br>
"Is my application healthy and ready?"

<br><br>â†“

<strong>Scheduling</strong>
<br>
"Where should this Pod run?"

<br><br>â†“

<strong>Autoscaling</strong>
<br>
"How many Pods or nodes do I need?"

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A production API suddenly receives heavy traffic.

Readiness probes prevent unhealthy Pods from receiving traffic.
The scheduler places Pods on suitable nodes. HPA increases the
number of application replicas when the workload requires more
capacity. If the cluster needs more nodes, Cluster Autoscaler can
adjust node capacity when supported/configured.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ================= PROBES ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What are Kubernetes Probes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes probes are health checks used by the kubelet to determine
the state of a containerized application.

The three important probes are:

<br><br>

<strong>1. Liveness Probe</strong> â†’ Is the application still alive?

<br>

<strong>2. Readiness Probe</strong> â†’ Can the application receive traffic?

<br>

<strong>3. Startup Probe</strong> â†’ Has the slow-starting application finished starting?

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Startup</strong>
â†’ "Has startup completed?"
<br>
â†“
<strong>Liveness</strong>
â†’ "Is it still alive?"
<br>
â†“
<strong>Readiness</strong>
â†’ "Can it receive traffic?"

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Liveness Probe</h2>

<div class="answer">

A liveness probe determines whether a container is still functioning.

If the liveness probe repeatedly fails, Kubernetes may restart the
container according to the Pod's restart policy and probe behavior.

</div>

<h3>HTTP example</h3>

<pre><code>livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080

  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

A Java application gets stuck internally and stops responding to
health requests.

The liveness probe detects the failure and Kubernetes can restart
the affected container.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Readiness Probe</h2>

<div class="answer">

A readiness probe determines whether a container is ready to serve
traffic.

When readiness fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from the endpoints
of Services that select it, so the Pod should not receive normal
Service traffic.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080

  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 3</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

A new application Pod starts successfully but is still loading
configuration and establishing database connections.

The container is alive, but not ready.

Readiness probe remains failed, so the Pod does not receive
application traffic until it becomes ready.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Startup Probe</h2>

<div class="answer">

A startup probe is designed for applications that take a long time
to initialize.

While the startup probe has not succeeded, Kubernetes does not run
the liveness and readiness probes in the normal way.

This prevents a slow-starting application from being incorrectly
restarted by an aggressive liveness probe.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /startup
    port: 8080

  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A legacy Java application takes several minutes to load a large
application context.

Without a startup probe, liveness could fail during startup and
continually restart the application.

Startup probe solves this type of problem.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Liveness vs Readiness vs Startup</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Probe</th>
<th>Main Question</th>
<th>Failure Effect</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Liveness</td>
<td>Is the application alive?</td>
<td>Container may be restarted.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Readiness</td>
<td>Can it receive traffic?</td>
<td>Pod is removed from Service traffic.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Startup</td>
<td>Has startup completed?</td>
<td>Protects slow-starting applications during initialization.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

"Liveness checks whether the application is still healthy enough to
continue running. Readiness checks whether it is ready to serve
traffic. Startup is useful for slow-starting applications and gives
them enough time to initialize before normal liveness and readiness
checks take effect."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Probe Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Usage</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>httpGet</td>
<td>Sends an HTTP request to an endpoint.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>tcpSocket</td>
<td>Checks whether a TCP connection can be established.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>exec</td>
<td>Runs a command inside the container.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>grpc</td>
<td>Performs a gRPC health check where supported/configured.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>TCP example</h3>

<pre><code>readinessProbe:
  tcpSocket:
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 10</code></pre>

<h3>Exec example</h3>

<pre><code>livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command:
    - cat
    - /tmp/healthy

  periodSeconds: 10</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 7. Probe Timing Parameters</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Parameter</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>initialDelaySeconds</td>
<td>Wait before starting the probe.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>periodSeconds</td>
<td>How frequently the probe runs.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>timeoutSeconds</td>
<td>How long to wait for a probe response.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>failureThreshold</td>
<td>Number of consecutive failures before failure is acted upon.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>successThreshold</td>
<td>Number of successful checks required for recovery in supported probe contexts.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Bad Probe Configuration</h2>

<div class="warning">

A common production mistake is configuring an aggressive liveness
probe that fails while the application is still initializing.

This can cause:

<br><br>

Pod starts â†’ liveness fails â†’ container restarts â†’ application starts
again â†’ liveness fails â†’ restart loop.

</div>

<div class="interview">

Use a Startup Probe for slow initialization and configure liveness
and readiness according to real application behavior rather than
using arbitrary values.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ================= RESOURCES ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. CPU and Memory Requests</h2>

<div class="answer">

A resource request tells Kubernetes how much CPU or memory a
container needs for scheduling purposes.

The scheduler uses resource requests when deciding whether a Pod
can fit on a node.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If a Pod requests:

<code>cpu: 500m</code>

the scheduler looks for a node with enough allocatable CPU according
to the Pod's requested resources.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Resource Limits</h2>

<div class="answer">

A resource limit defines the maximum amount of a resource a
container is allowed to consume, subject to Kubernetes behavior and
the resource type.

</div>

<pre><code>resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"

  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Memory is especially important.

If a container exceeds its memory limit and is terminated due to
memory pressure, you may see an <strong>OOMKilled</strong> state.

CPU overuse is generally throttled rather than causing the same
kind of OOM termination.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Requests vs Limits</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Requests</th>
<th>Limits</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used mainly for scheduling.</td>
<td>Defines an upper resource boundary.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Influences whether Pod fits on a node.</td>
<td>Controls resource consumption according to Kubernetes semantics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Important for capacity planning.</td>
<td>Important for workload protection.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Simple answer:</strong>

"Requests tell Kubernetes how much resource the Pod needs for
scheduling, while limits define the maximum resource boundary for
the container."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is CPU millicore?</h2>

<div class="answer">

CPU can be represented in millicores.

<pre><code>1000m = 1 CPU core
500m  = 0.5 CPU
250m  = 0.25 CPU
100m  = 0.1 CPU</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. QoS Classes</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes assigns Pods a Quality of Service class based on their
resource requests and limits.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>QoS</th>
<th>Concept</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Guaranteed</td>
<td>Every container has CPU and memory requests and limits set, with matching values for the relevant resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Burstable</td>
<td>Pod does not meet Guaranteed criteria but has at least some resource requests/limits.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>BestEffort</td>
<td>No CPU or memory requests/limits are specified.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Check QoS</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- ================= SCHEDULING ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. What is Kubernetes Scheduling?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Kubernetes scheduler selects an appropriate node for a newly
created Pod that is not yet assigned to a node.

It considers factors such as resource availability, constraints,
affinity, taints and tolerations, topology and other scheduling
rules.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pod Created
<br>
â†“
<br>
Scheduler
<br>
â†“
<br>
Filter unsuitable nodes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Score eligible nodes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Select node
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubelet starts Pod

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What happens if a Pod is Pending?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Pod may remain Pending when Kubernetes cannot find a suitable node
for it.

Common causes include:

<ul>
<li>Insufficient CPU.</li>
<li>Insufficient memory.</li>
<li>Taints without matching tolerations.</li>
<li>Node affinity rules.</li>
<li>NodeSelector mismatch.</li>
<li>Storage topology constraints.</li>
<li>Resource requests are too large.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<h3>First troubleshooting command</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<p>
Check the Events section for scheduler messages explaining why nodes
were rejected.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. nodeSelector</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>nodeSelector</code> is a simple way to constrain a Pod to nodes
having specific labels.

</div>

<h3>Label a node</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl label nodes worker-1 workload=backend</code></pre>

<h3>Pod</h3>

<pre><code>spec:
  nodeSelector:
    workload: backend</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Use case:

A team has dedicated nodes for backend workloads.

The nodes are labeled:

<code>workload=backend</code>

Pods using nodeSelector are scheduled only onto nodes with that
label.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Taints</h2>

<div class="answer">

A taint is placed on a node to repel Pods that do not have a matching
toleration.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl taint nodes worker-1 dedicated=backend:NoSchedule</code></pre>

<p>
Now normal Pods without a matching toleration should not be
scheduled onto that node.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Tolerations</h2>

<div class="answer">

A toleration allows a Pod to tolerate a matching node taint.

It does not automatically force the Pod onto that node.

</div>

<pre><code>tolerations:
- key: "dedicated"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "backend"
  effect: "NoSchedule"</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Important:</strong>

Taint = node says "keep Pods away."

Toleration = Pod says "I am allowed to run here."

Toleration alone does not mean "schedule me here."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Taint Effects</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Effect</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>NoSchedule</td>
<td>New Pods without a matching toleration are not scheduled.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>PreferNoSchedule</td>
<td>Scheduler tries to avoid placing Pods there when possible.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>NoExecute</td>
<td>Can prevent scheduling and can evict existing Pods that do not tolerate the taint.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Node Affinity</h2>

<div class="answer">

Node affinity provides more expressive rules for selecting nodes
based on labels.

It is more flexible than a simple nodeSelector.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>affinity:
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: workload
          operator: In
          values:
          - backend</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Use node affinity when scheduling rules become more complex than a
simple exact label match.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 21. required vs preferred affinity</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>requiredDuringScheduling...</th>
<th>preferredDuringScheduling...</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Hard requirement.</td>
<td>Soft preference.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pod cannot be scheduled if requirement is not satisfied.</td>
<td>Scheduler tries to satisfy it but can use another node.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Pod Affinity and Anti-Affinity</h2>

<div class="answer">

Pod affinity can encourage Pods to run near other Pods.

Pod anti-affinity can encourage Pods to run away from other Pods.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>High availability example:</strong>

Suppose an application has three replicas.

You do not want all replicas on the same node because a node failure
could take all replicas down.

Pod anti-affinity can help spread replicas across nodes.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Real-Time Scheduling Design</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Production application:

<ul>
<li>Backend nodes labeled <code>workload=backend</code>.</li>
<li>Backend nodes tainted with <code>dedicated=backend:NoSchedule</code>.</li>
<li>Backend Pods have a matching toleration.</li>
<li>Node affinity ensures they prefer/require backend nodes.</li>
<li>Pod anti-affinity spreads replicas across nodes.</li>
</ul>

This creates controlled workload placement and better failure
distribution.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ================= AUTOSCALING ================= -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. What is Kubernetes Autoscaling?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Autoscaling automatically adjusts resources or capacity according
to workload requirements.

The major autoscaling mechanisms are:

<br><br>

<strong>HPA</strong> â†’ Changes number of Pod replicas.

<br>

<strong>VPA</strong> â†’ Adjusts resource requests/limits recommendations
or updates according to its configured mode.

<br>

<strong>Cluster Autoscaler</strong> â†’ Adjusts node-group capacity
when configured and supported.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Traffic increases
<br>
â†“
<br>
HPA
<br>
â†“
<br>
More Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Insufficient node capacity
<br>
â†“
<br>
Cluster Autoscaler
<br>
â†“
<br>
More Nodes

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. HPA â€” Horizontal Pod Autoscaler</h2>

<div class="answer">

HPA automatically adjusts the number of Pod replicas based on
configured metrics such as CPU, memory or custom/external metrics.

</div>

<h3>Basic HPA</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler

metadata:
  name: api-hpa

spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api

  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10

  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. How HPA works</h2>

<div class="flow">

Metrics
<br>
â†“
<br>
Metrics API / metrics source
<br>
â†“
<br>
HPA Controller
<br>
â†“
<br>
Compare current vs target
<br>
â†“
<br>
Change Deployment replica count
<br>
â†“
<br>
Scheduler
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pods

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If average CPU utilization rises above the configured target, HPA
can increase replicas, subject to its configured behavior and
limits.

When load decreases, HPA can scale down after stabilization and
cooldown behavior as configured.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Why are resource requests important for HPA?</h2>

<div class="answer">

For CPU utilization-based HPA, utilization is calculated relative to
the container's requested CPU.

Therefore, correctly configured resource requests are important for
meaningful utilization-based scaling.

</div>

<div class="warning">

If requests are missing or badly sized, CPU utilization-based HPA
behavior may not work as expected.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. VPA â€” Vertical Pod Autoscaler</h2>

<div class="answer">

VPA adjusts or recommends CPU and memory resource requests for Pods.

It is focused on the resources assigned to individual Pods rather
than changing the number of replicas.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>HPA</th>
<th>VPA</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Changes number of Pods.</td>
<td>Changes/recommends Pod resource sizing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Horizontal scaling.</td>
<td>Vertical scaling.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful when workload replica count should respond to demand.</td>
<td>Useful when individual Pod resource sizing needs optimization.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

HPA and VPA can interact in problematic ways if both attempt to use
the same resource metric for scaling decisions. Design their
configuration carefully.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. Cluster Autoscaler</h2>

<div class="answer">

Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of nodes in a cluster or node
group based on unschedulable Pods and underutilized capacity,
according to its configuration and cloud integration.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

HPA increases replicas from 4 to 12.

The current nodes do not have enough capacity for the new Pods.

Some Pods remain Pending.

Cluster Autoscaler can increase node-group capacity so the scheduler
can place those Pods.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. HPA vs VPA vs Cluster Autoscaler</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Tool</th>
<th>What changes?</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HPA</td>
<td>Number of Pods</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>VPA</td>
<td>Pod CPU/Memory sizing</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Cluster Autoscaler</td>
<td>Number of Nodes</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy memory trick:</strong>

HPA = More/Fewer Pods

<br>

VPA = Bigger/Smaller Pods

<br>

Cluster Autoscaler = More/Fewer Nodes

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. HPA needs Metrics</h2>

<div class="answer">

Resource-based HPA depends on metrics being available through the
cluster's metrics infrastructure.

A common Kubernetes setup uses Metrics Server for basic resource
metrics.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

If <code>kubectl top</code> does not work, investigate the metrics
pipeline before assuming HPA itself is broken.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 32. HPA not scaling â€” Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Possible reasons:

<ul>
<li>Metrics are unavailable.</li>
<li>Target workload is incorrect.</li>
<li>CPU requests are missing or poorly configured.</li>
<li>HPA min/max replicas prevent expected scaling.</li>
<li>Metric target is not being reached.</li>
<li>Custom metrics configuration is broken.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get hpa
kubectl describe hpa &lt;hpa-name&gt;

kubectl top pods
kubectl top nodes

kubectl get deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Real-Time HPA Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">

An e-commerce application normally runs with 3 replicas.

During a flash sale, traffic increases dramatically.

CPU usage increases.

HPA detects the increased metric and scales:

<pre><code>3 Pods
â†“
5 Pods
â†“
8 Pods
â†“
10 Pods</code></pre>

If the existing cluster does not have enough capacity, some new
Pods may remain Pending.

Cluster Autoscaler can then add nodes when its configuration and
cloud provider integration allow it.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Why Pods can remain Pending even after HPA scales?</h2>

<div class="answer">

HPA only changes the desired number of replicas.

It does not automatically create node capacity.

If the cluster has no available resources, newly requested Pods can
remain Pending until capacity becomes available.

</div>

<div class="flow">

HPA
â†’ More Pods

<br>â†“<br>

Scheduler
â†’ Needs Node Capacity

<br>â†“<br>

No Capacity
â†’ Pods Pending

<br>â†“<br>

Cluster Autoscaler
â†’ More Nodes

<br>â†“<br>

Scheduler
â†’ Pods Placed

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIOS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 35. Production Scenario â€” Application becomes unhealthy</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

Application is running but is no longer responding correctly.

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Use liveness to detect a stuck application and allow Kubernetes to
restart the affected container.

Readiness should separately prevent unhealthy instances from
receiving traffic.

</div>

<div class="interview">

Never use readiness as a replacement for liveness.

They solve different problems.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 36. Production Scenario â€” Slow startup</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A Java application requires 2 minutes to start.

A liveness probe begins too early and kills the application before
startup completes.

<strong>Fix:</strong>

Use a startup probe or appropriately design initial startup timing,
then allow liveness/readiness to perform their normal functions after
startup.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 37. Production Scenario â€” Pod won't schedule</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Pod is Pending.

First command:

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Check Events.

If the message says insufficient CPU/memory, inspect:

<pre><code>kubectl describe nodes</code></pre>

If it mentions taints, inspect:

<pre><code>kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;</code></pre>

Then check Pod tolerations and scheduling rules.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 38. Production Scenario â€” HPA not scaling</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check in this order:

<pre><code>kubectl get hpa
kubectl describe hpa &lt;hpa-name&gt;

kubectl top pods
kubectl top nodes

kubectl get deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;</code></pre>

Then verify resource requests, metric availability, target values
and HPA min/max replica settings.

</div>

</div>


<!-- INTERVIEW -->

<div class="card">
