<!-- INTERVIEW ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Probes, Scheduling and Autoscaling"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes probes help maintain application availability.

I use liveness probes to detect containers that are unhealthy and
need restarting, readiness probes to control whether a Pod should
receive traffic, and startup probes for applications that take a
long time to initialize.

For scheduling, Kubernetes uses the scheduler to select suitable
nodes based on resources and constraints. I can use nodeSelector,
node affinity, taints and tolerations, and pod anti-affinity to
control workload placement.

For resource management, I define CPU and memory requests for
scheduling and limits to establish resource boundaries.

For autoscaling, HPA adjusts the number of Pods based on metrics,
VPA adjusts or recommends Pod resource sizing, and Cluster
Autoscaler adjusts node capacity when configured.

In a production environment, I combine these features carefully:
probes protect application health, scheduling controls placement,
and autoscaling handles changing workload demand."

</div>

<div class="icon">ðŸ”</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Kubernetes</a>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>RBAC & Security</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused revision covering RBAC, ServiceAccounts, Roles,
ClusterRoles, bindings, securityContext, least privilege,
NetworkPolicies and real-time security scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Kubernetes Security Mindset</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes security is mainly about controlling <strong>who can do what</strong>,
<strong>where they can do it</strong>, and <strong>what workloads are allowed to do</strong>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Identity
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Authentication</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Authorization / RBAC</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes API
<br>
â†“
<br>
Resources
<br><br>

Workload Security
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>securityContext</strong>
+
<strong>NetworkPolicy</strong>
+
<strong>Secrets Protection</strong>

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A DevOps team has a production Kubernetes cluster.

Developers should be able to view Pods and logs in the
<code>dev</code> namespace, but they should not be allowed to
delete production Deployments.

RBAC can enforce this least-privilege access.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Kubernetes RBAC?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>RBAC</strong> stands for Role-Based Access Control.

It controls which users, groups or ServiceAccounts can perform
which actions on which Kubernetes resources.

</div>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Subject</strong>
<br>
User / Group / ServiceAccount
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Role / ClusterRole</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Permission

</div>

<h3>Important verbs</h3>

<pre><code>get
list
watch
create
update
patch
delete</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"RBAC is Kubernetes' authorization mechanism. It defines permissions
through Roles or ClusterRoles and assigns those permissions to users,
groups or ServiceAccounts using RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Role vs ClusterRole</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Role</th>
<th>ClusterRole</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Namespace-scoped</td>
<td>Cluster-scoped</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Permissions within a namespace</td>
<td>Can define permissions for cluster-wide resources</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for application teams</td>
<td>Useful for cluster-level access</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Role example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]</code></pre>

<p>
This Role allows reading Pods only inside the <code>dev</code>
namespace.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>RoleBinding</strong> grants permissions within a namespace.

A <strong>ClusterRoleBinding</strong> grants the permissions of a
ClusterRole across the cluster.

</div>

<h3>RoleBinding example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: read-pods
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: developer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Avoid giving users <code>cluster-admin</code> unless it is genuinely
required. Excessive permissions increase the blast radius of mistakes
or compromised credentials.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. ServiceAccount</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>ServiceAccount</strong> provides an identity for workloads
running inside Kubernetes.

Pods can use that identity when communicating with the Kubernetes API
or other systems that integrate with Kubernetes identities.

</div>

<h3>Create ServiceAccount</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-sa
  namespace: dev</code></pre>

<h3>Use it in a Pod</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: dev
spec:
  serviceAccountName: app-sa

  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A Kubernetes workload needs permission to read specific Kubernetes
resources.

Instead of giving every Pod broad permissions, create a dedicated
ServiceAccount and bind only the required Role.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. ServiceAccount + Role + RoleBinding</h2>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
ServiceAccount
<br>
â†“
<br>
RoleBinding
<br>
â†“
<br>
Role
<br>
â†“
<br>
Allowed API Actions

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

---

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: app-read-access
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: app-sa
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io</code></pre>

<p>
The application can now use the ServiceAccount identity with only
the permissions granted by the Role.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Authentication vs Authorization</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Authentication</th>
<th>Authorization</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Who are you?</td>
<td>What are you allowed to do?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Verifies identity</td>
<td>Checks permissions</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Users / ServiceAccounts / external identity</td>
<td>RBAC policies</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Authentication verifies the identity, while authorization determines
what that identity is allowed to access or perform."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Least Privilege</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Least privilege</strong> means giving an identity only the
minimum permissions required to perform its job.

</div>

<h3>Bad approach</h3>

<pre><code>verbs: ["*"]
resources: ["*"]</code></pre>

<h3>Better approach</h3>

<pre><code>resources:
- pods

verbs:
- get
- list
- watch</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A monitoring application only needs to read Pod information.

Do not give it permission to create, update or delete Deployments,
Secrets or Nodes.

Give it only the permissions it actually needs.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is securityContext?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Kubernetes <code>securityContext</code> defines security-related
settings for a Pod or container, such as the user/group identity,
Linux capabilities and privilege settings.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true

  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - ALL</code></pre>

<h3>Important settings</h3>

<ul>
<li><code>runAsUser</code></li>
<li><code>runAsGroup</code></li>
<li><code>runAsNonRoot</code></li>
<li><code>allowPrivilegeEscalation</code></li>
<li><code>privileged</code></li>
<li><code>capabilities</code></li>
<li><code>readOnlyRootFilesystem</code></li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Why should containers run as non-root?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Running an application as a non-root user reduces the impact of a
container compromise.

If an attacker gains control of the application process, the attacker
does not automatically receive root privileges inside the container.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Non-root execution is one security layer. It does not replace RBAC,
network controls, image security or host-level security.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. Privileged Container</h2>

<div class="answer">

A privileged container receives significantly elevated access to the
host and should be avoided unless a legitimate infrastructure
workload requires it.

</div>

<h3>Example to avoid for normal applications</h3>

<pre><code>securityContext:
  privileged: true</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A normal web application should not require privileged access.

If an application can run without it, keep the container
unprivileged.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Linux Capabilities</h2>

<div class="answer">

Linux capabilities split traditional root privileges into smaller
permission units. Kubernetes can drop unnecessary capabilities from
containers.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop:
    - ALL</code></pre>

<p>
This follows the principle of removing privileges that the application
does not need.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. readOnlyRootFilesystem</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>readOnlyRootFilesystem: true</code> makes the container's root
filesystem read-only.

This can reduce the ability of a compromised application to modify
files inside the image filesystem.

</div>

<pre><code>securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If the application needs temporary writable space, provide a specific
writable volume such as an <code>emptyDir</code> rather than making
the entire root filesystem writable.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. NetworkPolicy</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>NetworkPolicy</strong> controls network traffic to and/or
from Pods when the cluster's networking implementation supports
NetworkPolicy enforcement.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pod A
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>NetworkPolicy</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Allowed / Denied Traffic
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod B

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database

  policyTypes:
  - Ingress

  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: api
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432</code></pre>

<p>
This expresses that traffic to the selected database Pods on port
5432 should be allowed from Pods matching the API label, subject to
the cluster's NetworkPolicy behavior.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Why use NetworkPolicy?</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Imagine a production namespace containing:

<br><br>

Frontend â†’ API â†’ Database

<br><br>

The database should not accept traffic from every Pod in the cluster.

A NetworkPolicy can restrict database access so that only the
required application Pods can communicate with it.

</div>

<h3>Security principle</h3>

<div class="answer">

Do not assume that Pods are automatically isolated from each other.
Define network access according to application requirements.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. Pod Security Standards</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes Pod Security Standards provide security profiles that
help define which Pod security configurations are permitted.

The commonly discussed levels are:

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Level</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Privileged</td>
<td>Unrestricted profile intended for trusted workloads.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Baseline</td>
<td>Prevents known privilege-escalation patterns.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Restricted</td>
<td>Strong security requirements for hardened workloads.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

For normal production workloads, aim for a restrictive security
posture while validating that the application's actual requirements
are compatible with it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Kubernetes Secret Security</h2>

<ul>
<li>Never commit Secrets directly to Git repositories.</li>
<li>Use RBAC to restrict Secret access.</li>
<li>Enable encryption at rest where appropriate.</li>
<li>Rotate credentials regularly.</li>
<li>Avoid exposing secrets in logs.</li>
<li>Use external secret-management systems when required.</li>
<li>Use short-lived credentials where possible.</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

A Secret containing base64 data should still be treated as sensitive.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. RBAC Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
A developer receives:
</p>

<pre><code>Error from server (Forbidden)</code></pre>

<h3>Check current identity</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl auth whoami</code></pre>

<h3>Check permission</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev

kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n production</code></pre>

<h3>Inspect RBAC objects</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get role -n dev
kubectl get rolebinding -n dev

kubectl get clusterrole
kubectl get clusterrolebinding</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Interview approach:</strong>

First identify the user or ServiceAccount, then check the relevant
Role/ClusterRole and binding, verify the namespace and requested
verb/resource, and use <code>kubectl auth can-i</code> to confirm
the effective permission.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Scenario: Developer needs Pod logs</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Requirement:</strong>

Developer should be able to view Pods and logs in the
<code>dev</code> namespace.

They should not be able to delete workloads.

<br><br>

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Create a namespace-scoped Role containing only the required
read permissions and bind it to the developer.

</div>

<pre><code>rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources:
  - pods
  - pods/log
  verbs:
  - get
  - list
  - watch</code></pre>

<p>
Do not add <code>delete</code> unless the job actually requires it.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Real-Time Scenario: Application needs Kubernetes API</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A controller or application running inside Kubernetes needs to
read ConfigMaps.

Instead of using a highly privileged ServiceAccount, create a
dedicated ServiceAccount with a minimal Role and RoleBinding.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
Dedicated ServiceAccount
<br>
â†“
<br>
RoleBinding
<br>
â†“
<br>
Minimal Role
<br>
â†“
<br>
Read ConfigMaps

</div>

<div class="interview">

This is an example of the least-privilege principle.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Real-Time Scenario: Pod Compromised</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

An attacker compromises a web application Pod.

<br><br>

<strong>Security layers that reduce impact:</strong>

<br><br>

1. Run the container as non-root.<br>
2. Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities.<br>
3. Disable privilege escalation.<br>
4. Use a read-only root filesystem where possible.<br>
5. Give the ServiceAccount minimal RBAC permissions.<br>
6. Restrict network access with NetworkPolicies.<br>
7. Keep Secrets tightly controlled.<br>
8. Use trusted and scanned container images.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Key interview point:</strong>

Kubernetes security should be layered. No single control should be
treated as the complete security solution.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 21 -->

<div class="card">

<ol>

</ol>

</div>


<!-- FOLLOW UPS -->

<div class="card">

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "How Do You Secure Kubernetes?"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"I follow a layered security approach.

First, I use RBAC and the principle of least privilege so users and
workloads receive only the permissions they need.

For workloads, I use dedicated ServiceAccounts and avoid excessive
permissions such as cluster-admin.

At the container level, I prefer non-root execution, disable
unnecessary privilege escalation, drop unnecessary capabilities and
use a read-only root filesystem where practical.

I also use NetworkPolicies to restrict unnecessary Pod-to-Pod
communication and protect Secrets with RBAC and appropriate
encryption controls.

Finally, I use secure images, vulnerability scanning, Pod security
controls, monitoring and regular credential rotation.

The main goal is to reduce the attack surface and limit the blast
radius if a workload or credential is compromised."

</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Kubernetes</a>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>Storage</span></h1>

<p>
PV, PVC, StorageClass, dynamic provisioning, access modes,
StatefulSets, AWS storage examples, troubleshooting and
real-time DevOps interview scenarios.
</p>

<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Kubernetes Storage Architecture</h2>

<p>
Containers are generally treated as ephemeral. If a container is
deleted and recreated, data stored only inside the container's
writable layer may disappear.
</p>

<p>
Kubernetes provides persistent storage abstractions so application
data can survive Pod or container recreation.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Application Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>PersistentVolume (PV)</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Storage Backend</strong>
<br>
<br>
AWS EBS / EFS / Cloud Disk / SAN / NFS / etc.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A PostgreSQL database is running in Kubernetes.

If the Pod crashes and Kubernetes recreates it, the database data
must still exist.

The database uses a PVC backed by persistent storage rather than
depending only on the container filesystem.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Why do we need persistent storage?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Container filesystems are normally tied to the lifecycle of the
container. Kubernetes workloads can be restarted, recreated or
rescheduled onto another node.

Persistent storage separates important application data from the
temporary container lifecycle.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pod Created
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application writes data
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod Deleted
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Persistent Volume still contains data</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is a PersistentVolume (PV)?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>PersistentVolume</strong> is a Kubernetes storage resource
representing storage available to workloads.

A PV can be backed by infrastructure such as cloud block storage,
file storage, NFS or another supported storage implementation.

</div>

<h3>Basic PV example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: app-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi

  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

  hostPath:
    path: /data/app</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

<code>hostPath</code> is mainly useful for local/testing scenarios.
It is generally not the preferred production storage solution for
multi-node clusters.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>PersistentVolumeClaim</strong> is a request for storage
made by a workload.

The application normally asks for storage through a PVC instead of
directly managing the underlying storage infrastructure.

</div>

<h3>PVC example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Developer / Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>PVC</strong>
<br>
"I need 5Gi storage"
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>PV / Storage Provisioner</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Actual Storage

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. PV vs PVC</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>PV</th>
<th>PVC</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Represents available storage</td>
<td>Requests storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Cluster resource</td>
<td>Namespace-scoped resource</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually managed/provisioned by infrastructure or platform teams</td>
<td>Usually requested by application teams</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Describes capacity and storage properties</td>
<td>Describes requested capacity and access requirements</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"PV is the storage resource available to the cluster, while PVC is
the application's request for that storage. Pods normally consume
the PVC rather than directly referencing the underlying storage."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is StorageClass?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>StorageClass</strong> defines a class of storage and allows
Kubernetes to dynamically provision persistent volumes through a
storage provisioner.

</div>

<div class="flow">

PVC
<br>
â†“
<br>
StorageClass
<br>
â†“
<br>
Provisioner
<br>
â†“
<br>
Cloud / Storage Backend
<br>
â†“
<br>
PV
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-storage

provisioner: example.com/provisioner

reclaimPolicy: Delete

volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer</code></pre>

<p>
The exact <code>provisioner</code> depends on the cluster and storage
platform.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Static vs Dynamic Provisioning</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Static Provisioning</th>
<th>Dynamic Provisioning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>PV is created beforehand</td>
<td>Storage is provisioned when requested</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More manual management</td>
<td>More automated</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for specific pre-created storage</td>
<td>Common in cloud environments</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Dynamic flow</h3>

<pre><code>PVC
  â†“
StorageClass
  â†“
Provisioner
  â†“
Cloud Storage
  â†“
PV automatically created
  â†“
PVC Bound</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Dynamic provisioning is one of the most important concepts to
understand for managed Kubernetes platforms such as Amazon EKS.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Access Modes</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Mode</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ReadWriteOnce (RWO)</td>
<td>Volume can be mounted read-write by a single node at a time.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ReadOnlyMany (ROX)</td>
<td>Volume can be mounted read-only by many nodes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ReadWriteMany (RWX)</td>
<td>Volume can be mounted read-write by many nodes.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

Do not assume every storage backend supports every access mode.
Always verify what the underlying storage implementation supports.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. RWO vs RWX Real-Time Example</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario 1 â€” Database:</strong>

A PostgreSQL database usually uses block storage such as an EBS-like
volume and commonly needs single-node read/write attachment.

RWO is a common access pattern.

<br><br>

<strong>Scenario 2 â€” Shared application files:</strong>

Multiple application Pods running on different nodes need to read
and write the same shared filesystem.

A storage system supporting RWX, such as an appropriate network
filesystem, may be required.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Using PVC in a Pod</h2>

<h3>PVC</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi</code></pre>

<h3>Pod</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: storage-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx

    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-storage
      mountPath: /data

  volumes:
  - name: app-storage
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: app-pvc</code></pre>

<p>
The application writes data under <code>/data</code>, which is backed
by the PVC.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Storage Lifecycle</h2>

<div class="flow">

PVC Created
<br>
â†“
<br>
PVC Pending
<br>
â†“
<br>
Storage Provisioned / PV Selected
<br>
â†“
<br>
PVC Bound
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod Uses PVC
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod Restart / Reschedule
<br>
â†“
<br>
Data Persists

</div>

<h3>Check status</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pv
kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc app-pvc</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. PVC Pending</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A PVC remains in:

<pre><code>Pending</code></pre>

Possible reasons include:

<ul>
<li>No suitable PV exists for static provisioning.</li>
<li>Incorrect StorageClass.</li>
<li>No dynamic provisioner is available.</li>
<li>Requested access mode is unsupported.</li>
<li>Requested capacity cannot be satisfied.</li>
<li>Storage backend/provisioner has an error.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<h3>Troubleshooting</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc app-pvc

kubectl get pv
kubectl get storageclass

kubectl describe storageclass &lt;storage-class&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Reclaim Policy</h2>

<div class="answer">

The PV reclaim policy determines what Kubernetes should do with the
underlying volume after the PVC is deleted.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Policy</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Retain</td>
<td>Keep the PV/storage so data can be preserved and handled manually.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Delete</td>
<td>Delete the volume according to the provisioner's behavior.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Recycle</td>
<td>Legacy behavior and generally not used for modern Kubernetes storage.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

For important production data, understand the reclaim policy before
deleting PVCs. A Delete policy can result in deletion of the
underlying dynamically provisioned storage.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Retain vs Delete</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Production database:</strong>

If accidental PVC deletion must not immediately destroy the data,
a Retain strategy may be appropriate depending on the organization's
backup and recovery design.

<br><br>

<strong>Temporary application environment:</strong>

For disposable environments, Delete may be appropriate so that
temporary storage is automatically cleaned up.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. What is volumeBindingMode?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>volumeBindingMode</code> controls when volume binding and dynamic
provisioning occur.

Two important modes are:

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Immediate</th>
<th>WaitForFirstConsumer</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provision/bind as soon as PVC is created.</td>
<td>Delay provisioning/binding until a Pod using the PVC is created.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<code>WaitForFirstConsumer</code> can help the scheduler choose a
storage location compatible with the Pod's placement and storage
topology.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. emptyDir vs PVC</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>emptyDir</th>
<th>PVC</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Temporary Pod storage</td>
<td>Persistent storage abstraction</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Deleted when Pod is removed from the node</td>
<td>Can survive Pod recreation according to storage lifecycle</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for temporary files/cache</td>
<td>Useful for databases and persistent application data</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>emptyDir example</h3>

<pre><code>volumes:
- name: temp-storage
  emptyDir: {}

containers:
- name: app
  image: nginx
  volumeMounts:
  - name: temp-storage
    mountPath: /tmp/app</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. StatefulSet + Persistent Storage</h2>

<div class="answer">

StatefulSets are commonly used for stateful applications that need
stable identities and persistent storage.

A StatefulSet can use <code>volumeClaimTemplates</code> to create a
PVC for each Pod.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: database
spec:
  serviceName: database
  replicas: 2

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: database

    spec:
      containers:
      - name: database
        image: postgres:16

        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data

  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data

    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce

      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

StatefulSet
<br>
â†“
<br>
database-0 â†’ PVC data-database-0
<br>
database-1 â†’ PVC data-database-1

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Why StatefulSet instead of Deployment for databases?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A StatefulSet provides stable Pod identities, stable network identity
when configured with the appropriate Service, and supports
per-Pod persistent storage patterns.

A Deployment is designed primarily for interchangeable replicas.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

For a database cluster, each member may need its own persistent
data volume.

A StatefulSet can provide:

<br><br>

database-0 â†’ its own PVC

<br>

database-1 â†’ its own PVC

<br>

database-2 â†’ its own PVC

</div>

<div class="warning">

A StatefulSet alone does not make a database highly available.
The database itself must support replication, failover and recovery,
and the storage/backup architecture must be designed appropriately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. AWS EBS vs EFS in Kubernetes</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>AWS EBS</th>
<th>AWS EFS</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Block storage</td>
<td>Managed network file system</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly associated with RWO workloads</td>
<td>Commonly suitable for shared filesystem access such as RWX patterns</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for many database/block-storage workloads</td>
<td>Useful when multiple Pods/nodes need shared file access</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>EKS example:</strong>

A database Pod needs block storage â†’ EBS-backed storage class.

Multiple application Pods need shared files across nodes â†’
EFS-backed storage class, assuming the appropriate CSI driver and
access mode support.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. CSI Driver</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>CSI</strong> stands for Container Storage Interface.

CSI provides a standard mechanism for Kubernetes to communicate
with storage systems.

Cloud platforms commonly provide CSI drivers for their storage
services.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes
<br>
â†“
<br>
CSI Driver
<br>
â†“
<br>
Cloud Storage
<br>
<br>
Example:
<br>
EKS â†’ EBS CSI / EFS CSI
</div>

<div class="interview">

The CSI driver is an important part of modern Kubernetes storage,
especially in managed clusters such as EKS.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 20. Static PV Example</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: manual-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi

  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce

  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain

  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data</code></pre>

<h3>Claim</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: manual-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi</code></pre>

<p>
The PVC may bind to a suitable available PV.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. StorageClass + PVC Dynamic Provisioning</h2>

<h3>StorageClass</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-storage

provisioner: example.com/csi

volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer

reclaimPolicy: Delete</code></pre>

<h3>PVC</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: dynamic-pvc

spec:
  storageClassName: fast-storage

  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce

  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

PVC
<br>
â†“
<br>
StorageClass
<br>
â†“
<br>
CSI Provisioner
<br>
â†“
<br>
20Gi Storage Created
<br>
â†“
<br>
PV
<br>
â†“
<br>
PVC Bound

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Default StorageClass</h2>

<div class="answer">

A cluster can have a default StorageClass.

If a PVC does not specify <code>storageClassName</code>, Kubernetes
can use the default StorageClass for dynamic provisioning when the
cluster is configured accordingly.

</div>

<h3>Check StorageClasses</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get storageclass

kubectl get sc</code></pre>

<h3>Inspect</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl describe storageclass &lt;name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

When troubleshooting a PVC stuck in Pending, checking whether the
cluster has an appropriate default StorageClass is one of the first
things to verify.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. PVC is Bound but Pod cannot start</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

PVC shows:

<pre><code>Bound</code></pre>

But the Pod remains Pending or fails during volume attachment/mount.

Possible reasons include:

<ul>
<li>Node does not satisfy storage topology.</li>
<li>CSI driver issue.</li>
<li>Volume attachment failure.</li>
<li>Mount permission problem.</li>
<li>Underlying storage unavailable.</li>
<li>Access mode or attachment limitation.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl describe pvc &lt;pvc-name&gt;

kubectl get pv

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Real-Time Scenario: Pod deleted</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A database Pod is deleted accidentally.

Kubernetes creates a replacement Pod.

If the database uses a correctly configured persistent volume,
the new Pod can mount the existing storage and continue using the
persisted data.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Old Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deleted
<br>
â†“
<br>
PVC remains
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
Same Persistent Storage
<br>
â†“
<br>
Data Available

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Real-Time Scenario: Pod moves to another node</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A node fails and Kubernetes schedules the workload onto another
eligible node.

Whether the persistent volume can be attached to the new node
depends on the storage backend, access mode, topology and CSI
implementation.

</div>

<div class="interview">

Do not simply say "the volume works on any node."

Storage attachment and topology rules matter, especially with
single-node-attached block storage.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Database Production Storage Strategy</h2>

<div class="scenario">

For a production database in Kubernetes, I would consider:

<br><br>

â€¢ Persistent storage through PVCs<br>
â€¢ Appropriate StorageClass<br>
â€¢ Correct access mode<br>
â€¢ StatefulSet when appropriate<br>
â€¢ Storage encryption<br>
â€¢ Regular backups<br>
â€¢ Snapshot strategy where supported<br>
â€¢ Monitoring<br>
â€¢ Tested restore procedures<br>
â€¢ Reclaim policy<br>
â€¢ Capacity planning

</div>

<div class="warning">

Persistent storage is not the same as backup.

A persistent volume can still be lost because of infrastructure,
operator error, corruption or deletion.

Backups and tested restoration are essential for important data.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Backup vs Persistent Storage</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Persistent Storage</th>
<th>Backup</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Keeps application data available across Pod lifecycle changes.</td>
<td>Provides a recoverable copy of data.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Supports normal application operation.</td>
<td>Used for disaster recovery and accidental deletion.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Not automatically a backup.</td>
<td>Should be stored according to recovery requirements.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

If an interviewer asks "Does PVC provide backup?", the answer is:

<strong>No.</strong> PVC provides persistent storage, not a complete
backup and disaster-recovery solution.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 28. Storage Security</h2>

<ul>
<li>Encrypt storage where supported.</li>
<li>Restrict access through RBAC.</li>
<li>Use appropriate filesystem permissions.</li>
<li>Protect sensitive data with application-level encryption where required.</li>
<li>Use secure StorageClasses and CSI drivers.</li>
<li>Monitor storage access and failures.</li>
<li>Use backups and tested recovery procedures.</li>
<li>Do not expose database storage unnecessarily.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<!-- ONE MINUTE ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Kubernetes Storage"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes Pods are generally ephemeral, so for applications that
need persistent data I use PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims.

A PersistentVolume represents available storage, while a PVC is the
application's request for storage.

For dynamic provisioning, I use a StorageClass. The PVC references
the StorageClass, and the provisioner creates the appropriate
persistent volume.

Access modes such as ReadWriteOnce and ReadWriteMany determine how
the storage can be mounted, depending on what the storage backend
supports.

For stateful applications such as databases, I can use StatefulSets
with volumeClaimTemplates so each Pod can have its own persistent
storage.

In AWS EKS, I would commonly consider EBS for block-storage workloads
and EFS for shared filesystem use cases, using the appropriate CSI
drivers.

Finally, I would configure reclaim policies carefully, monitor
storage, encrypt sensitive data, and maintain backups because
persistent storage itself is not a backup."

</div>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>Troubleshooting & Real-Time Scenarios</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused troubleshooting guide covering Pod failures,
CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending Pods, Services,

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Kubernetes Troubleshooting Mindset</h2>

<p>
In production, do not randomly change Kubernetes resources.
Troubleshoot from the outside toward the application and identify
the exact failing layer.
</p>

<div class="flow">

<strong>1. Check Status</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>2. Describe Resource</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>3. Check Events</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>4. Check Logs</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>5. Check Dependencies</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>6. Fix Root Cause</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>7. Verify Recovery</strong>

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Golden interview line:</strong>

"I first identify which Kubernetes layer is failing, then I use
status, describe, events and logs to narrow down the root cause
before making a change."

</div>

</div>


<!-- BASIC FLOW -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. First Commands to Run</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods -o wide

kubectl get svc
kubectl get deployments

kubectl get nodes

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

<p>
These commands provide the initial health picture of the cluster
and workload.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Describe the Problem Resource</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;

kubectl describe service &lt;service-name&gt;

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The <code>describe</code> output is especially useful for conditions,
events, scheduling failures, mounts, probes and other Kubernetes
control-plane information.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Check Pod Logs</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; -c &lt;container-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl logs -f &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If a container crashed and restarted, use:

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous</code></pre>

This is often critical for finding the error from the previous
container instance.

</div>

</div>


<!-- POD STATES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Pod is Pending</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Pending Pod has not successfully reached the running state.
Common causes include insufficient resources, scheduling
constraints, taints, node availability or volume-related issues.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Pod requests:

<pre><code>cpu: 4
memory: 8Gi</code></pre>

But available nodes cannot satisfy the request.

The scheduler cannot place the Pod, so it remains Pending.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

CrashLoopBackOff means the container repeatedly starts, crashes and
Kubernetes backs off before restarting it again.

It is a symptom, not the root cause.

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Application startup failure</li>
<li>Wrong environment variable</li>
<li>Missing Secret</li>
<li>Missing ConfigMap</li>
<li>Wrong command/entrypoint</li>
<li>Database connection failure</li>
<li>Probe configuration problem</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes cannot pull the requested container image.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -o yaml</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<ul>
<li>Image name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Registry availability</li>
<li>ImagePullSecrets</li>
<li>Registry credentials</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
</ul>

Example:

<pre><code>image: myregistry/payment:v5</code></pre>

If tag <code>v5</code> does not exist, the Pod cannot pull it.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Pod stuck in ContainerCreating</h2>

<div class="answer">

ContainerCreating indicates Kubernetes is still preparing the
container. The exact cause is shown through Pod events and
description.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Common causes:

<ul>
<li>Volume mount problems</li>
<li>Secret or ConfigMap mount issues</li>
<li>Container runtime problems</li>
<li>Network setup problems</li>
<li>Image pulling</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 8. Pod is Running but application is not working</h2>

<div class="answer">

Running only means the container process is running. It does not
guarantee that the application is healthy or reachable.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pod Running
<br>
â‰ 
<br>
Application Healthy

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get ingress</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- DEPLOYMENTS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Deployment rollout is stuck</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get deployment

kubectl rollout status deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;

kubectl rollout history deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;

kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Check whether new Pods are failing because of:

<ul>
<li>Bad image</li>
<li>Failed probes</li>
<li>Insufficient resources</li>
<li>Configuration errors</li>
<li>Scheduling problems</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Rollback a failed Deployment</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout history deployment myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment myapp

kubectl rollout status deployment myapp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time scenario:</strong>

A new application version is deployed and starts returning errors.

If the previous version was healthy:

<pre><code>kubectl rollout undo deployment myapp</code></pre>

Then investigate the new version separately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SERVICE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Service not reaching Pods</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Service selects Pods using labels.

If the selector does not match Pod labels, the Service can have no
backend endpoints.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get svc myapp-service -o yaml

kubectl get pods --show-labels

kubectl get endpoints myapp-service</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Service selector:

<pre><code>selector:
  app: frontend</code></pre>

Pod label:

<pre><code>labels:
  app: backend</code></pre>

No match â†’ no endpoints.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Service has no endpoints</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get endpoints &lt;service-name&gt;

kubectl get endpointslices

kubectl get pods --show-labels

kubectl describe service &lt;service-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

If the Service has no endpoints, verify the selector, Pod labels,
Pod readiness and namespace.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Service connection refused</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check the complete path:

<pre><code>Client
 â†“
Service
 â†“
TargetPort
 â†“
ContainerPort
 â†“
Application Process</code></pre>

Verify:

<pre><code>kubectl get svc &lt;service-name&gt; -o yaml

kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -o yaml

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

A common mistake is configuring the Service
<code>targetPort</code> differently from the port where the
application is actually listening.

</div>

</div>


<!-- NETWORKING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Kubernetes DNS troubleshooting</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get svc

kubectl get pods -n kube-system

kubectl exec -it &lt;pod-name&gt; -- nslookup &lt;service-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If:

<pre><code>backend-service</code></pre>

is in the same namespace, the application can normally resolve it
using the Service DNS name.

For cross-namespace communication:

<pre><code>backend-service.backend.svc.cluster.local</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Pod-to-Pod communication fails</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods -o wide

kubectl exec -it &lt;pod-name&gt; -- ping &lt;pod-ip&gt;

kubectl exec -it &lt;pod-name&gt; -- curl http://&lt;service-name&gt;:&lt;port&gt;</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>
<li>Pod IPs</li>
<li>Services</li>
<li>NetworkPolicies</li>
<li>DNS</li>
<li>Container ports</li>
<li>Application listening address</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 16. NetworkPolicy blocking traffic</h2>

<div class="answer">

NetworkPolicies can restrict which Pods are allowed to communicate
with other Pods.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get networkpolicy

kubectl describe networkpolicy &lt;policy-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

When troubleshooting networking, do not forget NetworkPolicies.
A Pod and Service can appear healthy while traffic is intentionally
blocked by policy.

</div>

</div>


<!-- CONFIG -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. ConfigMap not found</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get configmap -n &lt;namespace&gt;

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get configmap &lt;configmap-name&gt; -n &lt;namespace&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

ConfigMaps are namespace-scoped. Verify the name and namespace.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Secret not found</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get secrets -n &lt;namespace&gt;

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get secret &lt;secret-name&gt; -n &lt;namespace&gt;</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>
<li>Secret name</li>
<li>Namespace</li>
<li>Referenced key</li>
<li>Workload configuration</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- PROBES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Liveness Probe failure</h2>

<div class="answer">

A liveness probe determines whether the container is still alive.
Repeated liveness failure can cause Kubernetes to restart the
container.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Look for events such as probe failures.

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Application starts slowly but liveness probe checks too early.

The container may repeatedly restart even though the application
would eventually become healthy.

Use appropriate startup/readiness/liveness probe configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Readiness Probe failure</h2>

<div class="answer">

Readiness determines whether the Pod should receive traffic.

A failed readiness probe normally removes the Pod from Service
endpoints while allowing the container to continue running.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Readiness Failure
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod remains running
<br>
â†“
<br>
Removed from Service traffic
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application recovers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Traffic resumes

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 21. Startup Probe</h2>

<div class="answer">

Startup probes are useful for slow-starting applications.

They give the application time to start before liveness/readiness
checks become active according to the configured probe behavior.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Examples include:

<ul>
<li>Large Java applications</li>
<li>Applications with long initialization</li>
<li>Services that load large models or configuration</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- RESOURCES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. OOMKilled</h2>

<div class="answer">

OOMKilled means the container was terminated because it exceeded an
available memory limit or otherwise encountered memory pressure
leading to an out-of-memory termination.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -o yaml

kubectl top pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If a container has:

<pre><code>resources:
  limits:
    memory: 256Mi</code></pre>

and the application needs significantly more memory, it may be
terminated.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. CPU throttling / high CPU</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl top pods

kubectl top nodes

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>
<li>CPU requests</li>
<li>CPU limits</li>
<li>Application behavior</li>
<li>Traffic increase</li>
<li>Autoscaling</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Node NotReady</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get nodes

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

Possible causes:

<ul>
<li>Kubelet failure</li>
<li>Node resource pressure</li>
<li>Network problems</li>
<li>Disk pressure</li>
<li>Container runtime issues</li>
<li>Cloud infrastructure failure</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Node memory or disk pressure</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;</code></pre>

Look for conditions such as:

<pre><code>MemoryPressure
DiskPressure
PIDPressure
Ready</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If a node has insufficient disk space, image pulls, container
creation or other workloads may start failing.

Investigate node-level disk usage and container runtime storage.

</div>

</div>


<!-- STORAGE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. PVC stuck in Pending</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get pvc

kubectl describe pvc &lt;pvc-name&gt;

kubectl get storageclass

kubectl get pv</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Check whether the requested StorageClass exists and whether a
suitable volume can be dynamically provisioned.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Pod cannot mount volume</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl describe pvc &lt;pvc-name&gt;

kubectl get pv

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp</code></pre>

Common causes:

<ul>
<li>PVC not bound</li>
<li>Wrong volume name</li>
<li>StorageClass issue</li>
<li>Access mode mismatch</li>
<li>CSI driver problem</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- RBAC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Forbidden error</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

<pre><code>Error from server (Forbidden)</code></pre>

This commonly indicates an RBAC authorization problem.

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl auth can-i get pods

kubectl auth can-i create deployments

kubectl get role
kubectl get rolebinding

kubectl get clusterrole
kubectl get clusterrolebinding</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

The key question is:

<strong>"Does this identity have permission to perform this action
on this resource in this namespace?"</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- INGRESS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Ingress returns 404 / 502</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get ingress

kubectl describe ingress &lt;ingress-name&gt;

kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get pods</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>404:</strong>

Often check host/path/routing configuration.

<br><br>

<strong>502/503:</strong>

Often check backend Service, endpoints, application port and Pod
health.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DNS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 30. CoreDNS troubleshooting</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods -n kube-system

kubectl get svc -n kube-system

kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If applications cannot resolve Service names, investigate CoreDNS
Pods, Service configuration and network connectivity.

</div>

</div>


<!-- EVENTS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Why are Kubernetes Events important?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Events often provide the fastest clue about scheduling, image pulls,
mount failures, probe failures and other resource-level problems.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

When troubleshooting, I usually check Events alongside logs because
Events describe what Kubernetes itself observed while logs show what
the application process reported.

</div>

</div>


<!-- REAL TIME SCENARIOS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Scenario â€” Website is completely down</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Start from the outside and move inward:

<pre><code>DNS
 â†“
Load Balancer
 â†“
Ingress
 â†“
Service
 â†“
Endpoints
 â†“
Pods
 â†“
Application
 â†“
Database</code></pre>

Commands:

<pre><code>kubectl get ingress
kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpoints
kubectl get pods
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Do not immediately restart everything.

Identify the first broken layer.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Scenario â€” Pods are running but users get errors</h2>

<div class="answer">

Running Pods do not necessarily mean healthy applications.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods
kubectl get endpoints
kubectl get svc
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>
<li>Readiness</li>
<li>Application logs</li>
<li>Service routing</li>
<li>Backend dependencies</li>
<li>Database connectivity</li>
<li>Ingress</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Scenario â€” New deployment caused outage</h2>

<div class="scenario">

First stabilize the service.

<pre><code>kubectl rollout status deployment myapp

kubectl rollout history deployment myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment myapp</code></pre>

After recovery:

<ul>
<li>Inspect application logs.</li>
<li>Compare old and new configuration.</li>
<li>Check image version.</li>
<li>Check probes.</li>
<li>Check resource changes.</li>
<li>Reproduce the issue safely.</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 35. Scenario â€” Application cannot connect to database</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get secret

kubectl get configmap</code></pre>

Then verify:

<ul>
<li>Database Service name</li>
<li>DNS resolution</li>
<li>Database port</li>
<li>Credentials</li>
<li>NetworkPolicy</li>
<li>Database availability</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 36. Scenario â€” High restart count</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous</code></pre>

Possible causes:

<ul>
<li>CrashLoopBackOff</li>
<li>OOMKilled</li>
<li>Liveness probe failure</li>
<li>Application crash</li>
<li>Dependency failure</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 37. Scenario â€” Pod cannot schedule</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get nodes

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>
<li>CPU/memory availability</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations</li>
<li>Node selectors</li>
<li>Affinity/anti-affinity</li>
<li>Pod resource requests</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SYSTEMATIC PROCESS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 38. Production Troubleshooting Method</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>STEP 1</strong>
<br>
Identify symptom

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 2</strong>
<br>
Check resource status

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 3</strong>
<br>
Describe resource

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 4</strong>
<br>
Check Events

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 5</strong>
<br>
Check application logs

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 6</strong>
<br>
Check dependencies

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 7</strong>
<br>
Apply minimal safe fix

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 8</strong>
<br>
Verify health

<br><br>â†“

<strong>STEP 9</strong>
<br>
Document root cause

</div>

</div>


<!-- COMMAND CHEAT SHEET -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Kubernetes Troubleshooting Command Cheat Sheet</h2>

<pre><code># Cluster
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;

# Pods
kubectl get pods
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; -c &lt;container-name&gt;

# Deployments
kubectl get deployments
kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;
kubectl rollout status deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;
kubectl rollout history deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;
kubectl rollout undo deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;

# Services
kubectl get svc
kubectl describe svc &lt;service-name&gt;
kubectl get endpoints
kubectl get endpointslices

# Config
kubectl get configmaps
kubectl get secrets

# Storage
kubectl get pv
kubectl get pvc
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl describe pvc &lt;pvc-name&gt;

# Resources
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods

# RBAC
kubectl auth can-i get pods
kubectl auth can-i create deployments

# Networking
kubectl get networkpolicy
kubectl get ingress
kubectl get ingressclass

# Events
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

# Debug
kubectl exec -it &lt;pod-name&gt; -- sh</code></pre>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "How do you troubleshoot Kubernetes?"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"I follow a systematic approach rather than randomly changing
resources.

First, I identify the affected resource and check its status using
kubectl get. Then I use kubectl describe to inspect conditions and
Events. For application-level problems, I check container logs and
previous logs if the container restarted.

If the problem involves networking, I check Services, endpoints,
DNS, NetworkPolicies and Ingress. For scheduling issues, I check
nodes, resource requests, taints, tolerations and affinity. For
storage problems, I check PVs, PVCs and StorageClasses.

For deployment failures, I check rollout status and history and,
if necessary, rollback to the last known healthy version.

Finally, I verify that the application is healthy and document the
root cause and preventive action.

My goal is not just to restart the Pod, but to identify and fix the
actual root cause."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸš€ 60-Second Revision</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Pending</strong>
â†’ Scheduling / resources / constraints

<br><br>

<strong>CrashLoopBackOff</strong>
â†’ Container repeatedly crashing

<br><br>

<strong>ImagePullBackOff</strong>
â†’ Image cannot be pulled

<br><br>

<strong>OOMKilled</strong>
â†’ Memory-related termination

<br><br>

<strong>No Endpoints</strong>
â†’ Selector / labels / readiness

<br><br>

<strong>Readiness Failure</strong>
â†’ Pod removed from traffic

<br><br>

<strong>Liveness Failure</strong>
â†’ Container may be restarted

<br><br>

<strong>PVC Pending</strong>
â†’ Storage provisioning/binding issue

<br><br>

<strong>Forbidden</strong>
â†’ RBAC authorization issue

<br><br>

<strong>Node NotReady</strong>
â†’ Investigate kubelet/node health

<br><br>

<strong>Golden Flow</strong>
â†’ get â†’ describe â†’ events â†’ logs â†’ dependencies â†’ fix â†’ verify

</div>

</div>

</main>

DaemonSets, HPA, RBAC and production Kubernetes.
</p>

<div class="flow">

<div class="tip">

<strong>Interview Strategy:</strong>

Do not memorize Kubernetes definitions only.

For every Kubernetes concept, understand:

<strong>What is it?</strong> â†’ <strong>Why is it needed?</strong>

<!-- SECTION 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Kubernetes?</h2>

<h3>Q. What is Kubernetes?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform used
to deploy, manage, scale and maintain containerized applications
across a cluster of machines.

</div>

<h3>Why do we need Kubernetes?</h3>

<p>
Running one or two Docker containers manually is simple. But in a
production environment we may have hundreds of containers running
across multiple servers.
</p>

<p>
We need automation for scheduling, scaling, service discovery,
self-healing, rolling updates, configuration management and
resource management.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Problem</th>
<th>Kubernetes Solution</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container crashes</td>
<td>Self-healing / container restart</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Server has limited capacity</td>
<td>Schedule workloads across nodes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Need more application instances</td>
<td>Scale replicas</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Application IP keeps changing</td>
<td>Service provides stable networking</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Need application update without downtime</td>
<td>Rolling updates</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Need to manage hundreds of containers</td>
<td>Container orchestration</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Suppose an e-commerce application runs as 10 container replicas.

If one container crashes, Kubernetes can replace it.

If traffic increases from 10,000 requests/minute to 50,000 requests/minute,
the application can be scaled from 10 Pods to more replicas.

If a node becomes unavailable, Kubernetes can reschedule workloads
on available nodes depending on the workload configuration and
cluster capacity.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform.
It automates deployment, scaling, networking and management of
containerized applications. In production, it helps us maintain
application availability through mechanisms such as self-healing,
replica management, service discovery and rolling deployments."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why Kubernetes when we already have Docker?</h2>

<h3>Q. Is Kubernetes a replacement for Docker?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes and Docker solve different problems.

Docker is primarily used to build, package and run containers.
Kubernetes is used to orchestrate and manage containerized workloads
across a cluster.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Docker</th>
<th>Kubernetes</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build container images</td>
<td>Manage containerized workloads</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Run individual containers</td>
<td>Manage workloads across multiple nodes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container runtime / tooling ecosystem</td>
<td>Container orchestration platform</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Dockerfile</td>
<td>Pod / Deployment / Service YAML</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>docker run</td>
<td>kubectl apply</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

A company has 50 microservices. Running each container manually
would be difficult.

Kubernetes can schedule these workloads across worker nodes,
restart failed workloads, expose services and scale applications.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not say:

" Kubernetes is used to create Docker containers."

A better answer is:

"Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Kubernetes Cluster</h2>

<h3>Q. What is a Kubernetes cluster?</h3>

<div class="answer">

A Kubernetes cluster is a group of machines that work together to
run containerized workloads. It consists conceptually of a
<strong>control plane</strong> and one or more <strong>worker nodes</strong>.

</div>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Kubernetes Cluster</strong>

<br><br>

â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”
<br>
<strong>Control Plane</strong>
<br>
API Server | Scheduler | Controllers | etcd
<br>
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜

<br><br>

â†“

<br><br>

â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”
<br>
<strong>Worker Nodes</strong>
<br>
Kubelet | Container Runtime | kube-proxy
<br>
Pods
<br>
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜

</div>

<h3>Two major parts</h3>

<ol>

<li>
<strong>Control Plane</strong> â€” manages cluster state and makes
control decisions.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Worker Nodes</strong> â€” run application workloads.
</li>

</ol>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Control Plane Components</h2>

<h3>Important components</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kube-apiserver</td>
<td>Central API endpoint through which Kubernetes API operations are handled.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>etcd</td>
<td>Distributed key-value store containing Kubernetes cluster state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kube-scheduler</td>
<td>Selects suitable nodes for newly created Pods.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kube-controller-manager</td>
<td>Runs controllers that continuously work to make actual state match desired state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>cloud-controller-manager</td>
<td>Integrates Kubernetes with cloud-provider functionality where applicable.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Simple architecture</h3>

<div class="flow">

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>
