<br>
â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"The control plane manages the Kubernetes cluster. The API server
provides the Kubernetes API, etcd stores cluster state, the scheduler
selects nodes for Pods, and controller components continuously work
to maintain the desired state."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is kube-apiserver?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The kube-apiserver is the central API component of Kubernetes.
It exposes the Kubernetes API and acts as the main entry point for
cluster management operations.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<p>
When you execute:
</p>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods</code></pre>

<p>
kubectl communicates with the Kubernetes API server.
The API server processes the request and returns the relevant
cluster information.
</p>

<div class="flow">

kubectl
<br>
â†“
<br>
API Server
<br>
â†“
<br>
Cluster Data / Components
<br>
â†“
<br>
Response

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

A DevOps engineer wants to inspect application Pods in production.

Instead of directly connecting to every worker node, the engineer
uses kubectl to communicate with the Kubernetes API.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is etcd?</h2>

<div class="answer">

etcd is a distributed key-value store used by Kubernetes to store
important cluster state and configuration data.

</div>

<h3>What kind of information?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Cluster configuration</li>
<li>Object metadata</li>
<li>Desired state information</li>
<li>Resource definitions</li>
<li>Other Kubernetes control-plane state</li>

</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

If you create a Deployment with 3 replicas, Kubernetes needs to
know the desired state.

The cluster's state information is persisted through the Kubernetes
control plane, with etcd serving as the backing store for that state.

</div>

<div class="warning">

etcd is critical infrastructure.

In production clusters, etcd backup and recovery are important
because loss of the required cluster state can affect the ability
to recover the control plane.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is kube-scheduler?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The kube-scheduler watches for Pods that do not yet have a node
assigned and selects an appropriate worker node for them.

</div>

<h3>What does it consider?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Available resources</li>
<li>CPU and memory requirements</li>
<li>Node constraints</li>
<li>Affinity / anti-affinity</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations</li>
<li>Other scheduling rules</li>

</ul>

<div class="flow">

Pod Created
<br>
â†“
<br>
API Server
<br>
â†“
<br>
Scheduler
<br>
â†“
<br>
Select Suitable Node
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod Gets Scheduled
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubelet Runs Pod

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Suppose Node A has only 200 MB memory available while Node B has
8 GB available.

If a Pod requires significant memory, Kubernetes scheduling logic
may select an appropriate node based on resource requirements and
other scheduling constraints.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is kube-controller-manager?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The controller manager runs controllers that continuously compare
the desired state with the current state and take actions to move
the cluster toward the desired state.

</div>

<h3>Desired State vs Actual State</h3>

<div class="flow">

Desired State
<br>
"3 Pods should run"
<br>
â†“
<br>
Controller observes cluster
<br>
â†“
<br>
Actual State = 2 Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Controller takes action
<br>
â†“
<br>
3 Pods running

</div>

<div class="scenario">

You define:

<pre><code>replicas: 3</code></pre>

If one Pod disappears, the relevant controller detects that the
actual state no longer matches the desired state and works toward
restoring the required number of replicas.

</div>

<div class="tip">

This is one of the most important Kubernetes concepts:

<strong>Kubernetes is declarative and continuously works toward the
desired state.</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Worker Node</h2>

<h3>Q. What is a worker node?</h3>

<div class="answer">

A worker node is a machine in the Kubernetes cluster where
application workloads, usually in the form of Pods, run.

</div>

<h3>Important node components</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Kubelet</td>
<td>Agent running on the node that communicates with the API server and manages Pods assigned to the node.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container Runtime</td>
<td>Runs containers for Pods.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kube-proxy</td>
<td>Provides node-level networking functionality for Kubernetes Services according to the cluster's networking implementation.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Worker Node
<br><br>

Kubelet
<br>
Container Runtime
<br>
kube-proxy
<br>
CNI / Networking
<br><br>
â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What is kubelet?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubelet is the primary node agent. It runs on every worker node
and ensures that Pods assigned to that node are running and healthy
according to their specifications.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

The scheduler assigns a Pod to Node-1.

The kubelet on Node-1 receives the Pod specification through the
Kubernetes control plane and works with the container runtime to
ensure the required containers are running.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Kubelet is the Kubernetes node agent. It runs on each worker node,
communicates with the control plane and ensures that the containers
specified for Pods assigned to that node are running."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is a Container Runtime?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A container runtime is the software responsible for running
containers on a Kubernetes node.

Modern Kubernetes uses the CRI (Container Runtime Interface) to
communicate with supported container runtimes.

</div>

<h3>Important point</h3>

<p>
Docker Engine is not the required Kubernetes runtime itself.
Kubernetes can use CRI-compatible runtimes such as
<strong>containerd</strong> and <strong>CRI-O</strong>.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Interview trap:</strong>

Do not simply say:

"Kubernetes uses Docker to run containers."

A better answer is:

"Kubernetes uses a CRI-compatible container runtime such as
containerd or CRI-O to run containers."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is a Pod?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Pod is the smallest deployable and schedulable unit in Kubernetes.
A Pod contains one or more containers that share networking and can
share storage.

</div>

<h3>Why doesn't Kubernetes directly manage individual containers?</h3>

<p>
Kubernetes uses the Pod as its basic workload unit. A Pod provides
the context in which one or more tightly coupled containers run.
</p>

<h3>Most common pattern</h3>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Container

</div>

<h3>Multi-container Pod</h3>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Application Container
<br>
â””â”€â”€ Sidecar Container

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A Java application runs in one container.

A sidecar container may collect or process data closely associated
with that application.

Both containers are part of the same Pod and can communicate over
the Pod's network namespace.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

"A Pod is the smallest deployable and schedulable unit in Kubernetes.
It can contain one or more tightly coupled containers. Containers in
the same Pod share the Pod network namespace and can share volumes.
Normally we run one main application container per Pod and use
multiple containers when they need to work closely together."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Pod Networking</h2>

<h3>Important concept</h3>

<p>
Containers inside the same Pod share the Pod network namespace.
They can communicate with each other using <code>localhost</code>
and different ports.
</p>

<pre><code>Pod IP: 10.244.1.15

Container A â†’ localhost:8080
Container B â†’ localhost:9000</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Containers in the same Pod do not normally receive separate Pod IPs.
The Pod has the network identity.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Pod Lifecycle</h2>

<h3>Common Pod phases</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Phase</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pending</td>
<td>Pod has been accepted but one or more containers are not yet running.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Running</td>
<td>Pod has been scheduled and at least one container is running or starting.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Succeeded</td>
<td>All containers terminated successfully.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Failed</td>
<td>All containers terminated and at least one failed.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Unknown</td>
<td>Pod state could not be obtained, usually due to communication issues.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Useful command</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Pod vs Container</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Pod</th>
<th>Container</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Kubernetes workload unit</td>
<td>Application execution unit</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can contain one or more containers</td>
<td>Runs application process</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Has network identity</td>
<td>Shares Pod networking when inside a Pod</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed by Kubernetes</td>
<td>Run by container runtime</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Desired State vs Actual State</h2>

<h3>Q. What is desired state?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Desired state is the state that we declare we want Kubernetes to
maintain.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>replicas: 3</code></pre>

<p>
This tells Kubernetes that the workload should have three replicas.
</p>

<h3>Actual state</h3>

<p>
The actual state is what is currently running in the cluster.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Desired State
<br>
3 replicas
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Controllers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Actual State
<br>
3 replicas

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If one Pod crashes:

<br><br>

Desired = 3

<br>

Actual = 2

<br>

Kubernetes works toward restoring:

<br>

Actual = 3

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Very important interview statement:</strong>

"Kubernetes continuously reconciles the actual state with the
desired state."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Declarative vs Imperative Approach</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Declarative</th>
<th>Imperative</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Describe desired state</td>
<td>Tell Kubernetes specific commands/actions</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually YAML manifests</td>
<td>Often kubectl commands</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for version control and GitOps</td>
<td>Useful for quick operational tasks</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Declarative example</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml</code></pre>

<h3>Imperative example</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx</code></pre>

<div class="tip">

For production and GitOps, declarative configuration is especially
important because Kubernetes manifests can be version controlled
and reviewed through Git.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Kubernetes YAML Basics</h2>

<h3>Common fields</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion:
kind:
metadata:
spec:</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Field</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>apiVersion</td>
<td>API version used by the resource definition.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kind</td>
<td>Type of Kubernetes object.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>metadata</td>
<td>Name, namespace, labels and other identifying information.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>spec</td>
<td>Desired configuration of the object.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Example Pod YAML</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod

metadata:
  name: nginx-pod

spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:latest
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Most Kubernetes manifests describe the API version, resource kind,
metadata and desired specification. The spec is where we define
what we want Kubernetes to maintain."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Kubernetes Object</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Kubernetes object is a persistent representation of a resource
that describes the desired state of part of the cluster.

</div>

<h3>Common objects</h3>

<div>

<span class="badge">Pod</span>
<span class="badge">Deployment</span>
<span class="badge">Service</span>
<span class="badge">ConfigMap</span>
<span class="badge">Secret</span>
<span class="badge">Namespace</span>
<span class="badge">StatefulSet</span>
<span class="badge">DaemonSet</span>
<span class="badge">Job</span>
<span class="badge">CronJob</span>

</div>

<p>
Each object has its own purpose. Kubernetes controllers and other
control-plane components use these object definitions to manage
cluster state.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. What are Labels?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Labels are key-value pairs attached to Kubernetes objects.
They are commonly used to identify and organize resources and to
select related workloads.

</div>

<pre><code>metadata:
  labels:
    app: payment
    environment: production</code></pre>

<h3>Why are labels important?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Identify applications</li>
<li>Group resources</li>
<li>Enable selectors</li>
<li>Connect Services to Pods</li>
<li>Support operational organization</li>

</ul>

<div class="scenario">

A Deployment creates Pods with:

<pre><code>app: payment</code></pre>

A Service can use a selector matching:

<pre><code>selector:
  app: payment</code></pre>

The Service can then target the appropriate Pods.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Labels vs Annotations</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Labels</th>
<th>Annotations</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for identification and selection</td>
<td>Used for storing additional metadata</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be used by selectors</td>
<td>Not normally used for selection</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Important for Services and workload grouping</td>
<td>Useful for tooling and extra information</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>metadata:
  labels:
    app: payment

  annotations:
    owner: devops-team</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. What is kubectl?</h2>

<div class="answer">

kubectl is the command-line tool used to communicate with the
Kubernetes API and manage Kubernetes resources.

</div>

<h3>Most important commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl get nodes

kubectl get deployments

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl exec -it &lt;pod-name&gt; -- /bin/sh

kubectl apply -f file.yaml

kubectl delete -f file.yaml</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time troubleshooting:</strong>

A production Pod is not working.

A DevOps engineer might start with:

<pre><code>kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

These commands help identify scheduling, image, container,
configuration and runtime-related problems.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. What is a Namespace?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Namespace provides a logical scope for Kubernetes resources within
a cluster. It helps organize and isolate groups of resources.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes Cluster
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ dev
<br>
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ Pods
<br>
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ Services
<br>
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ Deployments
<br>
â”‚
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ staging
<br>
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ Pods
<br>
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ Services
<br>
â”‚
<br>
â””â”€â”€ production
<br>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;â”œâ”€â”€ Pods
<br>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;â””â”€â”€ Services

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get namespaces

kubectl create namespace dev

kubectl get pods -n dev

kubectl get all -n dev</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A company may use separate namespaces for development, staging
and production workloads within a cluster, together with appropriate
RBAC and resource policies.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 24. What is a Kubernetes Context?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A kubectl context defines which cluster, user/credentials and
namespace kubectl should use by default for commands.

</div>

<h3>Useful commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl config get-contexts

kubectl config current-context

kubectl config use-context &lt;context-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Always verify the current context before running destructive
commands against production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. How does kubectl apply work?</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

YAML Manifest
<br>
â†“
<br>
kubectl
<br>
â†“
<br>
API Server
<br>
â†“
<br>
Object State
<br>
â†“
<br>
Controllers / Scheduler
<br>
â†“
<br>
Worker Node
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod

</div>

<p>
The manifest declares the desired configuration. Kubernetes then
works to make the cluster state match that configuration.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. What happens when we create a Pod?</h2>

<h3>Interview question</h3>

<p>
"Explain the flow when I run a Kubernetes manifest."
</p>

<div class="flow">

<strong>1. kubectl</strong>
<br>
Reads YAML
<br><br>
â†“
<br><br>

<strong>2. API Server</strong>
<br>
Validates / processes API request
<br><br>
â†“
<br><br>

<strong>3. Cluster State</strong>
<br>
Desired object state is recorded
<br><br>
â†“
<br><br>

<strong>4. Scheduler</strong>
<br>
Selects a suitable node
<br><br>
â†“
<br><br>

<strong>5. Kubelet</strong>
<br>
On selected node
<br><br>
â†“
<br><br>

<strong>6. Container Runtime</strong>
<br>
Runs containers
<br><br>
â†“
<br><br>

<strong>7. Pod Running</strong>

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready answer:</strong>

"When I apply a Pod manifest, kubectl sends the request to the API
server. Kubernetes stores the desired state and the scheduler
selects an appropriate node. The kubelet on that node works with
the container runtime to start the containers. Kubernetes then
continues monitoring the workload."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. What happens if a Pod crashes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes behavior depends on how the Pod is managed and the
container's restart policy. For Pods managed by controllers such as
Deployments, the controller also works to maintain the desired
number of replicas.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Production example:</strong>

Suppose a Deployment requires:

<pre><code>replicas: 3</code></pre>

If one Pod becomes unavailable, the Deployment's controller works
to restore the desired number of available replicas, subject to
cluster capacity and the specific failure.

</div>

<div class="tip">

For production applications, we normally manage Pods through
higher-level workload controllers such as Deployments rather than
creating individual Pods manually.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Why don't we normally create Pods directly?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A standalone Pod does not provide the same desired-state management
and rollout capabilities as a Deployment or other workload
controller.

</div>

<p>
If a standalone Pod is deleted, Kubernetes does not automatically
create a replacement Pod simply because that Pod existed.
</p>

<p>
A Deployment, on the other hand, maintains a desired number of
replicas and manages rollout behavior.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Deployment
<br>
â†“
<br>
ReplicaSet
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Containers

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Pod vs Deployment</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Pod</th>
<th>Deployment</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Smallest deployable unit</td>
<td>Workload controller</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs containers</td>
<td>Manages replicated Pods</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>No built-in rollout strategy</td>
<td>Supports rolling updates and rollout management</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Not ideal for production application management</td>
<td>Common for stateless applications</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"A Pod runs the application containers, while a Deployment manages
the desired number of replicated Pods and provides rollout and
rollback capabilities for stateless workloads."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 30. Kubernetes Self-Healing</h2>

<div class="answer">

Self-healing means Kubernetes continuously works to maintain the
desired state of workloads, including restarting failed containers
according to the Pod's restart policy and recreating Pods when a
controller such as a Deployment determines that replicas are missing.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose:

<pre><code>replicas: 3</code></pre>

Current state:

<pre><code>Pod-1
Pod-2
Pod-3</code></pre>

If Pod-2 becomes unavailable, the workload controller can work
toward restoring the desired replica count.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 31 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 31. What is Kubernetes Service Discovery?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes Services provide a stable network endpoint for reaching
a set of Pods selected by labels. This is important because Pod IPs
are not intended to be the stable application endpoint.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Frontend Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Service</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Backend Pods
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Pod 1
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Pod 2
<br>
â””â”€â”€ Pod 3

</div>

<p>
Services are covered in detail in the Kubernetes Services section,
but this concept is essential to understand the Kubernetes basics.
</p>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 32 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 32. Kubernetes Networking Basic Concept</h2>

<p>
At a high level, Kubernetes networking allows Pods to communicate
with each other and allows Services to provide stable access to
workloads.
</p>

<h3>Important interview points</h3>

<ul>

<li>Each Pod gets a network identity.</li>
<li>Containers in the same Pod share the network namespace.</li>
<li>Services provide stable virtual endpoints.</li>
<li>Kubernetes networking is implemented using a CNI plugin.</li>

</ul>

<div class="warning">

Do not confuse:

<strong>Pod IP</strong> â†’ individual Pod networking

<br>

<strong>Service IP</strong> â†’ stable Service endpoint

<br>

<strong>Node IP</strong> â†’ worker machine networking

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 33 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Kubernetes Resource Requests and Limits â€” Basic Idea</h2>

<div class="answer">

Resource requests indicate the amount of CPU or memory a container
is requesting for scheduling purposes. Limits define an upper
boundary for resource usage.

</div>

<pre><code>resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"

  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"</code></pre>

<h3>Why important?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Helps scheduler make placement decisions</li>
<li>Prevents uncontrolled resource consumption</li>
<li>Improves cluster capacity planning</li>
<li>Important for production workloads</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 34 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Kubernetes Health Checks â€” Basic Idea</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes supports probes that help determine whether a container
is alive, ready to receive traffic, or has started successfully.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Probe</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Liveness Probe</td>
<td>Helps determine whether a container needs to be restarted.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Readiness Probe</td>
<td>Determines whether the application should receive traffic.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Startup Probe</td>
<td>Gives slow-starting applications time to initialize before other probes take over.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A Spring Boot application takes 60 seconds to start.

A startup probe can prevent Kubernetes from treating the application
as unhealthy too early. Once startup succeeds, readiness and liveness
checks can take over.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 35 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 35. Common Kubernetes Commands</h2>

<pre><code># Cluster
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes

# Namespaces
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get ns

# Pods

kubectl delete -f file.yaml

# Execute inside container

# Current context
kubectl config current-context

# Contexts
kubectl config get-contexts</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 36 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 36. Real-Time Scenario â€” Pod is Pending</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

You deploy an application and the Pod remains in:

<pre><code>Pending</code></pre>

<strong>What would you check?</strong>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Look at the Events section.

Possible causes include:

<ul>

<li>Insufficient CPU or memory</li>
<li>Scheduling constraints</li>
<li>Node selectors</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations</li>
<li>Affinity rules</li>
<li>No suitable node available</li>

</ul>

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"If a Pod is Pending, I would first run kubectl describe pod and
check the Events section. I would verify node availability, resource
requests, taints, tolerations, selectors and other scheduling
constraints."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 37 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 37. Real-Time Scenario â€” Pod is CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A Pod repeatedly starts and crashes.

<br><br>

<strong>First checks:</strong>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Possible causes:

<ul>

<li>Application startup failure</li>
<li>Incorrect environment variables</li>
<li>Missing configuration</li>
<li>Incorrect command or arguments</li>
<li>Dependency unavailable</li>
<li>Probe failure</li>
<li>Application exits immediately</li>

</ul>

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Important:</strong>

CrashLoopBackOff is not the root cause itself.

It means Kubernetes is repeatedly restarting a container and applying
a backoff delay between restart attempts.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 38 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 38. Real-Time Scenario â€” ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Pod cannot start because the container image cannot be pulled.

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Look for image-related events.

Possible causes:

<ul>

<li>Wrong image name</li>
<li>Wrong image tag</li>
<li>Private registry authentication issue</li>
<li>Image does not exist</li>
<li>Registry connectivity issue</li>
<li>Image pull credentials problem</li>

</ul>

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would inspect the Pod events using kubectl describe pod. Then I
would verify the image name and tag, registry availability and, for
private registries, the image-pull credentials."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 39 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 39. Real-Time Scenario â€” Pod is Running but Application is Not Accessible</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Do not assume that:

<pre><code>STATUS = Running</code></pre>

means the application is reachable.

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl get pods -o wide

kubectl get svc

kubectl describe svc &lt;service-name&gt;

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Possible issues:

<ul>

<li>Service selector does not match Pod labels</li>
<li>Wrong targetPort</li>
<li>Application listening on wrong port</li>
<li>Readiness probe failing</li>
<li>Network policy or external networking issue</li>

</ul>

</div>

</div>

<!-- SECTION 43 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Explain Kubernetes in 1 Minute</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration platform used
to deploy, manage and scale containerized applications.

A Kubernetes cluster consists mainly of a control plane and worker
nodes. The control plane includes components such as the API server,
etcd, scheduler and controllers, while worker nodes run application
Pods using components such as kubelet and a container runtime.

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes and can contain
one or more tightly coupled containers.

Kubernetes follows a declarative model where we define the desired
state, usually through YAML manifests. Controllers continuously
reconcile the actual state with the desired state.

For example, if a Deployment requires three application replicas
and one becomes unavailable, Kubernetes works to restore the desired
replica state.

In DevOps, Kubernetes provides capabilities such as self-healing,
scaling, service discovery, rolling deployments and resource
management, making it suitable for running containerized
applications in production."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SECTION 44 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸš¨ Common Kubernetes Interview Traps</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Question</th>
<th>Correct Understanding</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Is Kubernetes the same as Docker?</td>
<td>No. Docker provides container tooling; Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Is a Pod the same as a container?</td>
<td>No. A Pod can contain one or more containers.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does Kubernetes normally create containers directly?</td>
<td>Kubernetes manages Pods through the control plane and node agents, which work with a container runtime.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does a Pod always have multiple containers?</td>
<td>No. The common pattern is one main application container per Pod.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does Running mean the application is healthy?</td>
<td>No. Readiness and application-level health must also be considered.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does CrashLoopBackOff mean the image is wrong?</td>
<td>Not necessarily. It indicates repeated container restart attempts with backoff.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does Pending mean the application crashed?</td>
<td>No. Pending commonly indicates scheduling or startup prerequisites have not been satisfied.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Is a Pod IP permanent?</td>
<td>No. Pods are replaceable and their IPs should not be treated as permanent endpoints.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does etcd run application containers?</td>
<td>No. etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does scheduler run containers?</td>
<td>No. Scheduler selects suitable nodes for Pods.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

<!-- ARCHITECTURE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Kubernetes Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Control Plane</strong>

<br><br>

API Server â†’ Scheduler â†’ Controller Manager â†’ etcd

<br><br>

â†“

<br><br>

<strong>Worker Nodes</strong>

<br><br>

kubelet â†’ Container Runtime â†’ Pods

<br><br>

kube-proxy / Networking

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>API Server</td>
<td>Entry point for Kubernetes API requests.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>etcd</td>
<td>Stores Kubernetes cluster state and configuration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Scheduler</td>
<td>Decides which node should run a newly scheduled Pod.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controller Manager</td>
<td>Runs controllers that continuously reconcile desired and actual state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kubelet</td>
<td>Runs on worker nodes and ensures assigned Pods are running.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container Runtime</td>
<td>Runs containers through the Kubernetes container runtime interface.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>kube-proxy</td>
<td>Provides node-level Service networking behavior.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Kubernetes follows a control-plane and worker-node architecture.
The API Server receives requests, etcd stores cluster state, the
Scheduler assigns Pods to nodes and Controllers maintain the desired
state. Worker nodes run Pods using kubelet and a container runtime."

</div>

</div>


<!-- DESIRED STATE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Desired State vs Actual State</h2>

<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Controllers
<br>
â†“
<br>
Actual State
<br>
â†“
<br>
Reconciliation

</div>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes continuously compares the desired state defined by the
user with the current state of the cluster and takes action to
reduce the difference.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

Deployment requests:

<pre><code>replicas: 3</code></pre>

If one Pod crashes, the Deployment/ReplicaSet mechanism works toward
restoring the desired number of replicas.

â†“

â†“
Traffic continues</code></pre>

<!-- RESOURCES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Requests and Limits</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Request</strong> is the amount of CPU/memory Kubernetes uses
when making scheduling decisions.

<strong>Limit</strong> is the maximum resource amount enforced for
the container according to the resource type.

</div>

<pre><code>resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"

  limits:
    cpu: "500m"
    memory: "512Mi"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If a Pod requests more resources than available on eligible nodes,
the Scheduler may leave the Pod Pending.

If a container exceeds its memory limit, it can be terminated with
an OOMKilled status.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCHEDULING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Kubernetes Scheduling</h2>

Important concepts:

<span class="badge">Node Selector</span>
<span class="badge">Node Affinity</span>
<span class="badge">Pod Affinity</span>
<span class="badge">Pod Anti-Affinity</span>
<span class="badge">Taints</span>
<span class="badge">Tolerations</span>

<div class="answer">

The Scheduler evaluates whether a node satisfies the Pod's
requirements and selects an appropriate node.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

A workload must run only on nodes labelled:

<pre><code>workload=production</code></pre>

A nodeSelector or node affinity rule can be used to constrain
placement.

</div>

</div>


<!-- AUTOSCALING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Autoscaling</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HPA</td>
<td>Scales workload replicas based on metrics such as CPU/memory or configured custom metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>VPA</td>
<td>Adjusts Pod resource requests/limits according to observed usage, depending on configuration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Cluster Autoscaler</td>
<td>Adjusts the number of cluster nodes based on scheduling/resource needs.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Traffic Increase
<br>â†“
<br>
HPA
<br>â†“
<br>
More Pods
<br>â†“
<br>
Cluster Capacity
<br>â†“
<br>
Cluster Autoscaler if needed

</div>

</div>


<!-- RBAC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. RBAC</h2>

<div class="answer">

RBAC controls which identities can perform which actions on
Kubernetes resources.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Object</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Role</td>
<td>Permissions within a namespace.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ClusterRole</td>
<td>Cluster-scoped permissions or reusable permissions depending on binding.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>RoleBinding</td>
<td>Binds a Role or ClusterRole to subjects within a namespace.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ClusterRoleBinding</td>
<td>Binds a ClusterRole at cluster scope.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>kubectl auth can-i get pods

kubectl auth can-i create deployments

kubectl get role
kubectl get rolebinding</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SECURITY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Kubernetes Security</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use least-privilege RBAC.</li>
<li>Protect Secrets.</li>
<li>Use NetworkPolicies where required.</li>
<li>Use trusted and scanned container images.</li>
<li>Run containers with appropriate security settings.</li>
<li>Avoid privileged containers unless required.</li>
<li>Keep Kubernetes and node components updated.</li>
<li>Restrict API access.</li>
<li>Use image scanning and admission controls where appropriate.</li>
<li>Monitor cluster activity.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>DevSecOps example:</strong>

Git push â†’ CI scan â†’ image build â†’ vulnerability scan â†’ registry â†’
Kubernetes deployment â†’ runtime monitoring.

</div>

</div>


<!-- HELM -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. Helm</h2>

<div class="answer">

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. It uses Charts to package
Kubernetes resources and templates.

</div>

<pre><code>helm create myapp

helm install myapp ./myapp

helm list

helm upgrade myapp ./myapp

helm rollback myapp 1

helm uninstall myapp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Instead of maintaining many almost-identical YAML files for Dev,
QA and Production, Helm values can be used to provide environment
specific configuration.

</div>

</div>

<!-- NAMESPACE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 20. Namespace</h2>

<div class="answer">

Namespaces provide logical isolation within a Kubernetes cluster and
are commonly used to separate teams, applications or environments.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get namespaces

kubectl get pods -n dev

kubectl get svc -n production

kubectl create namespace dev</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

<pre><code>dev
qa
production</code></pre>

The same application can exist in separate namespaces with
environment-specific configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- LABELS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Labels and Selectors</h2>

<div class="answer">

Labels identify and organize Kubernetes objects.

Selectors are used by resources such as Services and controllers to
find matching objects.

</div>

<pre><code>labels:
  app: frontend

selector:
  app: frontend</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

A very common troubleshooting issue is a mismatch between Service
selectors and Pod labels.

</div>

</div>

<!-- PROJECT INTERVIEW -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Project Interview Answer</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In my DevOps project, I used Kubernetes to deploy and manage the
containerized application.

I used Deployments to maintain application replicas and rolling
updates. Services provided stable internal access to Pods, while
Ingress handled external HTTP/HTTPS routing.

I separated configuration using ConfigMaps and Secrets and used
persistent storage through PV/PVC where required.

I configured readiness and liveness probes for application health
and resource requests and limits for predictable scheduling and
resource management.

For security, I used RBAC and followed least-privilege principles.
For observability, I integrated monitoring using Prometheus and
Grafana.

For deployment automation, Kubernetes can be integrated with CI/CD
and GitOps tools such as Argo CD.

When troubleshooting, I use kubectl get, describe, events and logs
to identify the root cause before applying a fix."

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ 34. If Interviewer Says: "Explain Kubernetes"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform used to automate
the deployment, scaling and management of containerized applications.

It follows a desired-state model. The control plane consists of
components such as the API Server, etcd, Scheduler and Controller
Manager, while worker nodes run application Pods through kubelet and
the container runtime.

I use Deployments for stateless applications, Services for stable
network communication and Ingress for external HTTP/HTTPS routing.
ConfigMaps and Secrets help separate configuration and sensitive
data from application images.

For persistent workloads, Kubernetes provides PV, PVC and
StorageClass. Readiness, liveness and startup probes help manage
application health.

For scalability, I use resource requests and limits and HPA.
RBAC and NetworkPolicies help control access and communication.

In production, I combine Kubernetes with CI/CD, monitoring and
GitOps practices. When issues occur, I troubleshoot systematically
using kubectl get, describe, events and logs instead of making
random changes."

</div>

</div>

<!-- GOLDEN RULES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  36. Kubernetes Golden Rules</h2>

<ul>

<li>
<strong>Pod is not the application architecture.</strong>
Use appropriate workload controllers.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Service is not the same as Pod.</strong>
Service provides stable networking.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Running does not always mean healthy.</strong>
Use readiness and application health checks.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Base64 is not encryption.</strong>
Protect Secrets appropriately.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Requests influence scheduling.</strong>
Limits constrain resource usage.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Don't blindly restart Pods.</strong>
Find the root cause.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Don't expose everything publicly.</strong>
Use appropriate Services, Ingress and security controls.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Don't hard-code environment-specific configuration.</strong>
Use configuration management.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Don't give excessive permissions.</strong>
Follow least privilege.
</li>

<li>
<strong>Always verify after fixing.</strong>
</li>

</ul>

</div>

<h1>Kubernetes <span>Services & Networking</span></h1>

<p>
DevOps interview-focused revision covering Services, ClusterIP,
NodePort, LoadBalancer, DNS, Service Discovery, Endpoints,
Ingress, NetworkPolicy and real-time troubleshooting.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ What You Must Know</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes networking is one of the most frequently asked areas
in DevOps interviews. The interviewer normally checks whether you
understand how Pods communicate with each other and how users reach
applications running inside the cluster.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Pod IP</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Service</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Stable Virtual IP / DNS
<br>
â†“
<br>
Other Pods / External Users
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Ingress / LoadBalancer</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
External Traffic

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Kubernetes Networking?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes networking provides communication between Pods,
Services and external clients inside or outside the cluster.

The main goal is to allow applications running in different Pods
and services to communicate reliably.

</div>

<h3>Four important networking requirements</h3>

<ul>
<li>Pod-to-Pod communication</li>
<li>Pod-to-Service communication</li>
<li>Service-to-Service communication</li>
<li>External-to-Service communication</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Suppose an application has:

<br><br>

Frontend Pod â†’ Backend Pod â†’ MySQL Pod

<br><br>

The frontend should not depend on the backend Pod's changing IP.
Instead, it communicates with a Kubernetes Service that provides
a stable endpoint.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. How does Pod-to-Pod communication work?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Every Pod normally receives its own IP address. Kubernetes networking
is designed so that Pods can communicate with each other directly
without requiring NAT between Pods.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pod A
<br>
10.244.1.5
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Network
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod B
<br>
10.244.2.7

</div>

<h3>Important interview point</h3>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Each Kubernetes Pod gets an IP address. Pods can communicate with
other Pods across nodes through the cluster networking implementation,
usually provided by a CNI plugin."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Why do we need a Kubernetes Service?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Pod IP addresses are not stable. Pods can be deleted, recreated,
rescheduled or scaled, causing their IP addresses to change.

A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name for accessing
a group of Pods.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pod
â†’
Pod
â†’
Pod

<br><br>

â†“ Labels

<br>

<strong>Service</strong>

<br><br>

Stable IP + DNS

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Suppose the backend has 3 Pods:

backend-1 â†’ 10.244.1.10  
backend-2 â†’ 10.244.2.12  
backend-3 â†’ 10.244.3.15

If backend-2 dies, Kubernetes creates another Pod with a different
IP.

The frontend should not track these changing IPs.

Instead:

<code>backend-service</code>

provides a stable endpoint.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is a Kubernetes Service?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Kubernetes Service is an abstraction that exposes a group of
Pods through a stable network endpoint.

The Service selects Pods using labels.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-service

spec:
  selector:
    app: backend

  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

  type: ClusterIP</code></pre>

<h3>Important fields</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Field</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>selector</td>
<td>Selects Pods using labels.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>port</td>
<td>Port exposed by the Service.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>targetPort</td>
<td>Port where the application is listening inside the Pod.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>type</td>
<td>Determines how the Service is exposed.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Kubernetes Service Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>ClusterIP</strong></td>
<td>Internal cluster communication. Default Service type.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>NodePort</strong></td>
<td>Exposes the Service through a port on each node.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>LoadBalancer</strong></td>
<td>Exposes the Service externally using a cloud load balancer.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>ExternalName</strong></td>
<td>Maps a Service name to an external DNS name.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is ClusterIP?</h2>

<div class="answer">

ClusterIP is the default Kubernetes Service type.

It exposes the application internally inside the cluster and is
normally not directly reachable from the public internet.

</div>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-service

spec:
  type: ClusterIP

  selector:
    app: backend

  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time use:</strong>

Frontend and backend are both running inside Kubernetes.

Frontend:

<code>frontend-service</code>

communicates with:

<code>backend-service:80</code>

No public IP is required for the backend.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is NodePort?</h2>

<div class="answer">

NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on each Kubernetes node.

External traffic can reach:

<code>NodeIP:NodePort</code>

which is then forwarded to the Service and its backend Pods.

</div>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service

spec:
  type: NodePort

  selector:
    app: web

  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
      nodePort: 30080</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

User
<br>
â†“
<br>
Node IP : 30080
<br>
â†“
<br>
NodePort Service
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pod : 8080

</div>

<div class="warning">

NodePort is useful for development, testing and some specific
architectures, but production cloud environments commonly use
LoadBalancer or Ingress for external access.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is LoadBalancer?</h2>

<div class="answer">

LoadBalancer exposes a Kubernetes Service externally using a
cloud provider's load balancing capability.

In cloud environments such as AWS, Azure or GCP, the cloud
integration can provision the corresponding load balancer.

</div>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service

spec:
  type: LoadBalancer

  selector:
    app: web

  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Internet
<br>
â†“
<br>
Cloud Load Balancer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Service
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Feature</th>
<th>ClusterIP</th>
<th>NodePort</th>
<th>LoadBalancer</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Internal access</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>Yes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>External access</td>
<td>No direct public exposure</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>Yes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Default</td>
<td>Yes</td>
<td>No</td>
<td>No</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Typical production use</td>
<td>Internal services</td>
<td>Limited</td>
<td>Common</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What is targetPort vs port?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>port</strong> is the port exposed by the Service.

<strong>targetPort</strong> is the port on which the application
inside the Pod is listening.

</div>

<pre><code>ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

User connects to:

<code>backend-service:80</code>

Kubernetes forwards the traffic to:

<code>Pod:8080</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. How does Service select Pods?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Service uses label selectors to identify the Pods that should
receive traffic.

</div>

<h3>Pod</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod

metadata:
  name: backend
  labels:
    app: backend</code></pre>

<h3>Service</h3>

<pre><code>spec:
  selector:
    app: backend</code></pre>

<p>
Because the labels match, the Service sends traffic to the Pod.
</p>

<div class="warning">

If the Service selector does not match the Pod labels, the Service
may have no backend endpoints.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What are Endpoints / EndpointSlices?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes maintains the network destinations associated with a
Service. Modern Kubernetes primarily uses EndpointSlices to represent
these backend endpoints.

They help Kubernetes track which Pod IPs are currently available
behind a Service.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get endpointslices

kubectl describe service backend-service</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Troubleshooting:</strong>

Service exists, but application is unreachable.

First check:

<code>kubectl get endpoints backend-service</code>

If no backend endpoints are present, check the Service selector
and Pod labels.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is Kubernetes DNS?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes provides DNS-based service discovery.

Services normally receive DNS records, allowing applications to
communicate using Service names instead of hard-coded IP addresses.

</div>

<div class="flow">

backend-service
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes DNS
<br>
â†“
<br>
Service ClusterIP
<br>
â†“
<br>
Backend Pods

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>curl http://backend-service:80</code></pre>

<p>
A Pod in the same namespace can normally resolve the Service using
its Service name.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. How do Pods communicate across namespaces?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Service can be addressed using its DNS name.

For example:

<code>backend-service.dev.svc.cluster.local</code>

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>DNS Form</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Service name</td>
<td>backend-service</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Service + namespace</td>
<td>backend-service.dev</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Full DNS</td>
<td>backend-service.dev.svc.cluster.local</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

Frontend is in namespace:

<code>frontend</code>

Backend is in:

<code>backend</code>

Frontend can communicate with:

<code>backend-service.backend.svc.cluster.local</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What is kube-proxy?</h2>

<div class="answer">

kube-proxy is a node-level Kubernetes component responsible for
implementing Service networking rules so traffic destined for
Services can be directed toward the appropriate backend Pods.

</div>

<p>
Depending on the cluster configuration, these rules may be implemented
using mechanisms such as iptables or IPVS.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"kube-proxy runs on nodes and helps implement Kubernetes Service
networking by maintaining the rules required to forward Service
traffic to backend Pods."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. What is Ingress?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Ingress is a Kubernetes API resource used to define HTTP and HTTPS
routing rules for external traffic entering the cluster.

It commonly provides host-based or path-based routing.

An Ingress requires an Ingress Controller to actually implement
the routing.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Internet
<br>
â†“
<br>
Load Balancer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Ingress Controller
<br>
â†“
<br>
Ingress Rules
<br>
â†“
<br>
Services
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Ingress Example</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress

metadata:
  name: app-ingress

spec:

  rules:

  - host: app.example.com

    http:

      paths:

      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix

        backend:

          service:
            name: backend-service
            port:
              number: 80

      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix

        backend:

          service:
            name: frontend-service
            port:
              number: 80</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time architecture:</strong>

<code>app.example.com/</code>

â†’ frontend-service

<br><br>

<code>app.example.com/api</code>

â†’ backend-service

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Ingress vs LoadBalancer</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Ingress</th>
<th>LoadBalancer Service</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTP/HTTPS routing</td>
<td>Exposes a Service externally</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can route multiple applications</td>
<td>Normally exposes one Service</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Supports host/path rules</td>
<td>Does not provide the same application-level routing model</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Requires Ingress Controller</td>
<td>Implemented through Service/cloud integration</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"If I have multiple web applications and want centralized
HTTP/HTTPS routing using host or path rules, I would commonly use
Ingress with an appropriate Ingress Controller."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. What is a CNI plugin?</h2>

<div class="answer">

CNI stands for Container Network Interface.

A CNI plugin provides the networking implementation used by the
Kubernetes cluster for Pod networking.

</div>

<p>
Examples include implementations such as Calico, Cilium and
cloud-specific networking solutions.
</p>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Important:</strong>

Do not say Kubernetes itself provides the complete Pod networking
implementation. The networking behavior is provided through the
cluster's networking/CNI implementation.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. What is NetworkPolicy?</h2>

<div class="answer">

NetworkPolicy controls which network traffic is allowed to or from
selected Pods.

It can be used to implement network-level access restrictions such
as allowing frontend Pods to access backend Pods while preventing
other Pods from doing so.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Without proper restrictions:

Frontend â†’ Backend  
Test Pod â†’ Backend  
Unknown Pod â†’ Backend

<br><br>

With NetworkPolicy:

Frontend â†’ Backend âœ…

Test Pod â†’ Backend âŒ

Unknown Pod â†’ Backend âŒ

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. NetworkPolicy Example</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy

metadata:
  name: backend-policy

spec:

  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend

  policyTypes:
  - Ingress

  ingress:

  - from:

    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend

    ports:

    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

This policy selects backend Pods and allows ingress traffic on
port 8080 only from Pods labeled <code>app: frontend</code>,
assuming the cluster's networking implementation enforces the policy.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. What is Service Discovery?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Service discovery is the mechanism by which applications find and
communicate with Services without manually knowing changing Pod IPs.

Kubernetes commonly provides service discovery through DNS.

</div>

<pre><code>frontend Pod
     |
     | HTTP request
     â†“
backend-service
     |
     â†“
Kubernetes DNS
     |
     â†“
Backend Pods</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. What is Headless Service?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A headless Service is created by setting:

<code>clusterIP: None</code>

Instead of providing a normal virtual ClusterIP, DNS can return
the individual Pod addresses associated with the Service.

</div>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Service

metadata:
  name: database

spec:
  clusterIP: None

  selector:
    app: database

  ports:
  - port: 3306</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Headless Services are commonly useful for stateful applications
where clients need to discover individual Pods, such as certain
database or distributed-system architectures.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 24. What is ExternalName?</h2>

<div class="answer">

ExternalName maps a Kubernetes Service name to an external DNS name.

It does not create a normal ClusterIP.

</div>

<pre><code>apiVersion: v1
kind: Service

metadata:
  name: external-db

spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: database.example.com</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. What happens when a Pod dies?</h2>

<div class="answer">

If the Pod is managed by a controller such as a Deployment,
Kubernetes can create a replacement Pod.

The replacement may receive a different IP.

The Service continues to provide a stable endpoint and updates
its backend endpoint information accordingly.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Old Pod
<br>
âŒ
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deployment
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pod IP
<br>
â†“
<br>
Service
<br>
â†“
<br>
Traffic continues

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Real-Time Scenario: Service has no traffic</h2>

<h3>Problem</h3>

<p>
Service exists, but requests are failing.
</p>

<h3>Step 1 â€” Check Service</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get svc</code></pre>

<h3>Step 2 â€” Check Endpoints</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get endpoints
kubectl get endpointslices</code></pre>

<h3>Step 3 â€” Check Pods</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods --show-labels</code></pre>

<h3>Step 4 â€” Compare selector and labels</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl describe svc backend-service</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Most common issue:</strong>

Service:

<code>selector: app=backend</code>

Pod:

<code>app=backend-api</code>

Labels do not match â†’ Service has no matching backend Pods.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Real-Time Scenario: Pod cannot reach another Service</h2>

<h3>Troubleshooting flow</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get pods

kubectl describe svc backend-service

kubectl describe pod frontend-pod</code></pre>

<p>
Then test DNS and connectivity from inside a temporary/debug Pod.
</p>

<pre><code>kubectl exec -it frontend-pod -- sh

# Inside container
nslookup backend-service

# Or
curl http://backend-service:80</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview approach:</strong>

"I first verify that the Service exists, then verify that it has
healthy endpoints, check DNS resolution, confirm the target port,
and finally investigate NetworkPolicy or application-level issues."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Real-Time Scenario: DNS not resolving</h2>

<div class="answer">

If a Pod cannot resolve a Service name, I would verify the Service,
namespace, DNS configuration and DNS components.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get svc

kubectl get pods -n kube-system

kubectl get svc -n kube-system</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

Frontend is in namespace <code>frontend</code>.

Backend Service is in namespace <code>backend</code>.

Using:

<code>backend-service</code>

may not resolve to the intended Service.

Use:

<code>backend-service.backend.svc.cluster.local</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Real-Time Scenario: Application works inside Pod but not externally</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify the external exposure layer step by step.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>

<br>

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl get svc

kubectl describe svc &lt;service-name&gt;

kubectl describe ingress &lt;ingress-name&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Important Service Commands</h2>

<pre><code># Services
kubectl get svc

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Kubernetes Networking"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes networking allows Pods, Services and external clients
to communicate with each other.

Each Pod gets an IP address, but Pod IPs are not stable because
Pods can be recreated or rescheduled. Therefore, Kubernetes
Services provide a stable virtual endpoint and use label selectors
to route traffic to the appropriate Pods.

ClusterIP is mainly used for internal communication, NodePort
exposes a Service through a port on each node, and LoadBalancer
provides external exposure through cloud load balancing.

For HTTP and HTTPS routing, we can use Ingress together with an
Ingress Controller.

Kubernetes also provides DNS-based service discovery, so
applications can communicate using Service names instead of
hard-coded IP addresses.

For security, NetworkPolicies can restrict which Pods are allowed
to communicate with each other.

In a production troubleshooting scenario, I would check the Pod
status, Service configuration, labels, endpoints, DNS resolution,
ports, Ingress or LoadBalancer configuration and NetworkPolicies
step by step."

</div>
