<h1>Kubernetes <span>Workloads</span></h1>

<p>
DevOps interview-focused guide covering Pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets,
StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, rollout, scaling,
self-healing and real-time workload scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ What Are Kubernetes Workloads?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A workload is an application running on Kubernetes.

Kubernetes provides workload resources such as Deployments,
StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs to manage Pods according
to the application's requirements.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Workload Controller</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Pods</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Containers

</div>

<p>
The key interview point is that we normally don't manually manage
individual application Pods in production. Controllers manage the
desired state of those Pods.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Pod?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes.

A Pod can contain one or more containers that share the same
network namespace and can share storage volumes.

</div>

<h3>Simple architecture</h3>

<pre><code>Pod
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ Container
â”‚
â””â”€â”€ Container (optional)
</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A normal web application may have one application container in a Pod.

A sidecar architecture may have:

Application Container
+
Logging/Proxy Sidecar

Both containers share the Pod's network namespace.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why don't we usually create Pods directly?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A standalone Pod is not automatically recreated by Kubernetes if it
fails.

For production workloads, controllers such as Deployments manage
Pods and maintain the desired number of replicas.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Standalone Pod</th>
<th>Deployment</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Directly created</td>
<td>Manages Pods through ReplicaSets</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>No automatic desired replica management</td>
<td>Maintains desired replicas</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Limited production use</td>
<td>Common for stateless applications</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is a Deployment?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Deployment is a Kubernetes workload resource used mainly to manage
stateless applications.

It manages ReplicaSets, which in turn maintain the required number
of Pods.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Deployment
<br>
â†“
<br>
ReplicaSet
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Containers

</div>

<h3>Deployment responsibilities</h3>

<ul>
<li>Maintain desired replicas</li>
<li>Rolling updates</li>
<li>Rollback</li>
<li>Scaling</li>
<li>Self-healing through ReplicaSets</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Deployment YAML</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment

metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment

spec:

  replicas: 3

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx

  template:

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx

    spec:

      containers:

      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27

        ports:
        - containerPort: 80</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The Deployment declares that three Pods should normally exist,
and the Pod template defines how those Pods should be created.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is ReplicaSet?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A ReplicaSet ensures that a specified number of Pod replicas are
running.

For example, if the desired replica count is 3 and one Pod fails,
the ReplicaSet works to create a replacement Pod.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Desired = 3
<br><br>

Pod 1 âœ…
&nbsp;&nbsp;
Pod 2 âŒ
&nbsp;&nbsp;
Pod 3 âœ…
<br><br>

â†“
<br><br>

ReplicaSet creates replacement
<br><br>

â†“
<br><br>

Pod 1 âœ…
&nbsp;&nbsp;
Pod 2 âœ…
&nbsp;&nbsp;
Pod 3 âœ…

</div>

<div class="warning">

In normal application deployments, you generally create a Deployment
rather than manually creating a ReplicaSet.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Deployment vs ReplicaSet vs Pod</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Resource</th>
<th>Main responsibility</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pod</td>
<td>Runs one or more containers.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ReplicaSet</td>
<td>Maintains the desired number of matching Pods.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Deployment</td>
<td>Manages ReplicaSets and provides rollout/rollback functionality.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and ReplicaSets maintain the
desired number of Pods. The Pods actually run the containers."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is self-healing in Kubernetes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Self-healing means Kubernetes controllers continuously compare the
actual state with the desired state and take corrective action when
they differ.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Deployment requires:

<strong>3 replicas</strong>

Current state:

<strong>2 healthy Pods</strong>

Kubernetes detects the difference and creates another Pod.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Desired State
<br>
3 Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Actual State
<br>
2 Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Controller
<br>
â†“
<br>
Create Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
3 Pods

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What happens if a Pod crashes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The exact behavior depends on how the Pod is managed.

If it is managed by a Deployment/ReplicaSet, the controller ensures
the desired replica count is maintained.

Kubernetes may restart containers inside a Pod, and controllers may
create replacement Pods when necessary.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Production example:

A backend Deployment has 3 replicas.

One Pod crashes.

Kubernetes detects that the desired replica count is no longer met
and creates a replacement so the application returns to the desired
state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is Rolling Update?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A rolling update gradually replaces old Pods with new Pods instead
of stopping the entire application at once.

This helps reduce downtime during application updates.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Old Version
<br>
3 Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Version starts
<br>
â†“
<br>
Old Pods gradually removed
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pods become ready
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Version
<br>
3 Pods

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. How do you update a Deployment?</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment \
nginx=nginx:1.28</code></pre>

<p>Check rollout:</p>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment

kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deployment</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually moves
traffic/workload from the old version to the new version according
to the rollout strategy.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is Rollback?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Rollback means returning a Deployment to a previous revision when a
new deployment has a problem.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deployment

kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment

kubectl rollout status deployment/nginx-deployment</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time scenario:</strong>

Version 2 of the application causes HTTP 500 errors after deployment.

The DevOps engineer checks the rollout and quickly rolls back to
the previously working version while investigating the issue.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is StatefulSet?</h2>

<div class="answer">

StatefulSet is a Kubernetes workload resource designed for stateful
applications that require stable identity, stable network identity
and/or persistent storage characteristics.

</div>

<h3>Typical examples</h3>

<ul>
<li>Databases</li>
<li>Kafka</li>
<li>ZooKeeper</li>
<li>Distributed stateful systems</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

StatefulSet
<br>
â†“
<br>
pod-0
<br>
pod-1
<br>
pod-2
<br>
â†“
<br>
Stable identities

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. StatefulSet vs Deployment</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Deployment</th>
<th>StatefulSet</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Primarily stateless workloads</td>
<td>Stateful workloads</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pods are interchangeable</td>
<td>Pods have stable identities</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually does not require stable Pod identity</td>
<td>Stable network identity</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Storage is not inherently tied to Pod identity</td>
<td>Can use stable persistent storage per Pod</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Simple answer:</strong>

"Deployment is normally preferred for stateless applications,
while StatefulSet is used when Pods need stable identity or
persistent state characteristics."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. StatefulSet Example</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet

metadata:
  name: web

spec:

  serviceName: "web"

  replicas: 3

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web

  template:

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web

    spec:

      containers:

      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27</code></pre>

<p>
The Pods can have stable ordinal identities such as:
</p>

<pre><code>web-0
web-1
web-2</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What is DaemonSet?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A DaemonSet ensures that a Pod runs on each eligible node, or on
each node matching the DaemonSet's scheduling constraints.

</div>

<h3>Common use cases</h3>

<ul>
<li>Node-level logging agents</li>
<li>Monitoring agents</li>
<li>Security agents</li>
<li>Node networking components</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Node 1 â†’ Agent Pod
<br>
Node 2 â†’ Agent Pod
<br>
Node 3 â†’ Agent Pod
<br>
Node 4 â†’ Agent Pod

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Suppose an organization runs a logging agent on every Kubernetes
node to collect container logs.

A DaemonSet can ensure each eligible node has one logging agent Pod.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Workload</th>
<th>Best suited for</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Deployment</td>
<td>Stateless web applications and APIs</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>StatefulSet</td>
<td>Stateful applications requiring stable identity/storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>DaemonSet</td>
<td>One Pod per eligible node</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. What is a Job?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Job creates one or more Pods and ensures that the required
successful completions are achieved.

Jobs are intended for tasks that run to completion rather than
long-running services.

</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<ul>
<li>Database migration</li>
<li>Batch processing</li>
<li>Data processing</li>
<li>One-time administrative task</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Job YAML</h2>

<pre><code>apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job

metadata:
  name: database-migration

spec:

  template:

    spec:

      restartPolicy: Never

      containers:

      - name: migration
        image: myapp:1.0
        command:
        - /bin/sh
        - -c
        - "python migrate.py"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

The migration Pod runs the migration script.

If the task completes successfully, the Job reaches completion.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. What is CronJob?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A CronJob creates Jobs on a repeating schedule using a cron
expression.

</div>

<h3>Typical use cases</h3>

<ul>
<li>Scheduled backups</li>
<li>Cleanup tasks</li>
<li>Reports</li>
<li>Periodic data processing</li>
</ul>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob

metadata:
  name: backup-job

spec:

  schedule: "0 2 * * *"

  jobTemplate:

    spec:

      template:

        spec:

          restartPolicy: OnFailure

          containers:

          - name: backup
            image: backup-image:1.0
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - "backup.sh"</code></pre>

<p>
This schedule runs approximately every day at 02:00 according to
the CronJob's configured time interpretation.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Job vs CronJob</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Job</th>
<th>CronJob</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs a task to completion</td>
<td>Creates Jobs on a schedule</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>One-time/batch execution</td>
<td>Recurring execution</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: migration</td>
<td>Example: daily backup</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. What is desired state?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Desired state is the configuration that we tell Kubernetes we want.

Kubernetes continuously works to make the actual state match the
desired state.

</div>

<pre><code>replicas: 3</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Desired state = 3 Pods

Actual state = 2 Pods

Controller action = create another Pod

Final state = 3 Pods

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. What is declarative configuration?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Declarative configuration describes the desired end state rather
than specifying every individual operation required to reach it.

Kubernetes controllers then work to achieve that state.

</div>

<pre><code>spec:
  replicas: 3

  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.28</code></pre>

<p>
This configuration describes what should exist. Kubernetes handles
the reconciliation process.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. What is a Replica count?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The replica count specifies how many Pod replicas a workload should
maintain.

</div>

<pre><code>spec:
  replicas: 3</code></pre>

<p>
This is commonly used with Deployments and ReplicaSets.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. How do you scale a Deployment?</h2>

<h3>Imperative scaling</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl scale deployment nginx-deployment --replicas=5</code></pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get deployment

kubectl get pods</code></pre>

<h3>Declarative scaling</h3>

<pre><code>spec:
  replicas: 5</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Production example:

Traffic increases during a sale.

The application may need more replicas to handle increased demand.

For long-term automated scaling, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can be
used when the application and cluster are configured appropriately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. What is HPA?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically adjusts the number of Pod
replicas based on observed metrics such as CPU utilization,
memory or configured custom/external metrics.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Low Traffic
<br>
â†“
<br>
2 Pods
<br><br>

Traffic increases
<br>
â†“
<br>
HPA evaluates metrics
<br>
â†“
<br>
5 Pods

</div>

<div class="warning">

HPA does not increase the CPU or memory of an individual Pod.
It changes the number of replicas.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. HPA vs Vertical Scaling</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Horizontal Scaling</th>
<th>Vertical Scaling</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Increase/decrease number of Pods</td>
<td>Increase resources assigned to a Pod</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More replicas</td>
<td>More CPU/memory</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HPA is commonly used</td>
<td>VPA can be used in supported/configured environments</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. What are readiness and liveness probes?</h2>

<h3>Readiness Probe</h3>

<div class="answer">

Determines whether a container is ready to receive traffic.

If the readiness check fails, Kubernetes can remove the Pod from
Service endpoints.

</div>

<h3>Liveness Probe</h3>

<div class="answer">

Determines whether a container is considered healthy enough to
continue running. If the liveness probe repeatedly fails, kubelet
can restart the container.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Application starts slowly.

Without readiness:

Traffic may reach the application before it is ready.

With readiness:

Traffic is sent only after the application passes its readiness
check.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Readiness vs Liveness vs Startup</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Probe</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Readiness</td>
<td>Should this Pod receive traffic?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Liveness</td>
<td>Should this container be restarted?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Startup</td>
<td>Has a slow-starting application completed startup?</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy memory trick:</strong>

<br><br>

Readiness â†’ "Can I send traffic?"

<br>

Liveness â†’ "Is it still alive?"

<br>

Startup â†’ "Has it finished starting?"

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. Deployment Strategy</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes Deployments commonly support strategies such as:
</p>

<ul>
<li>RollingUpdate</li>
<li>Recreate</li>
</ul>

<h3>RollingUpdate</h3>

<div class="answer">

Gradually replaces old Pods with new Pods.

This is commonly preferred when application availability should be
maintained during updates.

</div>

<h3>Recreate</h3>

<div class="answer">

Existing Pods are terminated before the new Pods are created.

This can cause downtime and is useful only when the application's
requirements justify it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. What are maxUnavailable and maxSurge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

During a RollingUpdate:

<strong>maxUnavailable</strong> controls how many Pods can be
unavailable during the update.

<strong>maxSurge</strong> controls how many additional Pods can be
created above the desired replica count during the update.

</div>

<pre><code>strategy:

  type: RollingUpdate

  rollingUpdate:

    maxUnavailable: 1
    maxSurge: 1</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If desired replicas = 3 and maxSurge = 1,

Kubernetes can temporarily have up to 4 Pods during the rollout.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 31 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Real-Time Scenario: New deployment is failing</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A new application version is deployed, but Pods are failing.

</div>

<h3>Check Deployment</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get deployment

kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Check ReplicaSets</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get rs</code></pre>

<h3>Check Pods</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Rollback if required</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout undo deployment/&lt;deployment&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 32 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Real-Time Scenario: Pods are in CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

CrashLoopBackOff means a container is repeatedly starting and
crashing, and Kubernetes is backing off before restarting it again.

</div>

<h3>Investigation</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt; --previous</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Application error</li>
<li>Wrong environment variable</li>
<li>Missing configuration</li>
<li>Incorrect command</li>
<li>Dependency unavailable</li>
<li>Permission problem</li>
<li>Probe configuration issue</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 33 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Real-Time Scenario: Pods are Pending</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Pending Pod has not successfully reached the running state.

The scheduler may be unable to place it on a suitable node, or
another condition may be preventing startup.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl get nodes

kubectl describe node &lt;node&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Common causes:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Insufficient CPU or memory</li>
<li>Node selector mismatch</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations</li>
<li>Affinity rules</li>
<li>Unbound persistent volume claim</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 34 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Real-Time Scenario: Deployment says Available replicas are low</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would inspect the Deployment, ReplicaSet and Pods to identify why
the desired replicas are not becoming available.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get deployment

kubectl get rs

kubectl get pods

kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment&gt;

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt;</code></pre>

<p>
Readiness failures, image problems, resource issues and application
startup failures are common areas to investigate.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 35 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 35. Important Workload Commands</h2>

<pre><code># Pods
kubectl get pods

kubectl get pods -o wide

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt; --previous


# Deployments
kubectl get deployments

kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment&gt;

kubectl rollout status deployment/&lt;deployment&gt;

kubectl rollout history deployment/&lt;deployment&gt;

kubectl rollout undo deployment/&lt;deployment&gt;


# ReplicaSets
kubectl get rs


# Scaling
kubectl scale deployment &lt;deployment&gt; --replicas=5


# StatefulSets
kubectl get statefulset


# DaemonSets
kubectl get daemonset


# Jobs
kubectl get jobs


# CronJobs
kubectl get cronjobs</code></pre>

</div>

<!-- FINAL INTERVIEW ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Kubernetes Workloads"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Kubernetes workloads are resources used to run and manage
applications in a Kubernetes cluster.

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit and contains one or more
containers. For stateless applications, I commonly use a
Deployment. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and the ReplicaSet
maintains the required number of Pods.

Deployments also provide rolling updates, scaling and rollback.

For stateful applications that need stable identity or persistent
storage characteristics, I would use StatefulSet.

DaemonSet is used when a Pod needs to run on each eligible node,
for example a logging or monitoring agent.

For tasks that need to run to completion, I would use a Job, and
for scheduled recurring tasks, I would use a CronJob.

Kubernetes continuously compares the actual state with the desired
state and controllers work to maintain the desired state. This is
one of the key reasons Kubernetes provides self-healing behavior.

In production, I would also use readiness and liveness probes,
appropriate resource configuration, controlled rolling updates and
rollback mechanisms to maintain application availability."

</div>

<div class="icon">âš™ï¸</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Terraform</a>

<h1>Terraform <span>Advanced Concepts</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Data Sources, Locals, Functions,
Expressions, count, for_each, depends_on, Dynamic Blocks,
Provisioners and real-time Terraform scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Why These Concepts Matter</h2>

<p>
These features help Terraform work with existing infrastructure,
reuse values, dynamically create resources and express complex
infrastructure logic without unnecessary duplication.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Data Sources
â†’ Read Existing Infrastructure

<br><br>

Locals
â†’ Reuse Calculated Values

<br><br>

Functions / Expressions
â†’ Transform Values

<br><br>

count / for_each
â†’ Create Multiple Resources

<br><br>

depends_on
â†’ Explicit Dependency

<br><br>

Dynamic Blocks
â†’ Generate Nested Blocks

<br><br>

Provisioners
â†’ Last-resort Configuration Actions

</div>

</div>


<!-- DATA SOURCES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Terraform Data Source?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A data source allows Terraform to read information about existing
infrastructure or external data without creating that object.

The keyword used is:

<pre><code>data</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

An AWS VPC already exists.

Terraform should use that VPC instead of creating another one.

Terraform can retrieve the existing VPC using a data source.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DATA SOURCE EXAMPLE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. AWS VPC Data Source</h2>

<pre><code>data "aws_vpc" "existing" {

  filter {
    name   = "tag:Name"
    values = ["production-vpc"]
  }
}</code></pre>

<h3>Use the VPC ID</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_subnet" "app" {

  vpc_id = data.aws_vpc.existing.id

  cidr_block = "10.0.10.0/24"

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Here Terraform reads the existing VPC and uses its ID when creating
the subnet.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DATA SOURCE VS RESOURCE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Resource vs Data Source</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Resource</th>
<th>Data Source</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates or manages infrastructure.</td>
<td>Reads existing information.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>resource</code></td>
<td><code>data</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Terraform manages its lifecycle.</td>
<td>Terraform does not create the object.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: create VPC.</td>
<td>Example: find existing VPC.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy interview answer:</strong>

"Resource is used to create or manage infrastructure. Data source is
used to retrieve information about existing infrastructure."

</div>

</div>


<!-- AMI -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Real-Time AWS AMI Data Source</h2>

<pre><code>data "aws_ami" "amazon_linux" {

  most_recent = true

  owners = ["amazon"]

  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["al2023-ami-*-x86_64"]
  }

  filter {
    name   = "state"
    values = ["available"]
  }
}</code></pre>

<h3>Use it</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  ami           = data.aws_ami.amazon_linux.id
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Instead of hard-coding an AMI ID that can change between regions,
Terraform can dynamically look up a suitable AMI.

</div>

</div>


<!-- LOCALS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What are Terraform Locals?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Locals allow you to assign reusable names to expressions or computed
values inside a module.

They help avoid repeating the same expression multiple times.

</div>

<pre><code>locals {

  environment = "production"

  common_tags = {
    Environment = local.environment
    Project     = "payment-app"
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }

}</code></pre>

<h3>Use local value</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" {

  bucket = "payment-${local.environment}"

  tags = local.common_tags

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- LOCALS VS VARIABLES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Variables vs Locals</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Variables</th>
<th>Locals</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Input supplied to a module.</td>
<td>Value calculated or reused inside a module.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can change between environments.</td>
<td>Usually derived from configuration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>var.environment</code></td>
<td><code>local.environment</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Remember:</strong>

Variable = external input.

Local = internal reusable value.

</div>

</div>


<!-- FUNCTIONS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Terraform Functions</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform functions transform or manipulate values.

Common functions include:

</div>

<ul>
<li>length()</li>
<li>join()</li>
<li>split()</li>
<li>lookup()</li>
<li>merge()</li>
<li>concat()</li>
<li>contains()</li>
<li>toset()</li>
<li>tolist()</li>
<li>tomap()</li>
<li>upper()</li>
<li>lower()</li>
<li>replace()</li>
<li>file()</li>
<li>templatefile()</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- FUNCTION EXAMPLES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Important Function Examples</h2>

<h3>length()</h3>

<pre><code>locals {
  subnet_count = length(var.subnets)
}</code></pre>

<h3>join()</h3>

<pre><code>locals {
  name = join("-", ["prod", "web", "01"])
}</code></pre>

<h3>merge()</h3>

<pre><code>locals {

  tags = merge(
    var.common_tags,
    {
      Environment = "production"
    }
  )

}</code></pre>

<h3>contains()</h3>

<pre><code>contains(["dev", "qa", "prod"], var.environment)</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- EXPRESSIONS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Terraform Expressions</h2>

<div class="answer">

Expressions allow Terraform configuration to calculate values,
reference resources and make decisions.

</div>

<pre><code>name = "app-${var.environment}"

instance_type = var.environment == "prod"
  ? "t3.medium"
  : "t3.micro"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

For Production:

<pre><code>instance_type = "t3.medium"</code></pre>

For Dev:

<pre><code>instance_type = "t3.micro"</code></pre>

The conditional expression avoids duplicating the resource.

</div>

</div>


<!-- CONDITIONAL -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Conditional Expression</h2>

<pre><code>instance_type = var.environment == "production"
  ? "t3.large"
  : "t3.micro"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Syntax:

<pre><code>condition ? true_value : false_value</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="interview">

A common real-time use case is selecting different infrastructure
sizes or settings based on the environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- COUNT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is count?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>count</code> creates multiple instances of a resource based on
a numeric value.

</div>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  count = 3

  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

}</code></pre>

<p>
Terraform creates three instances:
</p>

<pre><code>aws_instance.app[0]
aws_instance.app[1]
aws_instance.app[2]</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- COUNT WITH LIST -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. count.index</h2>

<pre><code>variable "instance_names" {

  default = [
    "web",
    "api",
    "worker"
  ]

}

resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  count = length(var.instance_names)

  tags = {
    Name = var.instance_names[count.index]
  }

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<code>count.index</code> gives the numeric index of the current
resource instance.

</div>

</div>


<!-- FOR EACH -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is for_each?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>for_each</code> creates multiple resource instances from a map
or set.

It is useful when each instance has a meaningful key.

</div>

<pre><code>variable "instances" {

  default = {
    web    = "t3.micro"
    api    = "t3.small"
    worker = "t3.medium"
  }

}

resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  for_each = var.instances

  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = each.value

  tags = {
    Name = each.key
  }

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- COUNT VS FOREACH -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. count vs for_each</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>count</th>
<th>for_each</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses a number.</td>
<td>Uses map or set.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses numeric index.</td>
<td>Uses meaningful keys.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>count.index</code></td>
<td><code>each.key</code> / <code>each.value</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for identical or index-based instances.</td>
<td>Good when instances have distinct identities.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I prefer for_each when resources have meaningful identities because
the keys make resource addressing clearer and can reduce unwanted
index-related changes."

</div>

</div>


<!-- FOREACH SET -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. for_each with a Set</h2>

<pre><code>variable "users" {

  type = set(string)

  default = [
    "dev",
    "qa",
    "admin"
  ]

}

resource "aws_iam_user" "users" {

  for_each = var.users

  name = each.value

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- DEPENDS ON -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. What is depends_on?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>depends_on</code> explicitly tells Terraform that one resource
depends on another resource or module.

Terraform normally builds dependencies automatically from references,
so <code>depends_on</code> should be used only when the dependency
cannot be inferred automatically.

</div>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

  depends_on = [
    aws_iam_role_policy.app
  ]

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- IMPLICIT VS EXPLICIT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Implicit vs Explicit Dependency</h2>

<h3>Implicit dependency</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  subnet_id = aws_subnet.app.id

}</code></pre>

<p>
Terraform automatically knows that the instance depends on the
subnet because the instance references its ID.
</p>

<h3>Explicit dependency</h3>

<pre><code>depends_on = [
  aws_iam_role_policy.app
]</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Use explicit dependencies only when Terraform cannot determine the
relationship from resource references.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DYNAMIC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. What is a Dynamic Block?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A dynamic block generates repeated nested configuration blocks from
a collection.

It is useful when a resource contains nested blocks that need to be
created dynamically.

</div>

<pre><code>dynamic "ingress" {

  for_each = var.ingress_rules

  content {

    from_port   = ingress.value.from_port
    to_port     = ingress.value.to_port
    protocol    = ingress.value.protocol
    cidr_blocks = ingress.value.cidr_blocks

  }
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- DYNAMIC REAL TIME -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 19. Dynamic Block Real-Time Example</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose a security group has different inbound rules for:

<br><br>

HTTP â†’ 80

<br>

HTTPS â†’ 443

<br>

SSH â†’ 22

<br><br>

Instead of writing many repeated nested blocks manually, a dynamic
block can generate them from a variable.

</div>

<pre><code>variable "ingress_rules" {

  default = {
    http = {
      from_port   = 80
      to_port     = 80
      protocol    = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
    }

    https = {
      from_port   = 443
      to_port     = 443
      protocol    = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
    }
  }

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- PROVISIONERS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 20. What are Terraform Provisioners?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Provisioners allow Terraform to perform actions on or after resource
creation.

Examples include:

<ul>
<li>local-exec</li>
<li>remote-exec</li>
<li>file</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Provisioners are generally considered a last resort.

Terraform is designed to manage infrastructure declaratively.
Configuration-management tools, cloud-init, images and other
mechanisms are often preferable for application setup.

</div>

</div>


<!-- LOCAL EXEC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 21. local-exec Example</h2>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

  provisioner "local-exec" {

    command = "echo Instance created"

  }

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<code>local-exec</code> runs the command on the machine where
Terraform is executing.

It does not run the command inside the EC2 instance.

</div>

</div>


<!-- REMOTE EXEC -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 22. remote-exec Example</h2>

<pre><code>provisioner "remote-exec" {

  inline = [
    "sudo apt-get update",
    "sudo apt-get install -y nginx"
  ]

  connection {

    type        = "ssh"
    host        = self.public_ip
    user        = "ubuntu"
    private_key = file("key.pem")

  }

}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

For production systems, prefer immutable images, cloud-init,
configuration management or other appropriate automation instead of
relying heavily on remote-exec.

</div>

</div>


<!-- PROVISIONER FAILURE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 23. What happens if a Provisioner fails?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Provisioner behavior depends on the resource lifecycle and
provisioner configuration.

By default, a creation-time provisioner failure can cause the
resource to be marked as tainted in older Terraform terminology and
lead to recreation behavior.

Modern Terraform workflows should be designed carefully rather than
depending on provisioners for critical configuration.

</div>

<div class="interview">

The important interview point:

<strong>Provisioners are not the preferred way to configure
applications.</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- DATA SOURCE MULTIPLE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 24. Data Source with Filters</h2>

<pre><code>data "aws_subnet" "private" {

  filter {
    name   = "tag:Tier"
    values = ["private"]
  }

  filter {
    name   = "tag:Environment"
    values = ["production"]
  }

}</code></pre>

<p>
Filters allow Terraform to identify the required existing object.
</p>

</div>


<!-- LOCALS COMPLEX -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 25. Locals for Common Tags</h2>

<pre><code>variable "environment" {
  type = string
}

variable "project" {
  type = string
}

locals {

  common_tags = {
    Environment = var.environment
    Project     = var.project
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
    Owner       = "DevOps"
  }

}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" {

  bucket = "${var.project}-${var.environment}"

  tags = local.common_tags

}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This pattern is commonly useful when many AWS resources need the same
standard tags.

</div>

</div>


<!-- CONDITIONAL COUNT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 26. Conditional Resource Creation</h2>

<pre><code>variable "create_monitoring" {
  type    = bool
  default = true
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "app" {

  count = var.create_monitoring ? 1 : 0

  name = "/app/logs"

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

If <code>create_monitoring = true</code>, Terraform creates one
resource.

If false, Terraform creates zero instances.

</div>

</div>


<!-- FOR EXPRESSION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 27. For Expressions</h2>

<div class="answer">

For expressions transform one collection into another collection.

</div>

<pre><code>variable "names" {

  default = [
    "web",
    "api",
    "database"
  ]

}

output "upper_names" {

  value = [
    for name in var.names : upper(name)
  ]

}</code></pre>

<p>
Result:
</p>

<pre><code>[
  "WEB",
  "API",
  "DATABASE"
]</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- REAL WORLD -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Real-Time Architecture Example</h2>

<div class="flow">

Existing AWS VPC
<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>

<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>for_each</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Web / API / Worker
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Locals</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Common Tags
<br>
â†“
<br>
AWS Infrastructure

</div>

<div class="scenario">

This demonstrates how advanced Terraform features work together
instead of existing as isolated concepts.

</div>

</div>


<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. Troubleshooting count / for_each</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A resource unexpectedly wants to be destroyed and recreated after
changing from <code>count</code> to <code>for_each</code>.

<br><br>

<strong>Why?</strong>

The resource addressing model changed.

For example:

<pre><code>aws_instance.app[0]</code></pre>

may become:

<pre><code>aws_instance.app["web"]</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="answer">

When changing resource addressing, carefully plan state migrations
using appropriate Terraform state commands or configuration
techniques.

</div>

</div>


<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING DATA -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 30. Data Source Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Error:</strong>

Terraform cannot find the requested AMI, VPC or subnet.

<br><br>

Check:

<ul>
<li>AWS region</li>
<li>Account</li>
<li>Filters</li>
<li>Tags</li>
<li>Resource state</li>
<li>Permissions</li>
</ul>

</div>

<pre><code>terraform plan

terraform providers

aws sts get-caller-identity

aws configure list</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- BEST PRACTICES -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Advanced Terraform Best Practices</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use data sources for existing infrastructure.</li>
<li>Use locals for reusable calculated values.</li>
<li>Use variables for external inputs.</li>
<li>Prefer for_each when resources have meaningful identities.</li>
<li>Use count when numeric repetition is appropriate.</li>
<li>Prefer implicit dependencies through references.</li>
<li>Use depends_on only when necessary.</li>
<li>Use dynamic blocks only when they improve maintainability.</li>
<li>Treat provisioners as a last resort.</li>
<li>Keep expressions readable.</li>
<li>Validate inputs where appropriate.</li>
<li>Review terraform plan before production apply.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Advanced Terraform Concepts"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Terraform provides several features that help us build reusable and
dynamic infrastructure.

I use Data Sources when I need to retrieve existing infrastructure,
such as an existing VPC or the latest suitable AMI, instead of
creating it again.

I use locals for reusable calculated values such as common tags, and
functions and expressions to transform values or implement
conditional logic.

For creating multiple resources, I use count when numeric repetition
is sufficient and for_each when resources have meaningful keys.

Terraform automatically creates dependencies when resources reference
each other. I use depends_on only when an explicit dependency cannot
be inferred.

Dynamic blocks can generate repeated nested configuration, while
provisioners are treated as a last resort because Terraform is
primarily designed for declarative infrastructure management.

These features help make Terraform configurations reusable,
maintainable and suitable for real-world DevOps environments."

</div>

<h1>Terraform <span>Basics</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused Terraform foundation covering Infrastructure as Code,

<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Terraform in One Picture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Configuration
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>terraform init</strong>

â†“

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Instead of manually creating an AWS VPC, subnets, EC2 instances and
security groups through the AWS Console, Terraform can define the
infrastructure as code.

The same Terraform code can then be reused for Dev, QA and Production
with different variables.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Terraform?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool used to define,
provision and manage infrastructure using declarative configuration
files.

It can manage resources across cloud providers and many other
platforms through providers.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Terraform is a declarative Infrastructure as Code tool. We define
the desired infrastructure in configuration files, and Terraform
creates and manages the required resources by comparing the desired
state with the current state."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why Terraform?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Infrastructure can be managed as code.</li>
<li>Infrastructure changes can be version controlled.</li>
<li>Reduces manual configuration.</li>
<li>Provides repeatable infrastructure.</li>
<li>Supports multiple providers.</li>
<li>Supports planning before applying changes.</li>
<li>Helps maintain consistent environments.</li>
<li>Supports reusable modules.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

A company needs the same VPC architecture in Dev, QA and Production.

Instead of manually creating resources three times, the team creates
Terraform code once and supplies environment-specific variables.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is Infrastructure as Code?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Infrastructure as Code means defining infrastructure using
machine-readable configuration files instead of manually creating
resources through a graphical console.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Manual Infrastructure</th>
<th>Infrastructure as Code</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Manual console operations</td>
<td>Configuration files</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Difficult to reproduce exactly</td>
<td>Repeatable</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Harder to review changes</td>
<td>Can use Git</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Higher chance of human error</td>
<td>Automation reduces manual work</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Declarative vs Imperative</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform is primarily <strong>declarative</strong>.

You describe what the desired final infrastructure should look like,
rather than writing every individual command required to create it.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

Instead of saying:

"Create subnet â†’ then create route table â†’ then attach route table"

Terraform configuration declares the desired resources and their
relationships.

Terraform determines the actions needed to reach that state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Terraform Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Configuration
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Core
<br>
â†“
<br>
Provider Plugin
<br>
â†“
<br>
Cloud / API
<br>
â†“
<br>
Infrastructure

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Terraform Core</strong> reads configuration, state and
dependency information and determines the required changes.

<br><br>

<strong>Provider</strong> acts as the integration layer between
Terraform and an external platform such as AWS, Azure or GCP.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Provider?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A provider is a Terraform plugin that allows Terraform to interact
with an external API or platform.

</div>

<h3>AWS Provider Example</h3>

<pre><code>terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "ap-south-1"
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Here Terraform uses the AWS provider to communicate with AWS APIs
and manage resources such as VPCs, EC2 instances, IAM resources and
many others.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is a Resource?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A resource represents an infrastructure object that Terraform creates,
updates or manages.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app_bucket" {

  bucket = "my-company-demo-bucket"

}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Here:

<code>aws_s3_bucket</code> = resource type

<br>

<code>app_bucket</code> = local Terraform name

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Basic Terraform File Structure</h2>

<pre><code>terraform-project/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ main.tf
â”œâ”€â”€ variables.tf
â”œâ”€â”€ outputs.tf
â”œâ”€â”€ providers.tf
â”œâ”€â”€ terraform.tfvars
â””â”€â”€ .terraform.lock.hcl</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>File</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<td>main.tf</td>
<td>Main infrastructure resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>variables.tf</td>
<td>Variable declarations.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>outputs.tf</td>
<td>Important values exposed after deployment.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>providers.tf</td>
<td>Provider configuration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>terraform.tfvars</td>
<td>Values assigned to variables.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>.terraform.lock.hcl</td>
<td>Records selected provider dependency versions and checksums.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“
<br>

<br>â†“
<br>

<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. terraform init</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>terraform init</code> initializes the working directory.

It downloads required providers and prepares Terraform for further
operations.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform init</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>When do you run it?</strong>

Usually when starting a Terraform project, after changing provider
requirements, or when initializing a copied/cloned configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. terraform validate</h2>

<div class="answer">

Validates the syntax and internal consistency of Terraform
configuration.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform validate</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

It helps detect configuration problems before creating infrastructure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. terraform plan</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform plan shows the proposed changes before Terraform applies
them.

It compares the configuration and current state and determines what
actions are required.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time:</strong>

Before production deployment, a DevOps engineer runs
<code>terraform plan</code> and reviews whether Terraform will create,
modify or destroy important resources.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. terraform apply</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform apply executes the planned changes and creates, updates or
destroys infrastructure as required.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

<p>
Terraform normally asks for confirmation before applying changes
unless automatic approval is explicitly provided.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. terraform destroy</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform destroy removes resources managed by the current Terraform
configuration and state.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform destroy</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Never blindly run <code>terraform destroy</code> against a production
workspace or state.

Review the proposed changes carefully.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Variables</h2>

<div class="answer">

Variables make Terraform configurations reusable by allowing values
to be supplied from outside the resource definition.

</div>

<h3>variables.tf</h3>

<pre><code>variable "aws_region" {
  description = "AWS region"
  type        = string
  default     = "ap-south-1"
}</code></pre>

<h3>Usage</h3>

<pre><code>provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. terraform.tfvars</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <code>.tfvars</code> file can provide values for Terraform input
variables.

</div>

<pre><code>aws_region = "ap-south-1"

project_name = "nandu-project"

instance_type = "t3.micro"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

The same Terraform code can use different variable values for
different environments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Outputs</h2>

<div class="answer">

Outputs expose useful values from Terraform after resources are
created.

</div>

<pre><code>output "instance_public_ip" {
  description = "Public IP of EC2 instance"
  value       = aws_instance.app.public_ip
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

In a real project, outputs can expose values such as load balancer
DNS names, VPC IDs, subnet IDs or instance addresses.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Terraform State</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state records information about resources Terraform manages
and helps Terraform determine the relationship between configuration
and real infrastructure.

The default local state file is:

<code>terraform.tfstate</code>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Terraform state can contain sensitive information depending on the
resources being managed.

Do not casually commit <code>terraform.tfstate</code> to Git.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Why is Terraform State Important?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform uses state to understand what resources it manages and to
determine what changes are required during planning.

Without correct state management, collaboration and infrastructure
tracking become difficult.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Configuration
<br>
+
<br>
Terraform State
<br>
+
<br>
Real Infrastructure
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Plan

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Local State vs Remote State</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Local State</th>
<th>Remote State</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stored on local machine.</td>
<td>Stored in shared remote backend.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple for learning.</td>
<td>Better suited for team collaboration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Risk of loss if not backed up.</td>
<td>Can provide centralized storage and locking depending on backend.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

For a production team, remote state is generally preferred so team
members and CI/CD systems can work with a shared source of Terraform
state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Terraform Backend</h2>

<div class="answer">

A backend determines where Terraform state is stored and, depending
on the backend, how state locking and related operations are handled.

</div>

<h3>AWS S3 Backend Example</h3>

<pre><code>terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "company-terraform-state"
    key    = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

The exact backend configuration should follow your organization's
current Terraform and AWS design, including appropriate state
protection and locking strategy.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. What is Idempotency?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Idempotency means repeatedly applying the same desired configuration
should not continuously create duplicate resources.

Terraform checks the current state and determines whether changes
are actually required.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If an EC2 instance already matches the Terraform configuration,
running plan/apply again should normally result in no unnecessary
change.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Dependency Management</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform builds a dependency graph to determine the order in which
resources should be created, changed or destroyed.

</div>

<h3>Implicit dependency</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_subnet" "app" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
}</code></pre>

<p>
Terraform understands that the subnet depends on the VPC because the
VPC ID is referenced.
</p>

<h3>Explicit dependency</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  depends_on = [
    aws_iam_role.app
  ]

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. terraform fmt</h2>

<div class="answer">

Formats Terraform configuration files according to Terraform's
standard formatting conventions.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform fmt

terraform fmt -recursive</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Important Terraform Commands</h2>

<pre><code>terraform init

terraform validate

terraform fmt

terraform plan

terraform apply

terraform destroy

terraform show

terraform output

terraform state list

terraform state show &lt;resource&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Terraform vs CloudFormation</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Terraform</th>
<th>AWS CloudFormation</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Multi-provider IaC tool</td>
<td>AWS-native IaC service</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses HCL</td>
<td>Uses YAML/JSON</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Terraform state is important</td>
<td>AWS manages CloudFormation stack state</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Works across AWS, Azure, GCP and other providers</td>
<td>Primarily AWS focused</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

Terraform is often preferred when an organization wants one IaC
tool across multiple providers.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Terraform vs Ansible</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Terraform</th>
<th>Ansible</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Primarily infrastructure provisioning and management</td>
<td>Primarily configuration management and automation</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Declarative infrastructure model</td>
<td>Automation/playbook model</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses state</td>
<td>Does not use Terraform-style infrastructure state</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates cloud resources</td>
<td>Configures systems/applications</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time combination:</strong>

Terraform creates the AWS infrastructure.

Ansible can then configure operating systems and applications on
those instances.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Terraform Lifecycle</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>lifecycle</code> block allows control over certain resource
change behaviors.

</div>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  # resource configuration

  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Common lifecycle arguments include:

<br><br>

<code>create_before_destroy</code>

<br>

<code>prevent_destroy</code>

<br>

<code>ignore_changes</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. What is Drift?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Drift occurs when the real infrastructure is changed outside
Terraform and no longer matches what Terraform configuration and
state expect.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

Terraform created an EC2 security group allowing port 443.

Someone manually changes the security group in the AWS Console.

Now the real infrastructure differs from the Terraform-managed
configuration.

Running:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

can reveal changes Terraform wants to make to reconcile the
infrastructure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Real-Time Terraform Workflow</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A company needs:

<br>

<br>
â€¢ Public subnets
<br>
â€¢ Private subnets
<br>
â€¢ Internet Gateway

<br>
â€¢ Load Balancer
<br>
â€¢ Application instances
<br>
â€¢ Database

<br><br>

The DevOps engineer defines the infrastructure in Terraform.

</div>

<div class="flow">

</div>

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Terraform"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Terraform is a declarative Infrastructure as Code tool used to
provision and manage infrastructure.

We define the desired infrastructure using Terraform configuration
files. Terraform uses providers to communicate with platforms such
as AWS.

The typical workflow is terraform init, validate, plan and apply.

Terraform maintains state so it can understand the resources it
manages and determine the changes required to reach the desired
state.

In a real-time DevOps environment, I can use Terraform to provision
AWS networking, compute, security and other infrastructure in a
repeatable and version-controlled way.

For team environments, I would use remote state with appropriate
access control and state-protection practices, and I would review
terraform plan output before applying production changes."

</div>

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Terraform?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Terraform</strong> is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool
used to define, provision and manage infrastructure using
declarative configuration files.

Instead of manually creating AWS resources through the console,
we define the desired infrastructure in code and Terraform
creates or updates it.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Code
<br>â†“<br>
Terraform Plan
<br>â†“<br>
Review Changes
<br>â†“<br>
Terraform Apply
<br>â†“<br>
Cloud Infrastructure

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Instead of manually creating a VPC, subnets, security groups and
EC2 instances in AWS, I can define them in Terraform and create
the same architecture repeatedly.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why Terraform?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Infrastructure as Code</li>
<li>Repeatable infrastructure</li>
<li>Version control through Git</li>
<li>Automation</li>
<li>Consistent environments</li>
<li>Reusable modules</li>
<li>Change preview using plan</li>
<li>Works with multiple providers</li>
<li>Suitable for CI/CD automation</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview wording:</strong>

"Terraform helps us provision and manage infrastructure
consistently through code. It provides repeatability, version
control, automation and a clear plan of infrastructure changes."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Declarative vs Imperative</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Declarative</th>
<th>Imperative</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Defines the desired end state.</td>
<td>Defines step-by-step instructions.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Terraform</td>
<td>Traditional scripts</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Terraform determines required actions.</td>
<td>User explicitly specifies actions.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

Terraform is primarily <strong>declarative</strong>.

You describe what infrastructure should look like and Terraform
determines how to reach that state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Terraform Core Workflow</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Write</strong>

<br>â†“<br>
<strong>terraform validate</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>terraform plan</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>terraform apply</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>terraform destroy</strong> when intentionally required

</div>

<pre><code>terraform init
terraform fmt
terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply</code></pre>

</div>

<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Provider</h2>

<div class="answer">

A provider is a Terraform plugin that allows Terraform to interact
with an external platform such as AWS, Azure, GCP or Kubernetes.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "ap-south-1"
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The provider translates Terraform resource configuration into API
operations for the target platform.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Resource</h2>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

  tags = {
    Name = "web-server"
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

A resource represents an infrastructure object that Terraform
manages.

Examples include EC2, S3, VPC, IAM role, security group and load
balancer.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Variables</h2>

<pre><code>variable "instance_type" {
  description = "EC2 instance type"
  type        = string
  default     = "t3.micro"
}</code></pre>

<p>Use the variable:</p>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  instance_type = var.instance_type
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Variables make Terraform configurations reusable and reduce
hard-coded values.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 9. Variable Types</h2>

<pre><code>variable "name" {
  type = string
}

variable "count" {
  type = number
}

variable "enabled" {
  type = bool
}

variable "ports" {
  type = list(number)
}

variable "tags" {
  type = map(string)
}

variable "config" {
  type = object({
    environment = string
    region      = string
  })
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. tfvars</h2>

<pre><code>instance_type = "t3.medium"
environment   = "production"</code></pre>

Terraform can automatically load:

<pre><code>terraform.tfvars
*.auto.tfvars</code></pre>

Or explicitly:

<pre><code>terraform plan -var-file="prod.tfvars"</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Locals</h2>

<pre><code>locals {
  project_name = "payment-app"

  common_tags = {
    Project     = local.project_name
    Environment = "production"
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Locals are useful for calculated or reusable expressions inside
a Terraform configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Outputs</h2>

<pre><code>output "instance_id" {
  value = aws_instance.web.id
}

output "public_ip" {
  value = aws_instance.web.public_ip
}</code></pre>

Run:

<pre><code>terraform output</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Outputs expose useful values after Terraform creates infrastructure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. Data Sources</h2>

<div class="answer">

Data sources allow Terraform to read existing information without
creating that resource.

</div>

<pre><code>data "aws_ami" "amazon_linux" {
  most_recent = true

  owners = ["amazon"]
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Instead of hard-coding an AMI ID, Terraform can query for a suitable
AMI dynamically.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Terraform State</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state is Terraform's record of the infrastructure it
manages and the relationship between configuration and real-world
resources.

Common file:

<pre><code>terraform.tfstate</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not commit production Terraform state files to Git.

State may contain sensitive infrastructure information.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Local vs Remote State</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Local State</th>
<th>Remote State</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stored locally</td>
<td>Stored in a shared backend</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Suitable mainly for simple/local use</td>
<td>Better for teams and CI/CD</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Difficult collaboration</td>
<td>Centralized access</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Limited locking depending on setup</td>
<td>Can support state locking depending on backend</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Remote Backend</h2>

<pre><code>terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "company-terraform-state"
    key    = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

A remote backend allows a team or CI/CD system to work with
centralized Terraform state.

The backend should be secured with appropriate access controls,
encryption and recovery mechanisms.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. State Locking</h2>

<div class="answer">

State locking prevents multiple Terraform operations from modifying
the same state simultaneously when the selected backend supports
locking.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If another Terraform process is already using the state, a second
operation should not blindly modify it.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Never use force-unlock simply because Terraform reports a lock.
First confirm that the lock is stale and no active operation is
running.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Terraform Plan</h2>

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Plan compares the desired configuration with the current state and
provider information and shows proposed changes before apply.

Typical symbols:

<pre><code>+   create
-   destroy
~   update
-/+ replace</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Terraform Apply</h2>

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Apply executes the approved changes required to make the actual
infrastructure match the desired configuration.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

In production, apply should normally happen through a controlled
workflow with review and appropriate approvals.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Terraform Destroy</h2>

<pre><code>terraform destroy</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Destroy removes resources managed by the selected Terraform
configuration.

Never run it blindly against production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Modules</h2>

<div class="answer">

A module is a reusable collection of Terraform configuration.

</div>

<pre><code>module "vpc" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"

  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
}</code></pre>

Example structure:

<pre><code>terraform/
â”œâ”€â”€ modules/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ vpc/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ ec2/
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ security/
â”‚
â””â”€â”€ environments/
    â”œâ”€â”€ dev/
    â”œâ”€â”€ qa/
    â””â”€â”€ prod/</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. count vs for_each</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>count</th>
<th>for_each</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for indexed identical resources.</td>
<td>Good for uniquely identified resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>resource[0]</code></td>
<td><code>resource["web"]</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  count = 2

  ami           = var.ami
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
}</code></pre>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  for_each = {
    web = "t3.micro"
    api = "t3.small"
  }

  ami           = var.ami
  instance_type = each.value
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. depends_on</h2>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  depends_on = [
    aws_iam_role_policy.app
  ]

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Terraform normally creates dependencies automatically when one
resource references another. <code>depends_on</code> is useful when
the dependency cannot be inferred from an expression.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 24. Lifecycle Rules</h2>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "web" {

  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true

    prevent_destroy = true

    ignore_changes = [
      tags
    ]
  }

}</code></pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Rule</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>create_before_destroy</td>
<td>Create replacement before destroying old resource when supported.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>prevent_destroy</td>
<td>Protect against Terraform destroying the resource.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ignore_changes</td>
<td>Ignore selected configuration differences.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 25. Provisioners</h2>

<div class="answer">

Provisioners allow Terraform to perform actions such as running
commands after resource creation.

However, they should generally be avoided when a better native
resource, cloud-init/user-data, configuration-management tool or
other approach exists.

</div>

<pre><code>provisioner "local-exec" {
  command = "echo Instance created"
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Provisioners can make infrastructure less predictable and harder to
maintain.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Terraform Import</h2>

<div class="scenario">

An EC2 instance already exists in AWS but is not managed by
Terraform.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform import aws_instance.web i-0123456789abcdef0</code></pre>

Then:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Import associates an existing real-world resource with a Terraform
resource address. Configuration should then be aligned with the
actual resource.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Terraform Drift</h2>

<div class="answer">

Drift occurs when infrastructure is changed outside Terraform.

Example:

Terraform says:

<pre><code>instance_type = "t3.micro"</code></pre>

Someone manually changes AWS to:

<pre><code>t3.medium</code></pre>

Run:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

to identify the difference.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. State Commands</h2>

<pre><code>terraform state list

terraform state show &lt;resource&gt;

terraform state mv &lt;old&gt; &lt;new&gt;

terraform state rm &lt;resource&gt;

terraform show</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

State manipulation is powerful. Always understand the effect before
changing production state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. State Rename</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Resource address changes from:

<pre><code>aws_instance.web</code></pre>

to:

<pre><code>aws_instance.frontend</code></pre>

</div>

<pre><code>terraform state mv \
  aws_instance.web \
  aws_instance.frontend</code></pre>

This tells Terraform that the address changed while the underlying
managed object is intended to remain the same.

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Terraform Validation & Formatting</h2>

<pre><code>terraform fmt

terraform validate</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>fmt</strong> formats Terraform files.

<strong>validate</strong> checks whether the configuration is
syntactically valid and internally consistent for the initialized
configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 31 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Terraform CI/CD</h2>

<div class="flow">

Git Push
<br>â†“<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“<br>
terraform fmt
<br>â†“<br>
terraform validate
<br>â†“<br>
terraform plan
<br>â†“<br>
Review
<br>â†“<br>
Approval
<br>â†“<br>
terraform apply
<br>â†“<br>
Verify Infrastructure

</div>

<div class="answer">

This workflow provides version control, automated validation,
reviewable plans, approvals and auditability.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 32 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Terraform Security</h2>

<ul>
<li>Do not commit secrets to Git.</li>
<li>Protect remote state.</li>
<li>Encrypt state at rest where supported.</li>
<li>Use least-privilege IAM.</li>
<li>Use short-lived credentials where possible.</li>
<li>Protect CI/CD credentials.</li>
<li>Enable secret scanning.</li>
<li>Restrict production access.</li>
<li>Review destructive plans.</li>
<li>Maintain state backups/recovery mechanisms.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 33 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Terraform State and Secrets</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state can contain sensitive information depending on the
resources and expressions being managed.

Therefore state should be treated as sensitive infrastructure data.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not assume that marking an output as sensitive means the value
cannot exist in state. Sensitive values may still be stored in the
state required by Terraform.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 34 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Existing Resource Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Terraform says a resource already exists.

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Import the existing resource, inspect the configuration and state,
then run a plan.

<pre><code>terraform import &lt;address&gt; &lt;id&gt;

terraform plan</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 35 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 35. Apply Failed Halfway</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Never assume everything was rolled back.

Check:

<pre><code>terraform plan
terraform state list
terraform show</code></pre>

Fix the root cause and run the plan again.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Terraform records successful operations in state, so after resolving
the error it can usually continue toward the desired state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 36 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 36. AWS Authentication Troubleshooting</h2>

<pre><code>aws sts get-caller-identity

aws configure list

aws configure get region

terraform plan</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>
<li>Credentials</li>
<li>IAM role/user</li>
<li>Expired credentials</li>
<li>Profile</li>
<li>Region</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 37 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 37. Terraform Works Locally but Fails in CI</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would compare:

<ul>
<li>Terraform version</li>
<li>Provider versions</li>
<li>AWS credentials</li>
<li>AWS profile</li>
<li>AWS region</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Variable files</li>
<li>Backend</li>
<li>Working directory</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 38 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 38. Dev / QA / Production</h2>

<div class="flow">

Reusable Modules
<br>â†“<br>
Dev State
<br>â†“<br>
QA State
<br>â†“<br>
Production State

</div>

<div class="answer">

Keep environment state isolated so a Dev operation cannot
accidentally modify Production.

The exact implementation can use separate root configurations,
workspaces or other environment-management approaches depending on
the organization's requirements.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 39 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 39. Workspace</h2>

<pre><code>terraform workspace list

terraform workspace new dev

terraform workspace select dev

terraform workspace show</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Workspaces allow multiple state instances for the same configuration.
They can be useful in some scenarios, but teams should not assume
workspaces alone provide all environment isolation or security
controls required for production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 40 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 40. Provider Version Locking</h2>

Terraform creates a dependency lock file:

<pre><code>.terraform.lock.hcl</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The lock file records selected provider versions and checksums so
different machines and CI environments can use consistent provider
versions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 41 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 41. Terraform Version Management</h2>

<pre><code>terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6, < 2.0"
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Version constraints help ensure the project is executed with a
compatible Terraform version.

Teams should also standardize the version used by developers and
CI/CD.

</div>

</div>
