<!-- 46 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸš¨ 46. Common Terraform Mistakes</h2>

<ul>
<li>Running apply without reviewing the plan.</li>
<li>Storing state in Git.</li>
<li>Hard-coding credentials.</li>
<li>Using AdministratorAccess unnecessarily.</li>
<li>Ignoring state locking.</li>
<li>Blindly using force-unlock.</li>
<li>Using provisioners for everything.</li>
<li>Creating one huge Terraform configuration.</li>
<li>Mixing production and development state.</li>
<li>Ignoring provider version changes.</li>
<li>Running destructive commands against production.</li>
<li>Ignoring drift.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 47 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ 47. "Explain Terraform" â€” Interview Answer</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool that allows us to
define and manage infrastructure using declarative configuration.

I use Terraform to provision resources such as VPCs, subnets,
security groups, EC2 instances, IAM resources and other cloud
components.

The normal workflow is terraform init, validate, plan and apply.

Terraform maintains state to track the relationship between the
configuration and real infrastructure. In a team environment I
prefer a secure remote backend with appropriate state protection and
locking.

I use variables, outputs, locals and reusable modules to make the
configuration maintainable.

For production, infrastructure changes go through Git and CI/CD.
The pipeline validates the code, generates a plan and applies
approved changes.

I also handle real-time situations such as drift, importing
existing resources, state issues, authentication failures and
failed deployments.

The main benefit is repeatable, version-controlled and automated
infrastructure management."

</div>

</div>

<li>â˜‘ Resources</li>
<li>â˜‘ Variables</li>
<li>â˜‘ tfvars</li>
<li>â˜‘ Locals</li>
<li>â˜‘ Outputs</li>
<li>â˜‘ Data sources</li>
<li>â˜‘ State</li>
<li>â˜‘ Remote backend</li>
<li>â˜‘ State locking</li>
<li>â˜‘ Modules</li>
<li>â˜‘ count / for_each</li>
<li>â˜‘ depends_on</li>
<li>â˜‘ lifecycle</li>
<li>â˜‘ provisioners</li>
<li>â˜‘ Import</li>
<li>â˜‘ State commands</li>
<li>â˜‘ Drift</li>

<li>â˜‘ Security</li>
<li>â˜‘ AWS troubleshooting</li>
<li>â˜‘ Production scenarios</li>
<li>â˜‘ Interview answers</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Final goal:</strong>

You should be able to explain not only "what Terraform is", but also
<strong>how you would use Terraform safely in a real production
DevOps environment.</strong>

</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Terraform</a>

<h1>Terraform <span>Real-Time Scenarios</span></h1>

<p>
Production-style Terraform interview scenarios covering state,
drift, imports, failed deployments, AWS authentication,
dependencies, locking, modules, CI/CD and disaster recovery.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ How to Approach Terraform Scenarios</h2>

<p>
In a real DevOps interview, the interviewer may not ask only
definitions. They may describe a production problem and ask what
you would do.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Understand the Problem
<br>â†“<br>
Check Terraform State
<br>â†“<br>
Check Cloud Infrastructure
<br>â†“<br>
Identify Configuration vs State Difference
<br>â†“<br>
Run <strong>terraform plan</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Fix Safely
<br>â†“<br>
Review Plan
<br>â†“<br>
Apply
<br>â†“<br>
Verify

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Terraform says Resource Already Exists</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong>

An AWS S3 bucket was manually created in AWS.

Later, you add the same bucket to Terraform.

When you run:

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

Terraform reports that the resource already exists.

</div>

<h3>Why?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Terraform does not know that the existing AWS resource should be
managed by this Terraform configuration because it is not currently
represented in Terraform state.

</div>

<h3>Solution</h3>

<pre><code>terraform import aws_s3_bucket.app existing-bucket-name</code></pre>

Then:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I would import the existing resource into Terraform state rather
than trying to recreate it. Then I would run terraform plan and
align the Terraform configuration with the actual infrastructure."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Infrastructure was changed manually</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A developer manually changes an EC2 instance type from:

<pre><code>t3.micro</code></pre>

to:

<pre><code>t3.medium</code></pre>

But the Terraform configuration still contains:

<pre><code>instance_type = "t3.micro"</code></pre>

</div>

<h3>What happens?</h3>

<div class="answer">

Terraform refreshes its knowledge of infrastructure and compares
the actual infrastructure with the desired configuration.

The plan may show a change required to return the instance to the
configuration defined in Terraform.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

This is an example of <strong>configuration drift</strong>.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is Terraform Drift?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Drift occurs when the real infrastructure changes outside Terraform
and becomes different from what Terraform configuration and state
expect.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Configuration
<br>â†“
<br>
Desired State
<br>â‰ 
<br>
Actual AWS Infrastructure
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Drift</strong>

</div>

<h3>How do you detect it?</h3>

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Someone manually changes a security group rule in AWS Console.

Terraform detects the difference during planning and may propose
changing the infrastructure back to the desired configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Terraform Apply Failed Halfway</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose Terraform is creating:

<ul>
<li>VPC</li>
<li>Subnets</li>
<li>Security Groups</li>
<li>EC2</li>
<li>Load Balancer</li>
</ul>

The apply fails while creating the Load Balancer.

</div>

<div class="answer">

I would not immediately delete everything.

First I would inspect the error and state:

<pre><code>terraform plan
terraform state list
terraform show</code></pre>

Terraform tracks successfully created resources in state.

After fixing the root cause, I would run:

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

Terraform should continue toward the desired state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Terraform State Lock Error</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Two engineers or CI/CD jobs try to run Terraform against the same
remote state at the same time.

Terraform reports that the state is locked.

</div>

<div class="answer">

The lock protects the state from concurrent modifications.

First check whether another legitimate Terraform operation is
currently running.

Do not blindly force-unlock a state that another process is using.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform plan
terraform apply</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Use <code>terraform force-unlock</code> only when you have verified
that the lock is stale and no active Terraform operation is using
the state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Two Engineers Run Terraform Apply</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Engineer A runs:

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

At the same time Engineer B runs:

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

against the same environment.

</div>

<div class="answer">

With a properly configured remote backend that supports state
locking, one operation should acquire the lock while the other waits
or fails with a lock-related message.

</div>

<div class="interview">

In production, Terraform should generally use a shared remote state
with locking rather than independent local state files.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Terraform AWS Authentication Error</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Terraform returns an AWS authentication error such as:

<pre><code>InvalidClientTokenId</code></pre>

</div>

<h3>What would you check?</h3>

<ol>
<li>Configured AWS credentials</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>AWS profile</li>
<li>Credential expiration</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
<li>AWS region</li>
<li>STS identity</li>
</ol>

<pre><code>aws sts get-caller-identity

aws configure list

terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

I would first verify which AWS identity Terraform is using before
changing the Terraform configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Wrong AWS Region</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Terraform expects an AMI or resource in:

<pre><code>ap-south-1</code></pre>

but the data source or provider is configured for another region.

</div>

<h3>Check provider</h3>

<pre><code>provider "aws" {
  region = "ap-south-1"
}</code></pre>

<h3>Verify AWS CLI</h3>

<pre><code>aws configure get region</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

AWS resources such as AMIs are often region-specific. A valid AMI
ID in one region may not exist in another.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Terraform Plan Wants to Destroy a Resource</h2>

<div class="scenario">

You run:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

and see:

<pre><code>-/+ resource</code></pre>

or Terraform proposes destroying a production resource.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Do not blindly run <code>terraform apply</code>.

First identify why Terraform wants to replace it.

Check:

<ul>
<li>Changed immutable argument</li>
<li>Resource address changed</li>
<li>count / for_each changes</li>
<li>State mismatch</li>
<li>Manual infrastructure changes</li>
<li>Provider behavior</li>
<li>Configuration changes</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Production destruction should always be reviewed carefully before
approval.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Terraform State File Lost</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose a local <code>terraform.tfstate</code> file is accidentally
deleted.

</div>

<div class="answer">

If the project uses a remote backend, the state should be retrieved
from the backend rather than relying on a local copy.

If there is no remote state and no backup, recovery becomes much more
difficult because Terraform has lost its record of managed
resources.

</div>

<div class="interview">

This is one reason remote state, locking and state backups are
important for production Terraform environments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Someone Deleted an AWS Resource Manually</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Terraform state contains an EC2 instance, but an administrator
deleted that EC2 instance manually from AWS.

</div>

<h3>What happens?</h3>

<div class="answer">

During planning/refresh, Terraform can detect that the object no
longer exists and may propose creating it again to satisfy the
configuration.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Terraform's goal is to reconcile infrastructure toward the desired
configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Terraform Resource Was Renamed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Original:

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ...
}</code></pre>

Changed to:

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "frontend" {
  ...
}</code></pre>

Terraform may interpret the change as one resource being removed and
another being created.

</div>

<div class="answer">

If the rename is intended to represent the same real infrastructure,
use an appropriate state move so Terraform understands the address
changed.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform state mv \
  aws_instance.web \
  aws_instance.frontend</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Always review the state operation and resulting plan before applying
changes to important infrastructure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. count Changed to for_each</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Original resource address:

<pre><code>aws_instance.app[0]</code></pre>

After changing configuration to <code>for_each</code>:

<pre><code>aws_instance.app["web"]</code></pre>

Terraform may think the old resource and new resource are different.

</div>

<div class="answer">

The state addresses need to be handled carefully so the existing
resource can be associated with the new address rather than
unnecessarily recreated.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform plan
terraform state list</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. Terraform Module Change</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A production environment uses a reusable VPC module.

You update the module to change subnet configuration.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Before applying:

<pre><code>terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan</code></pre>

Review exactly which resources will change.

Module changes can affect many resources, so the plan should be
carefully reviewed before production deployment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Dev, QA and Production Architecture</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A company has three environments:

<ul>
<li>Development</li>
<li>QA</li>
<li>Production</li>
</ul>

The infrastructure code should be reusable.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Reusable Terraform Modules
<br>â†“<br>
Dev Configuration
<br>â†“<br>
QA Configuration
<br>â†“<br>
Production Configuration

</div>

<div class="answer">

Common approaches include separate root configurations, separate
state per environment and reusable modules.

The key requirement is to prevent one environment's state from
being accidentally applied to another environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Terraform CI/CD Pipeline</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Push
<br>â†“<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“<br>
Terraform fmt
<br>â†“<br>
Terraform validate
<br>â†“<br>
Terraform plan
<br>â†“<br>
Review / Approval
<br>â†“<br>
Terraform apply
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Infrastructure

</div>

<div class="interview">

A production pipeline should separate plan and apply appropriately,
protect credentials, use remote state and require approval for
sensitive changes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Terraform Plan in CI but Apply Locally</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A team generates a Terraform plan in CI but then manually runs
<code>terraform apply</code> from a laptop.

</div>

<div class="answer">

This creates governance and reproducibility concerns.

A better production workflow is to keep the plan/apply process in a
controlled CI/CD environment with:

<ul>
<li>Protected credentials</li>
<li>Remote state</li>
<li>Approvals</li>
<li>Auditing</li>
<li>Consistent Terraform version</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Terraform Secret Accidentally Committed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

An AWS access key or database password is committed to Git.

</div>

<h3>Immediate response</h3>

<ol>
<li>Assume the credential is compromised.</li>
<li>Revoke or rotate it immediately.</li>
<li>Check where it was exposed.</li>
<li>Remove the secret from active configuration.</li>
<li>Clean repository history when necessary.</li>
<li>Enable secret scanning.</li>
<li>Use a secure secret-management solution.</li>
</ol>

<div class="warning">

Deleting the secret from the latest commit is not sufficient if it
remains in Git history.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Terraform State Contains Sensitive Information</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state can contain sensitive infrastructure information and
sometimes values that should not be broadly exposed.

Therefore state should be protected like sensitive infrastructure
data.

</div>

<h3>Best practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Use a secure remote backend.</li>
<li>Restrict access using IAM/RBAC.</li>
<li>Enable encryption at rest.</li>
<li>Use state locking where supported.</li>
<li>Do not commit state files to Git.</li>
<li>Restrict CI/CD access.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Terraform Backend Configuration</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A team wants multiple engineers and CI/CD systems to work with the
same infrastructure.

Instead of local state, they configure a remote backend.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "company-terraform-state"
    key    = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The exact backend configuration depends on the organization's
security, locking and operational requirements.

The important design principle is centralized, protected state with
controlled access.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 21. Provider Version Changed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A team updates the AWS provider version.

After running:

<pre><code>terraform init -upgrade</code></pre>

the plan changes unexpectedly.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Provider upgrades can change behavior, schemas or resource handling.

Before production rollout:

<ol>
<li>Review release notes.</li>
<li>Test in a lower environment.</li>
<li>Run terraform validate.</li>
<li>Run terraform plan.</li>
<li>Review the changes carefully.</li>
<li>Promote through environments.</li>
</ol>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Terraform Version Mismatch</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Developer uses one Terraform version while CI/CD uses another.

This can produce inconsistent behavior.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Pin and standardize the Terraform version for the project.

Example:

<pre><code>terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6, < 2.0"
}</code></pre>

Teams may use version managers or CI images to keep execution
consistent.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. Terraform Destroy in Production</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Someone accidentally runs:

<pre><code>terraform destroy</code></pre>

against the production configuration.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Production Terraform should have strong controls.

Examples:

<ul>
<li>Separate production credentials.</li>
<li>Restricted permissions.</li>
<li>Protected CI/CD workflows.</li>
<li>Manual approvals.</li>
<li>Clear environment separation.</li>
<li>Careful review of plans.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not rely only on a human remembering not to run
<code>terraform destroy</code>. Production access should be designed
to reduce the possibility and impact of mistakes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. AWS IAM Permission Denied</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Terraform returns:

<pre><code>AccessDenied</code></pre>

</div>

<h3>Debugging flow</h3>

<pre><code>aws sts get-caller-identity

aws configure list

terraform plan</code></pre>

<p>
Then identify the AWS API action Terraform attempted and verify that
the executing IAM role or user has the required permissions.
</p>

<div class="interview">

Do not solve IAM errors by blindly attaching
<code>AdministratorAccess</code>. Grant the minimum required
permissions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Dependency Problem</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Terraform creates an application before a required policy or
supporting resource is ready.

</div>

<div class="answer">

First check whether the dependency can be represented naturally by
referencing the required resource.

Example:

<pre><code>role = aws_iam_role.app.arn</code></pre>

This creates an implicit dependency.

Only if Terraform cannot infer the relationship should you consider:

<pre><code>depends_on = [
  aws_iam_role_policy.app
]</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 26. Terraform Configuration Works Locally but Fails in CI</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Local:

<pre><code>terraform plan
```

works.

CI:

<pre><code>terraform plan
```

fails.

</div>

<h3>Check differences</h3>

<ul>
<li>Terraform version</li>
<li>Provider versions</li>
<li>AWS credentials</li>
<li>AWS region</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Backend configuration</li>
<li>Working directory</li>
<li>Variable files</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

A reliable CI environment should explicitly define its Terraform
version, credentials, variables and backend configuration rather
than depending on a developer's local machine.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Production Terraform Change Workflow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Create Branch
<br>â†“<br>
Modify Terraform
<br>â†“<br>
terraform fmt
<br>â†“<br>
terraform validate
<br>â†“<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“<br>
CI Checks
<br>â†“<br>
terraform plan
<br>â†“<br>
Review
<br>â†“<br>
Approval
<br>â†“<br>
terraform apply
<br>â†“<br>
Verify AWS
<br>â†“<br>
Monitor

</div>

<div class="interview">

This provides reviewability, consistency and auditability for
production infrastructure changes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Disaster Recovery for Terraform</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose the Terraform backend or state becomes unavailable.

</div>

<div class="answer">

A production setup should have:

<ul>
<li>Remote state</li>
<li>Encryption</li>
<li>State versioning / backups where supported</li>
<li>Restricted access</li>
<li>Documented recovery process</li>
<li>Recovery testing</li>
</ul>

The goal is not merely to keep the Terraform code. The state and
backend recovery process must also be understood.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Large Terraform Project</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A company manages networking, security, databases and application
infrastructure in one huge Terraform configuration.

Planning becomes slow and changes become risky.

</div>

<div class="answer">

I would consider modularization and logical separation.

For example:

<pre><code>terraform/
â”œâ”€â”€ modules/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ vpc/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ security/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ database/
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ compute/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ environments/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ dev/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ qa/
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ prod/</code></pre>

The exact repository structure depends on the team's operational
model.

</div>

</div>

<!-- SCENARIO 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Interview Scenario: "How would you deploy AWS infrastructure?"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"I would first organize the infrastructure into reusable Terraform
modules where appropriate.

I would configure a secure remote backend for state and separate
state between environments.

The code would be stored in Git and changes would go through pull
requests.

CI would run terraform fmt, validate and plan. After review and
approval, the controlled pipeline would run terraform apply.

I would protect AWS credentials, use least-privilege IAM, review
plans carefully and monitor the resulting infrastructure.

For production, I would also have state backup/recovery procedures
and strong controls around destructive operations."

</div>

</div>

<!-- SCENARIO 31 -->

<div class="card">

<!-- FINAL -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Final Interview Answer: "How do you use Terraform in Production?"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In production, I treat Terraform as the source of truth for
infrastructure and use Git-based workflows for all infrastructure
changes.

I use reusable modules, environment-specific configurations and a
secure remote backend with state protection.

For every change, I run formatting and validation, generate a
Terraform plan and review the proposed changes before applying them.

The apply operation is controlled through CI/CD with appropriate
authentication, approvals and auditability.

If drift occurs, I investigate the difference between the desired
configuration and actual infrastructure before deciding whether to
reconcile it.

For existing manually created resources, I can import them into
Terraform state.

I also protect Terraform state, use least-privilege IAM, avoid
unnecessary provisioners and have recovery procedures for state and
backend failures.

The main goal is safe, repeatable and auditable infrastructure
automation."

</div>

<div class="icon">ðŸ—„ï¸</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Terraform</a>

<h1>Terraform <span>State & Backends</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Terraform state, remote backends,
S3 state, state locking, drift, state commands, collaboration,
state security, recovery and real-time production scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
Terraform state is one of the most important concepts in Terraform.
It allows Terraform to keep track of infrastructure resources that it
manages and compare the desired configuration with the current
managed state.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Configuration
<br>
+
<br>
Terraform State
<br>
+
<br>
Real Infrastructure
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>terraform plan</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Required Changes

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A Terraform project creates an AWS VPC and EC2 instance.

Later, a developer changes the Terraform code to increase the EC2
instance size.

Terraform uses its configuration and state information to determine
what resource needs to change rather than blindly creating another
instance.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Terraform State?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state is a record of infrastructure resources managed by
Terraform.

The default local state file is usually:

<code>terraform.tfstate</code>

Terraform uses state information to map configuration resources to
real infrastructure objects.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Terraform state stores information about the infrastructure managed
by Terraform. Terraform uses it to track resource identities and
attributes and to determine what changes are required during plan and
apply."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why does Terraform need State?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform configuration describes the desired infrastructure, while
state helps Terraform understand the resources it is already
managing.

Without reliable state, Terraform cannot safely perform normal
incremental management of the infrastructure.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Desired Configuration
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform State
<br>
â†“
<br>
Real Infrastructure
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform determines difference

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is terraform.tfstate?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>terraform.tfstate</code> is the default local state file created
when Terraform manages resources using the local backend.

It contains Terraform's recorded representation of managed resources
and their attributes.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Never treat the state file like a normal source-code file.

Depending on the infrastructure being managed, state can contain
sensitive information.

Do not commit it to a public Git repository.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Local State vs Remote State</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Local State</th>
<th>Remote State</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stored on the local machine.</td>
<td>Stored in a shared remote backend.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple for learning and small experiments.</td>
<td>Better suited for teams.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Harder to collaborate safely.</td>
<td>Centralized access.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Backup is your responsibility.</td>
<td>Backend can provide durability and operational controls.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Concurrency is difficult.</td>
<td>Can support state locking depending on backend.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is a Terraform Backend?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Terraform backend determines where Terraform stores state and how
state-related operations are handled.

Terraform supports local state by default and can use remote backends
for team environments.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Production example:</strong>

A DevOps team has five engineers and a CI/CD pipeline.

If every engineer stores a separate local state file, Terraform can
lose the shared view of infrastructure.

A remote backend provides a centralized state location.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Why use Remote State?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Centralized state management.</li>
<li>Team collaboration.</li>
<li>Better backup and durability options.</li>
<li>CI/CD systems can access the same state.</li>
<li>State locking may prevent concurrent operations.</li>
<li>Access can be controlled using IAM or equivalent permissions.</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

For production Terraform, remote state is generally preferred over
keeping state only on an engineer's laptop.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. AWS S3 Backend</h2>

<div class="answer">

An S3 backend can store Terraform state in an Amazon S3 bucket.

A typical design uses:

<br><br>

<strong>S3</strong> â†’ state storage

<br>

<strong>Versioning</strong> â†’ recovery from accidental state changes

<br>

<strong>IAM</strong> â†’ access control

<br>

<strong>Encryption</strong> â†’ state protection

<br>

<strong>Locking</strong> â†’ prevent conflicting concurrent operations,
using the locking mechanism supported by the Terraform/backend setup

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "company-terraform-state"
    key    = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Why S3 Versioning?</h2>

<div class="answer">

S3 versioning keeps previous versions of objects.

For Terraform state, this can help recover from accidental state
replacement or corruption when the organization's backend design
uses versioning.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

A bad state update occurs.

If bucket versioning is enabled, the team can investigate previous
object versions and recover the state through the organization's
approved recovery procedure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is State Locking?</h2>

<div class="answer">

State locking prevents multiple Terraform operations from modifying
the same state concurrently when the backend supports locking.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Engineer A
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Operation
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>State Lock</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
State Updated
<br>
â†“
<br>
Lock Released
<br>
<br>
Engineer B waits or is prevented from conflicting operation

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Without proper locking, two engineers or CI jobs could attempt
conflicting state operations at the same time.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What happens if two engineers run Terraform simultaneously?</h2>

<div class="answer">

With a properly configured locking-capable remote backend, Terraform
can prevent conflicting state operations by acquiring a state lock.

The second operation generally waits or fails instead of modifying
the same state concurrently.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Never solve a locking problem by blindly deleting or manipulating
locking information.

First identify the running Terraform operation and verify that no
legitimate process is using the state.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is State Drift?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Drift occurs when the actual infrastructure changes outside
Terraform and no longer matches the configuration and Terraform's
managed state expectations.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Terraform creates:

<pre><code>EC2 instance
type = t3.micro</code></pre>

Someone manually changes the instance to:

<pre><code>t3.large</code></pre>

Now the infrastructure has changed outside the Terraform workflow.

Running:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

can reveal differences that Terraform wants to reconcile.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. How do you detect Drift?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The normal first step is to run:

<pre><code>terraform plan</code></pre>

Terraform refreshes relevant information from the provider and
compares it with the configuration and state to determine proposed
changes.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

In a production pipeline, drift detection can be performed
periodically so the team knows when infrastructure has been changed
outside the approved IaC workflow.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is terraform state list?</h2>

<pre><code>terraform state list</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Lists resource addresses currently recorded in Terraform state.

</div>

<h3>Example output</h3>

<pre><code>aws_vpc.main
aws_subnet.public
aws_instance.app</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. What is terraform state show?</h2>

<pre><code>terraform state show aws_instance.app</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Displays detailed state information for a specific resource address.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Useful when troubleshooting what Terraform currently knows about a
specific resource.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What is terraform state rm?</h2>

<pre><code>terraform state rm aws_instance.app</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Removes a resource address from Terraform state without destroying
the actual remote resource.

</div>

<div class="warning">

This is an advanced state operation.

Removing a resource from state does not mean Terraform deletes the
real infrastructure.

Use it only when you understand the desired ownership and recovery
impact.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. What is terraform import?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform import associates an existing infrastructure resource with
a Terraform resource address so that Terraform can begin managing
it.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>terraform import aws_instance.app i-0123456789abcdef0</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A company has an EC2 instance that was created manually.

Instead of deleting it and rebuilding it, the DevOps engineer can
import the existing resource and then create matching Terraform
configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. What happens if terraform.tfstate is deleted?</h2>

<div class="answer">

If local state is deleted, Terraform loses its local record of the
resources it was managing.

The real infrastructure may still exist, but Terraform no longer has
the expected state mapping.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not immediately run <code>terraform apply</code> after losing state.

Depending on the configuration and provider, Terraform may propose
creating resources that already exist.

First recover the correct state or reconstruct/import the resources
using a controlled procedure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. How do you recover lost Terraform State?</h2>

<ol>
<li>Stop automated Terraform runs.</li>
<li>Identify the affected backend and workspace.</li>
<li>Check backend backups or object versions.</li>
<li>Restore the correct state if available.</li>
<li>Verify resource mappings.</li>
<li>Run <code>terraform plan</code>.</li>
<li>Review all proposed changes carefully.</li>
</ol>

<div class="scenario">

For an S3-backed state design, bucket versioning can provide an
important recovery mechanism for previous state object versions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. State Security</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state can contain sensitive infrastructure information and
sometimes sensitive values.

Therefore state should be protected like other sensitive
infrastructure data.

</div>

<ul>
<li>Use a private backend.</li>
<li>Restrict access using IAM/RBAC.</li>
<li>Enable encryption where appropriate.</li>
<li>Enable state-storage versioning when supported and required.</li>
<li>Audit access.</li>
<li>Do not commit state files to Git.</li>
<li>Do not expose state files publicly.</li>
<li>Use separate state for appropriate environments.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Should terraform.tfstate be committed to Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Normally, no.

Terraform state should generally be stored in an appropriate
backend rather than committed to a source-code repository.

</div>

<h3>.gitignore</h3>

<pre><code>*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
.terraform/</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Ignoring state in Git is not a replacement for secure remote state
management.

The remote backend itself must also be properly protected.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. What is .terraform directory?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>.terraform</code> directory contains Terraform working
directory data such as downloaded provider plugins and other
initialization-related files.

It is not the Terraform state itself.

</div>

<pre><code>.terraform/</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not confuse:

<br><br>

<code>.terraform/</code> â†’ working directory data

<br>

<code>terraform.tfstate</code> â†’ Terraform state

<br>

<code>.terraform.lock.hcl</code> â†’ provider dependency selections/checksums

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. terraform state mv</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>terraform state mv</code> moves a resource address in Terraform
state.

It is useful when refactoring configuration without wanting Terraform
to interpret the resource as a completely new object.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform state mv \
  aws_instance.old \
  aws_instance.app</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This can be useful when renaming resources or reorganizing resources
into modules, provided the state operation matches the intended
configuration refactor.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. State and Modules</h2>

<div class="answer">

When resources are managed inside modules, Terraform state records
resource addresses that include the module path.

</div>

<pre><code>module.network.aws_vpc.main

module.compute.aws_instance.app</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This allows Terraform to distinguish resources belonging to
different module instances.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Separate State for Dev, QA and Production</h2>

<div class="answer">

Production environments should be isolated from development
environments through an appropriate state architecture.

One common approach is using separate state files/backend keys for
different environments.

</div>

<pre><code>prod/
  network/terraform.tfstate

qa/
  network/terraform.tfstate

dev/
  network/terraform.tfstate</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This reduces the risk of a development operation accidentally
targeting production state.

The exact environment architecture should match the organization's
Terraform design.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Terraform Workspaces</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform workspaces allow multiple state instances to be associated
with one Terraform configuration.

They can be useful for certain environment or workflow designs.

</div>

<pre><code>terraform workspace list

terraform workspace new dev

terraform workspace select dev

terraform workspace show</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Workspaces are not automatically a complete security boundary.

For critical production environments, separate state/backend
architecture is often easier to reason about and control.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Remote State Data Source</h2>

<div class="answer">

One Terraform configuration can consume outputs from another
Terraform-managed state using the <code>terraform_remote_state</code>
data source.

</div>

<pre><code>data "terraform_remote_state" "network" {
  backend = "s3"

  config = {
    bucket = "company-terraform-state"
    key    = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "ap-south-1"
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

The networking stack creates a VPC.

The application stack consumes the VPC ID from the networking stack's
outputs.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. State Refresh Concept</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform obtains current information from the provider during normal
planning and other operations so that it can evaluate differences
between configuration, recorded state and real infrastructure.

</div>

<div class="interview">

Modern Terraform workflows should generally use normal plan/apply
behavior rather than relying on the old standalone
<code>terraform refresh</code> workflow.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. State Locking Failure</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Terraform reports that it cannot acquire the state lock.

<br><br>

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Another Terraform operation is currently running.</li>
<li>A previous operation terminated unexpectedly.</li>
<li>Backend locking information needs investigation.</li>
<li>CI/CD has another active Terraform job.</li>
</ul>

</div>

<div class="answer">

First verify whether another Terraform operation is actually running.

Do not force-unlock state blindly.

If the lock is genuinely stale, follow the backend and Terraform
recovery procedure carefully.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Real-Time Scenario: Team Terraform</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Company setup:</strong>

<br><br>

5 DevOps engineers

<br>
1 CI/CD pipeline

<br>
AWS infrastructure

<br>
S3 remote state

<br>
IAM-controlled access

<br>
State protection/versioning

</div>

<div class="flow">

Engineer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Git Pull Request
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Format / Validate
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Plan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Code Review
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Apply
<br>
â†“
<br>
Remote State

</div>

<div class="interview">

This workflow provides controlled infrastructure changes instead of
allowing engineers to manually modify production resources.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Real-Time Scenario: Someone Changed AWS Manually</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

A developer manually changes a production security group in the AWS
Console.

<br><br>

The Terraform repository still contains the original configuration.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Manual AWS Change
<br>
â†“
<br>
Infrastructure Drift
<br>
â†“
<br>
terraform plan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Review Difference
<br>
â†“
<br>
Choose:
<br>
Terraform Configuration Change
<br>
OR
<br>
Reconcile Infrastructure
<br>
â†“
<br>
Apply Controlled Change

</div>

</div>


<!-- 31 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Real-Time Scenario: Terraform State Lost</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

The local laptop containing <code>terraform.tfstate</code> is lost.

<br><br>

If the project used only local state, the team has lost its local
Terraform management record.

If the project used a properly configured remote backend, Terraform
state remains available through the backend.

</div>

<div class="interview">

This is one of the main reasons production teams use remote state
instead of keeping the only state copy on an engineer's machine.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 32 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Real-Time Scenario: Two CI Jobs Run Together</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

Two GitHub Actions workflows attempt:

<pre><code>terraform apply</code></pre>

against the same infrastructure.

</div>

<div class="answer">

A properly configured locking-capable backend prevents conflicting
state operations.

The pipeline should also be designed so that production Terraform
applies are serialized and protected by appropriate approval and
concurrency controls.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 33 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. State Best Practices</h2>

<ul>
<li>Use remote state for team environments.</li>
<li>Protect state with strong access controls.</li>
<li>Enable encryption where appropriate.</li>
<li>Use state versioning/recovery mechanisms.</li>
<li>Use state locking when supported.</li>
<li>Separate production state from non-production state.</li>
<li>Never commit state to public Git repositories.</li>
<li>Do not manually edit the state JSON.</li>
<li>Use Terraform state commands carefully.</li>
<li>Review plan output before production apply.</li>
<li>Control CI/CD access to production state.</li>
<li>Monitor and audit infrastructure changes.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 34 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Important State Commands</h2>

<pre><code># List resources
terraform state list

# Show a resource
terraform state show aws_instance.app

# Move resource address
terraform state mv aws_instance.old aws_instance.app

# Remove resource from state
terraform state rm aws_instance.app

# Import existing resource
terraform import aws_instance.app i-0123456789abcdef0

# Inspect current plan
terraform plan

# Show state
terraform show</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

State commands can have significant consequences.

Always understand the desired state ownership before using
<code>state mv</code> or <code>state rm</code>.

</div>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Terraform State"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Terraform state is the record Terraform uses to track the
infrastructure resources it manages.

It helps Terraform compare the desired configuration with the
resources it knows about and determine what changes are required.

For local learning, Terraform can store state in terraform.tfstate.
For a production team, I would use a remote backend, for example an
S3-based backend in AWS, with appropriate access control, encryption,
versioning and locking according to the organization's design.

State is sensitive and should not be committed to Git.

If infrastructure is changed manually outside Terraform, it can
create drift, which I can identify and review using terraform plan.

For team environments, remote state and safe locking are important
because multiple engineers or CI/CD jobs may otherwise attempt
conflicting operations.

I would also maintain separate state for production and
non-production environments and protect production state carefully."

</div>

<h1>Terraform <span>Variables & Modules</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering input variables, tfvars, locals,
outputs, data sources, types, validation, sensitive values,
modules, module inputs and outputs, reusable infrastructure and
real-time DevOps scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
Terraform variables and modules are the foundation of reusable
Infrastructure as Code. Variables make configuration flexible,
while modules allow infrastructure patterns to be packaged and
reused.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Reusable Terraform Code
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Variables</strong>
â†’ Environment-specific values
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Modules</strong>
â†’ Reusable infrastructure
<br>
â†“
<br>
Dev / QA / Production

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A company creates the same VPC architecture for Dev, QA and
Production.

Instead of maintaining three completely different Terraform files,
the team creates a reusable VPC module and passes different CIDRs,
availability zones and environment values through variables.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Terraform Variable?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Terraform input variable allows a configuration to accept values
from outside the resource definition.

Variables make Terraform configurations reusable and avoid hard-coding
environment-specific values.

</div>

<h3>variables.tf</h3>

<pre><code>variable "instance_type" {
  description = "EC2 instance type"
  type        = string
  default     = "t3.micro"
}</code></pre>

<h3>Usage</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  ami           = var.ami_id
  instance_type = var.instance_type
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why use Variables?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Avoid hard-coded values.</li>
<li>Reuse the same configuration.</li>
<li>Support multiple environments.</li>
<li>Improve maintainability.</li>
<li>Make modules configurable.</li>
<li>Allow CI/CD pipelines to supply values.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Instead of changing the resource code:

<pre><code>instance_type = "t3.micro"</code></pre>

for every environment, define:

<pre><code>instance_type = var.instance_type</code></pre>

and provide different values for Dev and Production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Variable Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>string</td>
<td><code>"ap-south-1"</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>number</td>
<td><code>2</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>bool</td>
<td><code>true</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>list</td>
<td><code>["a","b","c"]</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>set</td>
<td><code>toset(["a","b"])</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>map</td>
<td><code>{env="dev", team="cloud"}</code></td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>object</td>
<td>Structured collection of named attributes</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>tuple</td>
<td>Ordered collection with defined element types</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. String, Number and Boolean Variables</h2>

<pre><code>variable "project_name" {
  type    = string
  default = "nandu-project"
}

variable "replica_count" {
  type    = number
  default = 2
}

variable "enable_monitoring" {
  type    = bool
  default = true
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. List and Map Variables</h2>

<h3>List</h3>

<pre><code>variable "availability_zones" {
  type = list(string)

  default = [
    "ap-south-1a",
    "ap-south-1b"
  ]
}</code></pre>

<h3>Map</h3>

<pre><code>variable "tags" {
  type = map(string)

  default = {
    Environment = "Dev"
    Project     = "Cloud"
  }
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is terraform.tfvars?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <code>.tfvars</code> file provides values for Terraform input
variables.

</div>

<pre><code>aws_region    = "ap-south-1"
instance_type = "t3.micro"
environment   = "dev"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

The same Terraform configuration can be used with different
<code>.tfvars</code> files for different environments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Variable Precedence</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform supports multiple ways to provide variable values.

Common sources include:

</div>

<ol>
<li>Variable defaults</li>
<li>Environment variables such as <code>TF_VAR_name</code></li>
<li>Automatically loaded <code>terraform.tfvars</code> and
<code>*.auto.tfvars</code></li>
<li>Explicit <code>-var</code> and <code>-var-file</code> arguments</li>
</ol>

<div class="interview">

When multiple sources provide the same variable, Terraform follows
its documented precedence rules. Explicit command-line variable
arguments have higher precedence than automatic variable files.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Using -var and -var-file</h2>

<pre><code>terraform plan \
  -var="environment=dev"</code></pre>

<h3>Using variable file</h3>

<pre><code>terraform plan \
  -var-file="dev.tfvars"</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This is useful in CI/CD when the pipeline needs to select the
appropriate environment configuration.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What are Locals?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Local values allow you to assign reusable expressions or computed
values within a Terraform module.

They are useful when the same derived value is used in multiple
places.

</div>

<pre><code>locals {
  common_tags = {
    Project     = "Nandu"
    Environment = "Dev"
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }
}</code></pre>

<h3>Usage</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" {

  bucket = "nandu-demo-bucket"

  tags = local.common_tags
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Variable vs Local</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Variable</th>
<th>Local</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Input supplied to the module.</td>
<td>Value calculated or defined inside the module.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be changed by the caller.</td>
<td>Not directly supplied as module input.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for configurable values.</td>
<td>Used for reusable internal expressions.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Simple answer:</strong>

Variable = external input.

<br>

Local = internal reusable value.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Variable Validation</h2>

<div class="answer">

Variable validation allows Terraform to reject invalid input before
infrastructure is created.

</div>

<pre><code>variable "environment" {

  type = string

  validation {
    condition = contains(
      ["dev", "qa", "prod"],
      var.environment
    )

    error_message = "Environment must be dev, qa or prod."
  }
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This prevents someone from accidentally supplying:

<pre><code>environment = "productionn"</code></pre>

when the module expects only approved values.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Sensitive Variables</h2>

<div class="answer">

Sensitive variables prevent Terraform CLI output from displaying the
value in normal situations.

</div>

<pre><code>variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong>

Marking a variable as sensitive does not mean the value is magically
encrypted everywhere.

Sensitive values can still exist in Terraform state depending on
how they are used.

Protect the state backend appropriately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What are Outputs?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Outputs expose useful values from a Terraform module.

</div>

<pre><code>output "vpc_id" {
  description = "VPC ID"
  value       = aws_vpc.main.id
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

A networking module can output a VPC ID.

The application module can consume that output.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Sensitive Outputs</h2>

<pre><code>output "admin_password" {
  value     = var.admin_password
  sensitive = true
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Sensitive output values should still be treated as sensitive data.
The <code>sensitive</code> flag mainly controls how Terraform
displays the value.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What is a Data Source?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A data source allows Terraform to read information from an existing
resource or external system without managing that object as a new
resource.

</div>

<h3>AWS AMI Example</h3>

<pre><code>data "aws_ami" "amazon_linux" {

  most_recent = true

  owners = ["amazon"]

  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["al2023-ami-*-x86_64"]
  }
}</code></pre>

<h3>Use it</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_instance" "app" {

  ami           = data.aws_ami.amazon_linux.id
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Resource vs Data Source</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Resource</th>
<th>Data Source</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates or manages infrastructure.</td>
<td>Reads existing information.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: aws_instance</td>
<td>Example: aws_ami</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Terraform manages lifecycle.</td>
<td>Terraform queries existing information.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

Resource = "Create/manage this."

<br><br>

Data source = "Find/read this."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. What is a Terraform Module?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Terraform module is a collection of Terraform configuration files
that can be reused as a logical unit.

The directory containing Terraform configuration is itself a module;
the root configuration is called the root module, and reusable
child modules can be called from it.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Instead of writing VPC resources repeatedly for every project, create
a reusable VPC module and call it with different inputs.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Root Module vs Child Module</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Root Module</th>
<th>Child Module</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Configuration where Terraform commands are executed.</td>
<td>Module called by another module.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Contains the main environment configuration.</td>
<td>Contains reusable infrastructure logic.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Calls child modules.</td>
<td>Accepts inputs and exposes outputs.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Basic Module Structure</h2>

<pre><code>terraform-project/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ main.tf
â”œâ”€â”€ variables.tf
â”œâ”€â”€ outputs.tf
â”‚
â””â”€â”€ modules/
    â””â”€â”€ vpc/
        â”œâ”€â”€ main.tf
        â”œâ”€â”€ variables.tf
        â””â”€â”€ outputs.tf</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The module directory contains reusable Terraform configuration.

The root module supplies values to it and consumes its outputs.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Calling a Module</h2>

<h3>Root module</h3>

<pre><code>module "vpc" {

  source = "./modules/vpc"

  vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"

  environment = "dev"

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<code>source</code> tells Terraform where the module comes from.

The other arguments are values passed to module input variables.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Module Input Variables</h2>

<h3>modules/vpc/variables.tf</h3>

<pre><code>variable "vpc_cidr" {
  type = string
}

variable "environment" {
  type = string
}</code></pre>

<h3>modules/vpc/main.tf</h3>

<pre><code>resource "aws_vpc" "main" {

  cidr_block = var.vpc_cidr

  tags = {
    Name        = "${var.environment}-vpc"
    Environment = var.environment
  }

}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Module Outputs</h2>

<h3>modules/vpc/outputs.tf</h3>

<pre><code>output "vpc_id" {
  value = aws_vpc.main.id
}</code></pre>

<h3>Root module</h3>

<pre><code>module "vpc" {
  source   = "./modules/vpc"
  vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

output "application_vpc_id" {
  value = module.vpc.vpc_id
}</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Root Module
<br>
â†“
<br>
Module Input
<br>
â†“
<br>
VPC Module
<br>
â†“
<br>
Module Output
<br>
â†“
<br>
Root Module

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Why use Modules?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Code reusability.</li>
<li>Consistency across environments.</li>
<li>Reduced duplication.</li>
<li>Standardized infrastructure patterns.</li>
<li>Easier maintenance.</li>
<li>Clear separation of infrastructure components.</li>
<li>Useful for large Terraform codebases.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

A company can create standard modules for:

<br><br>

VPC â†’ EKS â†’ RDS â†’ ALB â†’ IAM

<br><br>

Teams consume the approved modules instead of rebuilding the same
infrastructure pattern differently.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Local Module vs Registry Module</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Local Module</th>
<th>Registry/Remote Module</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>source = "./modules/vpc"</code></td>
<td>Module downloaded from a registry or remote source.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Maintained inside the project/repository.</td>
<td>Can be shared across projects.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for organization-specific modules.</td>
<td>Useful for reusable published modules.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Module Versioning</h2>

<div class="answer">

Remote modules can be versioned so teams can control which module
release they use.

</div>

<pre><code>module "vpc" {

  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "x.y.z"

}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

In production, pin module versions intentionally and upgrade them
through a controlled review process.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Module Composition</h2>

<div class="flow">

Root Module
<br>
â†“
<br>
VPC Module
<br>
+
<br>
Security Module
<br>
+
<br>
EKS Module
<br>
+
<br>
Monitoring Module

</div>

<div class="answer">

Large Terraform projects are often divided into logical modules
instead of putting every resource into one enormous file.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Passing Module Output to Another Module</h2>

<pre><code>module "vpc" {
  source = "./modules/vpc"
}

module "app" {

  source = "./modules/app"

  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id

}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The application module consumes the VPC module's output.

Terraform can infer the dependency through this reference.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 28. for_each with Modules</h2>

<div class="answer">

Modules can be created multiple times using <code>for_each</code>.

</div>

<pre><code>module "environment" {

  for_each = {
    dev  = "10.10.0.0/16"
    prod = "10.20.0.0/16"
  }

  source   = "./modules/vpc"
  vpc_cidr = each.value

}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

This can be useful when the same module needs to create multiple
similar infrastructure instances.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 29. count vs for_each with Modules</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>count</th>
<th>for_each</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses numeric indexes.</td>
<td>Uses keys.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for simple repeated instances.</td>
<td>Better when instances have meaningful identities.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>module.app[0]</code></td>
<td><code>module.app["dev"]</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

When individual instances have meaningful names such as
<code>dev</code>, <code>qa</code> and <code>prod</code>, I generally
prefer <code>for_each</code> because the keys describe the instances.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Real-Time Multi-Environment Design</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose a company has:

<br><br>

<strong>Dev</strong> â†’ smaller instances

<br>

<strong>QA</strong> â†’ medium instances

<br>

<strong>Production</strong> â†’ larger instances

</div>

<h3>Reusable module</h3>

<pre><code>module "app" {

  source = "./modules/application"

  instance_type = var.instance_type

  environment   = var.environment

}</code></pre>

<h3>dev.tfvars</h3>

<pre><code>environment   = "dev"
instance_type = "t3.micro"</code></pre>

<h3>prod.tfvars</h3>

<pre><code>environment   = "prod"
instance_type = "m7i.large"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Same module.

Different input values.

Different environment infrastructure.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 31 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Real-Time VPC Module Example</h2>

<div class="flow">

Root Terraform
<br>
â†“
<br>
VPC Module
<br>
â†“
<br>
VPC
<br>
â†“
<br>
Public Subnets
<br>
â†“
<br>
Private Subnets
<br>
â†“
<br>
Route Tables
<br>
â†“
<br>
Outputs
<br>
â†“
<br>
EKS / EC2 / ALB Modules

</div>

<div class="interview">

This modular approach keeps infrastructure organized and allows
different teams or environments to reuse standardized components.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 32 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Common Module Mistakes</h2>

<ul>
<li>Creating extremely large modules.</li>
<li>Hard-coding environment-specific values.</li>
<li>Passing too many unnecessary variables.</li>
<li>Not documenting module inputs and outputs.</li>
<li>Not validating inputs.</li>
<li>Using unpinned remote module versions in production.</li>
<li>Exposing sensitive values unnecessarily.</li>
<li>Duplicating the same module logic across repositories.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 33 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Variables + Modules + State Relationship</h2>

<div class="flow">

Variables
<br>
â†“
<br>
Module Inputs
<br>
â†“
<br>
Resources
<br>
â†“
<br>
Module Outputs
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform State

</div>

<div class="answer">

Variables control what values enter the configuration.

Modules organize reusable infrastructure.

Outputs expose useful results.

State records the infrastructure Terraform manages.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 34 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Interview: How do you design reusable Terraform code?</h2>

<div class="interview">

"I separate reusable infrastructure into modules and expose only the
configuration values that consumers actually need through input
variables.

I use validation for important inputs, locals for repeated internal
expressions, and outputs for values that other modules need.

For different environments, I keep the infrastructure logic reusable
and supply environment-specific values through variables or approved
environment configuration.

For production, I also version reusable modules and review module
upgrades before adoption."

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Terraform Modules"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Terraform modules are reusable collections of Terraform
configuration.

I use modules to avoid duplicating infrastructure code and to
standardize common components such as VPCs, IAM roles, EKS clusters
or application infrastructure.

The root module calls a child module and passes values through input
variables. The child module creates the required resources and
exposes important values through outputs.

For example, I can create one reusable VPC module and use it for Dev,
QA and Production by passing different CIDRs and environment values.

I also use variable validation, locals and versioned modules to make
the Terraform code easier to maintain and safer to reuse."

</div>

<h2>04. Credentials & Security</h2>
