<h1>Jenkins <span>Basics</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Jenkins architecture, Controller and
Agents, Jobs, Builds, Plugins, Workspace, CI/CD workflow and
real-time DevOps usage.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
<strong>Jenkins</strong> is an open-source automation server mainly
used to implement Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery /
Deployment pipelines.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>
â†“
<br>
Git Repository
<br>
â†“
<br>
Webhook
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Jenkins</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan â†’ Package
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Image / Artifact
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deployment

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A developer pushes code to GitHub. A webhook triggers Jenkins.
Jenkins checks out the code, builds the application, runs tests,
creates a Docker image and pushes it to a container registry.
The pipeline can then deploy the application to Kubernetes or AWS.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins is an open-source automation server used to automate
software build, test, integration and deployment activities.

It is widely used in DevOps to create CI/CD pipelines.

</div>

<h3>Interview Answer</h3>

<div class="interview">

"Jenkins is an open-source automation server that helps automate
CI/CD processes. We can integrate Jenkins with Git, Docker, cloud
platforms, Kubernetes and many testing or security tools to automate
the software delivery lifecycle."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why do we use Jenkins?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Automate application builds.</li>

<li>Run automated tests.</li>

<li>Integrate with Git repositories.</li>

<li>Build CI/CD pipelines.</li>

<li>Create Docker images.</li>

<li>Push artifacts to repositories.</li>

<li>Deploy applications automatically.</li>

<li>Integrate security and code-quality tools.</li>

</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Without Jenkins:</strong>

Developer manually builds, tests and deploys the application.

<br><br>

<strong>With Jenkins:</strong>

A Git push can automatically trigger the complete workflow.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Jenkins Architecture</h2>

<div class="answer">

Modern Jenkins commonly follows a controller-agent architecture.

<strong>Controller:</strong> manages Jenkins configuration,
jobs/pipelines and coordinates execution.

<strong>Agent:</strong> provides the environment where build or pipeline
steps execute.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Jenkins Controller
<br>
â†“
<br>
Pipeline / Job Scheduling
<br>
â†“
<br>
Agent 1 â†’ Build
<br>
Agent 2 â†’ Test
<br>
Agent 3 â†’ Docker
<br>
â†“
<br>
Artifacts / Deployment

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Controller vs Agent</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Controller</th>
<th>Agent</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Manages Jenkins configuration.</td>
<td>Executes assigned build or pipeline work.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Schedules jobs.</td>
<td>Runs commands and tools.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stores Jenkins configuration.</td>
<td>Provides execution environment.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can manage multiple agents.</td>
<td>Can be labeled for specific workloads.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview tip:</strong>

Do not say the controller must execute every build.

A production Jenkins setup can use dedicated agents so workloads
are distributed and the controller is not overloaded.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is a Jenkins Job?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Jenkins Job is a configured task that Jenkins can execute.

Depending on the setup, it can represent a build, test,
pipeline or another automated process.

</div>

<h3>Common examples</h3>

<ul>

<li>Freestyle project</li>

<li>Pipeline</li>

<li>Multibranch Pipeline</li>

<li>Organization Folder</li>

</ul>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

<strong>Payment-Service-CI</strong> can be configured to checkout
code, run tests, build a Docker image and publish the image.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Build?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A build is an execution of a Jenkins job or pipeline.

Every execution can produce a build result such as
<strong>SUCCESS</strong>, <strong>FAILURE</strong>,
<strong>ABORTED</strong> or <strong>UNSTABLE</strong>, depending on
the job and configuration.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>Build #101 â†’ SUCCESS
Build #102 â†’ SUCCESS
Build #103 â†’ FAILURE
Build #104 â†’ SUCCESS</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

When a build fails, I first inspect the console logs and identify
which stage or command failed before changing the pipeline.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is a Jenkins Plugin?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Jenkins plugin extends Jenkins functionality and allows Jenkins
to integrate with external tools and platforms.

</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<ul>

<li>Git integration</li>

<li>Pipeline functionality</li>

<li>Credentials management</li>

<li>Docker integration</li>

<li>Kubernetes integration</li>

<li>Notifications</li>

</ul>

<div class="warning">

Do not install unnecessary plugins.

A production Jenkins installation should keep plugins controlled,
compatible and regularly maintained.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is Jenkins Workspace?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A workspace is the directory where Jenkins performs operations
such as source-code checkout, compilation, testing and artifact
generation for a build.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Agent
<br>
â†“
<br>
Workspace
<br>
â†“
<br>
Git Checkout
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build / Test
<br>
â†“
<br>
Artifacts

</div>

<h3>Useful troubleshooting command</h3>

<pre><code>pwd
ls -la</code></pre>

<p>
Inside a Jenkins pipeline, shell commands execute in the workspace
unless another directory is specified.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Jenkins CI/CD Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Developer</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
git push
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>GitHub</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Webhook
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Jenkins</strong>
<br>
â†“
<br>
Checkout
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Test
<br>
â†“
<br>
Security Scan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Docker Build
<br>
â†“
<br>
Push Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Deploy
<br>
â†“
<br>
<strong>Application</strong>

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time DevOps example:</strong>

GitHub â†’ Jenkins â†’ Maven â†’ SonarQube â†’ Docker â†’ ECR â†’
Kubernetes/EKS.

This is a common pattern for an end-to-end CI/CD workflow.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Freestyle Job vs Pipeline</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Freestyle</th>
<th>Pipeline</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Configured mainly through Jenkins UI.</td>
<td>Pipeline can be defined as code.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Suitable for simple jobs.</td>
<td>Better for complex CI/CD workflows.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Harder to version configuration.</td>
<td>Jenkinsfile can be stored in Git.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less suitable for complex stages.</td>
<td>Supports stages, conditions and reusable logic.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"For modern CI/CD, I prefer Pipeline as Code using a Jenkinsfile
because the pipeline definition can be version-controlled along
with the application source code."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is Pipeline as Code?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Pipeline as Code means defining the CI/CD workflow in a file,
commonly called a <strong>Jenkinsfile</strong>, instead of relying
only on Jenkins UI configuration.

</div>

<h3>Basic example</h3>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    stages {

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Building application'
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                echo 'Running tests'
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                echo 'Deploying application'
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. What is Continuous Integration?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Continuous Integration means developers frequently integrate code
changes into a shared repository and automated processes build and
test those changes.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Developer pushes code.

<br>
â†“

Jenkins starts automatically.

<br>
â†“

Code is compiled and tested.

<br>
â†“

Failure is reported quickly.

</div>

<p>
The main goal is to detect integration problems early.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Continuous Delivery</th>
<th>Continuous Deployment</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Software is kept ready for release.</td>
<td>Successful changes are automatically released.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>May require manual production approval.</td>
<td>Production deployment can happen automatically.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

Example:

<strong>Delivery:</strong> Jenkins builds and tests the application,
then waits for production approval.

<br><br>

<strong>Deployment:</strong> Jenkins automatically deploys the
successful build to production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. How does Jenkins trigger a pipeline?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Jenkins job can be triggered through several mechanisms,
depending on configuration.

</div>

<ul>

<li>GitHub/GitLab webhook</li>

<li>Manual trigger</li>

<li>Scheduled trigger</li>

<li>SCM polling</li>

<li>Another Jenkins job</li>

<li>API or automation</li>

</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Preferred modern approach:</strong>

Git push â†’ Webhook â†’ Jenkins pipeline.

This avoids Jenkins repeatedly polling the repository just to
discover changes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. How do you troubleshoot a failed Jenkins build?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I follow a systematic approach rather than randomly changing the
pipeline.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Build Failed
<br>
â†“
<br>
Open Console Output
<br>
â†“
<br>
Identify Failed Stage
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check Exact Error
<br>
â†“
<br>
Verify Agent / Workspace
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check Credentials / Permissions
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check Tool / Dependency
<br>
â†“
<br>
Fix â†’ Re-run

</div>

<h3>Useful areas to inspect</h3>

<ul>

<li>Console output</li>
<li>Pipeline stage logs</li>
<li>Agent availability</li>
<li>Workspace files</li>
<li>Credentials</li>
<li>Docker / Kubernetes connectivity</li>
<li>Disk space</li>
<li>Network access</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Scenario: Agent Offline</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Jenkins pipeline is waiting because the required agent is offline.

<br><br>

<strong>Approach:</strong>

1. Check the agent status.
<br>
2. Check connectivity.
<br>
3. Verify agent process/service.
<br>
4. Check resource availability.
<br>
5. Verify labels match the pipeline requirement.
<br>
6. Reconnect or replace the agent if required.

</div>

<div class="interview">

I would not immediately restart the entire Jenkins controller.
First I identify whether the issue is isolated to the agent.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: Build is very slow</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Possible causes:

<ul>

<li>Insufficient CPU or memory.</li>
<li>Slow dependency downloads.</li>
<li>Large Docker builds.</li>
<li>Too many builds on one agent.</li>
<li>Disk or workspace problems.</li>
<li>Unnecessary stages.</li>
<li>Network latency.</li>

</ul>

<strong>Solution:</strong>

Use appropriate agents, parallelize independent stages, cache
dependencies where suitable and optimize Docker/build processes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Jenkins Production Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use Pipeline as Code.</li>

<li>Store Jenkinsfiles in Git.</li>

<li>Use dedicated agents for workloads.</li>

<li>Use credentials management instead of hard-coded secrets.</li>

<li>Apply least-privilege access.</li>

<li>Keep plugins maintained and controlled.</li>

<li>Monitor Jenkins disk, CPU and memory.</li>

<li>Back up important Jenkins configuration and data.</li>

<li>Use webhooks for event-driven CI where appropriate.</li>

<li>Keep production pipelines reproducible.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

</ol>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Jenkins"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"Jenkins is an open-source automation server widely used for CI/CD.
In a typical DevOps workflow, a developer pushes code to GitHub and
a webhook triggers Jenkins.

Jenkins checks out the source code and executes a pipeline on an
appropriate agent. The pipeline can build the application, run
tests and security scans, create a Docker image and push it to a
container registry. The image can then be deployed to platforms
such as Kubernetes or AWS.

For production, I prefer Pipeline as Code using Jenkinsfiles,
dedicated agents, secure credential management, controlled plugins
and proper monitoring and backups."

</div>

<strong>Core idea:</strong>

Jenkins automates the software delivery process by connecting source
control, build, test, security, packaging and deployment stages into
an automated pipeline.

</div>

<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins is an open-source automation server widely used to implement
CI/CD pipelines.

It can automate activities such as source checkout, compilation,
testing, security scanning, Docker image creation, artifact
publishing and deployment.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready:</strong>

"Jenkins is an automation server used to implement CI/CD. It
integrates with tools such as Git, Maven, Docker, cloud platforms and
Kubernetes to automate the software delivery lifecycle."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Jenkins Architecture</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controller</td>
<td>Manages Jenkins configuration, jobs, scheduling and orchestration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Agent</td>
<td>Executes build and deployment workloads.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Executor</td>
<td>Represents a slot that can run a build on a node.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Plugin</td>
<td>Extends Jenkins capabilities and integrations.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Workspace</td>
<td>Directory where a job operates on checked-out files.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Controller
<br>â†“
<br>Schedule
<br>â†“
<br>Agent
<br>â†“
<br>Executor
<br>â†“
<br>Workspace
<br>â†“
<br>Build

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Freestyle vs Pipeline</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Freestyle</th>
<th>Pipeline</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Configured mainly through Jenkins UI.</td>
<td>Pipeline is defined as code.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Good for simple jobs.</td>
<td>Better for complex CI/CD workflows.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less version-control friendly.</td>
<td>Jenkinsfile can be stored in Git.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Limited structure compared with Pipeline.</td>
<td>Supports stages, conditions, parallelism and post actions.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

"For modern CI/CD, I prefer Pipeline as Code because the pipeline
definition can be version controlled and reviewed along with the
application."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Declarative Pipeline Structure</h2>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    environment {
        APP_NAME = 'payment-app'
    }

    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                checkout scm
            }
        }

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                sh 'mvn clean package'
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                sh 'mvn test'
            }
        }

        stage('Docker Build') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t payment-app:${BUILD_NUMBER} .'
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        success {
            echo 'Pipeline successful'
        }

        failure {
            echo 'Pipeline failed'
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Important Pipeline Concepts</h2>

<span class="badge">pipeline</span>
<span class="badge">agent</span>
<span class="badge">stages</span>
<span class="badge">stage</span>
<span class="badge">steps</span>
<span class="badge">environment</span>
<span class="badge">when</span>
<span class="badge">post</span>
<span class="badge">credentials</span>
<span class="badge">parallel</span>

<div class="answer">

<strong>pipeline</strong> â†’ Complete pipeline definition.

<br>

<strong>agent</strong> â†’ Where the pipeline executes.

<br>

<strong>stages</strong> â†’ Logical collection of stages.

<br>

<strong>stage</strong> â†’ Major step such as Build or Test.

<br>

<strong>steps</strong> â†’ Commands executed inside a stage.

<br>

<strong>environment</strong> â†’ Environment variables.

<br>

<strong>when</strong> â†’ Conditional execution.

<br>

<strong>post</strong> â†’ Actions after a stage/pipeline completes.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Git + Jenkins</h2>

<div class="flow">

git push
<br>â†“
<br>GitHub
<br>â†“
<br>Webhook
<br>â†“
<br>Jenkins
<br>â†“
<br>Checkout
<br>â†“
<br>Build

</div>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins can integrate with Git repositories and use webhooks,
polling or manual/API triggers to start builds.

</div>

<h3>Webhook vs Poll SCM</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Webhook</th>
<th>Poll SCM</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Event-driven notification.</td>
<td>Jenkins periodically checks the repository.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually immediate.</td>
<td>Depends on polling schedule.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Jenkins + Docker</h2>

<div class="flow">

Source Code
<br>â†“
<br>Build
<br>â†“
<br>Test
<br>â†“
<br>Docker Build
<br>â†“
<br>Docker Image
<br>â†“
<br>Registry

</div>

<h3>Important commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t app:42 .

docker images

docker tag app:42 registry/app:42

docker push registry/app:42</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not rely only on <code>latest</code> for production traceability.
Use meaningful version, build or source-revision tags.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Jenkins Credentials</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins Credentials provides centralized storage and controlled use
of sensitive information such as passwords, API tokens and SSH keys.

</div>

<pre><code>withCredentials([
    string(
        credentialsId: 'api-token',
        variable: 'API_TOKEN'
    )
]) {

    sh '''
    ./deploy.sh
    '''
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Never hard-code:

<pre><code>PASSWORD=MyPassword123</code></pre>

inside a Jenkinsfile or repository.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Jenkins Security</h2>

<ul>

<li>Authentication</li>
<li>Authorization</li>
<li>RBAC</li>
<li>Least privilege</li>
<li>Credential management</li>
<li>HTTPS/TLS</li>
<li>CSRF protection</li>
<li>Plugin maintenance</li>
<li>Agent isolation</li>
<li>Cloud IAM permissions</li>

</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Golden rule:</strong>

"Never give Jenkins more access than the pipeline actually needs."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Jenkins Controller vs Agent</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Controller</th>
<th>Agent</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Schedules and orchestrates jobs.</td>
<td>Executes build workloads.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stores Jenkins configuration.</td>
<td>Provides execution environment.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Should not be treated as a general build machine.</td>
<td>Can be specialized for different workloads.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. CI vs CD</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Continuous Integration</strong>

<br><br>

Git â†’ Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan â†’ Package

<br><br><br>

<strong>Continuous Delivery / Deployment</strong>

<br><br>

Artifact â†’ Deploy â†’ Verify

</div>

<div class="answer">

CI focuses on integrating and validating code changes frequently.

CD focuses on reliably delivering or deploying validated artifacts
to environments.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Common Jenkins Troubleshooting</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Problem</th>
<th>First checks</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Git checkout failure</td>
<td>Repository URL, credentials, branch, Git installation, network.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build failure</td>
<td>Build logs, Java/Maven version, dependencies, disk.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Docker not found</td>
<td>Docker installation and PATH on agent.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Docker daemon error</td>
<td>Docker service, permissions, runtime/socket.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Docker push denied</td>
<td>Registry login, repository and permissions.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build stuck in queue</td>
<td>Executors, agent status and labels.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Kubernetes deployment failure</td>
<td>Cluster access, namespace, identity, manifest, events.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Disk full</td>
<td>Workspace, Docker data and artifact retention.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Real-Time Scenario: Pipeline Failed</h2>

<div class="flow">

Pipeline Failed
<br>â†“
<br>Find Failed Stage
<br>â†“
<br>Read Exact Error
<br>â†“
<br>Check Agent
<br>â†“
<br>Check Credentials
<br>â†“
<br>Check Dependency / Network
<br>â†“
<br>Reproduce Command
<br>â†“
<br>Fix Root Cause
<br>â†“
<br>Re-run

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview tip:</strong>

Do not say "I rerun the pipeline."

Say:

"I first identify the failed stage and analyze the exact error from
the console output. Then I validate the agent, credentials,
dependencies and external services before fixing the root cause."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Scenario: Secret Exposed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

If a credential appears in Jenkins logs:

<br><br>

<strong>1.</strong> Treat it as compromised.

<br>

<strong>2.</strong> Revoke or rotate it.

<br>

<strong>3.</strong> Remove unsafe logging.

<br>

<strong>4.</strong> Investigate where it was exposed.

<br>

<strong>5.</strong> Review access/audit logs.

<br>

<strong>6.</strong> Prevent recurrence.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Deleting the log or Git file alone does not make an exposed credential
safe. Rotate it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: Wrong Docker Image Deployed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Production is running an unexpected image.

<strong>Possible cause:</strong>

A mutable tag such as <code>latest</code> was reused or the deployment
was not updated as expected.

<strong>Better:</strong>

Use unique image tags.

</div>

<pre><code>payment-app:105
payment-app:git-a8f32c1</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Scenario: Kubernetes Deployment Fails</h2>

<div class="scenario">

If:

<pre><code>Docker Push â†’ SUCCESS
Kubernetes Deploy â†’ FAILURE</code></pre>

Check:

<ul>

<li>Cluster connectivity.</li>
<li>kubectl configuration.</li>
<li>Identity and RBAC.</li>
<li>Namespace.</li>
<li>Deployment manifest.</li>
<li>Image name/tag.</li>
<li>Pod events.</li>
<li>Application logs.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get nodes

kubectl get pods -n production

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt; -n production

kubectl get events -n production</code></pre>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Best Interview Answer: "Explain Your Jenkins CI/CD Pipeline"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In my CI/CD workflow, developers push application code to GitHub.
A webhook triggers Jenkins automatically.

Jenkins checks out the source code and runs the build and automated
tests. After successful validation, security checks can be performed
and Jenkins builds a Docker image.

I tag the image using a unique build number or source revision and
push it to a container registry such as Amazon ECR.

The deployment stage then updates the target environment, such as
Kubernetes/EKS, to use the validated image.

For security, I store credentials in Jenkins Credentials or use
appropriate workload identity mechanisms rather than hard-coding
secrets.

If a pipeline fails, I identify the failed stage, read the exact
console error, check the agent and dependencies, validate external
services and fix the root cause before rerunning.

This gives us an automated, repeatable and traceable path from Git
commit to deployed application."

</div>

</div>

<h1>Jenkins <span>Git + Docker + CI/CD</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Git integration, GitHub Webhooks,
SCM triggers, Docker builds, container registries, image tagging,
Jenkins credentials and an end-to-end production-style CI/CD flow.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
A common Jenkins CI/CD workflow starts with a Git push and ends with
a tested application artifact or Docker image being deployed.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>GitHub</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Webhook
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Jenkins</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Container Registry
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
<br>â†“<br>
Application

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A developer pushes a Java application to GitHub. Jenkins is triggered
through a webhook, checks out the code, runs Maven tests, builds a
Docker image, pushes it to Amazon ECR and deploys the new image to
Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. How does Jenkins integrate with Git?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins can connect to Git repositories and automatically checkout
source code before executing build and test stages.

The repository can be GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or another supported
SCM system.

</div>

<h3>Typical flow</h3>

<pre><code>git push
    â†“
GitHub Repository
    â†“
Webhook
    â†“
Jenkins
    â†“
Checkout Source
    â†“
Build / Test</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Webhook vs Poll SCM</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Webhook</th>
<th>Poll SCM</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Git provider notifies Jenkins when an event occurs.</td>
<td>Jenkins periodically checks the repository.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Event-driven.</td>
<td>Polling-based.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Usually faster reaction to changes.</td>
<td>Can generate unnecessary repository checks.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"For modern CI/CD, I generally prefer webhooks because the Git
provider can notify Jenkins immediately when a relevant event occurs,
instead of Jenkins repeatedly polling the repository."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What happens when a developer pushes code?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>git push</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub
<br>â†“<br>
Webhook Event
<br>â†“<br>
Jenkins Trigger
<br>â†“<br>
Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Push Image

</div>

<div class="interview">

The important point is that Jenkins does not magically know that
code changed. A trigger such as a webhook, polling mechanism or
manual/API trigger starts the job.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Jenkins Git Checkout</h2>

<h3>Simple checkout</h3>

<pre><code>stage('Checkout') {

    steps {
        checkout scm
    }
}</code></pre>

<p>
For a Pipeline job configured with SCM, <code>checkout scm</code>
checks out the source configured for that job.
</p>

<h3>Explicit Git checkout</h3>

<pre><code>stage('Checkout') {

    steps {

        git branch: 'main',
            url: 'https://github.com/example/app.git'
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

For private repositories, credentials should be configured securely
through Jenkins Credentials rather than putting usernames or tokens
directly into the Jenkinsfile.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Why do we use Docker with Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker packages an application together with its runtime dependencies
into a portable container image.

Jenkins can automate building, testing and publishing that image.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Without containerization, an application may behave differently
between build and deployment environments.

With Docker:

<strong>Source Code â†’ Docker Image â†’ Same Image â†’ Deployment</strong>

This improves consistency between environments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Docker Build in Jenkins</h2>

<pre><code>stage('Docker Build') {

    steps {

        sh '''
        docker build \
          -t payment-app:${BUILD_NUMBER} .
        '''
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<code>BUILD_NUMBER</code> is a Jenkins-provided build identifier.
Using a unique tag helps identify which Jenkins build produced an
image.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Docker Image Tagging Strategy</h2>

<p>
Avoid using only <code>latest</code> for production deployments.
Use identifiable immutable or versioned tags where possible.
</p>

<pre><code>payment-app:42
payment-app:1.4.2
payment-app:git-a8f32c1</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

Jenkins Build #42 creates:

<pre><code>123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/payment-app:42</code></pre>

If deployment fails, you can identify exactly which build/image was
used.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Push Docker Image to Registry</h2>

<div class="answer">

A container registry stores Docker images so deployment systems can
pull them later.

Examples include Amazon ECR, Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry
and other OCI-compatible registries.

</div>

<h3>Generic example</h3>

<pre><code>docker login &lt;registry&gt;

docker tag payment-app:42 \
  &lt;registry&gt;/payment-app:42

docker push \
  &lt;registry&gt;/payment-app:42</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Registry credentials should not be written directly into the
Jenkinsfile or shell commands.

Use Jenkins Credentials or an appropriate workload identity mechanism.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Jenkins + Docker + ECR</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A common AWS workflow:

<div class="flow">

GitHub
<br>â†“<br>
Jenkins
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Amazon ECR
<br>â†“<br>
EKS / ECS
<br>â†“<br>
Application

</div>

Jenkins builds the image and pushes it to ECR. The deployment
platform then pulls the image from ECR.

</div>

<h3>Conceptual commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t payment-app:${BUILD_NUMBER} .

docker tag payment-app:${BUILD_NUMBER} \
  ${ECR_REPOSITORY}:${BUILD_NUMBER}

docker push ${ECR_REPOSITORY}:${BUILD_NUMBER}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Complete Jenkins Git + Docker Pipeline</h2>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    environment {

        IMAGE_NAME = 'payment-app'
        REGISTRY = '123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com'
        IMAGE_TAG = "${BUILD_NUMBER}"
    }

    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {

            steps {
                checkout scm
            }
        }

        stage('Build') {

            steps {
                sh 'mvn clean package'
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {

            steps {
                sh 'mvn test'
            }
        }

        stage('Docker Build') {

            steps {

                sh '''
                docker build \
                  -t ${IMAGE_NAME}:${IMAGE_TAG} .
                '''
            }
        }

        stage('Docker Tag') {

            steps {

                sh '''
                docker tag \
                  ${IMAGE_NAME}:${IMAGE_TAG} \
                  ${REGISTRY}/${IMAGE_NAME}:${IMAGE_TAG}
                '''
            }
        }

        stage('Push Image') {

            steps {

                sh '''
                docker push \
                  ${REGISTRY}/${IMAGE_NAME}:${IMAGE_TAG}
                '''
            }
        }
    }

    post {

        success {
            echo 'CI pipeline completed successfully'
        }

        failure {
            echo 'CI pipeline failed'
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

This demonstrates the pipeline flow. Authentication to ECR and
other external systems should be implemented through secure Jenkins
credentials or AWS identity mechanisms rather than hard-coded
credentials.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Docker Build vs Docker Push</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>docker build</th>
<th>docker push</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Creates an image locally/on the build agent.</td>
<td>Uploads an image to a registry.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses Dockerfile and build context.</td>
<td>Requires access to the target registry.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: <code>docker build -t app:42 .</code></td>
<td>Example: <code>docker push registry/app:42</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. How do you securely authenticate to Docker Registry?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Credentials should be stored in Jenkins Credentials or supplied
through a secure identity mechanism.

The pipeline should reference the credential rather than embedding
the password or token in source code.

</div>

<h3>Conceptual Jenkins example</h3>

<pre><code>withCredentials([
    usernamePassword(
        credentialsId: 'docker-registry',
        usernameVariable: 'REGISTRY_USER',
        passwordVariable: 'REGISTRY_PASS'
    )
]) {

    sh '''
    echo "$REGISTRY_PASS" | \
      docker login \
      --username "$REGISTRY_USER" \
      --password-stdin registry.example.com
    '''
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Never commit:

<pre><code>docker login -u admin -p MyPassword</code></pre>

into a Jenkinsfile or Git repository.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What if Docker build fails?</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<br><br>

1. Dockerfile syntax.
<br>
2. Build context.
<br>
3. Required files.
<br>
4. Base image availability.
<br>
5. Network connectivity.
<br>
6. Docker daemon access.
<br>
7. Disk space.
<br>
8. CPU/memory resources.

</div>

<h3>Useful commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker version
docker info
docker images
docker ps
df -h</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. What if Docker Push fails?</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Common causes:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Registry authentication failure.</li>
<li>Wrong repository name.</li>
<li>Wrong image tag.</li>
<li>Repository does not exist.</li>
<li>Insufficient registry permissions.</li>
<li>Network connectivity problems.</li>
<li>Registry service issue.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<h3>Debugging approach</h3>

<pre><code>docker images

docker login &lt;registry&gt;

docker push &lt;registry&gt;/app:42</code></pre>

<p>
Then inspect the exact error and verify credentials and repository
permissions.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What if Jenkins cannot access Docker?</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Pipeline reports that the Docker command cannot connect to the
Docker daemon.

<br><br>

<strong>Check:</strong>

1. Is Docker installed on the Jenkins agent?
<br>
2. Is Docker running?
<br>
3. Does the Jenkins execution user have permission?
<br>
4. Is the correct Docker socket/runtime available?
<br>
5. Is the agent containerized?
<br>
6. Are security restrictions blocking Docker access?

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker version
docker info
docker ps</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Git Branch-based Deployment</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A common strategy is:

<strong>develop</strong> â†’ Dev

<br>
<strong>release/*</strong> â†’ QA/Staging

<br>
<strong>main</strong> â†’ Production

</div>

<h3>Jenkins condition</h3>

<pre><code>stage('Production Deploy') {

    when {
        branch 'main'
    }

    steps {
        sh './deploy-production.sh'
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The exact branch strategy depends on the organization's Git workflow.
The important concept is that deployment rules should be explicit
and controlled.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. End-to-End Production Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Scenario: Jenkins Build Works but Deployment Fails</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose:

<br><br>

Git checkout â†’ SUCCESS

<br>
Maven build â†’ SUCCESS

<br>
Tests â†’ SUCCESS

<br>
Docker build â†’ SUCCESS

<br>
Docker push â†’ SUCCESS

<br>
Deployment â†’ FAILURE

<br><br>

Do not rebuild everything immediately.

First inspect the deployment layer:

<ul>

<li>Image name/tag.</li>
<li>Registry availability.</li>
<li>Deployment manifest.</li>
<li>Kubernetes credentials.</li>
<li>Cluster connectivity.</li>
<li>Namespace.</li>
<li>Pod events and logs.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Real-Time Scenario: Wrong Docker Image Deployed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Production is running an unexpected image.

<strong>Likely cause:</strong>

The pipeline uses a mutable tag such as <code>latest</code> or
deployment configuration was not updated correctly.

<strong>Better approach:</strong>

Use unique version/build/commit-based tags.

</div>

<pre><code>payment-app:105
payment-app:git-a8f32c1</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

This improves traceability because you can map a deployed image
back to a specific source revision and Jenkins build.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. CI vs CD</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>CI</th>
<th>CD</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Continuous Integration</td>
<td>Continuous Delivery / Deployment</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build and test code changes.</td>
<td>Release and deploy validated artifacts.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Find integration issues early.</td>
<td>Automate software delivery.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

CI
<br>
Git â†’ Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan â†’ Package

<br><br>

CD
<br>
Artifact/Image â†’ Deploy â†’ Verify

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Jenkins + Git + Docker Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Keep Jenkinsfile in Git.</li>

<li>Use webhooks for event-driven triggering where appropriate.</li>

<li>Use unique image tags.</li>

<li>Avoid relying only on <code>latest</code>.</li>

<li>Never hard-code credentials.</li>

<li>Use Jenkins Credentials or workload identity.</li>

<li>Scan images before deployment.</li>

<li>Keep Docker images small and reproducible.</li>

<li>Use immutable artifacts where possible.</li>

<li>Promote the same tested image across environments rather than
rebuilding different images unnecessarily.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<!-- FINAL -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Jenkins CI/CD with Git and Docker"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In a typical CI/CD workflow, a developer pushes code to GitHub.
A webhook triggers the Jenkins pipeline.

Jenkins checks out the source code and runs the build and automated
tests. If the tests pass, Jenkins builds a Docker image and tags it
with a unique build or source revision identifier.

The image is then pushed to a container registry such as Amazon ECR.
The deployment stage updates the target environment, for example
Kubernetes or EKS, to use that image.

For security, I don't hard-code Git, registry or cloud credentials
inside the Jenkinsfile. I use Jenkins Credentials or appropriate
cloud identity mechanisms.

For production, I also prefer immutable/versioned image tags,
security scanning and traceability between the Git commit, Jenkins
build and deployed container image."

</div>

</div>


</main>

<div class="icon">ðŸš€</div>

<h1>Jenkins <span>Pipelines</span></h1>

<p>
Complete interview-focused guide covering Jenkins Pipeline,
Jenkinsfile, Declarative and Scripted Pipelines, stages,
steps, parameters, environment variables, conditions,
post actions, parallel execution and real-time CI/CD examples.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
A Jenkins Pipeline defines the complete CI/CD workflow as code.
Instead of manually configuring every build step in the Jenkins UI,
we define the workflow in a <strong>Jenkinsfile</strong>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git Push <br>â†“<br>
Jenkins <br>â†“<br> <strong>Pipeline</strong> <br>â†“<br>
Checkout â†’ Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan â†’ Package <br>â†“<br>
Docker Build â†’ Push <br>â†“<br>
Deploy

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A Java application is pushed to GitHub. Jenkins starts the pipeline,
checks out the code, runs Maven build and tests, performs a quality
scan, builds a Docker image, pushes it to ECR and deploys the
application to Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Jenkins Pipeline?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Jenkins Pipeline is a collection of automated steps that define
how software moves through stages such as build, test, security
scan, packaging and deployment.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Jenkins Pipeline is a way of defining the complete CI/CD workflow
as code. It allows us to automate multiple stages such as checkout,
build, test, Docker image creation and deployment."

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is a Jenkinsfile?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Jenkinsfile is a text file containing the Jenkins Pipeline
definition. It is commonly stored in the application's Git
repository.

</div>

<h3>Basic structure</h3>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    stages {

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Building'
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                echo 'Testing'
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                echo 'Deploying'
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Why keep it in Git?</strong>

It provides version control, code review, history and the ability
to reproduce previous pipeline versions.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Declarative vs Scripted Pipeline</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Declarative</th>
<th>Scripted</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Structured and easier to read.</td>
<td>More flexible and programmatic.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses <code>pipeline {}</code>.</td>
<td>Uses Groovy scripting.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Preferred for most standard CI/CD pipelines.</td>
<td>Useful for complex custom logic.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Has built-in pipeline structure.</td>
<td>Provides greater programming flexibility.</td>
</tr>
</table>

<h3>Declarative example</h3>

<pre><code>pipeline {
    agent any

    stages {
        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Build'
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"I generally prefer Declarative Pipeline because it provides a
clear structure and is easier to maintain. Scripted Pipeline is
useful when more advanced Groovy-based logic is required."

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is an Agent?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>agent</code> tells Jenkins where the pipeline or a stage
should execute.

</div>

<h3>Any available agent</h3>

<pre><code>pipeline {
    agent any

    stages {
        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Running build'
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<h3>Stage-specific agent</h3>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent none

    stages {

        stage('Build') {

            agent {
                label 'linux'
            }

            steps {
                sh 'mvn clean package'
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Pipeline Stages</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <code>stage</code> represents a logical section of the CI/CD
workflow.

Typical stages include:

</div>

<div class="flow">

Checkout <br>â†“<br>
Build <br>â†“<br>
Test <br>â†“<br>
Security Scan <br>â†“<br>
Docker Build <br>â†“<br>
Push <br>â†“<br>
Deploy

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre><code>stages {

    stage('Build') {
        steps {
            sh 'mvn clean package'
        }
    }

    stage('Test') {
        steps {
            sh 'mvn test'
        }
    }

    stage('Deploy') {
        steps {
            sh './deploy.sh'
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Step?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A step is an individual action executed inside a stage.

</div>

<pre><code>stage('Build') {
    steps {
        echo 'Starting build'
        sh 'mvn clean package'
    }
}</code></pre>

<p>
Here <code>echo</code> and <code>sh</code> are steps.
</p>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Common Jenkins Pipeline Steps</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Step</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>echo</code></td>
<td>Print a message.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>sh</code></td>
<td>Execute Linux shell commands.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>bat</code></td>
<td>Execute Windows batch commands.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>checkout</code></td>
<td>Checkout source code.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>input</code></td>
<td>Wait for manual approval/input.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>archiveArtifacts</code></td>
<td>Archive build artifacts.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Environment Variables</h2>

<div class="answer">

Environment variables allow configuration values to be provided to
the pipeline without hard-coding them repeatedly.

</div>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    environment {
        APP_NAME = 'payment-app'
        ENVIRONMENT = 'production'
    }

    stages {

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo "Building ${APP_NAME}"
                echo "Environment: ${ENVIRONMENT}"
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not put passwords or API keys directly inside the <code>environment</code> block. Use Jenkins Credentials instead.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Pipeline Parameters</h2>

<div class="answer">

Parameters allow users or automation to provide values when
starting a pipeline.

</div>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    parameters {
        choice(
            name: 'ENV',
            choices: ['dev', 'qa', 'prod'],
            description: 'Select environment'
        )
    }

    stages {

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                echo "Deploying to ${params.ENV}"
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time use:</strong>

The same deployment pipeline can be used for Dev, QA and Production
by selecting the required environment.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What is the <code>when</code> condition?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>when</code> directive controls whether a stage should
execute based on a condition.

</div>

<pre><code>stage('Production Deploy') {

    when {
        branch 'main'
    }

    steps {
        echo 'Deploying production'
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

For example, production deployment can be restricted to the <strong>main</strong> branch.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is <code>post</code>?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>post</code> section defines actions that should happen
after the pipeline or a stage completes.

</div>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    stages {

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Building'
            }
        }
    }

    post {

        success {
            echo 'Pipeline succeeded'
        }

        failure {
            echo 'Pipeline failed'
        }

        always {
            echo 'Pipeline completed'
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Common uses include notifications, cleanup and publishing test
reports.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Manual Approval using <code>input</code></h2>

<div class="answer">

The <code>input</code> step pauses a pipeline and waits for human
approval before continuing.

</div>

<pre><code>stage('Production Approval') {

    steps {

        input message: 'Deploy to production?'

        echo 'Approved'
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Continuous Delivery example:</strong>

Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan â†’ Staging â†’ Manual Approval â†’ Production.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Parallel Stages</h2>

<div class="answer">

Independent tasks can run in parallel to reduce total pipeline
execution time.

</div>

<pre><code>stage('Tests') {

    parallel {

        stage('Unit Tests') {
            steps {
                sh 'mvn test'
            }
        }

        stage('Security Scan') {
            steps {
                sh './security-scan.sh'
            }
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">

If unit tests and security scans do not depend on each other,
running them in parallel can reduce pipeline duration.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Complete Real-Time Jenkins Pipeline</h2>

<pre><code>pipeline {

    agent any

    environment {
        APP_NAME = 'payment-app'
        IMAGE = 'payment-app:v1'
    }

    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                checkout scm
            }
        }

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                sh 'mvn clean package'
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                sh 'mvn test'
            }
        }

        stage('Security Scan') {
            steps {
                sh 'trivy fs .'
            }
        }

        stage('Docker Build') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE .'
            }
        }

        stage('Push Image') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker push $IMAGE'
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                sh 'kubectl apply -f k8s/'
            }
        }
    }

    post {

        success {
            echo 'Deployment successful'
        }

        failure {
            echo 'Pipeline failed'
        }

        always {
            echo 'Pipeline completed'
        }
    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

This is an interview-oriented example. In production, registry
authentication, cloud credentials and Kubernetes access should be
handled securely through Jenkins Credentials or appropriate
identity mechanisms rather than hard-coded secrets.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. How does Jenkins Pipeline handle failure?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Normally, when a step fails, the current stage fails and the
pipeline can stop unless the pipeline explicitly handles the
failure.

The <code>post</code> section can still run cleanup or notification
logic.

</div>

<pre><code>post {

    success {
        echo 'Success'
    }

    failure {
        echo 'Failure notification'
    }

    always {
        echo 'Cleanup'
    }
}</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 16. How do you skip a stage for certain branches?</h2>

<pre><code>stage('Deploy') {

    when {
        branch 'main'
    }

    steps {
        sh './deploy.sh'
    }
}</code></pre>

<p>
This prevents the deployment stage from executing for branches that
do not satisfy the condition.
</p>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. How do you pass artifacts between stages?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Files created during one stage can remain in the workspace for
subsequent stages when those stages run in the same suitable
workspace.

For more explicit artifact management, Jenkins provides artifact
archiving and other mechanisms depending on the pipeline design.

</div>

<pre><code>stage('Build') {
    steps {
        sh 'mvn package'
        archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'target/*.jar'
    }
}</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Jenkins Pipeline Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Pipeline failed:</strong>

Do not immediately rerun it repeatedly.

<br><br>

1. Open Console Output.

   <br>
2. Identify failed stage.

   <br>
3. Find the exact command that failed.

   <br>
4. Check agent availability.

   <br>
5. Verify workspace files.

   <br>
6. Check credentials.

   <br>
7. Check external services.

   <br>
8. Reproduce the command manually where appropriate.

   <br>
9. Fix the root cause.

   <br>
10. Run the pipeline again.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Real-Time Scenario: Production Deployment</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A company wants automatic deployment to Dev and QA, but Production
requires approval.

<div class="flow">

Git Push <br>â†“<br>
Build <br>â†“<br>
Unit Test <br>â†“<br>
Security Scan <br>â†“<br>
Docker Build <br>â†“<br>
Dev Deploy <br>â†“<br>
QA Deploy <br>â†“<br> <strong>Manual Approval</strong> <br>â†“<br>
Production Deploy

</div>

This can be implemented using stages, conditions and the <code>input</code> step.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Pipeline Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Keep Jenkinsfiles in Git.</li>

<li>Use meaningful stage names.</li>

<li>Keep pipelines modular and readable.</li>

<li>Do not hard-code credentials.</li>

<li>Use environment variables for non-sensitive configuration.</li>

<li>Use Jenkins Credentials for secrets.</li>

<li>Fail fast when critical stages fail.</li>

<li>Use parallel stages when tasks are independent.</li>

<li>Use manual approval for controlled production releases where required.</li>

<li>Keep deployment logic reproducible.</li>

<li>Use dedicated agents for specialized workloads.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<div class="card">

â†’ Where pipeline runs

<br><br>

â†’ Logical section

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Jenkins Pipeline"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"A Jenkins Pipeline is an automated CI/CD workflow defined as code,
usually inside a Jenkinsfile.

I normally structure it into stages such as checkout, build, test,
security scanning, Docker image creation, image push and deployment.

The pipeline runs on Jenkins agents. I use environment variables
for normal configuration and Jenkins Credentials for sensitive
information.

Using Declarative Pipeline, I can define conditions with <code>when</code>, post-build actions with <code>post</code>,
manual production approval with <code>input</code> and parallel
execution for independent tasks.

Keeping the Jenkinsfile in Git gives us version control,
reviewability and reproducibility."

</div>

<header>

<div class="icon">ðŸ”</div>

<a href="index.html" class="back">â† Back to Jenkins</a>

<h1>Jenkins <span>Security & Troubleshooting</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering Jenkins security, authentication,
authorization, credentials, secrets, agents, CSRF protection,
common pipeline failures, logs, troubleshooting methodology and
real-time DevOps scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Core Concept</h2>

<p>
Jenkins is part of the CI/CD control plane, so securing Jenkins is
critical. A compromised Jenkins instance can potentially expose
source code, credentials, build artifacts and deployment access.
</p>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¤ User
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ” Authentication
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ›¡ï¸ Authorization
<br>â†“<br>
âš™ï¸ Jenkins Job
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ”‘ Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ–¥ï¸ Agent
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸš€ Build / Deploy

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Security principle:</strong>

Give users, jobs and agents only the permissions they actually need.
Avoid giving broad administrator or cloud privileges unnecessarily.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Authentication vs Authorization</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Authentication</th>
<th>Authorization</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Determines who the user is.</td>
<td>Determines what the user is allowed to do.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Login / identity verification.</td>
<td>Permissions / access control.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: Jenkins login.</td>
<td>Example: permission to configure a job.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Authentication verifies the identity of a user, while authorization
determines what that authenticated user is allowed to access or
perform."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Jenkins Credentials</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins Credentials provides a centralized way to store sensitive
information such as passwords, SSH keys, API tokens and other
credential material used by jobs.

</div>

<h3>Common credential types</h3>

<ul>

<li>Username and password</li>
<li>Secret text</li>
<li>SSH private key</li>
<li>Certificates</li>
<li>Cloud/provider credentials depending on installed integrations</li>

</ul>

<div class="warning">

Never put passwords, API keys or private keys directly inside a
Jenkinsfile or Git repository.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. How do you use Jenkins Credentials?</h2>

<pre><code>withCredentials([
    usernamePassword(
        credentialsId: 'docker-registry',
        usernameVariable: 'REGISTRY_USER',
        passwordVariable: 'REGISTRY_PASS'
    )
]) {

    sh '''
    echo "$REGISTRY_PASS" | \
    docker login registry.example.com \
    --username "$REGISTRY_USER" \
    --password-stdin
    '''
}</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The Jenkinsfile references a credential ID instead of storing the
actual secret in source control.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is RBAC in Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Role-Based Access Control allows permissions to be assigned according
to users or groups and their roles.

For example, developers may build applications while a smaller group
has permission to administer Jenkins.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Developer â†’ Build / Read

<br>
Release Engineer â†’ Build / Deploy

<br>
Jenkins Administrator â†’ Manage Jenkins

</div>

<div class="warning">

Avoid giving every user full administrator access.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Principle of Least Privilege</h2>

<div class="answer">

Users, Jenkins jobs and agents should receive only the permissions
required to perform their tasks.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If a Jenkins job only needs to push an image to ECR, it should not
automatically receive unrestricted permissions to every AWS service.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Protecting Secrets in Jenkins</h2>

<ul>

<li>Store secrets in Jenkins Credentials.</li>

<li>Do not commit credentials to Git.</li>

<li>Do not echo secrets into build logs.</li>

<li>Use masking features where applicable.</li>

<li>Rotate credentials periodically.</li>

<li>Limit credential scope and access.</li>

<li>Use short-lived credentials where practical.</li>

<li>Prefer workload identity mechanisms when supported.</li>

</ul>

<div class="warning">

Secret masking is not a guarantee that every possible way of
exposing a secret is prevented. Pipeline scripts should be designed
so secrets are never unnecessarily printed or passed into unsafe
commands.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Jenkins Controller vs Agent Security</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Jenkins controller coordinates jobs, while agents execute build
work.

Build workloads should generally run on agents rather than
performing arbitrary build commands directly on the controller.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Jenkins Controller
<br>â†“
<br>Schedule Job
<br>â†“
<br>Jenkins Agent
<br>â†“
<br>Build / Test / Docker
<br>â†“
<br>Artifact

</div>

<div class="warning">

Agents execute build commands, so an untrusted or compromised build
can be dangerous. Isolate agents appropriately and avoid giving
unnecessary access to the controller or production credentials.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 8. Jenkins Agent Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

Pipeline says:

<pre><code>There are no nodes with the label...</code></pre>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Is the agent online?</li>
<li>Does the required label exist?</li>
<li>Is the agent connected?</li>
<li>Does the agent have required tools?</li>
<li>Is there enough CPU/memory/disk?</li>
<li>Can the agent communicate with Jenkins?</li>

</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. CSRF Protection</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins supports protection against Cross-Site Request Forgery
(CSRF) attacks.

CSRF protection helps prevent unauthorized requests from being
submitted to Jenkins through a user's authenticated session.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not disable security protections simply to make an integration
work. Investigate the authentication, API and integration setup
properly.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. Jenkins Security Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Keep Jenkins and plugins updated.</li>

<li>Remove unused plugins.</li>

<li>Use strong authentication.</li>

<li>Use role-based permissions.</li>

<li>Protect Jenkins from direct public exposure where possible.</li>

<li>Use HTTPS/TLS.</li>

<li>Store credentials in Jenkins Credentials.</li>

<li>Restrict agent permissions.</li>

<li>Use least privilege for cloud access.</li>

<li>Monitor Jenkins logs.</li>

<li>Back up Jenkins configuration appropriately.</li>

<li>Review user and credential access regularly.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- TROUBLESHOOTING -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Jenkins Troubleshooting Method</h2>

<div class="answer">

When a Jenkins pipeline fails, do not randomly rerun it.

Follow a structured troubleshooting process.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pipeline Failure
<br>â†“<br>
Identify Failed Stage
<br>â†“<br>
Read Exact Error
<br>â†“<br>
Check Agent
<br>â†“<br>
Check Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
Check Dependencies
<br>â†“<br>
Reproduce Command
<br>â†“<br>
Fix Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
Re-run

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Pipeline fails during Checkout</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Wrong repository URL.</li>
<li>Invalid credentials.</li>
<li>Branch does not exist.</li>
<li>Network/DNS problem.</li>
<li>Git is not installed on the agent.</li>
<li>Repository access permissions are missing.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>git --version
git ls-remote &lt;repository-url&gt;</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Pipeline fails during Maven Build</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Java version.</li>
<li>Maven installation.</li>
<li>pom.xml.</li>
<li>Dependency download access.</li>
<li>Disk space.</li>
<li>Environment variables.</li>
<li>Build command.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<pre><code>java -version
mvn -version
df -h</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Docker command not found</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Error:</strong>

<pre><code>docker: command not found</code></pre>

<strong>Likely cause:</strong>

Docker is not installed or is not available in the Jenkins agent's
PATH.

<strong>Fix:</strong>

Install/configure Docker on the appropriate agent or use an
appropriate containerized build environment.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Cannot connect to Docker daemon</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

<pre><code>Cannot connect to the Docker daemon</code></pre>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<pre><code>docker version
docker info
docker ps</code></pre>

Also verify:

<ul>

<li>Docker daemon status.</li>
<li>Jenkins user permissions.</li>
<li>Docker socket/runtime configuration.</li>
<li>Agent environment.</li>

</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Docker Push permission denied</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Registry authentication failure.</li>
<li>Wrong repository.</li>
<li>Missing push permissions.</li>
<li>Incorrect image tag.</li>
<li>Registry policy restrictions.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<pre><code>docker images
docker login &lt;registry&gt;
docker push &lt;registry&gt;/app:42</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Kubernetes deployment fails from Jenkins</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Pipeline:</strong>

<pre><code>docker push â†’ SUCCESS
kubectl apply â†’ FAILURE</code></pre>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Is kubectl installed?</li>
<li>Can Jenkins reach the cluster?</li>
<li>Is the kubeconfig/identity valid?</li>
<li>Is the namespace correct?</li>
<li>Does the deployment manifest contain errors?</li>
<li>Does the identity have sufficient permissions?</li>
<li>Is the image available?</li>

</ul>

<h3>Useful commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl version
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -n &lt;namespace&gt;
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt; -n &lt;namespace&gt;
kubectl get events -n &lt;namespace&gt;</code></pre>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Jenkins Credentials not working</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Wrong credential ID.</li>
<li>Credential type mismatch.</li>
<li>Credential is not available to the job.</li>
<li>Incorrect variable usage.</li>
<li>Permission/scope issue.</li>
<li>Credential was rotated or revoked.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not print the credential value while troubleshooting.

Verify the credential configuration and test the authentication
operation safely.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Pipeline is stuck in Queue</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

The build remains in:

<pre><code>Waiting for next available executor</code></pre>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Are agents online?</li>
<li>Are executors available?</li>
<li>Does the job require a specific label?</li>
<li>Is the required agent disconnected?</li>
<li>Is another build consuming all executors?</li>

</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Pipeline is slow</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<ul>

<li>Build duration by stage.</li>
<li>Agent CPU and memory.</li>
<li>Dependency download time.</li>
<li>Docker build time.</li>
<li>Network latency.</li>
<li>Unnecessary repeated builds.</li>
<li>Tests that can safely run in parallel.</li>
</ul>

<strong>Possible improvements:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Parallelize independent stages.</li>
<li>Use caching appropriately.</li>
<li>Use optimized Dockerfiles.</li>
<li>Use suitable agents.</li>
<li>Avoid unnecessary workspace operations.</li>

</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Real-Time Scenario: Secret accidentally exposed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

A developer accidentally printed a cloud credential in Jenkins
console output.

<strong>Immediate response:</strong>

1. Treat the credential as compromised.
<br>
2. Revoke/rotate the credential immediately.
<br>
3. Remove unsafe logging.
<br>
4. Investigate where the value was exposed.
<br>
5. Review access/audit logs.
<br>
6. Replace it with secure credential handling.
<br>
7. Prevent recurrence with scanning and review.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not assume deleting the console output or deleting the Git commit
makes an already exposed credential safe. Rotate the credential.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Real-Time Scenario: Jenkins server compromised</h2>

<div class="scenario">

If there is evidence that Jenkins itself has been compromised:

<br><br>

1. Isolate the affected instance where appropriate.
<br>
2. Preserve relevant logs and evidence.
<br>
3. Rotate credentials accessible from Jenkins.
<br>
4. Review users, jobs, plugins and configuration.
<br>
5. Inspect connected agents.
<br>
6. Check downstream cloud and deployment systems.
<br>
7. Rebuild from a trusted configuration when necessary.
<br>
8. Restore only verified configuration/data.
<br>
9. Review security controls before returning to service.

</div>

<div class="interview">

The key interview point is that Jenkins can hold high-value
credentials, so a Jenkins compromise can have a much wider blast
radius than a normal application server compromise.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Jenkins Logs</h2>

<div class="answer">

Logs are one of the first places to look when diagnosing Jenkins
problems.

</div>

<h3>Check from Jenkins UI</h3>

<ul>

<li>Build Console Output</li>
<li>Pipeline Stage Logs</li>
<li>System Log</li>
<li>Agent logs</li>
<li>Plugin-related logs</li>

</ul>

<h3>Useful Pipeline diagnostics</h3>

<pre><code>echo 'Debug message'

sh 'pwd'
sh 'ls -la'
sh 'whoami'
sh 'java -version'
sh 'docker version'</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Never use debug commands that intentionally print passwords,
tokens or private keys.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 24. Jenkins Disk Full</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Symptoms:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Builds fail unexpectedly.</li>
<li>Docker builds fail.</li>
<li>Artifacts cannot be created.</li>
<li>Workspace operations fail.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>df -h
du -sh *</code></pre>

<strong>Possible solutions:</strong>

<ul>

<li>Clean old workspaces.</li>
<li>Remove unnecessary Docker images/layers.</li>
<li>Review artifact retention.</li>
<li>Increase disk capacity.</li>
<li>Configure appropriate cleanup policies.</li>

</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Jenkins Security + Troubleshooting Checklist</h2>

<ul>

<li>Authentication configured?</li>
<li>Authorization/roles configured?</li>
<li>Least privilege applied?</li>
<li>Credentials stored securely?</li>
<li>Secrets excluded from Git?</li>
<li>HTTPS/TLS enabled?</li>
<li>Plugins maintained?</li>
<li>Agents isolated appropriately?</li>
<li>Cloud permissions restricted?</li>
<li>Build logs reviewed?</li>
<li>Disk space checked?</li>
<li>Agent availability checked?</li>
<li>Git connectivity checked?</li>
<li>Docker availability checked?</li>
<li>Registry authentication checked?</li>
<li>Kubernetes access checked?</li>

</ul>

</div>

<!-- FINAL INTERVIEW -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "How do you secure and troubleshoot Jenkins?"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"I secure Jenkins using strong authentication, role-based
authorization and the principle of least privilege.

Sensitive information such as passwords, tokens and SSH keys is
stored using Jenkins Credentials instead of hard-coding them in
Jenkinsfiles or Git.

I also keep Jenkins and its plugins maintained, protect the Jenkins
endpoint with appropriate network controls and HTTPS, and isolate
build agents according to the workload and trust level.

For troubleshooting, I first identify the failed pipeline stage and
read the exact console error. Then I check the agent, credentials,
dependencies, network connectivity and external services.

For example, if Docker push fails, I verify registry authentication,
image tags and permissions. If Kubernetes deployment fails, I check
cluster connectivity, identity permissions, namespace, manifests,
events and pod status.

If a secret is accidentally exposed, I immediately treat it as
compromised and rotate or revoke it rather than simply deleting the
log or source file."

</div>

<h1>CI/CD <span>Basics</span></h1>

<p>
Core CI/CD concepts for DevOps interviews â€” Continuous Integration,
Continuous Delivery, Continuous Deployment, pipeline stages,
automation, benefits and real-world workflow.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- INTRO -->

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is CI/CD?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>CI/CD</strong> is a software delivery approach that automates
the process of integrating code, validating changes, building
artifacts and delivering or deploying applications.

</div>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸ“¦ Git Repository
<br>â†“
<br>
âš™ï¸ CI
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸ§ª Build + Test + Scan
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸ“¦ Artifact / Image
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸš€ CD
<br>â†“
<br>
â˜¸ï¸ Deployment

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Real-time example:</strong>

A developer pushes code to GitHub. A pipeline automatically builds
the application, runs tests and security checks, creates a Docker
image and deploys it to Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- CI -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is Continuous Integration?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Continuous Integration (CI)</strong> is the practice of
frequently integrating code changes into a shared repository and
automatically validating those changes through builds and tests.

</div>

<h3>Typical CI Flow</h3>

<div class="flow">

Code Commit
<br>â†“
<br>
Build
<br>â†“
<br>
Unit Tests
<br>â†“
<br>
Code Quality
<br>â†“
<br>
Security Scan
<br>â†“
<br>
Artifact

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"Continuous Integration means developers frequently merge their
changes into a shared repository, where an automated pipeline builds
and tests the code to detect problems early."

</div>

</div>


<!-- CONTINUOUS DELIVERY -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is Continuous Delivery?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Continuous Delivery</strong> means the application is
automatically built, tested and prepared for release so that it is
always in a deployable state.

The production deployment may require a manual approval.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Code
<br>â†“
<br>
CI
<br>â†“
<br>
Build + Test
<br>â†“
<br>
Package
<br>â†“
<br>
Staging
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Manual Approval</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Production

</div>

<div class="interview">

The key idea is:

<strong>Software is always ready to be deployed, but production
release may still require human approval.</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- CONTINUOUS DEPLOYMENT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is Continuous Deployment?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Continuous Deployment</strong> automatically deploys changes
to production after they successfully pass the required automated
checks.

There is no manual production approval in the normal successful
path.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Code
<br>â†“
<br>
Build
<br>â†“
<br>
Test
<br>â†“
<br>
Security
<br>â†“
<br>
Deploy Production
<br>â†“
<br>
Monitor

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If a company has strong automated testing, security controls,
deployment verification and monitoring, it may use Continuous
Deployment to release changes automatically.

</div>

</div>


<!-- DIFFERENCE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. CI vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Concept</th>
<th>Main Focus</th>
<th>Production Deployment</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>CI</strong></td>
<td>Integrate, build and test code frequently</td>
<td>Not the main purpose</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Continuous Delivery</strong></td>
<td>Keep software ready for release</td>
<td>Usually requires approval</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Continuous Deployment</strong></td>
<td>Automatically release validated changes</td>
<td>Automatically deployed</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy interview trick:</strong>

<br><br>

CI = <strong>Integrate + Validate</strong>

<br>

Continuous Delivery = <strong>Always Ready to Deploy</strong>

<br>

Continuous Deployment = <strong>Automatically Deploy</strong>

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

â†“

</div>

<!-- AUTOMATION -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Why do we automate CI/CD?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Reduce manual errors.</li>
<li>Get faster feedback.</li>
<li>Release software more frequently.</li>
<li>Standardize deployment processes.</li>
<li>Detect bugs earlier.</li>
<li>Improve release consistency.</li>
<li>Support repeatable deployments.</li>
<li>Reduce operational effort.</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

Instead of manually copying application files to servers after every
release, the pipeline performs the same validated deployment process
consistently.

</div>

</div>


<!-- BENEFITS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Benefits of CI/CD</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Benefit</th>
<th>Explanation</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Faster Releases</td>
<td>Automation reduces manual release effort.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Early Bug Detection</td>
<td>Automated tests run soon after code changes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Consistency</td>
<td>The same pipeline process can be reused for deployments.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Better Quality</td>
<td>Testing and quality checks are integrated into delivery.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Lower Risk</td>
<td>Small, frequent changes are generally easier to validate and roll back.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- DEVOPS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. CI/CD and DevOps</h2>

<div class="answer">

CI/CD is an important part of DevOps because it helps automate the
software delivery lifecycle and creates faster feedback between
development, testing, security and operations.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Development
<br>â†“
<br>

<br>â†“
<br>

</div>
