<!-- ARTIFACT -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. What is an Artifact?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An <strong>artifact</strong> is a versioned output produced by the
build process that can be stored and used later for deployment.

</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<ul>
<li>JAR file</li>
<li>WAR file</li>
<li>ZIP package</li>
<li>Docker image</li>
<li>Compiled application package</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

For example, a Java pipeline may build:

<pre><code>payment-service-1.5.0.jar</code></pre>

That artifact can then be promoted through different environments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ENVIRONMENTS -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. CI/CD Across Environments</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Development</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Testing</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>QA</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Staging</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Production</strong>

</div>

<div class="answer">

A mature pipeline promotes a validated build through environments
using controlled configuration and deployment policies.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Avoid rebuilding different application binaries for every environment
when the goal is to promote the same tested artifact. Environment-
specific configuration should normally be handled separately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- WEBHOOK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. What triggers a CI/CD pipeline?</h2>

<p>A pipeline can be triggered by different events.</p>

<ul>
<li>Git push</li>
<li>Pull request</li>
<li>Merge to a branch</li>
<li>Tag creation</li>
<li>Scheduled execution</li>
<li>Manual execution</li>
<li>API or webhook events</li>
</ul>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Common example:</strong>

A developer pushes code to the <code>main</code> branch â†’ Git provider
sends a webhook â†’ CI/CD server starts the pipeline.

</div>

</div>


<!-- FAILURE -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What happens when a pipeline fails?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The pipeline should normally stop at the failed stage and prevent
the invalid build from progressing to later deployment stages.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Build
<br>â†“
<br>
Test âŒ
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Pipeline Stops</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Developer Investigates
<br>â†“
<br>
Fix
<br>â†“
<br>
New Pipeline Run

</div>

<div class="interview">

A failed pipeline is useful because it provides fast feedback before
a bad change reaches later environments.

</div>

</div>


<!-- ROLLBACK -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Why is rollback important?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Rollback allows the team to return to a previously known-good version
when a deployment introduces a serious problem.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Version 1.4
<br>â†“
<br>
Version 1.5 ðŸš€
<br>â†“
<br>
Production Issue âŒ
<br>â†“
<br>
Rollback
<br>â†“
<br>
Version 1.4 âœ…

</div>

<p>
Rollback strategies are discussed in more detail in the
<strong>CI/CD Pipeline Strategies</strong> module.
</p>

</div>


<!-- REAL TIME -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Real-Time End-to-End Example</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A developer modifies a payment application.

<br><br>

1. Code is pushed to GitHub.

<br>

2. CI pipeline is triggered.

<br>

3. Application is built.

<br>

4. Unit and integration tests execute.

<br>

5. Code and dependencies are scanned.

<br>

6. Docker image is created.

<br>

7. Image is pushed to a container registry.

<br>

8. Deployment is triggered.

<br>

9. Kubernetes deploys the new version.

<br>

10. Health checks and monitoring verify the deployment.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready summary:</strong>

<br><br>

"I would design the CI/CD pipeline so that every code change is
validated through automated build, testing and security stages.
After producing a versioned artifact or container image, the
validated version is promoted through environments and deployed using
a controlled deployment strategy. Monitoring and health checks then
verify the release."

</div>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain CI/CD"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"CI/CD is an approach used to automate and improve the software
delivery lifecycle.

Continuous Integration means developers frequently integrate code
changes into a shared repository and automatically build and test
those changes.

Continuous Delivery keeps the application in a deployable state,
usually with an approval before production.

Continuous Deployment goes one step further by automatically
deploying successfully validated changes to production.

A typical pipeline includes source control, build, testing, security
checks, artifact creation, deployment and monitoring.

In a real DevOps environment, tools such as Git, Jenkins, Docker,
Kubernetes and cloud services can work together to create an
automated and repeatable delivery process."

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Continuous Delivery vs Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Continuous Delivery:</strong>

The application is automatically built, tested and prepared for
release, but production release may require approval or another
controlled step.

<br><br>

<strong>Continuous Deployment:</strong>

Every change that passes the required automated checks can be
automatically deployed to production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Jenkins Role</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins is an automation server commonly used to implement CI/CD
pipelines.

It can integrate with Git, build tools, Docker, security scanners,
cloud platforms and Kubernetes.

</div>

<pre><code>Git
 â†“
Jenkins
 â†“
Build
 â†“
Test
 â†“
Docker
 â†“

 â†“
Kubernetes</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. GitHub Actions Role</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions provides CI/CD automation directly inside GitHub.
Workflows are defined using YAML files under:

<code>.github/workflows/</code>

</div>

<pre><code>Git Push
   â†“

   â†“

   â†“

   â†“

   â†“

<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Docker in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker packages the application and its runtime dependencies into a
container image.

This helps create consistent environments between development,
testing and deployment.

</div>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0 .

docker tag myapp:1.0 registry/myapp:1.0

docker push registry/myapp:1.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Why Use Image Tags?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Tags identify different versions of an image.

A strong CI/CD practice is to use immutable identifiers such as
commit SHA or release version.

</div>

<pre><code>myapp:1.0.0
myapp:1.1.0

myapp:git-a83f91c</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Avoid relying only on <code>latest</code> for production deployments
because it does not clearly identify the exact application version.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Artifact Repository</h2>

<div class="answer">

An artifact repository stores build outputs such as packages,
libraries or container images.

Examples include:

</div>

<span class="badge">Amazon ECR</span>
<span class="badge">Docker Hub</span>
<span class="badge">JFrog Artifactory</span>

<div class="flow">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Kubernetes Role in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes provides the platform where containerized applications can

<div class="answer">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Blue-Green Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

Blue-Green keeps two environments so traffic can be switched between

Rollback can be fast by switching traffic back.

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Canary Deployment</h2>

<div class="flow">

<div class="answer">

Canary deployment releases a new version to a small percentage of

<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Rolling Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

A rolling deployment gradually replaces old application instances
with new ones rather than replacing everything simultaneously.

</div>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“
<br>

<br>â†“

<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Rollback</h2>

<div class="answer">

Rollback returns the application to a known-good version when a
release causes unacceptable problems.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Application rollback does not automatically make a destructive
database migration reversible.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Pipeline Security</h2>

<ul>

<li>Never hard-code credentials.</li>

<li>Use secret management.</li>

<li>Apply least privilege.</li>

<li>Scan source and dependencies.</li>

<li>Scan container images.</li>

<li>Protect production environments.</li>

<li>Use short-lived/federated credentials where possible.</li>

<li>Do not expose secrets in logs.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ 25. Best Interview Answer: Explain Your CI/CD Pipeline</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In my CI/CD approach, developers push code to GitHub, which triggers
the CI pipeline.

The pipeline checks out the code, builds the application and runs
automated tests. I can integrate code-quality and security scanning
before creating the Docker image.

The Docker image is tagged with a unique version such as the commit
SHA and pushed to a container registry such as Amazon ECR.

For deployment, Kubernetes runs the application, while GitOps tools
such as ArgoCD can continuously reconcile the desired deployment
state from Git.

Finally, monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana helps detect
application and infrastructure issues.

If a production deployment causes problems, I prioritize restoring
service, stop the rollout or rollback to a known-good version, and
then perform root-cause analysis."

</div>

</div>

<h1>CI/CD <span>Pipeline Strategies</span></h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide covering pipeline design, artifact promotion,

<div class="intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Complete Pipeline Strategy</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Code
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸ“¦ Git

<br>
ðŸ”¨ Build

<div class="answer">

A good CI/CD strategy focuses not only on automation, but also on
safe promotion, traceability, validation and recovery.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Build Once, Deploy Many</h2>

<div class="answer">

The preferred approach is to build and validate an application once,
create a versioned artifact, and promote that same artifact through
different environments.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Source Code
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Build Once</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Artifact v1.8
<br>â†“
<br>
Dev
<br>â†“
<br>
QA
<br>â†“
<br>
Staging
<br>â†“
<br>
Production

</div>

<div class="warning">

Avoid rebuilding the application separately for every environment
when the goal is to promote the same tested artifact. Environment-
specific configuration should be supplied separately.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Environment Promotion</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Environment</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Development</td>
<td>Early integration and developer validation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>QA / Testing</td>
<td>Functional, integration and regression testing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Staging</td>
<td>Production-like final validation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Production</td>
<td>Serve real users.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

A release should normally progress through controlled gates rather
than directly moving every untested change into production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Rolling Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>Rolling Deployment</strong> gradually replaces old
application instances with new instances instead of replacing
everything at once.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Old Version
<br>
ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦
<br>â†“<br>

Replace Gradually
<br>
ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ¦
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ¦
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ©
<br><br>
New Version

</div>

<h3>Advantages</h3>

<ul>
<li>Usually no need for a completely separate environment.</li>
<li>Gradual rollout.</li>
<li>Can reduce deployment risk.</li>
<li>Common in Kubernetes.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Disadvantages</h3>

<ul>
<li>Old and new versions may temporarily coexist.</li>
<li>Rollback can be more complicated for stateful changes.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Blue-Green Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

Blue-Green deployment maintains two environments or versions.
Traffic is directed to one version while the other is prepared.

</div>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Blue</strong>
<br>
Version 1.4
<br>
ðŸ‘¥ Traffic
<br>
â¬‡
<br>
Production

<br><br>

<strong>Green</strong>
<br>
Version 1.5
<br>
Testing
<br>
â¬‡
<br>
Ready

<br><br>

Traffic Switch
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>Green â†’ Production</strong>

</div>

<h3>Rollback</h3>

<div class="scenario">

If the new Green version fails after the switch, traffic can be
redirected back to Blue, assuming the architecture and state
management support this safely.

</div>

<h3>Advantages</h3>

<ul>
<li>Fast traffic switch.</li>
<li>Easy conceptual rollback.</li>
<li>Full new version can be tested before switching traffic.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Disadvantages</h3>

<ul>
<li>Can require additional infrastructure.</li>
<li>Database compatibility must be handled carefully.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Canary Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

A <strong>Canary Deployment</strong> releases the new version to a
small percentage of users or traffic first.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Version 1.4
<br>
90% Traffic
<br>
ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥ðŸ‘¥
<br><br>

Version 1.5
<br>
10% Traffic
<br>
ðŸ‘¥
<br><br>

Monitor
<br>â†“<br>
Success?
<br>â†“<br>
Increase Traffic
<br>â†“<br>
100%

</div>

<h3>Monitor</h3>

<ul>
<li>Error rate</li>
<li>Latency</li>
<li>HTTP 5xx responses</li>
<li>CPU / memory</li>
<li>Business metrics</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

Canary reduces blast radius because only a portion of traffic is
exposed to the new release initially.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Rolling vs Blue-Green vs Canary</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>Core Idea</th>
<th>Main Benefit</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Rolling</td>
<td>Gradually replace instances.</td>
<td>Controlled incremental rollout.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Blue-Green</td>
<td>Maintain old and new versions and switch traffic.</td>
<td>Fast switch and rollback.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Canary</td>
<td>Send a small amount of traffic to the new version.</td>
<td>Small blast radius.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Easy memory:</strong>

<br><br>

Rolling â†’ <strong>Replace gradually</strong>

<br>

Blue-Green â†’ <strong>Switch environments</strong>

<br>

Canary â†’ <strong>Release to a small percentage</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Zero-Downtime Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

Zero-downtime deployment aims to keep the application available
while a new version is released.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Load Balancer
<br>â†“
<br>
Healthy Instances
<br>
ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ©
<br><br>
Deploy New Version
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ© ðŸŸ©
<br>+
<br>
ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦
<br><br>
Health Checks
<br>â†“
<br>
Remove Old Instances
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦ ðŸŸ¦

</div>

<h3>Important requirements</h3>

<ul>
<li>Multiple application instances.</li>
<li>Load balancing.</li>
<li>Health checks.</li>
<li>Graceful shutdown.</li>
<li>Backward-compatible changes.</li>
<li>Safe database migration strategy.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Rollback Strategy</h2>

<div class="answer">

Rollback means returning the application to a previously known-good
version after a failed or unsafe release.

</div>

<div class="flow">

v1.0 âœ…
<br>â†“
<br>
v1.1 ðŸš€
<br>â†“
<br>
Production Error âŒ
<br>â†“
<br>
Detect
<br>â†“
<br>
Rollback
<br>â†“
<br>
v1.0 âœ…

</div>

<h3>Good rollback practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Keep previous versions available.</li>
<li>Use immutable/versioned artifacts.</li>
<li>Automate rollback where appropriate.</li>
<li>Monitor deployment health.</li>
<li>Test rollback procedures.</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

Application rollback does not automatically mean database rollback.
Database changes require separate compatibility and migration
planning.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Manual Approval Gates</h2>

<div class="answer">

An approval gate pauses the pipeline before a sensitive action, such
as production deployment, until an authorized person approves it.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Build
<br>â†“
<br>
Test
<br>â†“
<br>
Security
<br>â†“
<br>
Staging
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Approval â¸ï¸</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Production

</div>

<div class="scenario">

This is common when an organization wants automated validation but
requires human authorization for production changes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. Feature Flags</h2>

<div class="answer">

A feature flag allows application functionality to be enabled or
disabled through configuration without necessarily deploying a new
application version.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

Example:

A new payment feature is deployed but initially disabled.

After validation, the team enables it for a small group of users and
then gradually increases exposure.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Feature flags should be managed securely and cleaned up when they are
no longer needed. Old flags can create unnecessary application
complexity.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Release vs Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Deployment</strong> means installing or making a version
available in an environment.

<strong>Release</strong> means making functionality available to
users.

These can be separated using techniques such as feature flags.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

A new application version can be deployed to production while a new
feature remains disabled. The deployment happened, but the feature
has not yet been released to users.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Immutable Artifacts</h2>

<div class="answer">

An immutable artifact should not be modified after it is built and
validated.

</div>

<pre><code>payment-app:1.8.0
payment-app:git-a82f31c
payment-app:build-245</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Avoid overwriting the same production artifact tag with different
content. Immutable versioning improves traceability and rollback.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Deployment Verification</h2>

<div class="flow">

Deploy
<br>â†“
<br>
Health Check
<br>â†“
<br>
Application Logs
<br>â†“
<br>
Metrics
<br>â†“
<br>
Error Rate
<br>â†“
<br>
Business Validation
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Success / Rollback</strong>

</div>

<p>
A deployment should not be considered successful simply because the
deployment command returned exit code zero. The running application
must be healthy.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Production Release Strategy</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A safe production workflow can look like:

<br><br>

1. Build artifact.

<br>
2. Run automated tests.

<br>
3. Perform security checks.

<br>
4. Publish immutable artifact.

<br>
5. Deploy to staging.

<br>
6. Validate staging.

<br>
7. Obtain approval if required.

<br>
8. Deploy using Rolling, Blue-Green or Canary.

<br>
9. Monitor health and business metrics.

<br>
10. Roll back if defined failure thresholds are reached.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Scenario: Production Deployment Failed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

A new version is deployed and error rates increase sharply.

<br><br>

<strong>Response:</strong>

1. Confirm the issue through monitoring and logs.
<br>
2. Stop further rollout.
<br>
3. Assess impact.
<br>
4. Roll back or shift traffic to the known-good version.
<br>
5. Investigate the root cause.
<br>
6. Fix and validate the new version.
<br>
7. Retry deployment through the normal pipeline.

</div>

<div class="interview">

The priority is to restore service safely first, then investigate the
root cause.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: Zero Downtime</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Question:</strong>

"How would you deploy a new version without downtime?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer approach:</strong>

Use multiple healthy instances behind a load balancer, deploy the new
version gradually, configure readiness/health checks, wait for new
instances to become healthy, then remove old instances.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Scenario: Canary Failure</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Suppose 10% of traffic is sent to version 2.0.

Monitoring shows:

<pre><code>Error Rate: 0.5% â†’ 8%
Latency:    200ms â†’ 900ms</code></pre>

The rollout should be paused and the traffic can be shifted back to
the stable version while the issue is investigated.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. How to Choose a Deployment Strategy?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Requirement</th>
<th>Possible Choice</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple gradual replacement</td>
<td>Rolling</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Fast switch between complete versions</td>
<td>Blue-Green</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Small initial user exposure</td>
<td>Canary</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Very high-risk release</td>
<td>Canary + strong monitoring</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Need quick traffic reversal</td>
<td>Blue-Green can be suitable</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="warning">

There is no universally best deployment strategy. The choice depends
on application architecture, traffic, infrastructure cost, data
compatibility, monitoring maturity and business risk.

</div>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain Deployment Strategies"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In CI/CD, deployment strategies define how a new application version
is introduced into an environment.

With Rolling Deployment, old instances are gradually replaced with
new ones.

With Blue-Green Deployment, we maintain the old and new versions and
switch traffic between them, which can make rollback quick.

With Canary Deployment, we expose the new version to a small
percentage of users first, monitor metrics such as error rate and
latency, and gradually increase traffic if the release is healthy.

For zero-downtime deployment, I would use multiple instances,
load balancing, health checks and a controlled rollout.

I also prefer building an immutable versioned artifact once and
promoting that same artifact across environments. If a deployment
causes a production issue, monitoring should detect it and we can
pause or roll back to the known-good version."

</div>

</div>

<h1>CI/CD <span>Real-Time Scenarios</span></h1>

<p>
Production-focused DevOps interview scenarios covering Jenkins,

<div class="card intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ How to Approach Any CI/CD Scenario</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>1. Identify the failure</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>2. Find the affected layer</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>3. Check logs / status / metrics</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>4. Fix or mitigate</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>5. Verify</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>6. Prevent recurrence</strong>

</div>

<div class="answer">

In interviews, don't immediately jump to random commands.
First identify where the failure is occurring, then troubleshoot
layer by layer.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Jenkins Pipeline Suddenly Fails</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Question:</strong>

"Your Jenkins pipeline was working yesterday but suddenly started
failing. What will you do?"

</div>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<ol>
<li>Check which stage failed.</li>
<li>Read Jenkins console output.</li>
<li>Identify whether the failure is code, dependency, credential,
agent, network or infrastructure related.</li>
<li>Compare with the last successful build.</li>
<li>Check recent changes.</li>
<li>Fix the root cause and rerun safely.</li>
</ol>

<pre><code>Jenkins
â†’ Build History
â†’ Failed Build
â†’ Console Output
â†’ Failed Stage
â†’ Root Cause</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready:</strong>

"I would first identify the exact failed stage rather than assuming
Jenkins itself is broken. Then I would inspect console logs, compare
the failed build with the last successful build, check recent code or
environment changes, validate credentials and dependencies, fix the
root cause and rerun the pipeline."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Jenkins Agent Is Offline</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A pipeline cannot start because the Jenkins agent is offline.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Agent status in Jenkins.</li>
<li>Machine availability.</li>
<li>Network connectivity.</li>
<li>Jenkins agent process/service.</li>
<li>Disk space.</li>
<li>CPU and memory.</li>
<li>Java/runtime compatibility.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

The key is to distinguish between a Jenkins controller problem and
an agent execution problem.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Git Webhook Is Not Triggering Jenkins</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Developer pushes code to Git, but Jenkins does not start.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Git Push
<br>â†“
<br>
Webhook
<br>âŒ
<br>
Jenkins

</div>

<h3>Troubleshooting</h3>

<ol>
<li>Check whether the webhook exists.</li>
<li>Check webhook delivery history.</li>
<li>Verify Jenkins URL.</li>
<li>Check webhook secret if configured.</li>
<li>Check Jenkins job trigger configuration.</li>
<li>Check network/firewall accessibility.</li>
<li>Check branch/filter configuration.</li>
</ol>

<div class="warning">

A successful Git push does not guarantee that the webhook reached
Jenkins successfully.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Docker Build Fails in Jenkins</h2>

<div class="scenario">

The pipeline reaches the Docker build stage and fails.

</div>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0.0 .</code></pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Dockerfile syntax.</li>
<li>Build context.</li>
<li>Missing files.</li>
<li>Base image availability.</li>
<li>Network access.</li>
<li>Docker daemon availability.</li>
<li>Agent permissions.</li>
<li>Disk space.</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

I would inspect the exact Docker build error first. Common causes
include an invalid Dockerfile, missing files in the build context,
base-image pull failures or Docker daemon/permission problems.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Docker Image Push Fails</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Image builds successfully but the push to the registry fails.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Docker Build
<br>âœ…
<br>â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>âœ…
<br>â†“
<br>
Registry Push
<br>âŒ

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ol>
<li>Registry URL.</li>
<li>Authentication.</li>
<li>Repository name.</li>
<li>Image tag.</li>
<li>Network connectivity.</li>
<li>Registry permissions.</li>
<li>Credential configuration.</li>
</ol>

<pre><code>docker images

docker login &lt;registry&gt;

docker push &lt;registry&gt;/myapp:1.0.0</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Kubernetes Cannot Pull the Image</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Pod status:

<pre><code>ImagePullBackOff
ErrImagePull</code></pre>

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ol>
<li>Image name.</li>
<li>Image tag.</li>
<li>Registry availability.</li>
<li>Image existence.</li>
<li>Registry authentication.</li>
<li>Image pull secret if required.</li>
<li>Node network access.</li>
</ol>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get events</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The most useful first command is often
<code>kubectl describe pod</code> because Kubernetes events can reveal
why the image pull failed.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Pod Goes Into CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="scenario">

The image is pulled successfully, but the container repeatedly exits.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<h3>Common causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Application startup error.</li>
<li>Wrong environment variables.</li>
<li>Missing configuration.</li>
<li>Database connection failure.</li>
<li>Incorrect command or arguments.</li>
<li>Application exits immediately.</li>
<li>Resource problems.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Kubernetes Deployment Is Stuck</h2>

<div class="scenario">

The pipeline succeeds, but the new deployment never becomes healthy.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Deployment
<br>â†“
<br>
ReplicaSet
<br>â†“
<br>
Pods
<br>â†“
<br>
âŒ Not Ready

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get deployment

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get events</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Check whether the issue is image pulling, scheduling, startup,
readiness probes, configuration, resources or networking.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Readiness Probe Is Failing</h2>

<div class="scenario">

The application is running, but Kubernetes keeps the Pod out of
service because the readiness probe fails.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Probe path.</li>
<li>Probe port.</li>
<li>Application startup time.</li>
<li>Service binding address.</li>
<li>Application health endpoint.</li>
<li>Network policy if applicable.</li>
</ul>

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Readiness means "can this Pod receive traffic?"

Liveness means "is this container still healthy enough to keep
running?"

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Production Deployment Causes Errors</h2>

<div class="scenario">

After deploying version 2.0, HTTP 5xx errors increase.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Deploy v2
<br>â†“
<br>
5xx â†‘
<br>â†“
<br>
Stop Rollout
<br>â†“
<br>
Assess Impact
<br>â†“
<br>
Rollback / Shift Traffic
<br>â†“
<br>
Restore Service
<br>â†“
<br>
Root Cause Analysis

</div>

<div class="interview">

My first priority would be restoring service. I would stop further
rollout, verify the impact through monitoring, roll back or shift
traffic to the known-good version, and then investigate the root
cause.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. How Do You Roll Back Kubernetes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes Deployments maintain rollout history that can be used to
return to a previous revision.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Rollback of the application version does not automatically solve an
incompatible database migration. Application and database changes
must be designed for safe compatibility.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Terraform Stage Fails in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Pipeline reaches Terraform and <code>terraform plan</code> fails.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ol>
<li>Terraform syntax.</li>
<li>Provider configuration.</li>
<li>Credentials/identity.</li>
<li>Backend configuration.</li>
<li>State locking.</li>
<li>Variable values.</li>
<li>Cloud permissions.</li>
<li>Provider/resource changes.</li>
</ol>

<pre><code>terraform fmt -check

terraform init

terraform validate

terraform plan</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Terraform State Lock Error</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Two CI jobs attempt to modify the same Terraform state.

</div>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state locking prevents concurrent operations from modifying
the same state simultaneously when the backend supports locking.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not blindly force-unlock a state. First confirm whether another
Terraform operation is actually running.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. ArgoCD Shows OutOfSync</h2>

<div class="scenario">

ArgoCD reports:

<pre><code>OutOfSync</code></pre>

</div>

<h3>Possible causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Git desired state differs from cluster state.</li>
<li>Manual kubectl changes.</li>
<li>Application configuration drift.</li>
<li>Manifest generation differences.</li>
<li>Synchronization is disabled or pending.</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">

Git Desired State
<br>â‰ 
<br>
Cluster Actual State
<br>â†“
<br>
ArgoCD Detects Drift
<br>â†“
<br>
Sync
<br>â†“
<br>
Desired State Restored

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. ArgoCD Application Is Degraded</h2>

<div class="scenario">

ArgoCD successfully synchronizes the manifests, but the application
is marked degraded.

</div>

<div class="answer">

This means Git synchronization itself may have succeeded, but the
resulting Kubernetes resources are not healthy.

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl get deployment

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

ArgoCD can report the Kubernetes application health, but the actual
root cause may be inside Kubernetes resources or the application.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Pipeline Is Slow</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A pipeline that previously took 8 minutes now takes 25 minutes.

</div>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<ol>
<li>Identify the slowest stage.</li>
<li>Compare current and previous build durations.</li>
<li>Check dependency downloads.</li>
<li>Check Docker build caching.</li>
<li>Check test execution.</li>
<li>Check Jenkins agent resources.</li>
<li>Check external service latency.</li>
</ol>

<div class="answer">

Optimize the bottleneck instead of blindly adding more parallel
stages.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Pipeline Works Manually but Fails Automatically</h2>

<div class="scenario">

The developer runs the same command manually and it works, but the
Jenkins pipeline fails.

</div>

<h3>Common reasons</h3>

<ul>
<li>Different environment variables.</li>
<li>Different working directory.</li>
<li>Different user permissions.</li>
<li>Different PATH.</li>
<li>Missing credentials.</li>
<li>Different runtime version.</li>
<li>Different agent environment.</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

I would compare the runtime environment between the successful manual
execution and the Jenkins agent rather than assuming the command is
wrong.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. Secret Accidentally Appears in Jenkins Logs</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A cloud credential appears in build output.

</div>

<h3>Immediate response</h3>

<ol>
<li>Stop exposing the secret.</li>
<li>Rotate/revoke the compromised credential.</li>
<li>Check whether logs were accessible externally.</li>
<li>Remove insecure logging.</li>
<li>Move credentials into secure secret storage.</li>
<li>Review pipeline permissions.</li>
</ol>

<div class="warning">

Treat an exposed credential as compromised even if the log was
generated accidentally.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Zero-Downtime Deployment Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Question:</strong>

"How would you deploy a new version without downtime?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong>

"I would run multiple application instances behind a load balancer.
I would deploy the new version gradually, use readiness and health
checks, wait until the new instances are healthy, and then remove
the old instances. Depending on the application, I could use Rolling,
Blue-Green or Canary deployment."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Canary Deployment Failure</h2>

<div class="scenario">

10% of users receive version 2.0.

Monitoring shows:

<pre><code>Error Rate: 0.4% â†’ 7%
Latency:    180ms â†’ 850ms</code></pre>

<strong>Action:</strong>

Pause the rollout, reduce or stop traffic to version 2.0, restore the
stable version if necessary, investigate the issue and only continue
after validation.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Database Migration Breaks Deployment</h2>

<div class="scenario">

A new application version requires a database schema change. After
deployment, the old application version can no longer work with the
new schema.

</div>

<div class="answer">

This is a compatibility problem.

A safer strategy is often to use backward-compatible database changes
first, deploy application changes that work with both schema versions,
migrate data if needed, and remove old compatibility later.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Never assume application rollback automatically makes a destructive
database migration safe to reverse.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 22. Build Passed but Production Failed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

"All CI tests passed. Why can production still fail?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

CI tests may not cover every production condition.

Possible causes include:

<ul>
<li>Environment-specific configuration.</li>
<li>Missing production secrets.</li>
<li>Different infrastructure.</li>
<li>External dependency failure.</li>
<li>Production traffic patterns.</li>
<li>Database differences.</li>
<li>Resource limits.</li>
<li>Networking or DNS issues.</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. How Do You Prevent Failed Releases?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Automated Tests
<br>â†“
<br>
Code Quality
<br>â†“
<br>
Security Scans
<br>â†“
<br>
Staging
<br>â†“
<br>
Smoke Tests
<br>â†“
<br>
Approval / Automated Gate
<br>â†“
<br>
Canary / Rolling
<br>â†“
<br>
Monitoring
<br>â†“
<br>
Rollback

</div>

<div class="answer">

The goal is not to guarantee that failures never happen. The goal
is to reduce release risk, detect problems quickly and recover safely.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Production Is Down After Deployment</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

Users report that the application is unavailable immediately after
a release.

<strong>Response:</strong>

1. Confirm the incident through monitoring.
<br>
2. Identify whether the release caused the problem.
<br>
3. Stop further deployment.
<br>
4. Check application, Pod, Service and Ingress health.
<br>
5. Roll back if required.
<br>
6. Verify recovery.
<br>
7. Preserve logs and evidence.
<br>
8. Perform root-cause analysis after stabilization.

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Priority:</strong>

Restore service â†’ stabilize â†’ investigate â†’ prevent recurrence.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Complete End-to-End Failure Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong>

Developer pushes code. Jenkins succeeds. Docker image is pushed to
ECR. ArgoCD syncs successfully. But users receive HTTP 503.

<br><br>

<strong>Layer-by-layer investigation:</strong>

<br><br>

â†’ Code exists

<br>
Jenkins
â†’ Build succeeded

<br>
Docker
â†’ Image exists

<br>
Registry
â†’ Image available

<br>
ArgoCD
â†’ Desired state synchronized

<br>
Kubernetes
â†’ Check Pods

<br>

â†’ Check endpoints

<br>
Ingress
â†’ Check routing

<br>
Application
â†’ Check logs and health

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get ingress

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

This is a strong troubleshooting approach because each layer is
validated independently instead of blaming the last tool in the
pipeline.

</div>

<!-- MASTER ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Master Interview Answer: CI/CD Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="interview">

"When troubleshooting a CI/CD issue, I first identify the exact
stage where the failure occurred. I don't assume that the last tool
used is necessarily the root cause.

I check the logs and status of the affected component and compare
the failed execution with the last successful execution.

For example, if the pipeline fails during Docker push, I check the
registry URL, authentication, repository, image tag and permissions.

If Kubernetes deployment fails, I check Pod status, events, image
pulling, application logs, readiness probes and resource issues.

For a production failure after deployment, my first priority is to
restore service. I would stop the rollout, assess the impact and
rollback or shift traffic to a known-good version if appropriate.

After recovery, I investigate the root cause and add preventive
controls such as better testing, monitoring, validation or automated
deployment gates."

</div>

</div>

<h1>CI/CD <span>Tools Integration</span></h1>

<p>
How Git, Jenkins, Docker, container registries, Kubernetes,
Terraform and ArgoCD fit together in a real-world DevOps workflow.
</p>

<div class="card intro">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Complete CI/CD Toolchain</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Git / GitHub</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Jenkins / CI Server</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Build + Test + Scan
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>

</div>

<div class="answer">

The tools do different jobs. CI/CD is the overall delivery process;
Jenkins is one automation engine, Docker packages applications,
Kubernetes runs containers, and monitoring tools observe the running
system.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Git's Role in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="answer">

Git is used for source-code version control. The CI/CD pipeline can be
triggered when developers push code, create pull requests or merge
changes.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“
<br>
Git Branch
<br>â†“
<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“
<br>
Code Review
<br>â†“
<br>
Merge
<br>â†“
<br>
Pipeline Trigger

</div>

<h3>What Git provides</h3>

<ul>
<li>Version history</li>
<li>Branching</li>
<li>Pull requests</li>
<li>Code review workflow</li>
<li>Change traceability</li>
<li>Webhook events</li>
</ul>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong>

"Git acts as the source of truth for application code and pipeline
configuration. Repository events can trigger automated CI/CD
pipelines."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Git â†’ Jenkins Integration</h2>

<div class="flow">

Git Push
<br>â†“
<br>
Webhook
<br>â†“
<br>
Jenkins
<br>â†“
<br>
Jenkinsfile
<br>â†“
<br>
Pipeline

</div>

<div class="answer">

A common integration is to configure a webhook in the Git provider.
When a relevant repository event occurs, Jenkins receives the event
and starts the pipeline.

</div>

<h3>Typical Jenkinsfile flow</h3>

<pre><code>pipeline {
    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                checkout scm
            }
        }

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                sh './build.sh'
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                sh './test.sh'
            }
        }

    }
}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

The exact commands depend on the application and build system. The
important interview concept is the integration flow, not memorizing
one specific Jenkinsfile.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Jenkins + Docker</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins can automate Docker image creation after the application
passes its build and test stages.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>â†“
<br>
Jenkins
<br>â†“
<br>
Build Application
<br>â†“
<br>
Test
<br>â†“
<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“
<br>
Docker Image
<br>â†“
<br>
Registry

</div>

<h3>Example commands</h3>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:1.0.0 .

docker tag myapp:1.0.0 \
registry.example.com/myapp:1.0.0

docker push \
registry.example.com/myapp:1.0.0</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

The pipeline should preferably use immutable/versioned image tags so
that a specific deployment can be traced back to a specific build.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Container Registry</h2>

<div class="answer">

A container registry stores Docker/OCI images so that deployment
systems can retrieve the exact image version they need.

</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<span class="badge">Amazon ECR</span>
<span class="badge">Docker Hub</span>
<span class="badge">GitHub Container Registry</span>
<span class="badge">Azure Container Registry</span>
<span class="badge">Google Artifact Registry</span>

<div class="flow">

Jenkins
<br>â†“
<br>
Build Image
<br>â†“
<br>
Push
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Container Registry</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Pull
<br>â†“
<br>
Kubernetes

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Docker â†’ Kubernetes</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes schedules and runs containerized workloads. A Kubernetes
Deployment references a container image, and Kubernetes pulls that
image from the configured registry when creating Pods.

</div>

<pre><code>apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment

metadata:
  name: myapp

spec:
  replicas: 3

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp

    spec:
      containers:
        - name: myapp
          image: registry.example.com/myapp:1.0.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Registry
<br>â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Deployment
<br>â†“
<br>
ReplicaSet
<br>â†“
<br>
Pods
<br>â†“
<br>
Containers

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Jenkins â†’ Kubernetes Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins can deploy a new application version to Kubernetes by
updating Kubernetes manifests or using deployment tooling.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Jenkins
<br>â†“
<br>
Build Image
<br>â†“
<br>
Push Image
<br>â†“
<br>
Update Deployment
<br>â†“
<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“
<br>
New Pods
<br>â†“
<br>
Health Checks

</div>

<h3>Simple example</h3>

<pre><code>kubectl set image deployment/myapp \
myapp=registry.example.com/myapp:1.1.0

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

In a GitOps model, Jenkins does not necessarily change the cluster
directly. Instead, the pipeline updates the desired-state repository,
and ArgoCD reconciles that change into Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Terraform's Role in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform is primarily used for Infrastructure as Code. It can be
integrated into CI/CD to validate, plan and apply infrastructure
changes under controlled processes.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>â†“
<br>
Terraform Code
<br>â†“
<br>
terraform fmt
<br>â†“
<br>
terraform validate
<br>â†“
<br>
terraform plan
<br>â†“
<br>
Approval
<br>â†“
<br>
terraform apply

</div>

<h3>Common commands</h3>

<pre><code>terraform fmt
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply</code></pre>

<div class="interview">

Terraform manages infrastructure; CI/CD orchestrates automation around
that infrastructure and application delivery.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. CI/CD + Terraform + Application Deployment</h2>

<div class="flow">

Infrastructure Code
<br>â†“
<br>
Terraform
<br>â†“
<br>
AWS / Azure / GCP
<br>â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Cluster
<br>â†“
<br>
Application Deployment
<br>â†“
<br>
Monitoring

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Example:</strong>

Terraform can create the VPC, IAM resources, load balancers and
Kubernetes cluster infrastructure. A separate application pipeline
can then build and deploy the application.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not treat application deployment and infrastructure provisioning as
the same problem. They can be connected through automation, but they
have different responsibilities and lifecycles.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. GitOps and ArgoCD</h2>

<div class="answer">

In a GitOps model, Git contains the desired state of the application
or infrastructure. ArgoCD continuously compares that desired state
with the Kubernetes cluster and reconciles differences.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“
<br>
Application Code
<br>â†“
<br>
CI Pipeline
<br>â†“
<br>
Build Image
<br>â†“
<br>
Container Registry
<br>â†“
<br>
Update Manifest Repository
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>ArgoCD</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

<div class="interview">

A common separation is:

<strong>CI builds and validates.</strong>

<br>

<strong>ArgoCD handles GitOps-based Kubernetes delivery.</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Jenkins vs ArgoCD</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Jenkins</th>
<th>ArgoCD</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Automation server</td>
<td>GitOps continuous delivery tool</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can build and test applications</td>
<td>Primarily reconciles desired state</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can build Docker images</td>
<td>Deploys/synchronizes Kubernetes state</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can run Terraform</td>
<td>Focused on Kubernetes delivery</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pipeline-driven</td>
<td>Reconciliation-driven</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

They are not necessarily competitors. They can work together in a
modern DevOps platform.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Complete Modern DevOps Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>GitHub</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Jenkins</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Build
<br>â†“
<br>
Test
<br>â†“
<br>
SonarQube / Quality
<br>â†“
<br>
Trivy / Security
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Docker</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Amazon ECR</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Update GitOps Manifest
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>ArgoCD</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
<strong>Kubernetes / EKS</strong>
<br>â†“
<br>
Prometheus
<br>â†“
<br>
Grafana

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview-ready explanation:</strong>

"The developer pushes code to Git. Jenkins detects the change and
runs the CI pipeline. It builds and tests the application, performs
quality and security checks, creates a Docker image and pushes it to
a container registry.

For GitOps-based delivery, the deployment manifest is updated in a
Git repository. ArgoCD detects the desired-state change and
synchronizes it with Kubernetes. The application then runs on the
cluster and is monitored using tools such as Prometheus and Grafana."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What happens if the Docker push fails?</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check:

<br><br>

1. Registry URL.
<br>
2. Registry authentication.
<br>
3. Repository existence.
<br>
4. Image tag.
<br>
5. Network connectivity.
<br>
6. Permissions.
<br>
7. Registry credentials configured in the CI system.

</div>

<pre><code>docker login &lt;registry&gt;

docker push &lt;registry&gt;/myapp:1.0.0</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Never hard-code registry passwords or access tokens inside a
Jenkinsfile.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Secrets in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="answer">

Credentials should be stored in a secure secret-management mechanism
rather than committed into Git or written directly into pipeline
source code.

</div>

<h3>Examples</h3>

<ul>
<li>Jenkins Credentials</li>
<li>AWS IAM roles</li>
<li>AWS Secrets Manager</li>
<li>HashiCorp Vault</li>
<li>Kubernetes Secrets</li>
<li>Cloud-native identity mechanisms</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

Never commit:

<pre><code>AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
DOCKER_PASSWORD=...</code></pre>

to a source repository.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Artifact Traceability</h2>

<div class="answer">

Every production deployment should ideally be traceable back to the
source commit, build and artifact that produced it.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Git Commit
<br>â†“
<br>
Build #245
<br>â†“
<br>
Image
<br>
<code>myapp:git-a82f31c</code>
<br>â†“
<br>
Deployment
<br>â†“
<br>
Production

</div>

<div class="scenario">

If production reports an issue, the team can identify which commit
and build produced the running version.

</div>

</div>

<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: New Application Release</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Requirement:</strong>

Deploy a new version of a Java application to Kubernetes.

<br><br>

<strong>Flow:</strong>

1. Developer pushes code.
<br>
2. Git webhook triggers Jenkins.
<br>
3. Jenkins checks out source.
<br>
4. Application is built.
<br>
5. Tests execute.
<br>
6. Code/security checks run.
<br>
7. Docker image is created.
<br>
8. Image is pushed to ECR.
<br>
9. GitOps repository is updated with the new image version.
<br>
10. ArgoCD detects the Git change.
<br>
11. ArgoCD synchronizes Kubernetes.
<br>
12. New Pods start.
<br>
13. Readiness checks verify them.
<br>
14. Prometheus/Grafana monitor the release.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. If Kubernetes Deployment Fails</h2>

<div class="scenario">

Check the issue layer by layer:

<br><br>

<strong>1. Image</strong>
â†’ Does the image exist?

<br><br>

<strong>2. Registry</strong>
â†’ Can the cluster pull it?

<br><br>

<strong>3. Manifest</strong>
â†’ Is the Deployment configuration valid?

<br><br>

<strong>4. Pod</strong>
â†’ Check Pod status and events.

<br><br>

<strong>5. Application</strong>
â†’ Check container logs.

<br><br>

<strong>6. Health Checks</strong>
â†’ Check readiness/liveness probes.

<br><br>

<strong>7. Service / Ingress</strong>
â†’ Check networking.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl get events
kubectl get deployment</code></pre>

</div>

<!-- FINAL ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ If Interviewer Says: "Explain How Your CI/CD Tools Work Together"</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In my CI/CD workflow, Git is the source of truth for the application
code. A push or pull request can trigger Jenkins.

Jenkins checks out the code, builds the application, runs tests and
security checks, and creates a Docker image. The image is pushed to a
container registry such as Amazon ECR.

For Kubernetes delivery, I can use a GitOps approach. Instead of
directly changing the cluster from Jenkins, the pipeline updates the
desired image version in a GitOps repository. ArgoCD detects that
change and synchronizes the desired state with Kubernetes.

Terraform is used separately to provision and manage infrastructure
such as networking, IAM and Kubernetes cluster resources.

Finally, Prometheus and Grafana provide monitoring and visibility
into the deployed application and infrastructure."

</div>

<h1>GitHub Actions <span>CI/CD</span></h1>

<p>
Practical CI/CD implementation using GitHub Actions,
Docker, container registries, AWS and Kubernetes.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. GitHub Actions CI/CD Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub Repository
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Security Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Amazon ECR
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes / EKS
<br>â†“<br>
Application

</div>

<div class="answer">
This is a common cloud-native CI/CD flow. GitHub Actions performs
the automation, ECR stores the container image, and Kubernetes runs
the application.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Basic CI Pipeline</h2>

<pre><code>name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:

  build-test:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
This pipeline validates code whenever changes are pushed or a pull
request is created.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. CI Pipeline with Docker</h2>

<pre><code>name: Docker CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:

  docker-build:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build Docker Image
        run: |
          docker build \
            -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: List Docker Images
        run: docker images</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Using <code>github.sha</code> gives the image a unique identifier
associated with the commit that produced it.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Docker Build â†’ Registry Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Source Code
<br>â†“<br>
Dockerfile
<br>â†“<br>
docker build
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Image
<br>â†“<br>
docker tag
<br>â†“<br>
Registry Login
<br>â†“<br>
docker push
<br>â†“<br>
Container Registry

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Push Docker Image to Docker Hub</h2>

<pre><code>- name: Login to Docker Hub
  uses: docker/login-action@v3
  with:
    username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
    password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

- name: Build Image
  run: docker build -t myuser/myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

- name: Push Image
  run: docker push myuser/myapp:${{ github.sha }}</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Docker Hub credentials should be stored in GitHub Secrets and never
hard-coded in the workflow.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. GitHub Actions + Amazon ECR</h2>

<div class="answer">
Amazon ECR can be used as the private container registry for images
that will later be deployed to AWS workloads such as EKS or ECS.
</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Authentication
<br>â†“<br>
ECR Login
<br>â†“<br>
Push Image
<br>â†“<br>
EKS / ECS

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. ECR Login Example</h2>

<pre><code>- name: Configure AWS Credentials
  uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
  with:
    role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
    aws-region: ap-south-1

- name: Login to Amazon ECR
  id: login-ecr
  uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
For production, prefer short-lived credentials through GitHub OIDC
and an AWS IAM role rather than storing long-lived AWS access keys.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Complete Docker + ECR Pipeline</h2>

<pre><code>name: Build and Push

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

env:
  AWS_REGION: ap-south-1
  ECR_REPOSITORY: myapp

jobs:

  build-push:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Configure AWS
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ env.AWS_REGION }}

      - name: Login to ECR
        id: login-ecr
        uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

      - name: Build Image
        run: |
          docker build \
            -t ${{ steps.login-ecr.outputs.registry }}/${{ env.ECR_REPOSITORY }}:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Push Image
        run: |
          docker push \
            ${{ steps.login-ecr.outputs.registry }}/${{ env.ECR_REPOSITORY }}:${{ github.sha }}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Why Use GitHub OIDC with AWS?</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions can use OpenID Connect to obtain temporary AWS
credentials by assuming an IAM role.

This avoids storing long-lived AWS access keys inside GitHub.

</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
OIDC Token
<br>â†“<br>
AWS IAM
<br>â†“<br>
Assume Role
<br>â†“<br>
Temporary Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Resources

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. GitHub Actions + Kubernetes</h2>

<div class="answer">
After an image is pushed to a registry, the workflow can update a
Kubernetes deployment directly or update a GitOps repository that
ArgoCD reconciles.
</div>

<div class="flow">

Git Push
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Kubernetes Deployment Example</h2>

<pre><code>kubectl set image deployment/myapp \
  myapp=123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:${GITHUB_SHA}

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Direct cluster deployment from CI is possible, but many production

</div>

<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. GitHub Actions + ArgoCD GitOps</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<div class="answer">
In this model, GitHub Actions handles CI and image creation, while
ArgoCD handles continuous delivery and reconciliation.
</div>

<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. GitHub Actions Updating a GitOps Repository</h2>

<pre><code>- name: Update Image Tag
  run: |
    sed -i "s|image: .*|image: ${{ steps.login-ecr.outputs.registry }}/myapp:${{ github.sha }}|" \
      k8s/deployment.yaml

- name: Commit Changes
  run: |
    git config user.name "github-actions"
    git config user.email "github-actions@github.com"
    git add k8s/deployment.yaml
    git commit -m "Update image to ${{ github.sha }}" || exit 0
    git push</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
The exact implementation depends on repository structure. The key
idea is that CI updates the desired state, and ArgoCD detects and
reconciles that change.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Multi-Stage CI/CD Pipeline</h2>

<pre><code>jobs:

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploy application"</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. CI/CD with Security Scanning</h2>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Docker Image Security</h2>

<pre><code>- name: Scan Image
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
    severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    exit-code: '1'</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
The pipeline can fail when security policy thresholds are violated.
The exact action version and security policy should be reviewed
before using it in production.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Deployment Strategies</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Strategy</th>
<th>Idea</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Rolling</td>
<td>Gradually replace old instances.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Blue-Green</td>
<td>Switch traffic between two environments.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Canary</td>
<td>Release to a small percentage first.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Rollback</h2>

<div class="answer">
A rollback restores a previously working version when a deployment
causes unacceptable problems.
</div>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp</code></pre>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Production scenario:</strong><br>
If error rates suddenly increase after deployment, first stabilize
the service. Stop or roll back the release when appropriate, then
investigate the root cause.
</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Real-Time Scenario: Docker Push Failed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

Docker image builds successfully but push to ECR fails.

<br><br>

<strong>Check:</strong>

1. AWS authentication.
<br>
2. IAM permissions.
<br>
3. ECR repository name.
<br>
4. AWS region.
<br>
5. Registry URL.
<br>
6. Image tag.
<br>
7. ECR login step.
<br>
8. OIDC trust relationship if OIDC is being used.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Real-Time Scenario: Kubernetes Deployment Failed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Situation:</strong>

Pipeline succeeds until deployment, but Kubernetes deployment fails.

<br><br>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<pre><code>kubectl get pods

kubectl describe deployment myapp

kubectl get events

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt;</code></pre>

Then check:

<br>
â€¢ Image name/tag<br>
â€¢ Registry authentication<br>
â€¢ Deployment YAML<br>
â€¢ Environment variables<br>
â€¢ Secrets<br>
â€¢ ConfigMaps<br>
â€¢ Resource limits<br>
â€¢ Probes

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Real-Time Scenario: ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

ImagePullBackOff usually indicates Kubernetes is having trouble
pulling the container image.

Check:

<br><br>

1. Image repository.
<br>
2. Image tag.
<br>
3. Registry availability.
<br>
4. ImagePullSecrets if required.
<br>
5. Node/network access.
<br>
6. Registry permissions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Real-Time Scenario: CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and repeatedly exits,
causing Kubernetes to restart it.

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod&gt;</code></pre>

Possible causes include:

<br>
â€¢ Application error<br>
â€¢ Incorrect command<br>
â€¢ Missing environment variable<br>
â€¢ Missing secret/config<br>
â€¢ Port/configuration problem<br>
â€¢ Dependency failure

</div>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Production-Grade CI/CD Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Keep workflows small and readable.</li>

<li>Use reusable workflows where appropriate.</li>

<li>Use least-privilege permissions.</li>

<li>Prefer OIDC for AWS authentication.</li>

<li>Never hard-code credentials.</li>

<li>Use immutable image tags.</li>

<li>Run automated tests before deployment.</li>

<li>Scan dependencies and images.</li>

<li>Protect production environments.</li>

<li>Keep deployment configuration version-controlled.</li>

<li>Monitor deployments.</li>

<li>Have a rollback strategy.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Interview-Ready Answer</h2>

<div class="interview">

"In a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline, I would trigger the workflow
through a push or pull request.

The pipeline first checks out the source code, installs dependencies,
runs tests and performs code-quality and security checks.

Then I build a Docker image and tag it with an immutable identifier
such as the commit SHA. The image is pushed to Amazon ECR.

For AWS authentication, I prefer GitHub OIDC with an IAM role so
the workflow can obtain temporary credentials instead of storing
long-lived AWS access keys.

For deployment, I can deploy the image to Kubernetes directly, but
for a GitOps architecture I would update the desired state in Git
and let ArgoCD reconcile it into the EKS cluster.

Finally, Prometheus and Grafana can be used to monitor the
application and infrastructure."

</div>

</div>

<h1>GitHub Actions <span>Final Revision</span></h1>

<p>
Last-minute interview revision covering the most important concepts,

<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is GitHub Actions?</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions is a CI/CD automation platform integrated with GitHub.

It allows us to automatically build, test, scan and deploy
applications based on events such as code pushes, pull requests or
manual triggers.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Push
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Security Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Registry
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. GitHub Actions Architecture</h2>

<div class="answer">

The most important components are:

<br><br>

<strong>Workflow</strong> â†’ YAML automation definition

<br><br>

<strong>Event</strong> â†’ Trigger that starts workflow

<br><br>

<strong>Job</strong> â†’ Group of steps executed on a runner

<br><br>

<strong>Step</strong> â†’ Individual command or action

<br><br>

<strong>Runner</strong> â†’ Machine that executes the job

<br><br>

<strong>Action</strong> â†’ Reusable automation component

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Workflow â†’ Job â†’ Step</h2>

<pre><code>name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:

  build:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build
        run: echo "Building application"

      - name: Test
        run: echo "Running tests"</code></pre>

<div class="flow">

Workflow
<br>â†“<br>
Job
<br>â†“<br>
Steps

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Where is Workflow Stored?</h2>

<pre><code>.github/
â””â”€â”€ workflows/
    â””â”€â”€ ci.yml</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions workflow files are YAML files stored inside the
<code>.github/workflows</code> directory.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Common Workflow Triggers</h2>

<pre><code>on:

  push:
    branches:
      - main

  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

  workflow_dispatch:</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Common triggers:

<br><br>

â€¢ <code>push</code>
<br>
â€¢ <code>pull_request</code>
<br>
â€¢ <code>workflow_dispatch</code>
<br>
â€¢ <code>schedule</code>
<br>
â€¢ <code>workflow_call</code>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Runner?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A runner is the machine where a GitHub Actions job actually executes.

GitHub-hosted runners are managed by GitHub.

Self-hosted runners are machines managed by the organization.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>GitHub-Hosted</th>
<th>Self-Hosted</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed by GitHub</td>
<td>Managed by organization</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Easy setup</td>
<td>More control</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Temporary environments</td>
<td>Can use custom infrastructure</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is an Action?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An Action is a reusable unit of automation.

Example:

<pre><code>- uses: actions/checkout@v4</code></pre>

Instead of writing checkout logic manually, we use the existing
action.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. run vs uses</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>run</th>
<th>uses</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Executes shell commands.</td>
<td>Executes a reusable Action.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>run: npm test</code></td>
<td><code>uses: actions/checkout@v4</code></td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Job Dependencies with needs</h2>

<pre><code>jobs:

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Testing"

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<code>needs</code> creates a dependency between jobs.

Here, deployment starts only after the test job succeeds.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Environment Variables</h2>

<pre><code>env:
  APP_ENV: production

jobs:

  build:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - run: echo "$APP_ENV"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Environment variables store non-secret configuration values.

Sensitive information should be stored as secrets instead.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. GitHub Secrets</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Secrets are encrypted values used for sensitive information
such as tokens, passwords and credentials.

Example:

<pre><code>env:
  API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}</code></pre>

Never hard-code credentials inside workflow files.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. GITHUB_TOKEN</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub automatically provides <code>GITHUB_TOKEN</code> to workflows
for interacting with GitHub resources.

Its permissions should be restricted according to the workflow's
requirements.

</div>

<pre><code>permissions:
  contents: read</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. GitHub OIDC</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub OIDC allows a workflow to authenticate with cloud providers
using short-lived identity credentials instead of storing long-lived
cloud access keys.

</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
OIDC Token
<br>â†“<br>
AWS IAM
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Role
<br>â†“<br>
Temporary Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Resources

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. AWS OIDC Permissions</h2>

<pre><code>permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

<code>id-token: write</code> allows the workflow to request an OIDC
identity token.

The AWS IAM role trust policy then determines whether the GitHub
identity is allowed to assume the role.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Trust Policy vs Permissions Policy</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Trust Policy</th>
<th>Permissions Policy</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Who can assume the role?</td>
<td>What can the role do?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controls trusted identities.</td>
<td>Controls AWS actions/resources.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy memory:</strong>

<br><br>

Trust = <strong>WHO</strong>

<br>

Permissions = <strong>WHAT</strong>

</div>

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Docker Build & Push</h2>

<pre><code>docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

docker tag myapp:${{ github.sha }} \
  username/myapp:${{ github.sha }}

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. GitHub Actions + ArgoCD</h2>

<div class="answer">

In a GitOps architecture, GitHub Actions can build and scan the
application image and update the GitOps repository.

ArgoCD watches the GitOps repository and synchronizes the desired
state into Kubernetes.

</div>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Matrix Strategy</h2>

<pre><code>strategy:

  matrix:
    node: [18, 20, 22]

steps:

  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with:
      node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Matrix strategy allows the same job to run against multiple
configurations such as operating systems, language versions or
runtime versions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 22. Artifacts vs Cache</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Artifacts</th>
<th>Cache</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stores files produced by a workflow.</td>
<td>Speeds up repeated builds.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for reports/build outputs.</td>
<td>Useful for dependencies.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: test reports.</td>
<td>Example: npm cache.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. Reusable Workflows</h2>

<div class="answer">

Reusable workflows allow organizations to define common CI/CD logic
once and call it from multiple workflows.

This reduces duplication and improves standardization.

</div>

<pre><code>on:
  workflow_call:</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. How Do You Secure GitHub Actions?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use least-privilege permissions.</li>

<li>Never hard-code credentials.</li>

<li>Use GitHub Secrets.</li>

<li>Prefer OIDC for cloud authentication.</li>

<li>Restrict AWS IAM permissions.</li>

<li>Protect production environments.</li>

<li>Use branch protection.</li>

<li>Review third-party Actions.</li>

<li>Use secret scanning.</li>

<li>Scan dependencies and container images.</li>

<li>Be careful with untrusted pull requests.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Most Important Troubleshooting Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Workflow Not Triggering?
<br>â†“<br>
Check Event / Branch
<br><br>

YAML Error?
<br>â†“<br>
Check Syntax
<br><br>

Job Failed?
<br>â†“<br>
Read Logs
<br><br>

Build Failed?
<br>â†“<br>
Check Code / Dependencies
<br><br>

Docker Failed?
<br>â†“<br>
Check Dockerfile / Context
<br><br>

Push Failed?
<br>â†“<br>
Check Registry Authentication
<br><br>

AWS Failed?
<br>â†“<br>
Check OIDC / IAM
<br><br>

Kubernetes Failed?
<br>â†“<br>

<br><br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>
