<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Scenario â€” Workflow Not Triggering</h2>

<div class="question">

"My workflow is not running after I push code. What will you check?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

I would first verify the workflow file location and YAML syntax.
Then I would check the configured trigger and branch filters.

After that I would check whether the workflow is disabled or whether
repository settings are preventing the expected execution.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Scenario â€” Tests Fail Only in CI</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would compare the local and CI environments.

I would check:

<br><br>

â€¢ Runtime versions<br>
â€¢ Dependencies<br>
â€¢ Environment variables<br>
â€¢ Operating system<br>
â€¢ Database/service dependencies<br>
â€¢ Test configuration

Then I would reproduce the failure as closely as possible.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Scenario â€” Docker Push Failed</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify the image was built successfully, then check registry
login, credentials, repository name, image tag and registry
permissions.

For AWS ECR, I would additionally verify AWS authentication, OIDC,
IAM permissions and region.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Scenario â€” AWS OIDC Failed</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<br><br>

1. <code>id-token: write</code> permission.
<br>
2. AWS OIDC provider.
<br>
3. IAM trust policy.
<br>
4. Repository/branch conditions.
<br>
5. IAM role ARN.
<br>
6. Role permissions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 30. Scenario â€” Kubernetes ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would run:

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Then check the image name, image tag, registry access, authentication
and ImagePullSecrets.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 31 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 31. Scenario â€” CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would inspect the current and previous container logs and describe
the pod.

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Then check application startup, environment variables, Secrets,
ConfigMaps, commands and health probes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 32 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 32. Scenario â€” Bad Production Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

My priority would be to stabilize production.

I would check application health and logs, determine the impact and
rollback if required.

After recovery, I would investigate the root cause and add preventive
controls.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 33 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 33. Secret Accidentally Committed</h2>

<div class="answer">

The first priority is to revoke or rotate the exposed credential.

Then I would investigate possible usage, remove the secret from the
repository according to the organization's procedure, move it to
secure storage and enable preventive scanning.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Never assume that deleting the file from the latest commit makes the
credential safe.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 34 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 34. Green Pipeline but Application Is Down</h2>

<div class="answer">

A green pipeline only means the configured workflow steps succeeded.

I would verify the actual application using:

<br><br>

â€¢ Pod status<br>
â€¢ Application logs<br>
â€¢ Health probes<br>
â€¢ Service<br>
â€¢ Ingress/load balancer<br>
â€¢ Metrics<br>
â€¢ Alerts

</div>

<div class="flow">

CI Success
<br>â‰ <br>
Application Health

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¤ Final Interview Answer</h2>

<div class="interview">

"GitHub Actions is a CI/CD automation platform integrated with
GitHub. I use workflows defined in YAML to automate stages such as
checkout, build, testing, security scanning, Docker image creation
and deployment.

A workflow contains jobs, and jobs contain steps that execute on
runners.

For security, I use least-privilege permissions, GitHub Secrets and
prefer OIDC for AWS authentication instead of long-lived access
keys. The GitHub identity assumes a restricted IAM role through its
trust policy.

In a production CI/CD pipeline, I would build and test the
application, scan it, build and scan the container image, push it to
a registry and deploy it to the target environment.

For Kubernetes and GitOps, GitHub Actions can update the image or
GitOps repository while ArgoCD synchronizes the desired state to the
cluster.

For troubleshooting, I start from the failed workflow, identify the
failed job and step, read the logs, check configuration and
permissions, fix the root cause, rerun the workflow and finally
verify application health."

</div>

</div>

<!-- SCENARIO 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 1 â€” Workflow Does Not Start</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Interviewer:</strong><br>

"You pushed code to the main branch, but your GitHub Actions workflow
did not start. What will you check?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Step 1:</strong> Check whether the workflow file exists under:

<pre><code>.github/workflows/</code></pre>

<strong>Step 2:</strong> Check the YAML syntax.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 3:</strong> Check the trigger.

<pre><code>on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main</code></pre>

<strong>Step 4:</strong> Confirm that the push actually targeted
the expected branch.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 5:</strong> Check whether the workflow is disabled or
restricted by repository settings.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 2 â€” Workflow YAML Error</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"GitHub reports that the workflow file is invalid."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<br><br>

â€¢ YAML indentation<br>
â€¢ Incorrect key names<br>
â€¢ Missing colon<br>
â€¢ Incorrect expressions<br>
â€¢ Invalid workflow syntax<br>
â€¢ Incorrect <code>on</code> configuration<br>
â€¢ Unsupported action configuration

</div>

<pre><code>jobs:

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Build
        run: echo "Building..."</code></pre>

</div>

â€¢ Token permissions<br>

â€¢ Action version<br>
â€¢ Runner connectivity

</div>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<br><br>

<br>

<!-- SCENARIO 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 9 â€” AWS OIDC Authentication Failed</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"GitHub Actions says it cannot assume the AWS IAM role."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check the following in order:

<br><br>

<strong>1. Workflow permission</strong>

<pre><code>permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read</code></pre>

<strong>2. AWS OIDC provider</strong>

Confirm the GitHub OIDC provider exists in AWS.

<br><br>

<strong>3. IAM trust policy</strong>

Verify that the correct GitHub repository/branch or other intended
claims are trusted.

<br><br>

<strong>4. Role ARN</strong>

Verify that the workflow references the correct role.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 10 â€” Secret Is Empty or Unavailable</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"A GitHub Secret appears to be unavailable inside the workflow."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<br><br>

â€¢ Exact secret name<br>
â€¢ Repository vs environment secret<br>
â€¢ Correct environment<br>
â€¢ Workflow context<br>
â€¢ Repository permissions<br>
â€¢ Whether the secret actually exists

Example:

<pre><code>${{ secrets.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}</code></pre>

</div>

<div class="warning">

Do not print the secret value while troubleshooting.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div class="answer">

Separate the problem into two possibilities:

<br><br>

<strong>GitHub permission:</strong>

Check:

<pre><code>permissions:</code></pre>

<strong>Cloud permission:</strong>

Check AWS IAM, Azure RBAC, GCP IAM or the target platform's access
control.

<div class="flow">

<br>+
Cloud Permission
<br>â†“<br>

â€¢ Manifest configuration

<!-- SCENARIO 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 13 â€” ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Interviewer:</strong><br>

"Kubernetes shows ImagePullBackOff after your GitHub Actions
deployment. How do you troubleshoot?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

First inspect the pod:

<pre><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Check:

<br>

â€¢ Image repository<br>
â€¢ Image tag<br>
â€¢ ECR/registry access<br>
â€¢ ImagePullSecrets<br>
â€¢ Node network connectivity<br>
â€¢ Registry permissions

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 14 â€” CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"The deployment succeeds but the application enters
CrashLoopBackOff."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<pre><code>kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;</code></pre>

Possible causes:

<br><br>

â€¢ Application startup failure<br>
â€¢ Incorrect environment variables<br>
â€¢ Missing Secret/ConfigMap<br>
â€¢ Incorrect command<br>
â€¢ Port/configuration issue<br>
â€¢ Dependency unavailable<br>
â€¢ Failed health checks

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 15 â€” Pipeline Succeeds but Deployment Is Wrong</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"GitHub Actions is green, but Kubernetes is still running the old
image."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<br><br>

1. Image tag generated by CI.
<br>
2. Image actually pushed to registry.
<br>
3. Deployment manifest.
<br>
4. Deployment rollout.
<br>
5. Kubernetes image field.
<br>
6. GitOps repository if ArgoCD is used.
<br>
7. ArgoCD sync status.

</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub Actions
<br>â†“
Image Tag
<br>â†“
Registry
<br>â†“
Manifest
<br>â†“
ArgoCD
<br>â†“
Kubernetes

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 16 â€” ArgoCD Is Not Deploying the New Image</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"GitHub Actions pushed the image, but ArgoCD did not deploy it."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<br><br>

â€¢ Did CI update the GitOps repository?<br>
â€¢ Did the commit reach the correct branch?<br>
â€¢ Is ArgoCD tracking the correct repository?<br>
â€¢ Is ArgoCD tracking the correct path?<br>
â€¢ Is the application OutOfSync?<br>
â€¢ Are there manifest errors?<br>
â€¢ Is auto-sync enabled?

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 17 â€” Job Is Stuck</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"A GitHub Actions job remains queued for a long time."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<br><br>

â€¢ Runner availability<br>
â€¢ Self-hosted runner status<br>
â€¢ Runner labels<br>
â€¢ Concurrency restrictions<br>
â€¢ Organization/repository limits<br>
â€¢ Workflow queue

For self-hosted runners, verify that the runner is online and has
matching labels.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ Scenario 18 â€” Self-Hosted Runner Offline</h2>

<div class="answer">

Check:

<br><br>

1. Runner machine status.
<br>
2. Runner service/process.
<br>
3. Network connectivity.
<br>
4. Runner registration.
<br>
5. Labels.
<br>
6. Repository access.
<br>
7. Firewall/proxy configuration.

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<!-- SCENARIO 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 19 â€” Workflow Is Too Slow</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Interviewer:</strong><br>

"Your pipeline takes 30 minutes. How can you optimize it?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

Possible improvements:

<br><br>

â€¢ Cache dependencies<br>
â€¢ Run independent jobs in parallel<br>
â€¢ Avoid unnecessary checkout/build steps<br>
â€¢ Use matrix strategy carefully<br>
â€¢ Use reusable workflows<br>
â€¢ Optimize Docker builds<br>
â€¢ Use appropriate runners<br>
â€¢ Separate fast PR CI from heavier deployment pipelines

</div>

<pre><code>- uses: actions/cache@v4</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 20 â€” Need Different Environments</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"How would you design dev, staging and production deployments?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

A common design is:

<div class="flow">

develop
<br>â†“<br>

<br><br>

staging
<br>â†“<br>
Staging
<br><br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

Use environment-specific configuration and protection rules.

Production should normally have stronger approval and access

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 21 â€” Production Deployment Failed</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"Production deployment completed but the application is unhealthy."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Immediate priorities:

<br><br>

<strong>1.</strong> Check application health.
<br>
<strong>2.</strong> Check monitoring and logs.
<br>
<strong>3.</strong> Determine blast radius.
<br>
<strong>4.</strong> Roll back if required.
<br>
<strong>5.</strong> Investigate root cause.
<br>
<strong>6.</strong> Prevent recurrence.

</div>

<pre><code>kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 22 â€” Security Scan Failed</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"A Trivy/security scan failed the pipeline."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Do not immediately bypass the scan.

First determine:

<br><br>

â€¢ Vulnerability severity<br>
â€¢ Affected package/image layer<br>
â€¢ Whether a fixed version exists<br>
â€¢ Whether the issue is actually exploitable<br>
â€¢ Organization's security policy

Then update the vulnerable dependency/base image or handle an
approved exception through the security process.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 23 â€” Secret Accidentally Committed</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Interviewer:</strong><br>

"A developer accidentally committed an AWS access key. What do you
do?"

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>1.</strong> Immediately disable/rotate the exposed credential.
<br><br>
<strong>2.</strong> Check CloudTrail or relevant logs for suspicious
usage.
<br><br>
<strong>3.</strong> Remove the secret from source/history according
to the incident procedure.
<br><br>
<strong>4.</strong> Move credentials into secure storage.
<br><br>
<strong>5.</strong> Enable secret scanning/prevention.
<br><br>
<strong>6.</strong> Review why the control failed.

</div>

<div class="warning">

The most important first action is credential rotation/revocation,
not simply deleting the file from Git.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 24 â€” PR Workflow Security Issue</h2>

<div class="question">

<strong>Problem:</strong><br>

"A pull request from an untrusted contributor needs to run tests,
but the workflow also has access to production secrets."

</div>

<div class="answer">

Do not expose production secrets unnecessarily.

Separate untrusted PR validation from privileged deployment workflows.

Use:

<br><br>

â€¢ Minimal permissions<br>
â€¢ Appropriate PR triggers<br>
â€¢ Environment protection<br>
â€¢ Approval gates<br>
â€¢ Separate deployment workflow

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 25 â€” Need Manual Production Approval</h2>

<pre><code>jobs:

  deploy:

    environment:
      name: production

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying production"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Configure production environment protection rules so the deployment
requires the organization's intended approval process.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 26 â€” How Do You Debug a Failed Pipeline?</h2>

<div class="flow">

1. Open Workflow Run
<br>â†“<br>
2. Identify Failed Job
<br>â†“<br>
3. Identify Failed Step
<br>â†“<br>
4. Read Logs
<br>â†“<br>
5. Reproduce Locally if Possible
<br>â†“<br>
6. Check Recent Changes
<br>â†“<br>
7. Check Secrets / Permissions
<br>â†“<br>
8. Fix Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
9. Rerun
<br>â†“<br>
10. Verify

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong><br>

"I start from the failed workflow run and identify the exact job
and step. I read the logs, compare the failed run with the last
successful run, verify configuration, secrets and permissions, fix
the root cause and rerun the workflow. After it succeeds, I verify
the deployed application rather than assuming a green pipeline means
the release is healthy."

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ Scenario 27 â€” CI Green but Application Down</h2>

<div class="answer">

A successful CI/CD workflow only confirms that the defined pipeline
steps completed successfully.

It does not automatically prove that the application is healthy.

Check:

<br><br>

â€¢ Application logs<br>
â€¢ Kubernetes pods<br>
â€¢ Service endpoints<br>
â€¢ Ingress/load balancer<br>
â€¢ Health probes<br>
â€¢ Metrics<br>
â€¢ Alerts<br>
â€¢ Recent deployment

</div>

<div class="flow">

Pipeline Success
<br>â‰ <br>
Application Health

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ Scenario 28 â€” Need Rollback After Bad Release</h2>

<div class="answer">

If the application is unhealthy after deployment, first stabilize
the service.

For Kubernetes:

<pre><code>kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp</code></pre>

Then verify:

<pre><code>kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

kubectl get pods</code></pre>

After recovery, investigate the failed release.

</div>

</div>


<!-- SCENARIO 29 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ Scenario 29 â€” Multiple Jobs Should Run in Parallel</h2>

<pre><code>jobs:

  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test

  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Security scan"

  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm run lint</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Because these jobs have no dependency on each other, they can execute
independently.

If a deployment requires all three, a later job can use:

<pre><code>needs:
  - unit-tests
  - security
  - lint</code></pre>

</div>

</div>

<!-- FINAL INTERVIEW ANSWER -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Master Interview Answer</h2>

<div class="answer">

"When troubleshooting a GitHub Actions pipeline, I first identify
whether the issue is with the trigger, workflow syntax, runner,
application build, test, security scan, registry authentication,
cloud authentication or deployment.

I start from the failed workflow run, identify the failed job and
step, and inspect the logs. Then I compare the failed run with the
last successful run and check recent code or configuration changes.

For cloud-related failures, I verify authentication and permissions.
For AWS, I would check the OIDC configuration, IAM trust policy and
role permissions.

For Kubernetes failures, I check the deployment, pods, events,
logs, image configuration and RBAC.

After identifying the root cause, I make the smallest appropriate
fix, rerun the workflow and verify the actual application health.

If a production deployment causes an incident, I prioritize
stabilization and rollback when necessary, followed by root-cause
analysis and preventive actions."

</div>

</div>

<h1>GitHub Actions <span>Security</span></h1>

<p>
Secrets, GITHUB_TOKEN, permissions, OIDC, AWS IAM,
least privilege, environments and real-time security scenarios.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Why is GitHub Actions Security Important?</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions can access source code, cloud resources, deployment
systems and secrets. A poorly secured workflow can therefore become
an entry point into the infrastructure.

The main security goals are:

<br><br>

â€¢ Protect credentials<br>
â€¢ Limit permissions<br>
â€¢ Secure workflow execution<br>
â€¢ Prevent secret exposure<br>
â€¢ Control production deployments<br>
â€¢ Use short-lived credentials where possible

</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Workflow
<br>â†“<br>
Credentials / Permissions
<br>â†“<br>
Cloud Resources
<br>â†“<br>
Production

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What are GitHub Secrets?</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Secrets are encrypted values used to store sensitive
information such as API tokens, passwords, private credentials and
other secrets required by workflows.

They should not be hard-coded directly into workflow files.

</div>

<pre><code>- name: Deploy

  env:
    API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}

  run: ./deploy.sh</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Never commit passwords, access keys, private keys or tokens directly
into the repository.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Where Can Secrets Be Stored?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Scope</th>
<th>Use</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Repository Secret</td>
<td>Used by workflows in a repository.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Environment Secret</td>
<td>Used for a specific environment such as production.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Organization Secret</td>
<td>Can be shared across selected repositories.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

For production deployments, environment-level controls can be useful
because production credentials can be isolated from development
workflows.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. How Do You Use Secrets?</h2>

<pre><code>name: Deploy

on:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:

  deploy:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Deploy Application
        env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}

        run: |
          ./deploy.sh</code></pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not use commands such as:

<pre><code>echo "${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}"</code></pre>

because exposing secrets in logs is dangerous.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is GITHUB_TOKEN?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>GITHUB_TOKEN</code> is a token automatically provided to a
GitHub Actions workflow for interacting with GitHub resources.

Its permissions should be restricted to only what the workflow needs.

</div>

<pre><code>permissions:
  contents: read</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What are Workflow Permissions?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Permissions control what the workflow's GitHub token is allowed to
access.

A secure workflow should follow the principle of least privilege.

</div>

<pre><code>permissions:
  contents: read</code></pre>

<p>For example, if the workflow only needs to read repository files,
do not give it unnecessary write permissions.</p>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Least Privilege</h2>

<div class="answer">

Least privilege means giving a workflow, user or service only the
minimum permissions required to perform its task.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Required Permission
<br>â†“<br>
Minimum Access
<br>â†“<br>
Perform Task
<br>â†“<br>
No Unnecessary Privileges

</div>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Interview answer:</strong><br>

"I follow least privilege by restricting GitHub token permissions,
limiting AWS IAM permissions and using separate roles for different
environments."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is GitHub OIDC?</h2>

<div class="answer">

OpenID Connect allows GitHub Actions to authenticate with supported
cloud providers using short-lived identity credentials instead of
storing long-lived cloud access keys in GitHub Secrets.

</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
OIDC Identity Token
<br>â†“<br>
Cloud Identity Provider
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Role
<br>â†“<br>
Temporary Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
Cloud Resources

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Why Use OIDC with AWS?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Without OIDC, teams may store long-lived AWS access keys in GitHub
Secrets.

With OIDC, GitHub Actions can request temporary credentials by
assuming an AWS IAM role.

This reduces the risk associated with long-lived credentials.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Long-Lived Access Keys</th>
<th>OIDC</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Credentials stored and rotated</td>
<td>Short-lived credentials</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Higher credential exposure risk</td>
<td>Reduced credential storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Manual credential management</td>
<td>Federated identity</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. AWS OIDC Workflow</h2>

<pre><code>permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

steps:

  - name: Configure AWS Credentials
    uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
      aws-region: ap-south-1</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The workflow requests an OIDC token and uses it to assume the
configured AWS IAM role.

The IAM role's trust policy determines which GitHub identities are
allowed to assume it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. AWS IAM Role</h2>

<div class="answer">

The AWS IAM role defines what actions the GitHub Actions workflow can
perform after authentication.

For example, a deployment role may be allowed to push images to ECR
or interact with specific deployment resources.

</div>

<div class="flow">

GitHub Identity
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Trust Policy
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Role
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Permissions Policy
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Resources

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Trust Policy vs Permissions Policy</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Trust Policy</th>
<th>Permissions Policy</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Defines who can assume the role.</td>
<td>Defines what the role can do.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controls trusted identities.</td>
<td>Controls allowed AWS actions.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Authentication relationship.</td>
<td>Authorization permissions.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="interview">

<strong>Easy way to remember:</strong>

<br><br>

Trust Policy â†’ <strong>"Who can use this role?"</strong>

<br>

Permissions Policy â†’ <strong>"What can this role do?"</strong>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Example: Restrict AWS Permissions</h2>

<pre><code>{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
        "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
        "ecr:PutImage",
        "ecr:InitiateLayerUpload",
        "ecr:UploadLayerPart",
        "ecr:CompleteLayerUpload"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

In a real environment, permissions should be designed according to
the exact workflow requirements and resource scope.

Avoid giving a CI workflow unrestricted administrator permissions.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Production Environment Protection</h2>

<div class="answer">

Production deployments should have additional controls such as:

<br><br>

â€¢ Required reviewers<br>
â€¢ Environment-specific secrets<br>
â€¢ Deployment restrictions<br>
â€¢ Branch protection<br>
â€¢ Approval gates<br>
â€¢ Least-privilege credentials

</div>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“<br>
Review
<br>â†“<br>
CI Checks
<br>â†“<br>
Production Approval
<br>â†“<br>
Deployment

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Branch Protection</h2>

<div class="answer">

Branch protection helps prevent unsafe changes from being directly
merged into important branches such as <code>main</code>.

Typical controls include:

<br><br>

â€¢ Pull request requirement<br>
â€¢ Required approvals<br>
â€¢ Required status checks<br>
â€¢ Restrict direct pushes<br>
â€¢ Code review requirements

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Pull Request Security</h2>

<div class="warning">

Be careful when workflows execute code from untrusted pull requests,
especially when those workflows have access to secrets or elevated
permissions.

</div>

<div class="answer">

A malicious change in a pull request should not be able to freely
access production credentials or sensitive infrastructure.

Use appropriate workflow triggers, permissions and approval controls.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Why is pull_request_target Sensitive?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<code>pull_request_target</code> runs in the context of the base
repository and can have access to repository-level resources that
ordinary pull request workflows may not have.

Because of this, it must be used carefully when executing code or
processing untrusted pull request content.

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Interview point:</strong><br>

Never blindly execute untrusted pull request code with elevated
permissions or access to sensitive secrets.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Third-Party Actions Security</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions can use third-party actions from the marketplace or
other repositories.

However, an action executes code in the workflow environment, so its
source and permissions should be reviewed.

</div>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Best practice:</strong>

<br><br>

â€¢ Prefer trusted actions.<br>
â€¢ Review action source.<br>
â€¢ Pin versions carefully.<br>
â€¢ Minimize workflow permissions.<br>
â€¢ Keep actions updated through a controlled process.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 19. Why Pin Action Versions?</h2>

<pre><code>- uses: actions/checkout@v4</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

Pinning an action version provides more predictable workflow behavior
than blindly tracking an unknown moving version.

For highly controlled environments, organizations may pin actions to
specific commit SHAs according to their security policy.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Secret Leakage Prevention</h2>

<div class="answer">

To reduce accidental secret exposure:

<br><br>

1. Never hard-code secrets.
<br>
2. Use GitHub Secrets or an external secret manager.
<br>
3. Do not print secrets in logs.
<br>
4. Restrict workflow permissions.
<br>
5. Avoid unnecessary secret access.
<br>
6. Rotate compromised credentials immediately.
<br>
7. Prefer short-lived credentials where possible.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Secret Scanning</h2>

<div class="answer">

Secret scanning tools detect credentials or sensitive patterns that
may have accidentally been committed to source control.

Examples include:

<br><br>

<span class="badge">GitHub Secret Scanning</span>
<span class="badge">Gitleaks</span>

</div>

<pre><code>gitleaks detect --source .</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Security Pipeline</h2>

<div class="flow">

Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Dependency Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Secret Scan
<br>â†“<br>
SAST
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 23. Security Contexts</h2>

<div class="answer">

GitHub Actions provides contexts such as:

<br><br>

<code>github</code> â†’ repository, event and commit information

<br><br>

<code>secrets</code> â†’ encrypted secrets

<br><br>

<code>env</code> â†’ environment variables

<br><br>

<code>vars</code> â†’ configuration variables

<br><br>

<code>steps</code> â†’ outputs from previous steps

<br><br>

<code>needs</code> â†’ outputs/status from dependent jobs

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Real-Time Scenario: AWS Authentication Failed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Problem:</strong>

GitHub Actions cannot assume the AWS IAM role.

<br><br>

<strong>Check:</strong>

1. OIDC provider configuration.
<br>
2. <code>id-token: write</code> permission.
<br>
3. IAM trust policy.
<br>
4. Repository/branch restrictions.
<br>
5. Role ARN.
<br>
6. AWS account.
<br>
7. Region.
<br>
8. GitHub workflow claims.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 25 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. Real-Time Scenario: Secret Not Available</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<br><br>

â€¢ Incorrect secret name<br>
â€¢ Secret belongs to another repository<br>
â€¢ Environment not selected<br>
â€¢ Workflow is running from an untrusted context<br>
â€¢ Secret was deleted or renamed<br>
â€¢ Incorrect expression syntax

</div>

<pre><code>${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}</code></pre>

</div>


<!-- 26 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. Real-Time Scenario: Secret Accidentally Committed</h2>

<div class="answer">

If a credential is committed to Git:

<br><br>

<strong>1.</strong> Revoke or rotate the credential immediately.
<br><br>
<strong>2.</strong> Remove it from the repository.
<br><br>
<strong>3.</strong> Check whether it was used maliciously.
<br><br>
<strong>4.</strong> Update the application/workflow to use secure storage.
<br><br>
<strong>5.</strong> Review repository history and access.
<br><br>
<strong>6.</strong> Add secret scanning/prevention controls.

</div>

<div class="warning">

Deleting the secret from the latest commit alone does not make a
previously exposed credential safe. Rotate it.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 27 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. Secure GitHub Actions Workflow</h2>

<pre><code>name: Secure CI

on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:

  test:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install
        run: npm ci

      - name: Test
        run: npm test

      - name: Secret Scan
        run: |
          echo "Run secret scanning here"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">

The important ideas are:

<br><br>

â€¢ Read-only permissions by default<br>
â€¢ No unnecessary secrets<br>
â€¢ Automated validation<br>
â€¢ Security scanning<br>
â€¢ Controlled deployment

</div>

</div>


<!-- 28 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 28. Security Checklist</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use least-privilege workflow permissions.</li>

<li>Never hard-code credentials.</li>

<li>Use GitHub Secrets for required sensitive values.</li>

<li>Prefer OIDC for cloud authentication where supported.</li>

<li>Use restricted AWS IAM roles.</li>

<li>Protect production environments.</li>

<li>Use branch protection.</li>

<li>Review third-party actions.</li>

<li>Use secret scanning.</li>

<li>Scan dependencies and container images.</li>

<li>Do not expose secrets in logs.</li>

<li>Rotate credentials immediately after exposure.</li>

<li>Be careful with untrusted pull requests.</li>

</ul>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 29. Most Important Security Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>How do you handle an accidentally committed secret?</li>

<li>Why should third-party Actions be reviewed?</li>

<li>Why are pull request workflows security-sensitive?</li>

</ol>

</div>


<!-- 30 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Interview-Ready Answer</h2>

<div class="interview">

"To secure GitHub Actions, I start with least-privilege permissions
for the GITHUB_TOKEN and avoid hard-coding credentials.

For sensitive values, I use GitHub Secrets or an appropriate external
secret-management solution.

For AWS deployments, I prefer GitHub OIDC with an IAM role so the
workflow receives temporary credentials instead of storing long-lived
AWS access keys.

I also protect production environments with approvals and branch
protection, review third-party Actions, scan repositories for leaked
secrets, and perform dependency and container security scans.

For pull requests from untrusted sources, I make sure sensitive
secrets and elevated permissions are not exposed unnecessarily."

</div>

</div>

<h1>GitHub <span>Actions Core Concepts</span></h1>
<p>Important concepts, YAML structure, workflows, events, jobs, steps, actions, runners, variables, artifacts and interview questions.</p>
</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is GitHub Actions?</h2>

<div class="answer">
GitHub Actions is a CI/CD and automation platform integrated with GitHub.
It allows us to automatically build, test, scan and deploy applications
based on repository events.
</div>

<div class="flow">
Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Push
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
Build â†’ Test â†’ Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
</div>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Interview answer:</strong><br>
"GitHub Actions is GitHub's automation and CI/CD platform. We define
workflows using YAML files inside the repository, and those workflows
execute jobs on runners when specified events occur."
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Where are GitHub Actions workflows stored?</h2>

<div class="answer">
Workflow YAML files are stored inside the repository under:
</div>

<pre><code>.github/workflows/</code></pre>

<p>Example:</p>

<pre><code>project/
â”œâ”€â”€ src/
â”œâ”€â”€ Dockerfile
â””â”€â”€ .github/
    â””â”€â”€ workflows/
        â””â”€â”€ ci.yml</code></pre>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is a Workflow?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A workflow is an automated process defined in a YAML file. It specifies
when automation should run and what jobs should be executed.
</div>

<pre><code>name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - run: echo "Build application"</code></pre>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is an Event?</h2>

<div class="answer">
An event is something that triggers a workflow.
</div>

<table>
<tr><th>Event</th><th>Use</th></tr>
<tr><td>push</td><td>Run when code is pushed.</td></tr>
<tr><td>pull_request</td><td>Run when a pull request changes.</td></tr>
<tr><td>workflow_dispatch</td><td>Run manually.</td></tr>
<tr><td>schedule</td><td>Run on a schedule.</td></tr>
<tr><td>workflow_call</td><td>Call a reusable workflow.</td></tr>
</table>

<pre><code>on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main</code></pre>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is a Job?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A job is a collection of steps that runs on a runner.
A workflow can contain one or multiple jobs.
</div>

<pre><code>jobs:

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - run: echo "Build"

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - run: echo "Test"</code></pre>

<p>
Jobs can run independently or can be connected using
<code>needs</code>.
</p>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Step?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A step is an individual operation inside a job.
A step can execute a shell command or use an action.
</div>

<pre><code>steps:

  - name: Checkout
    uses: actions/checkout@v4

  - name: Install
    run: npm install

  - name: Test
    run: npm test</code></pre>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is an Action?</h2>

<div class="answer">
An Action is a reusable component that performs a specific task.
Actions prevent us from repeatedly writing common automation logic.
</div>

<pre><code>- name: Checkout repository
  uses: actions/checkout@v4</code></pre>

<p>
Here <code>actions/checkout@v4</code> is a reusable action used to
checkout repository code.
</p>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is a Runner?</h2>

<div class="answer">
A runner is the machine that executes a GitHub Actions job.
</div>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Runner</th>
<th>Description</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>GitHub-hosted</td>
<td>Machine managed by GitHub.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Self-hosted</td>
<td>Machine managed by the organization.</td>
</tr>
</table>

<pre><code>runs-on: ubuntu-latest</code></pre>

<div class="interview">
<strong>Interview point:</strong><br>
GitHub-hosted runners are convenient because GitHub manages the
execution environment. Self-hosted runners provide greater control
over the environment and infrastructure.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. GitHub-Hosted vs Self-Hosted Runner</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>GitHub-Hosted</th>
<th>Self-Hosted</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed by GitHub</td>
<td>Managed by organization</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Easy to configure</td>
<td>Requires infrastructure management</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Fresh environment generally provided for each job</td>
<td>Organization controls environment</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less maintenance</td>
<td>More control/customization</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Complete Basic Workflow</h2>

<pre><code>name: Basic CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm install

      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build</code></pre>

<div class="flow">
Event
<br>â†“<br>
Job
<br>â†“<br>
Runner
<br>â†“<br>
Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Install
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Build
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is <code>runs-on</code>?</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>runs-on</code> specifies the runner environment where the job
will execute.
</div>

<pre><code>runs-on: ubuntu-latest</code></pre>

<p>Other examples can include Windows or macOS runners:</p>

<pre><code>runs-on: windows-latest

runs-on: macos-latest</code></pre>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is <code>run</code> vs <code>uses</code>?</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>run</th>
<th>uses</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Executes shell commands.</td>
<td>Uses a reusable Action.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>run: npm test</code></td>
<td><code>uses: actions/checkout@v4</code></td>
</tr>
</table>

<pre><code>- name: Test
  run: npm test

- name: Checkout
  uses: actions/checkout@v4</code></pre>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Job Dependencies using <code>needs</code></h2>

<div class="answer">
The <code>needs</code> keyword makes one job wait for another job to
complete successfully.
</div>

<pre><code>jobs:

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Build"

  test:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Test"

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploy"</code></pre>

<div class="flow">
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. Parallel Jobs</h2>

<div class="answer">
If jobs do not depend on each other, they can execute independently
and potentially in parallel.
</div>

<pre><code>jobs:

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Build"

  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Security Scan"

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Tests"</code></pre>

<div class="flow">
Build â†˜
<br>
Security â†’ Independent Jobs
<br>
Test â†—
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Environment Variables</h2>

<div class="answer">
Environment variables store configuration values used during workflow
execution.
</div>

<pre><code>env:
  APP_ENV: production

jobs:

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - run: echo "$APP_ENV"</code></pre>

<p>
Variables can be defined at workflow, job or step level.
</p>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. GitHub Secrets</h2>

<div class="answer">
Secrets are encrypted values used to store sensitive information such
as tokens, passwords and credentials.
</div>

<pre><code>steps:

  - name: Deploy
    env:
      API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}

    run: ./deploy.sh</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Never hard-code passwords, private keys or cloud credentials inside
workflow YAML files.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Artifacts</h2>

<div class="answer">
Artifacts allow files produced during a workflow to be stored and
downloaded after the workflow or job completes.
</div>

<pre><code>- name: Upload Build
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: build-output
    path: dist/</code></pre>

<p>
Examples: test reports, compiled packages, logs and build outputs.
</p>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. Matrix Strategy</h2>

<div class="answer">
A matrix allows the same job to run against multiple combinations,
such as different language versions or operating systems.
</div>

<pre><code>strategy:
  matrix:
    node: [18, 20, 22]

steps:
  - run: echo "Node ${{ matrix.node }}"</code></pre>

<div class="flow">
Node 18
&nbsp;&nbsp; Node 20
&nbsp;&nbsp; Node 22
<br>â†“&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;â†“&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;â†“
<br>
Tests
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 19. Manual Workflow</h2>

<div class="answer">
<code>workflow_dispatch</code> allows users to manually start a workflow.
</div>

<pre><code>on:
  workflow_dispatch:</code></pre>

<p>
Useful for controlled deployments and operational tasks.
</p>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 20. Scheduled Workflow</h2>

<pre><code>on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * *"</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Scheduled workflows run according to cron expressions.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Permissions</h2>

<div class="answer">
The <code>permissions</code> section controls what the workflow's
<code>GITHUB_TOKEN</code> can access.
</div>

<pre><code>permissions:
  contents: read</code></pre>

<div class="warning">
Use least privilege. Give the workflow only the permissions it
actually requires.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Workflow Execution Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Event</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Workflow</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Job</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Runner</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Steps</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Commands / Actions</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Result</strong>

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Real-Time Scenario: Workflow Failed</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Question:</strong><br>
"Your GitHub Actions pipeline failed. How will you troubleshoot it?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong>

1. Open the failed workflow run.
<br>
2. Identify the failed job.
<br>
3. Identify the failed step.
<br>
4. Read the logs.
<br>
5. Compare with the last successful run.
<br>
6. Check recent code/configuration changes.
<br>
7. Check dependencies, secrets and permissions.
<br>
8. Fix the root cause.
<br>
9. Rerun and verify.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Real-Time Scenario: Secret Error</h2>

<div class="answer">

If a secret is not working, check:

<br><br>

â€¢ Secret name<br>
â€¢ Repository/environment scope<br>
â€¢ Workflow permissions<br>
â€¢ Event restrictions<br>
â€¢ Cloud-side permissions<br>
â€¢ Target account or role

</div>

<div class="warning">
Never print the secret value into workflow logs while troubleshooting.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 25. GitHub Actions + Docker</h2>

<pre><code>name: Docker CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:

  docker:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build Docker Image
        run: docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: List Images
        run: docker images</code></pre>

<div class="answer">
Using the commit SHA as an image identifier helps connect the image
to the exact source revision.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 26. GitHub Actions + Kubernetes</h2>

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 27. GitHub Actions vs Jenkins</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>GitHub Actions</th>
<th>Jenkins</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Built into GitHub ecosystem</td>
<td>Independent automation server</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>YAML workflows</td>
<td>Jenkinsfile / pipeline configuration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>GitHub-hosted runners available</td>
<td>Jenkins agents required</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Easy GitHub integration</td>
<td>Large plugin ecosystem</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed platform experience</td>
<td>More infrastructure control</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Interview-Ready Answer</h2>

<div class="interview">

"GitHub Actions is a CI/CD automation platform integrated with
GitHub. Workflows are written in YAML and stored under the
.github/workflows directory.

A workflow is triggered by events such as push or pull request.
It contains jobs, jobs contain steps, and steps can execute shell
commands or reusable Actions.

Each job runs on a runner. We can use GitHub-hosted or self-hosted
runners depending on the requirement.

For a production pipeline, I would use GitHub Actions to checkout
code, build and test the application, perform security checks,
build a Docker image, push it to a registry and deploy it to the
target environment.

For security, I would use Secrets or short-lived federated
credentials where supported, apply least-privilege permissions and
avoid exposing sensitive values in logs."

</div>
</div>

<h1>ArgoCD Applications & Sync</h1>

<p>
Applications, synchronization, OutOfSync, automated deployment,
self-healing, pruning, health status and real-time GitOps flow.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is an ArgoCD Application?</h2>

<p>
An ArgoCD Application is a Kubernetes custom resource that defines
which configuration should be deployed from a source repository to a
target Kubernetes cluster and namespace.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

An ArgoCD Application connects the desired state stored in Git with a
destination Kubernetes cluster and continuously manages the
application according to the configured synchronization policy.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Three Important Parts of an Application</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Source</strong></td>
<td>Where the desired configuration comes from.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Destination</strong></td>
<td>Where the application will be deployed.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Sync Policy</strong></td>
<td>Controls how synchronization should happen.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ“¦ Git Repository
<br>
<strong>Source</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ”„ ArgoCD Application
<br>â†“<br>
â˜¸ï¸ Kubernetes Cluster
<br>
<strong>Destination</strong>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Example ArgoCD Application</h2>

<pre>
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application

metadata:
  name: nginx-app
  namespace: argocd

spec:
  project: default

  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example/gitops-repo.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: manifests

  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: nginx

  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Remember:</strong><br>

<code>source</code> â†’ What should be deployed?<br>
<code>destination</code> â†’ Where should it be deployed?<br>
<code>syncPolicy</code> â†’ How should synchronization happen?

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is Sync?</h2>

<p>
Sync is the process of applying the desired state from Git to the
target Kubernetes cluster.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git Desired State
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
Compare With Live State
<br>â†“<br>
Differences Found
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>SYNC</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Updated

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is OutOfSync?</h2>

<p>
An application becomes <strong>OutOfSync</strong> when the desired state
in Git differs from the live state in Kubernetes.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>
replicas = 1
<br>â†“<br>
âš ï¸ <strong>OUT OF SYNC</strong>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

OutOfSync means there is a difference between the desired state stored
in Git and the live state running in the Kubernetes cluster.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is Synced?</h2>

<p>
An application is Synced when the live Kubernetes state matches the
desired configuration.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†•<br>
Kubernetes
<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>
âœ… <strong>SYNCED</strong>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Manual Sync</h2>

<p>
In manual synchronization, ArgoCD detects a difference but waits for
the user to trigger synchronization.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git Change
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Difference
<br>â†“<br>
âš ï¸ OutOfSync
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Engineer Clicks Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Updated

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Use Case:</strong><br>

Manual sync is useful when deployments, especially production
deployments, require an explicit human action.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Automated Sync</h2>

<p>
With automated synchronization enabled, ArgoCD can automatically apply
eligible changes detected in the desired Git state.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Change
<br>â†“<br>
Automatic Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Updated

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

Automated sync removes the need for an engineer to manually click the
Sync button for every eligible Git change.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is Self-Heal?</h2>

<p>
Self-healing allows ArgoCD to react to certain changes made directly
to Kubernetes that cause drift from the desired Git state.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>
Manual kubectl Change
<br>
replicas = 1
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Drift
<br>â†“<br>
Self-Heal
<br>â†“<br>
Cluster moves toward Git state

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

Self-heal helps ArgoCD automatically reconcile certain out-of-band
changes so that the live state moves back toward the desired Git state.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. What is Pruning?</h2>

<p>
Pruning removes resources that are no longer defined in the desired
application state when pruning is enabled.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>
Deployment + Service
<br>â†“<br>
Developer removes Service from Git
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Difference
<br>â†“<br>
Pruning Enabled
<br>â†“<br>
Service Removed From Cluster

</div>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

Pruning can delete Kubernetes resources. It should be enabled carefully,
especially for production environments.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Sync Policy</h2>

<p>
The sync policy defines how ArgoCD should synchronize the application.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Option</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Automated</td>
<td>Automatically synchronize eligible changes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Prune</td>
<td>Remove resources no longer desired.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Self-Heal</td>
<td>React to supported live-state drift.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Application Health</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD also monitors the health of application resources.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Status</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Healthy</td>
<td>Resources are operating as expected.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Progressing</td>
<td>Resources are still moving toward the expected state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Degraded</td>
<td>One or more resources are unhealthy.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Missing</td>
<td>An expected resource is not present.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Unknown</td>
<td>ArgoCD cannot determine the resource health.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Synced vs Healthy</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Status</th>
<th>Question It Answers</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Synced</strong></td>
<td>Does the live configuration match Git?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Healthy</strong></td>
<td>Are the deployed resources operating correctly?</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Example:</strong><br>

An application can be <strong>Synced but Degraded</strong> if Kubernetes
matches Git but the deployed application is unhealthy.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. Sync Waves</h2>

<p>
Sync waves allow resources to be applied in a controlled order.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Wave 0
<br>
Namespace
<br>â†“<br>

Wave 1
<br>
ConfigMap / Secret
<br>â†“<br>

Wave 2
<br>
Deployment
<br>â†“<br>

Wave 3
<br>
Ingress

</div>

<p>
This is useful when certain resources need to exist before dependent
resources are deployed.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Complete Sync Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ“¦ Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ” ArgoCD Detects Change
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ“¥ Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>
Manifest Generation
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ”„ Application Controller
<br>â†“<br>
Compare Desired vs Live
<br>â†“<br>
âš ï¸ OutOfSync
<br>â†“<br>
Sync
<br>â†“<br>
â˜¸ï¸ Kubernetes API
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸš€ Resources Updated
<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Interview Scenario</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
Your Git repository says the application should have three replicas,
but someone manually changes the Deployment to one replica using
<code>kubectl</code>.
</p>

<h3>What happens?</h3>

<ol>

<li>ArgoCD compares desired and live state.</li>

<li>It detects a difference.</li>

<li>The Application becomes OutOfSync.</li>

<li>If automated sync with self-heal is enabled, ArgoCD can reconcile
the drift.</li>

<li>The Kubernetes Deployment moves toward the Git-defined state.</li>

<li>ArgoCD checks the resulting application health.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"This is configuration drift. ArgoCD detects that the live state
differs from the desired state in Git. If self-healing is enabled,
ArgoCD automatically reconciles the supported drift and brings the
cluster back toward the Git state."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Most Important Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>What is an ArgoCD Application?</li>

<li>What is synchronization in ArgoCD?</li>

<li>What is OutOfSync?</li>

<li>What is Synced?</li>

<li>Manual sync vs automated sync?</li>

<li>What is self-healing?</li>

<li>What is pruning?</li>

<li>What is a sync policy?</li>

<li>What is the difference between Synced and Healthy?</li>

<li>What are sync waves?</li>

<li>What happens when someone changes a resource using kubectl?</li>

<li>Explain the complete ArgoCD synchronization flow.</li>

</ol>

</div>

<strong>Application</strong> â†’ Defines what and where to deploy.<br><br>

<strong>Sync</strong> â†’ Applies desired Git state to Kubernetes.<br><br>

<strong>OutOfSync</strong> â†’ Git and cluster differ.<br><br>

<strong>Synced</strong> â†’ Git and cluster match.<br><br>

<strong>Automated Sync</strong> â†’ Synchronization happens automatically.<br><br>

<strong>Self-Heal</strong> â†’ Reconciles supported live-state drift.<br><br>

<strong>Prune</strong> â†’ Removes resources no longer desired.<br><br>

<strong>Healthy</strong> â†’ Application resources are operating correctly.<br><br>

<strong>Sync Waves</strong> â†’ Control deployment order.

<h1>ArgoCD Architecture</h1>

<p>
Understand the main ArgoCD components, their responsibilities,
communication flow and how Git changes reach Kubernetes.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. ArgoCD Architecture Overview</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD follows a GitOps architecture where Git stores the desired
application state and ArgoCD continuously works to keep the Kubernetes
cluster aligned with that state.
</p>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ“¦ Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ”„ ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
â˜¸ï¸ Kubernetes API Server
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸš€ Application Resources

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

ArgoCD continuously monitors the desired state stored in Git,
compares it with the live state of Kubernetes and reconciles the
differences through the Kubernetes API.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Main ArgoCD Components</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Responsibility</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>API Server</strong></td>
<td>
Provides the API used by the ArgoCD Web UI, CLI and other clients.
Handles application and project operations.
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Application Controller</strong></td>
<td>
Monitors applications, compares desired and live state, detects drift
and performs reconciliation.
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Repo Server</strong></td>
<td>
Connects to Git repositories and generates Kubernetes manifests from
YAML, Helm, Kustomize and other supported sources.
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Redis</strong></td>
<td>
Used primarily as a caching layer to improve ArgoCD performance.
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Dex</strong></td>
<td>
Optional identity provider integration component used for
authentication with external identity systems.
</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>ApplicationSet Controller</strong></td>
<td>
Automates creation and management of multiple ArgoCD Applications.
</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. ArgoCD API Server</h2>

<p>
The API Server is the main entry point for users and external clients.
The ArgoCD Web UI and CLI communicate with the API Server.
</p>

<h3>Responsibilities</h3>

<ul>
<li>Provides ArgoCD APIs.</li>
<li>Handles requests from the Web UI.</li>
<li>Handles requests from the CLI.</li>
<li>Provides application information.</li>
<li>Supports authentication and authorization.</li>
<li>Handles application and project operations.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

The ArgoCD API Server acts as the interface between users or clients
and ArgoCD services. The UI and CLI communicate with it to manage and
inspect applications.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Application Controller</h2>

<p>
The Application Controller is the most important component for
reconciliation.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git Desired State
<br>â†“<br>
Application Controller
<br>â†•<br>
Kubernetes API
<br>â†“<br>
Live State

</div>

<h3>Main Responsibilities</h3>

<ul>
<li>Monitors ArgoCD Applications.</li>
<li>Compares desired state with live state.</li>
<li>Detects drift.</li>
<li>Determines Synced or OutOfSync status.</li>
<li>Performs reconciliation.</li>
<li>Monitors application health.</li>
<li>Triggers synchronization according to policy.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

The Application Controller continuously compares the desired state
from Git with the live Kubernetes state and reconciles differences
according to the configured policy.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Repository Server</h2>

<p>
The Repo Server is responsible for retrieving application configuration
from source repositories and generating Kubernetes manifests.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>
Manifest Generation
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Manifests
<br>â†“<br>
Application Controller

</div>

<h3>Common Configuration Sources</h3>

<ul>
<li>Plain Kubernetes YAML</li>
<li>Helm charts</li>
<li>Kustomize</li>
<li>Other supported configuration tools</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important Interview Difference:</strong><br>

<strong>Repo Server</strong> â†’ Gets configuration and generates manifests.<br><br>

<strong>Application Controller</strong> â†’ Compares states and reconciles the application.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 6. Redis</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD uses Redis mainly for caching.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

Redis is a cache used by ArgoCD to improve performance. It is not the
source of truth. Git remains the source of truth for the desired
application configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 7. Dex Server</h2>

<p>
Dex can be used as an identity broker between ArgoCD and external
identity providers.
</p>

<p>
It is mainly related to authentication and identity integration.
Authorization and permissions are handled through ArgoCD's access
control mechanisms.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­ 8. ApplicationSet Controller</h2>

<p>
ApplicationSet helps create multiple ArgoCD Applications from a common
template.
</p>

<div class="flow">

ApplicationSet
<br>â†“<br>
Generator
<br>â†“<br>
Application Template
<br>â†“<br>
Application 1
&nbsp;&nbsp; Application 2
&nbsp;&nbsp; Application 3

</div>

<p>
This becomes useful when the same application needs to be deployed to
multiple clusters or environments.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Complete Git â†’ Kubernetes Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ“¦ Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ” ArgoCD Detects Change
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ“¥ Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>
Manifest Generation
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ”„ Application Controller
<br>â†“<br>
Compare Desired vs Live State
<br>â†“<br>
â˜¸ï¸ Kubernetes API Server
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸš€ Deployment / Pods / Services

â¤ï¸ Health Status
<br>â†“<br>
âœ… Synced + Healthy

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. How Does ArgoCD Communicate With Kubernetes?</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD communicates with Kubernetes through the
<strong>Kubernetes API Server</strong>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

ArgoCD Application Controller
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes API Server
<br>â†“<br>
Deployments
<br>â†“<br>
ReplicaSets
<br>â†“<br>
Pods
<br>â†“<br>
Services / Ingress / ConfigMaps / Secrets

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

ArgoCD uses the Kubernetes API to inspect the live state of resources
and apply the desired configuration to the target cluster.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Desired State vs Live State</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>State</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Desired State</strong></td>
<td>Configuration stored in Git.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Live State</strong></td>
<td>Resources currently running in Kubernetes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Drift</strong></td>
<td>Difference between desired and live state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Reconciliation</strong></td>
<td>Process of bringing live state toward desired state.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What Happens When Git Changes?</h2>

<ol>

<li>Developer modifies Kubernetes configuration.</li>

<li>The change is committed and pushed to Git.</li>

<li>ArgoCD detects the updated desired state.</li>

<li>Repo Server retrieves the configuration.</li>

<li>Required manifests are generated.</li>

<li>Application Controller compares desired and live state.</li>

<li>The application becomes OutOfSync if there is a difference.</li>

<li>ArgoCD synchronizes the resources according to the configured policy.</li>

<li>Kubernetes API applies the changes.</li>

<li>ArgoCD monitors the resulting health.</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What Happens If Someone Uses kubectl?</h2>

<p>
Suppose Git says the Deployment should have three replicas, but an
engineer manually changes it to one replica using <code>kubectl</code>.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>
Manual kubectl Change
<br>
replicas = 1
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Difference
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>OutOfSync</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Self-Heal if configured
<br>â†“<br>
Cluster moves toward Git state

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Term:</strong>
This difference between Git and Kubernetes is called
<strong>configuration drift</strong>.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. What If Git Repository Is Unavailable?</h2>

<p>
If ArgoCD cannot access the Git repository, it cannot obtain fresh
desired-state information from that repository.
</p>

<div class="answer">

Existing workloads already running in Kubernetes do not simply disappear
because Git is temporarily unavailable. However, ArgoCD cannot fetch
new desired configuration from that repository until connectivity is
restored.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. What If Kubernetes API Is Unavailable?</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD may still be able to access repository information, but it
cannot inspect or modify the target Kubernetes cluster while the
Kubernetes API is unavailable.
</p>

<div class="answer">

Once Kubernetes API connectivity is restored, ArgoCD can resume
monitoring and reconciliation.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Component Responsibilities â€” Quick Revision</h2>

<table>

<th>Remember It As</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>API Server</td>
<td>UI / CLI / API entry point</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Application Controller</td>
<td>Compare + Reconcile</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Repo Server</td>
<td>Git + Manifest Generation</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Redis</td>
<td>Cache</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Dex</td>
<td>Identity Integration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ApplicationSet Controller</td>
<td>Multiple Applications</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Kubernetes API Server</td>
<td>Target Cluster Interface</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>

<h1>ArgoCD Final Revision</h1>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is ArgoCD?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

ArgoCD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
It continuously compares the desired state stored in Git with the live
state in Kubernetes and reconciles differences.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Desired State
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Cluster
<br>â†“<br>
Actual State
<br>â†“<br>
Reconciliation

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is GitOps?</h2>

<p>
GitOps is an operational model where Git acts as the source of truth
for infrastructure and application configuration.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“<br>
Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
Application

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Key Point:</strong><br>

Instead of manually changing Kubernetes resources, desired changes are
committed to Git and the GitOps controller reconciles the cluster.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. ArgoCD Architecture</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>API Server</td>
<td>Handles API requests, CLI and UI communication.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Application Controller</td>
<td>Monitors applications and reconciles desired state with live state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Repo Server</td>
<td>Connects to repositories and generates Kubernetes manifests.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Redis</td>
<td>Provides caching used by ArgoCD components.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Dex Server</td>
<td>Can support identity integration for authentication.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ApplicationSet Controller</td>
<td>Generates and manages applications from templates and generators.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is an ArgoCD Application?</h2>

<p>
An ArgoCD Application is a Kubernetes custom resource that connects

Kubernetes cluster and namespace.

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Sync Status vs Health Status</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Sync Status</th>
<th>Health Status</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Shows whether desired and live configuration match.</td>
<td>Shows whether resources are functioning correctly.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Synced / OutOfSync</td>
<td>Healthy / Degraded / Progressing</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important Interview Point:</strong><br>

An application can be <strong>Synced but Degraded</strong>.
ArgoCD may have successfully applied the desired configuration while
the Kubernetes workload itself is unhealthy.

</div>

<p>
Automated synchronization allows ArgoCD to automatically apply changes

</p>

Git Change
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Change
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Self-Healing</h2>

<p>

<div class="flow">

<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>

Manual kubectl Change
<br>
replicas = 1

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. OutOfSync Troubleshooting</h2>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app
argocd app diff my-app
</pre>

<p>
Compare the desired state with the live state and determine what
resource changed.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Typical Causes:</strong><br>

Manual kubectl changes, Git changes, generated manifest differences,
missing resources or incorrect configuration.

</div>

<!-- 18 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. SyncFailed Troubleshooting</h2>

<ol>
<li>Read the ArgoCD error.</li>
<li>Identify the failing resource.</li>
<li>Check Kubernetes events.</li>
<li>Check permissions.</li>
<li>Validate the manifest.</li>
<li>Fix the source configuration.</li>
<li>Retry synchronization.</li>
</ol>

<pre>
kubectl get events -A
kubectl describe &lt;resource&gt;
</pre>

</p>

<pre>

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Remember:</strong><br>

<strong>Synced â‰  Healthy</strong>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Production Deployment Failure</h2>

<div class="flow">

Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Production Deployment
<br>â†“<br>
Application Failure
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Reconciles
<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

In a production failure, I first identify the failing resource and
restore service safely. If the incident was caused by a recent Git
change, I can revert that change so Git returns to a known-good state,
then verify that ArgoCD reconciles the cluster successfully.

</div>

<strong>
"ArgoCD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
It uses Git as the source of truth and continuously compares the desired
state in Git with the live state in Kubernetes. Its Application
Controller performs reconciliation, while the Repo Server generates
manifests from sources such as YAML, Helm and Kustomize. ArgoCD supports
automated synchronization, self-healing, RBAC and Projects, which help
implement secure and reliable Kubernetes deployments."
</strong>

<h1>ArgoCD with Helm & Kustomize</h1>
<p>
How ArgoCD works with Helm charts and Kustomize configurations,
including interview questions and real-time deployment flow.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Why Use Helm or Kustomize with ArgoCD?</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD does not require every Kubernetes resource to be stored as
plain YAML. It can work with configuration tools such as
<strong>Helm</strong> and <strong>Kustomize</strong>.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Helm / Kustomize
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>
Generated Kubernetes Manifests
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Cluster
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
ArgoCD can use Helm and Kustomize as manifest generation tools.
The Repo Server processes the source configuration and produces the
Kubernetes manifests that ArgoCD deploys.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is Helm?</h2>

<p>
Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. It allows applications to be
packaged and deployed using reusable charts and configurable values.
</p>

<h3>Important Helm Concepts</h3>

<ul>
<li><strong>Chart</strong> â†’ Package containing Kubernetes resources.</li>
<li><strong>values.yaml</strong> â†’ Default configuration values.</li>
<li><strong>templates</strong> â†’ Kubernetes manifest templates.</li>
<li><strong>Release</strong> â†’ A deployed instance of a Helm chart.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
Helm simplifies Kubernetes application packaging and deployment by
using reusable charts and configurable values.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. How Does ArgoCD Use Helm?</h2>

<div class="flow">
Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Helm Chart
<br>â†“<br>
values.yaml
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>
Helm Template Rendering
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Manifests
<br>â†“<br>
Application Controller
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
</div>

<p>
ArgoCD can use Helm charts as a source and render them into Kubernetes
manifests before applying the resulting resources.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 4. Example Helm Repository Structure</h2>

<pre>
my-app/
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ Chart.yaml
â”œâ”€â”€ values.yaml
â”‚
â””â”€â”€ templates/
    â”œâ”€â”€ deployment.yaml
    â”œâ”€â”€ service.yaml
    â””â”€â”€ ingress.yaml
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Remember:</strong><br>
<code>Chart.yaml</code> â†’ Chart metadata<br>
<code>values.yaml</code> â†’ Configuration values<br>
<code>templates/</code> â†’ Kubernetes resource templates
</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Example ArgoCD Application Using Helm</h2>

<pre>

  name: my-app
  namespace: argocd

  project: default

<p>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is Kustomize?</h2>

<p>
Kustomize is a Kubernetes-native configuration customization tool.
It allows teams to customize Kubernetes YAML without using templates
in the same way Helm does.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
Kustomize allows Kubernetes manifests to be customized using
overlays and patches while keeping a common base configuration.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<p>
A common pattern is to maintain reusable base manifests and create

</p>

<pre>

â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ base/
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ deployment.yaml
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ service.yaml

â”‚
â””â”€â”€ overlays/
    â”œâ”€â”€ dev/
    â”‚   â””â”€â”€ kustomization.yaml
    â”‚
    â””â”€â”€ prod/
        â””â”€â”€ kustomization.yaml
</pre>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. How Does ArgoCD Use Kustomize?</h2>

<div class="flow">
Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Kustomize Base
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<p>
ArgoCD identifies the Kustomize configuration and generates the

</p>
