<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 9. Helm vs Kustomize</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Helm</th>
<th>Kustomize</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Package manager for Kubernetes.</td>
<td>Kubernetes configuration customization tool.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses charts and templates.</td>
<td>Uses bases, overlays and patches.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses values for configuration.</td>
<td>Uses overlays and patches for customization.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Useful for packaging reusable applications.</td>
<td>Useful for environment-specific configuration.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can manage application releases.</td>
<td>Focuses on customizing Kubernetes manifests.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Helm vs Kustomize â€” Interview Answer</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br><br>

Helm is a Kubernetes package manager that uses charts, templates and
values to package and configure applications.<br><br>

Kustomize is a Kubernetes-native customization tool that uses bases,
overlays and patches to customize existing manifests.<br><br>

In ArgoCD, both can be used as sources for generating the manifests
that are ultimately synchronized to Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. Can ArgoCD Deploy Helm Charts?</h2>

<p><strong>Yes.</strong></p>

<p>
ArgoCD can deploy applications from Helm chart sources and can use
Helm values to customize deployments.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Important:</strong><br>
ArgoCD uses Helm primarily for manifest generation. ArgoCD itself
manages the desired Kubernetes state and synchronization.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Can ArgoCD Deploy Kustomize?</h2>

<p><strong>Yes.</strong></p>

<p>
ArgoCD can detect a Kustomize application and generate the final
manifests before synchronization.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Dev and Production Example</h2>

</p>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What Happens When values.yaml Changes?</h2>

<ol>

<li>Developer changes a value in <code>values.yaml</code>.</li>

<li>The change is committed to Git.</li>

<li>ArgoCD detects the new Git revision.</li>

<li>Repo Server renders the Helm chart using the updated values.</li>

<li>ArgoCD compares the generated manifests with live resources.</li>

<li>The Application becomes OutOfSync if a difference exists.</li>

<li>ArgoCD synchronizes the new configuration.</li>

<li>Kubernetes updates the application.</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. What Happens When a Kustomize Overlay Changes?</h2>

<ol>

<li>Developer modifies an environment overlay.</li>

<li>Change is pushed to Git.</li>

<li>ArgoCD detects the new revision.</li>

<li>Repo Server processes the Kustomize configuration.</li>

<li>Final manifests are generated.</li>

<li>ArgoCD compares desired and live state.</li>

<li>Resources are synchronized.</li>

<li>Application health is monitored.</li>

</ol>

</div>

<li>How does ArgoCD work with Kustomize?</li>

<li>Helm vs Kustomize?</li>

<li>Can ArgoCD deploy Helm charts?</li>

<li>Can ArgoCD deploy Kustomize applications?</li>

<li>What happens when values.yaml changes?</li>

<li>What happens when a Kustomize overlay changes?</li>

</ol>

<div style="font-size:50px">ðŸ”</div>
<h1>ArgoCD RBAC & Security</h1>
<p>
Authentication, authorization, RBAC policies, projects, repositories,
Kubernetes permissions and important ArgoCD security practices.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is RBAC?</h2>

<p>
RBAC stands for <strong>Role-Based Access Control</strong>.
It controls what actions a user or service account is allowed to perform
based on assigned roles and permissions.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
ArgoCD RBAC controls which users or groups can perform actions such as
viewing, syncing, creating or deleting applications and projects.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Authentication vs Authorization</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Authentication</th>
<th>Authorization</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Who are you?</td>
<td>What are you allowed to do?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Login / identity verification.</td>
<td>Permissions and access control.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: SSO login.</td>
<td>Example: Can this user sync an application?</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¤ User
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Authentication</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Identity Verified
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Authorization / RBAC</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Allowed Actions

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. ArgoCD RBAC Components</h2>

<ul>
<li><strong>User / Group</strong> â†’ Identity requesting access.</li>
<li><strong>Role</strong> â†’ Collection of permissions.</li>
<li><strong>Policy</strong> â†’ Defines allowed or denied actions.</li>
<li><strong>Project</strong> â†’ Restricts applications, repositories and destinations.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Common ArgoCD RBAC Actions</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Action</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>get</code></td>
<td>View resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>create</code></td>
<td>Create resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>update</code></td>
<td>Modify resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>delete</code></td>
<td>Delete resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>sync</code></td>
<td>Synchronize an application.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>override</code></td>
<td>Override application source during supported operations.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. ArgoCD RBAC Policy Example</h2>

<pre>
p, role:developer, applications, get, dev-project/*, allow
p, role:developer, applications, sync, dev-project/*, allow

g, alice, role:developer
</pre>

<p>
The example gives the developer role permission to view and sync
applications under the specified project scope.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Tip:</strong><br>
Do not memorize only the syntax. Explain the principle:
developers should receive only the permissions required for their job.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Least Privilege</h2>

<p>
The principle of least privilege means giving users and systems only
the permissions they actually need.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
View + Sync Dev Applications
<br>â†“<br>
âŒ No Production Delete Permission

</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
In production, I would avoid giving broad admin permissions to every
developer. I would use project-level RBAC and grant only the required
actions.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is an ArgoCD Project?</h2>

<p>
An ArgoCD Project is a logical boundary used to organize applications
and restrict what those applications can access.
</p>

<h3>A Project Can Control:</h3>

<ul>
<li>Allowed source repositories</li>
<li>Allowed destination clusters</li>
<li>Allowed destination namespaces</li>
<li>Allowed resource kinds</li>
<li>Project roles</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
Projects provide an additional security and organizational boundary
for ArgoCD applications.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Why Use Projects?</h2>

<div class="flow">

ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>

Project: Development
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Dev Applications
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Dev Repository
<br>
â””â”€â”€ Dev Namespace

<br><br>

Project: Production
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Prod Applications
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Prod Repository
<br>
â””â”€â”€ Prod Namespace

</div>

<p>
This separation helps prevent accidental deployment of applications
into unauthorized environments.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Project Security Example</h2>

<pre>
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject

metadata:
  name: production
  namespace: argocd

spec:
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/example/prod-gitops.git

  destinations:
    - namespace: production
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Meaning:</strong><br>
This project can be configured so applications use approved Git
repositories and approved Kubernetes destinations.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Kubernetes RBAC vs ArgoCD RBAC</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>ArgoCD RBAC</th>
<th>Kubernetes RBAC</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controls access to ArgoCD resources and actions.</td>
<td>Controls access to Kubernetes API resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: Can user sync an ArgoCD Application?</td>
<td>Example: Can service account create Deployments?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Configured through ArgoCD RBAC policies.</td>
<td>Uses Role, ClusterRole and bindings.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>
They are separate authorization layers. A user being allowed to use
ArgoCD does not automatically mean they have unrestricted Kubernetes
permissions.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is SSO?</h2>

<p>
SSO stands for <strong>Single Sign-On</strong>. It allows users to
authenticate through an external identity provider rather than
maintaining separate credentials for every application.
</p>

<p>
ArgoCD can integrate with identity providers using supported
authentication mechanisms such as OIDC.
</p>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¤ User
<br>â†“<br>
Identity Provider
<br>â†“<br>
Authentication
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
RBAC
<br>â†“<br>
Allowed Application Actions

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Why Use SSO Instead of Local Users?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Centralized identity management.</li>
<li>Centralized access control.</li>
<li>Easier onboarding and offboarding.</li>
<li>Integration with organizational identity systems.</li>
<li>Reduced dependency on separate local credentials.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. How Should Production ArgoCD Be Secured?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use SSO / centralized identity where appropriate.</li>

<li>Apply least-privilege RBAC.</li>

<li>Separate environments using Projects.</li>

<li>Restrict allowed Git repositories.</li>

<li>Restrict allowed destination clusters and namespaces.</li>

<li>Avoid giving admin permissions unnecessarily.</li>

<li>Protect repository credentials and secrets.</li>

<li>Use TLS for access to ArgoCD.</li>

<li>Monitor and audit administrative actions.</li>

<li>Control who can perform production sync or deletion.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Real-Time Security Scenario</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
A developer needs to deploy applications to the development namespace,
but must not be able to modify production applications.
</p>

<h3>Solution</h3>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
SSO Group
<br>â†“<br>
Developer RBAC Role
<br>â†“<br>
Development Project
<br>â†“<br>
Dev Namespace
<br>â†“<br>
âœ… Allowed

<br><br>

Production
<br>â†“<br>
âŒ Access Denied

</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would use SSO groups with ArgoCD RBAC and AppProjects. The developer
role would have access only to development applications and would not
have production sync or delete permissions.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What If Someone Gets ArgoCD Admin Access?</h2>

<p>
An ArgoCD administrator can potentially control a large portion of the
applications managed by ArgoCD, depending on the configured permissions
and cluster access.
</p>

<div class="warning">
<strong>Security Risk:</strong><br>
ArgoCD is a powerful control plane. Administrative credentials must be
protected carefully and broad permissions should be minimized.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 16. Repository Access Security</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD may need credentials to access private Git repositories.
These credentials should be handled securely.
</p>

<ul>
<li>Use secure credential mechanisms.</li>
<li>Do not commit passwords or tokens to Git.</li>
<li>Limit repository access.</li>
<li>Rotate credentials when necessary.</li>
<li>Use dedicated credentials where possible.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 17. Common Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>What is RBAC?</li>

<li>Authentication vs authorization?</li>

<li>What is ArgoCD RBAC?</li>

<li>What is an AppProject?</li>

<li>Why are Projects important?</li>

<li>What is least privilege?</li>

<li>ArgoCD RBAC vs Kubernetes RBAC?</li>

<li>What is SSO?</li>

<li>How would you secure production ArgoCD?</li>

<li>How would you prevent developers from deploying to production?</li>

<li>How do you protect private Git repository credentials?</li>

<li>Why should ArgoCD admin access be restricted?</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  One-Minute Revision</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Authentication</strong> â†’ Who are you?<br><br>

<strong>Authorization</strong> â†’ What can you do?<br><br>

<strong>RBAC</strong> â†’ Role-based permissions.<br><br>

<strong>Project</strong> â†’ Application security boundary.<br><br>

<strong>Least Privilege</strong> â†’ Give only required permissions.<br><br>

<strong>SSO</strong> â†’ Centralized identity authentication.<br><br>

<strong>ArgoCD RBAC</strong> â†’ Controls ArgoCD actions.<br><br>

<strong>Kubernetes RBAC</strong> â†’ Controls Kubernetes API access.

</div>

</div>

<div style="font-size:50px">ðŸš€</div>
<h1>ArgoCD Real-Time Scenarios</h1>
<p>
Production-style ArgoCD interview scenarios with practical troubleshooting
approaches and interview-ready answers.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Git Change Is Not Reflected in Kubernetes</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
A developer changed the Deployment image tag in Git, but the Kubernetes
cluster is still running the old image.
</div>

<h3>What I Would Check</h3>

<ol>
<li>Verify the correct repository.</li>
<li>Verify the branch or revision.</li>
<li>Verify the application path.</li>
<li>Check whether ArgoCD detected the Git change.</li>
<li>Check whether automated sync is enabled.</li>
<li>Check Application events and sync status.</li>
</ol>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app
argocd app diff my-app
argocd app sync my-app
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would first verify that ArgoCD is tracking the correct repository,
revision and path. Then I would check whether the application is
OutOfSync and whether automated synchronization is enabled. If the
change is detected but not applied, I would inspect the sync error.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Application Shows OutOfSync</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
The application suddenly changes from Synced to OutOfSync even though
nobody changed Git.
</div>

<h3>Likely Cause</h3>

<p>
Someone may have manually modified a Kubernetes resource using
<code>kubectl</code>, causing configuration drift.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Git
<br>â†“<br>
Desired State
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†•<br>
Live Kubernetes State
<br>â†“<br>
âŒ Difference Detected
<br>â†“<br>
OutOfSync
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would run an ArgoCD diff and identify the changed resource. If the
change was made manually, I would either revert it or update Git if the
change is actually required.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Self-Healing Reverts a Manual Change</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
An engineer manually changes replicas from 3 to 1 using kubectl.
Within a short time, ArgoCD changes them back to 3.
</div>

<div class="flow">
Git
<br>
replicas: 3
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>
replicas: 1
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD detects drift
<br>â†“<br>
Self-Heal
<br>â†“<br>
replicas: 3
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
This is expected when automated sync with self-healing is enabled.
ArgoCD continuously reconciles the live state toward the desired state
stored in Git.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Sync Failed Because of an Invalid Manifest</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
A developer pushes a malformed Kubernetes YAML file. ArgoCD detects
the change but synchronization fails.
</div>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app
</pre>

<p>
Read the error and identify the resource that failed. Validate the YAML
and, depending on the source type, test Helm or Kustomize generation.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would not repeatedly retry the sync. I would identify the exact
manifest error, fix the configuration in Git, commit the correction
and allow ArgoCD to reconcile again.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Sync Succeeds but Pods Are Not Running</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
ArgoCD reports Synced, but the application is Degraded and Pods are
failing.
</div>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n production
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n production
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; -n production
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Application startup failure.</li>
<li>Missing environment variables.</li>
<li>Missing Secret or ConfigMap.</li>
<li>Image problem.</li>
<li>Readiness or liveness probe failure.</li>
<li>Insufficient resources.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Key Point:</strong><br>
Synced does not necessarily mean Healthy. Sync represents desired-state
application, while health reflects the runtime state.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Production Deployment Must Be Prevented</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
Developers should be able to deploy to Dev but must not be able to
deploy or delete Production applications.
</div>

<div class="flow">
Developer
<br>â†“<br>
SSO Group
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD RBAC
<br>â†“<br>
Development Project
<br>â†“<br>
Dev Namespace
<br><br>
Production â†’ âŒ Denied
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would use AppProjects and RBAC. The developer role would be restricted
to development applications and destinations, while production access
would be granted only to authorized teams.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 7. Private Git Repository Cannot Be Accessed</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
The ArgoCD Application cannot fetch manifests from a private GitHub
repository.
</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
argocd repo list
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect repository URL.</li>
<li>Invalid or expired credentials.</li>
<li>Insufficient repository permissions.</li>
<li>Network connectivity issue.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would verify the repository URL and credentials configured in ArgoCD,
confirm that the credential has access to the repository, and check
the repository connection status.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. ImagePullBackOff After Successful Sync</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
ArgoCD successfully applies the Deployment, but the Pod enters
ImagePullBackOff.
</div>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n production
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Wrong image name.</li>
<li>Wrong image tag.</li>
<li>Private registry authentication missing.</li>
<li>Image does not exist.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would inspect the Pod events first. Since ArgoCD already synchronized
the Deployment successfully, I would troubleshoot the Kubernetes image
pull process rather than the GitOps controller itself.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Rollback After a Bad Deployment</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
A new production version was deployed and the application became
unhealthy.
</div>

<h3>GitOps Approach</h3>

<div class="flow">
Bad Commit
<br>â†“<br>
Deployment
<br>â†“<br>
Application Failure
<br>â†“<br>
Revert Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Change
<br>â†“<br>
Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Previous Version Restored
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
With GitOps, I prefer reverting the problematic Git change so that Git
again represents the desired state. ArgoCD then reconciles the cluster
to that known-good configuration.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. ArgoCD Application Is Stuck During Sync</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
The sync operation appears to remain in progress for a long time.
</div>

<h3>Investigation</h3>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app

kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

kubectl get pods -A
</pre>

<p>
Identify the resource that is waiting. It could be a Deployment, Job,
Pod, Service, webhook or another dependency.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would identify the exact resource holding up the sync rather than
assuming the entire ArgoCD installation is unhealthy.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. ArgoCD Server Is Not Accessible</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
The ArgoCD UI suddenly becomes inaccessible.
</div>

<h3>Check ArgoCD Components</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n argocd
kubectl get svc -n argocd
kubectl get events -n argocd
</pre>

<h3>Important Components</h3>

<ul>
<li>argocd-server</li>
<li>argocd-repo-server</li>
<li>argocd-application-controller</li>
<li>argocd-redis</li>
<li>argocd-applicationset-controller</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I would first verify that the ArgoCD pods are running and then check
the Service, ingress or load balancer configuration used to expose
ArgoCD.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Application Controller Problem</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
Applications stop reconciling even though the ArgoCD UI is accessible.
</div>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n argocd
kubectl logs deployment/argocd-application-controller -n argocd
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
The Application Controller is responsible for continuously comparing
desired and live state and initiating reconciliation. I would inspect
its logs, pod status and resource availability.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. Repo Server Problem</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>
ArgoCD cannot generate manifests from Git.
</div>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n argocd
kubectl logs deployment/argocd-repo-server -n argocd
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
The Repo Server handles repository access and manifest generation.
Therefore, if applications fail during manifest generation, I would
check repository connectivity and Repo Server logs.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Emergency Production Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">
<strong>Production is down immediately after a deployment.</strong>
</div>

<h3>My Troubleshooting Sequence</h3>

<ol>
<li>Check ArgoCD Application health.</li>
<li>Check recent Git commit.</li>
<li>Check sync history.</li>
<li>Check Deployment and ReplicaSet.</li>
<li>Check Pod status.</li>
<li>Check application logs.</li>
<li>Check Kubernetes events.</li>
<li>Identify the root cause.</li>
<li>Rollback by reverting the Git change if required.</li>
<li>Verify application recovery.</li>
</ol>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
During a production incident, I focus first on restoring service safely.
I identify the failing layer, use the Git history to understand the
change, and revert to a known-good version when necessary. After
recovery, I investigate the root cause.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. ArgoCD Interview Golden Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
Application
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Sync Status</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Synced / OutOfSync
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Health Status</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Healthy / Degraded
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
Pods â†’ Services â†’ Ingress
<br>â†“<br>
Logs + Events
<br>â†“<br>
Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
Fix in Git
<br>â†“<br>
Reconciliation

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">
<h2>ðŸ§  One-Minute Revision</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>OutOfSync</strong> â†’ Desired and live state differ.<br><br>

<strong>SyncFailed</strong> â†’ ArgoCD could not apply a change.<br><br>

<strong>Degraded</strong> â†’ Resource/application health is bad.<br><br>

<strong>Git Error</strong> â†’ Check URL, credentials and connectivity.<br><br>

<strong>Manifest Error</strong> â†’ Check YAML, Helm or Kustomize.<br><br>

<strong>Pod Error</strong> â†’ Check describe, logs and events.<br><br>

<strong>Production Failure</strong> â†’ Identify change â†’ restore service â†’
revert Git if required â†’ verify recovery.

</div>

</div>

<header>
<div style="font-size:50px">ðŸ› ï¸</div>
<h1>ArgoCD Troubleshooting & Real-Time Scenarios</h1>
<p>
Practical troubleshooting for OutOfSync, SyncFailed, Degraded,
repository errors, Kubernetes failures and common production issues.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. How Do You Troubleshoot ArgoCD?</h2>

<p>
The first step is to identify whether the problem is related to the
Git repository, manifest generation, ArgoCD synchronization,
Kubernetes resources or application health.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
Repo Server
<br>â†“<br>
Manifest Generation
<br>â†“<br>
Application Controller
<br>â†“<br>
Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
Application Health
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I first check the Application status and events, then determine whether
the failure is in Git access, manifest generation, synchronization,
Kubernetes resources or application health. I troubleshoot from the
ArgoCD Application down to the underlying Kubernetes resources.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Application is OutOfSync</h2>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Git configuration changed.</li>
<li>Someone manually changed the Kubernetes resource.</li>
<li>Generated manifests differ from live resources.</li>
<li>Different Git revision is being tracked.</li>
<li>Expected resource is missing.</li>
</ul>

<h3>What I Check</h3>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app

argocd app diff my-app
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Approach:</strong><br>
I compare the desired state with the live state using the Application
details or CLI diff. Then I identify which resource differs before
performing a sync.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Application is SyncFailed</h2>

<p>
SyncFailed means ArgoCD attempted synchronization but one or more
operations failed.
</p>

<h3>Common Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Invalid Kubernetes manifest.</li>
<li>Insufficient Kubernetes permissions.</li>
<li>Resource already exists with conflicting ownership.</li>
<li>Invalid namespace.</li>
<li>Admission webhook rejection.</li>
<li>Immutable field modification.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Useful Commands</h3>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app

kubectl get events -n my-namespace

kubectl describe deployment my-app -n my-namespace
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Application is Degraded</h2>

<p>
A Degraded status generally means that the resources may match the
desired configuration but one or more resources are not healthy.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Git = Desired State
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Resource Created
<br>â†“<br>
Pod Fails
<br>â†“<br>
âŒ Application Degraded
</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n my-namespace

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n my-namespace

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; -n my-namespace
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Important:</strong><br>
If ArgoCD says the application is Degraded, do not immediately assume
ArgoCD itself is broken. The underlying Kubernetes workload may be
unhealthy.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Git Repository Connection Failed</h2>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect repository URL.</li>
<li>Invalid credentials.</li>
<li>Expired access token.</li>
<li>Private repository without valid credentials.</li>
<li>Network or certificate problem.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
argocd repo list

argocd repo get https://github.com/example/repo.git
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Approach:</strong><br>
I verify the repository URL, authentication configuration and whether
ArgoCD can successfully access the repository.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Manifest Generation Failed</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD may fail before synchronization if it cannot generate valid
Kubernetes manifests.
</p>

<h3>Common Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Invalid YAML.</li>
<li>Broken Helm template.</li>
<li>Invalid Kustomize configuration.</li>
<li>Missing Helm values.</li>
<li>Unsupported plugin or configuration.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
If manifest generation fails, I inspect the Application error message
and determine whether the source is plain YAML, Helm or Kustomize.
Then I validate the configuration independently before retrying.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 7. Namespace Not Found</h2>

<p>
A deployment may fail when the target namespace does not exist or the
application is configured with an incorrect destination.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get namespaces

kubectl get applications -n argocd

argocd app get my-app
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Fix:</strong><br>
Verify the destination namespace and configure namespace creation
where appropriate for the deployment model being used.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Pod is CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<p>
This is usually a Kubernetes workload problem rather than an ArgoCD
problem.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n my-namespace

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n my-namespace

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; -n my-namespace

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous -n my-namespace
</pre>

<h3>Common Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Application startup failure.</li>
<li>Incorrect environment variables.</li>
<li>Missing Secret or ConfigMap.</li>
<li>Incorrect command or arguments.</li>
<li>Health probe failure.</li>
<li>Dependency unavailable.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<p>
The Kubernetes node cannot successfully pull the required container
image.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n my-namespace
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect image name.</li>
<li>Incorrect image tag.</li>
<li>Private registry authentication issue.</li>
<li>Registry unavailable.</li>
<li>Image does not exist.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Important:</strong><br>
ArgoCD may have successfully synchronized the Deployment while the
application still remains unhealthy because Kubernetes cannot pull
the image.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. Sync is Hanging</h2>

<p>
A sync can appear stuck when a resource is waiting for readiness,
dependencies are unavailable or Kubernetes operations are blocked.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
argocd app get my-app

kubectl get pods -A

kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Approach:</strong><br>
I check the specific resource where the sync is waiting, inspect
Kubernetes events and verify whether the workload is becoming ready.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. ArgoCD Cannot Connect to Kubernetes</h2>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Cluster credentials problem.</li>
<li>Network connectivity issue.</li>
<li>Expired or invalid authentication.</li>
<li>API server unavailable.</li>
<li>Certificate problem.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
argocd cluster list
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I verify the cluster registration, connectivity to the Kubernetes API
server and the credentials used by ArgoCD for that cluster.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Useful ArgoCD CLI Commands</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Command</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd app list</code></td>
<td>List applications.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd app get APP</code></td>
<td>Show application details.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd app diff APP</code></td>
<td>Compare desired and live state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd app sync APP</code></td>
<td>Trigger synchronization.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd app history APP</code></td>
<td>View deployment history.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd repo list</code></td>
<td>List configured repositories.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><code>argocd cluster list</code></td>
<td>List registered clusters.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Useful Kubernetes Commands</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -A

kubectl get deployments -A

kubectl get services -A

kubectl get events -A

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; -n &lt;namespace&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; -n &lt;namespace&gt;

kubectl get nodes
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Golden Rule:</strong><br>
ArgoCD manages the desired state, but the actual workload still runs
inside Kubernetes. Always inspect Kubernetes when application health
is failing.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Scenario: Git Change but ArgoCD Does Not Update</h2>

<h3>Possible Reasons</h3>

<ol>

<li>Wrong branch configured.</li>

<li>Wrong repository path.</li>

<li>ArgoCD cannot access the repository.</li>

<li>Manifest generation failed.</li>

<li>Application is not configured for automated sync.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
I first check the Application source configuration, tracked revision
and path. Then I verify repository connectivity and manifest
generation. Finally I check whether the application requires manual
sync or has automated synchronization enabled.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Scenario: Manual kubectl Change Gets Reverted</h2>

<div class="flow">
Git
<br>
replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>
kubectl change
<br>
replicas = 1
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD detects drift
<br>â†“<br>
Self-Heal
<br>â†“<br>
replicas = 3
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Explanation:</strong><br>
This is expected behavior when the application is configured for
automated synchronization with self-healing. Git remains the desired
source of truth.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Scenario: Sync Succeeds but Application is Degraded</h2>

<div class="flow">
Git Configuration
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Sync
<br>â†“<br>
âœ… Sync Successful
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Pod
<br>â†“<br>
âŒ Application Failure
<br>â†“<br>
âš ï¸ Degraded
</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
A successful sync only means ArgoCD applied the desired resources.
The application can still be unhealthy. I would inspect Pods,
Deployments, events, logs and health probes.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Production Troubleshooting Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>1. Check Application Status</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Synced / OutOfSync?
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>2. Check Health</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
Healthy / Degraded?
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>3. Check Application Events</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>4. Check Git Repository</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>5. Check Manifest Generation</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>6. Check Kubernetes Resources</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

Pods â†’ Events â†’ Logs â†’ Services
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>7. Fix Root Cause</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>8. Sync / Reconcile</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

âœ… Verify Health

</div>

</div>

<li>What causes an application to become Degraded?</li>

</div>

<header>

<div style="font-size:50px">ðŸ”„</div>

<h1>GitOps & ArgoCD Basics</h1>

<p>
Core GitOps concepts and ArgoCD fundamentals explained in
interview-ready language with practical Kubernetes examples.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is GitOps?</h2>

<p>
GitOps is a way of managing application and infrastructure deployments
where <strong>Git acts as the source of truth</strong>.
The desired state of the system is stored in Git, and an automated
controller continuously works to make the actual environment match
that desired state.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
GitOps is a declarative deployment approach where the desired state of
applications and infrastructure is maintained in Git. A GitOps
controller such as ArgoCD continuously compares the Git state with the
Kubernetes cluster and reconciles differences.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why Do We Use GitOps?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Git provides version history.</li>
<li>Every configuration change can be reviewed.</li>
<li>Changes can go through Pull Requests.</li>
<li>Rollback becomes easier.</li>
<li>Deployment becomes consistent and repeatable.</li>
<li>Cluster configuration becomes auditable.</li>
<li>Manual <code>kubectl</code> changes can be reduced.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Key Idea:</strong><br>
Instead of manually telling Kubernetes what to do every time,
we declare what we want in Git and let automation maintain that state.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is ArgoCD?</h2>

<p>
ArgoCD is a <strong>Kubernetes-native continuous delivery and GitOps
tool</strong>. It monitors Git repositories containing Kubernetes
manifests or Helm/Kustomize configurations and synchronizes them with
the target Kubernetes cluster.
</p>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>
ArgoCD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes.
It continuously monitors the desired state stored in Git and
synchronizes that state with the Kubernetes cluster.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Traditional Deployment vs GitOps</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Traditional Approach</th>
<th>GitOps Approach</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Developer or operator may manually run deployment commands.</td>
<td>Git contains the desired state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Cluster state may not be fully tracked.</td>
<td>Configuration is version-controlled.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Rollback can require manual commands.</td>
<td>Previous Git versions can be restored.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Configuration changes may be difficult to audit.</td>
<td>Git history provides an audit trail.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Manual drift correction.</td>
<td>Controller can continuously reconcile drift.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Declarative vs Imperative</h2>

<h3>Imperative</h3>

<p>
You tell the system <strong>how</strong> to perform an action.
</p>

<div class="flow">
kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx
</div>

<h3>Declarative</h3>

<p>
You define <strong>what the final state should be</strong>.
Kubernetes determines how to reach that state.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>â†“<br>
deployment.yaml
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes

</div>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>
GitOps strongly favors a declarative model because the desired state is
explicitly stored and versioned.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Push-Based vs Pull-Based Deployment</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Push-Based</th>
<th>Pull-Based</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CI/CD system pushes changes into the cluster.</td>
<td>Agent/controller pulls desired state from Git.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Pipeline usually needs cluster credentials.</td>
<td>Cluster-side controller can access Git.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: CI pipeline running kubectl apply.</td>
<td>Example: ArgoCD.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Important:</strong><br>
ArgoCD follows the <strong>pull-based</strong> GitOps model.
ArgoCD continuously monitors the Git repository and reconciles the
desired state with Kubernetes.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. How Does ArgoCD Work?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Reads Desired State
<br>â†“<br>
Compares Git State with Cluster State
<br>â†“<br>
Detects Difference
<br>â†“<br>
Application Becomes OutOfSync
<br>â†“<br>
Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes API
<br>â†“<br>
Cluster Matches Git
<br>â†“<br>
Synced

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Desired State vs Actual State</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Term</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Desired State</strong></td>
<td>The configuration defined in Git.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Actual State</strong></td>
<td>The resources currently running in Kubernetes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Drift</strong></td>
<td>A difference between desired and actual state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td><strong>Reconciliation</strong></td>
<td>The process of bringing actual state toward desired state.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is Drift?</h2>

<p>
Drift occurs when the Kubernetes cluster no longer matches the
configuration stored in Git.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git says replicas = 3
<br>â†“<br>
Someone manually changes replicas to 1
<br>â†“<br>
Git State â‰  Cluster State
<br>â†“<br>
Drift Detected

</div>

<div class="answer">
If automated self-healing is enabled, ArgoCD can restore the cluster
toward the Git-defined state.
</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What is Sync?</h2>

<p>
Sync means applying the desired configuration from Git to the
Kubernetes cluster so that the cluster moves toward the desired state.
</p>

<p>
ArgoCD can perform synchronization manually or automatically depending
on the application's configuration.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is Reconciliation?</h2>

<p>
Reconciliation is the continuous process of comparing the desired
state with the actual state and identifying differences.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Wording:</strong><br>

ArgoCD continuously observes the application state and compares it with
the desired state in Git. If there is a difference, ArgoCD can take
action to reconcile the cluster according to the configured sync policy.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Sync vs Reconciliation</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Sync</th>
<th>Reconciliation</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Action that applies desired configuration.</td>
<td>Continuous comparison process.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can be manually or automatically triggered.</td>
<td>Continuously evaluates state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Moves cluster toward desired state.</td>
<td>Detects whether the cluster has drifted.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. What is Self-Healing?</h2>

<p>
Self-healing is the ability of ArgoCD to automatically correct certain
out-of-band changes so that the cluster returns toward the desired
state defined in Git.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Git
<br>
replicas: 3
<br>â†“<br>
Manual Change
<br>
replicas: 1
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Drift
<br>â†“<br>
Self-Healing
<br>â†“<br>
replicas: 3

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. What is Pruning?</h2>

<p>
Pruning removes Kubernetes resources that were previously managed by
ArgoCD but are no longer defined in the desired Git configuration,
when pruning is enabled.
</p>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Interview Caution:</strong><br>

Pruning can delete resources. It should be enabled carefully,
especially in production environments.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Why is Git the Source of Truth?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Git provides version control.</li>

<li>Changes are traceable.</li>

<li>Pull Requests can provide review and approval.</li>

<li>Previous versions are available.</li>

<li>Deployment configuration is centralized.</li>

<li>Teams can reproduce the desired environment.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. GitOps Deployment Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git Commit
<br>â†“<br>
Pull Request
<br>â†“<br>
Review & Merge
<br>â†“<br>
Git Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD Detects Change
<br>â†“<br>
Sync
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
Application Updated

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. ArgoCD + CI/CD</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub
<br>â†“<br>
GitHub Actions
<br>â†“<br>
Build + Test + Security Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Image
<br>â†“<br>
Container Registry
<br>â†“<br>
Update GitOps Repository
<br>â†“<br>
ArgoCD
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes / EKS

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

GitHub Actions handles CI activities such as build, test, security
scanning and image publishing. ArgoCD handles the CD/GitOps side by
monitoring the GitOps repository and synchronizing the desired state
into Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ 18. Most Important Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>What is GitOps?</li>

<li>What is ArgoCD?</li>

<li>Why do we use ArgoCD?</li>

<li>Why is Git called the source of truth?</li>

<li>Is ArgoCD push-based or pull-based?</li>

<li>What is desired state?</li>

<li>What is actual state?</li>

<li>What is drift?</li>

<li>What is synchronization?</li>

<li>What is reconciliation?</li>

<li>What is self-healing?</li>

<li>What is pruning?</li>

<li>How is GitOps different from traditional CI/CD?</li>

<li>What is the difference between declarative and imperative deployment?</li>

<li>How does ArgoCD work with GitHub Actions?</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  One-Minute Revision</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>GitOps</strong> â†’ Git is the source of truth.<br><br>

<strong>ArgoCD</strong> â†’ Kubernetes GitOps continuous delivery tool.<br><br>

<strong>Desired State</strong> â†’ Configuration stored in Git.<br><br>

<strong>Actual State</strong> â†’ Current Kubernetes state.<br><br>

<strong>Drift</strong> â†’ Desired state and actual state differ.<br><br>

<strong>Sync</strong> â†’ Apply desired state to the cluster.<br><br>

<strong>Reconciliation</strong> â†’ Continuously compare states.<br><br>

<strong>Self-Healing</strong> â†’ Automatically restore supported drift.<br><br>

</div>

<h2>ðŸ§  Key Concepts</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Monitoring</strong> â†’ Knowing the health and performance of systems.

<br><br>

<strong>Metrics</strong> â†’ Numeric measurements collected over time.

<br><br>

<strong>Prometheus</strong> â†’ Collects and stores time-series metrics.

<br><br>

<strong>PromQL</strong> â†’ Query language used to retrieve and analyze
Prometheus metrics.

<br><br>

<strong>Grafana</strong> â†’ Visualizes metrics through dashboards.

<br><br>

<strong>Alertmanager</strong> â†’ Handles and routes alerts generated

<!-- PROMETHEUS -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Prometheus â€” Must Know</h2>

<ul>
<li>Prometheus is an open-source monitoring and alerting system.</li>
<li>It primarily collects time-series metrics.</li>
<li>Prometheus usually uses a pull-based scraping model.</li>
<li>Targets expose metrics through an HTTP endpoint.</li>
<li>Prometheus stores metrics in its time-series database.</li>
<li>PromQL is used to query metrics.</li>
<li>Alert rules can be evaluated by Prometheus.</li>
<li>Alertmanager handles alert routing and notifications.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Important Components</h3>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Prometheus Server</td>
<td>Scrapes and stores metrics.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Service Discovery</td>
<td>Finds monitoring targets.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Exporters</td>
<td>Expose metrics for systems that do not natively expose Prometheus metrics.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>PromQL</td>
<td>Queries and analyzes metrics.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Alert Rules</td>
<td>Define conditions for alerts.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Alertmanager</td>
<td>Routes and manages alerts.</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

<!-- PROMETHEUS COMMANDS -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Important Prometheus Commands</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n monitoring

kubectl get svc -n monitoring

kubectl get prometheus -A

kubectl logs &lt;prometheus-pod&gt; -n monitoring

kubectl describe pod &lt;prometheus-pod&gt; -n monitoring
</pre>

<h3>Useful Checks</h3>

<pre>
curl http://localhost:9090/-/healthy

curl http://target:9100/metrics
</pre>
</div>

<!-- PROMQL -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. PromQL Quick Revision</h2>

<h3>Basic Metric Query</h3>

<pre>
up
</pre>

<p>
Returns the status of monitored targets.
</p>

<h3>CPU Example</h3>

<pre>
rate(node_cpu_seconds_total[5m])
</pre>

<h3>Memory Example</h3>

<pre>
node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes
</pre>

<h3>HTTP Error Example</h3>

<pre>
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Point:</strong>
PromQL allows filtering, aggregation and calculation over time-series
metrics.
</div>
</div>

<!-- GRAFANA -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Grafana â€” Must Know</h2>

<ul>
<li>Grafana is a visualization and observability platform.</li>
<li>It connects to data sources such as Prometheus.</li>
<li>Queries retrieve data from the configured data source.</li>
<li>Panels visualize the query results.</li>
<li>Multiple panels can be organized into dashboards.</li>
<li>Grafana can also participate in alerting.</li>
</ul>

<div class="flow">
Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>
Data Source
<br>â†“<br>
PromQL Query
<br>â†“<br>
Panel
<br>â†“<br>
Dashboard
</div>
</div>

<!-- GRAFANA INTERVIEW -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Common Grafana Questions</h2>

<h3>What is a Dashboard?</h3>
<p>
A dashboard is a collection of visualization panels that present
monitoring information in one place.
</p>

<h3>What is a Data Source?</h3>
<p>
A data source is the backend from which Grafana retrieves data.
Prometheus is a common monitoring data source.
</p>

<h3>Why use Grafana with Prometheus?</h3>

<div class="answer">
Prometheus is excellent at collecting and querying metrics, while
Grafana provides a powerful visual interface for analyzing those
metrics through dashboards.
</div>
</div>

<!-- ALERTING -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Alerting Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">
Metric
<br>â†“<br>
PromQL
<br>â†“<br>
Alert Rule
<br>â†“<br>
Condition Met
<br>â†“<br>
Alert
<br>â†“<br>
Alertmanager
<br>â†“<br>
Email / Slack / Other Notification
</div>

<h3>Important Difference</h3>

<p>
<strong>Prometheus:</strong> evaluates alert rules.
</p>

<p>
<strong>Alertmanager:</strong> handles grouping, routing,
silencing and notification management.
</p>
</div>

<!-- GOLDEN SIGNALS -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Four Golden Signals</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Signal</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Latency</td>
<td>How long requests take.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Traffic</td>
<td>How much demand the system receives.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Errors</td>
<td>How many requests are failing.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Saturation</td>
<td>How close the system is to its resource limits.</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>

<!-- METRICS LOGS TRACES -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Metrics vs Logs vs Traces</h2>

<table>
<tr>
<th>Observability Signal</th>
<th>Main Purpose</th>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Metrics</td>
<td>Numerical measurements and trends.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Logs</td>
<td>Detailed events and messages.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Traces</td>
<td>Track a request across distributed services.</td>
</tr>
</table>

<div class="flow">
Metrics â†’ What is wrong?
<br><br>
Logs â†’ What happened?
<br><br>
Traces â†’ Where did the request go / slow / fail?
</div>
</div>

<!-- SCENARIOS -->

<div class="card">
<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Top Troubleshooting Scenarios</h2>

<h3>CPU is 95%</h3>
<p>
Check the affected instance, process usage, traffic, deployments,
memory and scaling requirements.
</p>

<h3>Pod keeps restarting</h3>
<p>
Check <code>kubectl describe pod</code>, logs, events, probes,
configuration and OOMKilled status.
</p>

<h3>Prometheus target is DOWN</h3>
<p>
Check target connectivity, exporter, metrics endpoint, port,
service discovery and Prometheus configuration.
</p>

<h3>Grafana shows No Data</h3>
<p>
Check data source, Prometheus availability, PromQL query, time range,
dashboard variables and target status.
</p>

<h3>5xx errors increase</h3>
<p>
Check application logs, recent deployments, dependencies,
infrastructure metrics and database health.
</p>

<h3>Disk reaches 90%</h3>

<pre>
df -h
du -sh /var/log/*
df -i
</pre>

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ 14. Interview-Ready Answer: Monitoring in DevOps</h2>

<div class="answer">

"In a DevOps environment, monitoring helps us understand the health
and performance of applications and infrastructure. We can use
Prometheus to collect and query metrics and Grafana to visualize
those metrics through dashboards. Alerting can notify engineers when
defined thresholds or conditions are reached. During incidents, I
correlate metrics with logs and other available observability data,
identify the root cause, mitigate the impact and then implement a
permanent fix."

<h1>Grafana Basics</h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide to Grafana, dashboards, data sources,
panels, Prometheus integration, variables and monitoring scenarios.

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Grafana?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

Grafana is an open-source observability and visualization platform
used to query, visualize and monitor data from different data sources
through dashboards.

</div>

<p>
Grafana itself is commonly used as the visualization layer while
Prometheus provides the metrics.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why do we use Grafana?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Create monitoring dashboards.</li>
<li>Visualize metrics and trends.</li>
<li>Connect to multiple data sources.</li>
<li>Create panels for CPU, memory and application metrics.</li>
<li>Use variables for dynamic dashboards.</li>
<li>Support alerting workflows depending on configuration.</li>
<li>Help DevOps teams troubleshoot production systems.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Grafana + Prometheus Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Application / Infrastructure
<br>â†“<br>

Exporters / Metrics Endpoints
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>Prometheus</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

Metrics + TSDB
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>Grafana</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL
<br>â†“<br>

Panels
<br>â†“<br>

Dashboard

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Key Point:</strong><br>

Grafana does not replace Prometheus. Grafana can use Prometheus as
a data source and visualize the metrics returned by PromQL queries.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is a Data Source?</h2>

<p>
A data source is a backend system from which Grafana retrieves data
for queries and visualizations.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Data Source</th>
<th>Example Use</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Prometheus</td>
<td>Metrics monitoring.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Loki</td>
<td>Log aggregation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Elasticsearch</td>
<td>Search and analytics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>InfluxDB</td>
<td>Time-series data.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. How do you connect Prometheus to Grafana?</h2>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

Create Dashboard

</div>

<p>
Grafana uses the Prometheus HTTP API to execute queries and retrieve
metrics.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Dashboard?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A Grafana dashboard is a collection of visualizations that presents
monitoring information in one place.

</div>

<p>
A production dashboard can contain CPU usage, memory usage,
request rate, error rate, latency and infrastructure health.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is a Time Series Panel?</h2>

<p>
A Time Series panel displays metric values across time.

<br>â†’
<br>
Metric Values
<br>â†’

</div>

<p>
For example, CPU utilization can be plotted over the last hour.

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is PromQL in Grafana?</h2>

<p>
When Prometheus is configured as the data source, Grafana panels can
use PromQL queries to retrieve metrics.
</p>

<pre>
up
</pre>

<pre>
up{job="node-exporter"}
</pre>

<pre>
rate(http_requests_total[5m])
</pre>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What are Variables?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Grafana variables allow users to dynamically change dashboard
filters without creating separate dashboards for every environment,
service or instance.

</div>

<p>Examples:</p>

<ul>
<li>Environment â†’ dev / staging / production</li>
<li>Service â†’ frontend / backend / payment</li>
<li>Instance â†’ server-01 / server-02</li>
<li>Namespace â†’ dev / production</li>
</ul>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Why are Variables useful?</h2>

<p>
Instead of creating multiple dashboards, one dashboard can be reused
with different variable values.
</p>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is a Query?</h2>

<p>
A query retrieves data from the configured data source.
</p>

<p>
For Prometheus, Grafana sends a PromQL query to Prometheus.
</p>

<pre>
rate(http_requests_total[5m])
</pre>

<div class="answer">

The result of the query is then displayed using a Grafana panel.

</div>

Grafana provides alerting capabilities that can evaluate queries

</p>

<div class="flow">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: Production CPU Spike</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
The production CPU usage suddenly reaches 95%.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Step 1:</strong> Open the Grafana dashboard.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 2:</strong> Identify which node, Pod or service is consuming CPU.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 3:</strong> Use PromQL to inspect the metric.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 4:</strong> Check memory, traffic, errors and latency.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 5:</strong> Check recent deployments and application logs.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 6:</strong> Determine whether scaling or rollback is required.

</div>

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Troubleshooting "No Data"</h2>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<!-- 3 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Prometheus Server</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Prometheus Server is the central component responsible for
discovering targets, scraping metrics, storing time-series data,
evaluating recording/alerting rules and serving PromQL queries.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Target Discovery
<br>â†“<br>
Scrape
<br>â†“<br>
Parse Metrics
<br>â†“<br>
Store in TSDB
<br>â†“<br>
Query with PromQL

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is TSDB?</h2>

<p>
TSDB stands for <strong>Time Series Database</strong>.
Prometheus stores collected metric samples as time-series data.
</p>

<p>
A time series is identified by a metric name and its set of labels,
with values recorded over time.
</p>

<pre>
node_cpu_seconds_total{
    mode="idle",
    instance="server-01"
}
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

Prometheus's local storage is optimized for time-series metrics.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. How does Prometheus collect metrics?</h2>

<div class="flow">

1ï¸âƒ£ Discover Target
<br>â†“<br>

2ï¸âƒ£ Connect to Target
<br>â†“<br>

3ï¸âƒ£ Request Metrics
<br>â†“<br>

4ï¸âƒ£ Parse Response
<br>â†“<br>

5ï¸âƒ£ Attach Labels
<br>â†“<br>

6ï¸âƒ£ Store Samples
<br>â†“<br>

7ï¸âƒ£ Query / Alert

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Pull-Based Architecture</h2>

<p>
Prometheus normally pulls metrics from monitored endpoints instead of
waiting for applications to push every metric.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Prometheus
<br>â†“
<br>
HTTP GET
<br>â†“
<br>
<code>http://target:port/metrics</code>
<br>â†“
<br>
Metric Response
<br>â†“
<br>
Prometheus

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is Service Discovery?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Service discovery allows Prometheus to dynamically discover targets
that should be monitored.

</div>

<p>
This is particularly important in cloud-native environments because
instances, containers and Pods can be created and removed dynamically.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes API
<br>â†“<br>

Target Discovery
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

Scrape Targets

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Static vs Dynamic Target Discovery</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Static Configuration</th>
<th>Service Discovery</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Targets are manually specified.</td>
<td>Targets are discovered automatically.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Simple environments.</td>
<td>Dynamic environments.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less flexible.</td>
<td>Better for Kubernetes and cloud environments.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Exporters</h2>

<p>
Exporters translate or expose metrics from systems into a format
Prometheus can scrape.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Exporter</th>
<th>Monitoring</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Node Exporter</td>
<td>Linux system metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Blackbox Exporter</td>
<td>HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, TCP and ICMP probing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MySQL Exporter</td>
<td>MySQL metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Redis Exporter</td>
<td>Redis metrics.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Node Exporter Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Linux Server
<br>â†“<br>

Node Exporter
<br>â†“<br>

<code>/metrics</code>
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

Grafana

</div>

<p>
Node Exporter exposes operating-system and hardware-related metrics.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Prometheus Configuration</h2>

<p>
Prometheus commonly uses <code>prometheus.yml</code> to define global
settings and scrape configurations.
</p>

<pre>
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:

  - job_name: "node-exporter"

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "localhost:9100"
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is a Job?</h2>

<p>
A Prometheus scrape configuration uses a <code>job_name</code> to
logically group targets that perform the same monitoring role.
</p>

<pre>
scrape_configs:

  - job_name: "web-servers"

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "server1:9100"
          - "server2:9100"
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Labels in Architecture</h2>

<p>
Labels identify and differentiate time series.
</p>

<pre>
http_requests_total{
    job="frontend",
    instance="10.0.1.10:8080",
    status="200"
}
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Why labels matter:</strong><br>

They allow engineers to filter, group and aggregate metrics using
PromQL.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. PromQL</h2>

<p>
PromQL is the query language used to retrieve and analyze metrics
stored by Prometheus.
</p>

<pre>
up

up{job="node-exporter"}

rate(http_requests_total[5m])

sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Alerting Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

Alerting Rule
<br>â†“<br>

Condition Met
<br>â†“<br>

Alert
<br>â†“<br>

Alertmanager
<br>â†“<br>

Grouping / Routing / Silencing
<br>â†“<br>

Email / Slack / PagerDuty / Other Receiver

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Prometheus vs Alertmanager</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Prometheus</th>
<th>Alertmanager</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Evaluates alerting rules.</td>
<td>Receives alerts.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Determines when an alert condition is true.</td>
<td>Groups and routes alerts.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Generates alert events.</td>
<td>Handles notifications, silences and inhibition.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. What is Alertmanager?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Alertmanager handles alerts sent by Prometheus. It can group related
alerts, route them to receivers, silence alerts and apply inhibition
rules to reduce unnecessary notifications.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. What is Pushgateway?</h2>

<p>
Pushgateway is useful when certain short-lived or batch jobs cannot
be reliably scraped directly.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Short-Lived Job
<br>â†“<br>

Pushgateway
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus Scrapes Pushgateway
<br>â†“<br>

Metrics Stored

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

Pushgateway should not be treated as a general replacement for
Prometheus's normal pull model.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Grafana Integration</h2>

<div class="flow">

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana Data Source
<br>â†“<br>

Dashboard
<br>â†“<br>

Panel
<br>â†“<br>

Visualization

</div>

<p>
Grafana queries Prometheus and visualizes the returned metrics.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Kubernetes Monitoring Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes Cluster
<br>â†“<br>

Nodes + Pods + Services
<br>â†“<br>

Metrics Endpoints / Exporters
<br>â†“<br>

Kubernetes Service Discovery
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

TSDB
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Alertmanager

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. What if Prometheus cannot scrape a target?</h2>

<ol>

<li>Check target status in Prometheus.</li>

<li>Check whether the target endpoint is reachable.</li>

<li>Verify the metrics port.</li>

<li>Verify the <code>/metrics</code> endpoint.</li>

<li>Check firewall and network rules.</li>

<li>Check exporter status.</li>

<li>Check Prometheus configuration.</li>

<li>Check service discovery labels.</li>

</ol>

<pre>
up{job="node-exporter"}
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. High CPU Monitoring Scenario</h2>

<div class="flow">

CPU Spike
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus Metric
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL Query
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana Dashboard
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

Alertmanager
<br>â†“<br>

DevOps Notification
<br>â†“<br>

Troubleshooting

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Production Monitoring Example</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br><br>

A production Kubernetes application is experiencing increased
latency.

<br><br>

<strong>Approach:</strong>

<ol>
<li>Check Grafana latency dashboard.</li>
<li>Use PromQL to identify affected Pods.</li>
<li>Check request rate and error rate.</li>
<li>Check CPU and memory usage.</li>
<li>Check recent deployments.</li>
<li>Check application logs.</li>
<li>Check Kubernetes events.</li>
<li>Identify and resolve the root cause.</li>
</ol>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 24. Prometheus Data Flow â€” Interview Answer</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>
"Prometheus discovers monitoring targets through static configuration
or service discovery. It periodically scrapes metrics from those
targets, parses the metric data and stores the samples in its
time-series database. Engineers query the data using PromQL.
Alerting rules can generate alerts, which are handled by Alertmanager.
Grafana can use Prometheus as a data source to visualize the metrics."
</strong>

</div>

</div>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ“Š</div>

<h1>Prometheus Basics</h1>

<p>
Interview-focused guide to Prometheus, metrics, targets, scraping,
labels, exporters, PromQL and monitoring fundamentals.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- 1 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Prometheus?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

Prometheus is an open-source monitoring and alerting system designed
primarily for collecting and storing time-series metrics.

It uses a pull-based model where Prometheus periodically scrapes
metrics from configured targets.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Application / Server
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>Metrics Endpoint</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

<strong>Prometheus</strong>
<br>â†“<br>

Time-Series Database
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL
<br>â†“<br>

Dashboard / Alert

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why is Prometheus used?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Infrastructure monitoring.</li>
<li>Application monitoring.</li>
<li>Kubernetes monitoring.</li>
<li>CPU and memory monitoring.</li>
<li>Request and error monitoring.</li>
<li>Alerting based on metrics.</li>
<li>Performance troubleshooting.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Example:</strong><br>

If a Kubernetes application's CPU usage continuously increases,
Prometheus can collect the CPU metrics and an alert rule can notify
the DevOps team.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is a Metric?</h2>

<p>
A metric is a numerical measurement representing the state or behavior
of a system at a particular point in time.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Metric Example</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CPU usage</td>
<td>Processor utilization.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Memory usage</td>
<td>Memory consumed by a process or system.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTP requests</td>
<td>Number of requests received.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTP errors</td>
<td>Number of failed requests.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Network traffic</td>
<td>Amount of network data transferred.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. What is Time-Series Data?</h2>

<p>
Prometheus stores metrics as time-series data.
A time series consists of a metric name, labels and timestamped values.
</p>

<pre>
http_requests_total{
    method="GET",
    status="200"
}
</pre>

<div class="answer">

The same metric can contain different time series based on its labels.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. What is Scraping?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Scraping</strong> means Prometheus periodically sends an HTTP
request to a target's metrics endpoint and collects the exposed metrics.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Prometheus
<br>â†“
<br>
HTTP GET
<br>â†“
<br>
Target: <code>/metrics</code>
<br>â†“
<br>
Metrics Returned
<br>â†“
<br>
Prometheus Stores Metrics

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Pull Model vs Push Model</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Pull Model</th>
<th>Push Model</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Monitoring system pulls metrics.</td>
<td>Applications push metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Prometheus primarily uses pull.</td>
<td>Pushgateway can be used for certain short-lived jobs.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Prometheus controls scraping.</td>
<td>Application controls sending.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Tip:</strong><br>

Prometheus primarily follows a <strong>pull-based architecture</strong>.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is a Target?</h2>

<p>
A target is an endpoint that Prometheus monitors and scrapes for metrics.
</p>

<p>Examples:</p>

<ul>
<li>Linux server.</li>
<li>Application server.</li>
<li>Kubernetes node.</li>
<li>Database exporter.</li>
<li>Web server exporter.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is an Exporter?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An exporter is a component that exposes metrics from a system or
application in a format that Prometheus can scrape.

</div>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Exporter</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Node Exporter</td>
<td>Linux/Unix system metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Blackbox Exporter</td>
<td>Probe endpoints and network services.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MySQL Exporter</td>
<td>MySQL database metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Redis Exporter</td>
<td>Redis metrics.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Linux Server
<br>â†“<br>
Node Exporter
<br>â†“<br>
<code>/metrics</code>
<br>â†“<br>
Prometheus

</div>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is Node Exporter?</h2>

<p>
Node Exporter exposes hardware and operating-system metrics from
Unix-like systems so Prometheus can collect them.
</p>

<p>Examples include:</p>

<ul>
<li>CPU statistics.</li>
<li>Memory statistics.</li>
<li>Disk usage.</li>
<li>Filesystem statistics.</li>
<li>Network statistics.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. What are Labels?</h2>

<p>
Labels are key-value pairs attached to metrics that provide additional
dimensions for filtering and grouping.
</p>

<pre>
http_requests_total{
    method="GET",
    status="200",
    service="frontend"
}
</pre>

<p>
Here <code>method</code>, <code>status</code> and <code>service</code>
are labels.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Prometheus Metric Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Counter</td>
<td>Monotonically increasing value, such as total requests.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Gauge</td>
<td>Value that can increase or decrease, such as memory usage.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Histogram</td>
<td>Measures observations and groups them into buckets.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Summary</td>
<td>Calculates quantiles over observations.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Counter vs Gauge</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Counter</th>
<th>Gauge</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Normally only increases.</td>
<td>Can increase or decrease.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: total HTTP requests.</td>
<td>Example: current memory usage.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can reset when application restarts.</td>
<td>Represents current state.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is PromQL?</h2>

<div class="answer">

PromQL, or Prometheus Query Language, is used to select, filter,
aggregate and analyze time-series data stored in Prometheus.

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre>
up
</pre>

<p>
Returns the health status of monitored targets.
</p>

<h3>Example with label filtering</h3>

<pre>
up{job="node-exporter"}
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Common PromQL Examples</h2>

<pre>
up

rate(http_requests_total[5m])

sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))

node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes

node_cpu_seconds_total
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Tip:</strong><br>

Know the concepts behind <code>rate()</code>,
label filtering, aggregation and time ranges.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. What is the <code>up</code> Metric?</h2>

<p>
The <code>up</code> metric indicates whether Prometheus was able to
successfully scrape a target.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Value</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Target scrape succeeded.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>0</td>
<td>Target scrape failed.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Prometheus Configuration</h2>

<p>
Prometheus configuration is commonly stored in
<code>prometheus.yml</code>.
</p>

<pre>
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:

  - job_name: "node-exporter"

    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "localhost:9100"
</pre>

<p>
The configuration defines how frequently Prometheus scrapes targets
and which targets should be monitored.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. What is scrape_interval?</h2>

<p>
<code>scrape_interval</code> specifies how frequently Prometheus
collects metrics from targets.
</p>

<pre>
scrape_interval: 15s
</pre>

<p>
This means Prometheus attempts to scrape configured targets every
15 seconds unless overridden by a more specific configuration.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. What is Service Discovery?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Service discovery allows Prometheus to automatically discover
monitoring targets instead of manually configuring every target.

</div>

<p>
This is especially useful in dynamic environments such as Kubernetes,
where Pods and Services can change frequently.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Prometheus in Kubernetes</h2>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>

Pods / Nodes / Services
<br>â†“<br>

Service Discovery
<br>â†“<br>

Exporters / Metrics Endpoints
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Dashboard / Alerts

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Prometheus vs Grafana</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Prometheus</th>
<th>Grafana</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Collects and stores metrics.</td>
<td>Visualizes metrics.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides PromQL.</td>
<td>Provides dashboards and panels.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can evaluate alert rules.</td>
<td>Can visualize and alert depending on configuration.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Simple Interview Answer:</strong><br>

Prometheus is primarily the metrics collection and time-series
monitoring system, while Grafana is primarily the visualization
and dashboarding platform.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. What happens when a target goes down?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Target Down
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus Scrape Fails
<br>â†“<br>

<code>up = 0</code>
<br>â†“<br>

Alert Rule Evaluated
<br>â†“<br>

Alert Generated
<br>â†“<br>

Alertmanager
<br>â†“<br>

Notification

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Troubleshooting: Metric Not Available</h2>

<ol>

<li>Check whether Prometheus is running.</li>

<li>Check the target status.</li>

<li>Verify the metrics endpoint.</li>

<li>Check <code>up</code>.</li>

<li>Check Prometheus configuration.</li>

<li>Check network connectivity.</li>

<li>Check exporter logs.</li>

<li>Verify the metric name and labels.</li>

</ol>

<pre>
up
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->
<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Interview Scenario</h2>

<h3>Scenario:</h3>

<p>
Your application CPU usage suddenly reaches 95%. What would you do?
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Answer:</strong>

<br><br>

First, I would use Prometheus metrics to confirm the CPU spike and
identify the affected instance or Pod using labels.

Then I would check application traffic, recent deployments,
resource limits and application logs.

If the issue is caused by increased traffic, I would verify whether
scaling is working correctly. If it is caused by a faulty deployment,
I would investigate the recent change and roll back if required.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->
<div class="card">

<li><strong>Prometheus</strong> â†’ Metrics collection and storage.</li>

<li><strong>Scraping</strong> â†’ Prometheus pulls metrics.</li>

<li><strong>Grafana</strong> â†’ Visualization.</li>

<li><strong>Alertmanager</strong> â†’ Alert routing and notifications.</li>

</ul>

</div>
