<h1>Monitoring Real-Time Scenarios</h1>

<p>
Production-oriented Prometheus, Grafana, Kubernetes and DevOps
monitoring scenarios with interview-ready troubleshooting answers.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Production Monitoring Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Application / Infrastructure
<br>â†“<br>

Metrics
<br>â†“<br>

Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Dashboard / Alert
<br>â†“<br>

DevOps Engineer
<br>â†“<br>

Troubleshooting
<br>â†“<br>

Resolution

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Scenario: Server CPU is 95%</h2>

<h3>Problem</h3>

<p>
A production server suddenly shows 95% CPU utilization.
</p>

<h3>How would you troubleshoot?</h3>

<ol>

<li>Open the Grafana CPU dashboard.</li>

<li>Identify the affected instance.</li>

<li>Check when the CPU increase started.</li>

<li>Check running processes on the server.</li>

<li>Compare CPU with traffic/request rate.</li>

<li>Check recent deployments or configuration changes.</li>

<li>Check memory and disk activity.</li>

<li>Determine whether the workload needs scaling or optimization.</li>

</ol>

<div class="flow">

CPU Alert
<br>â†“<br>
Grafana
<br>â†“<br>
Identify Instance
<br>â†“<br>
Linux Process Investigation
<br>â†“<br>
Find Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
Fix / Scale

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would first identify the affected instance from Grafana and
determine when the CPU spike started. Then I would correlate CPU with
traffic, deployments and other system metrics. On the server I would
inspect processes and resource usage to identify the process causing
the spike. Based on the root cause, I would optimize, restart,
rollback or scale the workload."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Scenario: Memory Usage is Increasing</h2>

<p>
Memory usage continuously increases and reaches a critical threshold.
</p>

<h3>Investigation</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check memory dashboard.</li>

<li>Identify affected node or application.</li>

<li>Check whether the increase is gradual or sudden.</li>

<li>Check application memory usage.</li>

<li>Check container memory limits.</li>

<li>Check for OOMKilled events.</li>

<li>Review application logs.</li>

<li>Investigate possible memory leak.</li>

</ol>

<pre>
kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Scenario: Kubernetes Pod Keeps Restarting</h2>

<div class="flow">

Pod Restart Alert
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Identify Pod
<br>â†“<br>

kubectl describe pod
<br>â†“<br>

kubectl logs
<br>â†“<br>

Check Events
<br>â†“<br>

Find Root Cause

</div>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>

<li>Application crash</li>
<li>OOMKilled</li>
<li>Failed health probe</li>
<li>Configuration error</li>
<li>Missing Secret or ConfigMap</li>
<li>Image problem</li>
<li>Dependency failure</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Scenario: Application Latency is High</h2>

<p>
Users report that the application is responding slowly.
</p>

<h3>Metrics to compare</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>Why check it?</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Latency</td>
<td>Confirms response-time degradation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Request Rate</td>
<td>Identifies traffic spikes.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Error Rate</td>
<td>Identifies failing requests.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CPU</td>
<td>Checks resource saturation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Memory</td>
<td>Checks memory pressure.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Database Metrics</td>
<td>Checks database bottlenecks.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would correlate latency with request rate, CPU, memory, errors
and database performance. If latency increased together with traffic,
I would investigate capacity. If infrastructure metrics are normal,
I would investigate the application and downstream dependencies."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Scenario: HTTP 5xx Errors Increase</h2>

<div class="flow">

5xx Error Spike
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Identify Service
<br>â†“<br>

Check Application Logs
<br>â†“<br>

Check Recent Deployment
<br>â†“<br>

Check Dependencies
<br>â†“<br>

Rollback / Fix

</div>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>

<li>Application bug</li>
<li>Bad deployment</li>
<li>Database failure</li>
<li>Dependency unavailable</li>
<li>Configuration issue</li>
<li>Resource exhaustion</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Scenario: Disk Usage is 90%</h2>

<h3>Investigation</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check Grafana disk dashboard.</li>

<li>Identify affected server.</li>

<li>Check filesystem usage.</li>

<li>Identify large files/directories.</li>

<li>Check application and system logs.</li>

<li>Check log rotation.</li>

<li>Clean unnecessary files if safe.</li>

<li>Increase storage if required.</li>

</ol>

<pre>
df -h

du -sh /var/log/*

df -i
</pre>

<div class="warning">

Do not blindly delete production files. First determine what is
consuming the storage and whether the data is required.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Scenario: Prometheus Target is DOWN</h2>

<p>
A target appears as <code>DOWN</code> in Prometheus.
</p>

<h3>Checklist</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check target URL.</li>

<li>Check target network connectivity.</li>

<li>Check exporter status.</li>

<li>Check metrics endpoint.</li>

<li>Check port.</li>

<li>Check firewall/security rules.</li>

<li>Check service discovery configuration.</li>

<li>Check Prometheus logs.</li>

</ol>

<pre>
curl http://target:9100/metrics
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Scenario: Grafana Shows "No Data"</h2>

<h3>Check in this order</h3>

<ol>

<li>Grafana data source.</li>

<li>Prometheus URL.</li>

<li>Prometheus availability.</li>

<li>PromQL query.</li>

<li>Dashboard time range.</li>

<li>Dashboard variables.</li>

<li>Prometheus target status.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Best interview approach:</strong>

<p>
"I would isolate whether the problem is in Grafana, the query,
Prometheus or the monitored target instead of immediately assuming
Grafana is broken."
</p>

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Scenario: Alert is Not Triggering</h2>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>

<li>Alert expression is incorrect.</li>
<li>Metric is missing.</li>
<li>Threshold has not been reached.</li>
<li>Rule is not loaded.</li>
<li>Evaluation interval issue.</li>
<li>Alertmanager routing problem.</li>
<li>Notification receiver configuration issue.</li>

</ul>

<div class="flow">

Metric
<br>â†“<br>

PromQL
<br>â†“<br>

Alert Rule
<br>â†“<br>

Rule Evaluation
<br>â†“<br>

Alert
<br>â†“<br>

Alertmanager
<br>â†“<br>

Notification

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Scenario: Too Many Alerts</h2>

<p>
The monitoring system is generating hundreds of notifications.
</p>

<h3>How to handle it?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Group related alerts.</li>

<li>Review alert thresholds.</li>

<li>Remove noisy alerts.</li>

<li>Use inhibition rules where appropriate.</li>

<li>Use silences during planned maintenance.</li>

<li>Separate warning and critical alerts.</li>

<li>Ensure alerts represent actionable problems.</li>

</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

A good monitoring system should reduce alert fatigue rather than
generate notifications for every small metric fluctuation.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Scenario: Kubernetes Node is NotReady</h2>

<div class="flow">

Node NotReady
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana Alert
<br>â†“<br>

kubectl get nodes
<br>â†“<br>

kubectl describe node
<br>â†“<br>

Check Kubelet
<br>â†“<br>

Check CPU / Memory / Disk
<br>â†“<br>

Resolve Node Problem

</div>

<pre>
kubectl get nodes

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;

kubectl get pods -A
</pre>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Scenario: Pod is OOMKilled</h2>

<p>
A Kubernetes container is terminated because it exceeded its memory
limit.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<p>
Look for:</p>

<pre>
Reason: OOMKilled
</pre>

<h3>Possible Solutions</h3>

<ul>

<li>Investigate memory usage.</li>

<li>Check application behavior.</li>

<li>Review memory requests and limits.</li>

<li>Optimize the application if necessary.</li>

<li>Increase memory limit when justified.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Scenario: Traffic Suddenly Increases</h2>

<p>
Request rate suddenly increases from normal levels.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Traffic Spike
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Request Rate
<br>â†“<br>

CPU / Memory
<br>â†“<br>

Application Capacity
<br>â†“<br>

Scaling Decision

</div>

<p>
If the workload is designed for horizontal scaling, verify that the
appropriate autoscaling mechanism is responding correctly.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Scenario: Deployment Causes Errors</h2>

<div class="flow">

Deployment
<br>â†“<br>

Error Rate Increases
<br>â†“<br>

Grafana
<br>â†“<br>

Compare Before / After
<br>â†“<br>

Check Application Logs
<br>â†“<br>

Confirm Deployment Correlation
<br>â†“<br>

Rollback / Fix

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"If the error rate increases immediately after a deployment, I would
compare the monitoring metrics before and after the release, inspect
application logs and verify whether the deployment is responsible.
If confirmed and the impact is significant, I would follow the
rollback procedure."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Scenario: Database is Slow</h2>

<h3>What would you check?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Database latency</li>
<li>Connection count</li>
<li>CPU</li>
<li>Memory</li>
<li>Disk I/O</li>
<li>Slow queries</li>
<li>Application request rate</li>
<li>Database errors</li>

</ul>

<div class="answer">

Do not immediately blame the database. Correlate application
latency, database metrics and traffic to identify the bottleneck.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 17 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Scenario: Monitoring System Itself is Down</h2>

<p>
If Prometheus or Grafana becomes unavailable, monitoring visibility
is affected.
</p>

<h3>Recovery Approach</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check service/container/Pod status.</li>

<li>Check application logs.</li>

<li>Check resource availability.</li>

<li>Check storage.</li>

<li>Check configuration.</li>

<li>Check network connectivity.</li>

<li>Restore service.</li>

<li>Verify metrics collection after recovery.</li>

</ol>

<div class="warning">

Monitoring is itself a production dependency. It should also be
designed for reliability and appropriate backup/recovery procedures.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 18 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 18. Scenario: Metrics Suddenly Disappear</h2>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>

<li>Exporter stopped.</li>
<li>Target became unreachable.</li>
<li>Service discovery stopped finding the target.</li>
<li>Prometheus scrape configuration changed.</li>
<li>Prometheus is experiencing resource issues.</li>
<li>Metric name or labels changed after an application update.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 19 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Scenario: How do you investigate an Incident?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Alert
<br>â†“<br>

Confirm Impact
<br>â†“<br>

Identify Affected Service
<br>â†“<br>

Check Metrics
<br>â†“<br>

Check Logs
<br>â†“<br>

Check Recent Changes
<br>â†“<br>

Check Dependencies
<br>â†“<br>

Find Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>

Mitigate
<br>â†“<br>

Permanent Fix
<br>â†“<br>

Post-Incident Review

</div>

</div>


<!-- 20 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Golden Signals</h2>

<p>
Four commonly used service-level monitoring signals are:
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Signal</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Latency</td>
<td>How long requests take.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Traffic</td>
<td>How much demand the system receives.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Errors</td>
<td>How many requests are failing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Saturation</td>
<td>How close the system is to its resource limits.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

These signals help engineers understand both user impact and system
capacity.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 21 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Metrics vs Logs vs Traces</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Best For</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Metrics</td>
<td>Trends, thresholds and system health.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Logs</td>
<td>Detailed event information.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Traces</td>
<td>Request flow across distributed services.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="flow">

Metrics
<br>â†“<br>
"Something is wrong"
<br><br>

Logs
<br>â†“<br>
"What happened?"
<br><br>

Traces
<br>â†“<br>
"Where did the request slow/fail?"

</div>

</div>


<!-- 22 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 22. Complete Production Troubleshooting Example</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
Users report slow responses and intermittent errors.
</p>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check Grafana latency.</li>

<li>Check request rate.</li>

<li>Check error rate.</li>

<li>Check CPU and memory.</li>

<li>Identify affected Pods.</li>

<li>Check application logs.</li>

<li>Check database latency.</li>

<li>Check recent deployments.</li>

<li>Identify root cause.</li>

<li>Apply mitigation.</li>

<li>Verify recovery through monitoring.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Strong Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would first quantify the impact using monitoring metrics. Then I
would correlate latency and error rate with traffic, infrastructure
resources, application logs and downstream dependencies. I would
also check recent changes such as deployments. After identifying the
most likely root cause, I would mitigate the issue, verify recovery
using the same metrics and then work on the permanent fix."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 23 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 23. Monitoring Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Monitor user-facing services.</li>

<li>Create actionable alerts.</li>

<li>Avoid excessive alerting.</li>

<li>Monitor infrastructure and applications.</li>

<li>Use meaningful dashboards.</li>

<li>Track latency, traffic, errors and saturation.</li>

<li>Monitor the monitoring stack itself.</li>

<li>Use appropriate retention and storage policies.</li>

<li>Document incident response procedures.</li>

<li>Correlate metrics with logs and traces when available.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 24 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ 24. Top Scenario-Based Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>CPU usage suddenly reaches 95%. What will you do?</li>

<li>Memory usage continuously increases. How will you investigate?</li>

<li>A Pod keeps restarting. How will you troubleshoot?</li>

<li>Why is a Pod OOMKilled?</li>

<li>Prometheus target is DOWN. What will you check?</li>

<li>Grafana shows No Data. How will you troubleshoot?</li>

<li>Application latency suddenly increases. What will you check?</li>

<li>HTTP 5xx errors suddenly increase. What will you do?</li>

<li>Disk usage reaches 90%. How will you investigate?</li>

<li>Kubernetes node becomes NotReady. What will you check?</li>

<li>An alert is not triggering. How will you troubleshoot?</li>

<li>You receive too many alerts. How will you reduce alert fatigue?</li>

<li>A deployment causes production errors. What will you do?</li>

<li>Metrics suddenly disappear. What could be the reason?</li>

<li>How would you investigate a production incident end-to-end?</li>

</ol>

</div>

<header>
<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ”</div>
<h1>DevSecOps Basics</h1>
<p>
Security integrated into every stage of the software delivery lifecycle.
Interview-focused concepts, terminology and practical examples.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is DevSecOps?</h2>

<p>
<strong>DevSecOps</strong> means integrating security practices into
the DevOps lifecycle instead of treating security as a separate
activity performed only at the end.
</p>

<div class="flow">
Plan
<br>â†“<br>
Code
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Security
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
<br>â†“<br>
Monitor
</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"DevSecOps is an approach where security is integrated throughout
the software development and delivery lifecycle. Instead of finding
security issues only before production, we identify and fix them as
early as possible using automated security checks in the development
and CI/CD process."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. DevOps vs DevSecOps</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>DevOps</th>
<th>DevSecOps</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Focuses on development, operations and automation.</td>
<td>Adds security as an integral part of the lifecycle.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Security may be handled separately.</td>
<td>Security is shared across teams.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Security checks may happen later.</td>
<td>Security checks are shifted earlier.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CI/CD automation.</td>
<td>CI/CD + automated security controls.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Simple way to remember:</strong><br>

DevOps = Development + Operations + Automation<br>
DevSecOps = Development + Security + Operations + Automation

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. What is Shift-Left Security?</h2>

<p>
<strong>Shift-left security</strong> means moving security checks
earlier in the software development lifecycle.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Traditional
<br>
Code â†’ Build â†’ Test â†’ Deploy â†’ Security
<br><br>

Shift Left
<br>
Security â†’ Code â†’ Build â†’ Test â†’ Deploy

</div>

<p>
The objective is to identify vulnerabilities when they are cheaper
and easier to fix.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"Shift-left security means introducing security activities as early
as possible in the SDLC. For example, we can scan source code,
dependencies, secrets, Dockerfiles and infrastructure definitions
before they reach production."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Why is DevSecOps Important?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Detects vulnerabilities earlier.</li>

<li>Reduces security risks.</li>

<li>Automates security checks.</li>

<li>Reduces the cost of fixing vulnerabilities.</li>

<li>Improves compliance and governance.</li>

<li>Protects applications and infrastructure.</li>

<li>Reduces the possibility of insecure deployments.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Security Across the DevOps Lifecycle</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Stage</th>
<th>Security Activity</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Plan</td>
<td>Threat modeling, security requirements.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Code</td>
<td>SAST, secret detection, secure coding.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build</td>
<td>Dependency and artifact scanning.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Test</td>
<td>DAST and security testing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Containerize</td>
<td>Container image scanning.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Infrastructure</td>
<td>IaC security scanning.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Deploy</td>
<td>Policy and access controls.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Operate</td>
<td>Runtime monitoring and vulnerability management.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is SAST?</h2>

<p>
<strong>SAST â€” Static Application Security Testing</strong>
analyzes application source code or compiled code without executing
the application.
</p>

<p>
It can identify security weaknesses during development or CI.
</p>

<h3>Example</h3>

<p>
A developer pushes code â†’ CI pipeline runs SAST â†’ vulnerability is
detected â†’ pipeline can fail based on the configured policy.
</p>

<p>
<strong>Common example:</strong> SonarQube.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is DAST?</h2>

<p>
<strong>DAST â€” Dynamic Application Security Testing</strong>
tests a running application from the outside.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>SAST:</strong> Tests code.<br>
<strong>DAST:</strong> Tests a running application.

</div>

<p>
A commonly used DAST tool is OWASP ZAP.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is SCA?</h2>

<p>
<strong>SCA â€” Software Composition Analysis</strong> scans third-party
libraries and dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
</p>

<p>
For example, if an application uses a vulnerable version of a
dependency, SCA can identify the vulnerability.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. SAST vs DAST vs SCA</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>What it checks</th>
<th>When</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SAST</td>
<td>Source/application code</td>
<td>During development/build</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>DAST</td>
<td>Running application</td>
<td>During testing</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SCA</td>
<td>Third-party dependencies</td>
<td>During development/build</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Container Security</h2>

<p>
Container images can contain vulnerable packages, outdated operating
system components or insecure configurations.
</p>

<p>
A tool such as <strong>Trivy</strong> can scan container images.
</p>

<pre>
trivy image nginx:latest
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

"I would scan container images before deployment and configure the
CI/CD pipeline to block images that exceed the organization's
defined vulnerability threshold."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Secrets Management</h2>

<p>
Passwords, API keys, tokens and private credentials should never be
committed directly into source control.
</p>

<h3>Bad Practice</h3>

<pre>
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AKIA..."
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="..."
</pre>

<h3>Better Approach</h3>

<ul>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>GitHub Secrets</li>
<li>AWS Secrets Manager</li>
<li>HashiCorp Vault</li>
<li>Kubernetes Secrets with appropriate protection</li>
</ul>

<p>
Tools such as <strong>Gitleaks</strong> can detect accidentally
committed secrets.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is IaC Security?</h2>

<p>
Infrastructure-as-Code security means scanning infrastructure
definitions for insecure configurations before deployment.
</p>

<p>
Examples include Terraform, Kubernetes YAML and CloudFormation.
</p>

<p>
Typical checks can identify things such as overly permissive access,
public resources or insecure configuration.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Common DevSecOps Tools</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Tool</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SonarQube</td>
<td>Code quality and security analysis.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Trivy</td>
<td>Container, filesystem and IaC vulnerability scanning.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Gitleaks</td>
<td>Secret detection.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Hadolint</td>
<td>Dockerfile linting.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>OWASP ZAP</td>
<td>Dynamic application security testing.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 14 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. How DevSecOps Fits Into CI/CD</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer Push
<br>â†“<br>
Git
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
SAST
<br>â†“<br>
Dependency Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Secret Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Container Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
<br>â†“<br>
Runtime Monitoring

</div>

<div class="answer">

Security becomes an automated quality gate rather than a manual
activity performed only before production.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 15 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What Happens When a Security Scan Fails?</h2>

<ol>

<li>The security tool detects a vulnerability.</li>

<li>The pipeline evaluates the configured policy.</li>

<li>If the vulnerability violates the policy, the security gate fails.</li>

<li>The deployment can be blocked.</li>

<li>The developer/team investigates the vulnerability.</li>

<li>The issue is fixed or formally approved according to organizational policy.</li>

<li>The pipeline is executed again.</li>

</ol>

<div class="warning">

Do not automatically fail every pipeline for every low-severity
finding. Organizations normally define severity thresholds and
exception processes.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 16 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. DevSecOps vs Security Team</h2>

<p>
DevSecOps does not mean removing security teams.
</p>

<p>
Instead, security becomes a shared responsibility while security
teams continue to provide expertise, policies, governance,
risk management and advanced security practices.
</p>

</div>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ”’</div>

<h1>DevSecOps in CI/CD</h1>

<p>
How security checks are integrated into automated CI/CD pipelines
using practical stages, security gates and real-time examples.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Why Integrate Security into CI/CD?</h2>

<p>
CI/CD automates building, testing and deploying applications.
DevSecOps extends this automation by adding security checks into
the same delivery process.
</p>

<p>
This allows security issues to be detected before an insecure
artifact reaches production.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"We integrate security into CI/CD so that security checks become
automated and repeatable. The pipeline can scan source code,
dependencies, secrets, container images and infrastructure before
deployment."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Typical DevSecOps CI/CD Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer Push
<br>â†“<br>

Checkout Code
<br>â†“<br>

SAST
<br>â†“<br>

Secret Scan
<br>â†“<br>

Dependency Scan
<br>â†“<br>

Build
<br>â†“<br>

Docker Image
<br>â†“<br>

Container Scan
<br>â†“<br>

Push Image
<br>â†“<br>

Deploy to Test
<br>â†“<br>

DAST
<br>â†“<br>

Production

</div>

</div>


<!-- 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Where Should Security Scans Run?</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Pipeline Stage</th>
<th>Security Check</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Source Checkout</td>
<td>Secret scanning</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Code Analysis</td>
<td>SAST</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Dependency Installation</td>
<td>SCA</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Docker Build</td>
<td>Dockerfile linting</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Image Build</td>
<td>Container vulnerability scanning</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Infrastructure Validation</td>
<td>IaC security scanning</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Test Environment</td>
<td>DAST</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Deployment</td>
<td>Policy and access controls</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<!-- 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Security Gates</h2>

<p>
A security gate determines whether the pipeline can continue after
a security check.
</p>

<h3>Example Policy</h3>

<ul>
<li>Critical vulnerabilities â†’ Block deployment</li>
<li>High vulnerabilities â†’ Block or require approval</li>
<li>Medium vulnerabilities â†’ Track and remediate</li>
<li>Low vulnerabilities â†’ Track according to policy</li>
</ul>

<div class="warning">

The exact thresholds should be defined by the organization's
security policy. Do not assume that every vulnerability should
automatically fail every pipeline.

</div>

</div>


<!-- 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Example Jenkins Pipeline</h2>

<pre>
pipeline {

    agent any

    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                git 'https://github.com/example/project.git'
            }
        }

        stage('SAST') {
            steps {
                echo 'Run SonarQube analysis'
            }
        }

        stage('Secret Scan') {
            steps {
                echo 'Run Gitleaks'
            }
        }

        stage('Dependency Scan') {
            steps {
                echo 'Run dependency scanner'
            }
        }

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Build application'
            }
        }

        stage('Docker Build') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t myapp:latest .'
            }
        }

        stage('Container Scan') {
            steps {
                sh 'trivy image myapp:latest'
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                echo 'Deploy application'
            }
        }
    }
}
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

"The commands are examples. In a real project, I would configure
credentials, scanners, severity thresholds and quality gates based
on the organization's security requirements."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Example GitHub Actions Flow</h2>

<pre>
name: DevSecOps Pipeline

on:
  push:

jobs:

  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Secret Scan
        run: |
          gitleaks detect --source .

      - name: Build Docker Image
        run: |
          docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Container Scan
        run: |
          trivy image myapp:${{ github.sha }}

</pre>

<p>
In production, scanners should be pinned and configured according
to the organization's security and CI/CD standards.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What If Trivy Finds a Critical Vulnerability?</h2>

<ol>

<li>Trivy scans the image.</li>

<li>A critical vulnerability is detected.</li>

<li>The configured security policy evaluates the result.</li>

<li>If critical vulnerabilities are blocking conditions, the pipeline fails.</li>

<li>The image is not promoted to the next environment.</li>

<li>The vulnerable package or base image is updated.</li>

<li>The image is rebuilt and scanned again.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"If Trivy finds a critical vulnerability, I would check the affected
package and severity, apply the organization's policy, block the
image from promotion if it violates the policy, remediate the
vulnerability and rerun the pipeline."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What If Gitleaks Finds an AWS Credential?</h2>

<div class="warning">

<strong>First priority: revoke or rotate the exposed credential.</strong>

</div>

<ol>

<li>Stop the pipeline.</li>

<li>Identify the exposed credential.</li>

<li>Revoke or rotate it immediately.</li>

<li>Remove the secret from the source.</li>

<li>Clean repository history if required.</li>

<li>Store the replacement credential securely.</li>

<li>Run the pipeline again.</li>

</ol>

<p>
Deleting the secret from the current file alone may not remove it
from Git history.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. How Do You Store Secrets in CI/CD?</h2>

<p>
Never hard-code production credentials directly inside pipeline
files.
</p>

<h3>Common Options</h3>

<ul>
<li>GitHub Secrets</li>
<li>Jenkins Credentials</li>
<li>AWS Secrets Manager</li>
<li>HashiCorp Vault</li>
<li>Cloud-specific secret management services</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I store sensitive credentials in a dedicated secrets-management
solution or the CI/CD platform's protected credential store and
inject them only when required."

</div>

</div>


<!-- 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. How Do You Prevent Insecure Deployment?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Run automated security scans.</li>

<li>Configure security gates.</li>

<li>Use least-privilege credentials.</li>

<li>Protect production environments.</li>

<li>Require approvals where appropriate.</li>

<li>Scan container images.</li>

<li>Scan infrastructure definitions.</li>

<li>Monitor deployed applications.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. Security vs Pipeline Speed</h2>

<p>
Security checks should be designed so they provide strong protection
without unnecessarily slowing development.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Fast Checks</th>
<th>Slower Checks</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Secret scanning</td>
<td>Full DAST scans</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Basic SAST</td>
<td>Large dependency analysis</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Dockerfile linting</td>
<td>Deep security testing</td>
</tr>

</table>

<p>
A common approach is to run fast checks early and deeper tests at
appropriate later stages.
</p>

</div>


<!-- 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. Security Pipeline Failure Troubleshooting</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
"The deployment failed because the security stage failed."
</p>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<ol>

<li>Identify which security tool failed.</li>

<li>Read the scanner output.</li>

<li>Identify severity and affected component.</li>

<li>Determine whether the failure is expected.</li>

<li>Fix the vulnerability or configuration.</li>

<li>Rerun the scan.</li>

<li>Continue deployment only when policy requirements are satisfied.</li>

</ol>

</div>

<h1>DevSecOps Final Revision</h1>

<p>

tools, pipeline integration and real-time troubleshooting.

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is DevSecOps?</h2>

<div class="answer">

DevSecOps means integrating security throughout the software
development and delivery lifecycle instead of treating security
as a separate final-stage activity.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Plan â†’ Code â†’ Build â†’ Test â†’ Secure â†’ Deploy â†’ Monitor

</div>

<strong>Remember:</strong> Security is continuous.

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. DevOps vs DevSecOps</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>DevOps</th>
<th>DevSecOps</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Development + Operations collaboration</td>
<td>Development + Security + Operations collaboration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Automated delivery</td>
<td>Automated delivery with security controls</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Security may be added separately</td>
<td>Security is integrated throughout the lifecycle</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Important Security Testing Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
<th>Typical Stage</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SAST</td>
<td>Analyze source code for security issues</td>
<td>Code / CI</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>SCA</td>
<td>Find vulnerable dependencies</td>
<td>Build / CI</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Secret Scanning</td>
<td>Detect credentials and secrets</td>
<td>Commit / CI</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container Scanning</td>
<td>Find image vulnerabilities</td>
<td>Image build</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>IaC Scanning</td>
<td>Detect insecure infrastructure configuration</td>
<td>CI</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>DAST</td>
<td>Test running application</td>
<td>Test / Staging</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Must-Know Security Tools</h2>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Security Pipeline</h2>

<div class="flow">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is a Security Gate?</h2>

<p>
A security gate is a policy checkpoint that determines whether
a pipeline can continue.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Example:</strong><br>

If an image contains a critical vulnerability and the organization's
policy blocks critical vulnerabilities, the pipeline fails and the
image is not promoted.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What happens when Trivy finds a Critical CVE?</h2>

<ol>

<li>Identify the CVE and affected package.</li>

<li>Check severity and impact.</li>

<li>Check for a patched version.</li>

<li>Update dependency or base image.</li>

<li>Rebuild image.</li>

<li>Scan again.</li>

<li>Promote only when security policy is satisfied.</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What happens when a Secret is detected?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Secret Detected
<br>â†“<br>
Stop Pipeline
<br>â†“<br>
Verify Finding
<br>â†“<br>
Rotate / Revoke Credential
<br>â†“<br>
Remove Secret
<br>â†“<br>
Secure Storage
<br>â†“<br>
Run Pipeline Again

</div>

<strong>Important:</strong> Never expose credentials in source code,
logs or pipeline output.

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. How do you manage CI/CD Secrets?</h2>

<ul>

<li>GitHub Secrets</li>
<li>Jenkins Credentials</li>
<li>AWS Secrets Manager</li>
<li>HashiCorp Vault</li>

</ul>

<div class="answer">

"I avoid hard-coded credentials and use protected secret-management
mechanisms with least-privilege access."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Least Privilege</h2>

<p>
Least privilege means giving users, applications and CI/CD systems
only the permissions they actually need.
</p>

<pre>
CI/CD Pipeline
      |
      â””â”€â”€ IAM Role
             |
             â”œâ”€â”€ Required ECR access
             â””â”€â”€ Required deployment access
</pre>

<p>
Avoid giving a pipeline unrestricted administrator permissions when
they are not required.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. Shift Left Security</h2>

<div class="answer">

Shift-left security means identifying and fixing security issues
as early as possible in the software development lifecycle.

</div>

<div class="flow">

Developer
â†’ Code Scan
â†’ Dependency Scan
â†’ Build
â†’ Container Scan
â†’ Deploy

</div>

<strong>Goal:</strong> Find problems earlier when they are generally
easier and cheaper to fix.

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. False Positive</h2>

<p>
A false positive occurs when a security tool reports a problem that
is not actually a security issue in the application's context.
</p>

<h3>Correct Approach</h3>

<ol>

<li>Validate the finding.</li>
<li>Understand the affected component.</li>
<li>Check the evidence.</li>
<li>Document the analysis.</li>
<li>Use an approved exception process if appropriate.</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. How Do You Secure Docker?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use trusted and maintained base images.</li>

<li>Keep images updated.</li>

<li>Scan images for vulnerabilities.</li>

<li>Avoid running containers as root when possible.</li>

<li>Do not hard-code secrets in Dockerfiles.</li>

<li>Use minimal images where practical.</li>

<li>Do not expose unnecessary ports.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. How Do You Secure Kubernetes?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use RBAC.</li>

<li>Follow least privilege.</li>

<li>Secure Secrets.</li>

<li>Restrict container privileges.</li>

<li>Use NetworkPolicies where appropriate.</li>

<li>Scan container images.</li>

<li>Keep Kubernetes components updated.</li>

<li>Monitor cluster activity.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 15. How Do You Secure Terraform?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Scan Terraform code before deployment.</li>

<li>Review IAM permissions.</li>

<li>Avoid hard-coded credentials.</li>

<li>Protect Terraform state.</li>

<li>Use remote state with appropriate access controls.</li>

<li>Review security-sensitive changes.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Interview Scenario</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Question:</strong><br><br>

"Your pipeline passed all security checks but production still
has a security incident. What would you do?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong><br>

"I would first contain the incident and assess its scope. Then I
would identify the attack vector, affected resources and whether
credentials or application vulnerabilities were involved. I would
apply the required remediation, verify the fix and monitor the
environment. Finally, I would identify which preventive control was
missing and improve the CI/CD or runtime security process."

</div>

</div>

</ol>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸš¨</div>

<h1>DevSecOps Real-Time Scenarios</h1>

<p>
Production-style security situations, troubleshooting approaches
and interview-ready answers.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<!-- Scenario 1 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Trivy Finds a Critical Vulnerability</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

Your CI/CD pipeline builds a Docker image. Trivy reports a
CRITICAL vulnerability. What will you do?

</div>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check the vulnerability ID and affected package.</li>

<li>Confirm whether the vulnerability actually affects the application.</li>

<li>Check whether a patched package or newer base image is available.</li>

<li>Update the dependency or base image.</li>

<li>Rebuild the Docker image.</li>

<li>Run Trivy again.</li>

<li>Allow promotion only if the organization's security policy is satisfied.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would first analyze the vulnerability and affected package.
If it violates our security policy, I would block the image from
promotion, update the vulnerable dependency or base image, rebuild
the image and rerun the scan."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 2 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. AWS Secret Committed to Git</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

A developer accidentally commits an AWS access key to GitHub.
What do you do?

</div>

<h3>Immediate Actions</h3>

<ol>

<li>Revoke or rotate the exposed credential immediately.</li>

<li>Check CloudTrail or relevant logs for suspicious usage.</li>

<li>Remove the secret from the source.</li>

<li>Check Git history and clean it if necessary.</li>

<li>Store the replacement credential securely.</li>

<li>Add secret scanning to the CI/CD pipeline.</li>

</ol>

<div class="warning">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

Do not assume that deleting the key from the latest commit makes
the credential safe. The credential may still exist in Git history
or may already have been copied.

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"My first priority is credential revocation or rotation. Then I
would investigate possible usage, remove the secret, clean the
repository if required, replace it with a securely managed
credential and add secret scanning to prevent recurrence."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 3 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Gitleaks Fails the Pipeline</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

The Gitleaks stage fails during a deployment pipeline.
What do you check?

</div>

<ol>

<li>Read the Gitleaks output.</li>

<li>Identify the detected secret.</li>

<li>Determine whether it is a real secret or false positive.</li>

<li>If real, revoke or rotate the credential.</li>

<li>Remove the secret from the repository.</li>

<li>Use secure secret storage.</li>

<li>Rerun the pipeline.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would inspect the Gitleaks finding, verify whether it is a true
secret, immediately rotate it if necessary, remove it from source
control and rerun the pipeline after remediation."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 4 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. SonarQube Quality Gate Failed</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

The build passes, but the SonarQube quality gate fails.
Can you deploy?

</div>

<p>
Normally, if the quality gate is configured as a blocking condition,
the pipeline should not promote the artifact until the issue is
resolved or an authorized exception is applied.
</p>

<h3>What to Check?</h3>

<ul>

<li>Security vulnerabilities</li>

<li>Bugs</li>

<li>Code smells</li>

<li>Coverage requirements</li>

<li>Duplicated code</li>

<li>Quality gate configuration</li>

</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would inspect the failed quality gate conditions. If the gate is
configured as a blocking policy, I would fix the reported issues
before promoting the application."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 5 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Developer Says the Security Scan Is a False Positive</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

A scanner reports a vulnerability, but the developer believes it is
a false positive. What do you do?

</div>

<ol>

<li>Verify the finding manually.</li>

<li>Check the vulnerability details and affected component.</li>

<li>Confirm whether the vulnerable code path is actually used.</li>

<li>Review the scanner documentation and evidence.</li>

<li>Document the finding.</li>

<li>Follow the organization's approved exception process if it is genuinely a false positive.</li>

</ol>

<div class="warning">

Never simply suppress security findings without validation and
documentation.

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 6 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Vulnerable Base Image</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

Your Docker image uses an outdated Ubuntu or Alpine base image and
the scanner reports many vulnerabilities.

</div>

<h3>Solution</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check for a supported newer base image.</li>

<li>Update the Dockerfile.</li>

<li>Rebuild the image.</li>

<li>Run the vulnerability scan again.</li>

<li>Test the application.</li>

<li>Promote the new image after security checks pass.</li>

</ol>

<pre>
FROM ubuntu:24.04
</pre>

<p>
The exact base image version should be selected according to the
application's compatibility and organizational standards.
</p>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 7 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Critical Vulnerability Found in Production</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

A critical vulnerability is discovered in a production application.
What is your response?

</div>

<div class="flow">

Detect
<br>â†“<br>
Assess Risk
<br>â†“<br>
Contain
<br>â†“<br>
Patch / Mitigate
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy Fix
<br>â†“<br>
Monitor

</div>

<h3>Important Actions</h3>

<ul>

<li>Assess severity and exposure.</li>

<li>Identify affected systems.</li>

<li>Apply available patches or mitigations.</li>

<li>Restrict exposure if necessary.</li>

<li>Deploy the fix safely.</li>

<li>Monitor for exploitation.</li>

<li>Document the incident.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 8 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 8. Security Scan Makes Pipeline Too Slow</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

The security team added many scans and now CI/CD takes 45 minutes.
Developers are complaining.

</div>

<h3>Possible Approach</h3>

<ul>

<li>Run lightweight checks earlier.</li>

<li>Run deeper scans at appropriate pipeline stages.</li>

<li>Cache dependencies where appropriate.</li>

<li>Run independent security checks in parallel.</li>

<li>Avoid duplicate scanning.</li>

<li>Optimize scanner configuration.</li>

</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would optimize the pipeline rather than simply removing security.
Fast checks can run early, independent scans can run in parallel and
deeper security testing can run at appropriate stages."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 9 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Security Scan Passes but Production Is Still Compromised</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

All CI security scans passed, but a production security incident
still occurred. Does that mean DevSecOps failed?

</div>

<p>
Not necessarily. Security scanners cover specific classes of risks;
they do not guarantee that an application is completely secure.
</p>

<h3>Investigate</h3>

<ul>

<li>Application vulnerabilities</li>

<li>Cloud configuration</li>

<li>IAM permissions</li>

<li>Network exposure</li>

<li>Runtime vulnerabilities</li>

<li>Credential compromise</li>

<li>Monitoring and detection gaps</li>

</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Key Point:</strong><br>

"DevSecOps reduces security risk through continuous controls, but
security is a continuous process rather than a one-time guarantee."

</div>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 10 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 10. How Would You Secure a Jenkins Pipeline?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use Jenkins Credentials instead of hard-coded secrets.</li>

<li>Apply least-privilege permissions.</li>

<li>Keep Jenkins and plugins updated.</li>

<li>Restrict administrative access.</li>

<li>Use security scanning stages.</li>

<li>Protect production deployment stages.</li>

<li>Audit pipeline activity.</li>

<li>Secure Jenkins agents.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 11 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 11. How Would You Secure a Kubernetes Deployment?</h2>

<ul>

<li>Use RBAC.</li>

<li>Follow least privilege.</li>

<li>Scan container images.</li>

<li>Do not store sensitive credentials directly in manifests.</li>

<li>Use NetworkPolicies where appropriate.</li>

<li>Apply Pod Security controls.</li>

<li>Restrict container privileges.</li>

<li>Monitor workloads and cluster activity.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 12 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 12. IaC Scan Finds a Public AWS Resource</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

An IaC scanner reports that a Terraform resource could expose
something publicly. What do you do?

</div>

<ol>

<li>Identify the affected resource.</li>

<li>Understand why public access is configured.</li>

<li>Check whether it is actually required.</li>

<li>Restrict access if unnecessary.</li>

<li>Update the Terraform code.</li>

<li>Run the security scan again.</li>

<li>Apply the infrastructure only after validation.</li>

</ol>

</div>


<!-- Scenario 13 -->

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Complete Interview Scenario</h2>

<div class="scenario">

<strong>Question:</strong><br>

"Explain how you would implement DevSecOps for a project from
GitHub to production."

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br><br>

"I would start by integrating security into the CI/CD pipeline.
After a developer pushes code to GitHub, I would run secret scanning
and SAST. Then I would scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
After building the Docker image, I would scan the image using Trivy.
Infrastructure definitions can also be scanned before deployment.
After deployment to a test environment, I would run appropriate
dynamic security testing. Security gates would prevent artifacts
that violate the organization's defined policies from progressing
to production. Finally, I would monitor the production environment
and continuously remediate vulnerabilities."

</div>

</div>

</div>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ—ï¸</div>

<h1>Networking Architecture</h1>

<p>
Understand how real-world cloud applications communicate across
VPCs, subnets, routing components, NAT and load balancers.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Network Architecture?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Network architecture describes how network components are
organized and connected so that applications and systems can
communicate securely and reliably.

</div>

<p>
In Cloud and DevOps, architecture commonly includes:

</p>

<ul>
<li>VPC / Virtual Network</li>
<li>Subnets</li>
<li>Route Tables</li>
<li>Internet Gateway</li>
<li>NAT Gateway</li>
<li>Load Balancer</li>
<li>Security Groups / Firewalls</li>
<li>Application and Database tiers</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Typical Cloud Application Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸŒ Internet
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸŒ DNS
<br>â†“<br>
âš–ï¸ Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ–¥ï¸ Application Servers
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ—„ï¸ Database
<br><br>

<strong>Private Application Network</strong>

</div>

<p>
The public-facing components are normally separated from private
application and database resources.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. VPC</h2>

<p>
A VPC, or Virtual Private Cloud, is an isolated virtual network
where cloud resources can be deployed.
</p>

<pre>
VPC
CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16

        |
        +--------------------+
        |                    |
   Public Subnet        Private Subnet
   10.0.1.0/24          10.0.2.0/24
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"A VPC provides an isolated networking environment in the cloud
where I can define IP ranges, subnets, routing and network security
controls."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Public Subnet vs Private Subnet</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Public Subnet</th>
<th>Private Subnet</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Has a route toward an Internet Gateway.</td>
<td>Does not have a direct route to the Internet Gateway.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can contain resources that need direct Internet reachability.</td>
<td>Commonly used for application and database resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: public load balancer.</td>
<td>Example: private application server or database.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<strong>Important:</strong> A subnet being called "public" does not
automatically make every resource inside it publicly reachable.
Routing and security controls also matter.

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Route Table</h2>

<p>
A route table contains rules that determine where network traffic
should be sent.
</p>

<pre>
Destination       Target

10.0.0.0/16       local
0.0.0.0/0         Internet Gateway
</pre>

<p>
For a private subnet, a common outbound route is through a NAT
Gateway instead of directly through an Internet Gateway.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Internet Gateway</h2>

<p>
An Internet Gateway provides a path between a VPC and the public
Internet when the required routing and addressing configuration
exists.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Public Subnet
<br>â†“<br>
Route Table
<br>â†“<br>
Internet Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸŒ Internet

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. NAT Gateway</h2>

<p>
A NAT Gateway allows resources in a private subnet to initiate
outbound Internet connections without requiring those resources
to have public IP addresses.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Private EC2
<br>â†“<br>
Private Route Table
<br>â†“<br>
NAT Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
Internet Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸŒ Internet

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Question:</strong><br>
Why do we use NAT Gateway?

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong><br>

"We use a NAT Gateway to allow private resources to access external
services or download updates without giving those resources public
IP addresses."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Load Balancer Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

Client
<br>â†“<br>
âš–ï¸ Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>
â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”¬â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”
<br>
ðŸ–¥ï¸ App Server 1 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ðŸ–¥ï¸ App Server 2
<br>
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”´â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜
<br>â†“
<br>
ðŸ—„ï¸ Database

</div>

<h3>Why use a Load Balancer?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Distribute incoming traffic.</li>
<li>Improve availability.</li>
<li>Support horizontal scaling.</li>
<li>Perform health checks.</li>
<li>Provide a single entry point for clients.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Three-Tier Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Presentation Tier</strong>
<br>
Load Balancer / Web Layer
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Application Tier</strong>
<br>
Application Servers
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Data Tier</strong>
<br>
Database

</div>

<p>
A three-tier architecture separates responsibilities and helps
control access between layers.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Security Groups vs Network ACL</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Security Group</th>
<th>Network ACL</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Applied to supported network interfaces/resources.</td>
<td>Applied at subnet level.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stateful.</td>
<td>Stateless.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Rules control allowed traffic.</td>
<td>Rules can allow or deny traffic.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly used for instance-level access control.</td>
<td>Commonly used for subnet-level filtering.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Security Group Example</h2>

<pre>
Application Server Security Group

Inbound:

TCP 8080
Source: Load Balancer Security Group

SSH 22
Source: Trusted Administration Network

Outbound:
Only required traffic according to policy
</pre>

<p>
A strong design avoids exposing application ports directly to the
entire Internet when a load balancer can be used.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. DNS + Load Balancer Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

User
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>example.com</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
DNS
<br>â†“<br>
Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>
Application Servers
<br>â†“<br>
Database

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"DNS resolves the application domain to the appropriate endpoint,
the load balancer receives the request and distributes it to healthy
application targets."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Private Application Server: How Does It Access Internet?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Private Application Server
<br>â†“<br>
Private Route Table
<br>â†“<br>
NAT Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
Public Subnet
<br>â†“<br>
Internet Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸŒ Internet

</div>

<p>
The application server can initiate outbound connections without
being directly exposed through a public IP.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. High Availability Network Design</h2>

<div class="flow">

Availability Zone A
<br>
Public Subnet â†’ Load Balancer â†’ App Server
<br><br>

Availability Zone B
<br>
Public Subnet â†’ Load Balancer â†’ App Server
<br><br>

Both
<br>â†“<br>
Private Database / Managed Database

</div>

<h3>Benefits</h3>

<ul>
<li>Reduces dependency on a single Availability Zone.</li>
<li>Improves application availability.</li>
<li>Supports failure recovery.</li>
<li>Allows traffic distribution across healthy resources.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Real-Time Scenario</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Question:</strong><br><br>

"Your EC2 instance in a private subnet cannot download packages
from the Internet. How will you troubleshoot?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Check whether the subnet is actually private.</li>

<li>Check the subnet's route table.</li>

<li>Verify that the default route points to a NAT Gateway.</li>

<li>Check whether the NAT Gateway is available.</li>

<li>Verify the NAT Gateway is in a subnet with Internet connectivity.</li>

<li>Check security controls.</li>

<li>Check DNS configuration if the problem is hostname resolution.</li>

<li>Test connectivity from the instance.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Scenario: Application Not Reachable</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Check in this order:</strong>

<div class="flow">

DNS
â†’ Load Balancer
â†’ Listener
â†’ Target Group
â†’ Target Health
â†’ Security Group
â†’ Route Table
â†’ Application Port
â†’ Application Logs

</div>

<p>
This layered approach helps identify whether the issue is DNS,
load balancing, routing, security or the application itself.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ 17. Must-Know Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>What is a VPC?</li>

<li>Public subnet vs private subnet?</li>

<li>What is a route table?</li>

<li>Internet Gateway vs NAT Gateway?</li>

<li>Why do we use NAT Gateway?</li>

<li>What is a load balancer?</li>

<li>Explain three-tier architecture.</li>

<li>Security Group vs Network ACL?</li>

<li>How does a private EC2 instance access the Internet?</li>

<li>How would you design a highly available network?</li>

<li>How would you troubleshoot an unreachable application?</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Quick Revision</h2>

<div class="flow">

<h1>Networking Basics</h1>

<p>
High-priority networking concepts for Cloud and DevOps interviews.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is a Computer Network?</h2>

<div class="answer">

A computer network is a collection of connected devices that
communicate and exchange data using defined communication protocols.

</div>

<p>
In Cloud and DevOps, networking is essential because applications,
servers, containers, Kubernetes workloads and cloud services must
communicate securely.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is an IP Address?</h2>

<p>
An IP address uniquely identifies a device or network interface
within an IP network.
</p>

<h3>IPv4 Example</h3>

<pre>
192.168.1.10
</pre>

<h3>IPv6 Example</h3>

<pre>
2001:db8::10
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"An IP address identifies a network interface so that devices can
communicate with each other over an IP network."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Public IP vs Private IP</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Public IP</th>
<th>Private IP</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for communication over the public Internet.</td>
<td>Used inside private networks.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Must be globally routable.</td>
<td>Not directly routable over the public Internet.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Example: public cloud instance address.</td>
<td>Example: 10.0.1.20</td>
</tr>

</table>

<p>
Private IP ranges include:
</p>

<ul>
<li>10.0.0.0/8</li>
<li>172.16.0.0/12</li>
<li>192.168.0.0/16</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. MAC Address</h2>

<p>
A MAC address is a hardware-level address associated with a network
interface.
</p>

<pre>
Example:

00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Simple Difference:</strong><br><br>

IP address â†’ Logical network addressing<br>
MAC address â†’ Link-layer hardware addressing

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. TCP vs UDP</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>TCP</th>
<th>UDP</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Connection-oriented</td>
<td>Connectionless</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Reliable delivery</td>
<td>No delivery guarantee</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses acknowledgements and retransmission</td>
<td>No built-in retransmission</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More overhead</td>
<td>Lower overhead</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTP/HTTPS, SSH</td>
<td>DNS, streaming, real-time applications</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery using mechanisms such as
acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP is connectionless and has
lower overhead but does not guarantee delivery."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. OSI Model</h2>

</tr>

<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Physical</td>
<td>Cables, signals</td>
</tr>

</table>

<strong>Easy Memory Trick:</strong><br><br>

<strong>A</strong>ll<br>
<strong>P</strong>eople<br>
<strong>S</strong>eem<br>
<strong>T</strong>o<br>
<strong>N</strong>eed<br>
<strong>D</strong>ata<br>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. TCP/IP Model</h2>

<table>

<td>HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Transport</td>
<td>TCP, UDP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Internet</td>
<td>IP, ICMP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Network Access</td>
<td>Ethernet, ARP</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What is a Port?</h2>

<p>
A port identifies a specific network service running on a host.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Port</th>
<th>Service</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>22</td>
<td>SSH</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>80</td>
<td>HTTP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>443</td>
<td>HTTPS</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>53</td>
<td>DNS</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>25</td>
<td>SMTP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>3306</td>
<td>MySQL</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>5432</td>
<td>PostgreSQL</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>8080</td>
<td>Common alternative HTTP port</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is DNS?</h2>

<p>
DNS stands for <strong>Domain Name System</strong>.
It translates domain names into IP addresses.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User
â†’ www.example.com
<br>â†“<br>
DNS Resolver
<br>â†“<br>
DNS Server
<br>â†“<br>
IP Address
<br>â†“<br>
Web Server

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"DNS translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses so
clients can locate network services."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Common DNS Record Types</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Record</th>
<th>Purpose</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>A</td>
<td>Maps hostname to IPv4 address.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>AAAA</td>
<td>Maps hostname to IPv6 address.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>CNAME</td>
<td>Alias from one hostname to another.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>MX</td>
<td>Mail server information.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>TXT</td>
<td>Text information such as verification or policy records.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>NS</td>
<td>Authoritative name servers.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. HTTP vs HTTPS</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>HTTP</th>
<th>HTTPS</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Unencrypted application traffic.</td>
<td>HTTP protected using TLS.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Typically port 80.</td>
<td>Typically port 443.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Less secure for sensitive traffic.</td>
<td>Provides encryption and server authentication.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is a Firewall?</h2>

<p>
A firewall controls network traffic according to defined rules.
</p>

<p>
Rules can typically consider factors such as:
</p>

<ul>
<li>Source IP</li>
<li>Destination IP</li>
<li>Port</li>
<li>Protocol</li>
<li>Direction</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Cloud Example:</strong><br>

AWS Security Groups act as virtual firewalls for supported AWS
resources such as EC2 instances.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is a Subnet?</h2>

<p>
A subnet is a logical subdivision of an IP network.
</p>

<pre>
VPC
 |
 +-- Public Subnet
 |
 +-- Private Subnet
 |
 +-- Database Subnet
</pre>

<p>
In AWS, subnets are associated with a single Availability Zone.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. What is a Router?</h2>

<p>
A router forwards packets between different networks based on
routing information.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Network A
â†’ Router
â†’ Network B

</div>

<p>
In cloud environments, routing tables determine where network
traffic should be sent.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. What is NAT?</h2>

<p>
NAT stands for <strong>Network Address Translation</strong>.
It translates network addresses between different address spaces.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>AWS Example:</strong><br>

A NAT Gateway allows resources in a private subnet to initiate
outbound Internet connections without requiring those resources
to have public IP addresses.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. What is a Load Balancer?</h2>

<p>
A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple
backend servers or targets.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Client
<br>â†“<br>
Load Balancer
<br>â†“
<br>
Server 1 &nbsp;&nbsp; Server 2 &nbsp;&nbsp; Server 3

</div>

<h3>Benefits</h3>

<ul>
<li>High availability</li>
<li>Scalability</li>
<li>Traffic distribution</li>
<li>Health-based routing</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

</tr>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Networking Fundamentals</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Concept</th>
<th>Quick Answer</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>IP Address</td>
<td>Identifies a network interface or endpoint within an IP network.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Public IP</td>
<td>An address used for public network reachability when routing and security allow it.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Private IP</td>
<td>An address used within private network ranges and not directly routable on the public Internet.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>TCP</td>
<td>Connection-oriented transport protocol with reliable, ordered delivery.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>UDP</td>
<td>Connectionless transport protocol with lower overhead but no built-in delivery guarantee.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>DNS</td>
<td>Resolves domain names to IP addresses and other DNS records.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTP</td>
<td>Application-layer protocol commonly used for web communication.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>HTTPS</td>
<td>HTTP protected by TLS.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“
<br>

<br>â†“

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Public vs Private Subnet</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Public</th>
<th>Private</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Has a route toward an Internet Gateway.</td>
<td>Does not have a direct route to an Internet Gateway.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Common for internet-facing load balancers.</td>
<td>Common for application and database resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can support resources with public addressing.</td>
<td>Resources can use private addressing and controlled outbound paths.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Internet Gateway vs NAT Gateway</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Internet Gateway</th>
<th>NAT Gateway</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Provides VPC connectivity to the Internet when routes and addressing permit it.</td>
<td>Provides outbound Internet access for private resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used by public subnet routing.</td>
<td>Commonly used by private subnet routing.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Does not itself make a resource public.</td>
<td>Does not provide unsolicited inbound Internet access to private instances.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Security Group vs NACL</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Security Group:</strong><br>
Stateful â†’ resource/network-interface level â†’ allow rules.

<br><br>

<strong>NACL:</strong><br>
Stateless â†’ subnet level â†’ allow and deny rules.

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Scenario: Application Not Reachable</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I would troubleshoot layer by layer. First I would verify DNS
resolution, then network connectivity and routing. Next I would
check whether the required port is listening and whether firewall
or Security Group rules allow the traffic. If a load balancer is
involved, I would check the listener, target group and target health.
Finally, I would check the application logs."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Scenario: Private EC2 Cannot Access Internet</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I would verify the subnet route table and confirm that the default
route points to a NAT Gateway. Then I would verify that the NAT
Gateway has a valid path through the Internet Gateway, and check
Security Groups, NACLs and DNS configuration."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Scenario: Load Balancer Target Unhealthy</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ol>
<li>Target instance or pod is running.</li>
<li>Application is listening on the expected port.</li>
<li>Health-check path is correct.</li>
<li>Security Groups allow load-balancer traffic.</li>
<li>Network routing is correct.</li>
<li>Application returns the expected health-check response.</li>
<li>Review application and load-balancer logs.</li>
</ol>

</div>

</div>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ”</div>

<h1>Networking Security</h1>

<p>
High-priority networking security concepts for Cloud and DevOps
interviews, with practical AWS and Kubernetes examples.
</p>

</header>


<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Network Security?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Network security is the practice of protecting network resources,
systems and data from unauthorized access, attacks and unwanted
traffic.

</div>

<p>
In Cloud and DevOps, network security commonly involves:

</p>

<ul>
<li>Firewalls</li>
<li>Security Groups</li>
<li>Network ACLs</li>
<li>VPNs</li>
<li>Private Subnets</li>
<li>Encryption</li>
<li>Network segmentation</li>
<li>Least privilege</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Firewall</h2>

<p>
A firewall controls network traffic based on configured rules.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Incoming Traffic
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸ”¥ Firewall
<br>â†“<br>
Allowed â†’ Application
<br><br>
Denied â†’ âŒ Blocked

</div>

<p>
Rules can consider source, destination, protocol, port and direction.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. AWS Security Group</h2>

<p>
An AWS Security Group acts as a virtual firewall for supported
resources such as EC2 network interfaces.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important properties:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Stateful.</li>
<li>Controls inbound and outbound traffic.</li>
<li>Rules are allow-based.</li>
<li>Can reference another Security Group as a source or destination
where supported.</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Network ACL</h2>

<p>
A Network ACL is a subnet-level network traffic control mechanism.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important properties:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Stateless.</li>
<li>Supports allow and deny rules.</li>
<li>Associated with subnets.</li>
<li>Rules are evaluated in rule-number order.</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Security Group vs NACL</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Security Group</th>
<th>Network ACL</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Resource / network-interface level</td>
<td>Subnet level</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Stateful</td>
<td>Stateless</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Allow rules</td>
<td>Allow and deny rules</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>No explicit deny rules</td>
<td>Explicit deny possible</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly used for resource-level protection</td>
<td>Commonly used for subnet-level filtering</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Shortcut:</strong><br><br>

Security Group â†’ Stateful â†’ Resource level<br>
NACL â†’ Stateless â†’ Subnet level

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is Least Privilege?</h2>

<p>
Least privilege means providing only the minimum permissions and
network access required to perform a task.
</p>

<pre>
âŒ Bad:

Internet
   â†“
Application Server
Port 22, 80, 443, 8080
Source: 0.0.0.0/0

   â†“

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Network Segmentation</h2>

<p>
Network segmentation divides a network into separate zones to
reduce unnecessary communication and limit the impact of security
incidents.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Public Zone
<br>
Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>

<br>
Application Servers
<br>â†“<br>

<br>
