</div>

<p>
The database should not normally be directly accessible from the
public Internet.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Why Keep Databases in Private Subnets?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Databases are usually placed in private subnets so they are not
directly exposed to the public Internet.

Application traffic can reach the database through controlled
network paths and security rules.

</div>

<div class="flow">

ðŸŒ Internet
<br>â†“<br>
Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>
Application
<br>â†“<br>
Database

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. What is VPN?</h2>

<p>
VPN stands for Virtual Private Network. It creates an encrypted
connection between network endpoints over an underlying network.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Corporate Network
<br>â‡…<br>
ðŸ”’ Encrypted VPN Tunnel
<br>â‡…<br>
Cloud VPC

</div>

<p>
A common enterprise use case is securely connecting an on-premises
network with a cloud network.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. VPN vs Public Internet Access</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>VPN</th>
<th>Public Internet Access</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Encrypted tunnel between endpoints.</td>
<td>Traffic uses public network paths.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for private connectivity.</td>
<td>Used for public services.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Common for office-to-cloud connectivity.</td>
<td>Common for public websites and APIs.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Encryption in Networking</h2>

<p>
Encryption protects data by transforming readable information into
a form that unauthorized parties cannot easily understand.
</p>

<h3>Two Important States</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>State</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Data in Transit</td>
<td>Data moving across a network.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Data at Rest</td>
<td>Data stored on disks, databases or storage systems.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

HTTPS/TLS is commonly used to protect application traffic in transit.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is HTTPS?</h2>

<p>
HTTPS is HTTP transmitted over a TLS-protected connection.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Client
<br>â†“<br>
HTTPS : 443
<br>â†“<br>
TLS
<br>â†“<br>
Web Server

</div>

<h3>What does TLS provide?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Encryption</li>
<li>Integrity protection</li>
<li>Server authentication through certificates</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 13. What is a DDoS Attack?</h2>

<p>
A Distributed Denial-of-Service attack attempts to overwhelm a
service with a large amount of traffic or requests.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Many Sources
<br>â†“<br>
ðŸŒŠðŸŒŠðŸŒŠðŸŒŠðŸŒŠ
<br>â†“<br>
Target Application
<br>â†“<br>
Service Degradation / Unavailability

</div>

<h3>Common Defensive Measures</h3>

<ul>
<li>Traffic filtering</li>
<li>Rate limiting</li>
<li>Load balancing</li>
<li>CDN / edge protection</li>
<li>Managed DDoS protection services</li>
<li>Monitoring and alerting</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­ 14. Kubernetes Network Security</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes networking can be protected using several controls.
</p>

<ul>
<li>NetworkPolicies</li>
<li>RBAC</li>
<li>Pod security controls</li>
<li>Restricted container privileges</li>
<li>Secure ingress configuration</li>
<li>Private cluster networking where appropriate</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>NetworkPolicy:</strong><br>

Can restrict which pods or namespaces are allowed to communicate
with other workloads, depending on the network plugin and policy
support.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Secure CI/CD Networking</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
CI/CD System
<br>â†“<br>
Private Cloud Resources
<br>â†“<br>
Application
<br>â†“<br>
Database

</div>

<h3>Good Practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Restrict CI/CD network access.</li>
<li>Use private endpoints where appropriate.</li>
<li>Avoid exposing management ports publicly.</li>
<li>Use temporary credentials or roles.</li>
<li>Apply least privilege.</li>
<li>Monitor network activity.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. SSH Security</h2>

<p>
SSH is commonly used for secure remote administration.
</p>

<h3>Port</h3>

<pre>
TCP 22
</pre>

<h3>Security Practices</h3>

<ul>
<li>Prefer key-based authentication.</li>
<li>Restrict SSH source networks.</li>
<li>Avoid exposing SSH to the entire Internet unnecessarily.</li>
<li>Use bastion hosts or managed access mechanisms where appropriate.</li>
<li>Keep systems updated.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Real-Time Scenario: EC2 Port 22 Is Open to Everyone</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Question:</strong><br><br>

"An EC2 Security Group allows SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. Is that a good
security practice?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong><br>

"No. It exposes the SSH service to the entire Internet. I would
restrict the source to a trusted IP range or use a more secure
management approach such as a bastion host or AWS Systems Manager
where appropriate."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Real-Time Scenario: Database Is Publicly Accessible</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Approach:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Identify why public access is required.</li>

<li>Remove unnecessary public exposure.</li>

<li>Place the database in private subnets where appropriate.</li>

<li>Restrict inbound access to only required application sources.</li>

<li>Review route tables and network controls.</li>

<li>Monitor and verify the new configuration.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Security Incident: Unexpected Open Port</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Steps:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Identify the service using the port.</li>

<li>Determine whether the port is required.</li>

<li>Check the source of the traffic.</li>

<li>Review Security Group / firewall rules.</li>

<li>Restrict or remove unnecessary access.</li>

<li>Check logs for suspicious activity.</li>

<li>Document the remediation.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ 20. Most Important Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>What is network security?</li>

<li>What is a firewall?</li>

<li>What is a Security Group?</li>

<li>What is a Network ACL?</li>

<li>Security Group vs NACL?</li>

<li>What is least privilege?</li>

<li>Why are databases placed in private subnets?</li>

<li>What is network segmentation?</li>

<li>What is VPN?</li>

<li>How does HTTPS secure traffic?</li>

<li>What is a DDoS attack?</li>

<li>How do you secure Kubernetes networking?</li>

<li>How do you secure SSH?</li>

<li>How would you respond to an unexpectedly open port?</li>

</ol>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Quick Revision</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Firewall</strong> â†’ Controls Traffic

<br><br>

<strong>Security Group</strong> â†’ Stateful Resource-Level Control

<br><br>

<strong>NACL</strong> â†’ Stateless Subnet-Level Control

<br><br>

<strong>VPN</strong> â†’ Encrypted Private Connectivity

<br><br>

<strong>HTTPS/TLS</strong> â†’ Protects Data in Transit

<br><br>

<strong>Segmentation</strong> â†’ Separates Network Zones

<br><br>

<br><br>

<h1>Networking Troubleshooting</h1>

<p>
Real-time networking troubleshooting commands, methodology and
Cloud/DevOps interview scenarios.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. Networking Troubleshooting Approach</h2>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>â†“<br>
Port
<br>â†“<br>
DNS
<br>â†“<br>
IP Connectivity
<br>â†“<br>
Routing
<br>â†“<br>
Firewall / Security
<br>â†“<br>
Network Interface

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Tip:</strong><br>

Don't randomly run commands. Troubleshoot layer by layer and
identify exactly where communication is failing.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. ping</h2>

<p>
The <code>ping</code> command is commonly used to test basic
network reachability using ICMP.
</p>

<pre>
ping 8.8.8.8
ping 192.168.1.10
</pre>

<h3>What does it tell us?</h3>

<ul>
<li>Whether a destination responds to ICMP.</li>
<li>Approximate round-trip time.</li>
<li>Packet loss.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

A failed ping does not always mean the application is unreachable.
ICMP may be blocked while TCP traffic is still allowed.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. nslookup</h2>

<p>
Used to test DNS resolution.
</p>

<pre>
nslookup google.com
</pre>

<p>
If DNS resolution fails, investigate DNS configuration before
assuming there is an application connectivity problem.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. dig</h2>

<p>
<code>dig</code> provides detailed DNS query information.
</p>

<pre>
dig example.com
dig example.com A
dig example.com MX
</pre>

<h3>Useful Information</h3>

<ul>
<li>DNS server used</li>
<li>Answer records</li>
<li>TTL</li>
<li>Query status</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. curl</h2>

<p>
<code>curl</code> is extremely useful for testing HTTP/HTTPS
connectivity and APIs.
</p>

<pre>
curl http://example.com

curl -I https://example.com

curl -v https://example.com
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>DevOps Use Case:</strong><br>

When an application is not responding, curl helps determine whether
the HTTP endpoint itself is reachable and what response the server
returns.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. ss</h2>

<p>
<code>ss</code> displays socket and network connection information.
</p>

<pre>
ss -tulnp
</pre>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Option</th>
<th>Meaning</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>-t</td>
<td>TCP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>-u</td>
<td>UDP</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>-l</td>
<td>Listening sockets</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>-n</td>
<td>Don't resolve service names</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>-p</td>
<td>Show process information where permitted</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. ip addr</h2>

<p>
Displays network interfaces and their IP addresses.
</p>

<pre>
ip addr
</pre>

<p>
Use it to check whether the expected interface has an IP address
and whether the interface is up.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. ip route</h2>

<p>
Displays the system's routing table.
</p>

<pre>
ip route
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Question:</strong><br><br>

"What do you check if a server cannot reach another network?"

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong><br>

"I first verify the routing table to make sure there is a valid
route toward the destination."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. traceroute</h2>

<p>
Shows the network hops taken toward a destination.
</p>

<pre>
traceroute example.com
</pre>

<p>
On Windows, the equivalent command is:

</p>

<pre>
tracert example.com
</pre>

<p>
It can help identify where traffic appears to stop or experience
unexpected delay.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Test a Specific Port</h2>

<p>
Sometimes the network is reachable but a particular service port
is not accessible.
</p>

<h3>Linux</h3>

<pre>
nc -zv 10.0.1.10 8080
</pre>

<h3>Windows PowerShell</h3>

<pre>
Test-NetConnection 10.0.1.10 -Port 8080
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Key idea:</strong><br>

Ping tests basic ICMP reachability. A TCP port test checks whether
a specific service port can be reached.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. DNS Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>â†“<br>
Hostname
<br>â†“<br>
DNS Resolution
<br>â†“<br>
IP Address
<br>â†“<br>
TCP Connection
<br>â†“<br>
Application Response

</div>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre>
nslookup example.com
dig example.com
</pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Correct DNS record?</li>
<li>Correct DNS server?</li>
<li>DNS resolution working?</li>
<li>Correct IP returned?</li>
<li>Network route available?</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Application Not Reachable</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

An application is running on port 8080, but users cannot access it.

<br><br>

<strong>Troubleshooting:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Check whether the application process is running.</li>

<li>Check whether port 8080 is listening.</li>

<li>Check the server's IP address.</li>

<li>Check local firewall rules.</li>

<li>Check cloud Security Group / firewall rules.</li>

<li>Check subnet route table.</li>

<li>Check Network ACL where applicable.</li>

<li>Check load balancer listener and target health if a load balancer is used.</li>

<li>Test using curl or a TCP port test.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. EC2 Cannot Access Internet</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Scenario:</strong><br>

An EC2 instance cannot download packages or access an external
website.

<br><br>

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Does the instance have network connectivity?</li>

<li>Is the subnet public or private?</li>

<li>Check the route table.</li>

<li>For private subnets, verify NAT Gateway configuration.</li>

<li>Verify NAT Gateway has a working path to the Internet Gateway.</li>

<li>Check Security Group rules.</li>

<li>Check Network ACL rules.</li>

<li>Check DNS resolution.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. DNS Works but Website Doesn't</h2>

<div class="flow">

DNS
<br>â†“
<br>
IP returned successfully
<br>â†“
<br>
TCP connection
<br>â†“
<br>
Port 80 / 443
<br>â†“
<br>
HTTP response

</div>

<p>
If DNS resolves correctly, the next step is to test TCP and HTTP
connectivity rather than repeatedly checking DNS.
</p>

<pre>
curl -v https://example.com

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Connection Refused vs Timeout</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Connection Refused</th>
<th>Connection Timeout</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Host is reachable but the connection was rejected.</td>
<td>No response was received within the expected time.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Possible service not listening.</td>
<td>Possible routing or firewall issue.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Wrong application port is another possibility.</td>
<td>Security Group, NACL or network path may be involved.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Load Balancer Troubleshooting</h2>

<br>â†“

</div>

<li>Load balancer status</li>
<li>Listener configuration</li>
<li>Target group</li>
<li>Health check path</li>
<li>Target health</li>
<li>Security groups</li>
<li>Application port</li>
<li>Application logs</li>
</ul>

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Kubernetes Networking Troubleshooting</h2>

</pre>

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. EKS Architecture at a Glance</h2>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. EKS Control Plane</h2>

<p>
The EKS control plane runs Kubernetes control-plane components
required to manage cluster state and workloads.
</p>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Responsibility</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>API Server</td>
<td>Entry point for Kubernetes API requests.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>etcd</td>
<td>Stores Kubernetes cluster state.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Scheduler</td>
<td>Selects suitable nodes for Pods.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controllers</td>
<td>Continuously reconcile desired and actual state.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

AWS manages the underlying EKS control-plane infrastructure.
You interact with the Kubernetes API rather than managing the
control-plane servers yourself.

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. How Does a Request Reach a Pod?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"A user first resolves the application domain through DNS. The
request reaches an AWS load balancer, which forwards traffic to
the Kubernetes Service or its backend targets. The Service then
routes the request to an appropriate Pod, where the application
process handles the request."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. How Does a Pod Get Network Connectivity?</h2>

<div class="answer">

In a typical AWS VPC CNI setup, the CNI plugin assigns networking
from the VPC to Pods using available VPC IP resources. This allows
Pod traffic to integrate with AWS VPC routing and security controls.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. EKS Architecture Interview Scenario</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Question:</strong><br><br>

"Design a highly available EKS architecture for a production
application."

<br><br>

<strong>Answer:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Create an EKS cluster across multiple Availability Zones.</li>

<li>Use private subnets for worker nodes where appropriate.</li>

<li>Deploy multiple worker nodes across Availability Zones.</li>

<li>Use an internet-facing load balancer for public traffic.</li>

<li>Use Kubernetes Services to distribute traffic to Pods.</li>

<li>Use managed node groups or another appropriate compute model.</li>

<li>Use appropriate IAM and Kubernetes RBAC controls.</li>

<li>Use NetworkPolicies where supported and required.</li>

<li>Use persistent storage through appropriate CSI drivers.</li>

<li>Add monitoring, logging and alerting.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>

<li>How do worker nodes communicate with the control plane?</li>

<li>How does EKS integrate with VPC?</li>

<li>How does the AWS VPC CNI work at a high level?</li>

<li>How does traffic reach a Pod?</li>

<li>How does an Ingress expose an application?</li>

<li>How does IAM integrate with EKS?</li>

<li>What is the difference between IAM and RBAC?</li>

<li>Managed Node Group vs Fargate?</li>

<li>How would you design highly available EKS?</li>

<li>How would you secure an EKS cluster?</li>

</ol>

</div>

<h1>Amazon EKS Basics</h1>

<p>
High-priority Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service fundamentals
for Cloud & DevOps interviews.

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Amazon EKS?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Amazon EKS, or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service, is a managed
Kubernetes service provided by AWS.

AWS manages the Kubernetes control plane infrastructure, while
the customer manages workloads and worker compute according to
the chosen EKS architecture.

</div>

<h3>Simple Interview Answer</h3>

<p>
"EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes service. AWS manages the
Kubernetes control plane, while I deploy and manage my applications
on worker nodes or other supported compute options."
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Why Do We Use EKS?</h2>

<ul>
<li>Run containerized applications using Kubernetes.</li>
<li>Reduce operational effort for the Kubernetes control plane.</li>
<li>Integrate Kubernetes with AWS services.</li>
<li>Support scalable and highly available workloads.</li>
<li>Use Kubernetes orchestration, deployments and services.</li>
<li>Integrate with CI/CD and DevOps tooling.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. EKS High-Level Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

<br>
â”‚ Kubernetes Control Plane      â”‚
<br>
â”‚ API Server / etcd / Scheduler â”‚
<br>
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜
<br>
â†“
<br>
â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”

<br>
<strong>Pods â†’ Containers â†’ Applications</strong>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. EKS Control Plane</h2>

<p>
The EKS control plane contains the Kubernetes components responsible
for managing the cluster state and coordinating workloads.
</p>

<h3>Important Components</h3>

<ul>
<li>Kubernetes API Server</li>
<li>etcd</li>
<li>Scheduler</li>
<li>Controller Manager</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

AWS operates the EKS control-plane infrastructure for the managed
EKS service. As a user, you interact with it primarily through the
Kubernetes API and AWS APIs/tools.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Kubernetes API Server</h2>

<p>
The API Server is the main entry point to the Kubernetes control
plane.
</p>

<div class="flow">

kubectl
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes API Server
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Resources

</div>

<h3>Example</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pods
</pre>

<p>
The kubectl command communicates with the Kubernetes API Server.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. What is etcd?</h2>

<p>
etcd is a distributed key-value store used by Kubernetes to store
cluster state and configuration data.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"etcd stores Kubernetes cluster state, such as resource
configuration and metadata. The Kubernetes control plane uses it
as its backing data store."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. What is the Kubernetes Scheduler?</h2>

<p>
The scheduler determines which suitable node should run a newly
created Pod.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Pod Created
<br>â†“<br>
Scheduler
<br>â†“<br>
Select Suitable Node
<br>â†“<br>
Pod Runs on Node

</div>

<p>
It considers factors such as resource availability, scheduling
constraints, affinity and taints/tolerations.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. What are Worker Nodes?</h2>

<p>
Worker nodes provide compute capacity where Kubernetes workloads
run.
</p>

<div class="flow">

EKS Cluster
<br>â†“
<br>
Worker Node
<br>â†“
<br>
kubelet + Container Runtime
<br>â†“
<br>
Pods
<br>â†“
<br>
Containers

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. EKS Managed Node Group</h2>

<p>
A managed node group is a group of EC2 worker nodes that EKS helps
provision and manage as part of the cluster.
</p>

<h3>Benefits</h3>

<ul>
<li>Automated node provisioning.</li>
<li>Integration with EKS lifecycle operations.</li>
<li>Scaling support.</li>
<li>Managed node update workflows.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. EKS with Fargate</h2>

<p>
AWS Fargate can provide serverless compute for supported EKS Pods,
so you don't manage the underlying EC2 worker nodes for those Pods.
</p>

<div class="flow">

EKS
<br>â†“<br>
Pod
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Fargate
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Managed Compute

</div>

<h3>Managed Nodes vs Fargate</h3>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Managed Node Group</th>
<th>Fargate</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses EC2 worker nodes.</td>
<td>Runs supported Pods on serverless compute.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>You manage node-level configuration and capacity.</td>
<td>No EC2 worker node management for those Pods.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More control over node configuration.</td>
<td>Less infrastructure management.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. What is a Pod?</h2>

<p>
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Node
<br>â†“<br>
Pod
<br>â†“<br>
Container
<br>â†“<br>
Application

</div>

<p>
A Pod can contain one or more containers that share networking and
storage resources within the Pod.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. What is kubelet?</h2>

<p>
kubelet is the Kubernetes node agent that runs on worker nodes.
It communicates with the Kubernetes control plane and makes sure
the assigned Pods and containers are running as specified.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Remember:</strong><br>

API Server â†’ Control Plane<br>
kubelet â†’ Worker Node Agent

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. What is kube-proxy?</h2>

<p>
kube-proxy is a Kubernetes component traditionally responsible for
implementing service networking rules on nodes.
</p>

<p>
In AWS EKS, networking behavior also depends on the AWS VPC CNI and
the Kubernetes networking configuration.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. How Does kubectl Connect to EKS?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
kubectl
<br>â†“<br>
kubeconfig
<br>â†“<br>
EKS Kubernetes API Server
<br>â†“<br>
Cluster Resources

</div>

<h3>Common Command</h3>

<pre>
aws eks update-kubeconfig \
--region ap-south-1 \
--name my-eks-cluster
</pre>

<p>
This configures kubeconfig so kubectl can connect to the specified
EKS cluster using AWS authentication integration.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. EKS Cluster vs Kubernetes Cluster</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Self-Managed Kubernetes</th>
<th>Amazon EKS</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>You manage the Kubernetes control plane.</td>
<td>AWS provides the managed Kubernetes control plane.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>You handle control-plane infrastructure.</td>
<td>AWS handles the underlying control-plane infrastructure.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>You manage infrastructure integration yourself.</td>
<td>EKS integrates with AWS services.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>More operational responsibility.</td>
<td>Reduced control-plane operational burden.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. What is an EKS Cluster?</h2>

<div class="answer">

An EKS cluster is the Kubernetes environment running on AWS. It
includes the managed Kubernetes control plane and the compute
resources used to run workloads, such as managed node groups,
self-managed nodes or Fargate depending on the architecture.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. EKS and VPC</h2>

<p>
EKS integrates closely with AWS VPC networking.
</p>

<div class="flow">

AWS VPC
<br>â†“<br>
Subnets
<br>â†“<br>
EKS Cluster
<br>â†“<br>
Worker Nodes
<br>â†“<br>
Pods

</div>

<p>
The exact networking model depends on the EKS configuration, but
AWS VPC networking is a major EKS interview topic.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. EKS Authentication vs Authorization</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Authentication</th>
<th>Authorization</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Who are you?</td>
<td>What are you allowed to do?</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Identity verification.</td>
<td>Permission evaluation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>AWS IAM can participate in EKS authentication.</td>
<td>Kubernetes RBAC controls Kubernetes permissions.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Easy Interview Line:</strong><br>

IAM helps establish identity/access from the AWS side, while
Kubernetes RBAC determines what an authenticated identity can do
inside Kubernetes.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Common EKS Commands</h2>

<pre>

--name my-eks-cluster

--region ap-south-1 \
--name my-eks-cluster

</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Real-Time Scenario: Node Is Not Ready</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Approach:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Check node status.</li>

<li>Run <code>kubectl describe node</code>.</li>

<li>Check kubelet/node conditions.</li>

<li>Check CPU and memory availability.</li>

<li>Check networking and CNI status.</li>

<li>Check node IAM permissions.</li>

<li>Check system and Kubernetes events.</li>

<li>Check whether the node can communicate with the control plane.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Real-Time Scenario: Pod Stuck in Pending</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Possible Causes:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Insufficient CPU or memory.</li>
<li>Node selector mismatch.</li>
<li>Affinity rules.</li>
<li>Taints without matching tolerations.</li>
<li>Insufficient available nodes.</li>
<li>Storage or volume constraints.</li>
</ul>

<strong>First Command:</strong>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

</div>

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. What is Amazon EKS?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Amazon EKS is a managed Kubernetes service provided by AWS.
AWS manages the Kubernetes control-plane infrastructure while
customers manage workloads, worker capacity and cluster
configuration according to the chosen architecture.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. EKS High-Level Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¤ User

<br>

<br>â†“
<br>
Applications

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Control Plane vs Data Plane</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Control Plane</th>
<th>Data Plane</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Runs Kubernetes control components.</td>
<td>Runs application workloads.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed by AWS in EKS.</td>
<td>Uses compute capacity such as managed nodes, self-managed nodes or other supported compute models.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>API Server, scheduler and controllers are part of the Kubernetes control plane.</td>
<td>Worker nodes run Pods and container workloads.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<strong>Key Point:</strong><br>

EKS integrates Kubernetes networking with AWS VPC networking.
The AWS VPC CNI is commonly used to provide Pod networking.

<div class="answer">

Ingress defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules to Services.

resources to provision and configure Application Load Balancers.

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. IAM vs RBAC</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>IAM:</strong>
Controls AWS-level identity and permissions.

<br><br>

<strong>Kubernetes RBAC:</strong>
Controls authorization to Kubernetes resources.

<br><br>

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"IAM determines who can access AWS/EKS and what AWS permissions
they have, while Kubernetes RBAC determines what an authorized
identity can do inside Kubernetes."

</div>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Real-Time Scenario</h2>

<span class="badge">VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h3>Question:</h3>

<p>
Your application is running on EKS. Suddenly traffic increases
10x. How will you handle it?
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br><br>

"First, the load balancer distributes the increased traffic to
the application. HPA can detect increased resource utilization
and increase the number of Pod replicas. If the existing nodes
do not have enough capacity, a node provisioning mechanism such
as Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter can add compute capacity.
Once the new nodes are ready, pending Pods are scheduled.
I would monitor the application using metrics and logs and verify
that the system has recovered."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Real-Time Failure Scenario</h2>

<h3>Question:</h3>

<p>
A Pod is running but users cannot access the application.
How do you troubleshoot?
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Step 1:</strong> Check Pod status.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 2:</strong> Check application logs.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 3:</strong> Check Service.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 4:</strong> Check Endpoints / EndpointSlices.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 5:</strong> Check DNS.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 6:</strong> Check Ingress / Load Balancer.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 7:</strong> Check Security Groups and NetworkPolicies.

<br><br>

<strong>Step 8:</strong> Check AWS networking and routing.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Top 20 EKS Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. EKS Networking Overview</h2>

<div class="flow">

AWS VPC
<br>â†“<br>
Subnets
<br>â†“<br>
EKS Nodes
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<p>
EKS networking connects Kubernetes workloads with AWS VPC

</p>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. What is AWS VPC CNI?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Amazon VPC CNI plugin is the networking plugin used by EKS
to provide Kubernetes Pods with networking integrated with the
AWS VPC.

</div>

<h3>High-Level Flow</h3>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>â†“<br>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. How Does a Pod Get an IP?</h2>

<p>
With the AWS VPC CNI, Pods can receive IP addresses from the VPC
networking space using the networking resources available to the

</p>

<div class="flow">

Worker Node
<br>â†“<br>
VPC CNI
<br>â†“<br>
VPC Networking Resources
<br>â†“<br>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

Pod IP capacity is therefore influenced by the networking resources

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. EKS Subnets</h2>

<p>
EKS clusters commonly use multiple subnets across Availability

â””â”€â”€ Private Subnet

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Public vs Private Subnets in EKS</h2>

<tr>
<th>Public Subnet</th>
<th>Private Subnet</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Has a route toward an Internet Gateway.</td>
<td>No direct route to an Internet Gateway.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Commonly used for internet-facing load balancers.</td>
<td>Commonly used for worker nodes and internal workloads.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Can support public-facing infrastructure.</td>
<td>Can use NAT or private endpoints for required outbound access.</td>
</tr>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Kubernetes Service</h2>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. NodePort</h2>

<p>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<p>
NodePort is less commonly preferred as the primary production

<br>â†“<br>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Security Groups in EKS</h2>

<p>
AWS Security Groups control network traffic for AWS network

</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Example:</strong><br>

An application load balancer should be allowed to communicate
with the application targets on the required port, while unrelated
sources should not be granted unnecessary access.

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. NetworkPolicy</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy can restrict network communication
between Pods and other network endpoints, depending on the

</p>

<div class="flow">

Pod A
<br>â†“
<br>
NetworkPolicy
<br>â†“
<br>
Allowed â†’ Pod B
<br>
Denied â†’ Pod C

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

NetworkPolicy and AWS Security Groups operate at different layers
and should not be treated as replacements for one another.

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. How Do Pods Communicate?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Pods can communicate through Kubernetes networking. In an AWS VPC

Kubernetes Services provide stable endpoints for groups of Pods.

</div>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Pod-to-Service Communication</h2>

<div class="flow">

Frontend Pod
<br>â†“<br>
backend-service
<br>â†“<br>
Service Discovery
<br>â†“<br>
Backend Pods

</div>

<p>
Applications normally communicate with a Service rather than

</p>

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Pod-to-Internet Communication</h2>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. EKS Networking Troubleshooting</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Scenario:</strong> Pod cannot reach another service.

<br><br>

<strong>Check in order:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Is the Pod Running?</li>

<li>Does the target Service exist?</li>

<li>Does the Service selector match the Pods?</li>

<li>Are endpoints / EndpointSlices populated?</li>

<li>Is DNS resolution working?</li>

<li>Are NetworkPolicies blocking traffic?</li>

<li>Are AWS Security Groups or routing involved?</li>

<li>Check CNI health and node networking.</li>

<li>Check application listening port.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Pod Cannot Access Internet</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Check:</strong>

<ol>

<li>Pod IP / node networking.</li>

<li>Subnet configuration.</li>

<li>Route table.</li>

<li>NAT Gateway for private subnets.</li>

<li>Internet Gateway path.</li>

<li>Security Group rules.</li>

<li>NACL rules where applicable.</li>

<li>DNS resolution.</li>

<li>VPC CNI health and IP availability.</li>

</ol>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Pod IP Exhaustion</h2>

<p>
In VPC CNI networking, available IP capacity can become a scaling
constraint.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Possible causes:</strong>

<ul>
<li>Subnet has insufficient free IP addresses.</li>
<li>Node has reached its available Pod networking capacity.</li>
<li>High Pod density.</li>
<li>VPC CNI configuration or instance networking limits.</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<li>Explain EKS networking architecture.</li>

<li>What is Ingress?</li>

<li>How does an ALB work with EKS?</li>

<li>How do Pods communicate with each other?</li>

<li>How does a Pod access the Internet?</li>

<li>What is NetworkPolicy?</li>

<li>Security Group vs NetworkPolicy?</li>

</ol>

<h1>EKS Security</h1>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. EKS Security Architecture</h2>

<div class="flow">

ðŸ‘¤ User / Application
<br>â†“<br>
AWS IAM
<br>â†“<br>
EKS Access
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes API Server
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes RBAC
<br>â†“<br>

<br><br>

<br>â†“<br>

<br><br>

<br>â†“<br>

<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. IAM vs Kubernetes RBAC</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>IAM</th>
<th>Kubernetes RBAC</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>AWS-level identity and permissions.</td>
<td>Kubernetes-level authorization.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controls access to AWS resources.</td>
<td>Controls access to Kubernetes resources.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Uses IAM users, roles and policies.</td>
<td>Uses Roles, ClusterRoles and bindings.</td>
</tr>

</table>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"IAM controls access to AWS resources and EKS access, while
Kubernetes RBAC controls what an authenticated identity can do
inside the Kubernetes API."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. IAM Role for EKS</h2>

<p>
EKS commonly uses IAM roles for AWS service and workload access.
Using roles avoids embedding long-lived AWS access keys inside
applications.
</p>

<div class="flow">

IAM Role
<br>â†“<br>
Temporary Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
AWS API
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Resource

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. EKS Access Control</h2>

<p>
Access to an EKS cluster should be explicitly granted to the
identities that need it.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Best Practice:</strong><br>

Give users and automation only the permissions they require.
Avoid broad administrative permissions unless genuinely necessary.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Kubernetes RBAC</h2>

<p>
RBAC controls which Kubernetes API actions an identity can perform
on specific resources.
</p>

<div class="flow">

User / Service Account
<br>â†“<br>
Role / ClusterRole
<br>â†“<br>
RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Resources

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Role vs ClusterRole</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Role</th>
<th>ClusterRole</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Namespace-scoped.</td>
<td>Can define permissions at cluster scope.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Used for resources within a namespace.</td>
<td>Can be used for cluster-scoped resources and can also be
bound into namespaces.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>RoleBinding:</strong><br>
Grants permissions within a namespace.

<br><br>

<strong>ClusterRoleBinding:</strong><br>
Grants a ClusterRole across the cluster scope represented by the
binding.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Kubernetes Service Accounts</h2>

<p>
Service Accounts provide identities for workloads running inside

</p>

<div class="flow">

<br>â†“<br>

<br>â†“<br>
Identity
<br>â†“<br>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

Do not give every application broad permissions. Create dedicated
identities with only the permissions required.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. EKS Pod Access to AWS Services</h2>

<p>
Applications running in EKS may need to access services such as
S3, DynamoDB or Secrets Manager.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Service Account
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Role
<br>â†“<br>
AWS API
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Service

</div>

<p>
A common approach is to associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes
workload identity mechanism so the application receives controlled
AWS permissions without storing static access keys in the Pod.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Kubernetes Secrets</h2>

<p>
Kubernetes Secrets are designed to hold sensitive configuration
data such as passwords, tokens and keys.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl get secrets -A

kubectl describe secret &lt;secret-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Important:</strong><br>

Kubernetes Secrets should not automatically be treated as a
complete secret-management solution. Protect access to them and
consider dedicated secret-management services for sensitive
production workloads.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Encryption of Secrets</h2>

<p>
EKS can integrate with AWS encryption capabilities to protect
Kubernetes data at rest.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Kubernetes Secret
<br>â†“<br>
Encryption
<br>â†“<br>
Encrypted Data
<br>â†“<br>
Persistent Storage

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Security Groups</h2>

<p>
Security Groups provide stateful network access control for AWS
resources and network interfaces.
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Example:</strong><br>

Allow application traffic only from the expected load balancer or
trusted source instead of opening application ports to the entire
Internet.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Network Policies</h2>

<p>
NetworkPolicy can control allowed network communication between
Pods and other endpoints, depending on the networking implementation
and policy support.
</p>

<div class="flow">

Frontend Pod
<br>â†“<br>
NetworkPolicy
<br>â†“<br>
Allowed â†’ Backend Pod
<br>
Denied â†’ Untrusted Pod

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Security Groups vs NetworkPolicy</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Security Group</th>
<th>NetworkPolicy</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>AWS networking layer.</td>
<td>Kubernetes networking layer.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Controls traffic to AWS network interfaces/resources.</td>
<td>Controls Pod-level traffic according to supported implementation.</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Managed through AWS.</td>
<td>Managed through Kubernetes resources.</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Private EKS Cluster Endpoint</h2>

<p>
EKS cluster endpoint access can be configured to control how the
Kubernetes API endpoint is reached.
</p>

<div class="answer">

A private endpoint can reduce exposure of the Kubernetes API to
public networks. Access then needs appropriate connectivity from
the environments that administer the cluster.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. EKS Security Best Practices</h2>

<ul>

<li>Follow least-privilege IAM.</li>

<li>Use dedicated IAM roles for workloads.</li>

<li>Use Kubernetes RBAC carefully.</li>

<li>Avoid unnecessary cluster-admin permissions.</li>

<li>Use private subnets where appropriate.</li>

<li>Restrict network access with Security Groups.</li>

<li>Use NetworkPolicies where appropriate.</li>

<li>Protect Kubernetes Secrets.</li>

<li>Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit.</li>

<li>Regularly update Kubernetes and node components.</li>

<li>Enable appropriate logging and monitoring.</li>

<li>Scan container images for vulnerabilities.</li>

</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Scenario: Developer Needs Read-Only Access</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Approach:</strong>

<br><br>

Create or use an identity with read-only permissions and grant
access only to the required namespaces/resources.

Do not give the developer cluster-admin access simply because it
is easier.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Scenario: Pod Needs S3 Access</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would create a dedicated workload identity and associate it with
an IAM role containing only the required S3 permissions. I would
avoid storing AWS access keys directly inside the Pod."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Scenario: Unauthorized Kubernetes Access</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>

<li>Which identity is making the request?</li>

<li>Does the identity have EKS access?</li>

<li>What Kubernetes RBAC permissions exist?</li>

<li>Is the resource namespace correct?</li>

<li>Is the requested verb allowed?</li>

</ul>

<pre>
kubectl auth can-i get pods

kubectl auth can-i create deployments

kubectl auth can-i delete pods
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Scenario: Secure a Production EKS Cluster</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<br><br>

"I would use least-privilege IAM and Kubernetes RBAC, dedicated
workload identities, private networking where appropriate,
Security Groups and NetworkPolicies, protected Secrets, encryption,
regular patching, image scanning, logging and continuous monitoring."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ”¥ 21. Top EKS Security Interview Questions</h2>

<ol>

<li>Explain EKS security architecture.</li>

<li>IAM vs Kubernetes RBAC?</li>

<li>What is a Service Account?</li>

<li>How can a Pod access S3 securely?</li>

<li>Why should you avoid AWS access keys inside Pods?</li>

<li>What is least privilege?</li>

<li>Role vs ClusterRole?</li>

<li>RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding?</li>

<li>Security Group vs NetworkPolicy?</li>

<li>How do you secure Kubernetes Secrets?</li>

<li>How would you secure the EKS API endpoint?</li>

<li>How would you secure a production EKS cluster?</li>

<li>How do you troubleshoot an unauthorized request?</li>

</ol>

</div>

<h1>EKS Troubleshooting</h1>

<p>
Real-time Amazon EKS troubleshooting scenarios, diagnostic commands

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 1. EKS Troubleshooting Method</h2>

<div class="flow">

Problem
<br>â†“<br>
Identify Layer
<br>â†“<br>
Check Status
<br>â†“<br>
Check Events
<br>â†“<br>
Check Logs
<br>â†“<br>
Check Networking / IAM
<br>â†“<br>
Fix
<br>â†“<br>
Verify

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Rule:</strong>

Don't randomly change configurations. First identify whether the
problem is at the Pod, Node, Kubernetes, AWS networking, IAM or
application layer.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 2. Essential Troubleshooting Commands</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get nodes

kubectl get pods -A

kubectl get pods -o wide

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;

kubectl get events -A

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl get svc -A

kubectl get endpoints -A

kubectl get endpointslices -A

kubectl get ns

kubectl get deployments -A

kubectl get daemonsets -A

kubectl get configmaps -A

kubectl get secrets -A
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 3. Scenario: Pod Stuck in Pending</h2>

<span class="tag">VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
A Pending Pod means Kubernetes has not successfully scheduled or
started it yet.
</p>

<h3>Step 1 â€” Check Pod</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<h3>Step 2 â€” Describe Pod</h3>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Insufficient CPU or memory.</li>
<li>Node selector mismatch.</li>
<li>Affinity / anti-affinity.</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations.</li>
<li>Persistent volume constraints.</li>
<li>Scheduling events.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would first describe the Pod and inspect the Events section.
Then I would check node capacity, taints, tolerations, selectors,
affinity rules and storage constraints."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 4. Scenario: Pod in CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<span class="tag">VERY COMMON</span>

<p>
CrashLoopBackOff means a container is repeatedly starting and
crashing, with Kubernetes applying increasing restart delays.
</p>

<h3>Commands</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Application error.</li>
<li>Incorrect environment variables.</li>
<li>Missing configuration.</li>
<li>Missing Secret or ConfigMap.</li>
<li>Wrong command or arguments.</li>
<li>Dependency unavailable.</li>
<li>Health probe causing restarts.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 5. Scenario: Pod in ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<p>
The node cannot successfully pull the container image.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect image name.</li>
<li>Incorrect image tag.</li>
<li>Private registry authentication problem.</li>
<li>Registry unavailable.</li>
<li>Network connectivity problem.</li>
<li>Insufficient permissions.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Approach:</strong><br>

"I would inspect Pod events first. I would verify the image
repository and tag, registry authentication, node connectivity
and required permissions."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 6. Scenario: Node is NotReady</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get nodes

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;
</pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Node Conditions.</li>
<li>MemoryPressure.</li>
<li>DiskPressure.</li>
<li>PIDPressure.</li>
<li>NetworkUnavailable.</li>
<li>kubelet health.</li>
<li>Node connectivity to the control plane.</li>
<li>Instance health.</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would check the node conditions and Events first. Then I would
investigate kubelet health, resource pressure, networking,
instance health and connectivity with the EKS control plane."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 7. Scenario: High CPU or Memory</h2>

<pre>
kubectl top nodes

kubectl top pods -A
</pre>

<p>
If Metrics Server or another metrics provider is available, these
commands can show resource utilization.
</p>

<h3>Investigate</h3>

<ul>
<li>Which Pod consumes the resources?</li>
<li>Are resource requests configured?</li>
<li>Are resource limits appropriate?</li>
<li>Is HPA configured?</li>
<li>Does the node have enough capacity?</li>
<li>Should the node group scale?</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 8. Scenario: Service Not Reachable</h2>

<div class="flow">

Client
<br>â†“
<br>
Service
<br>â†“
<br>
Endpoints
<br>â†“
<br>
Pods

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get svc

kubectl describe svc &lt;service-name&gt;

kubectl get endpoints &lt;service-name&gt;

kubectl get endpointslices

kubectl get pods --show-labels
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect Service selector.</li>
<li>No healthy Pods.</li>
<li>Incorrect targetPort.</li>
<li>Application not listening on expected port.</li>
<li>NetworkPolicy blocking traffic.</li>
<li>DNS problem.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 9. Scenario: DNS Not Working</h2>

<h3>Check CoreDNS</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
</pre>

<h3>Check DNS Service</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get svc -n kube-system
</pre>

<h3>Test From a Pod</h3>

<pre>
kubectl exec -it &lt;pod-name&gt; -- nslookup kubernetes.default
</pre>

<h3>Investigate</h3>

<ul>
<li>CoreDNS Pods.</li>
<li>CoreDNS logs.</li>
<li>Service configuration.</li>
<li>Pod DNS configuration.</li>
<li>Network connectivity.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 10. Scenario: Pod Cannot Access Internet</h2>

<div class="flow">

Pod
<br>â†“
<br>
VPC CNI
<br>â†“
<br>
Node / VPC
<br>â†“
<br>
Route Table
<br>â†“
<br>
NAT Gateway
<br>â†“
<br>
Internet Gateway
<br>â†“
<br>
Internet

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Pod networking.</li>
<li>Subnet routing.</li>
<li>NAT Gateway.</li>
<li>Route tables.</li>
<li>Security Groups.</li>
<li>NACLs where applicable.</li>
<li>DNS.</li>
<li>VPC CNI health.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 11. Scenario: Pods Cannot Communicate</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ol>

<li>Are both Pods Running?</li>

<li>Can you resolve the Service DNS?</li>

<li>Does the Service have endpoints?</li>

<li>Is the correct port being used?</li>

<li>Are NetworkPolicies blocking traffic?</li>

<li>Is the CNI functioning correctly?</li>

<li>Are AWS networking controls involved?</li>

</ol>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -o wide

kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get networkpolicy -A
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 12. Scenario: Ingress / ALB Not Working</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get ingress -A

kubectl describe ingress &lt;ingress-name&gt;

kubectl get pods -n kube-system
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>AWS Load Balancer Controller problem.</li>
<li>Incorrect Ingress configuration.</li>
<li>Wrong target type.</li>
<li>Subnet tagging/configuration issue.</li>
<li>Security Group issue.</li>
<li>IAM permissions issue.</li>
<li>Incorrect Service configuration.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 13. Scenario: EKS Node Cannot Join Cluster</h2>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Incorrect node IAM permissions.</li>
<li>Incorrect cluster configuration.</li>
<li>Network connectivity issue.</li>
<li>Security Group rules.</li>
<li>Subnet or routing issue.</li>
<li>Incorrect bootstrap configuration.</li>
<li>Instance or launch configuration issue.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Investigate</h3>

<pre>
aws eks describe-cluster --name &lt;cluster-name&gt;

kubectl get nodes

kubectl get events -A
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Approach:</strong><br>

"I would verify the node IAM role, subnet and security-group
configuration, cluster endpoint connectivity and node bootstrap
logs."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 14. Scenario: Pod IP Exhaustion</h2>

<p>
A VPC CNI-based EKS cluster can experience IP capacity constraints
when the subnet or node networking capacity is exhausted.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Available subnet IP addresses.</li>
<li>Number of Pods per node.</li>
<li>Node instance networking limits.</li>
<li>VPC CNI status and logs.</li>
<li>Cluster scaling requirements.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 15. Scenario: Deployment Has No Available Pods</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get deployment

kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;

kubectl get replicaset

kubectl get pods
</pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Deployment desired replicas.</li>
<li>ReplicaSet status.</li>
<li>Pod scheduling.</li>
<li>Container image.</li>
<li>Configuration.</li>
<li>Readiness and liveness probes.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 16. Scenario: Readiness Probe Failing</h2>

<p>
A failed readiness probe means Kubernetes does not consider the
container ready to receive Service traffic.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Wrong health-check path.</li>
<li>Wrong port.</li>
<li>Application startup is slow.</li>
<li>Application dependency is unavailable.</li>
<li>Incorrect probe configuration.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 17. Scenario: Liveness Probe Causing Restarts</h2>

<div class="answer">

A liveness probe determines whether the container should be
restarted. If it repeatedly fails, Kubernetes may restart the
container.

Check the probe path, port, timing, initial delay and application
startup behavior before changing the configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 18. Scenario: Cannot Access EKS Cluster</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
aws sts get-caller-identity

aws eks describe-cluster \
--name &lt;cluster-name&gt;

kubectl cluster-info

kubectl get nodes
</pre>

<h3>Possible Causes</h3>

<ul>
<li>Wrong AWS identity.</li>
<li>Incorrect kubeconfig.</li>
<li>Insufficient EKS access permissions.</li>
<li>Cluster endpoint access configuration.</li>
<li>Network connectivity issue.</li>
<li>Expired or invalid authentication.</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 19. Scenario: Check EKS Control Plane Health</h2>

<p>
EKS manages the Kubernetes control-plane infrastructure, so
troubleshooting focuses on API availability, cluster status,
access configuration and Kubernetes resources rather than logging
into control-plane servers.
</p>

<pre>
aws eks describe-cluster \
--name &lt;cluster-name&gt;

kubectl cluster-info

kubectl get nodes
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 20. Troubleshooting Decision Tree</h2>

<div class="flow">

Is the Pod Running?
<br>
â†“ No
<br>
Check Events / Scheduling
<br><br>

Running but restarting?
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check Logs / Probes
<br><br>

Running but unreachable?
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check Service / Endpoints / DNS
<br><br>

Network issue?
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check CNI / Routes / SG / NetworkPolicy
<br><br>

Node problem?
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check Node Conditions / kubelet / Resources
<br><br>

Cluster access problem?
<br>
â†“
<br>
Check IAM / kubeconfig / Endpoint Access

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>â­â­â­â­â­ 21. Golden Troubleshooting Commands</h2>

<h1>AWS Real-Time Scenarios</h1>

<p>
Production-style AWS troubleshooting scenarios for DevOps interviews,
covering EC2, VPC, IAM, S3, Load Balancer, Auto Scaling and CloudWatch.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Scenario Approach</h2>

<div class="flow">

Identify Problem
<br>â†“<br>
Check Current State
<br>â†“<br>
Collect Evidence
<br>â†“<br>
Find Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
Fix
<br>â†“<br>
Verify
<br>â†“<br>
Prevent Recurrence

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. EC2 Instance Is Not Reachable</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
An EC2 instance was working earlier, but now you cannot connect
to it. How would you troubleshoot?
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Answer:</strong>

<br><br>

First I would check whether the instance is in the
<strong>running</strong> state.

Then I would check:

<ul>
<li>Security Group inbound rules</li>
<li>Network ACLs</li>
<li>Route table</li>
<li>Internet Gateway or NAT configuration</li>
<li>Public IP / Elastic IP</li>
<li>Subnet configuration</li>
<li>Instance status checks</li>
<li>SSH service and OS-level firewall</li>
</ul>

I would then use logs and connectivity tests to identify whether
the problem is at the AWS networking layer or inside the operating
system.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>2. SSH to EC2 Is Failing</h2>

<pre>
ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@PUBLIC_IP
</pre>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Correct public IP</li>
<li>Correct username</li>
<li>Private key permissions</li>
<li>Security Group port 22</li>
<li>Route to Internet Gateway</li>
<li>Instance is running</li>
<li>SSH daemon is running</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Point:</strong><br>

"I would troubleshoot from outside to inside: public connectivity,
Security Group, routing, instance status and finally the operating
system's SSH service."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. EC2 Has High CPU</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
An application server suddenly reaches 95% CPU. What will you do?
</p>

<div class="answer">

I would first confirm the metric using CloudWatch and then check
the processes consuming CPU inside the instance.

<pre>
top
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
uptime
</pre>

Then I would determine whether the cause is:

<ul>
<li>Traffic spike</li>
<li>Application process</li>
<li>Infinite loop</li>
<li>Background job</li>
<li>Insufficient instance capacity</li>
</ul>

Depending on the architecture, I could scale vertically,
scale horizontally using Auto Scaling, or fix the application
causing the CPU spike.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>4. EC2 Disk Is Full</h2>

<pre>
df -h

du -sh /* 2&gt;/dev/null

du -sh /var/* 2&gt;/dev/null
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would identify which filesystem and directory are consuming
the space. Then I would inspect logs, temporary files and
application data.

I would clean only safe files, rotate logs if required, and
increase the EBS volume if the workload genuinely requires
more storage.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>5. Application Cannot Access S3</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
An application running on EC2 suddenly receives AccessDenied
when accessing S3. What would you check?
</p>

<div class="flow">

EC2
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Role
<br>â†“<br>
IAM Policy
<br>â†“<br>
S3 Bucket Policy
<br>â†“<br>
S3 Object

</div>

<div class="answer">

I would check the IAM role attached to the EC2 instance,
its permissions, the bucket policy, explicit denies, object
ownership/access controls and the requested S3 action.

I would also verify that the application is actually using
the expected IAM role.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>6. IAM User Gets AccessDenied</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
A developer says they have an IAM policy but still receive
AccessDenied. What do you check?
</p>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Attached identity policies</li>
<li>Resource-based policies</li>
<li>Explicit Deny statements</li>
<li>Permission boundaries</li>
<li>Session policies</li>
<li>SCPs if AWS Organizations is being used</li>
<li>Correct AWS account and region</li>
<li>Exact resource ARN and requested action</li>
</ul>

<strong>Key Rule:</strong> An explicit Deny overrides an Allow.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>7. Application Behind Load Balancer Is Unhealthy</h2>

<div class="flow">

User
<br>â†“<br>
Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>
Target Group
<br>â†“<br>
EC2
<br>â†“<br>
Application

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Target health</li>
<li>Health-check path</li>
<li>Health-check port</li>
<li>Security Groups</li>
<li>Application listening port</li>
<li>Application logs</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong><br>

"I would start from the target group's health status, verify the
health-check configuration and then move toward the instance and
application layer."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>8. Load Balancer Returns 502</h2>

<p>
A 502 generally indicates that the load balancer could not get a
valid response from the target.
</p>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Backend application is running</li>
<li>Target port</li>
<li>Target health</li>
<li>Security Groups</li>
<li>Application response</li>
<li>Listener and target-group configuration</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>9. Auto Scaling Is Not Adding Instances</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>CloudWatch alarm</li>
<li>Auto Scaling policy</li>
<li>Desired, minimum and maximum capacity</li>
<li>Launch template</li>
<li>Subnet availability</li>
<li>Instance launch failures</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
<li>Auto Scaling activity history</li>
</ul>

The first objective is to determine whether the scaling policy
did not trigger or whether the new instance launch itself failed.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>10. VPC Instance Has No Internet Access</h2>

<div class="flow">

EC2
<br>â†“<br>
Subnet Route Table
<br>â†“<br>
Internet Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
Internet

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Public IP or Elastic IP</li>
<li>Route table</li>
<li>Internet Gateway</li>
<li>Security Group</li>
<li>Network ACL</li>
<li>Subnet configuration</li>
</ul>

<div class="answer">

For a private subnet, I would instead verify the NAT Gateway
and its routing path.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>11. Private Subnet Cannot Reach Internet</h2>

<div class="flow">

Private EC2
<br>â†“<br>
Private Route Table
<br>â†“<br>
NAT Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
Public Subnet
<br>â†“<br>
Internet Gateway
<br>â†“<br>
Internet

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>Private route table has a route to NAT Gateway</li>
<li>NAT Gateway is available</li>
<li>NAT Gateway is in a suitable public subnet</li>
<li>Public subnet route points to Internet Gateway</li>
<li>Security Groups and NACLs allow required traffic</li>
</ul>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>12. DNS Resolution Is Failing Inside VPC</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
nslookup example.com

dig example.com
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check VPC DNS support/hostnames, the configured resolver,
route and network connectivity, security controls, and whether
the problem affects one instance or the entire subnet/VPC.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>13. S3 Upload Is Failing</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<ul>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
<li>Bucket policy</li>
<li>Bucket name</li>
<li>Region</li>
<li>Object key</li>
<li>Encryption requirements</li>
<li>Explicit Deny</li>
</ul>

<pre>
aws s3 cp test.txt s3://my-bucket/
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>14. CloudWatch Alarm Is Not Triggering</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify the metric, namespace, dimensions, statistic,
period, evaluation periods, threshold and alarm state.

I would also verify that the resource is publishing the expected
metric and that the alarm action is configured correctly.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>15. Application Is Slow but EC2 Is Healthy</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would not assume the EC2 instance is the problem.

I would investigate the complete request path:

<div class="flow">

User
<br>â†“<br>
Load Balancer
<br>â†“<br>
Application
<br>â†“<br>
Database
<br>â†“<br>
External Services

</div>

Then I would compare latency, CPU, memory, network and application
metrics to identify the bottleneck.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>16. Production EC2 Instance Suddenly Stops</h2>

<h3>Approach</h3>

<ol>

<li>Check instance state.</li>

<li>Check system and instance status checks.</li>

<li>Review CloudWatch metrics.</li>

<li>Check CloudTrail for API activity.</li>

<li>Check application and OS logs.</li>

<li>Check Auto Scaling activity if applicable.</li>

<li>Determine whether it was infrastructure, application or human action.</li>

</ol>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Tip:</strong><br>

Always mention evidence collection before making a production
change.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>17. How Would You Secure an AWS Production Environment?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would use:

<ul>
<li>Least-privilege IAM</li>
<li>IAM roles instead of long-lived credentials</li>
<li>Private subnets for internal workloads</li>
<li>Security Groups with restricted access</li>
<li>Encryption at rest and in transit</li>
<li>CloudTrail for auditing</li>
<li>CloudWatch for monitoring</li>
<li>Secrets Manager or Parameter Store for secrets</li>
<li>Regular patching and vulnerability scanning</li>
<li>Backups and disaster-recovery planning</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ TOP INTERVIEW QUESTIONS</span>

<h2>18. Quick AWS Scenario Revision</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Scenario</th>
<th>First Things to Check</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>EC2 unreachable</td>

</tr>

<tr>
<td>SSH failure</td>
<td>Port 22 â†’ IP â†’ Key â†’ SSH service</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>High CPU</td>
<td>CloudWatch â†’ top â†’ process â†’ scaling</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Disk full</td>
<td>df -h â†’ du â†’ logs â†’ storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>S3 AccessDenied</td>
<td>IAM â†’ Bucket Policy â†’ Explicit Deny</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ALB unhealthy</td>
<td>Target Health â†’ Health Check â†’ SG â†’ App</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>ALB 502</td>
<td>Target â†’ Port â†’ Application Response</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Auto Scaling failure</td>
<td>Alarm â†’ Policy â†’ Activity â†’ Launch Template</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>No Internet</td>
<td>Route â†’ IGW/NAT â†’ SG â†’ NACL</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>DNS failure</td>
<td>Resolver â†’ VPC DNS â†’ Network</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Golden AWS Interview Formula</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>IAM</strong>
â†’ Who can access?

<br><br>

<strong>VPC</strong>
â†’ Where does traffic flow?

<br><br>

<strong>Security Group</strong>
â†’ Is traffic allowed?

<br><br>

<strong>Route Table</strong>
â†’ Where does traffic go?

<br><br>

<strong>CloudWatch</strong>
â†’ What is happening?

<br><br>

<strong>CloudTrail</strong>
â†’ Who changed it?

<br><br>

<strong>Logs</strong>
â†’ What failed?

<br><br>

<strong>Scaling</strong>
â†’ How do we handle increased demand?

</div>

</div>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ³</div>

<h1>Docker Real-Time Scenarios</h1>

<p>
Production-style Docker troubleshooting scenarios commonly asked
in DevOps interviews.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Docker Troubleshooting Approach</h2>

<div class="flow">

Container Status
<br>â†“<br>
Logs
<br>â†“<br>
Process
<br>â†“<br>
Network
<br>â†“<br>
Volumes
<br>â†“<br>
Image
<br>â†“<br>
Configuration
<br>â†“<br>
Root Cause â†’ Fix â†’ Verify

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. Container Starts and Immediately Exits</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
A Docker container starts but immediately stops. How would
you troubleshoot it?
</p>

<div class="answer">

First check the container status:

<pre>
docker ps -a
</pre>

Then check logs:

<pre>
docker logs &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

Then inspect the container:

<pre>
docker inspect &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

I would verify the container's main process and its
<strong>CMD / ENTRYPOINT</strong> configuration.

A container normally stays alive only while its main process
(PID 1) is running.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>2. Container Is Running but Application Is Not Accessible</h2>

<div class="flow">

Container
<br>â†“<br>
Application
<br>â†“<br>
Container Port
<br>â†“<br>
Host Port
<br>â†“<br>
Client

</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
docker ps

docker port &lt;container_id&gt;

docker logs &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

<p>
Also verify that the application is listening on the expected
port and that the port is correctly published.
</p>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. Port Mapping Is Wrong</h2>

<pre>
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
</pre>

<p>
Here:
<strong>8080</strong> = host port<br>
<strong>80</strong> = container port
</p>

<div class="answer">

If users access port 8080 on the host, Docker forwards the
traffic to port 80 inside the container.

Check the mapping with:

<pre>
docker port &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>4. Container Cannot Connect to Another Container</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check whether both containers are connected to the
same Docker network.

<pre>
docker network ls

docker network inspect &lt;network&gt;
</pre>

Create a network if required:

<pre>
docker network create app-network
</pre>

Run containers on it:

<pre>
docker run -d --name db --network app-network mysql
docker run -d --name app --network app-network myapp
</pre>

Containers on the same user-defined network can communicate
using container/service names.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>5. Docker Container Cannot Reach the Internet</h2>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
docker exec -it &lt;container&gt; sh

ping 8.8.8.8

nslookup google.com
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would distinguish between:

<ul>
<li>General network connectivity problem</li>
<li>DNS resolution problem</li>
<li>Docker network configuration problem</li>
<li>Host firewall or proxy configuration</li>
</ul>

I would also inspect the Docker network:

<pre>
docker network inspect bridge
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>6. Container Has High CPU Usage</h2>

<pre>
docker stats
</pre>

<p>
Then identify the process:
</p>

<pre>
docker top &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check application logs and determine whether the high
CPU is caused by traffic, an application problem, a runaway
process or insufficient resources.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>7. Container Is Using Too Much Memory</h2>

<pre>
docker stats
</pre>

<p>
Check container configuration:
</p>

<pre>
docker inspect &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would investigate application memory usage and, where
appropriate, configure container resource limits.

Example:

<pre>
docker run -d --memory=512m --cpus=1 myapp
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>8. Image Build Is Failing</h2>

<pre>
docker build -t myapp .
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would inspect the exact build step that failed.

Common causes:

<ul>
<li>Incorrect Dockerfile syntax</li>
<li>Wrong base image</li>
<li>Missing files in build context</li>
<li>Incorrect COPY path</li>
<li>Package installation failure</li>
<li>Network or registry issue</li>
<li>Permission problem</li>
</ul>

I would fix the first meaningful error rather than focusing
only on the final error message.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>9. Dockerfile COPY Is Failing</h2>

<pre>
docker build -t myapp .
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>File exists in the build context</li>
<li>Correct relative path</li>
<li>.dockerignore is not excluding the file</li>
<li>Correct capitalization</li>
<li>Build is being executed from the expected directory</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>10. Image Is Too Large</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would reduce image size by:

<ul>
<li>Using a smaller base image when appropriate</li>
<li>Using multi-stage builds</li>
<li>Removing unnecessary packages</li>
<li>Cleaning package caches</li>
<li>Using an effective .dockerignore</li>
<li>Copying only required application files</li>
</ul>

Example:

<pre>
.dockerignore

.git
node_modules
*.log
.env
README.md
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>11. Container Cannot Pull Image from Registry</h2>

<pre>
docker pull username/myapp:latest
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Image name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Registry availability</li>
<li>Authentication</li>
<li>Repository permissions</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
</ul>

For private registries:

<pre>
docker login
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>12. Container Data Is Lost After Container Removal</h2>

<div class="answer">

Container writable storage is ephemeral. For persistent data,
I would use Docker volumes or an external storage system.

Example:

<pre>
docker volume create app-data

docker run -d \
  --name app \
  -v app-data:/data \
  myapp
</pre>

Check volumes:

<pre>
docker volume ls
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>13. Docker Volume Is Not Mounting Correctly</h2>

<pre>
docker inspect &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Volume exists</li>
<li>Correct source and destination paths</li>
<li>Mount mode</li>
<li>Permissions</li>
<li>Application is writing to the expected path</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>14. Docker Compose Application Is Not Starting</h2>

<pre>
docker compose ps

docker compose logs

docker compose config
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would first validate the rendered Compose configuration,
then inspect individual service logs and dependencies.

I would also check:

<ul>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Ports</li>
<li>Volumes</li>
<li>Networks</li>
<li>Dependency configuration</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>15. Application Container Cannot Connect to Database</h2>

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Network
<br>â†“<br>
Database Container
<br>â†“<br>
Database Port

</div>

<div class="answer">

I would verify that both containers are on the same network,
the application uses the database service/container name rather
than an incorrect localhost address, and that the database is
actually listening.

For example, inside a Compose network:

<pre>
DB_HOST=db
DB_PORT=3306
</pre>

<strong>Important:</strong> Inside a container,
<code>localhost</code> refers to that same container.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>16. Docker Daemon Is Not Running</h2>

<h3>Linux</h3>

<pre>
systemctl status docker

systemctl start docker

systemctl enable docker
</pre>

<h3>Check Docker</h3>

<pre>
docker info
</pre>

<div class="answer">

If the daemon is unavailable, Docker CLI commands that require
the daemon will fail. I would check daemon status and logs.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>17. Container Logs Are Huge</h2>

<pre>
docker logs &lt;container_id&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would identify why excessive logging is happening and configure
appropriate Docker logging and rotation settings rather than
allowing unlimited log growth.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>18. Container Works Locally but Fails in CI/CD</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would compare the environments.

Check:

<ul>
<li>Dockerfile</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Secrets</li>
<li>Build context</li>
<li>CPU architecture</li>
<li>Registry credentials</li>
<li>Network access</li>
<li>Runtime configuration</li>
</ul>

<strong>Interview Point:</strong>

"The image should be treated as the same deployable artifact
across environments. I would identify environmental differences
rather than rebuilding different application logic for each
environment."

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>19. Security Vulnerability Found in Docker Image</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would:

<ul>
<li>Scan the image</li>
<li>Identify vulnerable packages</li>
<li>Update the base image</li>
<li>Upgrade vulnerable dependencies</li>
<li>Rebuild the image</li>
<li>Scan again</li>
<li>Prevent deployment if critical policy requirements are violated</li>
</ul>

Tools such as Trivy can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ TOP INTERVIEW REVISION</span>

<h2>20. Docker Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet</h2>

<table>

<tr>

<th>First Check</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container exited</td>
<td>docker ps -a â†’ docker logs</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Application inaccessible</td>
<td>docker port â†’ logs â†’ listening port</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Container networking</td>
<td>docker network ls / inspect</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>High CPU</td>
<td>docker stats â†’ docker top</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>High memory</td>
<td>docker stats â†’ inspect</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Build failure</td>
<td>Dockerfile â†’ build output</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Image pull failure</td>
<td>Registry â†’ login â†’ tag â†’ permissions</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Data lost</td>
<td>Volume configuration</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Compose failure</td>
<td>docker compose config â†’ logs</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Database connection</td>
<td>Network â†’ hostname â†’ port â†’ DB status</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">
