<div class="note">

<strong>ðŸ’¡ Interview Formula</strong>

<br><br>

When asked a scenario question, don't immediately give a random
command.

<br><br>

<strong>1. Understand the problem</strong><br>
<strong>2. Check the current state</strong><br>
<strong>3. Collect evidence</strong><br>
<strong>4. Identify the root cause</strong><br>
<strong>5. Apply the fix</strong><br>
<strong>6. Verify the result</strong><br>
<strong>7. Explain prevention</strong>

<br><br>

This structure makes your answer sound practical and
production-oriented.

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ”§</div>

<h1>Jenkins Real-Time Scenarios</h1>

<p>
Production-style Jenkins CI/CD troubleshooting scenarios
commonly asked in DevOps interviews.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Jenkins Troubleshooting Approach</h2>

<div class="flow">

Build Trigger
<br>â†“<br>
Jenkins Controller
<br>â†“<br>
Agent
<br>â†“<br>
Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Docker / Artifact
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
<br>â†“<br>
Verify

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. Jenkins Build Is Failing</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
A Jenkins pipeline suddenly starts failing. How would you
troubleshoot it?
</p>

<div class="answer">

I would first open the console output and identify the
<strong>first meaningful error</strong>.

Then I would determine which stage failed:

<ul>
<li>Checkout</li>
<li>Build</li>
<li>Test</li>
<li>Docker build</li>
<li>Registry push</li>
<li>Deployment</li>
</ul>

I would fix the root cause and rerun the pipeline.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>2. Jenkins Agent Is Offline</h2>

<pre>
Manage Jenkins â†’ Nodes
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Agent status</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
<li>Jenkins agent process</li>
<li>Java version</li>
<li>Disk space</li>
<li>Authentication</li>
<li>Controller-agent connection</li>
</ul>

If the agent runs on Linux:

<pre>
df -h
free -h
java -version
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. Jenkins Job Is Stuck in Queue</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check whether an eligible agent is available.

Possible reasons:

<ul>
<li>No available executor</li>
<li>Agent offline</li>
<li>Label mismatch</li>
<li>Concurrency restriction</li>
<li>Resource shortage</li>
</ul>

I would inspect the queue and node configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>4. Git Checkout Is Failing</h2>

<pre>
git clone &lt;repository-url&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Repository URL</li>
<li>Branch name</li>
<li>Git credentials</li>
<li>SSH key</li>
<li>Repository permissions</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
<li>Git installation on the agent</li>
</ul>

I would also verify that Jenkins is using the expected
credential.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>5. Jenkins Cannot Authenticate to GitHub</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify the configured Jenkins credential and its
permissions.

Depending on the setup, Jenkins may use:

<ul>
<li>SSH key</li>
<li>Personal access token</li>
<li>GitHub App credentials</li>
</ul>

I would also check whether the credential is correctly selected
in the pipeline or SCM configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>6. Docker Command Fails Inside Jenkins</h2>

<pre>
docker --version
docker ps
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check whether Docker is installed on the Jenkins agent
and whether the Jenkins user can access the Docker daemon.

For Linux:

<pre>
systemctl status docker

groups jenkins
</pre>

I would also verify the Docker socket and agent environment.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>7. Docker Image Build Works Locally but Fails in Jenkins</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would compare the local and Jenkins environments.

Check:

<ul>
<li>Docker version</li>
<li>Build context</li>
<li>Dockerfile</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>Credentials</li>
<li>Network access</li>
<li>File permissions</li>
<li>Architecture</li>
</ul>

The Jenkins console output should be used to identify the
specific failure.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>8. Jenkins Cannot Push Image to Docker Hub</h2>

<pre>
docker login

docker push username/myapp:latest
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Docker registry credentials</li>
<li>Credential ID configured in Jenkins</li>
<li>Repository name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Docker Hub permissions</li>
</ul>

I would avoid hardcoding the username or password in the
Jenkinsfile.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>9. Jenkins Cannot Push Image to Amazon ECR</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify AWS credentials and ECR permissions.

Typical required actions include permissions related to
authenticating and pushing image layers.

The flow is:

<div class="flow">

Jenkins
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Credentials
<br>â†“<br>
ECR Login
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Tag
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Push
<br>â†“<br>
Amazon ECR

</div>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>10. Jenkins Pipeline Is Not Triggering Automatically</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Webhook configuration</li>
<li>Repository webhook delivery</li>
<li>Jenkins URL accessibility</li>
<li>Job trigger configuration</li>
<li>Branch configuration</li>
<li>Webhook plugin/configuration</li>
</ul>

For GitHub integration, I would inspect the webhook delivery
logs to determine whether the event reached Jenkins.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>11. Jenkinsfile Has Syntax Error</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would inspect the pipeline syntax and validate the Jenkinsfile
before running it.

For declarative pipelines, the structure should follow:

<pre>
pipeline {
    agent any

    stages {
        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                echo 'Building application'
            }
        }
    }
}
</pre>

I would identify the exact parser error reported by Jenkins.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>12. Jenkins Credentials Are Not Working</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Credential exists</li>
<li>Credential ID matches Jenkinsfile</li>
<li>Credential type is correct</li>
<li>Credential has required permissions</li>
<li>Credential is available to the job</li>
</ul>

I would never print secrets directly into console output.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>13. Pipeline Is Taking Too Long</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would identify the slowest stage.

Possible causes:

<ul>
<li>Slow dependency downloads</li>
<li>Large Docker builds</li>
<li>Slow tests</li>
<li>Insufficient agent resources</li>
<li>Network latency</li>
<li>Unnecessary sequential stages</li>
</ul>

Where appropriate, independent stages can be parallelized.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>14. Jenkins Server Disk Is Full</h2>

<pre>
df -h

du -sh /var/lib/jenkins/*
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would identify whether the space is being consumed by:

<ul>
<li>Old builds</li>
<li>Workspace files</li>
<li>Artifacts</li>
<li>Logs</li>
<li>Docker images</li>
<li>Temporary files</li>
</ul>

Then I would implement build retention and cleanup policies
rather than manually deleting important Jenkins data.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>15. Workspace Has Corrupted or Stale Files</h2>

<div class="answer">

If a build is behaving unexpectedly because of workspace state,
I would clean the workspace and rerun the build.

In a Pipeline:

<pre>
cleanWs()
</pre>

I would first confirm that workspace cleanup is safe for the
job.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>16. Jenkins Deployment Stage Failed</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would determine whether the failure happened while deploying
to:

<ul>
<li>EC2</li>
<li>Docker</li>
<li>ECS</li>
<li>Kubernetes</li>
<li>EKS</li>
</ul>

Then I would check deployment logs, credentials, connectivity,
target health and the state of the deployed application.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>17. Kubernetes Deployment from Jenkins Fails</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods
kubectl get deployment
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>kubectl is installed on the agent</li>
<li>Kubeconfig or cluster credentials</li>
<li>Cluster connectivity</li>
<li>Namespace</li>
<li>RBAC permissions</li>
<li>Manifest validity</li>
<li>Image availability</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>18. Jenkins Pipeline Failed After Deployment</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would separate the problem into:

<div class="flow">

Build Successful
<br>â†“<br>
Deployment Successful?
<br>â†“<br>
Application Healthy?
<br>â†“<br>
Health Check
<br>â†“<br>
Rollback if Required

</div>

A deployment being technically successful does not necessarily
mean the application is healthy.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>19. How Do You Secure Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would use:

<ul>
<li>RBAC / least privilege</li>
<li>Credentials Manager</li>
<li>HTTPS</li>
<li>Restricted agent permissions</li>
<li>Plugin updates</li>
<li>Jenkins updates</li>
<li>Secret masking</li>
<li>Network restrictions</li>
<li>Audit logs</li>
<li>Separate production access</li>
</ul>

I would avoid storing passwords or cloud credentials directly
inside Jenkinsfiles.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>20. How Would You Design a Production Jenkins Pipeline?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer Push
<br>â†“<br>
Webhook
<br>â†“<br>
Jenkins
<br>â†“<br>
Checkout
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Unit Tests
<br>â†“<br>
Security Scan
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Push to ECR
<br>â†“<br>
Deploy
<br>â†“<br>
Health Check
<br>â†“<br>
Monitoring

</div>

<div class="answer">

I would include automated testing, security scanning, immutable
image tagging, secure credentials, deployment verification and
rollback capability.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ TOP INTERVIEW REVISION</span>

<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. Pod Is in CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
A Pod keeps restarting and shows <strong>CrashLoopBackOff</strong>.
How would you troubleshoot it?
</p>

<div class="answer">

First check the Pod:

<pre>
kubectl get pods
</pre>

Then inspect it:

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

Check logs:

<pre>
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

If the container restarted:

<pre>
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous
</pre>

I would investigate application errors, incorrect commands,
missing configuration, failed health checks, permissions or
resource problems.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>2. Pod Is in Pending State</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

The Events section is very important.

Common causes:

<ul>
<li>Insufficient CPU or memory</li>
<li>Node selector mismatch</li>
<li>Affinity/anti-affinity rules</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations</li>
<li>Unbound PersistentVolumeClaim</li>
<li>Scheduling constraints</li>
</ul>

I would identify the scheduler event explaining why the Pod
cannot be placed on a node.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. Pod Shows ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Image name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Registry availability</li>
<li>ImagePullSecrets</li>
<li>Private registry authentication</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
</ul>

The Events section normally provides the immediate reason for
the image pull failure.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>4. Pod Is Running but Application Is Not Accessible</h2>

<div class="flow">
Client
<br>â†“<br>
Service
<br>â†“<br>
Pod
<br>â†“<br>
Container
<br>â†“<br>
Application
</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl get svc
kubectl describe svc &lt;service-name&gt;
kubectl get endpoints &lt;service-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify that the Service selector matches the Pod labels
and that the target application is listening on the expected
container port.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>5. Service Has No Endpoints</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get endpoints &lt;service-name&gt;
kubectl describe svc &lt;service-name&gt;
kubectl get pods --show-labels
</pre>

<div class="answer">

The most common issue is a mismatch between the Service selector
and Pod labels.

For example:

<pre>
Service selector:
app: nginx

Pod label:
app: apache
</pre>

The Service will not select that Pod.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>6. Deployment Is Not Creating New Pods</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get deployment
kubectl describe deployment &lt;deployment-name&gt;
kubectl get replicaset
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check the Deployment desired replicas, ReplicaSet status,
Pod scheduling, resource constraints and image availability.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>7. New Deployment Version Is Failing</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would compare the new ReplicaSet with the previous working
ReplicaSet.

Check:

<ul>
<li>Image version</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>ConfigMaps</li>
<li>Secrets</li>
<li>Probes</li>
<li>Resource limits</li>
<li>Application logs</li>
</ul>

Then, if necessary, perform a rollback.

<pre>
kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>8. Readiness Probe Is Failing</h2>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

A readiness probe determines whether the Pod should receive
traffic.

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Probe path</li>
<li>Probe port</li>
<li>Application startup time</li>
<li>Initial delay</li>
<li>Timeout</li>
<li>Application health endpoint</li>
</ul>

A failed readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>9. Liveness Probe Keeps Restarting the Container</h2>

<div class="answer">

A liveness probe determines whether the container should be
restarted.

If it is too aggressive, a healthy but slow-starting application
may repeatedly restart.

I would review the probe configuration and application startup
behavior.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>10. Pod Is OOMKilled</h2>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

OOMKilled usually indicates that the container exceeded its
memory limit.

I would check:

<pre>
kubectl top pod
</pre>

Then compare actual usage with the configured resource requests
and limits.

Possible solutions include fixing a memory leak, optimizing the
application or adjusting the memory limit based on actual
requirements.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>11. Node Is NotReady</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get nodes

kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Node conditions</li>
<li>Kubelet status</li>
<li>Container runtime</li>
<li>CPU and memory pressure</li>
<li>Disk pressure</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
<li>Node events</li>
</ul>

On the node:

<pre>
systemctl status kubelet
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>12. Pods Are Stuck on One Node</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would investigate scheduling configuration:

<ul>
<li>Node selectors</li>
<li>Node affinity</li>
<li>Taints</li>
<li>Tolerations</li>
<li>Resource availability</li>
</ul>

Commands:

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl describe node &lt;node-name&gt;
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>13. DNS Is Not Working Inside Kubernetes</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get pods -n kube-system

kubectl get svc -n kube-system

kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
</pre>

<p>Test from a Pod:</p>

<pre>
nslookup kubernetes.default
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would investigate CoreDNS health, the DNS Service, Pod
networking and DNS configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>14. Ingress Is Not Working</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get ingress

kubectl describe ingress &lt;ingress-name&gt;

kubectl get svc
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Ingress Controller</li>
<li>Ingress rules</li>
<li>Host/path configuration</li>
<li>Backend Service</li>
<li>Service endpoints</li>
<li>DNS</li>
<li>TLS certificate if HTTPS is used</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>15. ConfigMap Changes Are Not Reflected in Application</h2>

<div class="answer">

The behavior depends on how the ConfigMap is consumed.

If configuration is injected as environment variables, existing
containers generally need to be restarted to receive updated
values.

If mounted as files, updates can be reflected into the mounted
volume depending on Kubernetes behavior and application handling.

A common approach is to trigger a controlled rollout when
configuration changes.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>16. Secret Is Not Available Inside Pod</h2>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl get secret
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Secret exists in the same namespace</li>
<li>Correct Secret name</li>
<li>Correct key</li>
<li>Volume or environment variable configuration</li>
<li>Pod specification</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>17. Kubernetes Deployment Rollback</h2>

<pre>
kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would first confirm the new deployment is unhealthy, identify
the cause, and then roll back to the previous known-good
revision if required.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>18. HPA Is Not Scaling Pods</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get hpa

kubectl describe hpa &lt;hpa-name&gt;

kubectl top pods
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Metrics Server</li>
<li>CPU/memory resource requests</li>
<li>HPA configuration</li>
<li>Current and desired metrics</li>
<li>Minimum and maximum replicas</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>19. Pod Cannot Mount PersistentVolume</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc &lt;pvc-name&gt;

kubectl get pv
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>PVC status</li>
<li>StorageClass</li>
<li>PV availability</li>
<li>Access mode</li>
<li>Requested storage</li>
<li>CSI driver</li>
<li>Events</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>20. Cluster Has Insufficient Resources</h2>

<pre>
kubectl top nodes

kubectl describe nodes
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would determine whether the problem is CPU, memory or another
resource.

Possible solutions:

<ul>
<li>Optimize Pod resource requests</li>
<li>Scale the node group</li>
<li>Add larger nodes</li>
<li>Use cluster autoscaling</li>
<li>Remove unnecessary workloads</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ TOP INTERVIEW REVISION</span>

<h2>21. Kubernetes Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet</h2>

</tr>

</tr>

</tr>

</div>

<header>
<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ§</div>
<h1>Linux Real-Time Scenarios</h1>
<p>
Production-style Linux troubleshooting scenarios commonly asked
in DevOps interviews.
</p>
</header>

<main class="container">

<div class="card">
<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Linux Troubleshooting Approach</h2>

<div class="flow">
Problem
<br>â†“<br>
Check System Health
<br>â†“<br>
Processes
<br>â†“<br>
Memory / CPU / Disk
<br>â†“<br>
Network
<br>â†“<br>
Logs
<br>â†“<br>
Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
Fix & Verify
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>
<h2>1. Server CPU Usage Is 100%</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>
<p>
A production Linux server suddenly reaches 100% CPU. How would
you troubleshoot it?
</p>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Step 1: Check overall CPU usage</strong>

<pre>
top
uptime
</pre>

<strong>Step 2: Find the process consuming CPU</strong>

<pre>
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head
</pre>

<strong>Step 3:</strong> Determine whether the process is expected,
a runaway process, application issue or traffic-related issue.

<strong>Step 4:</strong> Check application logs.

<strong>Step 5:</strong> Fix the root cause and monitor again.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>2. Server Memory Is Almost Full</h2>

<pre>
free -h
top
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would identify which process is consuming memory and determine
whether the system is under genuine memory pressure or whether
Linux is using memory for cache.

I would also check swap usage.

<pre>
swapon --show
</pre>

Then I would investigate the application for a memory leak or
increase capacity if required.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>
<h2>3. Disk Space Is 100% Full</h2>

<pre>
df -h
</pre>

<p>Then identify large directories:</p>

<pre>
du -sh /* 2&gt;/dev/null
du -sh /var/* 2&gt;/dev/null
</pre>

<div class="answer">

Common causes include:

<ul>
<li>Large application logs</li>
<li>Temporary files</li>
<li>Old packages</li>
<li>Large application data</li>
<li>Log rotation failure</li>
</ul>

I would clean only safe files, fix log rotation if necessary,
and increase disk capacity when required.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>4. Application Is Running but Users Cannot Access It</h2>

<div class="flow">
User
<br>â†“<br>
Network
<br>â†“<br>
Server
<br>â†“<br>
Port
<br>â†“<br>
Application
</div>

<h3>Check</h3>

<pre>
systemctl status application.service

ss -tulpn

curl localhost:8080
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify that the application process is running and
listening on the expected port. Then I would check firewall,
security rules and network connectivity.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>
<h2>5. Service Is Not Running</h2>

<pre>
systemctl status nginx

systemctl start nginx

systemctl enable nginx
</pre>

<p>For deeper investigation:</p>

<pre>
journalctl -u nginx
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would first check the service status, then inspect the service
logs and configuration, fix the root cause and restart the service.
After restarting, I would verify its status and application
connectivity.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>6. SSH Connection Is Failing</h2>

<h3>Check from client</h3>

<pre>
ssh user@server-ip
</pre>

<h3>Check on server</h3>

<pre>
systemctl status sshd

ss -tlnp | grep :22
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Server availability</li>
<li>Port 22 connectivity</li>
<li>SSH service</li>
<li>Firewall rules</li>
<li>User account</li>
<li>SSH key / password</li>
<li>sshd configuration</li>
<li>Authentication logs</li>
</ul>

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>7. Permission Denied Error</h2>

<pre>
ls -l file.txt

id

whoami
</pre>

<p>Check ownership:</p>

<pre>
chown user:group file.txt
</pre>

<p>Check permissions:</p>

<pre>
chmod 640 file.txt
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would first identify the user running the process and compare
that user's permissions with the file or directory ownership.
I would avoid blindly using <strong>chmod 777</strong>.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>
<h2>8. Which Process Is Using a Port?</h2>

<pre>
ss -tulpn
</pre>

<p>Or:</p>

<pre>
lsof -i :8080
</pre>

<div class="answer">

This helps identify which process is listening on the required
port and whether another application is causing a port conflict.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>9. Application Logs Are Growing Rapidly</h2>

<pre>
du -sh /var/log/*

tail -f /var/log/application.log
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would determine why the application is generating excessive
logs, check log rotation configuration and prevent the filesystem
from becoming full.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>10. How Do You Find a File?</h2>

<pre>
find /var/log -name "*.log"

find / -name "app.conf" 2&gt;/dev/null
</pre>

<p>Search inside files:</p>

<pre>
grep -R "ERROR" /var/log/
</pre>

</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>11. Server Load Average Is High</h2>

<pre>
uptime

top
</pre>

<div class="answer">

Load average indicates how much work is waiting for CPU or
other system resources. I would correlate load average with
CPU, memory, disk I/O and process information rather than
assuming high load always means high CPU.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>12. Disk I/O Is Very High</h2>

<pre>
iostat

iotop

vmstat
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would identify the process causing high disk activity and
determine whether the workload is application-related,
database-related or caused by insufficient disk performance.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>
<h2>13. DNS Is Not Working</h2>

<pre>
nslookup google.com

dig google.com

cat /etc/resolv.conf
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would determine whether the issue is DNS configuration,
network connectivity, resolver availability or an application-
specific DNS problem.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>14. Server Cannot Reach Another Server</h2>

<pre>
ping server-ip

curl -v http://server-ip:8080

nc -vz server-ip 8080
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would troubleshoot layer by layer:

<ul>
<li>DNS</li>
<li>Routing</li>
<li>Firewall</li>
<li>Port availability</li>
<li>Target service</li>
</ul>

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>15. Process Is Stuck</h2>

<pre>
ps aux | grep application

top
</pre>

<p>Inspect the process:</p>

<pre>
ps -p PID -f
</pre>

<p>If necessary, terminate gracefully:</p>

<pre>
kill PID
</pre>

<p>Force termination only when required:</p>

<pre>
kill -9 PID
</pre>

<div class="answer">
<strong>Interview Point:</strong>
Use SIGTERM first so the application has an opportunity to
clean up. SIGKILL should be a last resort.
</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>
<h2>16. Server Rebooted Unexpectedly</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would investigate:

<ul>
<li>System logs</li>
<li>Kernel messages</li>
<li>Cloud provider events</li>
<li>OOM events</li>
<li>Hardware / infrastructure events</li>
<li>Scheduled jobs</li>
<li>Manual administrative actions</li>
</ul>

Useful commands:

<pre>
journalctl -b -1
dmesg | tail -50
last reboot
</pre>

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>17. OOM Killer Terminated an Application</h2>

<pre>
dmesg | grep -i "out of memory"

journalctl -k | grep -i oom
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would identify which process consumed excessive memory,
check application behavior and determine whether memory limits
or instance capacity need adjustment.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>18. Cron Job Is Not Running</h2>

<pre>
crontab -l

systemctl status cron
</pre>

<p>Check logs:</p>

<pre>
grep CRON /var/log/syslog
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify the cron syntax, correct user, executable
permissions, absolute paths and environment variables.
Cron runs with a limited environment, so commands that work
interactively may fail in cron.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
<h2>19. Find the Top CPU and Memory Processes</h2>

<pre>
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head

ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
</pre>

<div class="answer">

These commands quickly help identify resource-heavy processes
during production troubleshooting.

</div>
</div>


<div class="card">
<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ TOP INTERVIEW REVISION</span>
<h2>20. Linux Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet</h2>

</tr>

</tr>

</tr>

<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ—ï¸</div>

<h1>Terraform Real-Time Scenarios</h1>

<p>
Production-style Terraform troubleshooting and infrastructure
scenarios commonly asked in DevOps interviews.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸŽ¯ Terraform Troubleshooting Approach</h2>

<div class="flow">

Code
<br>â†“<br>
terraform init
<br>â†“<br>
terraform validate
<br>â†“<br>
terraform plan
<br>â†“<br>
terraform apply
<br>â†“<br>
State
<br>â†“<br>
Cloud Resource
<br>â†“<br>
Verify â†’ Fix â†’ Prevent

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. Terraform Apply Fails</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
Terraform plan succeeds but terraform apply fails. What would
you do?
</p>

<div class="answer">

I would first read the exact provider error and identify whether
the failure is related to permissions, configuration, quotas,
dependencies or an existing cloud resource.

Then I would fix the root cause and run:

<pre>
terraform plan
terraform apply
</pre>

I would avoid randomly changing resources without understanding
the error.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>2. Terraform State File Is Missing</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Terraform state tracks the relationship between configuration
and infrastructure.

If the state is missing, Terraform may believe resources do not
exist.

I would first check whether the state is stored locally or in a
remote backend.

For production, I would prefer a remote backend with appropriate
locking and access control.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. Terraform State and Real Infrastructure Are Different</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
Someone manually changes an AWS resource. What happens when
Terraform runs?
</p>

<div class="answer">

This is called <strong>configuration drift</strong>.

I would run:

<pre>
terraform plan
</pre>

Terraform refreshes its understanding of the infrastructure and
the plan can show differences between the desired configuration
and actual infrastructure.

The correct solution is to bring the infrastructure back under
controlled Terraform management rather than making random manual
changes.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>4. Two Engineers Run Terraform at the Same Time</h2>

<div class="answer">

This can cause state consistency problems if both operations
modify the same state concurrently.

For production, I would use a remote backend with
<strong>state locking</strong> where supported.

Example AWS architecture:

<div class="flow">

Developer A
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Developer B
<br>â†“&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;â†“<br>
Terraform
<br>â†“<br>
Remote Backend
<br>â†“<br>
Shared State

</div>

The lock prevents conflicting state operations.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>5. Terraform State Is Locked</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
Terraform says the state is locked. What do you do?
</p>

<div class="answer">

First I would determine whether another Terraform operation is
actually running.

I would not immediately force-unlock the state.

Only after confirming that the original operation is no longer
running and the lock is stale would I consider:

<pre>
terraform force-unlock &lt;LOCK_ID&gt;
</pre>

<strong>Important:</strong> Force-unlock can be dangerous if another
Terraform operation is still running.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>6. Terraform Wants to Recreate an Important Resource</h2>

<pre>
terraform plan
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would carefully inspect why Terraform wants to replace the
resource.

Possible causes include:

<ul>
<li>Immutable attribute changes</li>
<li>Configuration changes</li>
<li>State mismatch</li>
<li>Drift</li>
<li>Provider behavior</li>
</ul>

I would not run apply blindly against a production resource.

I would understand the planned replacement first.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>7. Resource Exists in AWS but Terraform Wants to Create It</h2>

<div class="answer">

This usually means Terraform does not have that resource correctly
represented in its state.

If the resource was created outside Terraform, I would consider
importing it into state.

Modern Terraform supports import blocks, for example:

<pre>
import {
  to = aws_instance.app
  id = "i-0123456789abcdef0"
}
</pre>

The exact resource type and ID depend on the provider.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>8. Terraform Destroy Is Dangerous</h2>

<h3>Question</h3>

<p>
How would you safely destroy infrastructure?
</p>

<div class="answer">

First I would review:

<pre>
terraform plan -destroy
</pre>

I would verify the resources being removed and ensure that
production resources are protected through process and policy.

Where appropriate, lifecycle rules can prevent accidental
destruction:

<pre>
lifecycle {
  prevent_destroy = true
}
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>9. Terraform Provider Authentication Fails</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Credentials</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
<li>AWS profile</li>
<li>Region</li>
<li>Account</li>
<li>STS identity</li>
</ul>

For AWS:

<pre>
aws sts get-caller-identity
</pre>

This quickly confirms which AWS identity Terraform may be
expected to use.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>10. Terraform Plan Shows Unexpected Changes</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would investigate:

<ul>
<li>Recent code changes</li>
<li>Variable values</li>
<li>State</li>
<li>Manual cloud changes</li>
<li>Provider version</li>
<li>Resource defaults</li>
</ul>

Then I would compare the plan carefully before applying it.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>11. Terraform Variables Are Not Getting the Expected Value</h2>

<p>Check variable declaration:</p>

<pre>
variable "region" {
  type    = string
  default = "ap-south-1"
}
</pre>

<p>Check tfvars:</p>

<pre>
region = "ap-south-1"
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would verify variable precedence, variable names, tfvars files,
environment variables and command-line values.

I would also check whether Terraform is loading the expected
workspace and configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>12. Terraform Module Is Not Working</h2>

<pre>
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<ul>
<li>Module source</li>
<li>Module version</li>
<li>Required inputs</li>
<li>Outputs</li>
<li>Provider configuration</li>
<li>Module dependency</li>
</ul>

I would also inspect the module source itself if necessary.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>13. Terraform Init Fails</h2>

<div class="answer">

Common causes include:

<ul>
<li>Provider download failure</li>
<li>Backend configuration problem</li>
<li>Authentication issue</li>
<li>Network/proxy problem</li>
<li>Invalid module source</li>
</ul>

I would inspect the exact error before changing the configuration.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>14. Terraform Configuration Has Syntax Errors</h2>

<pre>
terraform fmt
terraform validate
</pre>

<div class="answer">

<strong>terraform fmt</strong> formats the configuration.

<strong>terraform validate</strong> checks whether the configuration
is syntactically and internally valid.

I would run both before creating infrastructure.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>15. Terraform Apply Fails Halfway Through</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform may have successfully created some resources before
another resource failed.

I would first inspect:

<pre>
terraform state list

terraform plan
</pre>

I would identify what already exists, understand the failed
resource and then safely continue after fixing the root cause.

I would not automatically destroy everything and start again.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>16. Terraform State Contains Sensitive Information</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform state can contain sensitive resource information.

I would:

<ul>
<li>Use a secure remote backend</li>
<li>Restrict backend access</li>
<li>Encrypt state at rest</li>
<li>Control IAM permissions</li>
<li>Avoid committing state files to Git</li>
<li>Protect state backups</li>
</ul>

Example .gitignore:

<pre>
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
.terraform/
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>17. Terraform Resource Was Deleted Manually</h2>

<p>
Someone deletes an EC2 instance manually from AWS.
</p>

<div class="answer">

Terraform still has the resource recorded in state.

During the next plan, Terraform detects that the real resource
is missing and may propose creating it again to match the desired
configuration.

I would review the plan and apply only after confirming that
recreation is expected.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>18. Different Environments Need Different Values</h2>

<p>
For example, development and production need different instance
sizes.
</p>

<div class="answer">

I would avoid hardcoding environment-specific values.

A common approach is:

<pre>
terraform.tfvars
dev.tfvars
prod.tfvars
</pre>

Or use workspaces/modules depending on the architecture.

Example:

<pre>
instance_type = "t3.micro"
</pre>

The exact approach should match the team's environment strategy.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>19. How Would You Manage Terraform in a Team?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would use:

<ul>
<li>Git for version control</li>
<li>Pull requests and code review</li>
<li>Remote state</li>
<li>State locking</li>
<li>Reusable modules</li>
<li>Separate environments</li>
<li>CI validation</li>
<li>Terraform plan before apply</li>
<li>Restricted production access</li>
</ul>

A typical pipeline:

<div class="flow">

Git Push
<br>â†“<br>
terraform fmt
<br>â†“<br>
terraform validate
<br>â†“<br>
terraform plan
<br>â†“<br>
Code Review
<br>â†“<br>
terraform apply

</div>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>20. Terraform Changes Must Be Applied Automatically</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would integrate Terraform into CI/CD.

The pipeline could run:

<pre>
terraform init
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform plan
</pre>

After approval, a controlled process can execute:

<pre>
terraform apply
</pre>

Production apply should have appropriate approval and access
controls rather than allowing every developer to change
infrastructure directly.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ TOP INTERVIEW REVISION</span>

<h2>21. Terraform Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet</h2>

<table>

<tr>
<th>Problem</th>
<th>First Check</th>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Apply failed</td>
<td>Error message â†’ provider â†’ permissions</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>State missing</td>
<td>Backend â†’ state storage</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>State drift</td>
<td>terraform plan</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>State locked</td>
<td>Check active operation â†’ stale lock</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Resource already exists</td>
<td>State â†’ import</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Unexpected replacement</td>
<td>Plan â†’ changed attributes â†’ drift</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Authentication failure</td>
<td>STS â†’ credentials â†’ IAM</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Module failure</td>
<td>Source â†’ version â†’ inputs â†’ outputs</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Init failure</td>
<td>Backend â†’ provider â†’ network</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Syntax issue</td>
<td>fmt â†’ validate</td>
</tr>

<tr>
<td>Team usage</td>
<td>Git â†’ remote state â†’ locking â†’ review</td>
</tr>

</table>

</div>


<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Golden Terraform Interview Formula</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Code</strong>
â†’ fmt â†’ validate

<br><br>

<strong>Preview</strong>
â†’ plan

<br><br>

<strong>State</strong>
â†’ Remote Backend + Locking

<br><br>

<strong>Drift</strong>
â†’ plan

<br><br>

<strong>Existing Resource</strong>
â†’ Import

<br><br>

<strong>Failure</strong>
â†’ Read Error â†’ Fix Root Cause â†’ Plan Again

<br><br>

<strong>Production</strong>
â†’ Review â†’ Approval â†’ Apply

</div>

<div class="architecture">

ðŸ‘¨â€ðŸ’» Developer

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Explanation:</strong>

<p>
The architecture starts with the developer pushing application
code to GitHub. Jenkins detects the change and starts the CI/CD
pipeline.
</p>

<p>
The pipeline performs build and testing activities and creates a
Docker image. The image is pushed to a container registry.
</p>

<p>
The container image is then deployed to Kubernetes running on AWS.
Prometheus collects metrics and Grafana provides visualization.
</p>

</div>

</div>

<h2>2. Explain the Request Flow</h2>

<div class="architecture">

User
<br>
â†“
<br>
Load Balancer / Service
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application Pod
<br>
â†“
<br>
Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
Database / External Services

</div>

<div class="answer">

When a user sends a request, the request reaches the exposed
application endpoint.

Kubernetes routes the request to an available application Pod.
The application processes the request and communicates with
required backend services.

</div>

</div>

<h2>4. Where Does Terraform Fit?</h2>

<div class="architecture">

Terraform Code
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Plan
<br>
â†“
<br>
Terraform Apply
<br>
â†“
<br>
AWS Infrastructure
<br>
â”‚
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ VPC
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Subnets
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Security Groups
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ EKS
<br>
â””â”€â”€ Node Groups

</div>

<div class="answer">

Terraform is used for the infrastructure layer.

Instead of manually creating AWS resources, the desired
infrastructure is defined as code and Terraform creates or
updates those resources.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>5. Why Separate Infrastructure and Application Deployment?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Infrastructure and application deployment have different
responsibilities.

<strong>Terraform:</strong> creates and manages infrastructure.

<strong>CI/CD:</strong> builds and deploys the application.

This separation makes the architecture easier to maintain and
reduces unnecessary infrastructure changes during application
deployments.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>6. Why Kubernetes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes provides the orchestration layer for containers.

It manages:

<ul>
<li>Pod scheduling</li>
<li>Service discovery</li>
<li>Scaling</li>
<li>Self-healing</li>
<li>Rolling deployments</li>
<li>Desired-state management</li>
</ul>

This is more suitable for managing multiple application
instances than manually running Docker containers.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>7. How Does Kubernetes Achieve High Availability?</h2>

<div class="architecture">

Deployment
<br>
â”‚
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Pod 1
<br>
â”œâ”€â”€ Pod 2
<br>
â””â”€â”€ Pod 3
<br>
â”‚
<br>
â–¼
<br>
Service
<br>
â”‚
<br>
â–¼
<br>
Traffic Distribution

</div>

<div class="answer">

Multiple replicas can run simultaneously.

If one Pod fails, Kubernetes can create another Pod based on the
desired state.

A Service provides stable access to the application Pods.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>8. What Happens When a Pod Fails?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Kubernetes controller continuously compares the actual state
with the desired state.

If a Pod managed by a Deployment fails, Kubernetes can create a
replacement Pod to maintain the desired replica count.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>9. Where Does Monitoring Fit?</h2>

<div class="architecture">

Application
<br>
â†“
<br>
Metrics
<br>
â†“
<br>
Prometheus
<br>
â†“
<br>
Grafana
<br>
â†“
<br>
Dashboard
<br>
â†“
<br>
Engineer

</div>

<div class="answer">

Prometheus collects and stores metrics.

Grafana queries Prometheus and presents the metrics through
dashboards.

This helps engineers identify resource usage, application
performance and operational problems.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>10. What Happens During a New Release?</h2>

<div class="architecture">

Developer Push
<br>
â†“
<br>
Jenkins
<br>
â†“
<br>
Build + Test
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Docker Image
<br>
â†“
<br>
Registry
<br>
â†“
<br>
Kubernetes Deployment
<br>
â†“
<br>
Rolling Update
<br>
â†“
<br>
New Pods
<br>
â†“
<br>
Health Check

</div>

<div class="answer">

The new application version is packaged as a new image and
deployed.

Kubernetes can perform a rolling update so that new Pods are
introduced while old Pods are gradually replaced.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>11. What If the New Deployment Fails?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would first check:

<pre>
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

I would identify whether the problem is related to:

<ul>
<li>Image</li>
<li>Configuration</li>
<li>Secrets</li>
<li>Resources</li>
<li>Networking</li>
<li>Application startup</li>
</ul>

If the release is unhealthy, I would use the deployment's
rollback capability where appropriate.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ INTERVIEW REVISION</span>

<h2>13. One-Minute Architecture Explanation</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
"The architecture follows a standard end-to-end DevOps workflow.
The developer pushes code to GitHub, which triggers Jenkins.
</p>

<p>
Jenkins performs the CI stages such as build, testing and
security checks. It then builds a Docker image and pushes it to a
container registry.
</p>

<p>
The application is deployed to Kubernetes running on AWS.
Terraform is responsible for provisioning the underlying cloud
infrastructure.
</p>

<p>
For observability, Prometheus collects metrics and Grafana
visualizes them through dashboards.
</p>

<p>
This gives us an automated, repeatable and observable deployment
process."
</p>

</div>

<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>3. What Happens When Developer Pushes Code?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
The developer pushes the code to GitHub.
</p>

<p>
GitHub sends an event through the configured webhook to Jenkins.
Jenkins receives the event and starts the pipeline.
</p>

<p>
The pipeline checks out the latest code and executes the defined
CI/CD stages.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>4. Explain Your Jenkins Pipeline</h2>

<pre>
pipeline {

    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                // Checkout source code
            }
        }

        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                // Build application
            }
        }

        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                // Run tests
            }
        }

        stage('Docker Build') {
            steps {
                // Build Docker image
            }
        }

        stage('Push') {
            steps {
                // Push image to registry
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                // Deploy application
            }
        }
    }
}
</pre>

<div class="answer">

The pipeline is divided into logical stages so that each phase
can be identified and troubleshot independently.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>5. Why Do You Build a Docker Image?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The Docker image packages the application and its dependencies
into a consistent artifact.

The same image can then be promoted through environments instead
of rebuilding the application differently for each environment.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>6. How Is the Docker Image Tagged?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would prefer an immutable tag such as a Git commit SHA or
release version instead of relying only on <code>latest</code>.

Example:

<pre>
myapp:1.0.0
myapp:&lt;git-commit-sha&gt;
</pre>

This makes it easier to identify exactly which version was
deployed.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>7. How Does Kubernetes Get the Image?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Container Registry
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes Node
<br>â†“<br>
Container Runtime
<br>â†“<br>
Application Container
<br>â†“<br>
Pod

</div>

<div class="answer">

The Kubernetes workload specifies the container image.

The cluster pulls the image from the configured container registry
when creating the Pod, subject to the required registry access.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>8. Explain Your Kubernetes Deployment</h2>

<pre>
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment

spec:
  replicas: 3

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp

    spec:
      containers:
      - name: myapp
        image: myapp:1.0.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
</pre>

<div class="answer">

The Deployment defines the desired state of the application.

For example, with three replicas Kubernetes attempts to maintain
three application Pods.

If a Pod fails, the controller can create a replacement.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>9. How Does Terraform Help Your Project?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform manages the infrastructure as code.

For example, the infrastructure can include:

<ul>
<li>VPC</li>
<li>Subnets</li>
<li>Security groups</li>
<li>EKS cluster</li>
<li>Node groups</li>
<li>IAM-related resources</li>
</ul>

Terraform allows infrastructure changes to be reviewed,
version-controlled and reproduced.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>10. How Do You Handle Terraform Changes?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Terraform Code
<br>â†“<br>
terraform init
<br>â†“<br>
terraform plan
<br>â†“<br>
Review Changes
<br>â†“<br>
terraform apply
<br>â†“<br>
Infrastructure Updated

</div>

<div class="answer">

I use <code>terraform plan</code> to review the proposed changes
before applying them.

This helps prevent unexpected infrastructure modifications.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>11. Explain Monitoring in Your Project</h2>

<div class="flow">

Application / Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
Metrics
<br>â†“<br>
Prometheus
<br>â†“<br>
Grafana
<br>â†“<br>
Dashboard
<br>â†“<br>
Engineer

</div>

<div class="answer">

Prometheus collects metrics from the monitored targets.

Grafana connects to Prometheus as a data source and displays
those metrics in dashboards.

This helps identify resource and application-level problems.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>12. What Happens If a Deployment Fails?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I first identify the failing layer.

For Kubernetes I would check:

<pre>
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl get events
</pre>

Then I determine whether the issue is related to the image,
configuration, secrets, resources, networking or application
startup.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>13. What Was Your Troubleshooting Method?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I follow a layer-by-layer approach instead of changing multiple
things at the same time.

<div class="flow">

Application
<br>â†“<br>
Container
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
Network
<br>â†“<br>
Cloud Infrastructure
<br>â†“<br>
CI/CD

</div>

I start with logs and the first meaningful error, then move
towards the underlying infrastructure if required.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>14. How Would You Make the Project Production Ready?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would add:

<ul>
<li>High availability</li>
<li>Autoscaling</li>
<li>Centralized logging</li>
<li>Secret management</li>
<li>Image vulnerability scanning</li>
<li>Automated rollback</li>
<li>Monitoring and alerting</li>
<li>Environment separation</li>
<li>Least-privilege IAM</li>
<li>Backup and disaster recovery strategy</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ FINAL REVISION</span>

<h2>15. 30-Second Project Explanation</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
"I built an end-to-end DevOps pipeline for deploying a
containerized application on AWS.
</p>

<p>
The code is maintained in GitHub and Jenkins automates the CI/CD
workflow. The application is tested, containerized using Docker
and the image is pushed to a registry.
</p>

<p>
Terraform is used for infrastructure provisioning and Kubernetes
handles container deployment and management.
Prometheus and Grafana provide monitoring and visualization.
</p>

<p>
The main objective was to make the deployment process automated,
repeatable and easier to monitor."
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

style="color:#93c5fd;text-decoration:none;font-weight:600;">

</a>

<h1>Project Interview Questions</h1>

<p>
High-priority project questions, follow-ups and interview-ready
answers for DevOps interviews.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>1. Explain Your Project.</h2>

<div class="answer">

I worked on an end-to-end Cloud and DevOps project focused on
automating application deployment.

The source code is maintained in GitHub. Jenkins automates the
CI/CD pipeline, Docker is used for containerization, Terraform
provisions infrastructure, and Kubernetes manages the deployed
containers.

Prometheus and Grafana are used for monitoring and visualization.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>2. What Was Your Role?</h2>

<div class="answer">

My role was focused on the DevOps implementation.

I worked on:

<ul>
<li>Cloud infrastructure</li>
<li>Terraform automation</li>
<li>Docker containerization</li>
<li>Jenkins CI/CD</li>
<li>Kubernetes deployment</li>
<li>Monitoring</li>
<li>Troubleshooting</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. Why Did You Choose AWS?</h2>

<div class="answer">

AWS provides a broad set of cloud services for compute,
networking, storage, security and managed Kubernetes.

It also allowed me to implement the project using real cloud
infrastructure instead of only local environments.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>4. Why Docker?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker packages the application and its dependencies into a
portable image.

This provides consistency between development, testing and
deployment environments and makes container-based deployment
easier.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>5. Why Kubernetes Instead of Docker Alone?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker can run containers, but Kubernetes provides orchestration
for multiple containers.

Kubernetes provides:

<ul>
<li>Scheduling</li>
<li>Self-healing</li>
<li>Scaling</li>
<li>Service discovery</li>
<li>Rolling updates</li>
</ul>

Therefore Kubernetes is more suitable for managing applications
at scale.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>6. Why Terraform?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform allows infrastructure to be defined as code.

It makes infrastructure:

<ul>
<li>Repeatable</li>
<li>Version controlled</li>
<li>Reviewable</li>
<li>Automated</li>
</ul>

It also reduces manual configuration through the cloud console.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>7. Why Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins automates the CI/CD lifecycle.

It can automatically build the application, run tests, create
Docker images, push them to a registry and trigger deployment.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>8. What Happens When Code Is Pushed?</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
â†’ GitHub
â†’ Webhook
â†’ Jenkins
â†’ Build
â†’ Test
â†’ Docker
â†’ Registry
â†’ Kubernetes

</div>

<div class="answer">

The Git push triggers Jenkins through the configured integration.
Jenkins checks out the latest code and executes the pipeline
stages.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>9. What If the Jenkins Pipeline Fails?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I first inspect the Jenkins console output and identify the first
meaningful error.

Then I determine which stage failed and troubleshoot that layer.

For example:

<ul>
<li>Git â†’ credentials or repository</li>
<li>Build â†’ dependency or code issue</li>
<li>Docker â†’ Dockerfile or daemon</li>
<li>Registry â†’ authentication or permissions</li>
<li>Kubernetes â†’ manifest, RBAC or image issue</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>10. What If the Pod Is Not Starting?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check:

<pre>
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
kubectl get events
</pre>

I would look for image-pull failures, configuration errors,
resource issues, scheduling problems or application startup
failures.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>11. What If the Docker Image Cannot Be Pulled?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would verify:

<ul>
<li>Image name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Registry availability</li>
<li>Image existence</li>
<li>Registry credentials</li>
<li>Kubernetes image-pull permissions</li>
</ul>

A common error is <strong>ImagePullBackOff</strong>.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>12. What If the Application Is Running but Not Accessible?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would check the request path layer by layer:

<div class="flow">

User
â†’ Load Balancer / Ingress
â†’ Service
â†’ Pod
â†’ Container Port
â†’ Application

</div>

I would verify Service selectors, endpoints, ports, network
configuration and application listening address.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>13. How Do You Monitor the Application?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Prometheus collects metrics and Grafana visualizes them.

I would monitor metrics such as:

<ul>
<li>CPU usage</li>
<li>Memory usage</li>
<li>Pod availability</li>
<li>Request metrics</li>
<li>Application performance</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>14. How Do You Handle Secrets?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would never hardcode passwords, tokens or cloud credentials in
source code or Dockerfiles.

Secrets should be stored using an appropriate secret-management
mechanism and accessed only by authorized workloads.

The principle is <strong>least privilege</strong>.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>15. How Would You Roll Back a Failed Deployment?</h2>

<div class="answer">

First I would confirm that the new version is unhealthy.

For a Kubernetes Deployment, I can inspect rollout history and
use the appropriate rollback mechanism.

The key objective is to restore the last known-good version
quickly while investigating the root cause.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>16. How Would You Scale the Application?</h2>

<div class="answer">

At the Kubernetes workload level, I can increase replicas.

For dynamic workloads, Kubernetes autoscaling can be used based
on suitable resource or application metrics.

At the infrastructure level, the worker capacity may also need
to scale so the cluster has enough resources.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>17. What Was the Biggest Challenge?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The biggest challenge was troubleshooting issues across multiple
layers such as CI/CD, Docker, Kubernetes and AWS.

Instead of making random changes, I learned to isolate the
failure layer first, inspect logs and then fix the root cause.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>18. What Would You Change If You Built It Again?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I would improve the project with:

<ul>
<li>Better secret management</li>
<li>Automated vulnerability scanning</li>
<li>Centralized logging</li>
<li>Automated rollback</li>
<li>More comprehensive alerting</li>
<li>Stronger IAM least-privilege policies</li>
<li>Separate environments</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­</span>

<h2>19. What Happens If AWS Goes Down?</h2>

<div class="answer">

For a production-critical application, I would design for
resilience rather than assuming a single environment is enough.

Depending on the business requirement, this could include
multi-AZ architecture, backups, disaster recovery and potentially
multi-region strategies.

The correct design depends on availability requirements and cost.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ FOLLOW-UP</span>

<h2>20. If I Remove Jenkins, Can the Project Still Work?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Yes.

Jenkins is the CI/CD automation tool. The application can still
run without Jenkins, but the automated build and deployment
workflow would need another CI/CD solution or manual execution.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ FOLLOW-UP</span>

<h2>21. If I Remove Kubernetes, Can Docker Run the Application?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Yes.

Docker can run the application directly on a host.

Kubernetes becomes valuable when we need orchestration features
such as scaling, self-healing, service discovery and rolling
deployments across multiple workloads.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ FOLLOW-UP</span>

<h2>22. What Is the Difference Between Terraform and Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Terraform</strong> manages infrastructure.

<strong>Jenkins</strong> automates CI/CD workflows.

They can work together, but they solve different problems.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ FINAL REVISION</span>

</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. Tell Me About Your Project</h2>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
I worked on an end-to-end Cloud and DevOps project where I
containerized an application and automated its build,
testing, infrastructure provisioning and deployment.
</p>

<p>
The main goal was to create a repeatable deployment process
instead of manually creating infrastructure and deploying the
application.
</p>

<p>
I used Git for source-code management, Jenkins for CI/CD,
Docker for containerization, Terraform for infrastructure
automation, Kubernetes for container orchestration, and AWS
services for cloud infrastructure.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>2. What Problem Does Your Project Solve?</h2>

<div class="answer">

The project reduces manual deployment effort and makes the
deployment process more consistent and repeatable.

Instead of manually:

<ul>
<li>Creating infrastructure</li>
<li>Building applications</li>
<li>Building Docker images</li>
<li>Deploying containers</li>
<li>Updating environments</li>
</ul>

the process is automated through DevOps tools and CI/CD.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>3. Explain the Overall Project Flow</h2>

<div class="flow">

Developer
<br>â†“<br>
Git / GitHub
<br>â†“<br>
Jenkins CI/CD
<br>â†“<br>
Build + Test
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Image
<br>â†“<br>
Container Registry
<br>â†“<br>
Kubernetes
<br>â†“<br>
AWS Infrastructure
<br>â†“<br>
Monitoring

</div>

<div class="answer">

A developer pushes code to the Git repository. Jenkins detects
the change and starts the pipeline.

The pipeline builds and tests the application, creates a Docker
image and pushes it to the container registry.

The image is then deployed to the Kubernetes environment running
on AWS.

Monitoring tools are used to observe the health and performance
of the deployed application.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>4. What Technologies Did You Use?</h2>

<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>5. Why Did You Use Docker?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Docker packages the application together with its dependencies
into a container image.

This makes the application environment more consistent across
development, testing and deployment.

It also makes the application easier to deploy and scale.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>6. Why Did You Use Kubernetes?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Kubernetes helps manage containers at scale.

It provides capabilities such as:

<ul>
<li>Container scheduling</li>
<li>Self-healing</li>
<li>Service discovery</li>
<li>Scaling</li>
<li>Rolling updates</li>
<li>Load balancing</li>
</ul>

Instead of manually managing individual containers, Kubernetes
provides an orchestration layer.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>7. Why Did You Use Terraform?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Terraform allows infrastructure to be defined as code.

Instead of manually creating AWS resources through the console,
I can define the infrastructure in Terraform configuration files.

This provides:

<ul>
<li>Repeatability</li>
<li>Version control</li>
<li>Consistency</li>
<li>Automation</li>
<li>Infrastructure change tracking</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>8. Why Did You Use Jenkins?</h2>

<div class="answer">

Jenkins automates the CI/CD process.

For example:

<div class="flow">

Code Commit
<br>â†“<br>
Build
<br>â†“<br>
Test
<br>â†“<br>
Docker Build
<br>â†“<br>
Image Push
<br>â†“<br>
Deployment

</div>

This reduces manual work and provides a repeatable deployment
workflow.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>9. What Was Your Role in the Project?</h2>

<div class="answer">

I worked on the DevOps side of the project.

My responsibilities included:

<ul>
<li>Creating cloud infrastructure</li>
<li>Writing Terraform configurations</li>
<li>Containerizing the application</li>
<li>Creating CI/CD pipelines</li>
<li>Working with Kubernetes deployments</li>
<li>Configuring monitoring</li>
<li>Troubleshooting deployment issues</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>10. What Was the Most Challenging Part?</h2>

<div class="answer">

One of the challenging parts was troubleshooting failures across
different layers of the stack.

For example, a deployment issue could originate from the Docker
image, Kubernetes configuration, credentials, networking or
infrastructure.

I learned to troubleshoot systematically by checking the failed
layer first instead of changing multiple things at once.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>11. How Would You Explain the Project in 60 Seconds?</h2>

<div class="answer">

<p>
"My project is an end-to-end Cloud and DevOps implementation
focused on automating application deployment.
</p>

<p>
The source code is maintained in GitHub. Jenkins handles the
CI/CD pipeline, where the application is built and tested and a
Docker image is created.
</p>

<p>
The image is stored in a container registry and deployed to
Kubernetes running on AWS. Terraform is used to automate the
underlying infrastructure.
</p>

<p>
Finally, monitoring tools such as Prometheus and Grafana are used
to monitor the application and infrastructure."
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>12. What Would You Improve in the Project?</h2>

<div class="answer">

In a production environment, I would improve the project by
adding:

<ul>
<li>Automated security scanning</li>
<li>Centralized logging</li>
<li>Stronger secret management</li>
<li>Automated rollback</li>
<li>High availability</li>
<li>Infrastructure state management</li>
<li>Better monitoring and alerting</li>
<li>Environment separation</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>
