<header>

<div style="font-size:55px">ðŸ› ï¸</div>

<h1>Project Troubleshooting</h1>

<p>
Real-time troubleshooting scenarios for an end-to-end
Cloud & DevOps project.
</p>

</header>

<main class="container">


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>1. Your Complete Troubleshooting Method</h2>

<div class="flow">

Identify Failure
<br>â†“<br>
Check Logs
<br>â†“<br>
Find First Meaningful Error
<br>â†“<br>
Identify Failed Layer
<br>â†“<br>
Verify Configuration
<br>â†“<br>
Fix Root Cause
<br>â†“<br>
Retest
<br>â†“<br>
Monitor

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Interview Answer:</strong>

<p>
"I don't immediately change multiple configurations. I first
identify where the failure occurred, check the logs and isolate
the root cause. Then I make the required change, rerun the
affected stage and verify the result."
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>2. Jenkins Pipeline Failed</h2>

<h3>Symptoms</h3>

<p>The CI/CD pipeline suddenly fails.</p>

<div class="answer">

First I open the Jenkins console output and identify the first
meaningful error.

Then I determine the failed stage:

<ul>
<li>Checkout</li>
<li>Build</li>
<li>Test</li>
<li>Docker build</li>
<li>Image push</li>
<li>Deployment</li>
</ul>

I troubleshoot only that layer first.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>3. Git Checkout Failed</h2>

<pre>
git clone &lt;repository-url&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I check:

<ul>
<li>Repository URL</li>
<li>Branch</li>
<li>Credentials</li>
<li>Repository permissions</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
<li>Git installation on the Jenkins agent</li>
</ul>

If authentication fails, I verify the Jenkins credential and
its permissions rather than changing unrelated pipeline stages.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>4. Docker Build Failed</h2>

<pre>
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I check the Docker build output and inspect:

<ul>
<li>Dockerfile syntax</li>
<li>Base image</li>
<li>Build context</li>
<li>File paths</li>
<li>Dependencies</li>
<li>Network access</li>
</ul>

I focus on the first actual error instead of the final generic
"build failed" message.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>5. Docker Container Exits Immediately</h2>

<pre>
docker ps -a

docker logs &lt;container-id&gt;

docker inspect &lt;container-id&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I check the container logs and inspect the configured command.

Typical causes include:

<ul>
<li>Application startup failure</li>
<li>Incorrect CMD or ENTRYPOINT</li>
<li>Missing environment variables</li>
<li>Missing dependencies</li>
<li>Process exits immediately</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>6. Docker Container Is Running but Application Is Not Accessible</h2>

<pre>
docker ps
docker logs &lt;container&gt;
docker inspect &lt;container&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I verify:

<ul>
<li>Application listening port</li>
<li>Container port</li>
<li>Host port mapping</li>
<li>Application listening address</li>
</ul>

Example:

<pre>
docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp
</pre>

Then test:

<pre>
curl http://localhost:8080
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>7. Docker Image Push Failed</h2>

<div class="answer">

I check:

<ul>
<li>Registry authentication</li>
<li>Image name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Repository permissions</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
</ul>

I also verify that the image actually exists locally:

<pre>
docker images
</pre>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>8. Kubernetes Pod Is Pending</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl get events
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I check for:

<ul>
<li>Insufficient CPU or memory</li>
<li>Node availability</li>
<li>Scheduling constraints</li>
<li>Taints and tolerations</li>
<li>Node selectors</li>
<li>Persistent volume issues</li>
</ul>

The <code>describe</code> output and events usually provide the
most useful clues.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY FREQUENT</span>

<h2>9. Kubernetes Pod Is in CrashLoopBackOff</h2>

<pre>
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;

kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; --previous

kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<div class="answer">

CrashLoopBackOff means the container repeatedly starts and then
fails.

I would investigate:

<ul>
<li>Application startup error</li>
<li>Incorrect configuration</li>
<li>Missing environment variables</li>
<li>Secrets</li>
<li>Dependency failures</li>
<li>Incorrect command</li>
<li>Health probe configuration</li>
</ul>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>10. Kubernetes Shows ImagePullBackOff</h2>

<div class="answer">

I check:

<ul>
<li>Image name</li>
<li>Image tag</li>
<li>Registry availability</li>
<li>Image existence</li>
<li>Registry credentials</li>
<li>Image pull permissions</li>
</ul>

Then:

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

I look at the Events section for the exact image-pull error.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>11. Application Is Running but Service Is Not Working</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get svc

kubectl get endpoints

kubectl get pods --show-labels
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I verify that the Service selector matches the Pod labels.

Then I verify that the Service port and targetPort match the
application configuration.

A Service with no healthy endpoints cannot route traffic to the
application Pods.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>12. Kubernetes Deployment Rollout Is Stuck</h2>

<pre>
kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp

kubectl get pods

kubectl describe deployment myapp
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I check whether new Pods are:

<ul>
<li>Failing to start</li>
<li>Unable to pull the image</li>
<li>Failing readiness probes</li>
<li>Unable to schedule</li>
<li>Missing configuration</li>
</ul>

If the release is confirmed unhealthy, I can consider rolling
back to the previous known-good revision.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>13. Terraform Apply Failed</h2>

<pre>
terraform plan
terraform apply
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I read the exact Terraform error and identify which resource
failed.

I then check:

<ul>
<li>AWS credentials</li>
<li>Region</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
<li>Resource limits</li>
<li>Resource dependencies</li>
<li>Existing resource conflicts</li>
<li>Terraform configuration</li>
</ul>

I avoid repeatedly running <code>apply</code> without understanding
the failure.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>14. Terraform Says Resource Already Exists</h2>

<div class="answer">

I first determine whether the resource was created outside
Terraform or already exists in the expected state.

Depending on the situation, the resource may need to be imported
into Terraform state or the configuration/state relationship may
need to be corrected.

The correct solution depends on how the resource was originally
created.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>15. AWS Authentication Error</h2>

<pre>
aws sts get-caller-identity
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I verify:

<ul>
<li>AWS credentials</li>
<li>Credential expiration</li>
<li>Configured profile</li>
<li>Region</li>
<li>IAM permissions</li>
<li>Environment variables</li>
</ul>

The STS identity command is a useful first check to confirm which
AWS identity the environment is actually using.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>16. EKS Cluster Is Working but kubectl Cannot Connect</h2>

<pre>
kubectl get nodes
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I check:

<ul>
<li>Kubeconfig</li>
<li>AWS identity</li>
<li>Cluster endpoint</li>
<li>Network connectivity</li>
<li>Cluster authentication</li>
<li>Authorization / RBAC</li>
</ul>

I would verify that kubectl is pointing to the correct cluster.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>17. Application Became Unhealthy After Deployment</h2>

<div class="flow">

Deployment
<br>â†“
<br>
Pods Running?
<br>â†“
<br>
Readiness Probe?
<br>â†“
<br>
Application Logs?
<br>â†“
<br>
Service Endpoints?
<br>â†“
<br>
External Dependencies?
<br>â†“
<br>
Root Cause

</div>

<div class="answer">

A Pod being in the Running state does not automatically mean the
application is ready to receive traffic.

I check readiness, logs, dependencies and Service endpoints.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>18. Monitoring Shows High CPU</h2>

<pre>
kubectl top pods
kubectl top nodes
</pre>

<div class="answer">

I identify whether the high CPU usage is caused by:

<ul>
<li>Application workload</li>
<li>Traffic increase</li>
<li>Resource limits</li>
<li>Application bug</li>
<li>Insufficient capacity</li>
</ul>

Then I correlate the Kubernetes metrics with application
behavior before deciding whether scaling is required.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­</span>

<h2>19. Grafana Dashboard Shows No Data</h2>

<div class="answer">

I check:

<ul>
<li>Prometheus is running</li>
<li>Prometheus is scraping targets</li>
<li>Grafana data source configuration</li>
<li>Prometheus URL</li>
<li>Query correctness</li>
<li>Target health</li>
</ul>

The first thing I verify is whether Prometheus itself has the
expected metrics.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ VERY IMPORTANT</span>

<h2>20. How Would You Handle a Production Incident?</h2>

<div class="answer">

My approach would be:

<ol>
<li>Understand the impact.</li>
<li>Identify the affected component.</li>
<li>Check monitoring and logs.</li>
<li>Stop further harmful changes.</li>
<li>Restore service using the safest known solution.</li>
<li>Verify recovery.</li>
<li>Investigate root cause.</li>
<li>Document the incident and preventive action.</li>
</ol>

The priority during an incident is to restore service safely,
then perform deeper root-cause analysis.

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ INTERVIEW GOLD</span>

<h2>21. One Troubleshooting Example to Remember</h2>

<h3>Scenario</h3>

<p>
"After a new deployment, the application became unavailable.
What would you do?"
</p>

<div class="answer">

<p>
<strong>Step 1:</strong> Check whether the Pods are running.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl get pods
</pre>

<p>
<strong>Step 2:</strong> Check Pod logs.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<p>
<strong>Step 3:</strong> Describe the Pod if necessary.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt;
</pre>

<p>
<strong>Step 4:</strong> Check Service and endpoints.
</p>

<pre>
kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpoints
</pre>

<p>
<strong>Step 5:</strong> Check whether the new image or configuration
caused the problem.
</p>

<p>
<strong>Step 6:</strong> If the new release is confirmed as the
cause, restore the previous known-good version and then investigate
the root cause.
</p>

</div>

</div>


<div class="card">

<span class="badge">ðŸ”¥ FINAL REVISION</span>

<h2>22. Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet</h2>

<div class="card">

<h2>ðŸ§  Golden Troubleshooting Formula</h2>

<div class="flow">

<strong>Observe</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Identify</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Check Logs</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Isolate Layer</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Find Root Cause</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Fix</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Verify</strong>
<br>â†“<br>
<strong>Prevent Recurrence</strong>

</div>

<div class="answer">

<strong>Best interview line:</strong>

<p>
"I don't troubleshoot by randomly changing configurations. I
first identify the failed layer, check the relevant logs and
events, isolate the root cause, apply the smallest appropriate
fix, and then verify that the system has recovered."
</p>

  </div>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      Tell me about a technical problem you faced.
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      While working on my EKS and Terraform project, I faced infrastructure
      and cluster-related configuration issues.

      One thing I learned from those situations was that the error message
      is evidence, but it isn't always the complete root cause.

      Initially, it was tempting to change multiple configurations at once.

      But I realised that doing that makes troubleshooting harder because
      I can't clearly identify which change actually fixed the problem.

      So I started following a more structured approach.

      I identify the layer where the problem occurred, check the relevant
      configuration and dependencies, make one meaningful change,
      observe the result and then continue.

      That experience improved not just my technical troubleshooting,
      but also the way I approach problems in general.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      Tell me about a failure.
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      One lesson I learned from my projects is that trying to solve
      everything at once can actually make a problem more difficult.

      When infrastructure or deployment issues occurred, my initial
      instinct was sometimes to change multiple things quickly.

      But I realised that this makes it difficult to understand the
      actual cause.

      I learned to slow down, isolate the problem, change one relevant
      thing at a time and observe the result.

      That experience taught me that troubleshooting is not about making
      more changes quickly. It is about making the right change based
      on evidence.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­â­</span>
      How do you handle a question you don't know?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      I don't like guessing and presenting something uncertain as a fact.

      If I haven't worked with something directly, I would honestly say:

      â€œI haven't worked with that directly yet, but based on what I know
      about the underlying concept, this is how I would approach it.â€

      Then I would explain whatever part I understand and describe how
      I would investigate the missing part.

      I believe being honest about my knowledge boundary is much better
      than giving a confident but incorrect answer.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      What if the interviewer challenges your answer?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      I would first listen carefully.

      Sometimes an interviewer may challenge an answer because they want
      to understand whether I actually know the concept deeply.

      If I realise that my answer is incorrect, I would acknowledge it
      instead of trying to defend a wrong answer.

      I see technical discussions as opportunities to improve my
      understanding rather than arguments that I need to win.

    </div>

  </article>


  <!-- PERSONALITY -->

  <div class="section-title">
    <span style="background:var(--green)"></span>
    <h2>ðŸŒ± Personality & Work Style</h2>
  </div>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      How do you keep learning?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      I learn best when I combine structured learning with hands-on
      implementation.

      I first understand the concept, then I try to implement it.

      When something fails, I treat the failure as part of the learning
      process rather than simply looking for a shortcut.

      My DevOps journey itself followed this pattern.

      Training gave me structure, projects gave me implementation,
      troubleshooting gave me deeper understanding, and mentorship
      helped me improve the way I approached problems.

      I also use AI tools as learning assistants when appropriate, but
      I make sure I understand and verify what I'm applying.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      Are you comfortable working with a team?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      Yes, definitely.

      In fact, communication and connecting with people are some of my
      natural strengths.

      I generally feel comfortable starting conversations and becoming
      part of a new environment.

      I believe technical teams work best when people communicate clearly,
      ask questions without hesitation and share information instead of
      working in isolation.

      So I actually enjoy the collaborative side of technical work.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      Are you comfortable working in shifts?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      Yes, I'm open to working according to the requirements of the role.

      I understand that Cloud infrastructure, production systems and
      support environments can sometimes require monitoring or
      operational coverage outside standard working hours.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      Are you willing to relocate?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      Yes, I'm open to relocation for the right opportunity.

      At this stage of my career, my priority is getting into a strong
      professional environment where I can learn, contribute and build
      solid Cloud and DevOps experience.

    </div>

  </article>


  <!-- SALARY -->

  <div class="section-title">
    <span style="background:var(--yellow)"></span>
    <h2>ðŸ’° Salary</h2>
  </div>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      What are your salary expectations?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      As a fresher, my first priority is finding the right opportunity
      where I can apply what I've learned, work with experienced engineers
      and gain real professional exposure.

      I'm open to the company's standard compensation for the role,
      and I'm happy to discuss the package based on the responsibilities
      and overall opportunity.

    </div>

  </article>


  <!-- ACHIEVEMENT -->

  <div class="section-title">
    <span style="background:var(--cyan)"></span>
    <h2>ðŸ† Achievement & Project Questions</h2>
  </div>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      What is your biggest achievement?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      One of my biggest achievements is the transformation in the way
      I understand technology.

      Initially, I was learning tools individually.

      Docker was one topic.
      Kubernetes was another.
      Terraform was another.
      AWS was another.

      But when I started building end-to-end projects, especially the
      EKS-based DevOps project, I began understanding how these technologies
      connect.

      That changed my mindset from:

      â€œI know this tool.â€

      to:

      â€œI understand where this tool fits and why it is needed.â€

      For me, that shift in understanding is one of the most valuable
      achievements of my learning journey.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      What was the most difficult part of your project?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      The hardest part wasn't learning an individual command.

      The challenging part was connecting multiple systems correctly.

      Terraform had to provision infrastructure.
      EKS had to provide Kubernetes.
      Docker had to package the application.
      GitHub Actions had to automate CI.
      Argo CD had to manage GitOps delivery.
      Prometheus and Grafana had to provide visibility.

      A problem in one layer could affect another layer.

      That taught me to stop looking at DevOps as a collection of tools
      and start looking at it as one connected system.

    </div>

  </article>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      What did you learn from your project?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      I learned three major things.

      First, automation is useful only when I understand the process
      underneath it.

      Second, troubleshooting is one of the most important DevOps skills.

      Third, architecture matters more than the number of tools I know.

      I could say I know 20 or 30 technologies, but the more meaningful
      question is whether I understand why they exist and how they
      interact.

      That became one of the biggest lessons from my projects.

    </div>

  </article>


  <!-- FUTURE -->

  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      <span class="priority">â­â­â­â­</span>
      If you had more time, what would you improve in your project?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      I would improve the project in several production-oriented areas.

      I would add stronger automated testing, better secret management,
      more comprehensive security scanning, improved observability and
      alerting.

      I would also work on reusable Terraform modules, environment
      separation, stronger networking controls, cost optimisation and
      disaster recovery considerations.

      The existing project gave me the foundation, but these improvements
      would make it closer to a mature production architecture.

    </div>

  </article>


  <!-- QUESTIONS TO ASK -->

  <div class="section-title">
    <span style="background:var(--purple)"></span>
    <h2>â“ Questions I Can Ask the Interviewer</h2>
  </div>


  <article class="question-card">

    <div class="question">
      What questions would you ask us?
    </div>

    <div class="answer">

      1. What does the current Cloud and DevOps architecture look like?

      2. Which cloud platform and CI/CD tools does the team primarily use?

      3. What would you expect a fresher in this role to accomplish
         during the first three to six months?

      4. How does the team currently handle monitoring and incidents?

      5. How are deployments and rollbacks handled?

      6. Will I get opportunities to work across infrastructure,
         automation and Kubernetes?

      7. How does the team support learning and mentorship for someone
         at the beginning of their professional journey?

    </div>

  </article>


  <!-- FINAL CLOSING -->

  <div class="closing">

    <h2>ðŸ”¥ Final Closing Statement</h2>

    <p>

      Thank you for the opportunity.

      I know I'm at the beginning of my professional career, but I've
      genuinely invested time in understanding Cloud and DevOps through
      hands-on work rather than only theoretical learning.

      What started as curiosity about what happens behind an application
      gradually became a serious interest in Cloud and DevOps.

      My training, projects, troubleshooting experiences and mentorship
      helped me turn that interest into practical understanding.

      I'm now looking for an environment where I can learn from experienced
      engineers, communicate well with the team, contribute wherever I can,
      and gradually take ownership of real infrastructure and automation
      problems.

      I may be a fresher, but I'm genuinely curious, comfortable learning,
      and ready to put that learning into practice.

    </p>

  </div>


  <!-- GOLDEN RULE -->

  <div class="highlight">

    <h3>ðŸ§  YOUR GOLDEN INTERVIEW RULE</h3>

    <p>
      Don't memorize these answers word-for-word.
      Remember the story behind them.
    </p>

    <p style="margin-top:10px;">

      <strong>
        ECE â†’ Curiosity â†’ Cloud â†’ DevOps â†’ Trainer â†’ Real-time learning
        â†’ Projects â†’ 30+ tools â†’ EKS â†’ Troubleshooting â†’ Mentorship
        â†’ Professional opportunity
      </strong>

    </p>

  </div>

  name: myapp

spec:
  replicas: 3

  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp

  template:

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp

    spec:

      containers:
        - name: myapp
          image: nginx:latest

          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
</pre>


<h3>Service</h3>

<pre>
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service

metadata:
  name: myapp-service

spec:

  selector:
    app: myapp

  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

  type: ClusterIP
</pre>


<h3>ConfigMap</h3>

<pre>
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap

metadata:
  name: app-config

data:
  APP_ENV: "production"
  APP_NAME: "myapp"
</pre>


<h3>Secret</h3>

<pre>
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret

metadata:
  name: app-secret

type: Opaque

stringData:
  DB_USERNAME: admin
  DB_PASSWORD: password
</pre>


<h3>Ingress</h3>

<pre>
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress

metadata:
  name: myapp-ingress

spec:

  rules:

    - host: myapp.example.com

      http:

        paths:

          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix

            backend:

              service:
                name: myapp-service

                port:
                  number: 80
</pre>


<h3>HPA</h3>

<pre>
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler

metadata:
  name: myapp-hpa

spec:

  scaleTargetRef:

    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: myapp

  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 5

  metrics:

    - type: Resource

      resource:

        name: cpu

        target:

          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
</pre>

<div class="note">

<strong>Priority:</strong>

Deployment â†’ Service â†’ ConfigMap/Secret â†’ Ingress â†’ HPA

</div>

</div>


<!-- TERRAFORM -->

<div class="card" id="terraform">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<h2>ðŸ—ï¸ 3. Terraform Code</h2>


<h3>AWS Provider</h3>

<pre>
terraform {

  required_providers {

    aws = {

      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"

    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {

  region = "ap-south-1"

}
</pre>


<h3>EC2 Resource</h3>

<pre>
resource "aws_instance" "web" {

  ami           = "ami-xxxxxxxx"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

  tags = {

    Name = "web-server"

  }
}
</pre>


<h3>Variable</h3>

<pre>
variable "instance_type" {

  description = "EC2 instance type"

  type = string

  default = "t3.micro"
}
</pre>


<h3>Output</h3>

<pre>
output "instance_public_ip" {

  value = aws_instance.web.public_ip

}
</pre>


<div class="note">

<strong>Possible interview questions:</strong>

<br><br>

Write Terraform code to create an EC2 instance.

<br>

How do you define a variable?

<br>

How do you create an output?

</div>

</div>


<!-- JENKINS -->

<div class="card" id="jenkins">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­â­ MUST KNOW</span>

<h2>ðŸ”§ 4. Jenkinsfile</h2>

<h3>Basic Declarative Pipeline</h3>

<pre>
pipeline {

    agent any

    stages {

        stage('Checkout') {

            steps {

                echo 'Checking out source code'

            }
        }


        stage('Build') {

            steps {

                echo 'Building application'

            }
        }


        stage('Test') {

            steps {

                echo 'Running tests'

            }
        }


        stage('Docker Build') {

            steps {

                sh 'docker build -t myapp:latest .'

            }
        }


        stage('Deploy') {

            steps {

                echo 'Deploying application'

            }
        }
    }
}
</pre>

<div class="note">

<strong>Possible question:</strong>

Write a basic Jenkins declarative pipeline.

</div>

</div>


<!-- GITHUB ACTIONS -->

<div class="card" id="github-actions">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­â­ GOOD TO KNOW</span>

<h2>âš™ï¸ 5. GitHub Actions YAML</h2>

<pre>
name: CI

on:

  push:

    branches:
      - main


jobs:

  build:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:

      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4


      - name: Build
        run: echo "Building application"


      - name: Test
        run: echo "Running tests"
</pre>

<div class="note">

<strong>Possible question:</strong>

Write a basic GitHub Actions workflow.

<!-- BASH -->

<div class="card" id="bash">

<span class="badge">â­â­â­ BASIC</span>

<h2>ðŸš 6. Bash Scripting</h2>

<h3>File Check</h3>

<pre>
#!/bin/bash

if [ -f "/etc/passwd" ]; then

    echo "File exists"

else

    echo "File does not exist"

fi
</pre>


<h3>Simple Backup Script</h3>

<pre>
#!/bin/bash

SOURCE="/var/www"

BACKUP="/backup"

DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)

mkdir -p "$BACKUP"

tar -czf "$BACKUP/backup-$DATE.tar.gz" "$SOURCE"

echo "Backup completed"
</pre>

<div class="note">

Basic Bash is enough unless the specific job requires
strong scripting skills.

</div>

</div>
